We eventually climbed to FL200 and stayed at 230 knots to protect the flap max altitude and flap speeds in case we had flaps out that were not indicating properly. Attempting to silence the takeoff configuration warning horn we brought the flaps to 1 and the alarm turned off. When we brought the flaps back to zero eventually the takeoff configuration warning came back on and could not be silenced. At this time I had my FO fly the airplane and talk to ATC while I contacted the company. Being on a 767-200 with no satcom or ACARS I used ARINC (Aeronautical Radio; Inc.) to get a phone patch to dispatch. Once I was communicating with Dispatch I advised them of our situation and got patched in with maintenance control. I explained the situation to maintenance control and then it took a few minutes for them to get back to me. They had us troubleshoot the alarm by reducing the thrust lever position. With the thrust lever reduced the alarm turned off. With this information maintenance control confirmed that there was a sensor issue causing the takeoff configuration warning to activate in flight. Communicating with maintenance control was difficult due to the horn and a weak and almost unreadable phone patch. After we determined this was a sensor issue; I was trying to ask if there was any way we could silence the alarm and got no response from maintenance. This whole process took until we were around the ZZZ2 area; about halfway to ZZZ1. At this time I heard a phone ringing sound over the radio and radio advised us that our phone patch had dropped. I advised them we needed to switch [frequencies] to stay in their radio coverage. Next; I requested to be patched back to Dispatch but after multiple attempts we were never able to be patched back to company. I tried two or three more times and never got the phone patch back. During the flight I was monitoring fuel. We were planned to land with 15;000lbs of fuel. Halfway in to the flight with us re-cruised to FL200 and 230 kts we were showing landing fuel of 17.8. I made the decision to continue to ZZZ1. At this point with our issue being confirmed as a sensor issue and plenty of fuel to make it to ZZZ1 and the takeoff configuration warning light; EICAS and horn were still on. The warning horn is very loud and very distracting. After talking with my FO we decided for the safety of the flight and our ability to communicate effectively to pull the aural warning circuit breakers to silence the aural warning horn. After doing this the horn stopped. I briefed my FO that we would not have altitude call outs on our approach. My FO had the idea and briefed me that once we had flaps deployed and the CONFIGURATION warning extinguished to reset the left aural warning circuit breaker so we would get normal aural alerts on approach and landing. This breaker is directly above the Captain's seat so it was easy to push back in. We landed uneventfully and with 17;000 some pounds of fuel in ZZZ1. Upon parking and talking with maintenance; they advised me that right nose wheel was showing cord down the middle of the tire. Their theory was that the tire was wearing too much on the scrubber after gear retraction and it was possible part ofthe tire destroyed the nosewheel air-ground sensor. Having this odd takeoff warning issue in flight was quite confusing and distracting with the warning horn blaring for 30 minutes while we were trying to fly; communicate and troubleshoot. This was an odd maintenance issue. Our plane was airworthy when we left ZZZ and the nosewheel tire was fine my FO and maintenance did exterior walk arounds and no defects were found. This weird situation took a lot of communication and troubleshooting. I think my FO and myself worked well and had good CRM during this event. I kept my FO in the loop with maintenance control and my FO kept me up with ATC. I think we made a good decision to stay low and slow to protect the flaps just in case there was some issue with a flap or slat hanging out that shouldn't have been. Being on a 767-200 with no SATCOM or ACARS makes communicating with the company difficult. Our VHF phone patch to the company was hard to understand and communicate. Multiple times I had to repeat myself; speaking slowly and deliberately. I had to tell maintenance control multiple times to speak up and slow down. When on with maintenance control I could hear multiple people in the background while we were talking. It seemed like they were using their phone on speaker phone; making it hard to understand them. Also I don't know why we lost the connection with them when I heard a phone ringing sound. ZZZ radio advised me that they hung up on us. This obviously was not good because I was unable to reestablish communication with the company and I don't understand why they would hang up on an airplane in flight. I would advise maintenance control to use their hand set or a head set while communicating with an aircraft in flight to help with communication clarity. SATCOM would have made communicating much easier than a VHF phone patch. I considered [requesting priority handling] but decided against it after troubleshooting with the company and determining this was just a sensor problem. Our flaps worked properly; we had plenty of fuel but we were distracted by the takeoff configuration horn blaring at us. In hindsight; [requesting priority handling] might have helped us get better communication with the company using ATC to help us communicate with them.
column123: While climbing out from ZZZ we started to get a takeoff configuration warning. We consulted the QRH then contacted MX and determined it was a sensor issue. However; we were unable to silence the alarm while the flaps were up; so in the interest of safety and reducing distractions; we pulled the aural warning circuit breakers while we were in cruise. As we configuration for the approach we pushed a circuit breaker back in to get the RA callouts for our approach and landing phase of flight. We also monitored fuel quality while flying at a different altitude and airspeed than planned.

column121: At the gate in ZZZ; almost ready for door closure and gate departure when we get a Lavatory Smoke warning. I called back to the aft cabin flight attendants and they tell me a passenger just exited one of the aft lavs and a cloud of smoke followed him. When confronted; the passenger denied smoking or vaping; and claimed the smoke was present before he entered the lavatory.I called for a customer service manager to come remove the passenger; and the manager; after talking with the passenger; informed me that he still denied smoking and that he was refusing to leave the airplane.After conferring with the manager and his supervisor; and confirming events with the aft cabin flight attendants; I decided to have the entire plane disembark and re-board without the offending passenger.As passengers were deplaning; the suspected smoker stopped at the L1 door and demanded his money back. From the cockpit; I instructed this gentleman to leave my airplane. He refused and was belligerent. I closed the cockpit door and called for law enforcement. After everyone deplaned; we re-boarded and left for ZZZ1.In the current economic/pandemic environment; the airline has been force to offer really low fares.  I feel this means some of our passengers are not frequent flyers and may not understand what's expected of them.I feel like the customer service manager initially was reluctant to have the passenger removed; due to the passenger claiming he hadn't smoked in the lavatory. The aft cabin flight attendants saw him step in the lavatory just prior to the smoke alarm being triggered. After I continued to advocate for his removal; the customer service team did as I requested. I'm not sure what was initially said to the suspected smoker; but when safety is involved; there shouldn't be an option of letting the passenger remain onboard.

column121: Began initial descent into ZZZZ. The controller called to change the STAR. I had to ask 3 times to repeat the prescribed STAR to be flown. His English was very broken. Traffic on the frequency was light. We determined a change of STARs. I input into the FMS and confirmed and executed with the Captain. By this time we were either over [the IAF] to or just past the point. The aircraft overflew [the fix]. The Captain went into heading select and turned to course. Two to three miles past [the fix]; the aircraft was back on an intercept outbound [from the fix]. Then the controller said turn to a heading to intercept inbound course; which we had already initiated. Continuing descent the controller instructed us to fly the circuit which was part of the STAR and we did as planned. During the descent the controller gave us 5 altitude step downs to comply with; 4 of the 5 were then subsequently modified back to a higher altitude. After the compliance with circuit instructions; controller changed the runway. I then reprogrammed the FMS; and confirmed execute with the Captain. After so many changes by the controller and workload was lowered in the cockpit; I queried the controller one final time to ensure we were all on same page. I stated to controller confirm ILS XXR; controller said negative ILS XXL; are you ready to commence approach. I quickly for 3rd time reprogrammed the FMS for ILS XXL confirmed with the Captain and executed. I then told controller ready to commence; and then briefed the Captain on differences of approaches; and new Baro; and landing distances. We landed uneventfully.Poor English by controller almost inaudible. Very late approach instructions modifications. Could be solved if controller gave us changes to STAR and approach a few minutes prior to descent instead of at last moment; and past Anchor points on STAR.
column123: We were filed to [the IAF] and we set up for the ILS Approach. As we approached [the fix] the controller issued a new arrival but we had difficulty understanding the new clearance [due to] language problems. Finally it was determined after 3 difficult queries what we were to fly. After installing the new clearance into the FMS the Aircraft did not make the turn towards [the] next point. As pilot flying I recognized the overshoot and made a correction back to course just prior to ATC issuing vectors. During the arrival numerous runway changes were issued and at least 5 or more altitude instructions given. Just prior to base turn the First Officer queried the controller one final time to confirm ILS XXR. The controller said negative ILS XXL. We quickly for 3rd time reprogrammed the FMS for the ILS XXL; briefed and executed an uneventful landing on XXL.Language problems which caused confusion and delayed FMS programming on our part. Late arrival insertion caused overshoot. Overshoot caused workload to increase. Do a better job anticipating what other options may be available to your crew and get an early confirmation on what arrival to expect. Better to reprogram the FMS after sequencing to the next point then forcing a FMS change close to a turn point.

column121: In VMC conditions; we were cleared by Center for the RNAV Approach. Reaching [the IAF] I noticed that the FMS was programmed to make a turn outbound. We had briefed a Visual Approach backed up by the RNAV Approach and had the runway in sight. I thought that there was an error in the programming of the FMS. Most RNAV approaches with a 90 degree T-shaped base to final turn do not include a procedure turn. This approach is an exception. I overlooked that detail. I disconnected the autopilot and turned inbound to the runway. I called for the flight director to be cleared and hand flew the rest of the approach visually with no flight director. The First Officer sequenced the FMS so I had lateral and vertical guidance in addition to the PAPI and runway; which I could see visually. The approach; landing; and taxi in was uneventful. The cause of the event was the expectation of doing a Visual Approach and not noticing that No PT was not depicted. With clear weather and the runway in sight; I was in the mindset of doing a visual approach even though we were cleared for the RNAV. Additionally; there were 2 other aircraft in the pattern. A light single engine aircraft and a military C-130. After crossing a fix I was thinking about the spacing between us and the other aircraft in the pattern based on making a turn inbound. We were warned that this airport was an unstable high energy approach airport; so I was focused on slowing and configuring for landing early. We are also experiencing light to moderate turbulence; so more attention than normal was required to maintain the desired airspeed. I selected continuous ignition during the approach due to moderate turbulence.We should have noticed that this approach was unusual in that it did not have No PT. We could have requested the visual approach from center; so we would not be required to fly the 7NM holding pattern in lieu of a procedure turn.

column123: Departing Runway XR we were cleared for takeoff. We followed the SID heading of 340 when ATC told us runway heading. Having been unfamiliar with this airports procedures I may have had some expectation bias towards just flying the SID and clearly missed the runway clearance; not to mention having not flown since April [and] a bit of tunnel vision during the before takeoff.

column121: Flight ABCD from ZZZZ to ZZZ I was the position C. After we landed in ZZZ; and taxiing of the aircraft was complete Flight Attendant A announced to the flight attendants to prepare the cabins for departure. I went to my forward service door and pulled the girt bar from the bracket and inserted back into the mount where it was disarmed then put the red flag back up. I turned around to cross check with FA A who I saw bend down to disarm the door. I then started talking to a first class passenger seated in X5. I heard FA A call the aft cabin via inter phone to verify their doors were disarmed. Then we waited till the agent came to knock on the forward entry door. I saw FA A give the thumbs up after the agent knocked and the agent starting opening the door. All of a sudden FA A said; 'stop' and I saw the slide peeping from the compartment after she moved to the side. FA A notified the flight deck of the situation and they called for a mechanic. Two mechanics came quickly and moved the slide out of the housing. We then began to deplane from the front entry door. Managers X and Y came to talk to me and FA A on the aircraft after all the passengers deplaned and was told by her to fill out a report as a partial inadvertent slide deployment.
column123: It was a routine flight; upon arrival at gate in ZZZ I did a P.A. for Flight Attendants to verify and disarm. I bent down to disarm the 1L door left side girt bar bracket and I was thinking what I had to do next: (turn on lights for passengers; all-call the back). For some reason I stood up to turn on the lights. That's not like me; I always focus and follow through on my doors when arming and disarming. The C [FA] had just beat me to the lights; then I did all-call to the back; then C mentions passengers are actually sitting down after health PA to stay seated; because they never listen and crowd the aisle. Then there were 2 knocks on the door from the agent; I gave them thumbs up and looked down and saw the girt bar attached; at same time the agent was gently cracking the door I said stop; the door had opened maybe 1 foot? and the agent and I were face to face; I said stop. The slide partially fell out of housing intact. The mechanics were called; they came fast; they held the bottom portion of the intact slide and they opened the door; and we started deplaning. When I got home my heart was pounding and body shaking from lack of sleep; low blood sugar; and wearing mask. Was a bad combination.Suggestions:*SLEEP- Circadian rhythm. Lack of sleep 4 nights in a row; early morning sign-ins. *FOOD- PLEASE on flights where you can't bring your food into other countries; or you can't bring your own food from the USA back into USA customs does not allow it; if it's too early or too late to get any food; places are closed or nothing is open; or lines are too long to make boarding. PLEASE have a little something for us to eat so our blood sugar does not drop so safety related accidents don't happen. *MASK- Sometimes feel headaches; feel suffocation; can't breathe; lack of oxygen.All of the above create fatigue which decreases the body's ability to focus; and decreased attention.

column121: An aircraft had an air return for the loss of number 1 engine; green; hydraulic pressure; no loss of fluid. The aircraft was moved to the hangar on day shift for repair. We motored the engine and observed the pressure coming from the pump: it increased to 3000 psi then fell off. The aircraft was moved inside and the cowlings were opened up for inspection of the EDP (Engine Driven Pump). There were no external leaks or external damage to the EDP. It was found that the fluid supply line had become disconnected at the pylon connection; it was further noticed that the locking section of the pylon side of the fluid supply line quick disconnect was not locking to the line side. We suspect the line vibrated off; starving the pump and the loss of pressure. The disconnect; pump; and case drain were replaced.

I immediately turned ninety degrees east to exit the TFR as quickly as possible. Fortunately a recent snowstorm had greatly dampened the fire and there was no air traffic fighting the fire at that time. This was very educational experience for me. column121: I completed the weight and balance paperwork; the preflight inspection; and prepared for departure from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2. I taxied to Runway XX from the FBO (Fixed Base Operator); announced my intentions on the CTAF frequency; taxied into position on Runway XX and held for a brief moment allowing for the engines to come up to 2000 RPM; and to look at the engine indications to ensure all indices were within operational limitations which they were; I released the brakes and the aircraft accelerated at the normal rate.Upon rotation and climbing above 500 ft.; I reduced power to 2500 RPM; turned to 090 degrees and contacted Departure. Departure gave me the standard departure for our CASW flights from ZZZ1 allowing me climb to 2;000 ft. MSL (Mean Sea Level) before turning to approximately 320 degrees North West towards ZZZZZ with a climb to 6;000 ft. MSL. I reached cruising altitude; reduced the throttle; set the mixtures; and adjusted pitch. The weather at the time was IMC (Instrument Meteorological Conditions) with moderate rain. Shortly after passing over the highway corridor and just south of ZZZZZ; Departure handed me off to Center. Center acknowledged the handoff; and issued me direct ZZZ2 when able. As I was inputting direct ZZZ2 in the Garmin 650 GNS; I noticed that there was increasing rudder pressure on my right foot. I immediately looked at the RPM gauge and noticed that I was losing power in the left engine. I looked at the oil pressure gauge and I still had pressure; the oil temp was within limits; and cylinder temp was good. Fuel flow was however low. There was no warning as to an impending power loss; no loss of oil pressure; no backfiring or popping noises coming from the engine; just silence. I immediately turned on the boost pump; and put the throttles; prop levers and mixture handles to full. The right engine responded; but the left continued to windmill. I notified ATC that I was having an issue with my left engine; and that I would get back with them. I then went to 'Memory Items' and began to shut down and feather the left engine. I pulled the throttle lever first; then the prop lever; and the mixture. The left engine continued to 'windmill' and cause significant drag. If I recall; ATC then asked if I was requesting priority handling. I do not recall if I did or not; but I believe I had requested priority handling. With a wind-milling prop; I was unable to maintain altitude and began a slow descent. At about 4000 ft. MSL; I broke out of the clouds and ATC notified me that ZZZ airport was available. I was continuing to descend; and despite trying to hold altitude I was unable to even with the #2 engine practically at full throttle. I then noticed my airspeed was dropping below 140; I then elected at that point to proceed directly to the ZZZ airport and land; and I notified ATC. On my way down I went through the emergency checklist for engine out; I however did not get to the abnormal procedure as I needed to concentrate on getting the airport lights on; and get lined up for the runway as I figured I only and one shot at it. Upon landing at the ZZZ airport; I was able to taxi into the ramp area on one engine. The Sheriff Department responded; and I spoke with the deputy. He gave me the contact number for Center and I called and notified them that I had made it to the ground safely without any damage to myself or the aircraft.After parking and securing the aircraft on the general aviation ramp at ZZZ; I inspected the aircraft. There was no sign of a catastrophic failure; no abnormal signs of oil on the outside of the engine cowling and no abnormal signs of oil on the inside of the cowling. The prop appeared to be in full feather; and I used the prop paddle to reset the prop to low pitch. I then attempted to start the engine; and to my surprise it started. I then brought the power up; and at about 1200 -1400 rpm the engine began to sputter and quit. I advanced the throttle and the engine backfired; coughed; sputtered a bit more; but then it regained full power and operated 'normally' at about 2000 RPM. Oil pressure was good; fuel flow was still low. I then shut down the engine and made no further attempt to restart.

column121: I executed a flight in a Piper Arrow 28R-200 in the practice area; in which we came back doing a no gear landing. Today was [the student's] introductory flight in this aircraft. After taking off and leveling at 1;000 ft.; I noticed that the Gear in Transit Light turned on. I put the gear lever in the down position and flew along [a highway] waiting for verification from Aircraft Y. The flight instructor radios that the gears were down but not secure. After cycling the gear and trying the emergency extension and realizing it was not working; I radioed ZZZ1 Tower and advise them of my situation. I did a low approach to verify if gears are down which I was told by tower that the nose gear did not appear to be down. After trying one more time in the pattern to cycle the gear and go over checklist and manual I decided to make the landing.

column121: After boarding was completed; I had the opportunity to listen to our Flight Attendant's safety briefing through my headset by selecting the 'CAB' button on my Audio Management Panel (AMP).  Our FA's are competent; safety oriented professionals and my hat is off to them in terms of all that they put up with from the traveling public and an airline that is sometimes tone deaf to their needs.  In listening the FA safety briefing; I realized that our passengers are NOT being given any procedural guidance to remove their masks / face shields / PPE in the event of a rapid decompression - the portion of the briefing dealing with the use of oxygen masks in the event of a loss of cabin pressure remains unchanged.  This is particularly troubling given that our airline and most other US airlines have adopted a 'zero tolerance' policy regarding the use of facial masks during the pandemic.  Not only has our airline adopted this zero tolerance policy; it is even 'banning' customers from our airline for failure to comply.  So in this draconian world of absolute zero tolerance for failure to wear a mask; where exactly is the procedural guidance in what to do with that snot and drool infested petri dish of nastiness once the oxygen masks drop during a real emergency?

column121: I was flying a J3 Cub to ZZZ. I'm a new sport pilot having only gotten my license about two weeks ago. I got caught up with finding the airport; making frequency changes; getting the winds from the automatic weather reporting station; and trying to figure out how I should enter the pattern. I was not scanning outside the aircraft because I was too focused on everything inside the aircraft. I did not see an aircraft; or hear it on CTAF because I was listening to the weather; departing a runway that I was crossing the extended centerline of. I was around 2 miles away. I finally saw the aircraft as it was coming up on my right side. We both turned left and it was fine; but it scared me quite a bit. After that scare; I just turned away from the airport and left while scanning for other aircraft. Things that I think contributed to this near miss are:-I did not plan the cross country because it was short and I figured I could figure it out on the fly by getting frequencies from my sectionals. -I did not make a radio call when I was close to the airport because I had not yet planned out how I would enter the pattern. -I was too focused on planning my pattern entry that I was not aware of my surroundings. -I did not expect traffic at the airport; because I had flown there the day before and had not seen or heard anyone at the airport. Thinking about what I will do differently; I will:1. Plan out every flight I do that is not just around my home airport. Route; frequencies; predicted weather; airport runways; traffic pattern direction; all available for quick reference on a knee board. 2. Make radio calls as soon as I am within 10 miles of an airport; even if I cannot say where I plan to enter the pattern in an initial call. 3. Keep an eye on airports for traffic below me and above me; and watch out for traffic on extended centerline. Next time I am at ZZZ I will try to avoid crossing centerline unless midfield. 4. Keep in mind that airport traffic can vary day to day.

The start went normally; oil pressure was back. I taxied down to the end of XX did another run up. Everything was in the normal range. Did a normal takeoff left hand pattern while watching the left engine. Proceeded to a normal approach rounded out; pulled power back then heard the gear unsafe warning. A split second later heard tick of a prop hitting the ground. My initial reaction was to push the power forward and take off but reason took over and I pulled power all the way back and bellied the plane in. Then I secured the plane and got out.I did several things wrong that day most importantly I did not follow the checklist and I did not do a GUMPS (Gas; Undercarriage; Mixture; Prop; Switches) check. I also had been driving 4 hours prior to the event. I am devastated. I should have followed the checklist.

column121: I was on an IFR Flight Plan from ZZZ to ZZZ1.  I had poor speed control on the approach.  I was legally IFR current; but; as it turned out; I was clearly not proficient.  The COVID-19 prevented me from flying with a (COVID safe) safety pilot and getting recent practice.  I was scheduled for simulator training for the following week.I flew VFR out to ZZZ for two days.  The weather was predicted VMC for the next several days.  The day after we arrived; the wind shifted and blew in severe smoke from forest fires.  We considered staying for a few more days; but there was no available lodging and the smoke was getting worse.  I reviewed an IFR plan to go back to ZZZ1 and when the destination weather improved enough; I filed IFR; got my clearance; and departed.  The departure; on route; and vectors to final were smooth and uneventful. There was an aircraft ahead that was going slower and ATC requested that I slow to 90 knots; which is what I should have already been slowing to.  I agreed and reduced power.  The autopilot was holding the altitude coming up to the IAF and I inadvertently pulled off too much power.  I was coming up on the IAF and descent and I was verifying that everything (else) was ready to go; when I noticed that the speed was rapidly reducing.  The autopilot (AP) was trimming nose up to maintain altitude.  I hit control wheel steering; nosed down; and added power.  I had to do a lot of trimming to get the nose back down and I over shot the altitude and rapidly picked up speed.  I got the nose back up; on altitude; and thought that the AP would acquire the glide slope.  Nope; in the excitement; I missed arming the approach and flew right through it.  Now I dove for the GS and picked up more speed again.  Now I'm on the GS and check to see if the AP would acquire it and no it started another excursion and so I shut it off and hand flew the rest of the way.  It was stabilized at this point; so I continued the approach and landed.Mistake 1.  I should have already been planning and reducing speed approaching IAF.Mistake 2.  I should have paid more attention to my speed reduction technique.Mistake 3.  I should have requested ATC to bring me around again to have time to set up properly.Mistake 4.  I should have done what I normally do and that is to turn off the AP and hand fly anytime things get weird.My takeaway is that my IFR currency should be done more often; even if it is done in a simulator.

column121: Required maintenance/inspection interval was inadvertently overflown. Upon investigation of the cause of the overflight the following root causes were identified. Bell 505 maintenance was developed in accordance with the MSG-3 methodology (Maintenance Steering Group-3). Different than other helicopters/airplanes that we have operated this method does not permit any tolerance for hourly inspection intervals and requires calendar based maintenance actions be conducted to the day rather than the calendar month. For example; a 1 year inspection conducted on May 3; 2019 is required on May 3; 2020 - not May 30 like many other aircraft. A review of the Bell 505 Maintenance Manual found that this information is present in the manual but is in the definitions section not in Chapter 5 where other manufacturer's include the data. The previous operator of the aircraft was not properly utilizing the block provided on each page of the aircraft log to record next maintenance due date and time information. This block is used on other aircraft to convey this information to the flight crew. It is unknown why flight crews and maintenance personnel did not utilize this block in the same manner that is done for the other helicopters. Maintenance planned to operate the aircraft up to 110 hours flight time since the last 100 hour inspection (10% overage as is allowed for other helicopters) or through 7/31/2020 (12 calendar months since last 1 year inspection) whichever came first. [Before the end of July] we made aware by the Bell Tech representative of the date and hour tolerances (none) for the 505 and operations were stopped until maintenance was completed.

column121: Aircraft X was given takeoff clearance and upon takeoff roll reported an aborted takeoff due to possible bird strike. After exiting the active runway they stopped to do a systems check and aircraft evaluation. They then requested that the fire department follow them to the gate in case of possible hot brakes. I alerted the fire department and they followed the aircraft toward the gate. At that time the Fire Chief advised that the aircraft needed to be evaluated before they could be allowed to go to the gate. I gave them a holding area on an unused taxiway. At that time it was determined that it was a hot brakes situation and the county declared it an alert 2 situation. Fire trucks were already on scene. Visual inspection by fire department personnel also discovered engine damage from the bird strike. After the brakes had cooled enough the aircraft taxied to the gate. No onboard injuries were reported. Alert 2 was canceled by county upon aircraft reaching the gate.
column123: Aircraft X; MKE to ZZZ pushed on time. We had an uneventful taxi to 19R. There was a medium transport aircraft that departed about 30-60 seconds before us. We were cleared into position and holding for about 30 seconds before we were cleared for takeoff. I did not observe any wildlife while we were in position on the runway. At approximately the 80 knots airspeed call I observed two large birds flying low on the center line of the runway. They were about 200 feet in front of us flying to the left of center line right towards us. One appeared to be some kind of large crane; and I could not tell what the other bird was. Later I found out it was a seagull. The crane impacted the left side of the aircraft and then was ingested into the left engine. The other bird also struck the aircraft and I believe was also ingested into the left engine. The left engine immediate had a notably different sound to it and was vibrating. I did not notice the VIB (vibrations) meter or any abnormal engine indications at that moment. I did not know the extent of damage to the left motor or if any damage had been done to the aircraft. Specifically the leading edge devices and the flaps. At that point I determined that the aircraft was in a condition that was unsafe/unable to fly and elected to abort the takeoff at approximately 100 knots. The aircraft came to a stop just past Runway 7R/25L on Runway 19R. The First Officer reported to Tower that we had rejected due to a bird strike. I made an announcement to the flight attendants / passengers to all remain seated. We then re-assessed the situation and I elected to taxi clear of the runway and do the brake cooling for the reject. Tower had us taxi clear of the runway onto Taxiway S then a left onto T. We came to a stop and computed the brake cooling while on Taxiway T. While on Taxiway T out of an abundance of caution we ask the Tower to alert Fire/Rescue to have them follow us to the gate. I also called back to the flight attendants and explained to them what happened and what our plan was. I then communicated with the passengers as to what had happened. We also contacted Dispatch to alert them. After computing the brake cooling it said we were okay to taxi to the gate. Fire/Rescue wanted to check for hot brakes before allowing us to the terminal. We taxied to Taxiway G where we held as Fire/Rescue checked our brakes. They reported that we had a small amount of smoke coming from the right brake and the temperature of the right brake was above 500 degrees fahrenheit and that the left brake was around 450. They wanted use to hold away from the terminal for about 30 minutes or until they saw that the brake temperature was trending down. Once again out of an abundance of caution we elected to follow Fire/Rescue guidance. I continued to make announcements to the passengers to keep them informed as to what was going on with Fire/Rescue. We also communicated with Dispatch via the radio to keep them informed. After about 20 to 25 minutes both brakes were reading below 350 degrees so we returned to the gate. At the gate I spoke to Dispatch and Maintenance Control; made a logbook entry for the bird strike/RTO (rejected takeoff) and then turned the aircraft over to the local Maintenance. There were no injuries reported by any passengers or crew and no one sought any medical attention.After the bird strike; the Tower made a comment to Airport Ops that they had 'several bird strikes that morning.' If this was true I think that MKE needs to have some better wildlife mitigation procedures.

column121: I was working two sectors during smoke and haze conditions requiring all aircraft to pick up IFR flight plans. A large TFR for firefighting was on the east side of my airspace and encroached on the finals for HWD and OAK departures which normally depart on 170 heading across the OAK [Runway] 30 final and towards SFO final which then have to be vectored back across the [Runway] 30 final to the northeast and across the HWD final and then the OAK [Runway] 28 final. Because of the TFR and traffic complexity; I issued a right turn of 040 and maintain 4000 ft. to HWD to issue to Aircraft Y. Per the NorCal TRACON and HWD LOA; released aircraft are to be airborne within 2 minutes. Aircraft X was approximately 11 miles from HWD and cleared for the ILS 30 approach to OAK when I released Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y took 3 mins and 7 seconds to tag up on radar; well outside the LOA requirements. I observed Aircraft Y going upwind and not turning which prompted me to call HWD Tower to confirm the heading to 040 which they affirmed. Aircraft Y was first observed in a turn at 1200 ft. and 1.5 miles upwind. This is well beyond expected pilot performance. Our Quality Control Department is stating that even if Aircraft Y had turned; it would not have been separated because divergence is not permitted with this aircraft. I have looked through JO 7110.65 and found nothing that should prevent me from applying the provisions of that paragraph. I contest that I had applicable divergence separation as Aircraft Y was assigned 040 (and not complying) and Aircraft X was assigned the ILS 30 which is a 296 heading.I am requesting the development of new departure headings and procedures to eliminate the congestion under the OAK final and eliminate the current procedures which are unsafe and nearly unusable given the noise abatement restrictions; which are in effect at all times; and wake re-categorization separation. I also propose new training for how management expects us to get HWD departure aircraft safely out of our airspace given such significant constraints. Also; I'm requesting a follow up to occur with the pilot since he failed to comply with his ATC assigned heading in a timely matter as this was clearly a pilot deviation. Furthermore; had HWD Tower complied with our LOA; I do not believe a conflict would have even been triggered through automation.

column121: Good rest; day VFR with clear skies throughout the flight. This was the second leg of the day; the first leg being a ferry flight. Uneventful flight. On arrival to the airport we both noticed and mentioned it to each other that ATC left us up a little high. Passing through 15;000 ft. or so and very close to what we thought was the airport. I mentioned 'rather than getting a lot of vectors let's just cancel and make a 360 to the left and go to ZZZZZ; which is the IAF on the RNAV GPS RWY XX); which we did. In no rush; I extended the outbound leg of the 360 turn. Coming out of the turn a little disoriented I asked; 'can you extend the centerline of the runway.' The SIC (Second In Command) which has little time in the plane and not very experienced with the FMS was having trouble putting in the centerline. I asked for a centerline from the RUNWAY; the SIC drew the path from ZZZZZ1; a fix on the approach. The approach is a 45 degree angle from the runway; so when he put the extended line it was from ZZZZZ1 not the runway. I asked again 'I don't think that's right; it doesn't line up.' It was still showing the 45-degree angle to the runway. I again queried him and said; 'What is the runway heading? Make the centerline off that; not any of the fixes.' By then; at around 1000 ft. AGL; we both saw RWY XX painted on the runway in front of us and thought; no worries; I see the numbers.On the landing roll out the chart did not pop up. I asked 'why are we not on the chart? The 350 shows the plane on all the charts'.Reaching the end of the runway the passenger came up and said 'guys; you are at the wrong field; ZZZ is 8 miles south of here; this is ZZZ1' He is a pilot also and was very sympathetic and said 'this happens so often; the operations people don't come out anymore.'I apologized and started planning the trip to ZZZ. I called dispatch and advised them of what happened and what we needed. We taxied back to the approach end of RWY XX and found a place to park and called the FODM (Flight Operations Duty Manager) while the SIC was getting the clearance from ATC. I was told 'he's not answering his phone'. I asked them to 'please find him; I need to talk to him'. A minute or so later [he] answered. I explained what happened. He was very calming and eager to work with me. We talked about the weather; the runway length and width; parachute activity in the area; VFR daytime only airport; he even gave me the frequencies to both airports. Our phones started to beep; at that time [he] said; 'I think they are trying to shut you down; I'll take care of it'. I mentioned that we both had plenty of duty time and felt fine to do the 8-mile flight. It is hard to recall every word but he mentioned something to the effect; 'ok; it looks good; let me check on something; I'll call you back'.After waiting a few minutes and thinking that we had covered everything we needed to for the flight; I decided to depart.The flight to ZZZ was uneventful. The passenger had no problem with the event and being a pilot himself in that area; he kept telling me 'don't worry it really does happen here a lot; ZZZ3 had a RWY XX also. They finally had to change the numbers to XY even though its heading is [different]'. We helped them load their car and they drove off.   Things we should/could have done...-Stayed with ATC and gotten better vectors to the airport.-Made sure the centerline was indeed off the runway NOT the FAF.

column121: On takeoff from PDX; in IMC conditions from takeoff up to about 15;000 ft. MSL. Everything seemed normal until 400 ft. AGL. The captain called 'verify NAV' and I did and then I noticed the EICAS displayed in cyan advisory messages 'Autoland 1 not available' and a second message which I believe was 'RNP (Required Navigation Performance) 0.1 not available.' I am certain about the first message but not about the second. I also noticed that the yellow square with 'RA' was displayed on the PFD in the bottom right corner. This seemed indicative of a radio altimeter malfunction or miscompare. The EICAS messages extinguished quickly and immediately we received an aural warning 'too low; terrain' GPWS message. I did not see a message on the PFD and there was no guidance provided; only the aural warning. I believe the aural warning was only announced once and then went away.This Aural warning is usually only for being low to terrain and not in a correct Landing configuration. We were taking off in takeoff configuration. The gear was up right after takeoff and the flaps were set to 2 for takeoff and had not been retracted since we had not achieved acceleration height. So the aural warning did not make any sense.We both quickly began scanning the instruments and found that the aircraft was already pitched to take off pitch of around 18 degrees nose up. Wings were mostly level. The aircraft was on the flight director. The altitude and vertical speed indicated a climb. Both PFDS displayed the same information. The backup instrument panel displayed the same. The MFD was on terrain display on the map page and showed black terrain in the immediate area and distant green terrain around the aircraft. And thrust was in the TOGA (Takeoff Go Around) position.So everything cross referenced to show a normal; terrain free; take off and climb. Also; we were already in full take off climb thrust; pitch; and configuration. So we continued flight.We got to acceleration height and retracted flaps and continued the remainder of the flight without issue. The issue did not repeat itself again.Another thought is that the IMC conditions were caused by smoke from wild fires. Perhaps the smoke particulates caused a radio altimeter malfunction and the RA briefly read the altitude as too low for only a split second.We were already in GPWS response pitch and configuration. So there was not much else to do. Especially when all indications seemed normal for climb out and the GPWS message was brief and seemed associated with RA malfunction. The only possible extra effort that could be made would be thrust to MAX but that didn't seem necessary in this case as the aural warning had already stopped.
column123: The flight departed PDX into immediate IMC because of fog and smoke in the area. Everything was functioning normal and it was standard takeoff and climb. At about 500-600 ft. MSL the FO's (First Officer) PFD indicated an issue with the radar altimeter: amber rectangle with RA. Two EICAS messages appeared. One of them was AUTOLAND 1 NOT AVAIL and I think the second message was something with the RNP (Required Navigation Performance). At which point the EGPWS warning 'TOO LOW; TERRAIN' was heard once. I immediately verified again that the aircraft is pitching up; climbing at takeoff power; on speed; and following the RNAV departure; according to standard profile. Terrain map did not indicate any colors but green and black on the MFD. After a few seconds all messages extinguished and the flight proceeded without any other malfunctions or anomalies.Upon discussing the event with my FO later in cruise; we both thought that it was a radar altimeter anomaly and that the aircraft was at all times operated following normal operating procedures and never outside the normal flight profile/envelope. We also discussed the possibility of an oversized vehicle on the I-205 bridge as that would have been about the point in the air this event occurred.Please monitor if this was a onetime occurrence or there is a trend.

column121: During an ILS approach to Runway XXR; the PF failed to slow early enough on final approach. PF configured later than desired considering the situation (fast due to earlier ATC request) resulting in the aircraft becoming high on glide path while slowing to configure for landing. PF needed to use a sink rate higher than desired to return to glide slope. We met the published parameters at all of our approach gates; but the first portion of the approach was unstable. We landed safely on XXR and proceeded routinely to the gate.The main lesson learned was to slow earlier on final approach to allow a more stable approach. We accomplished all checklists and procedures and landed safely; but the crew would have been more able to look for potential threats if the PF had flown a more stable approach during the first portion of the approach. PNF was just back from several months off - take away for PNF was to address a rapidly evolving situation sooner and prompt the PF to configure sooner.

column121: While on RNAV RWY 4 approach into UIN; between the initial fix (JISNA) and the FAF (WUSIS); we descended below the minimum altitude prescribed for that segment of the approach; which was 2100 ft. MSL . I did not recognize that we were below until about 1600 ft. MSL and by the time I had corrected our pitch and added power we between 1500 ft. and 1600 ft. MSL. We immediately climbed back up to 2100'; and at about 2 miles prior to the FAF; we re-evaluated our position; flight guidance panel and configuration and felt that we could resume the approach as normal; which was an autopilot coupled LPV approach. Part of the cause of this issue was my set up of the flight guidance panel. We had been descending from about 7000 ft. and navigating direct to the initial fix of JISNA. At some point in the descent; ATC cleared us for the approach and told us to maintain 2700 ft. until JISNA. We were given the frequency change from Center to CTAF at this point as well. At that point; I thought I was in VNAV mode and descending. I hit APPR (Approach); since we were cleared for the approach; and dialed my altitude selector to the bottom of the approach; which was 960 ft. MSL for the minimums. My assumption was that we would then VNAV to 2700 ft. at JISNA; or essentially just VNAV to 2100 ft. by WUSIS; grab the glideslope and continue the descent. I felt I had set it up so that all stepdown altitudes would be met. At that point; I may have become distracted with other radio calls and prepping for landing. During this time; the SIC (Second In Command) was running checklists; trying to reach the FBO  on unicom; and also conferring with ATC to ensure we had a good way to cancel IFR  once we were on the ground. Neither of us were totally focused on the task at hand; which was to monitor the plane as we were beginning this approach. I estimate we were doing about an 800 fpm descent rate. We may have been in VNAV mode; but I was not coupled to the glide path; so we were descending in such a way that would not allow the autopilot to level us off at each fix. 1. PIC/SIC should have been totally focused on the primary task at hand: entering; establishing; and flying the approach as published. This would have caught any errors in my programming of the descent and flight guidance panel before we descended below published altitude. 2. Both pilots should be looking at the flight guidance panel in these critical times to verify proper mode; and calling out altitudes around these fixes. 3. Once the altitude deviation was realized; I should have climbed up; executed a missed approach; and called ATC to vector us back around for the approach. 4. My decision not to go missed was influenced by my desire to keep my passenger's schedule. That is a hazardous attitude that I want others to be aware of and learn from.
column123: As our passengers were boarding the plane; they decided to change the destination to UIN due to the fact we were unlikely to be able to get into ZZZ due to low ceilings. The altitude deviation occurred on the RNAV (Area Navigation) approach to RW 4 at UIN. We had been cleared for the approach and we were to instructed to maintain 2700 ft. until established on the approach and had been approved to change to advisory frequency. I was the nonflying pilot and was busy verifying everything on the checklist had been completed and communicating with KC center and UNICOM at UIN to make position reports. I also verified with KC center that we would be able to contact them on the ground using that frequency or did we need to cancel our IFR through flight service. This took a little extra time to complete due to my lack of experience with the Proline Fusion avionics so I was not monitoring the PFD as closely as I should have. We were inside JISNA (IAF)and I was trying to determine our position from the airport in order to give an accurate position report when the pilot flying said something to the effect of wait why are we low. He immediately added power selected vertical speed up and set our altitude selector to 2100 ft. I was focused on other tasks in the cockpit so I cannot say with 100% certainty what autopilot modes were selected previously. We were somewhere between 1600 ft. and 1500 ft. MSL when he started the recovery. We reached 2100 ft. two miles prior to the WUSIS (FAF) intercepted the glide path and landed without further issue. During the debrief with my captain after the flight we discussed the need to treat such a critical phase of flight with the utmost respect and after getting established on the approach to keep all attention on the task at hand which is flying/monitoring the approach. We also discussed the need to make a verbal call out of all autopilot/ flight director mode changes to make sure both pilots are on the same page and are totally aware of what the automation is doing if it is engaged.

column123: After [the] Captain made [the] 'prepare for landing announcement' I; FA3 (Flight Attendant); walked up to [the] front and started clearing the cabin from there to [the] back. I finished preparing the cabin and headed up to my seat. When I was getting ready to sit; I saw that there was someone in front lavatory and asked FA1 if he saw anyone go in there. He explained that passenger 1F who came on [a] wheelchair had to use [the] lavatory last minute. I noticed how close we were getting to the ground so I started knocking on [the] door and told her; 'We are approaching landing and you need to come out;' to which she responded; 'I'm coming;' so I kept knocking on door and telling her she needed to come out already. Then; I noticed the landing gear is coming out. I then tell her; 'You need to come out NOW; landing gear is down we are about to land.' She said; 'Okay;' and seemed like she was going to come out but then didn't. That's when FA1 got up and told tell her to stay in the lavatory; which at that point; [was] so close to [the] ground and [since there was] such little time; [it] seemed like the best decision.We landed safely and checked on [the] passenger; she said she was okay. FA1 called [the] flight deck and explained to the Captain that we had someone in the lavatory [and] to let us know if we were going to make any stops so that we could have her go back to [her] seat safely since it takes her time to walk to her seat. The Captain told FA1; 'We are going to keep moving;' so [the] passenger remained in [the] lavatory until we came to a safe stop. The passenger came out and apologized for what she had done and said she understood she had done wrong but she really needed to go. Captain asked us why we didn't call him in the air we explained everything happened just so suddenly and we were so close to [the] ground with sterile flight deck and basically not much time.

column121: I was told to go to the gate at ZZZ airport to inspect a write up on an ERJ175. The write up stated that the pilots were not able to get cool air in the cockpit during cruise; but the packs worked and blew cool air on ground. It was written up previously and was a repeat write up. Because this was a repeat and there were no EICAS (Engine Indication and Crew Alerting System) messages reported; I decided to interrogate the CMC (Central Maintenance Computer) for active faults and faults stored on the previous flight. I found two fault codes on the current leg as active with no inactive time stamp showing it was resolved. I then went to active faults and both codes were stored as active there as well. The two fault codes were 21000020AM2 and 21000030AM2. Following the FIM (Fault Isolation Manual); the problem was a fault with SPDA (Secondary Power Distribution Assembly) 2 Module 26. I inspected the MEL (Minimum Equipment List) list and there was no deferral for this item. I informed my lead and ordered parts needed for repair. The parts would not arrive until the next morning so I was told it would be days. Shortly after arriving at work; I was informed that it was signed off as left pack deferred and flew out. Looking at the fault codes; the fault was for more than just the pack system which made it non-deferrable.Days did not follow the turn over stating that the faults were active and that the problem was with the SPDA 2 Module 26. They also did not look up fault in FIM and followed the procedures. This allowed for a broken plane to have a different part to be deferred while the actual problem was not addressed. Mechanics need to follow manuals and carefully read shift turnover.

column123: The crew and plane had arrived 4 hours earlier (XA:46) on an empty reposition leg. The passengers were originally scheduled to arrive at XC:00. The flight plan was delayed through handler 4 times due to uncertainty of passenger arrival time; with the most recent scheduled target takeoff time of XE:30.After engine start; the crew was instructed to taxi to Runway 05 holding point 'Hotel'. The aircraft initially stopped at H1 as a smaller business jet was taking Runway 05. We reported 'holding point H1' and the Controller responded 'holding point Hotel hold short Runway 05'. We moved forward the short distance from holding point Hotel 1 to Hotel. The Controller stated; 'Aircraft X; be prepared for an immediate takeoff. Do you have traffic 4 mile final in sight?' I responded 'affirmative; traffic in sight.' The Tower issued another instruction and I read back 'Line up and wait Runway 5; be ready for immediate takeoff.' We taxied ahead briefly then the Tower instructed us to 'hold position.' The Tower Controller stated that we were instructed 'Behind landing traffic; line up and wait Runway 5; be ready for immediate takeoff.' I replied that I heard 'Line up and wait Runway 5; be ready for immediate takeoff.'The Tower Controller was speaking with 2 inbound aircraft on the ILS (Instrument landing System) for Runway 5. There was another aircraft intercepting the ILS approximately 12 miles out. The inbound aircraft had been on a 4 mile final when we crossed the hold short point by approx. 100 ft. It was instructed to go around at approximately 2 miles out. After the inbound aircraft started its go-around; we were instructed to 'line up and wait; Runway 5.' We were cleared for takeoff and the Tower Controller stated that he would be submitting a report.A rough estimate indicates that the distance between holding point H and the actual runway is approximately 650 ft. We taxied about one 100 ft. across the hold short line but stopped approximately 500 ft. short of entering the runway. The term 'selective attention bias' seems appropriate here. I heard part of a message that included the phrase 'be ready for immediate takeoff' and was ready to act quickly. This situation was complicated by a language barrier and I missed or didn't understand the first part of the Controller's message of 'after landing traffic'. Operating frequently at busy Class B airports in the US where it's not unusual to be expected to expedite takeoff with closely spaced traffic; this situation was not out of the ordinary. In hindsight; it was the intention of the Controller to put us between the landing traffic and the next aircraft that was 12 miles out; not in front of the first aircraft that was landing.What both crew members could agree on is that we heard a transmission with an instruction to 'Line up and wait Runway 05. Be prepared for an immediate takeoff'.Contributing factors included language as LIEO is a popular international destination. There are many non-native English speakers on frequency. Phraseology can be different than what is used in the US and when accents and cultures are mixed; message transmission and reception aren't always in alignment.Time pressure [was a factor]. There had been numerous delays in the schedule. There was a sense of wanting to 'get things moving' since we were running 3 hours late. The weather at subsequent airports were forecast to have low ceilings and possible fog; so we didn't want to endure any unnecessary delays. The scheduled takeoff time of XE:30 was close to expiring.Also we were expecting to be sequenced into landing traffic and the pace was rapid. The instruction 'Be prepared for an immediate takeoff' had us ready to respond quickly. Recent landing experience [corroborated this]. Upon arrival 4 hours earlier; we were given landing clearance a few miles out. Instructions had a bit of a 'at the last minute' feel.PNF (Pilot Not Flying) had a Bose noise cancelling headset and PF(Pilot Flying) had a Telex over-the-ear headset. Neither pilot understood the first part of the ATC transmission. PF thought PNF might have understood the message better since he had a higher performance headset. What we did correctly [includes the following]. We read back what we thought we heard; assuming we would be corrected if wrong. We proceeded slowly across the hold short line. We stopped immediately when instructed and did not enter runway. We kept the incoming aircraft in sight and watched it go-around.What we did incorrectly [includes the following]. PNF missed or didn't understand the first part of an ATC transmission and didn't ask for clarification from the Controller or confirmation from the other pilot. With the 'Be prepared for immediate takeoff' instruction; we were spring-loaded to react versus stopping to ask for the message to be repeated or have a discussion between 2 pilots. [Also] since there was ambiguity in what we heard; we should have asked for clarification. After operating at busy class B airports in the US; there's a bit of hesitation in stopping to ask for an instruction to be repeated. Doing this at such an airport can result in getting lectured by ground and tower controllers.

column121: Apparently one of the flight school aircraft; a Cessna 172-L model; has been technically un-airworthy. The local mechanic shop did perform a pre-buy inspection when the flight school purchased the aircraft. The aircraft has undergone routine 100 hour inspections since the plane started working in the flight school. However; it wasn't until the most recent 100 hour inspection which was early September of this year that the local mechanic shop found that the aircraft was overdue on an Airworthiness Directive on a component on the propeller. It was overdue for about 500 hours on that particular AD. The mechanic shop was not certified to do the inspection on the propeller for that given AD for the propeller to be complied with. The flight school requested a ferry permit to fly the aircraft to the nearest propeller mechanic shop but was denied by the local FSDO. The next option was to remove the propeller and drive it to a propeller shop so that AD could be complied with. Such action was taken and the propeller shop found no defects with the propeller. The propeller was later driven back to the home airport to be placed back on the aircraft. Alas; the aircraft was complied with all known Airworthiness directives. The local mechanic shop staff admitted that they overlooked the AD. However; at the end of the day it is the owner/operator of the aircraft that is ultimately responsible for determining the airworthiness of the aircraft; which includes me; the flight instructor when using the aircraft to train student pilots. The flight school staff; meaning all the instructors and chief pilot were essentially responsible for this oversight of the airworthiness of the aircraft. I believe that the flight school staff trusted the mechanic shop to ensure the aircraft complies with all known AD's for every 100 hour inspection. The flight school has every intention to ensure the aircraft meets all inspections including ADs; and that by paying the mechanic shop for their services would suffice for ensuring the aircraft is airworthy. Over-relying on the mechanic shop in my opinion has been the root cause of this issue. I've personally shown the logbooks of the aircraft and ADs to my students prior to every checkride to show the aircraft is airworthy. I've even presented the ADs to my examiner for my CFI initial checkride. I honestly just never knew how to look up ADs or even know how to make sure that all ADs are complied with. The resolution that the chief pilot and I want to take to prevent this mishap from happening again is to learn how to look up ADs ourselves as a secondary check on top of the routine inspections done by the mechanics. Had I known that the AD wasn't complied with no one would've flown that aircraft until it is absolutely airworthy. A more thorough overview on the flight school's ADs is needed to make sure we are complying with them; and to make sure none have been overlooked. Again; the Chief pilot and I want to be able to double check AD compliance after routine inspections; and enhance communication between the instructors and mechanics.

column121: On approach into ZZZ on ILS XR we had been asked to keep our speed up until the marker. We complied with the request. The weather was very gusty winds and both myself and the pilot flying communicated as to what the V-ref target speeds should be. Sometime before 1000 feet the pilot flying was trying to control his speed and configure at the last minute in order to comply with the Tower's request. We had traffic about 3 1/2 miles in front of us. With the gusty winds and both of us pilots being relatively new to the aircraft and because this aircraft was an X type aircraft I had relayed to the pilot flying that we didn't want to have a tail strike with such gusty winds; so I suggested that at any time either one of us felt that we weren't going to land in the touchdown zone or we didn't feel we weren't going to make a normal landing then we needed to 'go-around.' About 1200 feet we got another gusty wind report from the Tower that caused me to readjust the target speed with my head being down and losing situational awareness (SA). We never got too fast for our configuration but I called the'1000 feet' call at approximately 930 feet. I had already configured the aircraft for the landing checklist except for final flaps. I feel the pilot flying got distracted by me changing the target speeds that he lost his SA and forgot to call for flaps 30/landing checklist. I initiated the checklist and realized we were hadn't gone to flaps 30 and he hadn't called for the checklist. I selected final flaps and finished the checklist. I called 500 feet and he responded stable and we landed uneventfully.
column123: On arrival into ZZZ I was configured flaps 15; 180 knots until the marker. About the time I was going to call flaps 30 we received a new gusting  wind report from tower that required an adjustment to our target speed. We discussed the wind and adjusted for about a 15 knot add over flaps 30 ref of about 148 target speed. Upon completing landing checklist which at this point was also delayed and we discovered that the flaps were not positioned yet to 30. We immediately positioned the flaps to 30 and landed. column121: All pilot crew members were present at scheduled report time; and pre-flight planning was accomplished as a crew. We arrived at the aircraft together approximately one hour before scheduled push time. Flight deck preparation duties were accomplished uneventfully in accordance with SOP. During flight deck preparation; I was designated by the Captain as the Pilot Monitoring for the first leg. The Captain accomplished the departure briefing; and I do not recall any deviations from the standard briefing. We pushed one minute early and proceeded uneventfully to Runway XXC. There were no aircraft anomalies during start and taxi. When cleared by ATC and after accomplishing runway verification; we initiated the takeoff roll. Another heavy aircraft had just departed on the same runway. The Captain made the 'check thrust' callout; and I replied with the 'thrust set' callout. After verifying all three airspeed indicators were matched and increasing; I focused my attention on the engine instruments while periodically cross-checking the airspeed indicator. All aircraft systems appeared to be performing normally; and I noticed normal aircraft acceleration. I glanced down the runway once prior to making the '100 knots' callout to verify that we were tracking centerline; then remained inside the cockpit until the Captain initiated the reject. I don't recall any significant yaw during the takeoff roll other than normal motion associated with the tracking of runway centerline. Approaching V1 (Takeoff Decision Speed); the Captain pulled the throttles to idle; initiating a rejected takeoff. I was surprised by this action; as I had not sensed a condition requiring a rejected takeoff. I did not hear a 'reject' callout. I noticed the speedbrake handle deploy and felt the RTO (Rejected Takeoff) brakes engage; but I do not remember looking to verify that the thrust reversers were in reverse. I heard the 'V1' callout shortly after the reject was initiated. I did not make the '80 knots' callout. When we were almost stopped; I made a 'remain seated; remain seated' PA announcement. I reported to ATC that we had rejected on runway XXC and that we were stopped on the runway between the five and six boards. I was confused about why the Captain had rejected the takeoff. I assumed he had seen something that I hadn't; and I was searching the instrument panel for the reason. The Captain said he felt a pronounced right swerve that felt like an engine failure; which prompted him to reject the takeoff. The IRO suggested looking at the wheels synoptic to check for a blown tire; but there was no indication of one. At the IRO's recommendation; we completed the rejected takeoff non-normal checklist. We did not request emergency vehicle response. We taxied clear of the runway and held position for a few minutes with the parking brake released while monitoring brake temperatures. I recall the hottest brake being number 7 with a value of 7.7. With brake temperatures no longer increasing; we elected to taxi to the gate; and coordinated with ATC; Operations and [Maintenance Control] for a gate return. We accomplished the BRAKE TEMP non-normal during the taxi back to the gate. Upon blocking in; we debriefed Maintenance in the cockpit and then departed the aircraft with the parking brake released after accomplishing all post-flight duties and a flight crew debrief. I spoke with [Operations] and completed a human factors questionnaire with her. While accomplishing flight deck preparation after plane swap and re-release; I was released from the trip.I recall V1 being 137 knots. I estimate the reject was initiated at approximately 130 knots; because I heard the automated 'V1' callout occur just after the reject was initiated. The 'V1' callout definitely occurred after the reject was initiated; because I remember being confused by sensing the deceleration at the same time as hearing the 'V1' callout. I suspect there was some residual acceleration after the throttles were pulled to idle which triggered the 'V1' callout; but by the time I heard the callout we were already decelerating.
column123: I was in the Jumpseat. It was the Captains takeoff runway XXC. At 120 to 130 knots; the Captain rejected the takeoff without announcing the Reject.The airplane came to a complete stop on the runway. A few seconds passed; I said; who's gonna say remain seated? The FO (First Officer) said; I will; and made the remain seated call over the PA.I said; we need to tell ATC we rejected. The FO then let ATC know.I realize that the ATC call comes before the remain seated call. My biggest concern at that moment was the possibility of an un-commanded passenger evacuation. And since no one in the cockpit was saying or doing anything yet; I strongly suggested that someone say; REMAIN SEATED.A few seconds went by. I said; should we do the Rejected takeoff checklist? The CA (Captain) agreed and called for it.The FO began to read the checklist; then the Cabin call message displayed. I asked the Captain; do you want me to get that? He said yes.The FA (Flight Attendant) on the phone asked if things were ok; then asked if we were going to make an announcement. I asked the Captain if he wanted to make a PA; he directed me to make an announcement. I said; ladies and gentlemen; we have rejected the takeoff due to an abnormality; we are running a checklist; please remain seated with your seatbelts fastened and follow your flight attendants instructions. As I finished the announcement; the FO was on step 5 of the rejected takeoff checklist.The CA announced that he wanted to taxi clear of the runway and he released the brakes. I said; should we make sure that the tires are ok first? The FO selected the gear synoptic page. All tire pressures were normal; but brake temperatures were 3.5 and rising. The FO then continued with the Rejected takeoff Checklist.I began to smell hot brakes in the cockpit; a hot rubber smell. Just then the cabin call light illuminated; I answered and the FA said that there was a hot rubber smell near door 3. I told her it was the brakes and that we would make an announcement. The Captain then directed me to make another announcement.I said; ladies and gentleman; what you are smelling is the elevated temperature of the brakes; the indications are within limits; please remain seated and follow the flight attendants instructions while we finish our checklists. The FO asked if we should call the fire trucks. The Captain said no I think we're ok.Tower then asked us what the reason was for the rejected takeoff. The Captain told the FO that the airplane had an un-commanded yaw to the right. The FO relayed that information to Tower.As we taxied clear of the runway the Captain said that he felt a yaw and thought that an engine had failed; that's why he rejected.The Captain said let's go back to the gate; and directed the FO to call [Operations]. I interjected and said do you think we should call maintenance first? He said yes.I called maintenance; explained the situation; I gave them the brake temps and asked their opinion on returning to the gate. Local maintenance said it would be fine to go to the gate. In hind sight; I should have called [Maintenance Control]; but at the time it was more efficient to call local maintenance on the radio.As we taxied to the gate I asked the Captain not to pull into the gate until I reviewed the rejected takeoff; and performance sections of the FM (Flight Manual). Even though I just asked maintenance; I wanted to be sure there were no restrictions on bringing an airplane with hot brakes to the gate.I pulled up and reviewed [the FM sections] with the CA and FO. A BRAKE TEMP advisory message was now displayed.We parked the airplane at the gate and maintenance came to the cockpit. One of the mechanics had a laptop. He asked the Captain what happened and typed the Captains response into his laptop. The Captain said he felt a severe yaw to the right; he thought it was an engine failure and he rejected the takeoff. [Maintenance] asked the FO if he felt the yaw; the FO said; not really. [Maintenance] asked me if I felt the yaw; I told him that I felt a yaw to the left after the CA began the rejected takeoff maneuver.[Maintenance] then said that he downloaded the data from the airplane and that no anomalies were found. The Captain said then maybe it was a gust of wind that yawed the airplane to the right. I told [Maintenance] that the Quick Turnaround Landing Weight Limit was not exceeded and I referenced the FM performance section with him. In hind sight; I should have advised the CA and FO to include the information outlined in FO in their rejected takeoff maintenance write up.The mechanics left; the Captain then debriefed. He said that he felt a significant yaw to the right; he said that he did not announce 'REJECT' and that he should have. He thanked us for backing him up.We went to the new airplane. I did the exterior preflight. I got a call from the [Flight Ops Manager] who asked me a list of HF (Human Factors) questions to gauge my stress level. I answered her questions.15 minutes later the Captain's phone rang; it was the chief pilot who advised us that a safety investigation is underway on the event and that we were being pulled off line with pay.

column121: I made a delayed turn from base to final approach while conducting the ILS XXR into ZZZ. The reason for the delayed turn was a momentary lapse in CRM skills. I was the flying pilot; my copilot was the monitoring pilot. We were on a base leg when the Controller gave us a turn towards the final approach. I remember dialing in the correct heading; but forgot to press heading select.  About ten seconds or so elapsed before the Controller asked if we were turning. I realized my error and immediately pressed heading select. The Controller gave us a new heading and an approach clearance. We turned onto final with a slight overshoot and above the glide slope. We configured for landing and used vertical speed mode to intercept the glide slope from above. We were on speed and altitude well before the 1;500 foot gate. Other than the late turn and the high glide slope intercept; there was no other incident or error.The fact is the I/we made an error by not following through with Verbalize Verify and Monitor. I know that we both verbalized the heading change; I recall we both Verified setting the heading; we both; however; forgot to monitor the FMAs for the change. I think that we realized the something wasn't right a split second before the controller queried us. There were many threats preceding this error. This is an all-night flight with an early morning low visibility arrival. The airspace is quite congested and there were many aircraft with similar sounding call signs. We had a runway change while on the arrival and the Controller kept us little higher and gave us a turn a little earlier than we had expected. I had a scheduling change in the middle of this pairing which reduced my rest time a day before this leg. Do to the current global pandemic and the reduced airline schedules; neither of us had flown very much in the past six months. I know I felt a bit rusty and tired.To mitigate this I gave what I thought was a good approach brief before top of descent; and we briefed the changed approach during the arrival. We still failed to monitor the FMA change at a crucial moment. It was an error I hope I/we don't repeat.

column121: This flight was planned on a route that went through ZZZZ.  In my pre-flight planning process; I checked the enroute NOTAMs by loading all the enroute FIR boundaries and then using 'control-F' and searching the enroute NOTAMs for applicable airways.  Today; there were no such hits when performing this NOTAM checking method.  Unfortunately; there was a NOTAM for ZZZZ that had been issued just before I arrived for work:...DUE TO COVID-19...ATS WILL NOT BE AVAILABLE. ATS CONTINGENCY PLAN(AIC A11/18) FOR ZZZZ1 FIR ACT.                                                                                     The flight had been airborne for some time; but was still in ZZZZ2 airspace when the crew advised me that they were being re-routed out of ZZZZ airspace - the re-route was minimal and after considerable effort (due to non-existent or out-of-date info in AIR for ZZZZ and ZZZZ3) I was finally able to speak with ZZZZ3 ATC and obtain an expected route through their airspace; and then I was able to advise the crew of the routing.  The amount of en-route FIR boundary NOTAMs is daunting - impossible to read these for every international flight --- therefore using the 'Control-F' to search for applicable airways allows the Dispatcher to quickly determine if there are any en-route implications to the flight.  Of course; if there are no associated airways with a NOTAM as in the case of the situation affecting this flight; then pertinent closures can be missed.  In addition; since the crews do not receive a copy of the FIR boundary NOTAMs; this scenario leaves the Dispatcher as the single point of failure.Be smarter when it comes to FIR boundary NOTAMs.  Utilize a resource like 'SmartNotam' to weed through all the FIR boundary NOTAMs and then provide both the crew and the dispatcher a condensed list of applicable FIR boundary NOTAMs to read and decipher.
