column121: During boarding Flight Attendant B let me know there was a passenger who was speaking on her cell phone while not wearing a mask. Flight Attendant B asked her to put the mask on and the passenger said she can't talk on the phone through a mask. Flight Attendant B insisted and the woman begrudgingly put the mask on. As I passed by the passenger she was again not wearing the mask and speaking on her phone. I stood by the seat in front of her waiting for a good break in the conversation for a time to talk with her and she wrapped up the conversation and said sorry and put the phone away. I told her it wasn't an issue with the phone; but the health and safety of those around her. She put her mask on. Shortly thereafter as we were preparing the cabin for departure I noticed her mask was below her nose. She was wearing her headphones and did not hear me; but when she saw me she pulled the mask up over her nose. Based on the attitude she gave Flight Attendant B and the fact that the mask was off again when I came by; and then not properly worn a third time Flight Attendant B and I concurred that if we had to speak with her again it would merit a disciplinary action. We also told the flight deck this; so that they would be aware. Throughout the flight we did have close eyes on her; as one does when a passenger has already exhibited behavior that is against the rules; but I tried not to hound on her. During service I saw her and some others wearing their mask below their nose or off in the long times between sips and I made a PA asking everyone to be compliant (in no way singling her out).Once it came time for final compliance for landing I came back through and again her mask was fully below her nose. I stopped and kneeled down and told her that we had already spoken with her about the mask and that wearing it under the nose does not comply. During the conversation that followed she did not pull her mask over her nose until after I had walked away.She told me that she has a medical condition that makes her light headed and that she has been doing her best with the mask. I told her that while for several months we had mask exemptions for medical cases for the last month it has been mandatory regardless of individual. She asked me for my full name and asked if she could take a picture of my name tag. I told her I was not comfortable giving my last name but if she reached out to the company they would know who I was. She said that I was rude for hounding her and briefly said the word 'Nazi' in reference to my strict adherence to the mask policy and 'targeting' of her.The specifics of timing between what was said during this conversation and what was said in the conversation after I brought disciplinary action and later during final compliance all kind of meld; but these things were said.She said that it was wrong to single out people who have medical conditions and that they don't have to share what the condition is. I reminded her that at no point did I ask her what her condition is and that she only shared that she had a condition at the end of the flight after things came to a head. I also explained again that regardless of condition the mask policy is for anyone who wants to fly.Some guests in the nearby rows thanked me for sticking to the policy as they had had concerns with the passenger in question not wearing her mask throughout the flight. I did my best to thank them for their support; but also to not rile up the non-compliant passenger nor the woman across the aisle who seemed to have befriended and come to the passenger's side (however this woman never spoke up to me or in my earshot). I did not want to put passengers against each other or cause more disruption.Passenger also said that she was not planning on flying [Airline] ever again. column121: VFR departure normal. Right turn at shoreline. I departed with flight following but was informed ATC would be too busy along my route and was told to squawk VFR. Limited to the Class Bravo shelf; I set my altitude select to 4500 ft. and engaged the autopilot in the climb. Monitoring the climb; I saw the plane continue the climb past 4500 ft. and where I expected it to settle back to 4500 ft.; instead go through 4600 ft. upon which I disengaged the auto pilot and pushed on the yoke. However; the trim up elevator wouldn't relax; I couldn't turn the trim wheel and all I could do was push hard against the yoke as I busted Bravo and the plane climbed at least another 400 ft. with the trim stuck. I pulled the circuit breaker but it still wouldn't release and I manually pushed the yoke hard to get the plane below the bravo. I cycled the breaker and the switch and finally got the trim under control. I hand flew at 4500 ft. until passing the shelf and continued on my flight climbing to 8500 ft. with no difficulties. Later; I determined that I have a faulty autopilot altitude switch. Getting it fixed tomorrow. In retrospect; I feel I handled the problem calmly but expeditiously.

column121: There are way too many airfields in Central/South Florida that are in somewhat close proximity on the same CTAF (Common Traffic Advisory Frequency) frequency 123.05.   These airfields include GIF Winter Haven; 2IS Airglades; X04 Apopka; PCM Plant City; X26 Sebastian; and X39 Tampa North. On busy days usually towards the end of the week including Thur; Fri; Sat and Sun when the weather is good and many people are out flying; this frequency is completely jammed up much of the day with radio calls from all of the different airfields all at once. It is difficult sometimes to even get a quick call in. Some of these airfields to include GIF; PCM; X04 and X26 are very busy with flight school traffic; local GA (General Aviation) traffic and skydiving (at X26). This creates an unsafe situation when pilots cannot even hardly get a word in on CTAF to give a standard traffic call. Often times pilots will step on each other making calls which creates a jamming type sound which further makes comm more difficult. There shouldn't be this many airfields this close on the same frequency.

column121: During a routine IFR training flight and upon departure from 0S9 (Port Townsend; WA - Jefferson County Intl); we were following the published Obstacle Procedure like we have many numerous times in training and filing IFR. On this day; it was Intermittent IMC above 1500 and VFR under and notable that day was 20 knots plus winds aloft from the Northwest. Upon departure from Runway 09; take off and turning right to heading 090 and in the climb; Turbulence and Tailwind were increasing; and IMC Conditions now present in and out of Cloud Banks. When I went to intercept the 166 radial off the Penn Cove VOR turning North; what was now strong tail winds and light to moderate chop; quickly became a pronounced quartering tail wind with well defined moderate turbulence present. I became disoriented with the leans as the plane was not easily coming level. This created the beginning of an unusual attitude that was best corrected by recovering out of the right turn and remaining in said turn to get back on what was now the controllers vectors of 320 vs As Filed; I was able to recover from this and then began working to comply with ATC as they were inquiring why we were deviating course. I explained to the controller after the plane was stable and back on course that I had entered IMC in Turbulence and experienced spatial disorientation and had to recover. Once the plane neared 4;000 MSL; turbulence lightened; and I was able to proceed on course and as filed to Friday Harbor with no further issue. The rest of the day we experienced strong winds into Bellingham and then back into Port Angeles but nothing else of note. I am writing this to call out what I learned and what I also believe is a risk to myself and other pilots. I believe this Obstacle Departure Procedure places aircraft and pilots while under a potentially heavy workload in IMC in an area that is well known and proven for strong weather convergence with little to no information to fully assess conditions in such a micro climate. I believe there is a safety issue here that could be mediated by reducing the greater than 45 degrees requirements that exists today from 090 degrees bearing to intercepting the 166 Radial and a 346 Bearing. This ODP creates risk and added another link in the chain against me that day; with the strong quartering wind; and turbulence created an unusual attitude and deviation to course. The Instructor and I briefed on what went right and wrong there. We concluded that unusual attitude training cannot be emphasized enough as part of initial and continued training. We also agreed that the use of the Autopilot in heading mode would have helped avoid this situation as I was hand flying through the strong quartering and side wind/turbulence. I also called out that the aircraft has a leaning tendency to the right which I believe was not a key item; but could have added another link in the chain as it may have magnified the strong action the plane took to shift/turn to the right. I am having a Mechanic from a certified service center further evaluate to ensure the plane is in proper rigging beyond what was observed in the last annual inspection.

column121: I was conducting a visual approach to [Runway] XXR backed up by the RNAV Y XXR. I was the Pilot Flying and the Captain was the Pilot Monitoring. We had briefed all the threats and the approach per the AOM prior to the TOD and were planning flaps full for the landing configuration. We were being vectored onto a base leg to join the final visually. I was faster than I should have been on the base for the distance we were out (180 selected speed I think) and so I had to delay calling for the flaps. I think the last altitude we were given was 8;000 feet on the base before we reported the field in sight and were cleared for the visual. The approach had been activated and I went to managed speed. We then set a lower altitude just above the altitude for the next fix after the one just ahead of us on the approach so I could use vertical speed to start down and stay on the path since the approach was not quite captured. I had armed the approach and it annunciated FINAL APP as we were joining the final and the aircraft continued descending on the path. I was using the auto pilot for lateral and vertical NAV until established on final. We extended the gear prior to joining the final to help with slowing the aircraft to flap deployment speeds. The vector had put us in closer than I had anticipated and I had also started slowing later than I should have. The speed did not come back very quickly; possibly because of a tailwind shifting to a headwind as were turning final; so I had to disconnect the autopilot and arrest the descent to get the aircraft slowed for flap deployment and also to prevent an overspeed. Both the Captain and I noticed the RA was close to 1;000 [feet] as we deployed final flaps; and our speed was still well above approach speed; but we were VMC and our assessment was that we had been in final configuration prior to 1;000 AGL. We continued the approach and were stable at 500 [feet] so we landed out of the approach within the required criteria. We were at the gate when the ACARS printed a Self-Assessment Flight Report. We weren't surprised to see Y for speed and descent; but we were surprised to see a Y for flap change. We discussed it; and although we were unstable at 1;000 [feet]; we felt that we had been configured and thought the report generated a flap change Y at 0974 RA because the terrain rises to the north and the spot elevations are around 300-600 feet higher than the airport elevation near where we selected final configuration. Regardless; the final configuration selection was closer to 1;000 AGL than it should have been and we decided we would file an report just in case. Normally; I call for gear down and managed speed at 2;000 AGL so as to have plenty of time to reach final configuration prior to 1;000 AGL; but I missed that cue because I was in the yellow due to being tighter and faster than I had anticipated; and I didn't realize it because I was busy trying to get back in the green slowing and turning final and descending to stay on the path. This is also a case where my experience exceeded my performance due to being new to being back in the right seat and not flying much in September. I also didn't say anything about being in the yellow; and so I didn't get as much help as I could have used. I also failed to brief that we may need to be configured on base depending on where the base leg is and to say something if I don't ask for the gear down by 2;000 AGL. The other factor was conducting a visual approach to a high-altitude airport where AGL altitudes happen at much higher MSL altitudes than were are used to and neither I nor the Captain had been into ZZZ in a long time. I will more thoroughly brief visual approaches regarding the gates I want for configuration and speed changes that provide plenty of margin for a stabilized approach.

We continued trying to solve the problem; going up and down the cabin seeing if it was stronger one place versus the other; and seeing if it was dissipating. Then Operations called and said it was a tug nearby that was leaking fuel. With this information; we decided we would pushback and see if it goes away after we left the gate area. We did and checked with the flight attendant twice during taxi to get an update. The first time she said it was dissipating; and on the before takeoff check to the line; she said it was gone. During descent; in the mid-teens; we got a call saying the smell was back. It wasn't busy so we asked for a quicker route to the airport; which was granted and we landed uneventfully. I have no good answer as to why I didn't write this up. I have thought about it since I got off the phone with Maintenance in ZZZ1; and I cannot think of a reason why I decided to not write this up. Referring to [the] manual. Mechanical Irregularities; D. Reporting Mechanical Irregularities; it does not specifically state to write anything in the MX Log. It's difficult to find a single reason on how to avoid this event. Perhaps more training on specific events that require Mx write ups.

It makes it very difficult to manage speed and altitude. Also; when in instrument conditions it provides an opportunity to become spatially disoriented with the turns and the assigned descent profile. I was PM and upon takeoff the Master Caution light came on for engine driven hydraulic pump for system A. The light went out and continued. Abeam ZZZ2 the master caution came back on for engine driven hydraulic pump number 1 system A. I pulled out the QRH and ran the Hydraulic Pump Low Pressure checklist which had us turn the pump switch off. We asked for a descent to FL 200 and told them we were working on a problem with our left engine. Since the OIL FILTER BYPASS indication remained illuminated the next step per the QRH was to shut the engine down. As a result we had to land at the nearest suitable airport. We decided that ZZZ3 was the best choice since it was close the weather was good and we were both familiar with the airport. I continued with the checklist as [the Captain] flew the aircraft; [requested priority handling]; and requested the diversion. We were cleared direct to the airport and a descent to FL 70. Shutdown and descent proceeded normally with me accomplishing the shutdown and [the Captain] continuing to fly and maintain communication with ATC. We then moved to the one engine inoperative and landing checklist which included calculating single engine landing distance. Hydraulic system A at this point had gone down to 25 percent. We prepared for the possibility of losing total system A pressure and a manual gear extension but was not a factor as the gear operated normally; [the Captain] performed a visual approach and landing with a safe landing in ZZZ3. We then sent a message to dispatch via ACARS that we were safe on the ground.
column123: First Officer and I deadheaded to ZZZ to pick up a 737-800; which had been down for maintenance due to failure of the number 1 engine driven hydraulic pump failure and loss of system A fluid. Upon arrival we did our normal preflight and found no problems with the aircraft. The 3 Tech OPS employees who fixed the aircraft were embarked and we prepared to fly.Start up; taxi; and takeoff were normal. I was flying pilot and [First Officer] was monitoring. Early in the climb master caution light for the hydraulics came on and [First Officer] noted that the low pressure light for the engine driven hydraulic pump on engine 1 was on then quickly went out. Thinking it was anomaly with sensor and hydraulic quantity and pressure normal we continued. We were abeam ZZZ2 and the master caution for Hydraulics once again illuminated and [First Officer] noted the Low Pressure light for engine driven hydraulic pump on the left (number 1) engine was illuminated and stayed on. [First Officer] pulled out the QRH and proceeded to run the Hydraulic Pump Low Pressure checklist which lead to the pump being turned off. With quantity and pressure still good using the electric pump we decided to continue. We did get one of the Maintenance Techs to come to the flight deck and we showed and conversed with him about the issue. Nothing changed our thought process so we continued.Soon after passing ZZZZZ intersection and headed directly to ZZZZZ1 intersection; the number 1 Engine Oil Filter Bypass indication on the upper engine MFD illuminated. [First Officer] once again pulled out the QRH and we decided I would continue to fly and talk and he would run the checklist. We were at FL300 and decided to request a lower altitude as we knew we could not maintain level flight for long with one engine at idle. We asked for and received a descent to FL200 and told him we were working on a problem with our left engine. [First Officer] worked our way through the checklist resulting with the OIL FILTER BYPASS indication remaining illuminated. Per the checklist the next step was to shut down the engine and as a result of that we would need to land. We chose ZZZ3.[First Officer] continued the checklist as I [requested priority handling] and requested to divert. We were cleared direct the airport and a descent to 7;000. Shutdown and descent proceeded normally with [First Officer] completing the shutdown checklist. With the engine secured we moved on to the one engine inoperative and landing checklist to include the non-normal single engine landing distance. As we got closer to ZZZ3 the hydraulic issue took another turn. The quantity began to change first climbing to 106 percent and then slowly starting to decrease to mid-70 percent and then working its way down slowly till as we were coming down final it was in mid-20's. [First Officer] brought up the possibility of losing the 'A' system; so both of us were both prepared should that happen. Fortunately we did not have to run that checklist. Visual approach and landing was uneventful and normal. Landed and taxied to parking spot.We sent a message to Dispatch using ACARS that we were safe on the ground. The call I got after we had been on ground for 15 min. or so from the FODM gave me the feeling that it didn't go through but it was sent. It was confirmed by maintenance that in fact the 'A' system was depleted to about 25 percent and still leaking.

During the initial part of our takeoff roll I was the Pilot Flying and I set takeoff power for a FLEX takeoff. My First Officer confirmed takeoff power was set. It was then that I noticed and felt a slight surging; and a tendency of the aircraft nose turning left. I immediately corrected the aircraft nose back to centerline using my rudders. It was then one second later that the aircraft nose abruptly went back to approximately 30 degrees left of centerline. I immediately initiated a low-speed Rejected Takeoff while bringing the aircraft nose back to centerline. I made my PA to tell our passengers to remain seated. I also briefly informed our passengers and crew what happened and why I elected In the interest of safety to discontinue our takeoff. We taxied the aircraft back to our new gate with no other incidents. After shutting down both engines and securing our aircraft we noticed In the E/WDU lower ECAM display in the class II messages that both ENG 1 FADEC (Full Authority Digital Engine Control) and ENG 2 FADEC were displayed in the lower right of the display...something I have never seen in my +XX years of flying the A320. column123: We were cleared for takeoff; set the power per SOPs and began the takeoff roll. Immediately the aircraft veered to the left. I don't really have an explanation as to why the event occurred. The power was set correctly and all engine indications showed stable thrust. When the aircraft veered to the left a second time; I thought it a good decision to reject the takeoff. I thought the decision to reject was a good one.

column121: We were on a 6 mile final when tower cleared a Cirrus to land in front of us. When this happened separation from the traffic began to decrease; tower then cleared the Cirrus for a low approach. This seemed to cause confusion in the Cirrus cockpit. We continued until the spacing was unsafe; the Cirrus appeared to be on the runway. At around 400 ft. we executed a go around. As we began to climb at go around thrust flaps 8 the Cirrus began to climb as well giving us a TA and tower asked us to side step to the right. I began a turn to the right as the pilot monitoring watched the traffic below us carefully. While our focus was on avoiding the traffic we neglected to call 'positive rate' and raise the gear. This led to a delay is raising the flaps form 8 to 0 to clean up the airplane. Since we were already at pattern altitude we made the decision to leave the gear down since we were moments away from needing to lower it again. Towers poor spacing was the initial cause of the event. However our focus on keeping visual separation from the traffic led us to neglect some of our duties. Although traffic avoidance was and should be our top priority in that situation. We could have called a go around earlier when we saw that there could be a potential conflict. This would have given us more time and led to less task saturation.
column123: While on about a six mile final tower cleared a Cirrus to perform a short approach to a touch and go in front of us. As we continued the rate of closure was greater than tower anticipated and tower changed the Cirrus clearance to a low approach only. We continued our approach until about 400 ft. AGL. At this time it appeared the Cirrus did a touch and go and was on the runway for a long time. I felt that the separation margin was too small and called for a go around. We completed the first portion of the go around but then the Cirrus had started his upwind and was directly in our path. We prioritized maintaining visual separation with the Cirrus and complying with ATC separation instructions and failed to bring gear up and do a climb sequence until we were on a downwind and ran the after takeoff and then another decent check. After this we completed all check lists and had a safe landing. Poor aircraft separation by ATC. It sounded like there were two controllers in the tower; one being trained and the other a supervisor. Waiting too long to call for the go around. We waited until a go around caused too much going on and made us miss checklists and call outs due to high work load. Misinterpreted instructions by the Cirrus. When ATC changed the landing clearance for the Cirrus it was unclear if they understood what ATC actually wanted. I think the biggest thing that could be done to avoid similar situations is to call for a go around earlier when we saw there might be a conflict with spacing. There were cues earlier in the approach indicating a potential for loss of separation; but it was also possible for us to land had the Cirrus followed instructions in a timely manner. We should have erred on the conservative side to not put us in an overloaded task situation.

At this point he realized we did not have our proper reserve fuel. We had plenty of fuel in the tank but we would have not been in compliance with the new limitation in place set by the MEL.Possibly more awareness on the flight plan of low passenger flights in conjunction for this MEL or a separate fuel column on the release when the fuel is to be used as weight so the crew can consider the fuel as unusable.

column121: While being vectored by Approach Control on approach to Runway XXC at ZZZ; we were held at 4;000 ft. on the base leg with instructions to maintain 210 KIAS. We were subsequently given clearance for a Visual Approach to Runway XXC. The pilot flying from the left seat was the PIC (Pilot in Command). I was the SIC (Second in Command)/pilot monitoring from the right seat and acknowledged the visual approach clearance. The pilot flying made appropriate use of power levers; speed breaks; flaps; and landing gear to set up for a stabilized approach as he attempted to descend and intercept a normal glide path on final approach to the runway; while maintaining the requested 210 knot speed restriction. Once established on final; but still above a normal glide path; the PIC asked me to query ATC as to whether we could resume normal approach speed. The controller replied; 'When I clear you for a visual approach; the speed restriction is removed.' Noting that we were still above the PAPI and glidepath on final approach as a result of being kept at high altitude on the base leg and while descending through approximately 2;000 ft.; both crewmembers agreed that the aircraft could likely be configured to salvage a stabilized approach. However; as we descended through approximately 1;000 ft.; we realized that we had not been handed off to the control tower. As the approach control frequency was busy; I attempted to switch to the control tower frequency automatically; and was trying to reference the approach chart on the pilot's side display for the appropriate frequency; as there were three listed for the various runways. As a break in communications presented itself; I quickly queried approach control; 'Aircraft X to tower?' The controller responded that we should already be on the tower frequency; which he had not yet instructed us to do; and which was not the published frequency for Runway XXC. As the aircraft was now on short final; slightly above glide path; notwithstanding the long length of the runway; and the fact that we had not received landing clearance from the tower; the crew immediately agreed to go around; and smoothly initiated a go around procedure. I checked in with ZZZ Tower to advise we were going around. We were vectored by tower in a left hand traffic pattern at an appropriate altitude; without speed restriction; and were able to properly configure; execute a visual approach and land without incident.The crew could have solicited a lower altitude from Approach on the base leg and/or stated that we were unable to maintain the 210 KIAS speed restriction in order to establish ourselves on the final approach course at an appropriate altitude and speed for a stabilized approach. We could also have solicited a handoff from approach to tower frequency sooner. The decision to go around was prudently made and smoothly executed. However; we should have made the decision to do so at 1;000 feet AGL due to our position above the normal glide path (unstable approach) and not having been handed off to tower.
column123: While being vectored for a visual approach to XXC at ZZZ; approach had us turning a close in base at 4;000 ft. and 210 knots as assigned. Once we were on the final approach course; we were cleared for the visual approach. I knew that we were both too high and too fast; however I thought with the use of drag devices we could become stable prior to 1000 ft. per our FOM. I noticed that we were on a 2-3 mile final and had not been switched to the tower controller yet and asked the PNF (Pilot Not Flying) to query the approach controller. The approach controller stated that he had handed us over to the tower controller; neither of us in the cockpit heard that or acknowledged that instruction. The PNF was searching on the approach chart for a tower frequency and there was some confusion as he was trying the read the chart and which frequency he should be on. By the time I could have the PNF query the controller again; I realized that we were not going to be stable within the parameters of the FOM. I made the decision to go-around and informed the PNF to tell the approach controller we were executing a missed approach. The approach controller gave us instructions to fly runway heading to 3000 ft. and vectored us around for another visual approach which ended up in a stable; uneventful landing.I should have realized earlier on in the approach that we were vectored onto the final approach course too fast and too high. The PNF should have preloaded the tower frequency into the Radio Tune page. The decision to execute a go-around was correct but could have possibly been made sooner.

column123: On taxiing for takeoff; my instructor and I noticed several people seemingly wandering out toward the runway environment. We waved them to go back toward the hanger area. We held our position in the run-up area for runway XX; and another taxiing plane confirmed that the individual was still on [the] taxiway; and still on the runway side of the hold markings. A few moments later; the plane that had landed with the person on the runway finally came over the radio and stated the individual was his instructor; and he was just soloing. We informed him to please reach out to him and have him move off the runway. No response. During this time; the individual was beyond visual range; so we waited to take the runway until the FBO resolved the issue. column121: Pilot and a singe passenger were returning for a landing in VMC (winds light and variable); and cleared For landing by Tower. After what appeared to be a normal landing; on-centerline and during roll-out;(the plane was rolling below 30 kts); the aircraft unexpectedly began to pull to the right. The pilot attempted to correct using left rudder pressure and toe brake. The combination of left rudder pressure and left toe brake did not appear to exert sufficient braking authority or correct the turn. The aircraft seemed very slow to correct direction. The pilot continued with left rudder pressure and applied the handbrake. The plane immediately slowed; but rolled off the right side of the marked runway (and onto the apron) as the pilot was able to regain directional control. This was just past the first taxiway; where the underside of the right wing scraped the top edge of the taxiway sign. There did not appear to be any damage to the sign; but the bottom skin of the right wing was later found to be torn; in a line perpendicular to the leading edge; on the outboard side of the wing; about half-way to the from the front of the wing; and the skin tear exposed the bottom edge of the wing spar; which appeared to be nicked. Using the handbrake only from that point on; the pilot was able to return to the runway centerline and taxi the plane on the runway to the next taxiway and then navigate to parking with no further directional control problems. The incident was promptly reported and the plane was grounded for inspection and repair at visual inspection by a qualified A&P.It had been noted that on one prior flight that the plane had unexpectedly pulled to the right; but that the problem had been evaluated and resolved. On pre-flight taxi and takeoff during the flight on which the incident occurred; the plane did not appear to be pulling excessively to the right; so the pilot believed that the earlier squawk had been resolved; and the pilot decided to conduct the flight as planned. The pilot was well-rested; in good health; and alert during the flight. A potential distractor was that the oil access door on the cowling popped open on climb-out after takeoff (this resulted in the decision to return to land and correct the issue before continuing the flight). It is possible that this issue may have distracted the pilot. Also; the pilot may not have reacted quickly enough when the plane began pulling to the right on roll-out; and may not have transitioned quickly enough from applying the toe brake (which did not appear to be effective)to using the handbrake (which applied effective braking on both mains). Finally; as a final possible preventive action; the pilot might have elected to touch-down on the left side of the wide runway; anticipating the possibility of the plane pulling to the right.

My impression is that BWI leadership; to the highest leadership levels; does not care to address or fix this ongoing problem. We need to collectively protect our engines from unnecessary damage resulting from FOD. On the scanner I changed the location to pit 4 so that the scanner would accept the close out. We pushed out the plane and on the way back to the gate the supervisor approached and asked about the DG being moved to pit 4 and I told her that I did that so the flight would close out on the scanner. She said that wasn't acceptable and that the plane would have to come back and be loaded correctly. She also told me to contact Load Planning and speak with them. Load Planning told me that they would reopen the flight. When the plane came back [we] moved bags and secured DG in pit 5. I told the supervisor that it was corrected and she left. We pushed the plane out and the scanner still would not let me close out the flight. I tried calling Load Planning again several times for advice but they weren't answering. Now that the flight was on taxiway and the DG was secure I thought that it was most important to close out the flight so on the scanner I moved the DG to pit 4 so it would close. column121: Cleared for visual approach and cleared to land on RWYXXL. [Commercial flight] canceled their take off clearance so [ZZZ] Tower told us to continue the visual approach with a canceled landing clearance. We were 7.5 miles out direct to the Final Approach Fix in LNAV (Lateral Navigation) and the armed glideslope had captured at about 3;000 MSL providing a constant descent. We were Flaps 5 at 180 kts. To create spacing I called for gear down and flaps 20 and rolled the speed back above 20 maneuvering speed. The plane began to slow and pitch down with flap extension. I called for flaps 25 when the gear showed 3 green and the EICAS (Engine Indication And Crew Alerting System) showed 'Autopilot' indicating it was still working but in a degraded mode. I then saw GS FMA (Glideslope Flight Mode Annunciator) now had a line thru it. At this point I disconnected the autopilot and leveled off visually. The altitude was about 1400 MSL; 1000 AGL. I told the Pilot Monitoring I was going to maintain 1000 AGL until established. Right after I leveled off the [ZZZ] Tower announced low altitude alert. During the debrief the Pilot Monitoring said he saw the glideslope go full scale below us and then shoot up to full scale above us near the autopilot disconnect. I continued to maneuver visually to the runway centerline at 1;000 ft. Once established we cycled the Flight Directors and the glideslope centered back to where we were on the approach. Continued visually and landed. Wrote up the discrepancy in the logbook.  Fatigue didn't cause it; but it may have slowed my processing of everything that was happening kind of at the same time.  Don't allow the glideslope to capture early. Choose another vertical mode until on or very close to the LOC (Localizer).
column123: We were cleared for the visual to [Runway] XXL and subsequently cleared to land approximately 10SW of the airport. We were level at 3000 when approach was armed and glideslope captured. Aircraft began descending on glideslope. ATC canceled our landing clearance and cleared a [Commercial flight] for takeoff on [Runway] XXL. In order to slow and create space the Pilot Flying called for gear and flaps 20. After we received an AUTOPILOT EICAS and the GS FMA (Glide Slope Flight Mode Annunciator) had an amber line through it. The Captain disconnected the autopilot and autothrottles and leveled the aircraft. We were approximately 1400 MSL (1000AFE). About this time [ZZZ] Tower called a low altitude alert. Contributing factors for this event would be the initial distraction resulting from the failure of ACARS. This lack of currency/proficiency was briefed as the threat in the brief for both the takeoff as well as the arrival. If task saturation begins to set in; notify the other pilot and let them assist you with reducing your saturation level. Always clearly understand where you are during any aspect of a flight. column121: I had just leveled off at 16;000 [feet] when ATC asked for what my assigned altitude was. I responded 16;000 [feet] [feet] and they informed me that I was showing 17;500 [feet]. I verified that I was showing 16;000 [feet] on my altimeter and then looked at my co-pilot altimeter and realized it was showing 17;600 [feet] and climbing. I communicated this discrepancy to ATC and began to troubleshoot while trying to maintain 16;000 [feet] on my altimeter until I had verified where the discrepancy lay. ATC had me turn off the mode C part of my transponder at this time. My first reaction was to run the icing encounter in flight do list in case it was an issue with icing. I then consulted the QRH (Quick Reference Handbook) and ran the static instrument malfunction do list. This 16;000 [feet] helped by raising my altimeter to approximately 16;700 [feet]. ATC then gave me a descent to 11;000 [feet]. At this time I looked at my airspeed indicator and noticed that while the captain speed was showing 160 knots the co-pilot airspeed was showing approximately 230 knots. I reduced power and referenced the co-pilot airspeed indicator for my speed in the descent. I leveled out at 11;000 [feet] on the 17;600 [feet]pilot altimeter and indicating 12;000 [feet] on the co-pilot altimeter. I requested to turn the mode C on my transponder back on and asked ATC for a readout on my altitude. They advised I was showing 12;000 [feet]. I then advised I was continuing my descent to 11;000 [feet] based off of my co-pilot altimeter. I subsequently flew the aircraft based on the co-pilot instruments. While descending I noticed that the airspeed and altitude on the pilot side was more closely matching to the co-pilot side as I got lower. I was able to visually identify the airport of destination and used the PAPI (Precision Approach Path Indicator) to verify my glide slope to the airport. Upon landing my speeds were within approximately 5 knots of each other and the altimeter was less than 200 foot difference. After shutdown the altimeters are less than 30 feet off of each other.I became aware of the event as I was leveling off at what I thought was 16;000 [feet] ft when ATC queried what my assigned altitude was. I then started to work the problem and work to rectify the instrument mismatch.There was a mismatch between the pilot static systems of my aircraft.I advised ATC that I was having an instrument mismatch and began working the problem to find a solution. I initially thought it might be an icing issue so I run the icing in flight do list. When that failed to resolve the issue I went to the QRH and ran the Static source malfunction do list. When that partially solved the issue I asked ATC to verify altitudes to work to determine what instruments were reading the most accurate information so I could plan and execute a plan of action as safely as possible. Not so much how to keep this from happening again but additional steps I could have taken. Once it became obvious to me that I was having an instrument mismatch and potential malfunction I should have declared an emergency. ATC was extremely helpful and assisted me completely but this could have been much more dangerous if the weather had been worse. I should also have requested the ILS (Instrument Landing System)to the opposite direction runway to have had that as a reference to the landing and terrain clearance instead of just the PAPI. I initially opted not to do this because it would have put me back in the clouds while getting vectored out for it.

column121: A friend who has a multi engine and instrument rating was interested in possibly buying my Cessna 310 so we flew to breakfast in IMC with me in the left seat acting as PIC. I suggested that on our return; he sit in the left seat and we fly to ZZZ where they had longer runways than our home field and he could practice some landings. While he was rated; I was still PIC from the right seat as he was not multi engine current and I was a multi engine CFI.We flew down and executed an RNAV/GPS (Area Navigation) approach to Runway XX in VMC conditions. I said that our first landing exercise would be to take the plane almost down to the runway and just fly a foot or so off of the deck to help visualize the sight picture; before cutting the throttles and landing. We'd then taxi back for more pattern work.The approach was very successful and everything went well until about 50 feet when he started to flare. I said we needed to keep coming down; we were nowhere near the altitude we needed to be at to begin the flare; but he leveled off; seeming to feel for the runway from that point. We quickly reached the midpoint of the runway and I began thinking that a go around would be necessary but I let him continue a bit further. Shortly thereafter I called for a go around but he cut the power; raised the nose; and landed firmly; about 2/3 of the way down the runway. I did not think we had room to stop on the remaining runway and at 80 knots we were close to flying speed. He told me to take over and I applied full power. At the end of the runway we still were slower than I would want to be but I raised the nose and we were airborne in ground effect. The plane was very slow to accelerate or climb and I felt my friend pulling back on the yoke. I pushed forward not wanting to stall or leave ground effect. At this point I realized that our gear was still down and that we had landing flaps. I knew that if I retracted landing flaps we had a very strong potential to sink into the ground so faced with that option I left the flaps down. I was not sure of the drag effect from gear retraction so I left it down as well. Again I felt him pulling back on the wheel while I yelled 'stop pulling' and pushed forward.Soon there was a row of trees in the windshield and I gathered we had gotten all of the speed we could for the time being and I pulled back on the yoke. The tower controller had seen what was going on and asked us if we were ok; did we need assistance; and did we see the trees. He also asked if we would be avoiding the trees. These calls were a distraction and I did not answer as my first priority was to fly the aircraft.We climbed out; retracting the gear and flaps. The controller asked if we wanted him to cancel IFR (Instrument Flight Rules) and for us to resume our pattern work. Shaken; I was not interested in pattern work and I asked him to cancel IFR and we would leave the area. Since he had questioned if we had hit the trees I decided to fly about 5 miles to an airport where I have maintenance done to have the plane inspected. Apparently we had made contact with the very top of the tree line as evidenced by some leaves on the nose gear. The mechanic came out to inspect the plane and could find no damage at all after inspecting the gear; flaps; wings; fuselage; and general condition.In retrospect; I had put my friend in a bad position. Even though he had watched me land many times; and had landed himself in the past; I should have demonstrated the first landing. I know better than to land outside the touchdown zone and yet we did. At the midpoint of the runway with limited runway ahead of us; I should have had an aggressive transfer of control and taken the plane around myself. If I had done that I have no doubt I would have raised the gear and flaps allowing a successful climb out; but in the uncertain transfer of control with the pilot monitoring suddenly and unexpectedly becoming the pilot flying; the sequence of a successful go around were lost.I can't help but think that I put the pilot flying into a bad position by not doing the go around sooner and not having the plane in proper climb configuration was a bad error. I have replayed this many times and reminded myself that in this situation; even though you are not the flying pilot; you have to stay on top of things mentally and be prepared to take over at any point.The better decision after the touch down would have been to get out of the mental go around mind set and just kept it on the ground. A couple of blown tires and a plane in the overrun would have been nothing compared to the threats of staggering into the air in a bad configuration with trees ahead.

column121: While conducting a Flight Review; my client pilot was practicing a power-off 180-degree approach to landing (simulated emergency) when we encountered wind shear. The winds were approximately 13 gusting 18 knots from 210 and the aircraft was on a modified left base while angling toward Runway XX at ZZZ. The descent path was normal for a glide to the beginning of the runway and airspeed was approximately 85 KT. At about 1;000 feet from the runway and 300 feet AGL; the pilot lowered the landing gear while passing into the lee of a dense woodlot that stands about 600 feet south and west of the extended runway centerline; and there we experienced a sudden and dramatic loss of airspeed; down to approximately 65 knots. (Of course; some loss of airspeed was expected as the gear deployed.) I called for power as the aircraft began to pitch down and descend. (The Pilot Flying was guarding the throttle.) I continued to shout for more power over the next 2-3 seconds as the aircraft descended to perhaps 15 feet AGL; still 500 feet short of the runway.I took control of the airplane as the pilot brought in full power. We were now grazing the tops of the corn in the field below us and I could see a 15' fence coming up quickly. I felt we had very little angle of attack available - perhaps just enough to climb 10' to clear the fence. I increased elevator as much as I dared; then lowered the nose again once past the fence. Because of our low airspeed and high angle of attack; though the propeller cleared the fence; the top of a fence post contacted and tore the skin of the airplane's belly just aft of the gear legs. As airspeed slowly recovered; I climbed to perhaps 20 feet AGL; then reduced power as we reached the runway and made a normal landing. I have been flying for more than XX years and I have never experienced such a dramatic loss of airspeed. My corrective action to prevent a similar crisis will include the following.1. I will not use the actual beginning of runways to practice power-off landings; but instead have clients treat the touch down zone (1;000 feet down the runway) as their landing target.2. I will be more prepared to push; move; or overpower client pilots if they do not immediately respond to verbal instructions. 3. I will be more mindful of the potential for wind shear; especially when operating downwind of significant obstacles (the wood lot; in this case) on windy days.

It just suddenly wouldn't transmit.  I checked my headset.  Then I switched the plug into the second set of holes.  I tried using the foot pedal instead of my button.  I tried switching to the backup transmitters.  I tried guard frequency.  The Supervisor tried to use the PET [radio].  I switched to the override orange box and could reach 2 or 3 of them; but then only about 1 of the 5 tries would go through and the responses were broken; unreadable or very static-y.  We tried to put everyone on our backup 133.575; but it had the same issues.  We could hear pilots; but were unable to transmit anything back.  I told Tower to keep everyone on their frequency they had; and everyone was point out approved.  We frantically kept trying to reach the aircraft sitting on my frequency as they began to go through final and some began to get dangerously close to MVAs.  Finally; the combination of everything and the frequency seemed to snap back to working.In the next hour; we had probably 25% of the transmissions to aircraft not be received.  At many altitudes in areas that would typically work.  I used aircraft I could reach to relay to the ones I couldn't.  It was a nightmare. I may have had separation losses.  I think I kept altitude separation; but it was too busy and chaotic for myself or the Supervisor to work it and see. The VFR photo guy just decided on his own to head east; directly across the two finals in front of aircraft on [an] approach; without me telling him to; or without me being able to issue any traffic to anyone.  One of the heavies I had on a right base to RWY 18 at 040 took it upon himself just to turn in to the airport.  He ended up overflying at 040 before finally switching himself to tower frequency to enter their frequency.  This was the 2nd scariest thing I've ever had while working.  Not okay. The frequency transmitter issues need to be identified and fixed.  Just because they start working again; is not good enough.  We also need a real backup that we can use that transmits from a different source.  When our backup seems to go out at the exact same time; it is useless.  Our Omaha and Offutt frequency options are not in range for low Lincoln sector aircraft.For the last 2-3 weeks; something is wrong with the transmitting capabilities of our Lincoln sector frequencies.  Our primary 124.0 frequency will all of a sudden just not go out to the pilots.  We try switching to main/stand-by and it makes no difference.  We switch and do all the coordination with other facilities to use our backup frequency; 133.575; but then it has the same issue.  Sometimes we can use the Orange Voice Backup Override boxes; but it is also intermittent and when it goes out is maybe 2 by 5 at best with a lot of static and crackling.  If we try to work them in by leaving them on Omaha and/or Offutt frequencies; 120.1 or 124.95; the range isn't good enough to reach low aircraft on the south/west side of Lincoln and we lose contact that way completely. This is an urgent; serious issue.  When we called it into MOCC (Mid-States Operations Control Center) a week or two ago; the tech responded to us that 'it was probably due to the storm passing through' even though there was only light (level 1 and 2 precipitation).  When it came back online they just called it back in service without fixing anything or identifying the problem.  Yesterday it occurred while I had around a dozen aircraft on frequency.  The sudden loss of communications nearly caused major incidents and could have been catastrophic.  Luckily I had most of them altitude separated as an additional precaution at the time; but we still had a near MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude) bust as a result and may have lost separation in the chaos.  The Supervisor tried to use the PET; but our range doesn't reach Lincoln on them; and when it did intermittently go through; only stepped on my transmissions I was making through the override box and made it worse.

However; the erroneous indications returned during the second flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2. After our conclusion; we returned the aircraft to normal flight; transferred the controls; and landed without further incident. Possible transponder malfunction. We wrote up the aircraft and discussed the event in great detail with Maintenance.

column121: We departed ZZZ without the flight release PIC signature.  The following summary is not offered as an excuse for this or to lessen the mistake that was made only to advise what happened and most importantly prevent it from happening again.  The weather for this flight was unusually good; only some forecast light chop at FL380 to FL410 for the first 200 miles of flight.  The FO (First Officer) and I spoke about this and decided to stop our climb at FL370 till past threat.  As we approached the gate I signed the release I thought; evidently the release did not go thru as expected.  The gate area was only partially full as our load was only 50 passengers. The aircraft was hot as the temperature was 106 degrees F and externally air was hooked to the aircraft. We dealt with that and unhooked the external air and started the APU to cool the aircraft.  During this time the FAs (Flight Attendants) boarded the aircraft and were briefed by me.  I was notified shortly after taken seat and starting the downloads to my EFB (Electronic Flight Bag) that the lights would not come on in the main cabin so we called Maintenance and they arrived quickly to fix the issue;  Quick fix and we continued; made the mask PA and we pushed early.  As we were pushing the FO noticed that the runway had changed to a west flow so runway change number 1; we completed the starting engines flows and set the parking brake and did not move.  We then got clearance to taxi and advise to set up for a south runway departure; change 2; we held position and as we completed this change we were advised we could depart on the north runway if we would be ready after the short taxi to Runway XX.  I called the FAs and asked if they would be ready for a short taxi; the response was yes. I accepted the short taxi; change 3.  We had set up for Runway XR before push; then after push Runway change XX; runway XYR and back to runway XX. Three runway changes after push along with checking and changing the route of flight as each runway has a different departure procedures and resetting the MCP 3 times.  Both the FO and myself have been on this aircraft for many years and both of us felt like we were in the green and had trapped all of the issues that had happened.  We never got an ACARS message saying the flight release had not been signed and during the distractions the final trap was missed as we briefed the takeoff data based on what we expected to happen.  The lesson which I learned on this flight is even when you feel like you're in the green; stop and run through your flows. This was the first time I ever took the runway without physically touching the closeout and it will be my last!  We were notified enroute that the release was not signed by Dispatch; signed release via ACARS and continued uneventfully to destination.  When you feel like your in the green; stop and run all the traps one final time before taking runway.

As we descended we checked for ice and there was still some on the right wing so I left the REF speeds to INCR. As we were approaching 3;000 ft we were fully configured and about 5 to 10 kts above open bug; which was about 115 to 120. The red line approached but we never exceeded it. When we got the stick shaker the FO (First Officer); who was pilot flying; just lowered the nose a bit to correct. It then stopped and we continued on with the approach and safe landing. column123: Operating Aircraft X from ZZZ1 to ZZZ as we began our approach and passed through 10;000 ft. We completed the approach checklist and checked wings for icing. I identified my wing still had icing present so we continued our decent with the ref speeds increased. As we continued our decent we went through our configuration checks and began slowing down. As we continued our decent a few moments later I checked my wing again and identified the icing was no longer present. Before we went through 1000 ft. my speed was set between solid bug and open bug in preparation for the approach; I noticed that the Vso speed was indicating near the open bug speed. I was maintaining approximately 5 knots above the open bug speed when I got a momentary stick shaker; I immediately increased pitch and announced 'stick shaker'. A quick scan to the ED (engine display) and I identified that the ref speeds were still increased and told the Captain; at that time he turned it off. We continued the remainder of the approach without incident. I am filing this report after being notified by Manager of Flight Safety that he recommended an ASAP should be filed. Lesson learned for me as a FO (First Officer) is that I should have verified that the ref speed switch was turned off after verifying that the icing was no longer present. And then again when I noticed the Vso speed was higher than I anticipated; I should have cued in that something wasn't set properly.

column123: We were descending on the ZZZZZ4 arrival. Approaching the ZZZZZ fix we were asked to slow to 210 on the speed early. ZZZZZ shows a 210 speed at 9;000 feet. We realized that I never reengaged VNAV after inserting the new 210 speed in the FMS computer thus the autopilot continued to descend toward the 6;000 foot altitude on the arrival. The rest of the arrival and approach were normal.Our wakeup call was at XA:30 in the morning body clock time. We had been flying for approximately X hours 45 minutes with each of us having a sleep break.This was my second pilot flying trip in over 7 months. This was the Captain's first flying trip in 7 months.Going to flight level change while still on a descend via arrival was a mistake on my part. column121: After passing waypoint JILNA on the RNP Z RWY 30L a scratch pad message showed; check altitude constraint. Cross checking the altitude the airplane was at; it was descending through 6800-6900 MSL and the altitude restriction is at 7000. JILNA was a melded waypoint on our flight plan off of the BRIXX 2 RNAV Arrival; that had been melded once we were cleared for the approach. Breakdown in cross check during higher demand phase of flight. While also forgetting about pilot bulletin XXXXX-X. Which pertains to this situation. Section XX of the bulletin states: VNAV not complying with altitude constraint during approach. When the last waypoint of a STAR procedure is common to the first waypoint of the instrument approach procedure; the FMS may automatically meld the waypoints. The altitude constraints contained in both procedures for that particular waypoint is expected to be melded as well. In other scenarios; the last STAR waypoint contains a 'fly vectors to intercept' leg. This waypoint can also be the first one for the approach procedure and the pilot may manually delete the 'fly vectors' or copy the approach waypoint of the same waypoint on the STAR; which will also meld both waypoints.Embraer has received reports of the airplane not complying with the published altitude constraints during transition from STAR to instrument approach procedure. Investigations have revealed that an altitude violation may occur when two common waypoints are melded; either automatically by the FMS or manually by the pilot; where the last waypoint of the STAR and the first waypoint of the approach procedure has the same name; but different altitude constraints. As a consequence; the FMS constructed vertical flight path may not respect the altitude constraint; despite the altitude constraint indications of the FMS FLT PLAN page; VSD (Vertical Situation Display) and PFD (Primary Flight Display) are correctly displayed. The VNAV guidance may result in a constructed flight path above or below the published constraint. To prevent the violation of an altitude constraint; after a common waypoint is melded automatically by the FMS or manually by the pilot; perform as follows; Delete the altitude constraint at the melded waypoint; manually re-insert the altitude constraint in the FMS.

column121: My student and I were performing TOLs [Take Off and Landings] at Coolidge on the morning of Month; date; when the pattern was relatively light. At that time; there were two other aircraft in the pattern executing touch and goes for Runway 23. At some point; Aircraft Y flew in on what may have been the GPS approach. I am not sure Aircraft Y made any calls on his way in. There were a few planes lining up on that approach and their call may have been lost with the others. I was watching my ADS-B and noticed this aircraft had gone 'missed' on 23 and began a 45 degree turn toward downwind. My initial thought was that they were probably offsetting. However; their course did not change. This was extremely unsettling because we were on downwind. By the time I put this all together (a few seconds); I realized that I could not get a visual fix on the aircraft. Why? Because they were on a direct collision course with us as they climbed up through my student's download leg (which was perfect; according to her). I noticed Aircraft X's altitude; which I believe was -200 from us; looked out again and saw them coming right at us. 'My controls'; power out and dive. I dropped us 400ft out of our pattern altitude. I believe this was the safest thing to do. I do not think I would have been able to safely out climb them and it was clear that they were oblivious to our presence. The aircraft passed over us at 2600 (right where we would have been). I cannot place myself in the mindset of the pilot; but what would possess a pilot or an instructor to fly into an established downwind pattern going the wrong way?ADS-B may have played a direct role in preventing a potentially fatal accident. Without ADS-B; the probability of making visual contact with Aircraft Y when the aircraft was angled at us and climbing was low. Knowing this makes me cringe a little when I think about the number of aircraft out there without this technology installed. Collision avoidance is not just about the skill level of the 'other guy'. There needs to be a moment of self reflection about what we do out there. Understanding that fact has given me pause about going back to P08 until I am able to justify the risks of being in an airspace with consistently unpredictable traffic. I am currently not able to convince myself that the risks are worth it. I can safely practice TOLs at Gateway; Chandler; or even (if one is cautious) Eloy. After about two more landings; my student and I decided to leave the pattern as more planes were joining from opposite directions on approaches. We came home to ZZZ where it was a busy; but safe environment. If I eventually decide to go back to that zoo for VFR flying I will do so with extra vigilance.

At the time of the incident; conditions were VFR - visibility of approximately 10 SM or greater with no cloud cover.The Aircraft X was returning to the Oceanside Municipal Airport; OKB; from ZZZ. Aircraft X received VFR flight following from SoCal Approach; flight following was canceled as Aircraft X crossed the Oceanside VORTAC (OCN) at 3000 ft MSL. SoCal Approach requested that Aircraft X remain at or above 3000 ft MSL until OCN to remain clear of traffic in the hold at OCN. After crossing OCN at 3000 ft MSL; Aircraft X switched to the OKB CTAF frequency and began a final descent into OKB tracking the VOR-A approach. At this time; Aircraft X also announced on the OKB CTAF that it was inbound on the VOR-A approach. Aircraft X initiated the approach at 3000 ft MSL; 500 ft higher than the published altitude at the IAF (OCN) to remain clear of the traffic in the hold. For the approach; the sole manipulator of the controls was an instrument rated commercial pilot; the safety pilot was a commercial pilot and flight instructor acting as PIC.Aircraft X terminated the approach approximately 2 nm from OKB at an altitude of approximately 2000 ft MSL and airspeed of approximately 95 kts; at which point it began a gradual descending right turn to join the upwind leg for RWY 25 to sequence into the traffic pattern for landing due to other aircraft in the pattern on downwind. At this time; the safety pilot took over as sole manipulator of the controls to fly the final approach and landing.At 1600 ft MSL and while still in a gradual descending right turn to join the upwind leg for RWY 25; Aircraft X took immediate evasive action by initiating a steep left turn to avoid a midair collision with the Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y was overtaking Aircraft X in a climbing right turn after departing RWY 25 at OKB and crossed from left to right underneath Aircraft X. Until the time at which Aircraft X took evasive action; neither pilot in Aircraft X had visual contact with Aircraft Y; nor did the pilots of Aircraft X hear any radio calls from Aircraft Y on the OKB CTAF. Aircraft Y took no evasive action to prevent a midair collision. The estimated miss distance was less than 200 ft vertically and less than 300 ft horizontally. The incident occurred approximately 1.5 NM west of the departure end of RWY 25 at OKB. The location of the incident does not coincide with the standard traffic pattern for departures from OKB; and Aircraft Y did not report it was initiating a crosswind turn to the right from runway heading. column121: I was conducting a ferry flight with another pilot on Aircraft X. The other pilot came with me in order to begin familiarizing himself with the airplane and its systems; particularly with the G1000 system as he had no previous experience operating a glass cockpit. While enroute I was providing some instruction [of] the various aspects of the G1000; including the radio. We were operating on an IFR flight plan and maintaining assigned altitude; but at one point I realized that a significant amount of time had elapsed since I had heard from ATC. I discovered that at some point; the radio volume had been turned down. I quickly turned up the radio and reestablished radio contact. The Controller informed me that he had been trying to get a hold of me and that he had to re-route some traffic in a MOA that I had flown through. He didn't tell me whether this resulted in an actual loss of separation; but either way I ended up flying through an active MOA while on an IFR flight plan and did not hear any instructions to descend below it. While retrieving my briefing; I saw that the MOA along in my route was active beginning at 8;000 feet. I filed for 11;000 expecting the Controller to descend me below it if necessary. Obviously; that did not happen in the NORDO situation.A lot factors played into this situation. First; I recently conducted several flights through very quiet airspace (especially after COVID) during which I would go 30 minutes or more before hearing anyone talk on the radio; whether to me or someone else. This made the silence a bit more normalized.Second; I was expecting ATC to keep me out of any airspace I needed to avoid. During previous flights; I would normally confirm with ATC that any restricted areas along my route were cold before flying through them; even while IFR. In this situation; I think I became overly reliant on ATC to keep up my situational awareness while instructing. I also didn't give as much consideration to the MOA as I could have since flying through an active one is more common than other types of special use airspace.Third; simply dealing with the student/pilot added to my workload. Had I not been working with the student; this probably would not have happened. I honestly can't remember now who turned down the radio; but either way; the situation would not have happened if training wasn't part of the mission on this flight.Of course; this simply comes down to a situational awareness issue. While I'm not a brand new instructor; I recognize that I always need to continue practicing and refining the art of teaching while dealing with the challenges of operating an aircraft. I constantly teach my students to aviate; navigate; and then communicate. In this case; I simply let the instructing take away from those priorities. Still; here are some other practical steps to take to prevent this in the future: Avoiding any special use airspace when flying with students unless the lesson specifically involves dealing with such airspace. While the primary purpose of this flight was not training; having the pilot/student on board was the primary factor contributing to the incident. While it may not have prevented the NORDO situation; everything could have been made less serious by simply filing around or below the MOA.Prior to this flight; we had covered some ground material concerning the G1000 and Aircraft X; but we never spent any time in the airplane on the ground. When I train students on the G1000; I normally spend at least an hour going over the system while the aircraft is on the ground powered by a GPU. We didn't do that in this situation because the primary mission was ferrying; not training. In the future though; I'll familiarize the student as much as possible with the system on the ground in all situations before flying.

column123: I was flying as the LCA and pilot monitoring.  While conducting new Captain IOE on Aircraft X; we were setting up for an autoland on Runway XXL in ZZZ.  The arrival and approach were briefed to include known and anticipated threats.  We were vectored around for the approach and cleared for the ILS XXL.  The approach mode was armed and the second autopilot engaged.  Just prior to intercepting the glideslope; the gear was lowered and flaps 5 was selected.  We were in VMC conditions with the runway in sight.  The touchdown zone altitude was set as we continued the approach.  The 1;000 feet call and 500 feet call were made by me acting as pilot monitoring.  The response to 'set missed approach altitude cleared to land' and 'flare armed stable' were made respectively by the IOE student.  After 500 feet we received GPWS alerts for 'Terrain' and as we approached the runway threshold; a 'Pull Up' warning was [received].  After observing that we were in normal landing position; I made the ill advised call to continue.  As the autopilot began to enter the flare we realized we were still at flaps 5 and not configured to land.  I immediately called for a Go-Around and the Go-Around procedure was executed.  We advised ATC and were vectored around for a second approach for [Runway] XXR.  We executed the approach and landed without further incident.  Upon arriving at the gate; we debriefed our errors as well as the breakdown in CRM/TEM monitor crosscheck and SOP.  We also debriefed our failure to adhere to the GPWS warning.  We concluded that the combination of limited currency; outside current distractions (COVID; displacements;) and a long duty day may have created a moment where we completely lost focus.  The decision to go-around saved our poor performance from becoming an accident.

column121: Momentary loss of control during takeoff. ORD ATIS indicated winds at 180/11 for our Runway 28R (full length) takeoff. Just prior to our takeoff ATC had cleared Aircraft Y to cross our runway and hold short of 28C; somewhere near mid-runway; if I recall correctly. While initial takeoff roll was uneventful; we had a sudden and aggressive yaw to the left which had me (as pilot flying) suspect we had an engine failure; but there was no loss of thrust. Aircraft responded well to corrective rudder inputs; but was destabilized by the event. Within second of the event we strongly suspected that the engine thrust of the freighter was causal to our sudden yaw to the left. Advised ATC upon being asked to switch to Departure frequency that we had concern over this event; but did not advise we would be submitting a report. However; given the possibility of far more negative consequences had the event occurred at a lower airspeed (such as if we had had an intersection departure); I now feel that a report is warranted to investigate the specific details of this event; and prevent a future loss of control on takeoff event which could lead to a hull loss and/or fatalities. Hold all heavy and larger aircraft facing runway so as to prevent engine thrust impact on landing and departing aircraft.

column121: The aircraft's left fuel indicator was MEL'd and was blank. Following the MEL procedure; the Captain spoke with the Maintenance crew about the fuel numbers. Before our arrival; Maintenance accomplished the fuel stick procedure to verify the amount of fuel in each wing and total fuel to upload. We where told each side was balanced and the total fuel load was 37;500 lbs. Maintenance provided us with the chart they used to load the fuel and their explanation in writing. Everything they showed us looked correct. However; in flight we began to wonder about the accuracy as the Captain examined the papers he gave us and the current readout on the remaining right indicator. The fuel flow was matched and consistent between both engines the entire flight. The calculated number in the FMC was off from the right side indicator. There is no other way to tell if we had an imbalance to my knowledge; that's why the starting fuel load is critical to have balanced. As we approached ZZZ the Captain disconnected the A/P to feel for an imbalance. The aircraft was trimmed perfectly and neither side felt heavy. The Captain landed the aircraft normally. On the post flight checks Maintenance was outside sticking the tanks. The Captain asked him what the numbers were and he said 11;000 lbs of fuel remained in the left tank; 6;000 lbs in the right and 600 pounds in the center. The Captain couldn't believe there seemed to be an imbalance of 5;000 lbs. I'm not sure that was true because the aircraft seemed to fly wings level in flight. When we left I never got the chance to see if Maintenance had incorrectly calculated those numbers of if there actually was an imbalance.

column121: During a flight to maintain currency an upset event occurred.  Aircraft X took off from ZZZ on a VFR flight with flight following.  After takeoff and communication hand off from ZZZ Tower to Departure; Aircraft X was instructed by ATC to maintain runway heading due to traffic.  After watching the traffic pass on the moving map display and no other traffic in the immediate area; asked ATC for permission to proceed on course.  ATC apologized for the delay and cleared Aircraft X to proceed on course.  Leveling off at 5;500 feet MSL and after visually and electronically checking for traffic; setup for slow flight and approach to stall practice.  Retarded throttle; airspeed was already below 165 knots so landing gear was extended; verified all gear was down and locked.  Held altitude while speed bleed off; applying flaps incrementally until fully extended.  Began stabilized slow flight; adjusting throttle and pitch as necessary to maintain 5;500 feet.  Winds at 5;500 MSL were 18 knots and there was some light turbulence.  After 1-2 minutes of steady slow flight the airspeed indicator dropped quickly even though there were no rapid throttle or control surface adjustments.  The stall horn began sounding continuously and the aircraft experienced very slight buffeting at which point full throttle and downward pitch were applied simultaneously and in the same instant the right wing dropped extremely rapidly as if the aircraft had been commanded into a snap roll.  The roll continued even as left aileron and left rudder were applied with no effect and in less than 2 seconds the aircraft was inverted.  At this point the nose dropped and the aircraft entered a right-hand spiral dive.  The throttle was immediately retarded and standard recovery efforts begun.  Attempts to level the wings were complicated by the g-forces as the pilot struggle to remain upright.  At least 5-7 right hand turns occurred in spite of left aileron input.  At approximately 500-700 feet AGL; control was reestablished and the aircraft returned to zero roll.  A climb was initiated and as the airspeed dropped the pilot remembered the aircraft was still in full landing configuration with the throttle at idle.  Power was added; flaps retracted one notch and the landing gear was retracted.  Continued retracting flaps one notch at a time as speed and altitude increased.After returning to a safer altitude; all aircraft controls were checked and seemed to be normal with no apparent explanation for the un-commanded roll.  Only after landing and examining the aircraft was the extreme damage noted.  Apparently during the spiral dive; the aircraft exceeded speed and g-force limitations even though the pilot does not recall an overspeed warning.
