I got out of my seat to see what was going on and prepare to close the door should things escalate. When I returned; I thought I had finished my flow completely but after pushback and engine start realized I had not turned on IRS3 when we got an ADR3 fault caution message.Knowing that there were warnings and conditions about aligning IRS's outside of the normal preflight I opened page X which has the ADIRS preflight information. The caution on that page said to make sure the flaps and slats were retracted before aligning; which was confirmed before I turned on IRS3. Since there was a GPS outage in our area; and we had moved in the pushback after aligning IRS1 and IRS2 I also decided to do another full alignment of those. When I selected all of the ADIRS off we got a master warning for the ADIRS 1+2+3 fail and other cautions which all resolved after I turned them on to align again. Knowing we had gotten out of our normal flow; and recognizing that I had gotten distracted with gate issue; during the alignment the FO and I went through the preflight items and reviewed our previous work to confirm we had not missed anything else. After the alignment was complete and all systems normal we departed for an otherwise uneventful flight. Once in cruise; I went back to review the manual and found on the next page Y a continuation of the ADIRS section with an additional second bullet point; one that said not to align the ADIRS with the engines running.

column121: On initial approach into ZZZ at first flap extension the flaps had an asymmetric condition that stopped the flaps between up and 1 degree; the LEDs (Leading Edge Devices) went to the extend position; no roll experienced. Upon noticing the FO elected to level off and follow the approach track and published missed approach. We informed ATC that we were experiencing a flight control problem and that we would be entering holding. We ran the flap trailing edge asymmetry QRH and decided not to land at ZZZ due to the short runway and degraded runway conditions. We then debated on proceeding to ZZZ1 or ZZZ2. We could not proceed to our filed alternate of ZZZ3 due to the increased fuel burn with the LEDs extended. With a quick rough calculation we decided we had enough fuel to proceed to ZZZ2 that had the longest runway. We contacted Dispatch and they concurred on proceeding to ZZZ2. We then climbed to FL190 and cruised at 220 knots IAS. We ran the ALL FLAPS UP QRH and landed at ZZZ2 uneventfully. column121: TCAS RA while flying inbound on ILS XXR ZZZ. Exceptionally busy local ZZZ Tower Controller with multiple VFR in pattern and adjacent Class D airspace including helicopter operations. Joined localizer inbound. [A] low level helicopter in pattern was consuming [the] majority of [the] Tower Controller instructions either due to training occurring in [the] helicopter; or [an] inability to comply with Tower instructions and widening their pattern out for [the] landing jet - us. Continuing inbound at the marker; I elected to stay one dot above glide slope due to [the] continuing inability of [the] helicopter to comply with Tower instructions to turn away from final approach course for us. Inside the marker one dot high; [I] received [a] TCAS RA from [the] helicopter turning base early towards us. PNF (Pilot not Flying) had helicopter in sight [the] entire time. Immediately started to arrest descent when TCAS RA abated. Continued [the] approach; reestablishing glide slope intercept without unusual maneuvering required; to an uneventful landing. ZZZ during VMC weather is always an exceptionally busy airport with mix of high and low speed traffic in addition to multiple flight schools based there. Slowing the aircraft significantly assisted us and likely ATC Tower with sequencing for landing XXR and smaller aircraft; XXL. Estimate [there was] one dozen aircraft in pattern; with more nearby. Additionally; staying high on glide slope using situational awareness VFR likely provided further altitude separation for this eventual encounter. Non-complying VFR pattern helicopter to Tower instructions for whatever reason; highlights perils at this airport and necessitates good crew situational awareness and CRM. I did not follow up with ZZZ Tower with non-complying instruction helicopter; deeming [the] encounter a good learning lesson for all of us.

column121: I fell victim to the dirty dozen; complacency. I was reading the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) to perform the leak test of the P1 and pitot S1 system when; in the middle of the test; I realized the airspeed indicator was not indicating correctly. I went back through the manual to realize that I had read it incorrectly. I saw that the circuit breakers needed to be 'opened' instead of 'closed;' which conflicted with what I thought I read. When I inspected the left and right pitot probes I saw the inner sleeve of our test equipment had melted around it and entered the probes; which caused the erroneous readings. After removing the damaged sleeves I realized that the test equipment; DPS1000; had a maximum limit of 60 HZ and should not have been plugged in to the aircraft galley outlet;which exceeds that limit. I did not see the limit on the test device due to it being on when I plugged it in. It booted up and tested normally so I did not look at that part of the device. I detected the problem by realizing the airspeed indication was not lining up correctly with the test equipment.It was my first time doing any work on pitot probes so I wanted to move slowly and read the manual; after being on the task for 6 hours and at the final stretch to finish it I began to lose focus. After I found the problem I began talking to my partner about writing a report and doing damage control by removing the damaged equipment.When I was looking through the manual my eyes went right to the breakers; glossing over the warnings and cautions. Maybe having those color coded; since we no longer have to print out papers due to the electronic systems in place; would be beneficial and more eye catching.

column121: This is a SAFETY concern. In order to issue the B737 MEL 35-XXX for the Passenger Oxygen Complete System inop; Boeing MEL 'M' procedure; step 'e' requires portable oxygen units to be provided for at least 10% of the passengers. Our 737 NG aircraft is configured for 160 passengers. If we multiply this number by 0.10%; [it] is equal to 16 portable oxygen units that are required to be in compliances with the MEL instructions. During the last MEL Rev 60-XX; a note was added to the 'M' procedure for clarification. This note reads the following. 'The B737 NG is equipped with sufficient portable oxygen CAPACITY to provide for 10% of the passengers; provided that no more than one bottle is inoperative or missing.' The information provided on this note contradicts the 'M' procedure and requirements to issue this placard. The 737 NG is not equipped with sufficient portable oxygen units for 10% of the passengers in accordance with our emergency equipment configuration. There are only 6 portable oxygen units available in the cabin for the passengers. The amount of oxygen available for the passengers should not be measured based on the CAPACITY of oxygen available in the aircraft; but the AMOUNT of units available to assist multiple; different passengers in the event of an emergency.This MEL is a SAFETY hazard for our passenger and flight crew; and should be corrected as soon as possible due to compliances.

column121: I coordinated my annual recurrent training with the instructor to take place yesterday. The instructor was Director of Training for Company for many decades; and even still provides insurance-required recurrent examinations; etc.; and I have been flying with him since I purchased Aircraft X in 2006. The instructor is also a recipient of the Wright Brothers Award from the FAA for 50 years of safe flying. With the weather situation; we decided to fly out of ZZZ. I met the instructor about noon after flying in from ZZZ1; and by the time we got Aircraft X started and taxied to Runway X for departure; we heard Aircraft Y announce 'downwind'. It took a few minutes to get to the approach end of Runway X; and we came to a full stop so we could carefully check for traffic before taking the active. In fact; the instructor and I examined just about every place we could look; including downwind and approach trying to locate any traffic; especially given the previous call. No traffic was depicted on the ADS-B (Automated Dependent Surveillance Broadcast) either. I specifically asked the instructor; 'do you see any reason we cannot take the active'; to which he replied he saw no reason not to. At the time; I even commented seeing what appeared to be either a large bird or an aircraft; but whatever it was it seemed to be moving out of the area and was therefore not a factor. Accordingly; I announced taking the active and departing Runway X for local air work with a northwest departure. After establishing Aircraft X on the runway and starting to advance the power; we suddenly heard Aircraft Y report 'short final'; after which Aircraft Y passed over Aircraft X and landed on the same runway in front of us. I aborted the departure and we watched Aircraft Y land far down the runway (it appeared to be well over halfway down from where we were sitting) at what seemed to be a very high speed; and then; after touchdown; generating all sorts of smoke in the aircraft's wake; either from the engine or from the brakes/tires. It appeared as though there wasn't much runway left and it eventually cleared the runway at the end; apparently using almost all of the 6;704 ft. runway. The instructor observed the smoke to be more 'whitish' in color; meaning it may have been coming from the tires (notably; the instructor provides recurrent training events in the TBM and Jet-prop aircraft as well).Following our recurrent event; the instructor and I thoroughly debriefed what had transpired. We could not understand why we had not visually observed Aircraft Y; given the careful examination of the area surrounding the airport we did prior to taking the active. We were in no hurry whatsoever; and would not have taken the active runway unless we were completely certain there was no conflicting traffic approaching; and we observed none. We examined the FlightAware record as well; but it did not become more obvious as to what may have transpired until today when the instructor and I were discussing the event. For example; Aircraft Y climbed to a cruising altitude of 30;000 ft. enroute from Columbus; Ohio to ZZZ. We believe the pilot may only possess a private pilot certificate; which brings into question whether he could legally be operating at that altitude under IFR (Instrument Flight Rules) conditions or on an IFR flight plan. The mysterious track Aircraft Y flew descending into ZZZ commenced with Aircraft Y descending to 12;500 ft.; presumably VFR (Visual Flight Rules); while still a significant distance from the destination airport. For whatever reason; Aircraft Y pilot apparently elected not to execute one of the three IFR approaches available for that airport at the time; including an ILS (Instrument Landing System) and two GPS (Global Positioning System) approaches. According to the FlightAware data; Aircraft Y first circled the area at 12;500 ft.; completing a 'racetrack' pattern in the immediate vicinity of the airport; while at the same time descending.After flying the racetrack pattern; Aircraft Y continued to descend in an even tighter circular pattern around the airport. It then commenced a base leg turn as it descended out of 5;300 ft.; and then; as it was approaching the airport; it completed an even tighter 360 degree turn at approximately 3;700 ft. As it descended out of that exceedingly tight turn onto final; it was closing on the airport very quickly at an altitude of 2;100 ft. Given our familiarity with the weather at the time; some of the cloud bases of a scattered to broken layer were approximately at 2000 ft. MSL (Mean Sea Level) or even slightly lower; with multiple layers above. In other words; it appears as though the pilot was descending in the vicinity of the airport in what was essentially a 'cloud break' procedure; instead of flying one of the three available instrument approaches. He apparently only relocated the airport visually when he was on a very high approach path already; which would explain the extended touchdown point and the use of most of the runway. It would also explain why we did not see him; as at 2;100 ft. Aircraft Y was likely obscured by the clouds at that point; when Aircraft Y would be located approximately a mile south of the approach end of Runway X.First; the airman made no callouts on Unicom other than flying 'downwind'; not mentioning he was at or above 6;000 ft. while on the downwind leg. Nor did the pilot tell anyone on Unicom he was orbiting the airport and descending trying to locate the runway visually. He made no callouts whatsoever between the original 'downwind' call we heard while taxiing Aircraft X initially; and then just the 'short final' call before Aircraft Y overflew Aircraft X; landing far down the runway in front of us.As the conditions were very similar when I arrived approximately 30 minutes previously; there was no problem maintaining VFR conditions in order to make a visual approach to runway X; and those conditions continued 45 minutes later when we concluded our flight. Visibility was at all times in excess of 10 miles. There appears to be a significant amount of desperation exhibited by the pilot in landing over Aircraft X after we had initiated the departure; as it seems he might have been in somewhat of a panic to get Aircraft Y on the ground; when the only prudent course of action at that point; given that neither of us visually located Aircraft Y; despite an extremely diligent search; and after announcing that we were taking the active runway for departure purposes; was to immediately go around and reenter the pattern.Quite a few of the preceding flights for Aircraft Y available on FlightAware appear to be training type missions; and it is unclear what put so much pressure on the pilot to complete the approach and landing; imperiling all involved; instead of merely executing a prudent go around and reentering the pattern; which the weather would certainly permit at the time. Quite frankly don't know what else we could have done to prevent this situation from occurring; as we used all due diligence before we took the active runway. Aircraft Y was likely above the clouds when we searched for traffic before departing. The two pilots on our flight deck at the time had over 100 years of [combined] flight experience; without incident or accident.

column121: On climb; I tried to start moving fuel forward with the gravity flow valve open and noticed that it didn't work. Our fuel from the wings kept getting low and after great coordination with controllers we were able to get safely to the ground. column121: I often fly late-day or evening; and routinely use the associated pilot-controlled airport lighting both to fix my position and for terminal guidance. Sky Manor has MIRL but does not have an airport beacon; so I often also turn on the lighting for Alexandria (N85); located approximately 2NM northwest; which has both MIRL and a rotating beacon. The frequency for this at Sky Manor is 122.975 (which doubles as the CTAF frequency); at Alexandria; 121.8 (with 122.975 as CTAF).On at least two separate occasions; coming from more than one direction; I have turned the airport lighting on for Alexandria and ended up momentarily distracting pilots and/or ATC by doing so. Alexandria is not very far away from Newark Liberty (EWR); or Lancaster (LNS); both of which use 121.8 as a Ground Control frequency and are apparently well within radio range and altitudes at and below 2000 ft MSL. Further research indicates that McGuire (WRI) may also be affected; as it's a similar distance as Newark.While I don't want to keep distracting others in the ATC system - and I've resolved the issue for myself by increasing familiarity with the airspace; which has reduced the necessity of me using the Alexandria airport beacon for guidance - I also realize that this has the capability to reduce my situational awareness; and at any event; aircraft intending to land at Alexandria at night must necessarily turn the airport lighting on; potentially distracting operations at the airports previously listed.I propose that the lighting frequency at Alexandria be changed; either to CTAF or to some other discrete frequency; with the intention of minimizing possible adverse operational implications for local controlled airports.

column121: We were conducting a long cross country for the student's commercial pilot requirements. This required us to deviate west and south of course due to not being cleared into the Class Bravo airspace and Class D airspace. We had a near miss with a powered parachute. The other operator was slightly below us; heading westbound. Our altitude at the time was 3500 feet eastbound; with flight following. Weather conditions were VMC; clear and unrestricted. Both I and the student were actively scanning for traffic outside due to the busy Bravo environment and using ADS-B to aid us. Since he was slightly below us; we did not see him until close; less than 1 mile separation and probably closer. I directed the student to immediately turn left to pass behind; but he started turning slowly; so I took controls to avoid the situation. The powered parachute passed behind; and we continued without further incident. The parachute's color caused it to really blended in until we were close. We were attempting to spot all traffic visually; but did not see them until late. I'm unsure if the parachute operator ever saw us; as we would've been coming out of the sun off his roughly 3 to 4 o'clock. I did not report this to Approach; mainly since we ourselves were getting into a high workload environment since we were close to our destination. Additionally; with the traffic was behind us; I was more concerned with flying the airplane and watching for other traffic; especially since it is a busy general aviation airport. That was probably my biggest self recommendation; is trying to report that if able to approach to warn other aircraft. The only other recommendation for myself is to be a little clearer when I need to assume controls.

column121: We were departing ZZZ to ZZZ1 after dropping our passengers off at their personal hangar. As we began taxiing out; we made a call on the CTAF that we were taxiing out and planning to takeoff on RWY XX. We heard an Air Force C130 on CTAF doing work in the pattern. We made a second call as we rounded the hangars on the NE side of the airport. At that time we heard a very faint radio call of a tail number (we could not make out the N#) saying that they 'were entering the pattern; ZZZ' That is all that we heard. I made a radio call asking for the aircraft to repeat the call; and heard nothing. As we were taxiing to the hold short line; I as the PNF (pilot not flying) called for our release from Center Radio. the PF (pilot flying) was monitoring CTAF the entire time; and heard no additional radio calls from the unidentified airplane in the pattern. We stopped at the hold short line and made another radio call that we were holding short and were going to be departing RWY XX. The C130 radio'd that he would extend his orbit so that we could take off. We heard no other radio calls during that time. We crossed the hold short line and I looked and verified the final approach area for RWY XX was clear; the PF looked and verified that RWY XY Final was clear. As we were taxiing into position we heard a very faint 'you guys hold up a minute' call over CTAF. We did not know who it was for and I called over the frequency 'say again' We heard nothing. We started our takeoff run. About 5 seconds later we saw a Cessna landing on RWY XY and aborted our takeoff at a speed of about 100 knots IAS. We called out on the radio that we had made radio calls saying that we were taking off. I do not recall the exact words but we were getting chewed out for taking off while a local was trying to land. We taxed clear of the runway; reset everything; checked our brake temperatures; made another radio call and proceeded to take off uneventfully.We try to be hyper vigilant operating a high performance jet out of uncontrolled fields. It is possible; but I believe unlikely that we missed radio calls from the aircraft in question; but it is possible that we did. I believe the problem arose from a weak transmitter on the Cessna; and non standard phraseology and lack of position report calls on the CTAF. I believe that we followed the AIM guidance for operating on an uncontrolled field; by making several radio calls stating our intentions; and listening for other traffic. We heard no other position reports from the Cessna such as 'entering downwind or turning base' etc. I am not saying the other pilot did not make the calls; I'm saying we did not hear them if he did. There is also a dip in the runway that prevents you from seeing the end of RWY XY from the end of RWY XX. In addition the pilot of the Cessna did not have his landing light on; which would have helped to identify him sooner. We asked for a repeat of his initial radio call; but heard nothing. We also heard no other radio reports from any aircraft other than the C130. In addition; this could have been avoided if a proper radio call such as 'ZZZ Traffic Aircraft Y short final; landing RWY XY ZZZ' had been made instead of 'You guys hold up a minute'. We can always be more vigilant in our actions. Taxiing out while getting a clearance and setting up the FMS is a very busy time; monitoring 2 radios can be distracting. Careful attention to detail and vigilant use of the checklist and PF/PNF duties all need to be done to ensure that nothing is missed; inside and outside the airplane while operating on an uncontrolled field.

column121: While conducting a CFI checkout in a Grob-103C; the canopy came open and separated from the aircraft during final approach with a forward slip.This was my second training flight in the glider; the purpose of the checkout was to allow me to provide flight instruction in the Grob-103C. I normally provide instruction in Aircraft Y. The Grob-103C we were flying was recently inspected - 100-Hour and Annual - and was flying frequently at the flight school. Before flight; we performed our standard pre-flight inspection and pre-takeoff checklist which included ensuring both canopies were closed and locked. I was seated in the front seat; having flown side secured canopies often; [I] closed the canopy latch and tested the canopy by pushing up on the side to ensure it was securely closed. I noted no problems during closing and locking the canopy.After executing our pre-takeoff procedure; my Instructor and I proceeded on aerotow to 3;000 AGL; released; and performed some basic maneuvers - stalls; slow flight; and thermalling. After gliding for approximately 15 minutes; we elected to enter the pattern on the downwind leg. While turning from base to final; we decided to slip the aircraft to practice flying without airbrakes. After slipping for approximately 8 seconds; the front canopy suddenly opened and departed the aircraft. I immediately came out of the slip; nosed down for approach speed; and opened the airbrakes. I was able to land the glider with normal maneuvers and noted no change to the controllability of the glider.Upon examination of the glider; there was no structural/significant damage. There were no injuries to either crew. There was a slight score to the fiberglass on the right wing and damage to the canopy hinges. The canopy was later recovered in a field where the fiberglass appeared to have shattered on impact. Analyzing the situation; I am still unsure why the canopy separation occurred; but if I could improve my process; I would have examined the canopy all along its edges after securing the latch to insure there were no gaps or leaks. In addition; I probably would have looked closer during preflight at the edges/seals of the canopy from the exterior to ensure there were no abnormalities on either canopy when closed and locked.

column121: While approaching the initial fix (IF) TNNER for the San Juan; Puerto Rico ILS Runway 10; we heard a commercial airline pilot ahead of us report that his cockpit had been illuminated by a green laser near TNNER.  Approach Control warned us of this laser strike. We asked for clearance to proceed to waypoint REMSY (IAF) instead of TNNER (IF) to allow us to avoid the area where the green laser strike had been reported. Immediately after being cleared to REMSY; our cockpit was illuminated by a very bright ground based green laser coming from the 1:30 clock code position at about six to eight miles from our position. We reported the green laser strike to ATC at approximately (XA:33) Z. The Approach Controller asked if either pilot had sustained any eye injury. We responded that we did not believe we had sustained any eye injuries. I estimated the laser to be approximately four miles southeast of TNNER; or 260 degrees at 8 NM from the SJU VOR. I estimate the source to be on the ground between the 436 feet tall tower and the 489 feet tall tower (shown on the SJU ILS Runway 10 Approach plate).  The green laser was an unnecessary distraction during a critical phase of flight (approach; configuration change; visually searching for arrival traffic; attempting to locate the runway visually; conducting the landing checklist; landing; etc.).  Law enforcement never met us at the airport to take a report. It did not appear that anyone at the FAA  or law enforcement were interested in gathering facts immediately after the event in order to pursue the perpetrators.  The San Juan; PR; TJSJ/SJU-1; (date); airport page says; 'Numerous LASER events have been recorded in area' as a warning to pilots. It seems like laser strikes have become so common in the area of the San Juan Airport that officials just accept this fact. Is law enforcement aggressively investigating these laser strikes in an attempt to hold the perpetrators accountable? Fortunately; tonight; the laser strike caused only a momentary distraction to the pilots. What happens when a persistent series of laser strikes causes the pilots eye injury; disorientation; and/or loss of aircraft with all passengers onboard. Will the FAA and law enforcement treat the event more seriously after such a catastrophic event?Will the FAA; FBI; NTSB; and/or law enforcement aggressively investigate and pursue the perpetrators who are pointing high intensity green lasers at commercial airline cockpits flying into San Juan Airport.

The First Officer had sent a message to this Captain confirming such. The ZZZ1 Chief Pilot was subsequently notified and a request was made for that office to contact my crew of this matter (I never received any communication about this event). This Captain was tested on Day 2; became symptomatic on Day 3 and obtained a positive test result on Day 5 prompting the message.Upon reviewing the message; I contacted my First Officer and the company On-duty Manager to notify each of the situation. Per company and CDC COVID protocol both the First Officer and I have been quarantined for a 14-day period commencing Day 0. As I compose this report; I am quarantined at the hotel; unable to travel home.The intent of this report is to question why didn't the company notify my crew of the COVID encounter? Apparently protocol wasn't followed or if it was; it should be modified to address this particular or similar scenarios. Flight crews should not be placed in a situation where they must quarantine away from home while on company business; especially if the company was previously notified to contact a crew which was exposed to a COVID positive employee. Had I not been received said message I would still be flying the line with the potential to infect others with this virus.

column121: This was a training flight. Occupants included student in left seat and instructor in right seat. ATIS reporting winds 300 degrees at 8 knots; SKC; visibility greater than 10 miles. Student confidently performed all preflight; taxi; and run up procedures. After run up; advised complete and cleared to hold short of the runway and monitor Tower. Takeoff clearance was north turnout approved cleared for takeoff. No additional wind direction or speed was given in the clearance. Student lined up appropriately and commenced takeoff roll. Once rolling; the plane veered towards the left of the runway while student continued the takeoff. As speed continued to increase; the student was unsuccessful in aligning the plane with the centerline and began to prematurely rotate in what appeared to be a moment of panic. With an excursion inevitable; instructor called 'abort my controls' retarded power and struggled to regain control. The aircraft may have momentarily became airborne. As the aircraft settled back onto the surface; a violent porpoising action proceeded. Instructor discovered student was applying full pressure on the brakes. Instructor demanded 'off the brakes' and eventually brought the aircraft under control towards centerline. Instructor canceled flight and taxied back to the ramp without further incident. Factors leading up to this event included too much confidence placed in student's ability as he done exceptionally well leading up to the takeoff; reported a very successful flight with a previous instructor; as well as having previous aircraft type experience. Additional factors would include lack of control inputs to counter the reported direct crosswind. Typically; a direct crosswind from the left would tend to cause a right deviation of centerline. It is possible the student inadvertently or over corrected the beginning takeoff roll with differential left brake after feeling the plane go to the right and did not transition to rudder steering once airspeed increased. It is also possible the 300 degree wind direction and runway assignment seemed coincident causing a lack of correction for winds. Regardless; lesson gained for instructor is to stay on the controls with student until student demonstrates safe takeoff procedures. Additionally; instructor should identify early on a rejected takeoff scenario that leaves enough space to safely recover.

column121: On arrival into ZZZ; descending via on the ZZZZZ3 Arrival just before the ZZZZZ waypoint; we checked on with approach; and they responded 'Company XXXX; cleared ILS X.' I had programmed the ILS X for our arrival; but didn't select any transition on the approach. The ZZZZZ3 STAR has the note to cross ZZZZZ at 6;000 feet; expect ILS or LOC Runway X. On receipt of the clearance; I paused for a moment as there was a discontinuity in the box after ZZZZZ and before ZZZZZ1 [waypoint]; and the remaining points on the ILS X. ATC had not given us a heading or guidance for after the last fix on the STAR; just cleared ILS X. I looked at my EFB to see what the text of the STAR said; and my Captain seeing my confusion; said 'you're cleared for approach; how about direct ZZZZZ1?' He had also queued up ZZZZZ1 in the box; and was poised to execute it. I still wasn't sure; but he seemed positive. I said 'OK;' he executed it and we began direct to ZZZZZ1. Within a few seconds; Approach queried us 'I show you left of course; what [are you] doing?' The Captain replied; 'we're direct ZZZZZ1 cleared for ILS X; is there something else you would like?' ATC responded that there was a ZZZZZ transition to the ILS X; and in future that is what he meant when he cleared us ILS X - to fly the ZZZZZ transition on the ILS from the STAR. Had I looked closer at the approach plate; and not just the STAR chart; after the issuance of the clearance; the ATC clearance intention would've become obvious to me. I let my Captain cause me to second guess my hesitation; and disregard my uncertainty over our clearance. I should have requested he ask for clarification from ATC instead of allowing him to execute a path I was unsure of. I have felt a bit slow in the cockpit lately; due to having flown very infrequent this year (light schedules/hindsight/scheduled time off) and I believe I made the false assumption I was missing something and he was correct. A simple query to ATC would have cleared up the matter.I should have taken a moment longer to review the appropriate charts to clarify the appropriate flight course; and failing that answering my question; I should have queried ATC for clarification. When programming the approach; closer examination of the plate would have shown the available lead in transition from ZZZZZ. I should have trusted my hesitation upon receipt of the clearance and not assumed I was wrong in needing clarification.

column121: It was from ZZZ1 to ZZZ IFR flight. Our flight plan and clearance was from ZZZ1..ZZZZZ5. ZZZ. During the descend; the ZZZ Approach Controller gave instruction to switch our runway to XXR. Captain and I programmed [the] FMS and switched our planned runway to XXR as well as review the fixes along the route. However; as we approach the fix ZZZZZ2; LNAV autopilot was switched to lateral mode [and the] airplane was late to turn to [the] final [approach] fix which is ZZZZZ3. As soon as Pilot Flying noticed the mode change in autopilot; Pilot Flying used heading bug to make a left turn to rejoin the course for the rest of arrival. Next time; we will review the fixes more carefully after making any changes on the runways or arrivals and make sure if there are any fixes that are duplicated; we will deleted it.
column123: On arrival to ZZZ we were descending via ZZZZZ5. Our dispatch release had planned [Runway] XXL and we had already briefed our approach prior to the beginning of the arrival as is common for preparation and safety. As an LCA (line check airman) I have been flying our route structure for over X;XXX hours in the left seat and this is common practice for myself. However; I am still trying to understand the traffic flows in ZZZ and as time progresses I am positive the other crews and I will get better at selecting runways based on flow and approaches utilized over time. ZZZ Approach Control gave us instructions for XXR somewhere after ZZZZZ5 I believe. I was the pilot monitoring. So I immediately went to work resetting FMS verifying ZZZZZ3 had now changed to ZZZZZ2. Altitudes were correct at said waypoint. Getting new landing data. Resetting both navigational aids for the correct runway. And since my FO (First Officer) was fairly new to the plane I began briefing his approach to him out loud; highlighting changes and re-briefing all pertinent information. It was in the middle of this brief that I heard the lateral NAV disconnection chime. The plane had entered ROL mode and within a second I and the FO were both reaching for the heading bug. He made the correction on the FGC (Flight Guidance Computer) about as quickly as anyone could. We recaptured the LNAV course to ZZZZZ2 and were given a number to call.I have been operating with this company for over X years; almost Y are as an LCA. In all my time I have never seen what I described above. After the fact I am aware of exactly what happened and I will explain and make suggestions to correct. Upon loading the runway change to XXR the FMS duplicated the ZZZZZ fix. I know this because the pilot observing told us when we got on the ground what he had witnessed and told us it was a current trend within our airline and they were trying to troubleshoot. I understand why that might happen in the mind of the FMS as it is trying to separate the arrival into parts. Initial arrival segment versus approach segment. However; reloading approaches or fielding runways changes are common in our route structure and not once in four years has this happened anywhere else. ZZZZZ4 in ZZZ2. Landing north transitions to ZZZZZ6 at 7000. Landing south your next fix might be ZZZZZ7 at 7000 for XXC. But never in four years has a reassigned runway and a reload of the approach caused ZZZZZ4 to duplicate. This is specific to ZZZ2. This is why we are just now seeing this throughout the pilot group in this airspace. I know there is verbiage within our books that states duplicated points must be removed for this very reason. However; in this event I was unable to catch the duplicated fix due to workload and I had never seen the issue before so my mental radar so to speak was focused on threats I have seen: monitoring our descent rate; monitoring speed control for arrival compliance; re-briefing navigational aid frequencies; briefing go-around and missed approach for the new runway. All the things I have seen cause errors in our flight on a normal day. So when this lateral break happened I was as stunned as the FO. I will say to his credit he corrected in the quickest fashion and made the correct adjustment for the situation. There was nothing more we could have done. I did not feel safety was at stake nor that the violation was hugely significant. I however do see that as a systemic issue the implications of this are massive and need to be corrected ASAP which is why I have my recommendations. I spoke with a sim pilot who was able to recreate the event and he confirmed what I had already suspected. Pilots need to be aware that this is common in ZZZ2. When receiving a new runway or a change to the approach. Look for duplicate fixes!

column121: I was Captain and the flying pilot for arrival into IAH. We were descending in VMC conditions on the LINKK1 Arrival for the assigned Runway 27. We had completed our Approach to Landing above the line and as we were approaching 10000' we were running our Approach to Landing checklist Below the Line when we were cleared by the Approach Controller for the ILS 27 Approach and to maintain 240 knots.I put on the appropriate lights and we finished our checklist. However I did not - in hindsight - set the lower 1500' at which we were to cross the FAF at REDOC. Between RDFSH and GEYGR we were queried as to whether we were going to make our crossing restriction of 4000 at GEYGR. We realized the error and started to descend on the approach. Shortly after not complying with the crossing restriction at GEYGR; we were broken off the approach and vectored back around-slowed to 210 and descended to rejoin the approach. We were given a phone number to call HOUSTON TRACON. We then completed the approach and landing. The error started when I did not select the lower altitude for the FAF of 1500. The timing of our clearance was a contributing factor but the error was in the failure to set lower FAF altitude. Typically we are double checking each other and we missed it. Greater vigilance would have eliminated this error. We were also discussing the fact we were at 240 as assigned still inside of RDFSH was also a factor. We debriefed this all on the ground in detail. I later spoke with TRACON about this. They informed me that there were no separation issues and he did note the timing of the clearance when they reviewed the tape.
column123: We were flying the LINKK 1 Arrival; runway 27 to IAH. We confirmed all points in the MCDU and set the altitude down to 6000 we both confirmed the altitude we were then given a speed of 240kts with a clearance of descend via the STAR. We both looked at each other to confirm everything before we started to descend down immediately. There was not enough time to report that we were not going to make the crossing restrictions at 240kts and also the altitude. We both realized at this time that the altitude had not been changed for the lower altitude of 1500ft. at REDOC. The controller gave us a 360-degree turn back on course as we lost our altitude. At this point we realized our error. The controller called back with a number to call Houston for TRACON; we completed the approach and landed. Timing of the clearance was a factor; as well as not selecting lower altitude for the FAF of 1500 or double checking each other. Also should have discussed that we were inside of RDFSH and still at 240. We talked when on the ground in detail.

column121: During the landing rollout; after all three wheels were firmly on the ground and brakes were being applied; the airplane began to yaw to the right. At the same time; the right suspension settled down and the left wing rose significantly. I could not steer the airplane back towards the center line. I then brought the airplane to a stop via braking. Upon coming to a stop; I applied power to attempt to move and steer the airplane with neither being successful. The entire event was felt the same as a blown tire would. I then told the tower we had blown a tire and requested to shut down engines. After gaining permission; we shut down the engines and awaited city employees. After a city car arrived and circled the airplane to inspect the damage; I alone exited the airplane to speak with him and inspect the airplane myself. He informed me there appeared to be no damage; and I verified this with my own inspection of the tires and landing gear struts. I then decided to start the engines and attempt to move the airplane. Upon advising the tower; I started engines and applied power. The airplane moved normally. We then taxied to the gate with no further incident. It is my opinion; after observing no bald spots on the tires; that a gust of wind from the left lifted the left wing significantly and at the same time the right brake locked up or would not release from an applied position. After letting the airplane rest for a few minutes; the sticky brake may have released itself allowing movement as normal.

column121: Before departure I randomly decided to look at the L1 door. I noticed that there was daylight coming from the aft vertical part of the door. I walked down from the upper deck to inspect the status of the door and noticed that the daylight was a 2-3 inch gap. The door handle was in the down and locked position and the forward part of the door was latched. Being that we were in a BCF (Boeing Converted Freighter); we had no way of knowing that the door was not secure because the BCF had no doors synoptic. I informed the Captain and he came down to inspect the door right about the time the ground crew personnel noticed the door was ajar. The door was then closed properly and we went on our way. The safety concern that we had as a crew was that we had no checklists or instructions to verify the L1 door was closed on the BCF; and without a doors synoptic page; we wouldn't of known it was still ajar. [Recommend incorporating] a check before departure from the crew to verify the L1 door is closed on BCFs that do not have door synoptic pages.

column121: I was positioning for a take-off at ZZZ. AWOS noted that the preferred calm wind runways are X for landing and XX for takeoff (with pilot discretion). Also announced was the fact that taxiway A was closed between A-2 and A-4 so all traffic should be aware of back-taxing aircraft on the runway. Winds were about 3 knots and a slight cross wind. The plane in front of me taxied to XX for takeoff; including the back taxi from A-4 to A-2. I was stuck at A-4. The amount of incoming traffic began to increase; with all of it calling for a landing on [Runway] X. So it made sense for me to switch to taking off on X to keep with the traffic direction for better safety. I decided to taxi on the runway from A-4 to A-5 since I could not turn around where I was. Then I could proceed down A to the end at [Runway] X.Sitting at A-4; I waited for a plane to land and clear my position at A-4. I called my intention and then proceeded onto the runway to move down to A-5. Seeing a plane on final (est. 3/4 mile); I added power for more speed. I arrived at A-5 sooner than I thought and with too much speed. I pulled back the power (too late) and applied the brakes (too hard) and entered the turn into A-5 with too much speed; skidding off A-5 several feet until the prop hit and destroyed a taxiway light. I immediately proceeded to the closest parking spot; with no noticeable prop vibration or noise; shut down the avionics and engine; inspected the plane; and went into the FBO to discuss the incident.In the very brief amount of time I had to make a decision; I rushed to decide to speed up on the runway to get well out of the way of the incoming traffic I could see on final. Even though I had announced my intentions and had the right of way; I should have maintained a safe speed and warned the incoming plane to watch out for me and be prepared for a go-around if I didn't get off the runway at A-5 in time for him to reach my position. I often visualize different scenarios that might occur in flying; but I obviously didn't envision this one so that my instincts might have been better in that very small window of decision-making time. So now our club has to not only replace the prop; but have the engine disassembled; inspected; tested; and reassembled after the prop strike; with all the associated costs and plane downtime.

Controller gave me taxi instructions and I replied 'Taxiway 3; Taxiway 4; cross Runway Y; into parking.' column123: Most of the 1 hr and 40 minutes I had been on position with positions combined during moderate to busy traffic. I had been held over for 2 hours and a Supervisor was working LC with Tower in-charge on a single runway; so we were not using LUAW (Line Up And Wait). Additionally Runway XXL was closed as well (which we use to offset small arrivals to allow for more departures on XXR) and all these factors were adding complexity to an already busy session.Aircraft X exited Runway XXR and was given taxi instructions 'Taxiway 2; Taxiway 3; Taxiway 4; cross Runway Y and taxi to park' (Runway Y is a closed runway in my control). The pilot read back the instructions correctly. I had other aircraft taxiing and needed a runway crossing between the steady stream of arrivals and departures. I coordinated for the crossing with LC and after Aircraft Y went through the intersection on takeoff roll; I cleared the aircraft waiting to cross Runway XXR at Taxiway 5 to cross. I watched him cross; checked another plane taxiing to the runway; checked the printer for clearances; checked back on my crossing; and informed LC the Taxiway 5/XXR crossing was complete. At that point Aircraft X keyed up and said something like 'Uh; GC? I think we took a wrong turn.' I did a quick scan of the runway and didn't see him initially because one of the poles was in the way. I started to key up to ask him where he was and stepped back to re-scan and realized he was on the north side of XXR half on the runway and half off. I immediately informed LC of the situation. I turned Aircraft X around and held him short of XXR and told local I was too busy to find a hole to cross him and to just call me when he had a place for me to cross him back over. I informed the pilot of his possible pilot deviation and gave him the phone number and then moved on to other planes and clearances. This is an intersection we have had multiple issues with for runway incursions and last I knew is identified as a hot spot on the chart. Recently the airport added wig-wags to make it clear that it is a runway intersection to help stop pilots from doing this. ZZZ needs some sort of ground radar because even with the new safety lights installed they still cross. Some sort of early warning from an ASDE would at least give us a chance to catch this sort of thing.While the Supervisor was doing a very good job of working LC; I was still trying to keep my eye on him because of how little pro-time they need; the regular decrease in traffic from COVID slowing our skills; and the high volume of traffic he was working as well. If the traffic is regularly that volume at that time of day; it's imperative that three people be in the Tower; not two. The only way I could have caught this aircraft would have been if I was staring directly at him as he made the turn. The distance from Taxiway 2 to Runway XXR on Taxiway 3; is very short and I was focused on verifying the completion of the runway crossing Taxiway 5.Recommend 3 people in the tower from XA-XC pm.

column121: As part of my job as a CFI for a local flight school; I was looking to add tailwheel instruction to my list of instruction services I provide. I have about 15 total tailwheel hours; but very little recent experience. In order to improve proficiency; I went up with an instructor the day before the ground loop to get tailwheel current and get some additional training. We flew for an hour and did four full stop landings on the airfield's grass runway; and all were straight; and no issues came up during any of these landings that would suggest I needed additional training. On the day of the ground loop; the winds had shifted to be about 8 knots directly down the asphalt runway so I chose to use that one rather than the grass which would have had a 90-degree crosswind. During my first approach; I made a low pass to verify the sight picture in my mind and double check any wind correction that may need to be done. I executed a go around and came around for another uneventful approach to a planned 3-point landing. After a smooth touchdown with the airplane rolling down the runway; a gust lifted the right wing and a yaw to the left. My corrective actions did not prevent the airplane from ground looping. Upon reflection; there was a moment where I should have applied power to try to stop the yaw and execute a go-around. However; I believe my ego got in the way since I've been flying more than I ever have that I could 'save' the landing despite teaching my students to default to a go-around when things aren't looking right. My overconfidence in my skills; combined with ego resulted in me trying to save the rollout rather than going around. I also believe more than an hour of recurrent training prior to flying a tailwheel airplane is required; even though I have been flying a lot lately.

column121: The first 3 flights were uneventful and on arrival in ZZZ we were swapped into Aircraft Y - a broken airplane for ZZZ - ZZZ1. We were then swapped into Aircraft X - an airplane coming from the hangar that was a first flight and had a deferred APU. There was no ground air available at the gate and we were now an hour late. We boarded 30 passengers and had a Company Dispatcher Jumpseater. We started one engine at the gate and taxied out and performed a cross bleed engine start for #1. ATIS was reporting wind shear and we used wind shear numbers for takeoff on XXR; [Taxiway] XX; with ignition ON.On the takeoff roll I noticed an intermittent IDG 1 caution message; followed by an intermittent CONFIG SPOILERS warning message; a BTMS 3 that was dashes and two probe/window heat messages. I called abort and should have executed an abort procedure. I believed the message to be associated with a MEL on a previous flight; and I said; 'Associated; continue;' and continued the takeoff. The winds were very gusty. After takeoff we had a GEN 1 caution message and I ran the QRH for GEN 1; and in the process I accidentally switched off GEN 2; resulting in the ADG deploying. We [requested priority handling] and returned to ZZZ; landing on XYR. CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) was there and escorted us to Gate XXX. No injuries or complaints were reported. We were met by Maintenance and then had a 5-way call with Company; Maintenance; [another person]; and one or two other people. I explained what had happened and told them of my mistake. I and the First Officer said that we were done flying and we were taken off our schedules. We then had a call with Maintenance and wrote up the airplane; including the #1 IDG; ADG deployment; and spoiler warning message.I called abort and should have executed an abort procedure. Once airborne; and running the QRH; I should have confirmed that the GEN1 switch was selected and confirmed with the flying pilot prior to actuating the switch.
column123: The day began early with an XA45 wake up to accommodate an XB45 van and [an] XC15 show. We completed the first three flights of the day without issue. Upon landing in ZZZ and swapping our good airplane for the plane we were taking to ZZZ1; we found out that that aircraft had maintenance issues and would require us to swap aircraft again. We were informed that there would be a delay in getting a new aircraft from the hangar. After waiting for about an hour the aircraft was finally coming from the hanger and we found out that it had an inoperative APU and it was its first flight of the day. Additionally; we would be having a Company Dispatcher in the jump seat. We were able to complete our first flight of the day items; acceptance checklist to include the first flight of the day items; complete an air start; push back; single-engine taxi out; and complete the cross bleed start without incident. We were set up for a wind shear takeoff with continuous ignition on.We were given a lineup and clearance and taxied onto the Runway of XXR at [Taxiway] XX. After a momentary wait; we were then given the takeoff clearance with a turn to the north. I was the flying pilot at the time; so I was given controls upon completion of the takeoff checklist. I pushed the thrust levers up and commanded for thrust to be set; the CA (Captain) confirmed thrust set and guarded the thrust levers. Shortly after this; a caution message appeared and the CA called out 'IDG 1' and called for the abort initially; but then said; 'Wait; that's associated.' The CA did not perform the abort; so I continued to fly the plane to ensure the positive control of the aircraft. Shortly after this; a warning message appeared momentarily; and the CA called out; 'Config Spoilers;' and the message disappeared. We continued the takeoff normally and began our turn to the north per ATC instructions.I was initially hand flying but shortly after reaching acceleration altitude; I called for the autopilot to be engaged. I called for the after takeoff checklist and noticed the caution messages that were present and called for the QRH. The Captain began to run the GEN 1 caution message QRH for the caution messages that were present. We noted the associated probe and window/windshield heat messages. While he was running the QRH he called out; 'GEN 1 off/reset; then on;' and reached up to perform this action. It appeared that he accidentally reset GEN 2 and the aircraft went dark momentarily; our EICAS and instrumentation screens went dark momentarily; and we heard the ADG automatically deploy. The CA immediately acknowledged his mistake and I continued flying by hand to maintain positive control of the aircraft while we sorted out the generator issue. The CA turned GEN 2 back on and communicated with me that we should return to ZZZ; I agreed.The CA then communicated to ATC that we needed to return to ZZZ and [requested priority handling]. The CA then communicated to Dispatch; the FA (Flight Attendant); and passengers that we were returning to ZZZ and to expect a normal landing. He did mention that there would be emergency vehicles near the aircraft; but that they were just a precaution and not to worry. We were then given vectors for the approach to Runway XYR; giving us time to brief our approach and landing; complete our in-range; approach; and landing checklists. We completed a normal landing; taxied back to our departure gate of XXX with an emergency escort; and arrived at the gate without issue.It would have been wise to perform the takeoff abort procedure at the earliest possible indication of an abnormal situation while the airspeed was still low and safe to do so. This would have prevented handling the aircraft issued in the air. Additionally; it is important to always confirm guarded switches with our fellow crew members to avoid making a stressful and abnormal situation worse.

column121: After sorting out an issue in ZZZ of not getting a cargo load report (CLR) notes on ACARS on any live animals. The flight crew simply asked [the] ramp agents to resend it. They were unable to do so so we simply asked for a paper CLR. The Ramp Lead became flustered with his scanner and went to go ask a manager for help. The manager came back about 10 minutes later after we had closed and gave the flight crew the notice to Captain form (first time we discovered there was dangerous goods onboard) and resent the CLR with the notes on DG (Dangerous Goods) and live animal (I noticed the bird and medical boxes on my walk around but didn't notice any markings on the medical boxes pertaining to DG). Already delayed pushing back we then became saturated with a runway change. Reaching cruise we became talking more about the lack of NOTOC (Notice to Captain) and an impending incident report. After talking for a few moments at cruise. I realized that we are not allowed to be carrying both dry ice and any live animals in the forward cargo bin together. After bringing that to light I began inquiring about possible diversion options. Including the destination of ZZZ1 40-45 minutes out. After the Captain messaged with Dispatch we decided to divert to ZZZ2 as that was the fastest option to separate the dry ice and live animal. Landing and taxing in we made sure we had a ramp crew that was informed of the situation and needing to open the fwd cargo door asap and remove the live animal. As well as a gate in ZZZ2. I went down to check as soon as the jet bridge was pulled up. And when I got down there the bird was out of the fwd cargo and in good health. The live bird was ok and the ramp agents took the bird into the office to be in the air conditioning and off the loud ramp environment while the ramp crew and flight crew figured out a new bag count. Cargo count. And any other required paperwork. I began calling for fuel. Loading in the new flight plan from the release while the Captain went down to talk to ramp managers as to what cargo is staying or going. A new and confirmed bag count after ZZZ2 rampers recounted bags and cargo (which did not match the original bag count out of ZZZ even though we only removed the DG) was received.After getting everything all figured out in ZZZ2 we calmly talked to the passengers and gave them a timeline of when we would expect to be pushing back and going to ZZZ1. After getting to ZZZ1. And finishing the flight. Deplaning. And; making sure the live animal was ok and in the possession of ZZZ1 Ramp Operations. The Captain and I began debriefing today's events. We reconstructed a timeline. No cargo load remarks. Called OPS. They began to get flustered about their system. We then just asked for a paper cargo load report to remedy the glitch in the system. The Ramp Manager came and threw though the window a notice to Captain. This was the very first time we realized we had any DG onboard. We then hyper focused on the problem of closing without a NOTOC and making sure to talk to OPS and Ground. When talking about this in the air. I realized the problem of the DG and live animal in the same compartment. We quickly then realized that this was not a situation that could continue. We began looking at diversion options. Talking to Dispatch and ZZZ2 OPS. We diverted and handled the situation at hand going forward. We talked about how there are numerous safeguards to never let a situation like this happen before it even gets to the airplane or airport/cargo processing counter for that matter. And how this is a prime example of reasons [for the] swiss cheese model. Starting early this morning with 3 runway changes and a wrong turn on a taxiway resulting in the first ASAP. Airline's ramp scanning system and software letting these be scanned together or a safeguard overridden to let this happen. Us hyperfocusing on discovering DG was onboard after closing with no NOTOC. And resulting in missing the combined DG and live animal in the same cargo compartment until cruise flight. Going forward and learning from this. This is a prime example of how to simply complete tasks and move on without hyperfocusing on the previous threats or errors.
column123: Today I; while operating Aircraft X from ZZZ-ZZZ1; made a grave mistake and allowed myself to depart ZZZ with dry ice and a parrot in the forward cargo bin. Upon discovering my mistake I contacted Dispatch and subsequently diverted to ZZZ2. The parrot was alive and we got some gas and continued onto ZZZ1 without further incident. While in ZZZ my FO (First Officer) noticed a big parrot and some medical looking boxes sitting outside cargo bin during preflight. He brought it to my attention. I was focused on making sure we had one or the other listed on load remarks. We got our baggage data but it did not generate a load remarks message. I released parking break while talking to [the] Ramp Lead via interphone. I inquired as to why we did not have a load remarks message. I asked if he could resend it. He was unsure of everything and went to find his supervisor. At this time I could not confirm if we had an animal or DG or both. I called Dispatch to see if he could look at stuff for me and he confirmed we got bag total the weight of some cargo thru close out but no load remarks. As a side bar I spoke with Name1 on the Hazmat hotline and he stated that company had to manually override scanner to allow for DG and animal at same time. Could this be why we didn't get load remarks? After about 10 minutes; [a] ramp agent returned but paced. He did not get back on intercom during most of this but when he did I explained he had a couple options. We could do a return to gate or they could give me a paper CLR (Cargo Load Report) thru [the]  window if they could not fix it with [the] scanner. He radioed someone and a minute or so later a supervisor came out of an office and did not look happy. He had a wad of paper. He came to FO side and tossed the wad of paper thru window which ended up being the NOTOC for the dry ice. At about the same time we received the load remarks and I was focused on the DG the live animal got past me. I did not do this on purpose. At the time I was more upset with blocking out without the knowledge of DG on board and focused on making sure I had all my correct paperwork and it matched since I had DG. We also had the remark 'EXST:9A'. This threw me for a loop because I didn't know what it meant. We figured it out to be that a passenger had bought a seat onboard a raft for an animal which I already knew about because of gate agents and flight attendants. We had wasted enough time so I decided to continue with the push. We had a runway change on taxi out so I focused on getting thru that and we as a crew focused on operating safely until we were in a low workload environment to talk about it again. At cruise I was filling out incident report for not getting NOTOC when I was talking my narrative out loud the FO was looking at [the] FOM and said we have both an animal and DG on board and he just realized it as he was reading and telling me. We immediately contacted Dispatch who advised us to go to ZZZ2 or ZZZ3 and divert. I chose ZZZ2. I alerted [the] flight attendants and we landed in ZZZ2 without further incident. There was confusion on [the] ground in ZZZ2 as to which item should continue with us. The bird or dry ice. I called Dispatch again and they chose the dry ice and while I was talking to ramp they said company wanted to keep bird to ZZZ1. While checking packages manually in cargo bin I discovered the DG also contained Blood. UN3373. After OPS and company agreed; we departed to ZZZ1 without further incident. After landing I called Hazmat hotline and submitted pictures of bird and DG and ACARS remarks to company.I did not purposefully depart without NOTOC or depart consciously knowing we had dry ice and a bird in same bin. I know it's one or the other. I was just hyper focused on being legal that I missed connecting the two together. I believe I realize now that I can take as much time as I need to make good decisions. No need to rush. I did and it got me nowhere. I hope someone can imagine getting a wadof paper thrown into flight deck and the distractions of finally realizing the gravity of I had almost departed without knowing what was in cargo bin. I had always believed there were safeguards in place to prevent this from happening. This is the first time in 15 years of safe flying I've had to divert for a bad decision I made. I feel horrible and I'm glad the animal was still alive. I know it could have been much worse. I believe this flight had a happy outcome because of Dispatch and my crew. I tried to thank them but I cannot thank them enough.

column121: Loss of control during student simulated soft field takeoff involving Diamond Aircraft Industries DA20 aircraft; began to depart from Runway XX; by practicing a simulated soft field takeoff. On board the aircraft were an instructor and student. The primary focus of this dual exercise was for the student to refine the skills needed to perform a simulated soft field takeoff required as a private pilot task for FAA-S-ACS-6B. Prior to the flight the instructor thoroughly briefed the student on the proper exchange of flight controls through several exercises and it was clear to the student. After practicing the takeoff the first time; where the student made the mistake of keeping the stick fully aft; instead of slowly reducing back pressure once in ground effect; the student kept the stick in a full aft position creating a takeoff stall. The instructor was able to recover the aircraft by taking the controls and breaking the stall by lowering the angle of attack and regaining airspeed appropriate for a positive rate of climb. After the unsatisfactory performance of the soft field takeoff; the instructor decided to give the student another chance exercising a simulated soft field takeoff after completing several traffic patterns. Prior to taxiing Runway XX for takeoff the instructor asked the student how are you going to perform the soft field takeoff.  The student responded with the proper procedure and the instructor reminded the student of his mistake last time he attempted a soft field takeoff. The student properly taxied to runway centerline using constant back pressure on the stick and increased throttle to full power.  The student then used the proper right rudder pressure to compensate for P-factor. Once 500 feet down the runway; the airplane was able to get into ground effect however the aircraft was too slow pitch for Vx and after the instructor stated 'release the back pressure slowly' the student increased the pitch up and kept constant right rudder (stalling the airplane again). At this point the instructor took the controls and said abruptly 'my flight controls!' twice. The student failed to positively exchange flight controls to the instructor and locking the grip and control inputs contrary to the instructors. This lead to the plane striking the right wing on the runway pointing and losing control of the aircraft over the grass field to the right of Runway XX.  The instructor then overpowered the students control movements to counter a possible cartwheeling right prop strike; banked left while reducing the throttle to idle which caused the airplane to strike its left wing on the grass where it landed.  The instructor immediately secured the aircraft; preventing any chances of an onboard fire. Both the student and instructor survived with no injuries. It is unclear what total damage was done to the plane however there was visible damage to both wings.

column121: I was scheduled to complete 3 takeoff and landings for currency.  The flight was completed uneventfully.  Today; I was contacted by a manager that it was discovered the aircraft registration had expired.  Typically we would be flying this aircraft frequently; but all of the passenger flights had been cancelled the remainder of the year due to COVID concerns. Crews (myself included) are scheduled at various times to complete currency takeoff and landings.  While we checked to make sure the registration was on board during our preflight; we did not notice that the date had expired.  When this was just discovered by management and maintenance of the expirations; our company self-notified to the appropriate agency.There are several factors that contributed to this. I had my own contribution to this error by not verifying the date on the registration was current. It was determined the paperwork got mailed to a central location to the company and not directly to our hangar location. With COVID causing a reduced workforce in the location of mail delivery; we never got the paperwork forwarded of renewal and it wasn't until the second notification (delayed by a several weeks) that we got the notification. We have also been shifting different service providers for flight/trip planning and never was a flag raised that we were close to expiration on this document. We also discovered this wasn't tracked specifically on a maintenance program. Lastly; we would typically fly an international trip several times a year (but haven't flown any in 2020) that the registration would also be copied and verified current. There was not just one; but several contributing factors to this error.  All these actions have already been corrected to prevent a future re occurrence. I have also learned from this that I made an assumption when checking to make sure the registration was on board that it was current; and that I didn't verify the date because I assumed it was tracked by several methods.  The take away that I have from this; even if I assumed somebody else has tracked and checked some of the items that was included on our interior inspection preflight; I need to be more detailed on some of my checks. This is even more prevalent in the current times when the flight hours are drastically reduced.
column123: I flew an aircraft with an expired registration for landing currency. I ensured that the document was on board; but am guilty of not checking the date. This is not an excuse for my actions; but I do believe it is a contributing factor in this event happening.We have already implemented corrective actions to ensure this never happens again. We hired a company to automatically renew our registrations and have them delivered directly to our hangar. Additional training and language will be added to our company manuals to emphasize the need to ensure that we have valid and current documents on board for every flight.

He came back and said that he couldn't continue the climb to 17000 ft. and would need to go back down to 15000 ft. He then had said he needed lower and I told him I had opposite direction traffic at 14000 ft. so if he needed lower I would need to turn him to the south. He said okay so I turned him to a 160 heading and gave him 14000 ft. He then said 'I stalled' and I noticed he began a rapid descent. I still had other aircraft and did a quick traffic scan and thought he was in a dive to regain airspeed to pull out of the stall. I thought the most helpful transmission I could give was to tell him what my MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) in the area was so if he was IMC he would know roughly what altitude he would impact the ground so he could plan his stall recovery dive accordingly. I decided in that moment to say only that and not use radio time/overwhelm him with the low altitude alert. I also wanted to leave the frequency open so he could make any requests like is there a road nearby to crash on or ask for a pilots assistance or recommendations. I thought he had seconds to a minute to live and felt like I needed to leave the frequency open. I also looked around for a topographical map of the ZZZ1 area which has disappeared or our atlas which is hard to locate so if he made a request of where the lowest possible terrain area or roads were. He pulled out of the dive; came back up on frequency; mentioned he didn't want to climb back into the clouds so I instructed him that I couldn't leave home IFR under the MIA. I asked if he was VMC; he said yes so I quickly gave him the option of canceling IFR and switching to VFR flight following so he could stay below the clouds and remain clear of ice. He lived.

column121: This is now the 4th Practice Approach (PA) issue we have documented in the past 30 days. ZZZ1 (TRACON) continues to not coordinate PA according to our LOA. They are introducing risk to the NAS by leading pilots to believe they are cleared for a PA and creating uncertainty. LC (Local Control) would have time to anticipate and better accommodate this pilot if ZZZ1 would have simply coordinated this procedure. Due to ZZZ1 not following their requirement in the LOA they are jeopardizing safety and not providing a good service to the flying public. We must get the answers to the following questions before we can move forward. Why did ZZZ1 issue a Practice Approach Letter to Airmen (PALTA) about 3 years ago? What are the reasons for it not reinstating the PALTA? Why was the workforce not briefed or trained on this change? What are the pros and cons of not having a PALTA?On (date); our General Manager signed the now expired PALTA in question. There were many requests from HQ for PA clarification and interpretations on this very topic throughout the past decade.Since the LTA expired on date; we have gradually started to see a thread of confusion among pilots and controllers. The very purpose of having a PALTA was to prevent this from happening. This has led to misinterpretations of many rules within the 7110.65 and the 7110.3. ZZZ ATCT has compiled over 10 falcon replays over the past 10 months that references this very trend and ZZZ2 ATCT has been experiencing similar issues as well. I would like those who review those replays to listen to the disappointment and frustration from the pilots. We are wasting their valuable time and not providing them with the best possible service. It must be clear there are only 3 possible separation rules that can be applied when handling a PA request. These rules are not to be applied by CPC choice at any given moment. 2 out of the 3 rules are defined on whether or not there is an effective LTA that lists your facility. With that being said; CPC and pilots must be trained and aware of these differences. Separation Rules (7110.65) a.1 [states that] IFR aircraft practicing instrument approaches must be afforded approved separation in accordance with Chapter 3; Chapter 4; Chapter 5; Chapter 6; and Chapter 7 minima until the aircraft lands; and the flight is terminated; or the pilot cancels the flight plan. For this argument we have not discovered any issues when complying.[Section] a.2 [states that] where procedures require application of IFR separation to VFR aircraft practicing instrument approaches; IFR separation in accordance with Chapter 3; Chapter 4; Chapter 5; Chapter 6; and Chapter 7 must be provided. Controller responsibility for separation begins at the point where the approach clearance becomes effective. Except for super or heavy aircraft; 500 ft. vertical separation may be applied between VFR aircraft and between a VFR and an IFR aircraft.The issue we have is some CPC are still following a.2 and some a.3. We must train our workforce on which they are to follow; which is dictated on whether or not we have an LTA. We can't allow them to apply a mixture of both these rules. For 2 years our effective LTA has dictated and conditioned pilots; instructors; students; examiners; and CPC that we must follow a.2. This basically implied to all users that they were going to be treated as if they were IFR doing a VFR PA. This was implemented to give VFR pilots and instructors the full experience so they can perfect the instrument approach procedures they are trying to practice. Various air traffic incidents have indicated the necessity for adoption of measures to achieve more organized and controlled operations where practice instrument approaches are conducted. Practice instrument approaches are considered to be instrument approaches made by either a VFR aircraft not on an IFR flight plan or an aircraft on an IFR flight plan. To achieve this and thereby enhance air safety; it is company policy to provide for separation of such operations at locations where approach control facilities are located and; as resources permit; at certain other locations served by ARTCCs or parent approach control facilities.We need to understand that a.2 is simple for all users involved and reduces risk to the NAS. Not to mention it provides a great and safe service to the flying public. The experience we afford the users when utilizing a.2 enhances safety; achieves a more organized and controlled operations where practice instrument approaches are conducted.[Section] a.3 [states] where separation services are not provided to VFR aircraft practicing instrument approaches; the controller must instruct the pilot to maintain VFR; advise the pilot that separation services are not provided; and provide traffic information or advise the pilot to contact the appropriate facility.The implementation of a.2 and the LTA requirement was to detour facilities from using this rule if they have existing resources. This rule creates confusing and is why we are now seeing unsafe trends since our LTA expired about a year ago. Some CPCs are following this rule and are lead to believe that no coordination is needed because they are not clearly them for the approach as they would when utilizing a.2. Some CPCs are still following a.2 and some are doing a mixture of both. We must train our workforce on which procedures must be followed when handling PA. We also need to brief the flying public as well. If ZZZ1 is not going to reinstate the LTA; all the LOAs with the towered airports listed in the LTA must be amended with detailed procedures on dealing with PA approaches; which include coordination requirements. I'm certain Mission Support would support my argument that we should follow a.2 and reinstate our LTA to achieve more organized and controlled operations where practice instrument approaches are conducted. The volume of VFR traffic in the ZZZ1 is on an upward trend and the last thing we need is uncertainty. We also must ask ourselves; why do most all other major approach control facilities in the NAS choose to issue a PALTA to enhance safety? Having the ability to issue a PALTA was given to us to migrate the very issue we are now having. By not choosing to issue a PALTA; ZZZ1 is jeopardizing safety by not creating a more organized environment where PA are being conducted. We understand that the approach control ATM has the discretion on whether or not they need to issue a PALTA however it is important that the workforce understands why they are making this decision. Especially when the data shows that we are now having mass confusion among pilots and CPC. A PALTA will mitigate this confusion immediately. Choosing to not reinstate an LTA on the sole purpose of pilot and CPC complaints is ludicrous and negligent. We did not see this chaos when the LTA was effective.   Over the past 2 years ZZZ ATCT has noticed and documented a trend with PA and other facility are starting to notice as well. Our workforce and all the users involved deserve the best possible service and training. Why are we choosing not to provide pilots with a.2 service and waste their valuable time with a subpar service (a.3) instead? I'm asking that the national recurrent training team design a course on this very argument.
