column121: I listened to the AWOS and noted wind at 5mph from 90 degrees with gusting to 10mph. On final approach for landing; I experienced light to moderate wind gusts that bounced the aircraft around a bit. Under those conditions; I decided to limit flaps to 20 degrees and maintain a slightly higher airspeed since the runway length was over 6;000 ft. and gusting was intermittent. Upon crossing over the runway threshold at 65kts; I reduced power to idle and flared 10 feet over the runway. The aircraft floated in the ground effect for a long distance and ultimately when the wheels made contact it bounced up into the air again and floated further in ground effect. At that moment; a wind gust pushed the tail to the left. I tried to correct with opposite rudder but the deflection did not correct the alignment before the wheels made contact with the runway. The aircraft was by then oriented at a 25-30 degree angle to the right of runway centerline. The aircraft then bolted violently to the right and rolled quickly off the runway into the grass; heading toward a rock lined; 4-ft deep drainage ditch just beyond a taxiway. As I attempted to maneuver the rolling aircraft back to the left; it began to skid and tip over to the right. I righted the aircraft to avoid driving the right wing and nose into the ground and potentially flipping the aircraft; but by then my only choice was to either roll toward the ditch or in the direction of hangars to the right. I braked but wasn't able to stop before the aircraft rolled into the ditch.The left wingtip; propeller and landing gear received damage. No injuries to myself or damage to airport property resulted. I immediately contacted the aircraft owner and airport authorities; who arrived to the scene quickly to assess the situation. The airport manager confirmed no damage to airport property. The aircraft owner and airport manager coordinated to make arrangements to remove the aircraft from the ditch.

column121: Prior to flight; I queried my flight school about the status of the aircraft following an ECU (engine control unit) B failure on the left engine I had experienced during a previous flight. They had a flight instructor meet with me before the flight and he described an operating procedure that they allegedly received from the aircraft manufacturer. This procedure included avoiding touch-and-go landings and keeping the engines below 1200 rpm on the ground. As I had not planned for any touch-and-go landings; I was not worried about adhering to that requirement. However; I found it difficult to adhere to the advice I received about keeping the engines below 1200 rpm while on the ground. The airplane itself idles at 900 rpm and that gives me very little throttle to work with in order to get the airplane to move. However; I was able to successfully taxi the airplane out of its home airport at ZZZ while adhering to this requirement. The flight to ZZZ1 went smoothly and I encountered no problems. However; I found it necessary to bring the airplane above 1200 RPM to taxi to the runway while attempting to leave ZZZ1. Due in part to the relatively high density altitude of 7000 feet combined with the upsloping taxiway out of ZZZ1; I had to bring the engines up to approximately 1700 RPM to taxi to the runway. I ran the before takeoff checklist before takeoff; which included an ECU health test on both engines. The aircraft indicated no problems with ECU health prior to takeoff.With an aircraft inbound with intentions to land in the opposite direction from the runway I intended to use for takeoff; I began my takeoff roll after coordinating with the incoming aircraft via CTAF. At approximately 60 knots and 1/2 way down the runway; I noticed a dual ECU failure on the right engine. I elected to continue the takeoff since the ability to stop in the remaining distance was questionable; and the severe dropoff at the end of the runway increased the hazard to me should I be unable to stop. The engine was still producing power; but I noted it was maxed at 80% load on the right engine and the prop was overspeeding at approximately 2200 RPM. I climbed to approximately 1000 feet AGL before beginning my troubleshoot procedure. I reduced power to approximately 65% load to prevent the overspeeding of the propeller and pulled out the Dual ECU Failure emergency checklist. I climbed to an altitude that would ensure safe single-engine diversion to ZZZ2 airport and followed the procedure; which called for reducing the power to zero on the problematic engine and bringing it back up to full power. Upon following this procedure; both of the ECU Failure warnings on the right engine disappeared and I monitored the engine instruments to verify proper operation. The problem seemingly cleared itself and I proceeded with my flight to the aircraft's home base in ZZZ. I encountered no more issues for the rest of the flight.At aircraft check-in; I wrote up the aircraft with an abbreviated description of my incident and left my phone number with the flight school in case they had any questions for me regarding my incident. I checked on the progress of the aircraft's maintenance about a week later and discovered that no one had translated my writeup of the aircraft to the electronic squawk list visible online. I asked what was being done to fix the problem and my flight school told me they could not replicate the problem and considered the aircraft safe. I became agitated and declared that I believe that by not putting my write-up in the squawk list and continuing to rent the airplane to potentially unsuspecting pilots that they are in effect renting an unsafe airplane. In what I feel is an act of retaliation for my challenge to their concern for safe operation of their aircraft; the flight school then pulled my qualifications on the airplane and refused to rent it to me (and only me; as far as I am aware) until I had completed another checkout with one of their instructors. As of date the aircraft is still being rented; and no mention of my incident has been written down and made available for other pilots.I feel that by renting an aircraft with the requirement to operate the aircraft in a manner inconsistent with the approved flight manual that they are subjecting their renters to unnecessary and avoidable risk. I do not feel as though company in ZZZ has the same concern for safety that I do and I have ceased my business there. I only worry that another pilot may encounter the same problem that I had with a different outcome.

column121: I was riding in the back of the aircraft on the flight from ZZZ to DEN. On arrival; the descent path took the aircraft straight through the middle of the enormous smoke column from the large wildfire in Colorado. The cabin immediately filled with smoke dense enough to make my eyes water and my throat burn. At the same time; there was nothing but dark orange light in the windows. The light; while not a Safety concern; was certainly eerie. Several passengers were visibly concerned and some pressed their call buttons to ask the Flight Attendant about the situation. We were in the column for several minutes. I was a little surprised when we landed in DEN to look back and realize that there were no other clouds in the sky. The smoke column looked; for all intents and purposes; like a thunderstorm. In my opinion; based on my experience in wildland fire fighting aviation; it would have been reasonable and prudent to ask for a deviation around the smoke column just as any of us would have for a thunderstorm. I've never been certain whether there is actually an aircraft Safety concern regarding flying through dense wood smoke but based on what I saw in the back of the aircraft yesterday there's definitely a passenger comfort concern. It might be worth addressing this in some kind of publication to the pilots.

column121: During descent to ZZZ for visual approach; FO PF (First Officer Pilot Flying); CA PM (Captain Pilot Monitoring). Crew called the airfield in sight and was frequency changed to tower. Once on tower frequency; we heard Tower call a Seneca directing them to clear the approach path of runway XX. The next call was to a departing aircraft calling out our aircraft for separation which they did not see us. TWR then called our aircraft saying traffic 12 o'clock 3600 ft. north northeast bound. We responded with leveling and we have them on TCAS. Noting on TCAS the aircraft climbing toward us and it's very close proximity and rapid closure rate; we leveled our aircraft. The approaching TCAS target continued climbing from less than 1;000 ft. below us at our 12 o'clock into our flight path rapidly. TCAS quickly displayed a climb for the RA OF 3;000 fpm. The PF added thrust to TO (Takeoff) power and climbed with the RA at 3;000 fpm. The PM called tower notifying them we were responding to an RA. The TCAS target continued climbing passing 400 ft. directly under the aircraft from the 12 o'clock position to the 6 o'clock position. After the RA was complete; the crew began the descent again coordinating with tower for a right 360 degree turn in order to reestablish the approach. The crew landed on runway XX without further incident. No heavy aircraft loading during climb and no passenger complaints on landing. No PA's were made to passengers [in] reference [to] this event.Frequency changed from approach to tower at 10 miles for the visual without any traffic notifications. Contacting tower we were given a traffic advisory with less than a 1;000 ft. separation descending while traffic climbed with a rate of closure of at least 400 knots.Before being given a frequency change by approach control crews should be given traffic advisories in the area in order to build situational awareness.
column123: While descending into ZZZ out of approximately 3500 ft. MSL; and on about a 10 mile left base for XX; we received an advisory and then an RA to climb. I switched to tower and heard the tower advising another aircraft to stay clear of the approach area. I checked in and was cleared to land. The tower then advised a Seneca that he needed to clear the approach area due to our approach and was advised to turn left. We then received a traffic advisory from the tower that was simultaneous with TCAS traffic alert; followed shortly by a RA to climb. I was looking outside and did not see the conflicting aircraft. The FO advised it passed underneath approximately 400 ft. below us. The entire event took less than 15 seconds as best I can recall. At that point we advised the tower we had complied with an RA and that we were high and needed a right 360 to re-establish on the approach. The tower responded that where we were was class E airspace and that the opposing Aircraft was not under radar control; and words to the affect that we were not in his airspace. He cleared us for the maneuver and again cleared us to land. Once on the ground we advised the tower via ground frequency that we would be filing a report for a near miss.Changed from approach control to tower after reporting field in sight without being given any traffic advisories before the frequency change. Also departing conflict aircraft departing along approach corridor.Approach controller should coordinate with tower to ensure approach path is clear prior to allowing frequency change.

column121: I'm not sure the best way to address this; so I figured I would write a report to document this event. On departure from ZZZ; the flap handle became momentarily stuck in the Flaps 20 detent. It required excessive; and unusual amounts of force to select the flaps from the takeoff setting of 20; to flaps 8 during the climb sequence. After landing I documented the maintenance irregularity per FOM Airworthiness procedures. The write up in the maintenance log I submitted was 'While selecting flaps from 20 to 8 on departure; flap handle sticks in the 20 position; requires excessive force to move to flaps 8.' I then left the aircraft in the care of the next crew. I explained to the Captain the Maintenance discrepancy. After getting home; and plugging my iPad in to charge; I happened to see the flight; and out of curiosity decided to review the Maintenance Log again to see what they did to address the discrepancy. In my professional opinion; an incorrect corrective action was applied. The Maintenance corrective action states. 'The CRJ-200 flap selector has a built in gate between flaps 8 and flaps 20 that requires the operator to depress the lever when passing the gate. This is normal operation. Ok for continued service.' This is not true however. There is a gate that prevents selecting flaps past 20; without depressing the flap handle during flap extension; and a gate at flaps 8 to prevent retraction past flaps 8 in the event of a go around and during normal climb flap retraction. There is not a need to depress the flap handle to move it from 20 to 8 during flap retraction however; as the corrective action states. According to the CRJ PRM (Pilot Reference Manual) for the CRJ-200; it states on page 9-18 'Two flap gates are incorporated within the flap lever quadrant. The forward gate at the 8-degree setting minimizes the possibly of accidental flap selection to 0 degrees during a go-around procedure. The rearward gate at the 20 degree setting; minimizes the risk of Vfe (Flaps 30) being exceeded.' I'm not sure how to address this further; but I do not believe this discrepancy was appropriately dealt with by our maintenance. Furthermore; I do not believe the mechanic that submitted this corrective action has a full and appropriate understanding of the CRJ flap handle mechanics and operation; and it might be appropriate to consider passing this information to Maintenance for a bulletin or some sort of 'heads up.' The CRJ-200 is sensitive to flap fail events; and this is a critical component to the flap system; it's important for it to work properly and without issue. We don't want the flap handle getting stuck between detents; or preventing a crew from selecting flaps 8 appropriately in the event of a go-around.Improper procedure applied by maintenance. Failure of maintenance personnel to fully understand the flap handle flight control system and operational mechanics. Most likely added pressure to get the next flight out on time.I would suggest first and foremost that this aircraft is pulled out of service; properly inspected; and fixed if necessary. The maintenance write up does not even say that the system was properly ops checked. It was very simply ignored by the maintenance personnel attending to the write up; and not properly inspected or checked. I believe that a maintenance bulletin describing the correct operation of the CRJ-200 flap handle and the flap gates would potentially help further the understanding of our maintenance personnel to be able to properly address this write up.

column121: I was PM for this leg back to ZZZ1. We were cleared for takeoff on Runway XX; lined up on the runway; and I gave the controls to the FO. He set the thrust levers to CLIMB and called 'set thrust.' I checked the stack and verified the N1 indications were in the carats and stated 'thrust set.' I failed to push the thrust levers into the TOGA detent and neither of us noticed. The remainder of the takeoff was uneventful. When performing the after takeoff flow I realized that the thrust levers were already in the climb detent.This was my first trip on the type aircraft since being checked out earlier this month. I have exclusively flown the different version of aircraft type for the last X months and have not become accustomed to setting the thrust in Aircraft X compared to the previous type aircraft. I was a type Y aircraft FO before upgrading into this type aircraft so my time in all three variants is very limited. I had only done three legs in this type aircraft as PM before today; the rest of the legs being as PF to practice landings. My habit of pushing the thrust levers past the climb detent and into the TOGA detent has not been set yet; as for the majority of my legs I was only setting them to CLIMB; then the PM pushing them up to TOGA before I put my hand back.I need to fly this type aircraft more often to become/stay proficient. It also would have been better to do OE in this type of aircraft sooner to start those habits earlier and not get into such a groove in only the other type aircraft. I guarantee I will never make the same mistake again as it was quite a shock when I realized what I had/had not done.

I then asked the Captain to see if he could feel the same thing.  We exchanged controls; and he confirmed that the controls were sticky about the pitch axis.  We then exchanged control of the airplane back; and I resumed flying the airplane.  The Captain then requested immediate vector to the nearest airport.  ATC then gave us a vector to ZZZ and a descent altitude.  We then engaged the yaw-damp; but left the autopilot off.  During the descent; we had at least four more events where the flight controls appeared to be stuck.  Each time I was able to over-power the control.  I also noticed that once I freed the controls; they appeared to be freed for 20-30 seconds.  During the descent; I was monitoring the outside temperature to detect when we got to warmer air; as I was concerned that all the rain that we had at ZZZ may have frozen and caused the controls to momentarily freeze.  After we passed the freezing level; I did not notice any more problems with the pitch control.  After landing at ZZZ; we de-planed the passengers at [the] FBO. column121: Filed flight plan about 20 minutes before calling to see if flight plan was in the system. I informed Ground Control that I would pick it up in the air but was just checking to see if it had arrived.  Ground did not have flight plan so I started up and taxied to runway figuring it would be out by the time we were at the hold line. Called at the runway hold line and still no flight plan - Ground suggested I just take off and have the Departure Controller enter one for me.  Just to be safe I quickly filed another one on my phone; did my checks and when I called for takeoff they told me it had just come through.  I had filed NAVHO intersection then BLD VOR on the first flight plan; then just direct BLD VOR on the second - rest of route to ZZZ the same for both plans.On VFR climb I skipped NAVJO because I thought it was the second flight plan that had popped up on the system.  Phoenix Approach was in a long conversation with a VFR plane so couldn't contact until I was at 14;500 feet - climbing to 16;500.  They told me I was almost out of their airspace and to call ABQ Center.  Level at 16;500 I called ABQ and they cleared us to ZZZ as filed.  Here's where there was a problem.  Just to be safe I asked if I should be going direct NAVHO then BLD and the controller said 'affirmative' as I was climbing to FL280.  I knew I wasn't at NAVHO yet so entered it in as 'NAVJO' (incorrect).  I noticed that the needle pointed over 30 degrees to the right as I engaged NAV - figuring something was wrong I disengaged NAV and turned back to something close to direct BLD and asked if I could just go direct BLD which I was given.  NAVHO was pretty much on a direct line from FLG to BLD so I was doing okay before entering 'NAVJO' which is way up to the North.Looking at the track log I never was more than 17 degrees off and that was for as long as it took to reverse the turn; but this was embarrassing.  Don't want to do this kind of thing when departing a NY Metro area airport.  Contributing factors:  Flight plan late arriving at FLG.  My desire to do a quick turn and keep the boss happy - this was a fuel stop.  Misspelling 'NAVHO' because I was rushing - trying to keep the controller happy.  Two flight plans in the system; each with a different initial fix.  I neglected to enter NAVJO because it would be departing VFR and it was pretty close to the airport. Ways to prevent this from recurring:  File my flight plans earlier just in case - even if I'm not sure we will use it.  I thought we may be able to make it all the way to ZZZ so didn't file the plan for departing from FLG (fuel stop).  Don't be so quick to engage NAV - make sure it looks correct first.  Don't rush when entering waypoints - if I had entered with the correct spelling there would not have been more than a few degree turn to the left involved.  Enter all the fixes when departing VFR - don't assume you won't get one of them.

Additionally; the Ground controller did not provide instruction nor information regarding the exiting regional jet to us; [with] no time for us to query either. Though dark; our aircraft lighting was on and operating normally; bright LED navigation lights; beacon; and taxi light. I will continue to be vigilant throughout every phase of flight.

column123: Completed all briefings prior to approach. We were expecting a VFR approach but briefed like full IFR approach and were prepared for the weather to change. We were preparing for a normal approach and landing to Runway XXL. ATIS Bravo showed three miles and overcast 4100 feet. ATIS BRAVO also advised RCC CODE 5-5-5 for Runways XXR; XXL; XYL. Planned a flap 15 landing. We used conservative number of CODE 4 RCC giving us Autobrakes 2; 1530 stopping margin. In essence 3000 feet; touchdown zone being the most restrictive of the 12;000 foot runway. On final approach;  Tower stated Braking Action Good to RJ in front of us.We landing uneventfully. I believe we landed within 3;000 TDZE; however; I do remember floating a little with 10 knots ice additive. We did not have any markings visible outside center line do to white snow. Decelerated to 60 knots; F/O called 60 knots. I stowed the thrust reversers and pressed brakes to disconnect autobrakes. Nothing seemed unusual at that point. Deceleration rate seemed normal up to that point. Tower stated: 'Roll to end; aircraft behind you two-mile final.'I depressed brakes to further decelerate and realized there was zero braking available. I stated 'No brakes' to F/O a couple of times. F/O immediately told Tower and aircraft behind us went around. I extended full reverse thrust again to try and get aircraft stopped. We drifted about 45 degrees toward intended exit. We never left hard surface of runway/taxiway. I briefed F/O to contact Ground immediately and notify 'NILL BRAKING LAST THIRD OF RUNWAY XXL.'I also had F/O ask for inspection of runway/taxiway lights to make sure aircraft had no damage before we taxied any further. He also notified Company Ops what had just occurred. I briefed what had happened to Passengers on PA. ZZZ Ground Ops notified there were no runway/taxiway lights damaged. We taxied aircraft to gate without any further issues. Maintenance was waiting for us at gate and we described what had occurred. They inspected aircraft and found an actual blue taxiway light laying on top of wheel carriage on right main. There was no aircraft damage noted by the Maintenance inspection. I put a note in logbook and we deadheaded to ZZZ1.I take briefings very seriously. This was not the type of flight that either Pilot was out of loop or just not having a bad day. We were configured at the marker and on speed the whole time on approach. I may have floated a little do to 10 knot increase of VREF. The ATIS reports from ZZZ were RCC 5-5-5. The two previous aircraft reports BRAG. The only difference was; the two previous aircraft exited 2nd high speed. We rolled past the second high speed for passenger comfort. We never expected NIL braking under light snow covered runway in front of us. The airport needs to actually test the runway; if they're going to advertise 5-GOOD. It was one of the worst feelings a Pilot can have realizing he/she has lost effective control of an aircraft. Had I not redeployed the thrust reversers; I believe we would have encountered aircraft damage and maybe even injuries even though aircraft would have been exiting hard surface at a slow speed. I am actually shocked the runway had not been prepared for arrivals with so much equipment and men available at that airport. Very disappointed.

column121: Climbing out; approximately XX00Z; the left engine had loss of thrust associated with compressor stall / surges. Flight attendants rang the call button and indicated they heard loud banging and wanted to verify we heard the same. We shallowed our climb then leveled off at FL 280 and [advised ATC]. Subsequent flight attendant chime indicated they saw flames had extended aft of the #1 engine. We had already begun to tackle the surge / stall QRC followed by QRH checklist when they called advised of flames. We recognized and agreed that ZZZ was our best option due to proximity (80 miles roughly ) off our nose with optimum field capabilities. We coordinated with flight attendants and talked with a non-rev commuting Company Captain who had been sitting on left side of cabin and had seen the flames. During this process; we coordinated with ATC for direct and began a descent to ZZZ [and] fired off a quick message to Dispatch indicating engine malfunction and plan to divert. We coordinated with crew of the precautionary landing and advised passengers of our intentions. In the descent we completed the appropriate checklists; acquired the [weight and balance] data for landing in addition to brake cooling then were vectored for a visual approach to [Runway] XXL. We landed uneventfully and taxied clear of the runway and we were met by Fire and Rescue. We shut down the #1 engine and awaited CFR to evaluate. CFR gave us the all clear and we taxied to gate and began to coordinate with all appropriate personnel.
column123: Normal climbout passing FL 282.  Initially heard banging outside of aircraft followed by a reduction in climb; decreasing airspeed and aircraft vibration.  Immediately followed by a call from the A F/A (flight attendant) reporting flame emanating from #1 engine.  Engine problem was confirmed in the cockpit by high temp (800 EGT) and diminished N1.  My F/O (First Officer) immediately notified ATC that we have an engine issue and need to maintain FL 280. I told him to [request priority] at that time. I reduced the thrust lever to observe changes in engine indications. The vibrations ceased and temperature reduction. We both believed we had a compressor stall. We were holding FL 280 on one engine; albeit with excessive thrust on #2 engine.  F/O asked for lower and we were cleared to FL 240. We had two jumpseaters onboard; so I got an experienced set of eyes on the engine.  He confirmed all that we knew and that the engine no longer had flames coming from the tailpipe. Assessing the non-normal together; I called for the QRC (quick reference checklist) Engine Limit or Surge or Stall Checklist.  The QRH (quick reference handbook) confirmed our assessment. We completed down to Step X (QRH) at that point. An engine shutdown was not required; but thrust lever remained at idle for remainder of flight.  ZZZ was 80 miles from our present position and we agreed was the nearest suitable airport.  ATC cleared us direct. While I was PF (pilot flying); F/O communicated with F/A's and passengers.  I sent a message to Dispatch about our diversion.  We ran the Diversion Checklist.  F/O ran weight and balance data for a 'One Engine Inoperative' approach and landing data.  We planned for and flew a 'One Engine Inoperative Landing'.  An uneventful landing in ZZZ culminated with a check of the engine/damage by Emergency Personnel.  We taxied under our own power to the gate.

In the curriculum; it shows the initial 3 sims all start engines running on the runway. There is no practicing flows; FMS work on the ground; starting engines; or normal ground ops getting to the runway which are some of the most high risk areas. There is no time built into the curriculum to work on procedures for people that have [not] flown for 8-9 months and didn't have much recency.I feel the company is focused on pushing through as many people through as quickly as possible when the company let them lose currency. I don't feel that the new re-qualification X course is appropriate or safe for all pilots that can be trained under it. column121: We flew the airplane in from ZZZ1 on Flight ABC; arriving late at XA:05L. We were late due to the previous flight arriving late into ZZZ1 and then circuitous ATC routing for an arrival from the NE (ZZZZZ Intersection; ZZZZZ1 STAR). Because of our late arrival our outbound flight was designated a quick turn. During this Pandemic; NO flight should be designated a quick turn or the time required to accomplish a quick turn should be greatly increased. During this Pandemic; designating a flight a quick turn leads to all the well-intentioned folks on the ground becoming rushed. Operations designates blame if the quick turn is not accomplished in the allotted time and this further complicates and rushes activities. Cleaning is rushed or inadequate; time required to spray the aircraft is not accounted for in the quick turn time. Catering is rushed; deplaning and boarding take much longer during the Pandemic; gate agents become rushed and mechanics are rushed to fix or defer any maintenance issues. This rushing leads to intense time pressure; mistakes in judgment and errors in execution; all of which could lead to an accident or incident. Fortunately; there was not an accident or an incident on this flight. There were a few errors; however. During the Pandemic; ZZZ Catering has not been boarding any special meals; so the Captain had to leave the airplane to obtain a meal that he could eat. This takes some time to accomplish in a crowded ZZZ Airport around dinner time.During the Pandemic; I (the Captain) accomplish a short pre-flight safety briefing to the passengers with special emphasis on seat belt usage during climbout; descent or during any en-route turbulence and proper mask wear throughout the flight to prevent the spread of COVID. Boarding had been completed; catering was finishing up as I started my PA with the cockpit door closed. The Gate Agent opened the cockpit door and without waiting a beat; announced loudly; 'You got everything you need?'  When I held up my hand to silence the Gate Agent because I was in the middle of making a PA; the Gate Agent turned to the FO and asked him loudly; 'Well; do you got everything you need?'  I stopped making my safety PA; put on my mask and told the Agent that 'I'll be done in a minute; I'd like you to leave the cockpit; so that I can finish making my PA. I'll come let you know when I'm done; please shut the door on your way out.' The Gate Agent turned and left the cockpit; but did not close the cockpit. I got up; slammed the cockpit door shut and made a few loud choice remarks to myself. The choice comments were definitely an error on my part. I composed myself and then finished making my safety PA. Shortly thereafter; I put my mask back on; exited the cockpit and told the Gate Agent that we had everything we needed and the Gate Agent could close the Cabin Door. The Gate Agent closed the cabin door; I returned to the cockpit and we accomplished the Before Push Checklist.I checked in with the ground crew and she told me that catering had noticed some large scratches around Door 1R and that the Mechanic was telling her not to push. I asked to speak with the Mechanic and she promptly put him on the headset. The Mechanic had invalidated our current maintenance release and explained that catering had noticed several large scratches around Door 1R. He would need to measure the scratches and then go check the aircraft maintenance history to see if they had previously been noted and properly recorded. I told the FAs; made an announcement about the delay and turned the seat belt sign off. I asked the FO to call Operations and have them bring the jetway back to the airplane. In a couple of minutes; the Agent returned the jetway to the aircraft and Door 1L was opened. During a Pandemic; it is not the time to keep passengers wearing masks; trapped on an airplane. Just having an opportunity to leave the airplane actually reduces the stress and anxiety to feel the need to do so. 15 minutesinto the delay; a Maintenance Supervisor got on the headset and said we'd have a new maintenance release in 7 - 10 minutes. We got a new maintenance release in about 8 minutes; closed Door 1L; turned on the seat belt sign and pushed back 38 minutes late. We arrived safely in ZZZ3; only 14 minutes late.Before departing; I quickly reviewed the new maintenance release; which looked OK in spite of it not showing a new write-up or a new / previously inspected / signed-off of the scratches around Door 1R. If it's important enough to delay an already late flight by another 25 minutes; it's important enough to write up the scratches or notate that those scratches were previously recorded and within limits. I don't believe there's anything wrong with adding a 2nd written sign-off to a previously recorded or to a verbally added maintenance gripe; but it would be helpful if the flight crew knew about it. Whenever pilots call in a maintenance gripe we are always advised to follow it up. If the rampers or catering verbally reports a maintenance gripe to a mechanic; then that mechanic should likewise have to make a written report of the gripe. He can then appropriately sign it off; defer it or notate as previously inspected. Verbally noting; recording and signing off of a valid maintenance gripe leaves much to be desired. I'll say it again; if it's important enough to delay an already late flight by another 25 minutes; it's important enough to write it up.

column121: After the parking checklist was completed we found a ACARS printout informing us of an overweight landing.  The printout listed the Max Structural Landing weight of 146;300; the actual landing weight section was blank.  Using our ZFW and arrival gate fuel we were approximately 200 pounds overweight on landing.   This overweight landing was due to two shortened routings we received by ATC saving time and fuel.  We completed a post flight debriefing which included a review of the OFP (Off-line Flight Planning) - FMS INIT LOAD section.  The flight was dispatched to land only 568 pounds below max structural landing weight.  We failed to identify this threat before departure or enroute which led to the subsequent error.Our expectation bias of recent low passenger loads and light aircraft combined with a lack of recency of experience was a threat we didn't identify properly.  Plus in past experiences if a potential landing weight concern exists; Dispatchers have highlighted this threat as a note in the OFP.
column123: After arrival to the gate we received an overweight landing message. After reviewing our ZFW and fuel load we determined that we landed approximately 200 lbs over max landing weight. After discussion between the CA and I we agreed a lack of CRM was the ultimate cause of the deviation. My thought process was as follows:Our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 was planned to land almost 1;000 lbs below MLW. As part of my pre-flight planning I always note the spread between both takeoff and landing weight verses the maximum values. A 1;000 lbs gap on landing did not stand out to me as something I would need to worry about. During our flight to ZZZ1 we received a number of shortcuts that shortened our route; and early in the flight we were certainly heavy on the fuel. However; as we neared the top of descent our fuel number vs the HOWGOZIT had dropped and was just several hundred pounds heavy.When requesting the landing data our FMC wt was about 3;000 lbs over MLW; and while it mentally recognized this; I did not verbalize it to make sure the CA was also aware (again in my mind I was not thinking landing weight was going to be an issue). I also did not mention our weight as a potential threat during my arrival briefing.

column121: COVID testing at ZZZ took approximately 45 minutes to complete. Any one individual crew member could probably have gotten through faster; but since most of the crew (pilots and flight attendants) was there at the same time; the process got very slow. The nasal swab was quite invasive. One of the pilots reported great discomfort after his test. He initially felt he was unfit for duty. However; his pain eventually subsided after approximately 15 minutes; and he decided he was fit enough to fly. We blocked-in to ZZZZ. It was complete and utter chaos on the aircraft for the flight attendants. The Purser and the language flight attendants did a tremendous job attempting to help the customers fill out the form. Many of the customers were extremely frustrated by the slow; confusing process. This is something that Customer Service in ZZZ absolutely should have assisted passengers with before departure. There is no reason that they should have waited until arrival in ZZZZ to start this process. It took exactly one hour after block-in to deplane the passengers and crew.After deplaning the crew was required to line up in approximately 6-7 different stations to have various health forms and passports checked; and to have our COVID-19 tests performed. The choice of tests were a nasal swab; a throat swab; or a blood test. After undergoing the uncomfortable nasal swab in ZZZ; most crew members chose the throat swab which was also uncomfortable and caused a lot of gagging; but generally better than the nasal swab. No one chose the blood test. At most of the stations the crew was simply mixed in line with the passengers. We finally exited customs; two and a half hours after block-in.The crew was then escorted on the 15 minute walk to the back service entrance of the hotel. The service entrance was dark; smelly; and in general disrepair. The entire area around the hotel was deserted; and there seemed to be no apparent reason we couldn't be processed in through the front entrance. We finally arrived at our rooms. The entire process took exactly 3 hours from block-in.Due to our late arrival at the hotel; we were unsure if we were going to be fed any dinner. When we initially inquired about our meals; we were told that dinner service [had] ended. It was unsettling to hear that we would not be afforded any meals since we were not allowed to leave our rooms. However; after several phone calls to the hotel/CDC staff by the Captain and the Purser; we were assured that meals would be forthcoming. Two hours and a half hours after arrival at the hotel and over five hours after block-in; meals for the crew started to arrive. Food quantity and quality were acceptable.I don't believe there is much the company can do about the foreign country government's procedures for processing passengers and crew. However; one area we need to immediately improve upon is caring for our customers by helping them to obtain required information prior to departure. This would be extremely helpful in expediting deplaning and preventing confusion and frustration for both customers and flight attendants.Another area we could improve upon is helping crews get through the rigorous process of health inspections and customs processing at ZZZZ. If the government would allow a company representative to be on hand; that would be extremely helpful. Our language flight attendants did their best; but at each station there were numerous question about what documents were needed; and what was to happen next.Hopefully this information will be helpful for upcoming passenger flights from the U.S. to ZZZZ.
column123: I got the bag of food and a list for the layover. I'll address each item on the layover list included in the bag.1. Let me start by saying this is the most slimy disgusting hotel I have ever stayed at. It is the ZZZZ1 airport hotel. I don't know who reviewed the hotel; but it is very run down; and lack of maintenance is very apparent; and feel that the conditions are not safe. We should not have any layovers in City Y as long as the COVID testing procedures are in effect and the government insists on keeping crews at this hotel.2. The internet at the hotel is so slow it is not usable. I am unable to log into company system.3. The hot oatmeal in the food bag is not edible; there is no safe water at the hotel; and no way to heat the water. The water is not safe to drink. They do offer bottled water on check-in. 4. We blocked in. We didn't get to the rooms till 3 hours [later]. This is time I am still on duty; but is not recognized.5. We were required to undergo another round of COVID tests on arrival. I asked for and was granted the mouth swab; a few flight attendants asked for this instead of the nasal probe and were denied. On the way to the testing; they wanted us to leave our bags unattended while we went outside; to the testing center. I said; no; we will not leave our bags unattended as it was a security issue. They were not gentle with the nasal probes. Several flight attendants had sore noses after the tests; and were crying. Many said they will not come to ZZZZ again because of the invasiveness of the testing. One pilot was taken away for further scrutiny at one customs station. We were never told why. I hung back to make sure he was not taken somewhere else. I strongly recommend to not ever leave any crew behind. Stay together.6. No company representatives were in attendance of our arrival; at least none I could tell. We could not tell who was who. No one knew what we were supposed to do. We finally; after an extensive delay found our security escort through the terminal. It took about an hour to get the passengers off the plane. Many did not have the COVID form filled out ahead of time; and were required to do this before they were let off the plane; which meant we were also held as long as there were passengers on the plane.7. We went through 3 different customs/COVID paperwork stations. At each station we waited for another set of paperwork to be filled out; greatly extending the time required to get to the hotel.8. A customs employee walked us to the hotel to the back entrance. Water damage; moldy; run down hallways; and a rusty elevator that looks like it hasn't been maintained for the last decade was our route.9. The room itself is not too bad; and is as described in the handout; except for temperature control.10. I called several times; and asked the hotel representative about the food; no one had any answers about when or what kind of food would come. Finally; 1.5 hours after we arrived; food was delivered to the room. However; no room service; no menu; no food choices at all. Again; no information of any kind was available.11. No fire sprinklers in the room; meaning it's not safe in the event of an emergency. If you have to leave the room in case of emergency; you do not have a room key and cannot get back into your room.12. Unable to control the temperature in the room. It was uncomfortably warm.13. The time to leave the hotel is set at 2 hours before departure. For a paper XX hour layover; we ended up with [4 hours less] in the room. These times need to be accounted for [to] make sure there is adequate layover time in the room; as well as duty day after block in; and prior to flight planning.In conclusion; the procedures the Country officials have in place for our arrival are excessive and unneeded. Due to the treatment during the COVID tests; I will not be coming back on this trip again. The hotel is abysmal. Nowhere near in contractual compliance. Why [are we] even entertaining allowing flights/layovers here with the disgusting conditions? We should not be staying here and we need to stop this ASAP. No one in charge knows anything about the procedures; or has any answers for our [foreign language] speakers.

column121: Captain (CA) was PF on takeoff from ZZZ [Runway] XR. In the high speed phase; CA air data (airspeed and altitude) blanked out showing flags. Takeoff continued. Missed initial turn on the ZZZZZ departure as both CA and FO lost flight directors. [I] guided CA back to SID using heading bug. Captain transferred controls to me as my air data seemed more reliable. Ran Unreliable Airspeed QRH. Determined that FO side was indeed working and regained automation per the procedure. As CA airspeed and altitude were intermittent; I became PF for rest of flight.Discussed with CA and both agreed as a crew it was safe to continue flight. However; we forgot to discuss that we had a single altimetry system and entered RVSM. We operated in RVSM for remainder of flight. Aside for intermittent issues on Captain side; rest of flight was uneventful. It is noteworthy that the Airspeed Unreliable procedure didn't have a note regarding potential RVSM issues in the scenario of recovering a back air data and automation on one side.
column123: During the takeoff roll; the Captain's primary airspeed and altitude display blanked and autothrottle disengaged. Captain was PF and continued the takeoff. FO manually set takeoff thrust. We were cleared to climb via the ZZZZZ2 [departure] ZZZZZ1 transition. I was slightly late making the initial turn and FO communicated this; then used HDG SEL to return to course. I asked for flaps 5 (we had taken off using flaps 10). Once at wings level; I asked FO to take the controls and a positive transfer of controls occurred. FO appeared to have good attitude; airspeed and altitude information. FO continued to fly; and we retracted the rest of the flaps on schedule. At this point; we ran the Airspeed Unreliable checklist. We were able to confirm that the FO indeed had reliable airspeed; altitude and attitude information. We were able to re-engage the FO's flight director; and ultimately he engaged the right autopilot as well. We also determined that the autothrottle was working with the FO's flight director as master. We monitored the autothrottle closely throughout the flight and it functioned normally. We discussed the prudence and safety of continuing the flight without reliable primary airspeed and altitude information. We ultimately agreed that with the FO's side working normally; as well as having reliable standby airspeed and altitude information; that it was safe to continue the flight. The Captain's airspeed and altitude would return to normal periodically during the flight; but then blank again. This occurred throughout the flight.I failed to notify ATC or dispatch about the failure; which would have been the correct thing to do; because of the requirements for entering RVSM airspace. Only after the flight did we realize this and debrief this as an error. We also debriefed the course deviation during the departure phase. The distraction of not having a primary display for altitude and airspeed was one reason for this deviation. Good crew communication from the FO was helpful in correcting this error and promptly returning to course. This aircraft had a similar write-up from the previous day; and maintenance had replaced the Captain side PFD. Several hours into the flight the Relief Pilot advised myself and the Captain that the actual load closeout in fact printed out a few minutes after rotation. After reviewing the load closeout I determined the takeoff was well within the performance data I imputed. However; that fact remains; we are required to review the load closeout prior to takeoff.Causal factors for me include...1. I am new on this type aircraft. I in fact picked the trip up in order to make sure I obtained enough hours to consolidate.2. I had not worked in the First Officer position in about two months which was when I was receiving line training. 3. This was my first time be it ground training; line training; or on line where is was required to get new runway takeoff data and was not familiar with the outputted format. 4. We were rushed due to a last minute runway change.I would be helpful if in the training environment pilots were required to at least once obtain new runway data to get the experience.

column121: Flying into ZZZ. Because of the weather we setup for a CAT 2 to Runway XXL. I briefed the CAT 2 off the pages. We were cleared for the approach. I armed the approach. CAT 3; dual. I was looking outside to pick up the runway. We got the Land green. I picked up the lead in lights then the runway. I said landing. At approximately 50 feet the aircraft said retard. I retarded the thrust levers. At approximately 30 feet and descending quickly I realize the aircraft was not going to flare. I pulled back on the stick and we landed firmly. We taxied to the gate. I called the maintenance control person and explained what went on. He look at the data. He said there was a 'momentary glitch' in the FMC. I don't know if we received a flare display and neither does the FO. I think when I said landing the FO also started looking outside. We debriefed the approach and landing sequence. I think also so many of our FOs are very distracted because of the virus situation; the furloughs; etc. If we were in the military it would be a good time for a Safety Stand-down. I understand we can't do that; but it is very tough out here for the line pilots; FA; Gate Agents etc. [I suggest] ensuring everyone does their job all the way to engine shutdown.
column123: On descent into ZZZ we were prepared for an ILS approach to [Runway] XXR when the weather was reporting below minimums for the approach. 3;000 RVR was reported and 4;000 RVR was needed. We requested an approach to XXL which has a CAT 2 ILS approach and were vectored around for the approach. The approach was loaded and CAT 2 autoland procedures briefed. The approach was normal breaking out at about 200 feet with blowing snow but fairly good visibility. As we approached the 40 foot flare point I was distracted and not looking at the PFD. The Captain noticed the aircraft was not flaring and turned off the autopilot and landed the airplane firmly.We briefed the autoland approach and I quickly reviewed the required callouts. I was distracted when we entered visual conditions and my sight was drawn outside the aircraft. I missed the flare annunciation and not sure if it was presented. Captain noticed the lack of flare and took the appropriate action landing the aircraft. If I had called out no flare at 40 feet a go-around probably would have been more appropriate. When conducting autoland approaches the First Officer needs to remain focused on the flight mode annunciator during the whole approach all the way through rollout. Emphasis needs to be placed on this importance during the briefing. We rarely conduct autoland approaches and thus can be overlooked along with the natural tendency to want to look up and out the window when going visual on an approach.

My lesson is to reset the brakes pressing hard on the brake pedals once I get back inside the plane.  I'll also avoid any seat adjustment after engine start-up. column121: While on final to RWY 1R we were following an A350 for 1R.  We elected to remain 1/2 dot - 1 dot above glideslope as the winds aloft and at surface were relatively calm with slightly quartering tailwind.  As we descended below 100 feet AGL we experienced the tell tale signs of wake turbulence.  Luckily the aircraft did not experience any violent pitch or roll oscillations.  A missed approach was executed and we immediately cleared the wake vortices.  We were given vectors for another visual to RWY 1R.  On the second approach we had momentary wake turbulence at 2000 feet MSL following an A320.  As stated earlier the wind conditions being calm at all altitudes were prime for wake turbulence. The main purpose of this report is to draw attention to hazards of wake turbulence.  While we all appreciate efficiency of the national airspace system; lots of separation I feel is the key to preventing these occurrences.  We had noticed the aircraft ahead of us was left and right of centerline on approach and feel there may have been glideslope deviations as well.  This very well may have caused staying high on the glideslope on our part to [be of] no benefit if they were high as well.
column123: While receiving vectors for the visual approach to RWY 1R we were told to follow a heavy A350. The controller notified us we were 3 1/2 miles in trail and to caution for wake turbulence. The Captain (pilot flying) told me he would stay above the glideslope to avoid the wake turbulence. We remained 1/2 dot to 1 dot above the glideslope for the entire approach with no signs of turbulence. As we descended below 100 feet AGL we experienced two rolling moments to the left; both of which were corrected by the Captain. These oscillations were not extreme; but were clearly due to the wake turbulence. As these occurred the Captain called and executed a go around; immediately exiting the heavy aircraft's vortices. We were then vectored around for a second visual approach to RWY 1R; this time following an A320. During the approach a light quartering tailwind was reported. We once again remained slightly above glideslope and only experienced minor turbulence on the approach. This situation would have been avoided with increased separation from a heavy aircraft. The efficiency gained from using minimal separation on landing aircraft does not outweigh the risks of wake turbulence. Even by remaining high on the glideslope we experienced an uncommanded roll at a low altitude.

column121: I was about to begin the flight portion of a lesson with my student. We were holding short of runway; allowing multiple planes to safely land before we had a good opportunity to depart. While holding short; another plane had landed and was about to pull off of the runway onto A3; but there was an Aircraft Y on the other side of the hold short line. A radio call was made asking what the Aircraft Y was doing; and then he taxied out of A3 and Aircraft Z was able to taxi back to midfield parking. After Aircraft Z was clear of the runway; another aircraft landed on Runway 18; did a touch and go; and took off for a south departure. After waiting for about 5 aircraft to land on 18; the traffic pattern was now not busy; there was one aircraft on the downwind. I was positioned to where I could see the upwind; left downwind; left base and final of the traffic pattern; as well as the entire runway and taxiway and determined it safe to now make my radio call announcing my departure. After the radio call was made; it was not blocked; again I visually inspected that the runway was clear and slowly rolled onto 18. It was my student's second flight lesson; and his mother accompanied us in the backseat. While talking him through how to taxi onto the runway; how to takeoff and where to be visually scanning; I performed a normal takeoff; lifting off at rotation speed; the runway was still clear. After about five to ten seconds after rotation; I looked down to see my ground track over the runway and saw Aircraft Y directly beneath me. While maintaining positive control of the aircraft; talking through what I was doing with my student I flew at the speed that safely allowed us to gain as altitude. I made a radio call asking what the pilot in the Aircraft Y was doing and if he had not heard or seen us take off and if he had us in sight at that moment. He did not respond. Then I said 'What the hell dude?' on the radio. Due to how fast everything happened; and trying to remain calm and fly the airplane safely; it was hard to determine exactly how close the aircraft actually was to me. At this point I determined the safest action was to get us as far away from this plane as I could. I continued on the upwind; to where I could not see the Aircraft Y anymore. I was hoping that he had aborted his takeoff. Continuing out and scanning; maintaining a calm demeanor for myself as well as my passengers; I then heard an early crosswind call and knew it was the pilot in the Aircraft Y. Another instructor from FBO said '[name]; what is going on with you today?' A few other aircraft responded 'Agreed;' 'Agreed.' After this I did not want to return to the pattern knowing the Aircraft Y was still flying. I decided to take my student to the practice area to where I could continue my lesson and also monitor the traffic pattern to know when it would be safe to return; as I always do. After about 30 minutes I determined it was safe to return to the airport and land; because I didn't hear or see anyone in the traffic pattern. We landed safely. My passengers did not even notice what was happening until we were almost clear of the traffic pattern; I had told them someone was trying to takeoff underneath us. Still; they do not know the severity of how close it was because of being distracted by it being one of their first flights and not paying attention to the radio calls or doing the constant visual scan. I am extremely fortunate that my passengers and I are alive. This pilot; name; is the definition of unsafe. He chooses to make extremely unsafe actions. I will never fly if I see this man at the airport and will tell every student I have and pilot I see to also not fly if this man is out. If he is not held accountable for his actions; I fear that someone could be tragically hurt. My coworker; another CFI was a witness standing at midfield parking near A3 taxiway; and said it was a miss of 5 feet.

column121: Departed empty on a quick-turn repositioning leg. I was PM (pilot monitoring). Shortly after a normal liftoff and commanding gear retraction; crew noticed a red 'R GEAR' lamp on the instrument panel. About the same time; the Tower radioed us and let us know our right main gear appeared to be fully extended; with the left and nose gears retracted. (all 3 green gear lights were extinguished). We continued our IFR departure and were handed off to Departure. ZZZ Tower had already informed ZZZ1 Departure of our gear issue; and Departure asked our intentions. I requested a level off and we referenced the 'Abnormal' checklist which directed us to lower the gear and land. I requested a change in destination to ZZZ1. During cruise to ZZZ1; I took the flight controls and became PF (pilot flying). The remainder of the flight and landing at ZZZ1 were normal. Visually checking the main gear after landing revealed no apparent problems. Gear locking pins were all accounted for and had been removed prior to our flight. After landing; I telephoned the Tower to gather more information. The Tower Controller re-confirmed that it was 'apparent' to him that the right main gear appeared to be fully extended while the nose and left had retracted.

column121: The issue arose when I was taxiing from the northernmost T hangars to Ramp C at DWH to perform a run-up before a VFR departure for a local flight. Several corporate jets were parked on Ramp C and upon entering my aircraft I could hear a jet engine running; but I couldn't tell which aircraft it was. Ramp C is where run-ups are performed on the north end of DWH; and I needed to taxi to the south end of Ramp C in order to access an open spot for run-up; however the way I was familiar with was blocked by a pickup-truck. I then elected to turn right on N and taxi north then turn left on Ramp C. There is normally room to taxi behind aircraft parked on that ramp; but because one of the jets was running at least one engine; it wasn't safe to taxi behind them. I then elected to taxi south on Ramp C in front of the parked jets; and as I did so I saw that there were people walking in front of them; and also a vehicle approaching them from the south; so I swung out wide to give plenty of clearance; proceeded to an empty spot; and performed a run-up. On my initial taxi out for the run-up I didn't see the white boundary line of Ramp C; and assumed that I was safely inside of it; based on my previous study of the Jeppesen airport diagram. However Ramp C does not extend out as far toward Taxiway P as it appeared on the diagram. This was only my second time operating out of the north side of the airport; and my first time taking this route at the north end of Ramp C; and unfamiliarity was a factor. I chose this route instead of taxiing around the south end of Ramp C because the way was blocked by a pickup truck. The area is very congested; and the airport is poorly marked. Many of the ground markings; taxi lines; etc. are faded. Additionally; many ground vehicles; such as the airport vehicle; fuel trucks; golf carts; and other vehicles for pilots; passengers; employees; and residents that live on the field routinely drive on some of the ramp and taxiways without communicating on the radio; blurring the lines between the movement and non-movement areas. Specifically fuel trucks and the official airport vehicle (marked with signage on the doors) operate on taxiway P without making radio calls. Though I didn't realize it at the time; it was when I swung wide while heading south on Ramp C that I feel I may have encroached into taxiway P. It was upon completion of the flight when taxiing back to the hangar via taxiways E and P that I was able to see the faded white line that designates the border of Ramp C and realized that I may have made an incursion onto taxiway P at the beginning of the flight. The next day I sought out a highly experienced instructor who has operated out of DWH for over forty years and asked him about Ramp C; the faded white line; and the boundary between Ramp C and Taxiway P. He informed me that the area is tighter than I realized; and that anything west of the white line is a movement area requiring a clearance. Most importantly; I should not have assumed; and simply called Ground and coordinated with them; that way there would not have been an issue. Additionally DWH has a reputation for being poorly marked and I should have sought out more help becoming familiar with an airport that is new to me. My perception based on looking at the airport diagram was erroneous; and it was poor judgment to not call Ground and simply get cleared into the movement area; instead of trying to squeeze along the edge inside of Ramp C. I'm comfortable talking to controllers; I thought I could safely and legally do it and didn't want to 'bother them'. The reality is that's what they are there for; and I am sure the controllers would have preferred a call if there was any doubt.  The biggest factor affecting performance was the difficulty to see the faded border line of Ramp C. Additional factors were a reluctance to bother ATC; and the movement of road vehicles all around that gave a false perception that the non-movement area was larger than it really is. Unfamiliarity with the airport; especially when operating out of the north end was also a factor. The major inaction was failing to contact ATC.

column121: I was operating on an IFR flight plan while VMC in cruise talking to Baton Rogue Approach en-route to Houston. I was cruising at 140 knots true with the autopilot engaged tracking direct to LFT. The event occurred at 6;000 ft. I was scanning outside the windscreen when out of the corner of my eye I saw a black object through the copilot's side windshield. My first reaction was a bird and it was too late to avoid. The object passed beneath my wing and I briefly lost line of sight before the object reappeared behind the starboard wing. At this moment; I identified that the object was not a bird and had four arms; rotors; and was a large; but standard looking quad copter style UAS with position lights. I estimated that the object passed with 50-150 feet of the aircraft and varied in altitude. It rapidly changed courses and as I passed the UAS it made a sharp turn and a rapid acceleration behind the aircraft's tail and out of sight. No further contact was made. I immediately contacted ATC and reported the event. ATC contacted me to follow up about 5 minutes after I reported to them and I relayed the coordinates and description of the UAS to them. The flight continued safely to its destination. While I also hold a UAS certificate and enjoy that side of aviation; this near mid-air collision was extremely unfortunate. There seems to be very little enforcement in this area of aviation. A collision would have likely resulted in an in flight breakup. As a manned pilot; I do not believe there is much I could have done to avoid this. I could coach my UAS friends in the law; but most of my peers are well versed and follow the regulations. It only takes one rogue individual to cause an issue. I also thought I might opt to fly at higher altitudes. I had chosen 6;000 for wind and visibility; but perhaps I should have been higher. I do not believe this is a compelling argument because some drones can climb to the flight levels...much higher than a piston GA. I think drones may need to have further hardware limitations (subject to overrides) that would keep them off of federal airways or on ADSB/Radar in order to ensure the safety of manned flight.

column121: When I arrived at work for my XB00-XJ00 shift there was a CIC on the Supervisor desk. The area was still combined at the mid sector (XX) except for sector XY which sits 4 inches from sector XX. Sector XY was open and staffed by a Supervisor not wearing a face covering over any part of his face other than his neck. This Supervisor has been repeatedly told to do so; but most of the time doesn't do so. The adjacent airspace was ATC zero for a positive COVID case that had been reported the previous afternoon. This Supervisor often opens this sector between XA00 and XC00 am to avoid going to stand up and also avoid any sort of volume or complexity in the airspace. I understand normally it's not an issue besides that it's an awkward configuration that confuses everyone in and around the area; but today it was much more than that. Today marked ZZZ's X confirmed positive COVID case in X days' time and X [number] in X weeks. This supervisor not wearing a mask and opening the sector to get time was not only dangerous but just plain rude as the controllers sitting next to him were forced to work the other sectors while properly adhering to mask wearing guidance. I wish this was the end of this report however the day progressed to be even worse. During the morning the contingency plan was abandoned and we were told we could go through the sterilized airspace however far 'we felt comfortable.' In fact we were told it would be OK to give IFR clearances off the ground in the sterilized airspace as well. I don't think this is a safe idea. One person's comfort level could be more than a different person's. We don't know how far frequency coverage goes into the sterilized airspace and this could result in NORDO aircraft in conflict in the airspace with no way to resolve the confliction. To add further to this; later in the day a D-side trainee was brought to the area to give an over the shoulder for the resumption of training. 4 people were plugged in to one sector while the same Supervisor still wore his mask around his neck. This put 3 more controllers at risk unnecessarily during the middle of a facility outbreak. This D-side trainee is now fully certified again on all the area D-sides after working a total of 1 week in the past 7 months which presents even more risk both to proficiency and also to proper social distancing measures. After this certification was complete he was used throughout the day and told to 'pick a D-side' at the instruction of the Supervisor further combating any social distancing guidelines that have been set in place by state health officials; NATCA; and facility management.If this is how ZZZ center is going to continue to operate this is only the tip of the iceberg with how much crossing paths there is since the return of normal schedules and staffing. column121: After pushing back from the gate the aircraft was deiced using Type 1 fluid to remove excessive ice buildup.  The aircraft had been RON for nearly 10 hours and spent most of its time exposed to FZRA (freezing rain) and -FZRA.  The deice crew completed spraying/decontaminating the aircraft and called 'aircraft deicing complete'.  At this point; I still could not even see out of the co-pilots number 3 window due to excessive ice buildup.  This made the Captain and I suspicious (identified a threat) and asked the ground crew to spray the window and to be sure that they observed a clean airplane.  They resprayed and said the aircraft was clean.  To be sure; I performed a 'wing check' prior to engine start and noticed the wings were completely saturated with at least a quarter inch of ice.  We called them back and asked for a complete re-do explaining how difficult it may be to remove the ice.  They completed a second total deice and stated the aircraft was clean.  We elected to perform another 'wing check' and noticed that nothing had changed.  In fact; on one side of the aircraft we were unable to view the wing from any of the passenger windows due to ice buildup.  At this point neither one of us felt confident in the aircraft's condition and the Captain elected to return to the gate to perform both a walk around as well as conference with all ground personnel.  His communication was effective.  As a note; during the walk around noticed icicles hanging from the leading edges and the upper wing surface was completely saturated with ice.  We pushed a 3rd time; deiced by a different crew member; performed a 'wing check' and were satisfied the wings and control surfaces were clear.  Departed nearly 4 hours late.  An unsuspecting crew could have very easily departed with an aircraft completely covered in ice.

column121: IOE (initial operating) student was attempting a flaps 22 landing. During the approach; gusty winds from outer bands of an approaching hurricane contributed to an unstable approach and generating two glide slope EGPWS annunciations. We initiated a missed approach and were put in sequence to reattempt the approach. The vectors from the second approach brought us in above the glideslope. We engaged the vs (vertical speed) mode initially at 1;200 feet per minute (per GOM) and then 1;000 feet per minute as we closed in on the glide slope and stabilized approach criteria. The student had NAV armed; not APP; which as PM (pilot monitoring) I should have caught. My attention was briefly diverted to reassessing our fuel; which was 200 pounds over final divert at the final approach fix. At 1;000; instruments cross checked; the GS (glideslope) was exact (though not captured). At this point; we had been in visual conditions for several minutes. The runway did not have visual guidance (PAPI nor VASI); I looked out the window to verify the runway was clear; of which I annunciated. At approximately 700 feet AGL; we fell below the glide slope; generating additional glide slope EGPWS annunciations. Due to the winds; fuel nature; incoming weather; and diversion airport expecting similar conditions; I used my command authority to take control of the airplane; reestablish ourselves on the glide path; and land without further incident.

In flight: 'L & R AUX Bus Fail' CAS Messages (normal ops single engine) During descent; crew saw LH Engine N1 indications between 10-15% N1. column121: I was acting as an instructor to a CPL who was new to flying the Aircraft X Type. He had spent all of his time up to this point flying the Aircraft Y Type; so I was helping him familiarize himself with the different aircraft. We were doing pattern work while several other aircraft were in the pattern.  Upon getting abeam the numbers and beginning our descent; there was an aircraft on long final (roughly 2-2.5 miles) that we did not hear on the radio.  We continued with our base; and final. The CPL whom I was instructing did not speak very strong english; and was having some trouble with the radio calls in the pattern; and occasionally neglecting to make them. In this instance; he neglected to call his base; and also neglected to call final.  I noticed this only after him turning final without saying anything; and immediately announced our one mile final. This set up a situation where a near miss occurred between us and the other aircraft who was on long final. The aircraft that was on a long final did not call an extended downwind; or a base.  They called final and neglected to give any mileage to indicate they had flown a much larger pattern than usual for a light general aviation plane. The other aircraft noticed us only because I called our final; and immediately broke off his final leg to avoid collision.  I spoke with their pilot after this incident and he said we were slightly above them and cut them off. I believe this incident was caused by a number of factors mentioned above; and could have been avoided with better radio work on the part of my aircraft and the other one on final.  I had a high workload at the moment; which caused my attention to lapse when the CPL turned base without making the call.  However; the pilot on the other aircraft also did not specify that he was purposely flying a large pattern with an extended downwind/base/final.  His failure and mine to accurately give position reports caused the incident.   I also believe that often pilots become complacent and fly a pattern which is far too large at this airport.  There are several times in a week where I have to extend my pattern to a point where I would not be able to make the runway in the event of an engine failure.  Routinely; general aviation aircraft at the airport fly a 2+ mile final; which should be considered a 'long' final.  Like in the incident mentioned; this can cause confusion when someone joins flying a smaller; more appropriate pattern.
