column121: During vectors into OKC from the east; the Approach Controller assigned us Runway 17R differently from the one we had setup (17L). After re-configuring for the ILS 17R; I asked the Pilot Monitoring to brief the approach so I can concentrate on flying (Approximately 14;000 feet MSL and descending to 4;000 feet). During the brief a bright shining white light; like a spotlight shined at us; caught our attention and cause a distraction. We still conducted the briefing; including the highest elevation figure. As I kept flying I was paying attention if the light shined us again; in the event it was a laser that needed to be reported. I had the terrain page setup from the previous briefing and both pilots were aware of the obstacle northeast of the airport (Antenna 2758 feet MSL). After the briefing was complete; we were given a vector (a 90 degree angle) for the approach within a close proximity of the Final Approach Fix (minimum altitude at FAF 3;000 feet MSL). This vector would have flown us south of the obstacle depicted in the plan view section of the approach chart. Approximately 18NM from the airport the Approach Controller queried the visual contact of the airport. Pilot Monitoring told me he had contact with it and after I picked it up in sight I asked to call for it if he still had it. At that point the Approach Controller cleared us for the visual approach for [Runway] 17R. Slightly after; the Approach Controller notified us of traffic on the approach to the parallel runway. Both pilots were trying to ID the traffic since it was below our altitude and we had to cross his approach path. We seemed clear of the traffic; but a strong wind from the south was drifting us north which cause a concern for us due to the known obstacle. The aircraft was just approaching 4;000 feet of altitude and started to level off; when I set 3;000n in the Altitude Select box. The aircraft transitioned into a shallow descent instead of holding 4;000 since it wasn't fully captured. While having a discussion about the wind I adjusted my heading and kept the descent to 3;000 feet so we could be close to level and slow when we intercepted the course outside of the FAF. Around 3500 feet we both remembered the obstacles when we saw its lights ahead and below us. I already started a transition into a climb when the Pilot Monitoring verbally reminded me of the obstacles. During the climb we got a 'Caution Obstacle'; due to the projected descent; which was removed shortly since we were already compensating. We were 500 to 700 feet above the highest obstacle. The obstacle represented on the MFD was not the highest elevation figure on the IAP chart. This depicted obstacle was part of another group of towers not depicted on the chart but they can be seen on the VFR chart in the Jeppesen app. Since it was a visual approach; I had focused on maintaining the airport inside; and started to descend and slow down so we could be on a good position for the stable approach. Following the event; we landed with no issues and had a discussion at the gate on how we could have mitigated our error. We were below the MSA and had loss awareness of the obstacles due to other distractions and the tight vector to the approach with the visual approach. Several factors played key roles for the loss of situational awareness that led us to be at a lower altitude for our location. Flags:-A night Visual approach into an airport were an obstacle is a threat.-A night Visual approach to an airport were the elevation of the airport is higher than we are normally used to.-An arrival consisting of an extended base into a visual approach rather than a downwind arrival.-The change of runway that led to a new setup and briefing.-The distractions caused by the wind-drift; traffic; and the bright light.-The tight vector given and accepted for the original approach. Our error was the premature descent to 3000 feet with the goal of not being high once we intercept the final course with short distance to the final fix. Although the setup for the approach included the awareness of terrain and using the terrain displayed as an aid; we should have use TEM to establish a plan to avoid the premature descent. A briefed plan of using the last assigned altitude of 4;000 feet until intercepting would have avoided this. During the approach brief; I should have asked my Pilot Monitoring to intervene in the event I set a lower altitude while maneuvering for the visual (mitigation plan in the vent of losing SA). I realized that our briefings cover informational items that could be threats but we should discuss mitigating plans for them. Other actions that could have been taken are: 1) denying the visual at night due to the obstacle; 2) requesting a vector for the visual; and 3) querying if a lower altitude was needed which would have led the Controller to keep us at 4;000 feet.
column123: I was Pilot Monitoring. Approximately 20min out we were giving the option to change our landings intentions from [Runway] 17L to 17R which we took. Captain asked me if I could brief the approach which I did and then we performed the runway change items from the checklist. During this briefing moment we both noticed a bright light from about a 12 o'clock position which caught our attention. Captain was aware of the obstacles to the northeast of the airport (antennas) and turned on the terrain. At approximately 18 miles out we were asked if we had the airport in sight. We both saw it and were cleared for the visual approach Runway 17R. Winds were out of the south at approximately 26kt pushing us to the north since we were coming from the east. We were at 4;000 ft. and began a gradual descent. ATC advised us of traffic at 11 o'clock landing on the parallel runway. Looking for the traffic we began to noticed the red lights of the obstacles (towers) on the northeast of the airport. I pointed them out as [did] the Captain. The altitude window was set for 3;000 ft. we were currently at 3;400 ft. Captain turned off the autopilot and began a climb. As we were climbing we received a Caution for the obstacle but it cleared quickly since the Captain had already began the climb. Once cleared we continue to intercept the final approach course and perform a normal landing. We both had a long discussion after the flight and both agreed that we should had mitigated this by simply staying at 4;000ft when cleared for the visual approach since we knew about the MSA which is 3;800 ft. Also the parallel traffic played a role on this since we started looking for it due to it being in our path for intercepting the final approach course of [Runway] 17R. As a Pilot Monitoring I should had advised the Captain that selecting 3;000 ft. and continuing the descent once cleared for the visual would had put us close to the highest obstacle stated in the approach plate. I will keep this in consideration for future flights to come ensuring we are not at a lower altitude than the MSA not established on a final approach course as well as keeping in mind obstacles around us at all times.

column121: Aircraft X was on heading 360 and instructed to descend to 6;000 ft.  I observed Aircraft X descend through 6;000 and at 5;800 I issued a low altitude alert; the MVA was 5;600. When I descended them to 6;000 and they indicated lower it was apparent something was wrong and I was immediately concerned about the MVA so I issued a low altitude alert before they went below the MVA and a climb to 6;000.A snowstorm had just blown through the airspace and there was still stiff winds out of the west gusting to 30 kts. I recall planning ahead; looking at strips; using the STARS (Standard Terminal Automation Replacement System) to determine how much the wind was pushing the vectors.  Also ZZZ had many taxiways closed from the snow so I was vectoring for much greater distance than usual (10 miles on final).  I must not have looked at Aircraft X's altitude when they checked on and just used the reported altitude.  While I am happy I got a low altitude alert out when they were near terrain; I wish that I had caught it on check-on.I found it strange that their altitude in STARS was accurate but not in the cockpit. column123: Descending into ZZZ through FL 180 we completed the Approach Checklist and verified 30.24 altimeter setting. The Approach Controller said that we were at 5;200 and for us to climb to 6;000 and turn to a heading of 030. I immediately clicked the autopilot/auto-throttles off and started my turn towards 030 heading and started climbing; as my Pilot Monitoring verbalized that we had the wrong altimeter setting of 30.24 instead of 29.24. We leveled off at 6;000 on a 030 heading; and at that time I engaged the autopilot and auto-throttles. We got vectored for approach and landed uneventfully on Runway XX. We were asked to contact TRACON on landline by the Ground Controller as we taxied to the gate. We realized that we had unintentionally set altimeter setting of 30.24 in error instead of 29.24 which directly led to the altitude deviation. We failed to catch our error during crosschecks as we ran the checklist due to expectation bias. Lack of digital ATIS was also a contributing factor; however; we should have trapped this error as we updated the new weather. We needed to be more vigilant to trap these kind of errors.

column121: I was in bed sleeping at XA:05am.  My scheduled shift for the day was supposed to begin at XE:00L.  I received a phone call at XA:05 from my operations manager.  He said that this phone call was not a joke and that he needed me to report to work ASAP because the Tower was being evacuated due to a COVID-19 case and the 'need for secondary cleaning.'  I was aware of the fellow colleague who had been out on quarantine. The colleague had last worked a shift on [date] in the Tower.  Apparently managers above me had become aware that this colleague had contracted the virus.  A telcon had been convened in the earlier hours of the morning and during that telcon it was determined that cleaning the Tower was necessary due to the COVID case of an employee who hadn't worked in the Tower in over XX days.  It was determined that this cleaning needed to take place ASAP.  No regard was given to the fact that the employee hadn't worked for XX days and that controllers had worked in the permanent Tower for close to two weeks. Even more frustrating was the fact that this cleaning would take place during the busiest and most complex traffic times of the facility.  There was no pre-planning for this transition to take place.  From the time I was awakened; I was on the phone communicating and preparing for a very complex transition to a temporary Tower.  As this was early in the morning; there were almost no resources available to prepare for and to facilitate this transition.In my opinion; those that made this decision were extremely short-sighted and negligent in considering the impact to the safety of the operation and to those working in the operation.  With the help of the ZZZ Airport Manager on Duty and my Operations Manager; I reported alone to a contingency Tower at the terminal at with two portable radios.  Prior to leaving the permanent Tower I met with one of the two controllers on duty for the graveyard shift and explained to them the transition.  These two controllers stayed beyond the end of their shifts to facilitate the transition.  Their actions were exemplary. By XF:00 am all X controllers who were scheduled to work the day shift were with me in the temporary Tower.  I had coordinated with the TRACON to have the Developmental Controller on shift stay in the TRACON to work flight data.  The actions of the controllers that morning were heroic.  Working with 3 radios; two telephones; and a few pads of paper and pens.  The controllers on shift safely moved the three busiest traffic banks of the day while the permanent Tower was cleaned.  I was in awe of their professionalism and commitment to safety.  Their expertise was truly heroic.At XH:00 am Local; the cleaning was completed and we were able to transition to the permanent Tower.  As a team we were proud of what we had accomplished in spite of very difficult circumstance.The timing of this event was horrific.  Those who demanded the cleaning take place took no regard for operational safety.  There is no reason that after XX days of working in the permanent Tower under possible exposure that it would not have hurt to delay the cleaning until the operation was in a better position to support cleaning.  This cleaning should have happened on a mid shift and the facility should have been closed for the duration of the cleaning.  I am aware of multiple enroute centers that have been closed for cleaning.  The cleaning is always done overnight and there is sufficient traffic management support and communication to the users about the event.  This decision to clean the Tower was made in the early hours of the morning and as the one who facilitated the transition I am aware of no support or awareness that come from outside the facility.  In this event I am not aware of any communications to the users that we were in a temporary Tower.  This event was mitigated by the expertise of air traffic controllers who have been heroically working for months through thispandemic.  They are already working short staffed in less than ideal conditions.  Instead of recognizing these circumstances; those on the telcon who mandated the cleaning ignored the safety of the operation.

column121: The Captain and I made a go around on our second attempt to landing. The first approach was discontinued due to RVR being reported below the minimums for the approach outside the final approach fix. Due to a glideslope anomaly on Runway 23. The glideslope a few hundred feet from reaching minimums made a quick movement towards half scale deflection down. The aircraft was on a constant rate of descent; airspeed and proper configuration; hand flown below 1700 feet per approach plate. At the point that I called runway in sight the Captain and I noticed that the aircraft was not going to touch down in the prescribed TDZ and accomplished the go around procedure. While being vectored for a 3rd attempt at landing; the Captain and I briefed that if the anomaly happened again; we would accomplished another go around. Before the 3rd approach; another flight was able to land on their first attempt. After requesting a PIREP from the crew; they said they were able to see the runway right at minimums. We were able to obtain visual reference with the runway right at minimums and complete a successful landing. In the hotel van with the other crew we asked them if they had issues with the glideslope and mentioned they did. They said it acted very similarly to our situation. It seems that this has been a recurring theme at CRW in the past as well. The cause of the second go-around was due to an inaccurate indication of the glideslope that put the crew in a situation where a landing would have been made outside of the TDZ. I think the FAA needs to take a deeper dive in what is causing glideslope anomalies for the ILS 23 into CRW. Especially coming into the winter months in mountainous areas where weather can deteriorate rapidly.

column121: We briefed the route and departure; to include the [engine failure] procedures. We confirmed the route in the FMS. After being cleared for takeoff and reaching 400 AGL; We turned to heading 189 and hit moderate or greater turbulence and mountain waves; which significantly affected us. I had trouble communicating with ATC and performing cockpit duties due to turbulence. Just before reaching 1;000 AGL; Tower said switch to departure. Upon contacting departure we were told 'upon reaching 8;000; proceed direct to a fix'; but the radio quality of the transmission was poor and we couldn't clearly hear the name of the fix. I realized the mountain was on our path and for an immediate left turn to avoid terrain. The Spokane Departure Controller cleared us direct to a fix by name but not the identifier or phonetic spelling; which I couldn't understand due to significant turbulence and poor radio quality. We continued normal flap retraction callouts and takeoff profile. We were given heading a 120; to which we turned; and it took several radio calls between the Captain and ATC to get clarification on the identifier to which we were cleared. This was due to scratchy radios; the turbulence; and some possible confusion on the part of the controller who was talking with us and another company aircraft. We were mistakenly trying to navigate to ENY VOR which caused us to be confused and task saturated. Once we got the correct identifier for HIA and entered into the FMS; we proceeded on course as cleared. However this delay resulted in us temporarily deviating from the charted procedure. This caused the controller to get a low altitude alert although we did not receive any terrain avoidance warnings from our aircraft. In retrospect; the controller admitted on our phone conversation afterwards that this situation is very common. There are a lot of risks and stressors associated with this MZULA.MSO RWY12 and I feel like our outside resources did not help the flight crew. We accept full responsibility for allowing this situation to develop; but changes to this procedure will greatly increase safety in the future.First our Jeppesen charts had no verbal narrative and left us needing FAA charts to understand the procedure. It would be a great help if the procedure could be simplified or the controller's expectations that are outside the procedure could be communicated before we hit significant turbulence. The controller was clearly frustrated with us which only made our situation worse by trying to give us a phone number during a high stress and high workload phase of flight in significant turbulence. This shows the controllers are not fully aware of what human factors the flight crews have and how to help safety of flight. Having poor radio transmission quality was also a significant factor.
column123: I was the First Officer and Pilot Flying departing MSO. I received and read back the clearance from ATC which included the MZULA5 Departure MSO transition. I programmed this into our FMS and the Captain and I thoroughly reviewed the route in the FMS and on our Jeppesen plates. We also briefed the procedure for engine failure departure. In my takeoff briefing I again described the departure we were assigned. After being cleared for takeoff and reaching 400 AGL; I turned to heading 189 as charted. Immediately we began to encounter moderate turbulence. Just before reaching 1;000 ft AGL; Tower said switch to Departure. Upon contacting Departure we were told 'upon reaching 8;000; proceed direct to ________ ' but it was very turbulent and we did not clearly hear the name of the fix. I immediately realized the flight director was not commanding a left turn in accordance with the charted procedure. The Captain asked to say again the fix; and the controller said the name but not the identifier or phonetic spelling. At 1;000 ft AGL; I called out 'flight level change'; followed by the normal flap retraction callouts and told him we needed a left turn since I knew from the charted SID that's what we were supposed to do. Meanwhile the Captain was trying to get clarification on the fix to which we were to proceed. We knew it would be a left turn so he asked for a left turn and we were given heading 120; to which we turned. During this entire time it was very turbulent and took a lot of effort and concentration to focus on safe flying. It took several radio calls between the Captain and ATC to get clarification on the identifier to which we were cleared. This was due to scratchy radios; the turbulence; and some possible confusion on the part of the controller who was talking with us and another company aircraft. Once we got the correct identifier and entered it into the FMS; we proceeded on course as cleared. However; this delay resulted in us temporarily deviating from the charted procedure. During this time; we had terrain radar displayed on our MFD and were well aware of our surroundings and the location of rising terrain; and at no time did we ever get a terrain caution or warning.Although the SID was correctly programmed into the FMS; for unknown reasons the Flight Director did not command the left turn to intercept the MSO 159 radial. The extreme turbulence and difficulty understanding ATC instructions caused a delay in turning to the assigned fix; resulting in a course deviation. First of all; given our route of flight; it would have made much more sense if; in the pre-departure clearance; we would have been given the Salmon transition. This fact was even stated by the ATC supervisor on the phone when I called him after we landed. He further stated they have had frequent problems with pilots and aircraft not following the procedure we were assigned. Second; I could have anticipated a potential issue; and tuned the MSO VOR in NAV 1 and 2; along with the radial to intercept prior to takeoff. If I return to MSO in the future; I will definitely do that as a backup in case this kind of thing should happen again. I realized we were supposed to be turning left; which is why we asked for a left turn in the interim while trying to get the identifier for the fix and get that loaded in the FMS. The significant turbulence and the communication difficulties with ATC were definitely contributing factors in this temporary deviation. Nonetheless; as a pilot it is my responsibility to safely and correctly fly the plane; so I will ensure I have a backup navigation source programmed and ready in the future. And if I go back there again and get assigned that same SID; I will ask for the Salmon transition rather than the MSO transition; as suggested by the ATC supervisor. Finally I will brief my Captain on what happened previously so we can be vigilant and prepared.

column121: We had just switched on to approach frequency and were given a heading and altitude for the visual approach. We both heard the altitude clearance as 5;000 ft. and the PM read back 5;000 ft. A few min after we had leveled off at 5;000 ft. ATC asked us to confirm altitude and gave us the altimeter. We responded with 5;000 ft. and verified we had the correct altimeter. ATC then responded the minimum vectoring altitude was 5;300 ft. for that area. As the PM (Pilot Monitoring) attempted to clarify we read back 5000 ft. in the initial clearance; I started a climb to 5;300 ft. ATC then asked if we had the field in sight which we did and then we were cleared for the visual approach using the GPS 14 approach plate as guidance. We landed normally.The cause of this event was a miscommunication with ATC. We both heard 5;000 ft. in the initial clearance not 5;300 ft. The PM read back 5;000 ft. and we didn't hear a correction from ATC. A contributing factor in my opinion was the fact that we were experiencing light to occasional moderate turbulence for most of the flight including the descent and that could have caused us to miss hear the original clearance and potentially the read back was hard for ATC to hear due to the PM's mic being jostled.In cases such as this we could have requested clarification if the altitude didn't sound correct but in my estimation the clearance seemed to make sense based on our position and the airport elevation and the location of obstacles and terrain which were not a factor from the direction we were arriving and they also seemed to be similar to the altitudes we would expect if on the GPS approach we were using as a backup. But it would be prudent in the future especially in turbulence to verify clearances considering the effect turbulence could have on radio transmissions.
column123: We had just checked in with approach and they gave use a heading to turn to for vectors and an altitude to descend to. I thought I had remembered reading backing 5;000 ft. as the captain who was the PF put 5;000 ft. in the FMA and we both confirmed the 5;000 ft. once set. After reaching 5;000 ft. the controller asked us to verify our altitude and I read back 5;000 ft. The controlled returned with 'the MDA is 5;300 in that sector do you have the field in sight?' We had the field in sight but the question led us to believe we descended to the wrong altitude. The controller didn't clarify the altitude at this point and said were cleared for the visual using the RNAV GPS 14 approach plate for guidance.The cause of the event was a miscommunication with ATC and I could have possibly read back a different altitude and thought that 5;000 ft. was what he said instead; after we had set 5000 ft. Also; we were in light to moderate turbulence during the entire flight and it might have caused me to mishear the controller or misread the altitude.I should have asked for clarification from the controller after we had set the altitude in the FMA. From where we were; the altitude of 5000 ft. made sense so it did not cue me to ask for clarification. We had briefed the approach plate as well and the higher rising terrain was on the other side of the field and we determined it would not be a factor for the altitude of 5000 ft. column121: On a relatively calm and clear day at ZZZ1; I departed southbound toward ZZZ. The takeoff was uneventful; I contacted Approach for flight following. Throughout the climb to 9;500 ft.; there was constant light to moderate turbulence; typical for this segment of flight throughout this area. Upon reaching cruise the severity increased to consistent moderate turbulence; again not abnormal for the route of flight; the aircraft was slowed. I reported the ride conditions to Approach; and they stated that a Cessna 208 had reported similar conditions and opted for lower. The airplane began to experience downdrafts; exceeding over 1000 fpm and airspeed fluctuations of +/- 20 knots. I elected to descend to 7;500 ft. based on the ride conditions reported by the aircraft in front of me. At 7;500 ft. I experienced consistent moderate to severe turbulence; with consistent up and downdrafts; accompanied by fluctuations in airspeed. Occasionally; I nearly hit my head on the ceiling of the airplane. I queried [ATC] and they stated that the aircraft had reported a better ride at 6000 ft.; at that time I descended to 6000 ft. At 6000 ft. the ride was much more manageable; and I was able to make it to ZZZ safely. I made the decision that the airplane did in fact fly through severe conditions and required an inspection. I wrote the airplane up and contacted Maintenance Control. The unstable nature of the valley I was flying over and the absence of weather reporting in the valley make it difficult to gauge the ride conditions. I should have slowed the airplane down; and descended to more manageable flight conditions.A solution would have been flying the airplane above the valley to avoid possible severe turbulence. I talked with my pilot supervisor and he advised that flying at 15;500 ft. over the valley is a viable option. This particular route is very abnormal; with respect to mitigating risk. This is a prime example of how quickly things can change when flying. The more we can do to try to mitigate these risks as a whole; the safer it will become.

column121: After a diversion to our planned alternate we had a routine enroute and descent phase. We contacted Tower on about a 10 mile final. We were approximately 5 miles in trail of a B737; and we heard them check in as well. I overheard tower tell them about a Medevac helicopter who was operating to the east of the airport and transiting to the west. Once we were on about a 5 mile final; tower provided us with a traffic call for the same helicopter. The first call we received was traffic at our 10 o'clock and about three miles; and that the traffic had us in sight and was maintaining visual separation. Due to the lights of the city; I did not see the traffic; and it was not yet showing up on our TCAS.Inside of a 4 mile final; at approximately 1200 ft. we received a Traffic Alert for the traffic. On TCAS it showed him at 200 ft. above us and inside a mile. I immediately saw the traffic visually and told the first officer that I had the traffic in sight. Based on the traffic's track and altitude; I very quickly suspected that we might receive an RA. I instructed the first officer to go slightly below the glide slope to increase our separation. Very shortly after that; at 1050 ft. we received a 'DESCEND DESCEND' TCAS Resolution Alert. The First Officer followed the TCAS guidance and I informed ATC. Due to the switch at 1000 ft. to Traffic Alert only we never received a clear of conflict; but we were able to visually identify that we were clear of conflict at about 800 ft. We were one dot low on the glide slope but correcting and all other approach criteria were stable so I quickly asked the First Officer if he felt stable. He responded that he did; so we agreed that we were okay to continue the approach. At our closest point; the helicopter was directly above us and approximately 200 ft. above; leading to a significantly reduced margin of separation.This event was caused by several factors. The helicopter pilot had us in sight and was maintaining visual separation; but in our opinion; the separation provided was not adequate. I was not able to visually identify the traffic until the Traffic Alert occurred; and at that point there was very little we could do to avoid a loss of separation. I do not believe we should have been sequenced by air traffic control to pass directly underneath the medevac's flight path. After landing I communicated my concerns to tower and he said that once the helicopter reported maintaining Visual Separation; he had no further responsibility to separate us. If that is correct; I believe it is a fundamentally unsafe procedure. In this event it led to us receiving a descending RA at 1000 ft. leaving us with very little maneuvering room. I should have made more of an effort to find the traffic prior to receiving a Traffic Alert; but with the city lights it was difficult. This was at the end of a very high workload; 3 hour blocked flight with significant weather; holding; a diversion; and fuel considerations. I believe that this type of event could have been prevented with better planning from air traffic control. There was clearly a difference in expectations between the helicopter pilot and us; and the helicopter pilot may have been comfortable with 200 ft. of separation; but we were not.
column123: We diverted due to weather. On final approach we received a TCAS Resolution Alert due to a medical helicopter crossing the final approach. I was Pilot Flying for the approach. I was manually flying a challenging approach due to high winds and did not recognize the threat until a few seconds before the Resolution Alert.

column121: Let me say to begin I am not familiar with Flight Check. By this I mean I never came across it in any of my FAA materials or non-FAA reading; online; or video materials. It was not on any of my private; instrument; or commercial FAA exams. It was never brought up to me on any flight checks or check rides. I have never seen anything written about it in any online materials. No CFI or CFII ever mentioned it to me. I have never seen Flight Check aircraft at my home airport or any other airport I've ever flown into. Yesterday I experienced a conflict with a Flight Check aircraft. Just after I made my routine call for my pattern entry '...6 miles to the northeast inbound for a left downwind...'; a Flight Check aircraft made the call they were on an approach to the same runway as me and that they would need to drive inbound on the final until just short of the approach end for on an obstacle check. We're looking for inbound traffic. Other calls by various aircraft as well as Flight Check and my aircraft were made. One of the flight check calls was stepped on however and was therefore not audible. What is important to note too; is that there was an aircraft 2 to 3 miles behind me following me in. Because Flight Check and I were on an entry for the same runway in opposite directions I felt the situation was beginning to become dangerous; I considered doing a 360 turn at 6 miles out just to give spacing to the Flight Check aircraft coming in from the wrong direction. However; I did not do this because there was an aircraft directly behind me and I felt a 360 might put me into him. Therefore; for safety reasons I decided against it. I felt the safest course of action was to proceed on because I felt a King Air at 6 miles out was going to arrive much sooner than I was at 6 miles out because of his faster speed and because he was doing a straight in and I was doing a standard approach. Additionally; he said he was not going to land but instead 'break off just short of the approach end...'. Lastly; he said he was 'looking for inbound aircraft' which I felt meant he was aware of me and would divert if needed. I also briefly considered the option of extending my downwind but felt that to be unsafe because other aircraft were in the area and I had lost track of exactly where everybody was due to the constant traffic chatter both for ZZZ and other nearby airports. It was becoming stressful and my goal was to fly the aircraft; look out the window; and either land or see and avoid this other aircraft. As our approaches proceeded and I turned final I could see an oncoming aircraft above me ascending and turning south as I was descending to land. As I was about 50 feet off the runway I received a tongue lashing from the Flight Check aircraft and my landing was hard and it took several moments for me to calm myself after parking. Only after going into the Fixed Base Operator and asking about what a Flight Check aircraft was did I understand what had just happened. I now understand; after I did my own investigation; what Flight Check is and what I should do if I encounter a Flight Check aircraft in the future. I will now avoid Flight Check if I ever encounter one. I will advise other pilots of what Flight Check is and to avoid them. What caused the problem and what can be done to prevent a recurrence or correct the problem.The problem was caused by me not knowing what Flight Check is and that they have the authority to fly wherever they want and however they want. I will stay away from all Flight Check aircraft in the future. Flight Checks should be included in NOTAMS. I checked NOTAMS prior to my departure and there existed no such NOTAM regarding Flight Check aircraft that day. ATC; such as Approach did not advise me of any Flight Check aircraft. Flight Check pilots should include such wording as; 'This is the Federal Aviation Administration advising all aircraft to avoid (airport name) until (time).' This should be repeated over the appropriate frequency every 1 to 2 minutes until Flight Check is clear of the area. Include Flight Check information in FAA teaching materials. Include Flight Check information in FAA testing materials. Flight Check pilots should avoid berating pilots on frequency especially just prior to them landing as this can cause an unsafe distraction.

column121: On an early evening flight to IAH we were descending via the DRLLR 5 RNAV arrival being set up and briefed for the RNAV Y 26R with our altitude set to 6000'. When checking on with the approach controller we were told to expect the runway 26L transition. We selected the new runway in the FMS but failed to reset our altitude selector to 7;000' at that time. As we neared ZOEEE Drag Required appeared on the FMS scratchpad and the Captain said; 'Careful not to be too hot at ZOEEE'. I deployed the speed brakes and slowed us to 210kts and checked the FMA and we were still in VNAV PATH. Shortly after passing ZOEEE; I noticed the FMA showed VNAV SPEED as we were leveling at 6;000' and I no longer showed SKLER as a waypoint on the screen. I then looked more closely at the DRLLR 5 chart and noticed the point we'd briefed as the lowest altitude on the arrival had (Runway 26R) beside it and thought we should've stopped at 7;000'. I brought it to the attention of the captain who then queried ATC. The ATC response was that we were ok and to now descend to 5;000'. We started the descent and shortly after were told by what sounded like a different voice on the radio to maintain 6;000'. We reversed the approximately 200' descent and returned to 6000'.The rest of the approach and landing were uneventful and the flight ended safely at the destination. I believe we should've stopped at 7;000' but am unsure since the controller didn't have a problem with us being at 6;000' so I listed the event as a possible altitude deviation.

column121: Upon arrival to Gate X in ZZZ we were asked to call OPS. The Captain called them and we were reminded that we should call ramp before entering the ramp next time. I couldn't believe that I had made such a mistake after over XXXXX hours on the fleet and almost XX years of flying at the company with many many ZZZ arrivals. I looked at the Captain and I said; 'I am sorry I have no excuse;' which is how I felt. I then called the ramp and apologized. I called them on the frequency that I had set on stby at Comm 2 prior to the top of descend when I was setting up for our arrival to ZZZ. As we debriefed I started questioning the why of my mistake and I realize that I am taking for granted my lack of situational awareness as a result of my 7 month absence from flying.When I went to ZZZ1 I was very serious about it; during my OE trip I was still very conscious of my weaknesses because of my lack of recency but now as I am finishing my second trip after OE I feel that 'I am back' which obviously I am not. There were a few other threats that contributed to my mistake. We had thoroughly briefed a [Runway] XXL arrival and taxi in but had spent way less time discussing [Runway] XYR. Our set up for XYR and execution was great but created a distraction and increased the workload. We cleared XYR on Taxiway 1; were given instruction to cross XYL on 1 and call Ground. Both myself and the Captain were anticipating taxi via 1; but when I called Ground we were told 'Taxi via 2; 3 hold short of 4 and at the half way point on November call Ground at XXX.YY.' A lot of information to digest especially if you aren't very familiar with the airport; you have been out for a long time (this is the Captain's first trip after RQ (Recurrent Qualification) training and OE). We were both expecting to go straight on Taxiway 1.I told the Captain to stop. Which he very nicely did as he was also figuring out that we were not suppose to continue on 1. The Captain taxied as instructed; I called Ground Control and was told to taxi via 3; 4 to the gate. After making the turn on 4 we were instructed to give way to opposite direction traffic on 4 that was turning on 5. We then were told to turn right on 5 and continue via 6 to the gate. As I am debriefing this I realized that ZZZ unlike ZZZ1 or ZZZ2 doesn't instruct you to contact ramp. They simply say taxi to the gate/ramp. Finally as we were approaching the gate area I was trying to time my APU start so it is running when we come to a full stop; and I also noticed that there was a lot of vehicle traffic traveling parallel to us and I was a little concerned on whether or not they will stop at X7 for our turn. There was no traffic in the alley and we taxied to Gate X uneventfully.

column121: We were assigned the ZZZZZX RNAV departure off Runway X at ZZZ.  The clearance was to climb via the SID; top altitude of FL230 was set in the MCP. All the fixes and altitude restrictions were correct in the FMC; I was the PM; the airplane was light; so we had a good climb rate. The PF was hand flying as we approached the first fix which has a crossing restriction of at or below 10;000. LNAV/VNAV and VNAV PTH was selected. Close to the first fix the PF called for the autopilot as the airplane started its turn to cross the fix that placed the sun directly into our face which affected our visibility. As I turned my head to get my sunshade; ATC asked if we were going to stop at 10;000 feet; we got as high as 10;300 the PF turned the autopilot off and went down to 10;000.  In this situation I think turning the autopilot on earlier would have helped. Also anticipating the sun and take steps earlier to mitigate the effects of the sun would have helped us to maintain better situational awareness.
column123: Our departure SID was the ZZZZZX.  Our departure plan was for Runway YYR per the ATIS.  During taxiout our runway assignment was changed to Runway X with the same SID.  My First Officer ran the runway change checklist and briefed me on the changes to the SID departing Runway X.  During the climbout I called for the autopilot sometime prior to 10;000 feet.  There is a fix named ZZZZZ that has a crossing altitude of 10;000 or below.  Our automation level was LNAV/VNAV with the autopilot engaged.  Approaching 10;000 feet I noticed that the FMA went to VNAV PTH.  About that time; I also got a face full of morning sunrise.  It briefly made it hard to see and I had not deployed my sunshade or put on my sunglasses yet.  When my vision adjusted to the glare of the sun I noticed that the aircraft did not level at 10;000 feet.  It overshot the altitude by 300 feet.  I disengaged the autopilot and returned to 10;000 feet.  The Controller did query us on our altitude during the overshoot.  One other piece of useful information is that the aircraft was very light.  I'm wondering if the system was respecting a G-Load vs. an altitude because I have no other explanation as to why it did not level at 10;000 feet.  Factors that I feel contributed to this event were the runway change on the ground; high airport elevation; sunrise; fatigue and maybe our light weight.  Next time I will not accept the immediate line up and wait from ATC.  Instead I would re-brief the SID so that my situational awareness would be better.

The flight was cleared to descend via the TBARR 1 RNAV Arrival with the Runway 16R transition. The transition ends at CLFFF intersection at 11;000' with a speed of 210 knots. ATC was informed that we could not accept an RNAV approach and we were told to expect a visual approach; which we backed up with the ILS approach. The flight was turned to a right base heading at 210 knots. While turning the FO requested a slower speed which ATC approved. ATC asked if we had the airport insight. When I replied that we had the runway insight we were cleared for the visual approach. The FO selected the approach mode. As the FO was selecting a slower speed I mentioned that she should turn toward MERYN intersection. She slowly selected a heading toward MERYN and over shot the final approach course. I think this was due to the angle in which the course was intercepted. I would suggest adding a discussion about accepting visual approaches to the approach briefing; as a possible threat.

column123: An amber L HYD QTY CAS message posted approx. 2 min after liftoff. The L HYD was showing a magenta RF; quantity was decreasing and pressure was approx. 3;500 PSI. T L hydraulic quantity was .016 and pressure was 70 PSI. We discussed it and decided to return to ZZZ. I [advised ATC] and asked for equipment to be standing by. We discontinued the approach and while over RWY XXC; CFR reported that our gear was 'Not Down'. The First Officer ran the GEAR DISAGREE checklist and alternate gear extension resulted in three down and locked. The First Officer then ran the L HYD SYS PRESS checklist. The L ELEC PUMP switch was placed to OFF. When we were ready; we recovered at F20 and Vref20 with a visual approach; backed up by the ILS XXC. Differential braking was used. The R reverser was used. They looked at the engine with their IR camera and declared that there was no risk if an immediate fire. Once CFR was behind us; we taxied off of [Runway] XXC and stopped on taxiway waiting a tug. The After Landing Checklist was completed. I chose to keep the R engine running until we were chocked or connected to the tug. column121: There was a line of storms crossing ZZZ.  We were told to expect holding at ZZZZZ.  We ended up holding.  We did one turn and then we got sent back on the arrival.  We ultimately got vectors from ZZZZZ1 and were following one Company aircraft.  The plan was to fly northeast about 30 miles at 5;000 ft to go around the weather and then come back south to land.  We couldn't get in front of it or through it.  Company turned around to try to get around the weather from the other direction.  We did the same thing.  We got a 270 heading and a descent to 4;000 ft and an assigned speed of 170 knots.  On that vector; I noticed airspeed decreasing and added some power.  Then the airspeed dropped to approximately 140 knots and the autopilot and autothrottles were disconnected.  I announced to the PM (Pilot Monitoring) that we were in windshear and I added power and started a climbing turn to the left.  The aircraft started accelerating and climbing; and we retracted the flaps.  The highest speed I saw during the recovery was 220 knots.  During this period; airspeed; pitch attitude and altitude was very difficult to control and we encountered what we believed to be severe turbulence.  The PM told ATC that we had severe turbulence and windshear and that we were turning to the left and climbing.  We tried to level at 5;000 ft and flew southwest.  ATC told us to climb to 6;000 ft for traffic.  I added power and the aircraft responded poorly.  Eventually; we got a climb going; but we were unable to stop the climb at 6;000 ft.  The aircraft continued to about 6;450 ft and ATC asked us what altitude we were going to.  PM told them that we were trying to get to 6;000 ft but were having a difficult time maintaining altitude with the turbulence.  On our way back down to 6;000 ft we got a TCAS TA for traffic at our 1-2 o'clock at 700-800 ft above us.  I continued down to about 5;800 ft to make sure we avoided that traffic.  We continued southwest and diverted to ZZZ1. If we had asked to stay in holding until we saw that the line had passed even further northeast of the field; it would have prevented this.  We had about 13.0 of fuel when we entered holding; so we had the time. [We were] unable to maintain assigned altitude; heading; and airspeed due to windshear and severe turbulence.

Last year when there were more runway closures there were events where aircraft overran closed sections of runway and I believe ATIS was primarily to blame.Ideas to make this better:-Get a faster talking robot; or make a human record it (that will eliminate some errors).-Move information that's always on there (like the bird strike thing) to the chart supplement.-Consolidate groups of information; like 'Taxiways closed: B; D; F; RH; RB'.-Maybe make a separate frequency with a 'long ATIS' for out of towners who want to hear about how bad the bird strike hazard is getting.We have a 20 min leg from ZZZ. column121: I was operating flight to ZZZ. The weather was good and after detecting inadequate fuel planning and requesting additional fuel we departed on time and flew the filed flight plan. We were clear direct to ZZZZZ. Our ATIS was showing that we were expecting to land on Runway XX left.Knowing it was early in the morning we did anticipate a possible runway opening of either XX right or XY. When we were about three minutes from ZZZZZ; We were given the instructions to depart ZZZZZ on a heading to intercept the XY localizer. Although we had planned for the possibility of XY; this was a fairly abrupt and last-minute instruction from ATC. As briefed; this falls under the 'slam dunk' which was is always a threat; as I briefed for departure.We departed ZZZZZ on the assigned heading and began to set up for the intercept of the XY localizer. We were given a descent to 9000; then very quickly a decent to 6000; then a speed reduction to 170 and then briefly after that another speed reduction to 160 (until 5 out). All of this seem to happen in [a] very quick sequence. I was set up to intercept; set up to descend and began to slow down According to our instructions.We established our self on the ILS [Runway] XY without incident but when I realized that we needed to slow down; I called for flaps 22 'out of sequence.' (Typically flaps 22 is called with 'Gear Down'). I had already called for flaps nine; and just naturally called for flaps 22 knowing I needed to slow down.My First Officer (FO) followed the command and put in flaps 22. I naturally look down and scanned my instruments as I always do after a change command and I immediately realized that we were above the 200 knot threshold. I immediately took action - I pressed in the TCS (Control Steering) button; pitched up and began to slow down. As quickly and as safely as I could I brought the aircraft under the 200 knot limitation and completed the rest of the flight without incident.Upon landing I called my dispatcher; explained what happened; maintenance came out; they completed a full inspection and downloaded the information from the airplanes computer. We swapped airplanes so that the inspection could be completed and by the time we landed in ZZZ1; I had heard back from the maintenance supervisor. He told me that the inspection was completed no defects were found and the airplane was returned to service.I detected the problem. I always do a brief scan during critical phases of flight to confirm that the command and input was followed. So I did my scan after calling for Flaps 22 and immediately realized the error. I did not alert FO; as it was not necessary and I simply made the adjustments to the pitch and speed by using the TCS button. I feel there were 2 factors contributing cause to this event. The first was the additional time we had to spend on considering our planned fuel situation. This was definitely an added concern that both FO and I collaborated on before we even left the gate. Then; as Runway XY was opened and we received the 'Slam Dunk' vectors onto the ILS XY; was a second major contributor to this situation. My suggestion as to how to avoid this situation is to simply avoid the 'slam dunk' vectors. Had I asked for better vectors; I'm certain that this situation could and would have been avoided.

column121: The flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ was dispatched under our new fuel management program. The 1 hour and 25 minute flight was dispatched with planned fuel of 5830 lbs. The FO and I both noticed and mentioned that the landing fuel numbers were very low for our standard operation. The NAV Log section of the release showed 1;829 lbs. which is planned fuel minus taxi and fuel burn. But the fuel calculation section showed 1;660 lbs. This concerned both the FO and I; as such a long flight with very little fuel to be landing with. We both discussed that the airplane was [under] fueled by at least 200 lbs. Therefore we both felt landing with 2;000 lbs. or worst case scenario 1;800 lbs. was low but a safer and acceptable number. The performance manual shows around 1;700 lbs. at 5;000 ft. is around 45 minutes of fuel. Knowing our fuel was tight; we did what we could to help conserve fuel by delaying the second engine start as long as possible; and we attempted a Flight Level Change climb by several and normal intermediate level off altitudes with only 7 miles in the opposite direction. We continued to monitor our fuel burn. Upon our initial descent; we noticed we had burned more than planned; but we had received a shortcut and still calculated landing with around 1;800 lbs. On a few turns before final; the right fuel gauge began to flash amber at us then continued to flash in and out as fuel moved around throughout the final approach. Upon landing; we had around 1;800 lbs. of fuel. I feel this margin of safety is extremely low for a safety conscious airline and program. The fuel management program should be providing us with more fuel not less fuel. We were [under] fueled and received no undue delays and were proactive in managing and conserving fuel. Our end result was landing with 1;800 lbs. of fuel. In a medium case scenario; if the airport shuts down for an aircraft emergency or anything else; a go around diversion to the closest company destination (ZZZ2 is 78 miles away); say 25 to 30 minutes at 8;000 ft. (1;100 lbs.); would have me landing with 400 lbs. of fuel and I would have had to make that decision immediately. ZZZ3 is the next closest at 117 miles. That is also if those stations both have personnel staffed to service the aircraft. While legal; and probably acceptable; this practice seems to create an unreasonable reduced margin of safety standards with the trade-off being cost savings. In addition; as a Check Airmen and experienced pilot; I have more wherewithal to be neurotically monitoring developing situations; and weather. I can see an average pilot easily being forced into a no-win situation or very unsafe situation with dire outcome.[We] detected and attempted to manage [the issue] upon review of the release and even with proactive measures; the aircraft still landed with an uncomfortable amount of fuel. [We] took proactive fuel burn reductions with no changes in landing fuel. The airline's new fuel management program and a lack of safety margins created by the program [were contributing factors].I suggest changing the standard practice of providing 45 minutes of cruise fuel from flight level altitudes and provide the crew with an accurate and manageable 45 minutes of fuel near 10;000 ft. which is where most people will need that extra fuel in the case of holding; delays; reroutes and diversions which more likely occur below the flight levels. Add fuel and increase the amount of minimum fuel required to be on the airplane for dispatch.

column121: Aircraft X apparently hit a set of stairs on pushback with their right wing tip unbeknownst to the crew or Marshaller. A ground crew member saw it and called it in to his supervisor; who called it in to the Ops (Airport Operations). The plane at this point was on takeoff roll and wasn't in contact with Ops via radio anymore. After getting airborne; Ops took it into their own hands and called Tower and told them to have the flight return to field. I received an message from the crew asking why the return to field; which is when I started to make calls. This happened while the crew was at 3;000 feet and turning around. Crew landed uneventfully and the plane was taken out of service with visible damage to the right wingtip. No request was issued for a return to field as I felt in the short time frame; and with how busy the crew would have been setting up an unexpected approach; that it would have been unsafe to add more to their workload. Operations staff need to be fully aware of their limitations in regards to operational control of flights. Perhaps there needs to be a rapid communication procedure for the ground personnel; as they had to make several calls to get the information to someone who could have made a difference quicker.
column123: After we took off and checked on with ZZZ Departure Control we were advised by the controller that Company wanted us to return to the airport. Upon questioning; the controller did not know the reason. I sent an ACARS message to our Dispatcher advising of an air turn back and asked why. His response was that he didn't know but would find out. We set up for the return to ZZZ and landed uneventfully and taxied to parking. Upon aircraft shutdown and secure a ZZZ maintenance representative met us inside the cockpit to advise us that the right wingtip possibly came into contact with a set of crew stairs during block out. We took a look at the wing and there was some minor damage to the right outboard leading edge slat just inside the right navigation light. At all times during the block out we were under the guidance and direction of the marshaller. Appropriate logbook entry made and reports submitted by both myself and First Officer. Reflecting upon blocking out; after engine start we cleared the mechanic and ascertained immediate area left and right were clear; I signaled the marshaller across the ramp and on the nose that we were ready to taxi out. We were marshaled straight out into the alley and given the signal for a left turn into the alley followed by a wave-off and salute. During the initial block out taxi roll; the First Officer mentioned the crew stairs seemed close; but from my position the stairs did not appear to be encroaching on the taxi lane and I continued to follow the marshaller's instructions. All marshaling signals were consistent with the aircraft being clear of any obstacles; and at no time did the marshaller give us a stop signal during the taxi out; nor did we feel any bump from the right wingtip possibly making contact with the crew stairs. I do not know if there was a wing-walker on the right wing due proximity of ground equipment between our aircraft and the aircraft to our right. I do recall a white ramp vehicle was encroached in the clear area to our right as we were blocking out; but the vehicle backed up out of the way. Recommendations: wing-walkers; all ground equipment clear; equipment safe boxes painted on the ground around the aircraft like in ZZZ1.

column121: During climb after departing ZZZ; we experienced light clear icing; which began around 12;000 ft and ended around 20;000 ft. The checklist drove us to press the wing ice protection button out; which we did. Almost immediately the EICAS message disappeared from view. At the end of our day; I made the next Captain aware of our event verbally when we got to ZZZ2.I wish that I had taken a picture after the wing valves were closed on the ice protection schematic on my MFD. column121: Upon arriving at MSO airport on [Date] at approximately XA:00 the winds were not favorable to execute the ILS to RWY (Runway) 12. The weather conditions to perform the RNAV GPS D were alternating between ceiling and visibility going below minimum conditions. We were communicating with Dispatch along the way and were discussing diverting to our first alternate; which [was] Billings (BIL). The ceiling and visibility at MSO was above minimums at time of arrival. We started the RNAV approach with a circle to land on RWY 30. After crossing the final approach fix at 6;800 ft.; and descending to our MDA of 4;700 ft.; we started to have some ground contact. The FO (First Officer) said that he saw the PAPI lights to the right of us. The approach did not allow for us to circle to land northeast of RWY 12/30. The only way to commence the circle was to fly over the airport and circle around to the west. We briefly discussed circling to the west and quickly decided that it would be unsafe to circle around the airport at night in low visibility with LLWS (Low Level Wind Shear) conditions in mountainous terrain. During the decision making phase I had inadvertently disconnected the auto throttle. We continued to the missed approach point. As we went around I had realized that the MAP fix was not in the box. As we looked at the approach plate and quickly made a climbing left turn on a heading of about 340. We asked ATC for a heading while we headed in the proper direction. Once WENKE was back in the box we realized we were right on course.At approximately 8;000 ft. we were back in radar contact and was giving a vector off the final approach course. ATC asked us if we wanted to commence another approach or divert to a different airport. After discussing the conditions that we saw and weather forecast to be deteriorating; we unanimously decided that it would be unsafe to conduct a circle to land night approach based on the current weather and forecasted conditions.We then told ATC that we were going to divert to BIL. We sent ACARS message to Dispatch telling them we were diverting as well. After landing at BIL; Dispatch told us that we were to refuel and proceed back to MSO. Dispatch then said the weather was not good enough to go back and was delaying our departure. After waiting about an hour Dispatch said the winds were improving and we should be able to do the ILS RWY 12 back into MSO. We departed BIL for MSO with BIL as our alternate if we could not get in. We executed the ILS to RWY 12. While in Billings we contacted ATC and they told us at that time that they did not have radar until about 8;000 ft. The controller said that he was not working at that time but discussed with the previous controller that we were right where we were supposed to be and we said we just were at a high work load and wanted to verify with them that we were on course.High workload with low ceilings; LLWS; at night in mountainous terrain. Having to circle with visibility below what was projected and inadvertently disconnected auto throttles to land.I feel like this approach is not a safe approach to do at night. I spoke with several carriers that land at this airport and this approach is not authorized.

column121: Crew was descending into ZZZ Airport at about [night] time. Weather revealed winds 350 with good visibility and MVFR conditions. With the higher winds out of the north; the crew elected to fly the RNP Approach which requires the PAPI to be operational to fly the approach. A review of the NOTAMs revealed this would not be an issue; though the REIL was out of service to this runway. Icing conditions on the approach prompted to crew to conduct a flap full landing with ice numbers. Additionally; Tower mentioned that they would be closing just prior to our arrival. The Captain; myself; briefed the autothrottles would be disconnected on the arrival; with the autopilot off once established inbound. I disconnected the autothrottles and left the autopilot on as briefed. We continued to configure through the landing checklist and saw the runway on the approach. Once we rounded out on final; I disconnected the autopilot and began slowing to our approach speed when the lights at the airport clicked off. I briefly shallowed the descent anticipating the possibility of a go-around and had my First Officer turn the lights to high which failed to bring the PAPI back online. Being VMC and within required company parameters for a safe approach; I inquired to my First Officer if he was comfortable with continuing under the conditions which he was. I corrected descent angle and the flight landed without any further incident.This was the flight crew's first time flying this approach; my first RNP approach in a while; and my fourth night landing in about 2.5 months. This RNP Approach requires the PAPI to be operational to use. With there being no PAPI NOTAM; it was determined that it would be appropriate to fly it. After we had landed we found that the Tower; attempting to enable the pilot controlled lighting; had inadvertently switched all lights off. This was corrected with my First Officer turning the lights back on but the action failed to turn the PAPI on. The ATIS had called for gusty winds out of the north but; once we were established on final; I noticed we had a quartering tailwind at 15 kt. which caused me some confusion. The light issue and shifting winds prompted me to shallow out the approach due to the possibility of a go-around. However; with the airport lights on minus the PAPI and in VMC conditions; I figured the safest course of action was to continue given the fact that we were within parameters required to continue the approach and land. My thinking was a go-around late at night; in mountainous terrain and icing conditions with a possible changing weather pattern; may not be the best idea given we were still within tailwind parameters and touchdown requirements for landing. To me; this incident illustrates how important it is to appropriately manage [non-forecasted] distractions; especially during high workload phases. Additionally; it's imperative that we strive to remain current even during prolonged periods of stagnation.When weather is in vicinity; ensure [that] the most accurate weather is obtained from Tower if necessary. Relay concerns of airport issues to ATC or go-around. Be wary of Tower closures near arrivals to airports. A reminder that higher elevation airports present unique challenges which must be reviewed and briefed prior to flying into them. A reminder to chair fly approaches to destination airports; especially if the approaches you intend to follow are unfamiliar. The importance of maintaining appropriate approach currency. Speed management and adequate monitoring during all flight phases. A reminder to fly the airplane first and; if mounting distractions cause confusion; go-around.

column121: We were navigating between coordinates at FL410 and M.80 assigned.  We received a CPDLC clearance that said; 'Resume normal speed'.  We reviewed the Europe Jeppesen Airway Manual section entitled 'Operations Without an Assigned Speed' to review this relatively new procedure. After agreeing on what it meant we accelerated to M.83 and advised ATC at XA:03z via CPDLC 'Present speed .83'.  ATC responded at XA:13z with 'Do you want M.83'.  We responded; 'Received normal speed CLNC and advising our speed is .83'.  At XA:17z ATC sent; 'You may want to read up on that. Resume normal speed means plus or minus mach .01 from cleared mach.'  We immediately changed speed to Mach .81 and replied; 'Roger speed now is .81 requesting M.83' (XA:18z). At XA:19z ATC sent 'Maintain .83M'. All communications were done via CPDLC. The rest of the flight was uneventful.  We disagree with the controller's interpretation of the 'Resume normal speed' clearance and request clarification from the company. Page 668 of the Jeppesen Airway Manual (Europe) says; 'If the aircraft then receives RESUME NORMAL SPEED (via CPDLC or Voice); the flight crew no longer needs to comply with a previously issued Mach. However; the flight crew shall advise ATC if; as the result of the RESUME NORMAL SPEED message; they intend to adjust their speed by plus or minus Mach 0.02 or more from their last assigned speed.'  Furthermore; in the operational example given on page 688 it says; '...message RESUME NORMAL SPEED will be sent.  The flight crew no longer needs to comply with a previously issued Mach. However; the flight crew shall advise ATC if; as the result of the RESUME NORMAL SPEED message; they intend to adjust their speed by plus or minus Mach 0.02 or more from their last assigned speed. In this case; with a previously assigned speed of .81; they must inform ATC if the flight either slows to M.79 or less or speeds up to M.83 or more.'  Finally; in the North America Jeppesen Airway Manual it says; ' When adherence to an assigned 'MACH' setting is no longer required; pilots will receive a controller-pilot data link communications (CPDLC) message to 'RESUME NORMAL SPEED;' at which point the flight crew can continue at their cost index. Refer to aeronautical information circular (AIC) 1/20 Operations Without an Assigned Fixed Speed (OWAFS) in the North Atlantic for more details.'  In looking at the ICAO NAT OPS Bulletin (2019_001); the text mimics what is published in the Jeppesen Airway Manual. In conclusion; I believe we were in full compliance with the 'Resume normal speed' clearance when we accelerated to M.83 and advised ATC but since the controller has a different understanding of the situation I would like to get clarification from the company.

column121: It was the Captain's leg on a return flight from ZZZ when we were given the ZZZZZ3 SID. We were given a standard take off clearance from Runway XXL (no heading; altitude; or fix to fly) and I; as the pilot monitoring; engaged the autopilot modes as directed. After double-checking I correctly engaged NAV mode; we were still in HDG with the only white needle navigation being from ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1 and then on the rest of the departure. Since we were still in HDG mode with what I remember was runway heading bugged; we were heading directly for the terrain off of the departure end of XXL. We received hasty instructions from ATC to turn left immediately to get away from the terrain; which we complied with. We were in VMC and could clearly see the terrain; which we had already climbed above when the instructions from ATC came through to start the immediate turn. We never received a GPWS terrain alert. Once established heading back to ZZZZZ on the departure; the Captain had disengaged and reengaged the NAV button to finally arm FMS mode. ATC then advised us to resume the departure and continue our assigned climb altitude to 17;000 feet. No further communications between us and ATC about what had happened. The rest of the flight went on normally and without incident. Really make sure on RNAV departures that when you select the NAV button that the FMS mode activates and if needed spin the heading bug to the headings provided on the charts to avoid conflicts like this.

column121: The crew departed ZZZ on time after calling maintenance to reset a Rudder Trim Limiter ECAM malfunction. Pushback; start; taxi; takeoff and climb out were uneventful. Passing FL260 for a cruise altitude of FL270 the First Officer (Pilot Monitoring) identified a flashing oil quantity advisory reading and a low oil pressure indication on the #1 engine system display. Due to the aircraft's momentum and vertical rate of climb the Captain (Pilot Flying) elected to level off at FL270 as planned. Initially the zero oil quantity and low 60 PSI pressure indication were not accompanied by an ECAM message and system status indicated normal. Within a couple of minutes a series of intermittent ECAM cautions and warnings occurred leading to an engine shutdown condition. The amber ENG 1 OIL LO PR Caution illuminated first on the ECAM display. The crew responded by initiating the company non-normal checklist strategy. The Captain announced 'my aircraft' then the First Officer verified that the ECAM was not a Quick Action or ECAM exception item. The Captain elected to remain flying and also took control of the radio. It was a crew awareness only caution so the FO (First Officer) then checked the QRH for follow up items. This Caution does not direct the crew to adjust thrust settings. During this process the caution [message] cleared itself without any inputs from the crew but the zero oil quantity and 60 PSI indications remained. At this point the ECAM display was clear and system status indicated normal. Shortly thereafter the red ENG 1 LO PR warning illuminated on the ECAM display. This occurred intermittently 3 times and then cleared itself each time resulting in a normal system status display on the ECAM. Oil quantity remained at zero and pressure was now steady at 40 PSI on the system display. These intermittent ECAM warnings lasted for approximately 2-3 seconds and then cleared to a normal status for roughly the same amount of time. The next time the ECAM warning illuminated it remained steady and the crew followed the ENG 1 LO PR warning procedures and shutdown the engine. The crew notified Center and requested a radar vector descent to final for the engine out approach at ZZZ1. The non-normal indications initially occurred just prior to the ETP (equal time point) between ZZZ and ZZZ1. However by the time the ECAM directed engine shutdown the flight had progressed passed the ETP and was at a normal descent point for ZZZ1. Dispatch was called using the iPad crew phone and notified of the nature of the emergency and decision to land at ZZZ1. The flight attendants and passengers were briefed about the Precautionary Landing at ZZZ1 and the possibility of airport fire vehicles near the aircraft. After shutting down the engine and notifying ATC; the crew requested and was given a vector and descent direct to a left 10 NM base at ZZZ1. Descent and approach were very stable and normal. The Captain flew the descent and approach with both the autopilot and auto thrust on. Crew requested ARFF (airport rescue fire department) for the landing and cleared the runway for a brief inspection of the engine. On request of the crew the fire department followed the aircraft to the gate. Shutdown at the gate and passenger deplaning were normal. Note: ATC handling by ZZZ Center; ZZZ1 Approach and Tower were outstanding. Handoff from Tower to ARFF at ZZZ1 was seamless and well coordinated. Flight Attendant performance was also outstanding and the passengers remained well informed throughout the emergency. Although oil fault indications were somewhat intermittent and erratic the fact that multiple independent sensors indicated a problem caused the crew to shutdown the #1 engine when directed by the ENG LO PR Warning ECAM. After the flight; maintenance personnel initially reported normal engine oil quantity on a sight gauge even though the engine instrument remained at zero. Initially crew suspects a partial blockage or pump failure in the system without oil loss. The engine oil quantity and pressure indications were initially both alarming and confusing. As the adrenaline level increased for the crew due to the perception there would be an engine shutdown there was also a level of doubt that the indications were accurate. Low oil pressure on the engine instrument should be accompanied by a Low Pressure ECAM Caution or Warning. Why did the pressure remain steady in the amber range with zero on the quantity? This is an uncomfortable situation because our training does not address multiple oil failures without ECAM warnings. It puts the flight crew into one of those gray areas where a Captain is expected to make a decision based on the information he has on hand in a situation not covered in training. The natural instinct of a pilot is to shutdown an engine before complete oil loss to prevent a catastrophic failure. In this occurrence engine indications identified a problem well in advance of ECAM warnings. Yet crew training and aircraft procedures generally do not address engine shutdown without ECAM warning checklist direction. Should crews be given shutdown discretion in the absence of ECAM warnings and checklist? In this situation the Captain elected to continue as the Pilot Flying while the crew worked through the non-normal checklist strategy. Even though most aspects of company's non-normal strategy were performed correctly the overall pace and structure were hampered by the Captain continuing to fly. In this case the checklist strategy would have been better managed if the Captain had delegated flying to the FO. For example; when the ECAM directed the 'Engine Master Switch-Off' both pilots confirmed it was the #1 engine but the Captain positioned it to off. Procedure dictates that the non-flying pilot position the switch to off.

The 150 continued downwind; turned base then final; when the biplane banked hard from downwind directly to final abeam the 150 and approximately 25 feet above. The 150 initiated a go-around and the biplane did the same; nearly colliding which each other. The 150 eventually landed on a second go-around while the biplane continued to execute high speed low passes over the runway at about 50 feet AGL. The problem likely arose because the biplane; which was NORDO; was engaged in a low level acrobatics display for a group of onlookers in the tiedown area and was not scanning for conflicting traffic. The 150 likely saw the biplane traffic near the airport; but the biplane's erratic behavior and rapid altitude and direction changes would have complicated efforts to maintain separation. The conflict could have been resolved if the biplane pilot refrained from low-level aerobatics in the vicinity of the traffic pattern; was visually scanning for traffic; and vacated the traffic pattern area when other traffic was inbound to land.

column121: During a Medevac flight to ZZZ1 from ZZZ I initiated an approach with less than the required RVR to do so. Our return flight had been delayed by 4 hours because the patient was very difficult to stabilize. I had checked the weather before departing ZZZ and it was above the minimums that were required for the approach. While enroute to ZZZ1; I acquired the ATIS and found that visibility had decreased to 1/8 mile. The situation at the two nearest options that would allow me to get the hospital was the same. I chose to go to ZZZ2 because it was near enough that we could get the patient to ZZZ1 and the automated weather was well above minimums for the approach. After two attempts at landing in ZZZ2; I realized that the weather was worse than reported there. While I had been maneuvering I was monitoring the conditions at ZZZ1 and they seemed to vary minute by minute. I decided to divert to ZZZ3 since the medic told me we had no time to waste with another approach as he was running low on medication for the patient. When I requested the change to ZZZ3; the controller asked me if I wanted to attempt an approach to ZZZ1. I saw the runway lights at 400 ft AGL and the runway at 200 ft AGL. I decided to land. As I was rolling out I noticed that ground visibility was very low and I realized I had landed with less than the required 2400 RVR that I was supposed to have. Contributing factors: I had the weather and forecast from when I left ZZZ1 6 hours prior printed out. I should have reviewed the forecast more thoroughly rather than just checking present conditions before returning to ZZZ1. I did not realize that night that I was getting sick. During the climb out I was queasy and I attributed this to a lack of horizon at night. The next day I had full flu like symptoms that precluded me from working. What I would do differently: I should have asked the medical team where they wanted to go if ZZZ1 did not work out. If I had that we could have all been prepared to go to a different hospital if the ZZZ1 airport did not work.
