column121: On date I was conducting training in an R22 Helicopter departing out of ZZZ at XA:45 local time to ZZZ1. Winds were predominantly out of the west at around 10 kts and we joined left closed traffic for RWY 26 at ZZZ1. There was high training volume and I estimate 7 aircraft were on the ground waiting to depart or actively in the Right Closed Traffic for RWY XX plus our Helicopter. At around XB:10 local time a Jet taxied to the active with no Radio (or no radio communication was made) as we were on a left downwind for [Runway] XX. Local pilots made calls on the radio so all would be aware of his departure and be vigilant/use caution. The jet took off without incident and departed to the North. As pilots worked together to sequence traffic we made our base and final leg before again departing XX to rejoin left closed traffic. At approximately XB:15 local time on the upwind of XX roughly 300ft AGL without warning the jet made a low pass on runway XY at very high speed. I would estimate the pilot was 300ft off our starboard side and about 100ft below our current altitude. I was able to track his flight after the incident to find his Ground Speed was in excess of 330mph. The Jet than proceeded back out to the North again and ended up circling to land on RWY XY this time to a full stop. (The following is my personal opinion) I believe this pilot does not have any remorse for his action. He has an attitude that the FAA can't/won't get him in trouble for this reckless behavior. He wasn't breaking any REG by operating without a radio in an ECHO airspace but his speed certainly was in violation of FAR 91.117(a) and given the high training volume being conducted on this day the pilot showed a clear disregard for other pilots or even his/her own safety.

column121: On [Date]; I was acting as Pilot in Command (PIC) of a UH-60 L Army National Guard Helicopter conducting a round-trip air movement of crew and passengers from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. I was sitting left seat; my Co-pilot (PI) sat right seat. I had two crewmembers in the gunner's seats (Row 2); and one passenger in Row 3. Total: 5 souls on board.Earlier in the day; we had flown IFR from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 for a fuel stop before heading to ZZZ. We had received a military weather briefing and were aware of an AIRMET Zulu for moderate icing along the route. We monitored PIREPS and determined as a crew that the risk of anything beyond moderate icing was minimal; as the few PIREPS observed were for light rime ice at flight levels above our planned flight altitude.The conditions observed on the flight from ZZZ2 to ZZZ were very stable. There was a stratiform cloud layer; approximately 1;000 to 2;000 ft. thick; that we either flew below or above the cloud layer the entire way to ZZZ. We observed no icing.We were on the ground for approximately two hours after landing at ZZZ. I continued to monitor weather conditions; and it appeared they had not changed from the time we landed. I observed the same AIRMET Zulu and a couple of PIREPS reporting light rime above our planned flight level.Prior to departure; my crew and I conducted de-ice checks in accordance with our aircraft's technical manual; which all passed.After an uneventful climb to our requested flight level of 7;000 ft. MSL; we leveled off. At this time the annunciator panel gave us a warning of 'MR ICE DETECTED'. We had discussed this as an expected possibility; acknowledged the caution; and monitored our ice rate meter; which read 'Light Icing Detected'.At this time; I asked ATC if they knew where the cloud tops were. We were informed that they were at approximately 8;000 ft. MSL. Faced with the decision to climb approximately 1;000 ft. through visible moisture; or descend approximately 4;000 ft. through visible moisture; I requested to climb to 10;000 ft. MSL. ATC gave a clearance to 9;000 ft. MSL. We began our climb.In approximately 1.5 minutes; our icing condition worsened. Our ice rate meter pegged out at its maximum indication of severe icing. The helicopter began to shake; and we lost a dangerous amount of our main rotor RPM (a true [anomaly]). I immediately pressed down on the collective to preserve our rotor RPM; took the controls from my co-pilot; [advised ATC] by announcing 'PAN PAN PAN' on ZZZ Approach frequency. I asked the controller to help me get out of the icing situation and was ultimately cleared down to 2;500 ft. MSL.My crew and I flew the helicopter well; in a level attitude at approximately 2;500 ft. per minute. We maintained 100% rotor RPM during our decent and exited the cloud layer at approximately 3;000 ft. MSL. I tested the controls as we got closer to the surface to ensure I would be able to arrest the helicopter's rate of decent. Upon exiting the clouds; the icing condition improved; and the rest of the flight home was uneventful and under VFR conditions.Chain Of Events:How the problem arose: The problem arose from the unexpected encounter into severe icing.How it was discovered: The severe icing was detected by on the on-board ice detection system; severe vibrations were felt by the crew; and the low rotor warning alarm sounded.Corrective actions: The Good: The crew responded to the [situation] well by manipulating the flight controls to preserve rotor RPM; communicating the [anomaly] to ATC; and flying the aircraft out of the icing conditions.The Bad: The crew did not respond correctly to the initial 'ICE DETECTED' caution. In accordance with the UH-60 Operators Manual; 'The ice rate meter activates the ICE DETECTED caution when the BLADE DE-ICE POWER switch is turned off; informing the pilot of the requirement to turn on the system'. Contributing Factors:Neither the UH-60 Operating Manual or checklist clearly emphasizes the immediatememory item actions required in the event of an icing [situation].An updated -1 weather brief was not obtained from the Air Force Operational Weather Squadron by the Pilot in Command.Human Performance Considerations:The perception of the Pilot in Command that the 'AUTO' function on the ice rate meter meant that the system will 'automatically operate upon detection of ice' was incorrect.The perception of the Pilot in Command that the weather conditions would be the same on the return flight as they were on the first portion was incorrect.The actions of both the Pilot in Command and Co-pilot ultimately saved the lives of the crew; however their inaction to turn the de-ice system on was detrimental to the safe operation of the aircraft.Factors affecting the quality of human performance:Neither the Pilot or Co-pilot complained of fatigue or other exogenous factors prior the flight. Both had a good night's rest and were well within the confines of their duty day at the time of the incident.Recommendations:Ensure aircrew are intimately familiar with the de-ice equipment and capabilities on their aircraft. Recommend that changes be made to the UH-60 Operator's Manual and checklist to emphasize the seriousness of an icing [situation] and the immediate response required. This should be an underlined step. Once the ICE DETECTED caution appears; the immediate action required is for the blade de-ice switch to be turned ON.

column121: On a flight from ZZZ to MPR; I flew a practice approach into MPR (RNAV 18) visually in VFR conditions with no view limiting device. I mention this because I believe this was the biggest contributing factor to the event with Aircraft X. Aircraft A was at 160 and he descended the aircraft to 10;000 thinking he was a ZZZ1/ZZZ2 arrival and to alleviate all potential traffic conflicts. The main problem was as soon as I sat down and signed in; the R-side was too busy to give me a brief but I was eager to help and to catch up on anything. As I was beginning my scan I noticed Aircraft X getting close to the ZZZ1 Approach airspace at 10;000 without a hand-off and I immediately jumped on the line to coordinate with the ZZZ1 Approach Controller. I began to try to APREQ the aircraft at 10;000 but the ZZZ1 Controller realizing he had an arrival to ZZZZZ [Intersection] already at 10;000 he instructed me to descend Aircraft X to 080; the R-side complied. There was no loss of separation between any aircraft; however; I have decided to report this event because I was talked to by management because of it. I advised my Supervisor in the X area that I did the best I could given I had just sat down and had just noticed the aircraft not handed off to ZZZ1 Approach. Given the coordination could have been done in a more efficient and timely manner I had to work with what I had.According to the safety board's review of the event there was an airspace violation as a result of this coordination. In my opinion this happened because the ZZZ1 Controller and his uncertainty of what needed to be done. I offered to descend Aircraft X to 080; but he advised me to just leave him at 10;000 and then instructed another aircraft to descend below the Aircraft X flight. This back and forth coordination and being reluctant to take the hand off is what resulted in Aircraft X entering his airspace without a hand off. I would like to add that overflights are not allowed over ZZZ NAVAID per our LOA; however the situation dictated a different solution. I would also like to emphasize that as the D-side Controller in this situation had I not immediately gotten on the line with the ZZZ1 Controller this would have been a much different and ultimately worse issue. I am almost certain a loss of separation would have occurred. My Supervisor agreed and the R-side backed me up on it. I have chosen to report this event because even though management advised me this was not disciplinary in any way shape or form; I would still like to bring this up to the safety council's attention.Because of COVID; staffing has been an issue and the traffic volume was high. We had staffing later in the day that helped tremendously but this particular situation we were at minimum. I would also like to receive guidance as to what I could have done better given I was forced into a bad situation and I did my best to separate aircraft and coordinate what I could before an incident may have occurred.

column121: Working in a north flow; with arrivals coming in on the downwind; spacing not really an issue; and I had just been in a rhythm bringing the arrivals in for visual approaches. My general method is to give a descent to 9;000 feet which is the downwind Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA) when clear of traffic; then slow to 180 knots 2 miles from the base turn; then turn to a 070 heading; then when the first turn is observed and they are now crossing the 9;000 foot MVA line into the 8;000 foot MVA; give a descent to 7;000 feet; then call the airport; then clear them for an approach with a turn to final. This sequence requires 5 or 6 transmissions per plane; but I feel like it is an expeditious way to safely get aircraft in with such a high MVA on the downwind. After having worked many aircraft in without issue and rather monotonously; Aircraft X checked on and was one of the last aircraft in the bank. I descended them to 9;000 feet; slowed to 180 knots at the normal place; then got distracted by something going on with another sector; I can't remember what; but I returned my focus to Aircraft X; incorrectly thinking that I had already given the base turn; and I was watching for the target to start a turn to the east. I saw the target move and started the transmission to descend. The pilot read it back; but I soon could tell that they were not in the turn and were not leaving the higher MVA for lower terrain. I asked the pilot if they were in the right turn heading 070 yet; and they responded that they were turning to 070 degrees; but in reality I had not yet issued it and didn't realize that until reviewing it afterward. The aircraft was soon in the base turn leaving the higher MVA; I called the airport and the pilot responded in sight; and I issued a visual approach clearance. It was my mistake that I did not catch it earlier. I will practice more vigilance in ensuring a complete turn out of the MVA before issuing the descent.

column121: Aircraft X. ARD had previous write-up about compressor stalls on #3 Engine. Maintenance said the morning crew rejected the takeoff for compressor stalls; we read the write-up and maintenance action in detail and discussed the issue. We identified this as a potential threat to our flight. On push back; while starting #1 Engine; we got ENG 1 FADEC ALTN alert; we referred to the QRH; it also identified 'action code' as SW. After engine start; the Captain said we could recycle the switch and asked if I was okay with that; I replied if he was okay; I was okay. We selected FADEC ALTN; then selected it again to the normal function; the alert went away. Later as we taxied out; I thought about the PDM process and not consulting maintenance; but the Captain's action corrected the alert to the proper configuration without any alerts and without an AML write-up; so I resolved my dilemma internally. Prior to taking the runway; the Captain announced he was gonna run-up all the engines a bit higher than usual while holding the brakes to ensure #3 Engine was operating correctly; I replied it was a good idea. It was my take-off (hand flown as briefed) and everything went normal up to about 700 ft. AGL.About 700 ft. AGL; with the gear up and flaps extended; we heard loud bangs associated with a compressor stall (I only heard this before in the sim) and a jolting in the plane; there were no differing indications on any of the engine instruments (all three N1; EGT; and N2 indications were identical). Around 1;000 ft. AGL; the Captain said he was gonna shut the engine down; I said okay with the bias of the previous write-up in the ARD; also thinking we'd go thru the process of 'Throttle-Idle; Fuel Shutoff Switch-Off' (I admit this wasn't the calm and rehearsed engine failure problem in the sim; and I was a bit anxious about the actual compressor stall). About that time; Tower called us and said we had intermittent flames shooting out of the left side (#1 Engine); the Captain said 'left side; I shut down [Engine] #3' (paraphrase). I looked down and noticed 0 fuel flow and the engine N2 decreasing while the banging continued. I exclaimed 'Let's start it back up' thinking #3 wasn't the problem and we definitely needed it if we had to shut down #1! The Captain quickly returned the fuel cutoff switch to on and I saw the N2 increase. I turned the autopilot on (as briefed if we had a problem) and announced I was disconnecting the auto throttles while the Captain told Tower we were returning to the field for compressor stalls and advised ATC. Tower told us to turn left downwind for [Runway] XX and I told the Captain 'I got the plane and the radios' and I replied to Tower. With the autopilot on and above 1;000 ft. AGL; the plane accelerated above Vf and I asked Tower if 2;000 ft. MSL was okay to level off; Tower replied yes. As I started the heading guided turn to the left; I adjusted the altitude to 2;000 ft. and manually retarded all the throttles for level off then selected airspeed 200 knots. With the throttles out of take-off power; the banging went away; I believe Tower said the flames stopped. While flying downwind abeam the field; I began to setup for the approach [Runway] XX; adjusted the minimums (already had it preselected); and announced I was moving the flaps to 15 degrees since they were still extended. Tower asked if we had the field insight; I replied yes and Tower cleared us the visual approach [Runway] XX and cleared to land; I repeated the clearance but said we were gonna fly out a bit to get our normal visual glidepath. After the Captain programmed the FMS and inserted the ILS frequency into the NavRad page; I called for the approach check and turned base to final; on dogleg; I began the descent on glidepath before intercepting the localizer and called for the gear down and before landing check. With the final configuration and checklist complete; I asked the Captain if he wanted the landing since we were an emergency; he took control of the plane with the autopilot on while I briefed him of the FMAs. Landing was uneventful.  We taxied clear onto taxiway XX and waited for the fire truck's inspection. With the all clear (no fire); we terminated the emergency and taxied to parking.Engine compressor stall.Some missteps between the crew while successfully resolving an engine compressor stall. Better crew coordination would simplify resolution.

column121: On [Date]; we operated Aircraft X from ZZZ-ROA and I was the CA (Captain) onboard. It was our Day 3 and Leg 4 of the day. I was the Pilot Flying; while my FO (First Officer) was Pilot Monitoring. Both of us were new to this airport; so we reviewed the 10-7 pages and airport diagram to make sure we selected an adequate runway for landing; because they both were relatively short runways in mountainous terrain surrounding area. Once we were in the air and leveled off at our cruising altitude; we started setting up for the approach and briefed it all. As we got closer to the airport and were with Approach; he descended us to 6;000 ft. We both saw the runway and reported it. The ATC asked us to give him at least 6 mile final and we concurred. We looked at the runway and descended down to 4;500 ft. approaching from the southwest to intercept [Runway] 34 localizer. As we got closer to the intercept point for the localizer; the aircraft annunciated 'Caution terrain' 'Pull up' simultaneously; there was no break in between at all. There was also no terrain data that displayed on the MFD on both of our screens. I disconnected the AP (Autopilot) and added power needed to climb immediately. The 'Pull up' annunciation was only said once and went away. We only climbed 500 ft. to 5;000 ft. and continued to intercept the course to land. We also reported the event to the ATC and they didn't say anything. The 'Master Warning' switch light also didn't go on. This event lasted about 2 seconds and we continued to land at the airport.Both of us were new the airport and should've stayed with ATC until intercepted and then call for visual.This event could've easily been avoided by simply just staying with the Approach Control until established on approach; because it is a very mountainous area. Being an unfamiliar crew flying to this area and going visual to land this runway can put you in this situation; even though being in VMC conditions and having runway in sight. column123: On [Date]; my Captain and I operated Aircraft X from ZZZ to ROA. It was Day 3; Leg 4 of our trip. On this leg; I was the Pilot Monitoring; while my CA (Captain) was flying the aircraft. This was the first time either of us operated to Roanoke; so we reviewed the 10-7 pages; and airport diagram to make sure we selected an adequate runway for landing; since they both were relatively short runways in a mountainous area. Once in cruise flight at our final altitude; we started setting up for the approach and briefed it as necessary. The plan was to set up for the visual backed up by the ILS for Runway 34. As we got closer to the airport and were with Approach; the controller descended us to 6;000 ft. We both saw the runway and reported it. ATC then cleared us for the visual; but asked us to give him at least 6 mile final and we concurred. We looked at the runway; surrounding terrain; and approach plate; and decided to descend down to 4;500 ft. approaching from the southwest to intercept the Runway 34 localizer. We figured this was a correct altitude; as the highest obstacle on the plate was 3;508 ft. As we got closer to the intercept point for the localizer; the aircraft annunciated 'Caution terrain' 'Pull up' simultaneously; there was no break in between at all. There was also no terrain data that displayed on the MFD on both of our screens. My Captain immediately disconnected the AP (Autopilot) and added power as necessary. The 'Pull up' annunciation and all other GPWS alerts were only said once and went away as soon as we started the climb. We only climbed 500 ft. to 5;000 ft. and continued to intercept the course to land. The event was reported to ATC as well; and they acknowledged. This event lasted about 2 seconds and we continued to land at the airport.This was the first time either of us have operated to this particular airport; and should have either stayed above the approach's MSA of 5;700 ft.; or even stayed with the Approach Controller; making him give us headings and altitudes rather than calling the airport in sight and getting cleared for the visual.This event could have easily been avoided by staying with the Approach Controller until established on the approach; rather than calling the airport in sight and getting cleared for the visual. A crew flying to this area that is unfamiliar with the surrounding terrain and conducting a visual approach to this runway can end up in this situation; even with VMC conditions and having the runway in sight. I would also like to suggest some guidance in the 10-7 pages to be added regarding landing at this airport and staying with ATC until cleared of the mountains and only going visual once cleared and over the valley. Something similar to the 10-7 pages for ZZZ regarding the GPWS events would be helpful to other crews in avoiding a similar situation.

column121: Being vectored onto the final approach course 26R; we had a brief encounter with a wake turbulence. And then again during the landing flare to the point where it was becoming a problem to maintain a stabilized approach path above the runway in ground effect. Did not have time to notify air traffic control that this happened. I don't know if we were behind a heavy previous arrival. But we were getting really close to having to go around from the landing flare. The roll motion was becoming such a problem with keeping the aircraft stabilized; and aligned with the runway. I was actually shocked that we touchdown as smooth as we did. I asked the pilot flying if he thought that was a bit unusual his statement was 'I was just one more jolt away from going around'. Wake turbulence encounters in Atlanta are becoming an every week problem; more like almost every inbound leg into Atlanta problem. Also it seems there is little consideration given to the fact that we may be departing behind something that might be a threat as well. I'm beginning to think that there's nothing much going to be done about it until something serious happens. Often the wake encounter threats are not much of a problem if there's sufficient crosswind push the wake away from trailing aircraft; from my experience it does not take much to all. However I've learned that this is still a problem at some point on the arrival or departure procedure. For example a crosswind on the departure runways will clear you of the wake threat for takeoff; but might present a very real problem in trail of a heavy navigating to a point; to the same on that departure or arrival. Especially if it's a direct head; or tailwind now.

column121: Upon stepping aboard Aircraft X; I immediately detected an odor that had a burnt wire smell.  The other FA's also made comments such as; 'What is that smell? I looked in the galley to see if any circuit breakers had popped and also looked in the oven to determine if the odor was from a forgotten burnt meal.  All circuits were in proper place and there was no food in oven.  I then walked down the aisle to determine if the burnt-wire smell was coming from the aft galley.  I stopped at Row 21; aircraft right and stepped up on Seat 21 D as the odor was very strong above the OH bin.  I could not visibly see any sign of smoke but the odor was quite strong. He stated that it had just arrived to ZZZ and the Captain of that flight informed him that a smoke alarm for the aft cabin activated upon landing.  Captain stated that this happens from time to time and poses no threat of fire.  All of us 4 FAs told him that we smelled a burnt wire odor in the cabin. Captain waited for the Maintenance personnel member to step off of the aircraft and then told us FA's that if we were not comfortable with the odor that he backed us and would insist that we fly a different aircraft to ZZZ1 or return to hotel if aircraft was not available.  All 4 of us FA's unanimously and instantly stated that we did not feel comfortable on this aircraft and we wanted to change aircraft in the interest of Safety First.  I then told the Captain that I noticed the odor was particularly strong by OH compartment of 21D.  We then walked to that row and Captain also noticed that it had a strong odor of either 'heated dust' or 'hot wire' on the lighting ballast.  He then asked me if I personally felt safe taking this aircraft. I told him that I am very safety minded and the odor was not normal or usual to me.  We all stayed in the first class seating area and continued personal conversations among us.  The Captain was not present as he was talking to Operations.  After approximately 15 minutes of remaining in the first class seating area; the other FAs noticed that my voice was getting hoarse and that I was beginning to lose my voice.   To the best of my recollection; I believe that C FA; and B FA; both stated that their throats felt scratchy.After approximately another 15 minutes of staying and waiting for a decision onboard; in the first class seating area; we were told by [the] Captain that we were changing into different aircraft for our flight back to ZZZ1.  We then deplaned the aircraft and walked to the other waiting aircraft.  My voice remained coarse for an additional 30 minutes and I developed a migraine during the boarding process.  I had the migraine the entire flight to ZZZ1; and it continued until early afternoon of date.  Additionally; I awoke on the morning of date with a sore and scratchy throat.  Both my migraine and scratchy throat subsided around 1400 hours on date.  I have had a continuous low-grade headache since date through present date.  I did not seek any medical attention as I 'normally' suffer from low grade sinus headaches regularly and use an OTC nasal spray along with Tylenol.I commend our Captain; for valuing and backing our decision to prioritize safety first.I would hope that Aircraft X was ferried back to ZZZ without full crew and guests in the pursuit of safety.

column121: I file this report for two reasons: to note a particular pilot's decision-making; and to talk about a larger potentially dangerous airport-environment situation.  Here is the relevant data:- The airport in question is Montgomery County Airpark; in Gaithersburg; Maryland; GAI. It is a very busy *uncontrolled* airport. It is within the DC SFRA; so pilots must obtain a discrete transponder code from Potomac Approach before taking off; and before re-entering the SFRA from outside. - The airport's only runway is 32/14; about 4000 feet long. The airport ATIS specifies that Runway 14 is preferred in calm-wind conditions. Also; the only approach to GAI is an RNAV/LPV approach to Runway 14. - There is a very; very active primary-training type airport. Nearly all of its students are [from] overseas; and the frequency of their flight means that the traffic-pattern at the airport is usually 'full.' It is typical to have one plane doing a runup; another taking off; another on downwind turning to base; and two or three others approaching from the north; all at the same time.- On the morning of this incident; winds had been in the 5 kt range--but from the north. So traffic through the morning had been all on Runway 32. - Now; the time in question. It was about XA:00 local EST. I was approaching from the north; and I received a code for entering the SFRA from Potomac Approach. As is usual practice; when I was about 12 miles north of GAI; I told Potomac; 'Gaithersburg in sight;' and they gave the formulaic response: 'Stay on discrete transponder code until landing; remain outside Class Bravo; switch to local frequency approved.' So I switched to the local UNICOM; 123.075.-I heard on the frequency what I also saw on my ADS-B display: That the pattern was; as usual; 'busy;' with three or four planes at various points in the circuit. And all of them were using Runway 32. (The winds at that moment were reporting calm on ATIS; but the pattern had been in steady use all day; on 32.)-Over the next eight minutes or so; between first radio contact and landing; I noticed two recurrent phenomena. One was many planes reporting their progress and position in a pattern for Runway 32.  I made calls; beginning at 8 miles out; with intentions to follow the established local practice. ('Forty-five to join right downwind for Runway 32.') The other notable entry was one airplane (Airplane X) that reported it was to the west; and 'straight in landing; Runway 14.'-A plane reports 'downwind 32.' Aircraft X says; 'straight in; Runway 14.' Another plane says; 'Aircraft X; we are using 32; please circle to land.' Aircraft pilot says; 'Straight in Runway 14.' At least twice; and I think three times; flight instructors say 'Aircraft X; PLEASE circle to land 32. We are all using 32.' Aircraft X replies; 'Straight in; 14.'-I kept reporting my own position; and said at one point 'Aircraft X; I am turning base to final for landing 32.' At that point I could see him descending to 14 -- i.e.; head on. The distances were such that it was clear to me that I could land safely and normally; and get off the runway; before he got too close.   And I proceeded to land. I turned off the runway halfway down; while he was still probably a mile out on opposite-direction final. All the other planes in the Runway 32 pattern extended their downwind etc.; to land. -The two planes landed at XA:07 pm EST; but in opposite directions.-Later; I saw someone who I assumed to be the Aircraft X pilot. He was; and I asked him: 'Why did you do that?' His answer was that he was fine-tuning the coupled-autopilot and wanted to fly an approach all the way down. -Note: I have been in this situation myself too; wanting to check out autopilots. But I choose airports where I can do so in keeping with the local traffic flow. -The main problem in this scenario was the Aircraft X pilot; who insisted on plowing ahead despite repeated requests on the frequency to switch to join the busy local traffic flow. I realize this is not an 'enforcement' forum; and I mention it just FYI.-The larger point is that the Gaithersburg airport has become unsustainably busy; for its uncontrolled status.  I have landed there probably X times over the past XX years. I *always* view the most challenging part of any trip to be the final 10 minutes of trying to fit into the uncontrolled but increasingly busy traffic pattern there.  With many primary students in training; they're often doing unexpected things in the pattern; or are uncertain in radio calls. Suggestion / request: Sooner or later there is going to be some safety incident at this airport; coming from too much traffic with too little control. A tower controller would *never* have allowed the situation I'm reporting to emerge. This is a problem waiting to happen at this airport.

column121: I was returning to BED from the West. It was dark. I tuned in the ATIS. The current ATIS was broadcasting that BED was 'landing and departing Runway 23.' After copying the ATIS; I called BED Tower and reported my position as near Minuteman Airport (6B6) and informed the Tower that I was inbound landing with ATIS. The Tower Controller initially cleared me to enter a right downwind for Runway 29.  This confused me because the ATIS had stated that BED was 'landing and departing Runway 23.' I asked the Controller for confirmation of the runway assignment and he acknowledged that he had 'made a mistake' and told me to enter a right downwind for Runway 23. After I entered the control space; and near the airport; I noticed the high intensity runway lights and landing traffic was on Runway 29; while runway 23 had their lights on 'dim'.  Since the ATIS had not mentioned simultaneous operations to intersecting runways; I became disoriented. I mistook Runway 29 for Runway 23. I was so concerned that I even called the Tower and asked the Controller: 'Is the Aircraft Y lined up with the right runway?'The Tower Controller realized that something was not right and called me and asked me to confirm that I was setting up for right downwind 23 and offered me a clearance to enter a right downwind for Runway 29. I told him that I thought I could still correct; but I ended up flying through the final for Runway 23 and ended up on a left downwind for 23. At about this time; another aircraft; which I later learned was Aircraft Z arriving from the west had also turned inbound to Runway 23 from the north. The Tower Controller told me to turn 20 degrees further right which I did to widen out my downwind leg. Thanks to the Controller; the Aircraft Z was able to land safely and so was I.I now realize that several other factors contributed to my confusion.  I was more tired than I realized. I had a very long work week; yet this night was an opportunity to start flying more night flights; after being absent from this experience for over 16 months.  The pandemic means hazard [but not] if I bring an instructor to help me re-acquaint to night flying.   I allowed myself to be fooled by the warm weather; the light winds and the great visibility into thinking that it would be a good night to re-acquaint myself to cross-country night flying.  Tonight; with the lights dimmed in the cockpit; and the high intensity lights on Runway 29; a plane landing on 29; the lights dimmed on Runway 23; and my lack of night flying practice did this happen.I now realize that I had vastly underestimated the combined effects of fatigue; distraction and 'rust.' Added to that; my confusion resulting from the initial mistaken clearance to enter a right downwind for 29; the combination of bright runway lighting on a conflicting runway without any warning that such operations were being conducted; and traffic operating in unexpected directions all combined to make for a much more confusing situation than I ever would have expected.The controllers explained to me that even when Runway 23 is the operating runway; they still allow traffic to land and depart Runway 29 because Runway 23 is too short for some aircraft that use the field. Nevertheless; I believe that safety would be greatly improved if; during nighttime operations; the ATIS included the warning concerning operations being conducted simultaneously to conflicting runways. This is especially true at BED where runway alignment issues are already an issue. I believe that such a warning would have eliminated my confusion at seeing traffic landing and departing on Runway 29 and then mistaking it for Runway 23.

column121: I was doing pattern work at ZZZ between XA:00 and XB:00. The airfield had a large amount of arriving traffic during the hours I was flying. After a touch & go on RWY XX; I was asked to extend the upwind before flying a right pattern. About mid-field on the downwind; tower requested a left-360. After my first 360; I was instructed to extend my downwind. A second plane [Aircraft Y] was approaching the airport from the northwest. Aircraft Y was asked to 'make a right 270; keep it tight and get ready to line up behind a [jet]'ATC then asked me to widen out my downwind and look for Aircraft Y making the right 270. At this point it was at my 11 o clock; 3 miles. About 5 seconds later I was able to identify the aircraft; let tower know that I had them in sight and was preparing to line up behind them. About 15 seconds later; tower called me up again; asking 'Aircraft X - extend it out a little bit; actually just follow behind and I'll call your base you will have to follow a jet behind on final'. I read back and confirmed.About 30 seconds later; tower called me up again; 'Aircraft X just so I don't get you too far from the field; make a left 360'. I read back the instruction and began my left 360. At this point; I was already thinking about Aircraft Y as I was planning on how I would get back on the downwind and line up behind them. I believe Aircraft Y was just about to finish its right 270 as I was about 90 degrees into my 360. I was able to spot and track the plane on Foreflight with Sentry; but since I had to make a 360 I lost visual when I initiated my turn. Tower; likely receiving a traffic alert called the other plane to make them aware of me: 'Aircraft X about a mile south making a left 360 - he has you in sight'. I do not think he asked them to confirm that they had me in sight and I can't tell from the live-ATC recording whether they read it back. The added statement 'he has you in sight' was extremely dangerous and could have been fatal. Yes; I had the traffic in sight when I was heading toward it and planning to get behind them; but once I started my left 360 there was no way of maintaining a visual with the other plane since I was now heading the opposite direction. I immediately recognized the potential conflict and started looking both outside the plane and on Foreflight trying to spot and track the other plane's relative position. The other plane did not make a 270 turn; but instead kept turning toward the airport/runway i.e. cutting into my path.As I was about 270 degrees into my 360 turn tower called 'Aircraft X - as you are coming out of that 360 turn do you still have Aircraft Y in sight?'At this point; I was already banking hard left in a steep turn trying to pull away from the converging traffic that I saw coming closer toward me. Turning right was not an option as it would have put me in the middle of final with jets arriving. I do not think the other plane confirmed whether or not they had me in sight. If they did; they flew way too close to me for my comfort and should have initiated an avoidance maneuver. In response to tower's question I responded 'Aircraft X unable' because I had to focus on flying the airplane away from the other traffic. We then passed by each other with much less separation than I feel comfortable. The other plane heading toward the runway; and me pulling hard left to the North-West; initiating a climb up to gain altitude. It is hard to tell exactly but horizontal distance could have been less than 500 feet Vertical distance was virtually the same. It happened very quickly. If I had not realized the potential conflict and mitigated by tracking on foreflight and pulling hard left this could have been a really really bad situation. The biggest mistake here; in my opinion; was ATC communicating to the other plane that I had them in sight AFTER I started my 360. There is no way one can maintain visual during such a maneuver while also flying safely and ATC shouldunder no circumstances make that statement. I also think that having two planes completing maneuvers in a way where their exit paths can conflict (right 270 and left 360) in close proximity should be prohibited.There were multiple safer options here. Aircraft Y could have flown a proper base rather than cutting it short onto final. I could have been asked to fly west; or I could have been asked to fly another 360 right after the first one. The fact that ATC changed its instructions relative to how I should fly behind/around the other traffic 3 times in a minute indicates to me that they were not planning ahead but rather responding to/running behind.In the future; I will call out if ATC tells other people that I have them in sight when I don't (i.e. after starting my left 360). I am also surprised nobody (tower/the other plane) complained about how close this was. I am glad to be back on the ground.  I hope this helps keep other people safe in the future!

column121: I was assigned today to operate SuperTug X; a towbarless aircraft tow tractor; while working at ZZZ.  After towing the aircraft to Gate X; after disconnecting the SuperTug and while attempting to maneuver away; I made light contact with the pushback tractor which was parked behind me.  At the time; I was feeling rushed; because I knew there were more tows scheduled for us and there was also someone waiting for me to clear the area so he could connect the ground power to the aircraft.  While backing up I felt that I had the proper radius in the turn to clear the parked pushback but apparently did not; and made a light inadvertent contact with either the SuperTug hitch or bumper.  I did notice that on this and a few other occasions that day; because I was wearing a different than usual but still company issued face mask; my depth perception seemed to be affected as the mask kept creeping up into my peripheral vision.  I think this was a factor in my misjudging the turn in what were already very confined conditions.  Another issue is that the SuperTug onboard GPU had recently been repaired; and we were using it for the first time in months; with a commensurate disruption to normal workflow.  Although I thought I had clearance at the time; in retrospect I should have taken a minute to move the pushback and reduce the risk.  There was no pushback parking spot painted at this gate; so it was parked right against the edge of the OSZ [Outer Safety Zone]; even there there was approximately 80 additional linear feet of space behind it available to park.  Even if I had moved it; I doubt there was a user check performed on it that day; and therefore moving it without doing one myself would technically put me in violation.  There are many more things that can be taken into consideration than just the blatantly obvious in a situational dynamic environment like an airport.  Because the contact I made felt light; and I know from experience that the equipment is built to take that kind of minor impact; I made the snap decision to continue with the operation.  If you take a look at any piece of airport ground equipment; including SuperTugs; it will immediately become apparent that it is literally covered with innumerable scratches and dents or varying severity; and if we would stop to report and investigate each one; the operation would literally grind to a halt.  Therefore; it was my decision in this instance; based on my experience; observations; and common sense to continue.  There were other factors which came into play in this decision; which I will briefly expand upon.  I need to be clear that if this situation had been one in which I had reason to suspect that there was damage to equipment or even the possibility of damage to an aircraft; that I would have stopped and reported it at once.  In this instance I deemed that it would be unreasonable to bring it up.Today was the X day back from my vacation of Y days; and when checking my work assignments for the month; this was only my Z day assigned to a SuperTug for the month; and the first assigned to X brand SuperTug.  The other days I was at work during this time I was assigned to auxiliary functions.  I believe this is significant in that it feels that this period of lack of hands-on experience caused a perception that my skills may have deteriorated or that I had become rusty.  To that point; I noticed that I was taking some calculated risks; most notably when maneuvering on the gate areas; especially around stationary ground equipment; while preparing to capture or egressing from the vicinity of aircraft.  My reasoning for this; and which I explained to the Supervisor during the course of the day; was that I was attempting to refresh or hone my skills; which I felt may have become dulled.  Another way to put it is that I was trying to find my corners; as persons who operate various types of vehicles say when describing how they feel or sense where the vehicle is in relation to the surrounding environment.  While doing this I felt that I was on point; secure and aware of myself and tasks at hand.  I could say that in fact I was over-zealous or over-confident; too gung ho; and I should have taken a step back at some point and put all this information together; which I only do now after the fact.  I would have to say that the primary reason I did not take that step back was workload / task saturation and distraction; described as follows:Because of the substantial number of people who were not able to work; apparently due to the public health crisis yet ongoing; the manpower available was at or just over half of which would normally be on the team on a given shift.  There was not a substantial reduction in workload; and we had what I would consider based on precedent to be a moderately but not excessively heavy day.  There was therefore an underlying perception of increased pressure to perform; especially in consideration of supporting the needs of the operation because of the diminished staffing during an unusually trying time.I had also noticed multiple issues during the day; which could have been brought to the attention of management or also could have been overlooked and dealt with at a time of less operational urgency.  The most notable of those issues were; a broken seat belt in the SuperTug; radios whose display units were not lighted and hence not visible after sunset; and all the fire extinguishers on the SuperTug were missing the inspection placards.  Additionally; no less than three sets or portable stairs that we used during the day had operational deficiencies which would have deemed them unsafe or usable; and which I have been seriously doing a report on.  For any or all of these reasons or others; I could have stopped the operation.  I chose not to so as not to interrupt the operational tempo but more so because these types of inconsistencies are regularly not recognized as such but instead accepted as the norm; and ignored and worked around; regularly and without second thought or concern.  For a company that emphasizes a focus safety as the primary value; in actuality the primary  focus appears more to be; unless there is a glaring issue present; in many but not all instances; getting the task accomplished with little or no regard given to risk mitigation.  This attitude is part of the culture of this workforce; is long going; omnipresent and systemic.  Combined with other negative attitudes and attributes it conspires to create a corporation which says one thing; and does another.  To an employee who wants to do the right thing because of the recognition of the fact that it is mutually beneficial to do so;  working in this environment can be disheartening; frustrating and disappointing.  To be frankly honest; I feel quite often that I am being singled out on occasion for attempting to bring these sorts of things to light; and that local management's attitude towards me is becoming that; if you want to hold us accountable then we will do the same towards you; watch you like a hawk and bring to bear any issue or inconsistency in your performance also.  This does feel to me to be somewhat unfair; at times.  When I decide to bring an issue to light; I give it careful consideration; more than I probably should; and more often than not I keep quiet about it; do my job and let management do theirs.  We should be striving to work together; especially in a critical time such as this now is.I do admit that at some point during the day; I should have recognized that the pressure levels were increasing and should have voluntarily and proactively taken a few minutes to step back and regain composure and reintegrate myself appropriately into the operational flow.  I did not do so largely because of operational pressure but also due to the distraction caused by various inconsistencies I described; keeping a running mental tally of these while still maintaining a focus on my tasks. Based on my analysis of the events of this situation; I consider that it would be more likely that I take a pause given another encounter of a similar chain of events.

column121: Descending into LUK on the LNAV 3R we first received a report from tower of a low altitude alert in between the FAF and the intermediate step down fix (ZUGMI at or above 1480). I had the aircraft in LNAV/VS with a commanded vertical speed mode of -700FPM. I glanced at the altimeter and saw 1550. This is above the step down altitude and above the MDA. The copilot and I both quickly agreed we were above MDA. At this point also I looked out and could see the runway. We briefly leveled off and planned to continue visually. At this point we received a too low PULL UP. Aural warning. Immediately we went around. After getting back level and configuring we talked about the approach and decided to do it again with less vertical speed and just stay a bit higher on the glide path. We got down to out MDA without issue and landed.I never saw any altitude any lower than the step down altitude on the approach. LUK airport is sunk in the valleys between some hills and I think I should've maybe thought to have a gentler vertical speed.Not accept a fairly close to minimums LNAV only approach with a lot of turbulence into Lunken when ZZZ is right around the corner. Fly the instrument profile at lowest possible vertical speed and visual only after VDP. Although we never busted any altitudes I could've made it a much gentler descent to MDA at the VDP since the VDP is 2.4 from the runway and there are lots of hills on the approach prior to the runway.IMC until ragged bases around 800 AGL to 1;000 AGL. Some Visual conditions at time of the event. Runway/PAPI were in sight.

column121: While departing ZZZ Runway X on the RVAV departure; we experienced a wind shear ahead alert shortly after rotation and after the gear was selected up. While climbing through approximately 500 feet AGL; we entered an area of moderate to severe turbulence followed by a gain and loss of 20+ knots of airspeed. Airspeed excisions were brief in nature; and climb rate decreased from near 3;000 FPM to 1;000 FPM and momentarily less while we transited the wind shear. During this time we also experienced multiple quick rolling and yawing moments that required nearly full control deflection to counter.  Both myself and my First Officer agreed that the aircraft was at times momentarily out of control. It is my recollection that the maximum intensity of the turbulence occurred from 500 feet AGL to approximately 3;500 feet AGL. Again these excursions were very quick left and right rolling and yawing motions. During the event; the aircraft energy state never decayed to a dangerous level; however; we were in a lightly loaded -700 with max thrust selected for wind shear avoidance.  Above 4;000 feet; we experienced continuous moderate turbulence and icing up to 14;000 feet; and only light turbulence above that.  There were no injuries reported; and we did not suspect any aircraft damage. The flight attendants and passengers were briefed before takeoff. Before departure; both myself and the First Officer consulted the Airport Wind System reports as well as reviewed the required wind limits for the departure. The ZZZ Tower and Dispatch were contacted to get a better assessment of what they were seeing with the winds as well.  At the time of the beginning of the takeoff roll; the Tower reported steady state wind from the south east 28 KT gusting to 38 KT. The Airport Wind System alert was not functioning; however;  [other weather station's] wind and the gust 2-6 Airport Wind System was reporting. All wind reports were within limits at the time of takeoff; and had been for most of the morning. The Dispatcher reported the 8 High Airport Wind System Alert was intermittent all morning. Both myself and my First Officer briefed the departure and took steps necessary to mitigate the perceived threats. Wind shear take off procedures and power settings were used during the take off.  After level off; myself and the First Officer consulted the FOM and we were in agreement that we experienced a situation where the aircraft was momentarily not in positive control. A pilot report of MOD to SEV turbulence was relayed to ARTCC as well as company. Dispatch was consulted at this time; and a plan was made to divert to ZZZ1 for maintenance inspection as Maintenance did not want the aircraft stuck in ZZZ2. The remainder of the flight was uneventful. Ensuring Airport Wind System has full functionality and wind profiles are working to the greatest extent possible.
column123: Preparing for departure from ZZZ we looked at weather reports including the ZZZ Airport Wind System and PIREPS.  Nothing indicated that we would encounter anything greater than moderate turbulence as we took off from Runway X. We gave ATC a PIREP and overflew our original destination of ZZZ2 at the request of Dispatch and Maintenance control to get the plane to a maintenance base.

column121: I was the Captain and Pilot Flying (PF) for Aircraft X from ZZZ to Richmond (RIC) on November XX; 2020; and observed the following. During cruise flight my First Officer and Pilot Monitoring (PM) alerted me that the last time (back in July) that she flew into RIC the airplane caught a false localizer signal and turned no where near the centerline of the respective runway. Having reviewed the Weather Briefing Package; I determined that RIC would be landing to the north; and elected to load the Runway 34 ILS approach. I confirmed all the waypoints with my PM and set up accordingly. I hard tuned the localizer frequency of 110.7; set the approach course of 337 degrees; and set the minimums of 370 feet on the Primary Flight Display (PFD). We received a clearance to cross the NEAVL intersection at 11;000 with a speed of 250 knots. We met that restriction; and then got a clearance to proceed to the KAFKA intersection and pilot's discretion to maintain 2;000 feet. That waypoint was loaded and confirmed. We began a descent. About 12 miles from the airport I slowed the aircraft to 210 knots and had selected Flaps 1. We were about 3;000 feet; and I slowed further to 180 knots; with a setting of Flaps 2. We were about 7 miles from the KAFKA waypoint; and confirmed the airport was insight. I began slowing the plane to 160 knots. About 3 miles from KAFKA; and the approach mode in the armed position; the airplane selected the LOC mode on the PFD and began to turn towards Runway 2. I turned the autopilot off; and manually continued to fly towards the KAFKA waypoint to lose more altitude. The airplane was about 2;300 feet; with 1;700 feet selected in the altitude selector. I continued the approach; and we landed safely. My First Officer questioned the Tower as to why this would happen. The Tower stated that both the Runway 34; and Runway 2 localizers were operational. He said that he would inform the staff at the airport.

column121: On approach to landing at my home lake I observed traffic parallel to my position.  The traffic; a larger single engine float plane; was also visible on my FIS-B.  I was over water and the other seaplane was over land. As I descended I noted the airplane turned to the east at low altitude away from the lake and over an adjoining swamp. Since other seaplanes commonly land on the lake I decided to land into the light wind close to the undeveloped shoreline.  This would permit the other seaplane unobstructed access to the main body of the lake. As I landed on the water and was in step taxi mode the other seaplane suddenly appeared out of a slough on the water and on a collision course.  I immediately turned to avoid the aircraft and the other pilot applied power; continued straight ahead; and departed the lake.  The two aircraft were within 100 ft of each other on the water at high speed taxi and in direct conflict. It had not occurred to me that the larger float plane would use the short; narrow slough to land on the water.  The slough is a posted waterway prohibiting entry due to the presence of endangered species.  Further; the slough is on a local canoe route in common use; particularly on a weekend.  It is a tight area for a large float plane to operate in. When I contacted the local seaplane operator he indicated it probably wasn't his aircraft involved; though he did say that the slough was sometimes used because it is 'scenic'.  I explained that landing there is prohibited by Florida statute and it is posted.  He said he was unfamiliar and would not use it in the future.

column121: During a clear day; and after long taxi; we conducted a standard engine Run Up and the aircraft performed flawlessly with strong power output. We were eventually cleared for takeoff and after an uneventful takeoff from Runway XX. Runway XY was CLOSED at ZZZ. Approximately 7 miles north I began to notice that the engine was performing slightly lower than usual. Within moments I saw the RPM drop to 2100 and the engine was 'rumbling'. I executed the emergency checklists at this time; mixture rich; carburetor heat on and power forward and it provided only slightly better performance but not much. I immediately called the Tower and advised them of the engine problem. The tower immediately acknowledged and I continued to bring the aircraft to best glide speed and trouble shoot. I know my aircraft usually likes to run lean so I tried leaning the mixture and it got worse so I immediately enriched the mixture and held it full forward as much as possible and the engine was performing better. In addition I saw that carburetor heat was producing no result so I turned off the carburetor heat and with Throttle; Mixture full forward and carburetor heat off; I was able to sustain over 2300 RPM without any engine shaking. I did a quick scan of the area; and calculation of winds aloft and looked back and saw that indeed I could likely make the ZZZ airport and at worst would have to land on XZ or runway XY; the closed runway but which was mostly vacant. I also calculated and knew; that the winds aloft were quite strong over 3000 ft. so I used full power to climb; catch the southerly winds and return immediately for the airport. I advised ZZZ of my intentions and they said that they would clear the area for me. At all times I was able to climb and if I touched the power controls to reduce them; there would be a decrease in power with more vibration; but at full power I was able to sustain good engine power. My climb worked and stronger winter winds aloft indeed pushed me back into downwind; albeit well above pattern altitude. Nonetheless; I determined that altitude would be the safest option since it would ensure ability to glide to the airport. I was cleared to land and the tower reiterated that the airport would be cleared for me.It is possible during this climb I may have slightly penetrated Class B area above ZZZ but it is not likely as the FlightAware and my handheld GPS did not indicate I reached that altitude. During the process I was always in contact with ZZZ and they had positive ID of my aircraft; so I did not squawk 7700 as I was concerned about moving my hands from the console. Eventually; when I was on a close downwind with landing assured and the only way to slow down to VFE would be to point the nose up as I did not want to risk pulling power and not regaining it. This technique worked and I safely deployed the flaps within operating limitations. I turned base and then final as I eventually deployed additional flaps and cut power. I advised the tower I would be landing and doing some S turns to descend. Landing was uneventful; on the runway just after the numbers. I was able to taxi under my own power however; my mechanic told me he was later unable to restart the engine; most likely due to engine failure. I believe the tower did an amazing job. I also did not hesitate to tell them my intentions. If at any time I thought I would not be able to circle back to Runway XX; I would have easily made Runway XZ or Runway XY if necessary. I do not believe that there were any deviations whether it be owner/operator/pilot related; or mechanical or ATC. It is my belief that everyone did what they had to. My mechanic did run compression checks and other diagnostic tests which are still in progress and the most likely issue was fuel starvation caused by the carburetor. I have acquired a refurbished one recently which will be inspected and installed and; once installed a complete diagnostic will be done once again to determine whether there were other issues.

The PACOTS east routing (Pacific Organized Track System) for that day was our original flight plan which had us departing the 130W longitude for DACEM onward to pick up the IRNMN arrival into LAX. However the Dispatcher rerouted us to fly from 140W bypassing 130W to begin an arrival using the RYDER arrival. This confused not only us but departure Area Control who had our original flight plan in their system. We departed the gate with the correct uploaded ATC flight plan but possessed on our iPads the amended flight plan from Dispatch... in addition our FO (First Officer) refused to coordinate with Dispatch to revise our our flight plan to its original format which resulted in erroneous flight progress forms from ACARS. To be clear the flight plan only deviated towards the latter end of the flight with the confusion resulting from the Dispatcher uploading an erroneous flight plan to remove a bend in the flight however that was not loaded to the PACOTS east routing for the day. Our FO contacted SFO radio to confirm our routing was correct with our FMS but neglected to inform Dispatch who thought we were still flying the amended route he had given us. It would be helpful if the company would provide guidance regarding how procedurally they would prefer crews coordinate changes to flight plans with ATC. Do they prefer we coordinate with ATC directly or would they prefer that we contact Dispatch and ask that they upload the correct route and that we check it with ATC. It would seem there is a loophole in regards to keeping Dispatch up to speed on changes to flight plans. I believe there is language in the FOM regarding any changes to the flight plan to notify Dispatch of those changes. In this case the changes were minimal however the arrival time differed by about 6-8 minutes from the original flight plan and the amended one from Dispatch. Dispatch was unaware that this stub flight was not flying the amended flight plan they sent us. When I; as the relief pilot; arrived from my break on the flight deck I noticed the erroneous flight progress forms and notified Dispatch who then sent us the revised flight plan. Dispatch was unaware that we were back on our original PACOTS routing. This was accomplished 2+45 into the flight. However if I had not done this it would not have gotten done as the FO refused to contact Dispatch to clear up the confusion. please advise. The First Officer refused input from both the Captain and myself; the relief pilot; to contact Dispatch and get them in the loop regarding discrepancies from filed flights from amended ones. Stub flights caused more confusion than necessary. Clear guidance is needed from company on how they prefer the crew to remedy route discrepancies from Dispatch versus filed. Do they prefer the crew to contact ATC and fix the problem ourselves or do they prefer Dispatch to get involved and fix the discrepancy.
column123: Just prior to pushback; we received a message from Dispatch with regards to a change in our flight planned route. We delayed pushback until receiving new flight plan. Only change was to end of route after waypoint at 140W. We then called Clearance Delivery and did a full route verification. They still only had the original; unchanged route. Since the only discrepancy between the flight plans was at the end of the flight; we opted to depart. After departure; we received the flight progress report that showed the modified route (after 140W). During flight; after checking in with San Francisco ARINC; we asked for a verification of our cleared routed. ARINC verified it was the original flight planned route. We then sent a message to Dispatch with our cleared route and received an update. Dispatch believed we requested a look at modifying our route to remove a 'dog leg' segment from our route which we hadn't.  We were a STUB flight and that might have been a factor as the original flight was near to the arrival time. The change to our flight plan wasn't requested and wasn't essential to safety. Unless critical to flight safety; last minute changes to flight plans (especially international) can cause miscommunications and errors in navigation and should be avoided.

column121: During climbout on a heading of east on the ZZZZZ2 SID while passing 8;000 feet between ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 we got a TCAS TA regarding traffic descending off ZZZZZ3 on the ZZZZZ4  flowing south at 1 o'clock; 3-5 miles ahead that was no factor.  This is something we see every day on climb out or descent in and out of ZZZ due to climb and descent rates.   ATC then called traffic at our '10-11 O'clock 3 miles descending to one one (11) thousand I called 'traffic in site no factor; they're passing above and behind us.'  ATC then asked our Altitude.  I replied 'level 10;000 feet.He asked our altitude again; I replied 'Level 10;000 feet; he said he saw us at 10;500 feet and gave us an updated Altimeter setting; and cleared us to climb to 17;000 feet.  Passing 12;000 feet he asked us what altitude we were passing.  I replied '12;000 feet.'  He then replied 'That's what we show as well.  For some reason I had you at 10;500 feet back there. I have a phone number to copy when you are ready.'  We took the number down; and he said 'Call us when you get to your destination to discuss a possible pilot deviation.'The Captain called when we got to ZZZ1.  The Controller Supervisor who answered said he had just sat down; had no idea what we were talking about; said he would do some research and call us back.  5 minutes later he called us back and said; 'After review; the previous Controller showed you slightly high and stopped traffic on the arrival at 12;000 feet (which I thought was at 11;000 based on his advisory call).  Then showed our altitude correct in the climb after he inquired again passing 12;000 feet.  Said there was no conflicts or loss of separation; not a big deal; and that he would just file it as an RA report and close It out; however; we had no known RA's; nor any TA/RA indications for the potential conflicting traffic passing above and behind us?  The ATC Supervisor didn't take any further action or questions; and wished us a safe rest of our day and left It at that.  We thought It would behoove of us to fill out this report regardless.Wrong altimeter setting.  We had a lot of distractions from multiple visitors on the flight deck at the gate while setting up cockpit and during the before start checklist (flight attendants; gate agents; deadheading crew and commuting pilots who we knew who stopped by to visit).  Flight attendants held off boarding passengers who were held up at the door; until catering; who arrived at the aircraft late; had cleared the forward galley and aisle; and got them their snack/sanitary packages set up to hand out.  So this backlogged the jet bridge; had the flight attendants coming in and out of the cockpit along with the commuting pilots; and gave us a lot of distractions.  This back log seemed to frustrate the agent; for It was the flight attendants who were keeping the passengers out of the way until they were ready for them.  For that; the gate agent was rushing to close the flight (We still pushed 10 min early).  The FA A seemed rushed; and just closed the flight deck door before verifying if we were ready or saying 'seated and stowed;' which was nonstandard.  These multiple interruptions (which seem to happen every flight these days) just added up; we had the current ATIS printed off; but when back tracked to get caught up; we missed the altimeter settings; which must have been set from a flight a day or two prior due to the difference in what It actually was at the time.Verify; Verify; Verify; Trap the Errors; Don't let the distractions of the daily operations knock you off your game.  It was a beautiful cold VFR morning; flying with a Captain I had enjoyed flying with in the past; so I felt we were both comfortable and familiar with how each other operates within the SOP's and as a person.  The Aircraft had sat overnight.  I would like to see more operational (non-flying) related distraction/awareness incorporated into training.  The day prior on a separate flight we had a passenger removed by law enforcement for non-compliance/and possible criminal related activity.  Gate agents are constantly under stress to get flights out on time or early.  To top It all off; everyone has been under stress of the pandemic; furlough related; or state of the airline related issues.-"

column121: On approach to ZZZ; the ATIS was obtained with reported winds of 340 @ 15 G 28. The airport was configured to land east; utilizing Runways XL and XXC. The First Officer (FO) and I discussed how this was odd and not desirable as the tailwind component with gusts was at our 10 knot limitation. Additionally; the ATIS stated there were wind shear advisories in the area. On final approach inside the FAF; maintaining target airspeed within Vref +10 was extremely difficult due to the high wind gusts; shifting winds; and shear. As pilot flying; my airspeed was hovering at +10 with occasional jumps up to +20. The wind vector on the MFD was showing winds at 030 between 20-35 knots until 100 feet or so; where the winds sheared to 340 at an unknown speed. I touched down within the touchdown zone but off centerline by approximately 10 feet. Taxi to the hanger was uneventful and no damage was noted. During the debrief; the FO and I agreed a go-around with a request to land on a Westerly direction should have been made. The cause of this event were gusty winds; poor traffic flow decision by ATC; and undesirable speed control by the Pilot Flying due to windshear.  ATC decision to land to the east with reported winds of 340 @ 15 G 28. This decision by ATC caused an unsafe tailwind condition when coupled with very strong and gusty crosswinds. Additionally; myself or the FO should have requested a landing to the west. However; the First Officer and I determined that any request would be denied as ZZZ has a reputation for not accommodating these types of request in order to maintain efficient traffic flows. There is pressure to land with the prevailing flow of traffic at a major airport like ZZZ when the crew sees other aircraft landing in the existing conditions; even if the crew would prefer an alternate runway. I strongly believe ATC created an unsafe situation that may have inadvertently pressured pilots into landing with a tailwind in gusty conditions. When I made the decision to conduct the approach; a go around would have been the correct action when the wind sheared at 100 feet.

column121: The Captain was flying. We got switched from the ZZZZZ to the ZZZZZ1 arrival and told to keep 300 knots. ZZZ was busier than normal since COVID and we got task saturated. Since ZZZ had wanted us at 300 knots we were in manual speeds. We descended below 10;000 feet at 300 knots and noticed it at about 9;300 feet. We leveled off to slow to 250 knots by 9;100 feet and continued as normal. It was a simple and common error caused by task saturation and typical ZZZ switching approaches 3 times and arrivals twice. ATC did not say anything.This is a common issue with ZZZ but also something we should have seen. We were more careful to monitor throughout the rest of the trip. This is also an issue of COVID and not flying much. No pilot is flying the amount that we used to. Especially Captains and First Officers on reserve. That is not an excuse; but an observation. column121: A line of scattered thunderstorms were moving west to east. We spoke with Clearance Delivery and Departure Control regarding the direction to go around these storms. Departure suggested we follow a flight which had just gone westbound to avoid the storms. We agreed. Departure Control said we should be given a turn in a few miles. We were then instructed to contact Center. The frequency was busy and they would not respond to our communications. We were at 23000 ft. and could not get Center to respond. We tried multiple times to check-in and ask for deviations; but no answer. We were using NEXRAD and on board radar. Our path was taking us through two storm cells separated by approximately 30 miles. The radar was showing light to moderate precipitation ahead of us. At no time did it show any red returns ahead of us. Center finally contacted us and told us to climb to 40000 ft. As we initiated the climb; we encountered moderate turbulence with approximately 10 seconds of severe turbulence. As we climbed through 26000 ft. we cleared the clouds and the turbulence abated. We had one passenger on board that was briefed on the expected turbulence and the seat belt sign was on. The passenger was seated with his seat belt on; but did hit his head on the ceiling of the cabin during the turbulence. He did not report any injuries. The cause of the problem was a saturated ATC system that couldn't handle the traffic load. Perhaps more controllers to handle the traffic load could alleviate the situation.

column121: Myself and my student departed ZZZ VFR to the east on [Date] at approximately XA:30 local time for a routine instrument training flight. We took Aircraft X which had been flown twice that day already with no issues. The preflight was normal; and run-up was normal. We found no indication of a potential malfunction. We had been maneuvering for approximately 15 minutes in the east practice area when [Student] began to make an altitude correction from 3;700 ft. MSL to 3;500 ft. MSL. He attempted to take out some power; but when he reduced the throttle towards the idle position there was no RPM change indicated. He stopped reducing the throttle when he noticed it was pulling out farther than he had ever seen it go before. With concern that the throttle may not be secured properly now; I moved the throttle to the full open position; then moved slightly toward the aft position (approx. 1/2 inch reduction). This reduction was successful and the power reduced to 2400 RPM. With power still being available; I took the flight controls via a positive three-way exchange; turned direct ZZZ visually immediately; called the tower; for partial engine failure. We were 10 miles due east of ZZZ at this time. I selected a field for a forced landing in case that became necessary; and as we got closer to ZZZ I verbally selected another field; and then finally a grass strip just [southeast] of ZZZ before I had ZZZ ensured.I requested to stay at 3;500 ft. MSL (or at least high enough to ensure gliding distance to XXL-the runway I wanted and later requested) and enter the pattern possibly that high. I reported two miles east of the field; got cleared to land; and once I had the runway ensured; I began to reduce the throttle. I remember only trying to reduce about 300-400 RPM; but the power went from 2400 RPM to 1300 RPM. I then put the throttle to the fully open position. At full open; the RPM indication was still 1300. I told the tower I was now in a full engine-out situation. I was approximately 1 to 1.5 nm [northeast] of the approach end of [Runway] XXL when the full failure happened. After getting lined up on final; I reduced the throttle to idle (I did not want a resurgence of power at an unexpected time) and did not attempt a restart. I had [Runway] XXL ensured; and I knew the best option was to commit to the forced landing on a large; paved runway rather than risk restarting an engine that may just die again. On final; [Student] opened his door to ensure at least one safe exit. I glided into [Runway] XXL and maintained positive aircraft control with a smooth touchdown. I did have to perform a forward slip with full flaps to ensure touchdown in the first 3rd of the runway- I recommend the flaps be inspected. I had enough energy to roll off on Taxiway Bravo; clear of [Runway] XXL. We then exited the aircraft and waited for a tow. [Student] told me once we were on the ground that he noticed the fuel flow was indicating 0 while I was on short final just after I had declared the full engine out. He said nothing else caught his eye during those seconds. He was trying to study the MVP50 [Electronic Engine Monitor] for any possible explanation as to the cause of the failure while I was flying.

column121: I was the Pilot Flying on this leg. After departing ZZZ1 while climbing through Flight Level 280 on our way up to FL340 Autopilot #1 disconnected and would not reengage. A/P (Autopilot) #2 would engage but after about 30 seconds it also disengaged along with the auto thrust going into THRUST LOCK mode. Then several ECAMs (Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor) appeared including RUD TRIM1 FAULT; YAW DAMPER 1; RUD TRV LIM 1. The First Officer ran the Quick Reference Handbook procedures for each of those problems which included resetting the FACs (Flight Augmentation Computer).We leveled at FL340 and the aircraft was exhibiting a slight Dutch Roll tendency so we descended to FL280 and no more Dutch Roll was observed. Autopilots could be intermittently engaged; flight directors would come and go; autothrust would disengage in THRUST LOCK mode. We consulted with Dispatch and [Maintenance Control] via phone patch. Without further attempting to engage autopilots or autothrust events seemed to stabilize and with consult with Dispatch we planned to continue to destination. We began evaluating along route alternates and asked Dispatch to do the same. Shortly thereafter the flight directors started to come and go repeatedly along with the previously described ECAMS. When each rudder ECAM came and went there was a discernible yaw felt. Other messages would appear momentarily then clear such as 2FD2; and BOTH PFDs (Primary Flight Display) on SINGLE SOURCE (not sure of the wording as it would momentarily flash then disappear).At this time we made the decision to divert and after evaluating the weather decided with dispatch concurrence to divert to ZZZ2. An [urgent situation] was declared with ATC and a clearance to ZZZ2 was obtained and a safe landing was made. ECAMS intermittently continued while enroute.The aircraft was always fully under control. After gate arrival I debriefed with the [Flight Manager] and maintenance log entries were submitted. Briefed local ZZZ2 maintenance personnel.
