column121: This was originally scheduled as [Flt Number; Route] However that flight was cancelled due to the inbound aircraft diverting due to a reported autopilot/ILS (Instrument Landing System) failure during an attempt at a Cat 3 Autoland approach. Flight [Number] was rescheduled as a ferry flight [Number] to ZZZ; using the diverted aircraft.The aircraft had some autopilot maintenance done at ZZZ1; and was signed off cleared for flight. Upon arrival at the gate in ZZZ2; the Captain reported that the problems with the autopilot and the ILS were not fixed. Both he and the First Officer stated that the exact same malfunctions occurred on both of the past two flights. They described the Captain's ILS as erratic--intermittent ident; azimuth and glide slope drifting stop to stop and blanking out. The aircraft did not intercept course or glide slope on a Cat 3 approach. On the inbound leg; they described a 30 degree left final approach course LOC (Localizer) intercept where instead of rolling left; the airplane rolled right and turned away from final approach course; prompting the Captain to take over manually. They continued to fly a visual approach due to improved weather conditions since their earlier attempt. The Captain said he had made several ACARS ELB (Aircraft Communications And Reporting System Electronic Logbook) entries at the gate in ZZZ2; but had not received any acknowledgement printouts. Because of this; he had notified ZZZ2 maintenance via radio. The gate agent asked my FO (First Officer) and me how soon we would be ready to push back for ZZZ. We replied that there were open write ups that first had to be worked out or deferred; then released. Shortly after that; a Station Operations Supervisor arrived at the gate and expressed an expectation that we would quick turn the aircraft and depart for ZZZ. There had been no maintenance on the aircraft; nor any service. A Maintenance Supervisor arrived and stated the jet was ok to fly as is; with no open write ups. It was clear that there had been a breakdown in communication between the previous crew and the ZZZ2 Station in regards to the status of this aircraft. They became pushy about getting us off the gate. I was clear that this could not happen until these known; reported discrepancies were written up and resolved. I asked about aircraft servicing (fuel) and catering (food and water). The Pilot Mobile app showed that we had crew meals on this flight. (Both of us require Special Meals due to dietary restrictions.) The Operations Supervisor then went on a tirade about no catering at ZZZ2 and how everyone knows that. Her vehement response surprised both of us; as there was no context or cause for it. The maintenance supervisor continued to insist the aircraft had been fixed in ZZZ1 and was good to fly. I called Dispatch to see if we could get some help from [Maintenance Control]. The controller noted there were no open ELB write ups and therefore no reason to delay departure. No one seemed to register that the previous crew had reported multiple malfunctions of navigation equipment on an evening where IMC (Instrument Meteorological Conditions) was a huge factor. So I said to [Maintenance Control]; with the ZZZ2 Maintenance Supervisor and Operations Supervisor within earshot; that I would have to refuse the aircraft unless they properly documented these discrepancies; and either fixed them or legally deferred them. Meanwhile; the First Officer had called the [Flight Manager]. He recommended that we stand our ground on the maintenance issues; continue to be professional; and if we refused the aircraft to follow protocol. We had showed up at the airport slightly hungry; expecting that our crew meals would be boarded as listed. This was becoming a safety of flight problem; as the airport had few options for food at all; and the ones available were in the process of closing down. It was clear that if we were to have any food and water for the 5+10 red eye flight to ZZZ; we wouldhave to stop what we were doing and go find it. I called Dispatch back and tried again to explain the legal operational aspects of why it was important to document these inbound discrepancies. He got a different [Maintenance Controller] on the line and we had a better discussion. The new controller called the previous Captain for a personal debriefing of the inbound flight. That; in turn; got the requisite ELB documentation generated and the maintenance process started. Troubleshooting revealed the problem was not the autopilot but a failed relay in the localizer antenna switch. Once we were confident that our [Company] procedures had been followed; we began preflighting the aircraft for ferry to ZZZ. We were running a little short of time (appx 1 hr before a CCO (Crew Critical Off) time); but not so much as to cause undue hurry. During this time; several of the ZZZ2 station personnel were hovering around us; looking over our shoulders as though we needed close supervision to do our jobs. It was a distraction and a bit creepy. Before closing the door; the Ops supervisor reappeared in the jetway; blamed me for the delay; berating me for threatening to refuse the aircraft over crew meals and bottled water; and for not knowing there is no catering in ZZZ2. Ironically; even though we pushed back with 30 minute's; cushion; we nearly went over our CCO time while waiting at the hold short for the final weight numbers from Station Operations. We lifted off and had an otherwise uneventful flight to ZZZ.

column121: Following two previous approach attempts into ZZZ1 followed by diversions to our Filed Alternates; on [consecutive evening and morning flights] of Aircraft X. I was advised by Dispatch that if the Crew was willing; they would like us to fly back to ZZZ1 and make yet a third attempt. I immediately said I did not feel safe operating the flight as I didn't feel the approach was safe based on the current conditions at the airport; and the weather we had experienced during the last two attempts. I then stated I would not be willing to make another attempt. During the first attempt (Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1) we experienced moderate turbulence; gusty winds; heavy rain; in IMC at night followed by a Windshear Warning and Escape Maneuver at 150 ft. AGL; following this up with a consecutive approach the next morning (Aircraft X ZZZ2-ZZZ1) resulting in an early Go-Around / Diversion to alternate due to Heavy Rain; Moderate to Severe Turbulence on Approach; Strong Crosswinds on Final; Changing (Increasing) Gusting Wind Conditions on the surface and the previous aircraft making a Severe Turbulence Encounter Report on Final with the Controller inquiring as to passenger injuries on board. This led to a phone call from my direct Supervisor; who tried to convince me the operation was safe. I clearly stated to both persons; that our Dispatch Release reads; and I quote.. 'By Signing this Dispatch Release we are affirming our belief that this flight can be made safely'. I was very clear that after my previous two attempts; I did not feel comfortable operating the flight. The Initial Plan was for us to depart in just 30 minutes after refueling; which again I stated I did not feel safe operating the flight. Followed by yet another phone call from my Supervisor who reviewed the weather with me. Explaining things were much better now and we can depart. Again; I expressed my concerns as to the safety of the flight based on recent experience in the storm system; and inaccuracies experienced with the past weather reports that allowed us to dispatch prior. I felt I was being pushed to operate the flight. My Supervisor continued to tell me of other carriers that made it into ZZZ1 today. Once again I explained they didn't deal with what we had to do; and again relayed I was not comfortable making a flight to ZZZ1 today. After some discussion; it seemed my Supervisor was becoming agitated stating that if I didn't fly he would have to. I remained silent as this was not pertinent to my decision. I was again asked to operate - to which I repeated my opinion that I didn't feel it was a safe operation and I would not even go there as a passenger if you asked me to at that time. I was then told I was being pulled from the flight; I was being relieved of all duty pending an investigation and I would hear from someone in the company. The phone call was then disconnected by the other party.I feel this was an attempt to force a flight crew to accept a flight that I had clearly stated I didn't feel it was safe to operate. I feel that this is a violation of the Captain's joint Authority with Dispatch to operate a flight and is in direct conflict with PIC's (Pilot in Command) responsibility and authority. It also seems to me to be in conflict with the creation of a 'Just Culture: required be FAA in implementing a SMS. A pilot should never be coerced to accept a mission he/she feels is unsafe. In this situation; the PIC was being asked to Dispatch into an area where an URGENT PIREP was broadcast via Center Frequencies advising of Moderate to Severe Turbulence reported below 11;000 ft. by an aircraft on Final Approach to ZZZ1. Another aircraft should not be dispatched to fly an approach in Severe Turbulence. The most basic principle is Dispatchers; Managers; and Supervisors need to listen to the people under their charges. Air Carriers need to stress the importance of Safety; by not just stating they have a culture based on Safety; but by actually exercisingone especially when performance metrics may not be met but safety goals will be achieved. As Pilots; I feel we are all mission-oriented; but the need to complete the mission can never exceed operational safety.

column121: During final approach to ZZZ; We were instructed by Approach to descend and maintain 7000 ft. and expect vectors for visual approach Runway XX. When we were crossing approximately 9000 ft. and 235 KIAS PF (Pilot Flying) requested flaps 9. PM (Pilot Monitoring) double checked the airspeed and proceeded to select flaps 9 position. Right after moving the handle to the 9 position; we got the EICAS message FLAP FAIL. PF took the radios and requested ATC to stop the descent at 8000 ft. because we have to run a checklist and ATC cleared us to stay at 8000 ft. PF leveled off and PM took the QRH and started looking for the associated procedure. PF and PM agreed to follow procedure XXX-XX-X FLAP FAILURE and PM started to read every step in the checklist. In that moment PF requested a Hold while we solved the issue but after receiving confusing ATC holding instructions; PF requested a square box flying vectors and [advised ATC] due to Flaps Failure. We followed every step in the checklist; verified the new approach speed; the new required landing distance; Pulled the J7 CB; sent an ACARS msg to company and advised FA (Flight Attendant) of the issue. After double checking that conditions were safe to land and the available runway landing distance was suitable for the situation; we decided to continue with the approach to Runway XX and advised ATC. ATC gave us vectors for the visual approach and a normal landing was performed. Brake temperatures were ok after landing and no further issues were found during the rolling after the touchdown; then we requested a normal taxi to the ramp and a normal deplane process occurred. No injuries were reported. At the gate; captain pulled out the information from maintenance messages and FLAP JAMMING and FLAP LH MOTOR BRAKE FAIL were found.
column123: On descent to 7000; we were at speed 220 and I asked for flaps 9. We received EICAS message flaps fail. I asked FO (First Officer) to recycle back to zero. We asked ATC to hold and they had us stop the descent maintain 8000. We leveled off and requested box turns. We ran flap fail checklist. Communicated with Dispatch and FA (Flight Attendant). [Advised ATC]; landed with no issue. I [Advised ATC] because at zero flaps; possible long landing with higher approach speed is expected as well as potential for hot brakes. So we wanted to err on the caution side. Great CRM by crew.

column121: Attempted to de ice as per station procedure for light frost appproximately 10 ft. from the gate. De ice personnel used absolutely no standard phraseology. Sprayed left wing and left for approximately 30 minutes to return for right wing. We were informed by the crew chief that it was for the truck to heat to the required temperature. I asked the crew chief to inspect the left wing. He reported that it was now all ice. The First Officer and I both inspected the wing and it was indeed a significant layer of clear ice. We informed the station manager that the wing and also the right wing would need to be de iced at proper temperature of the fluid. The Crew chief and ramp personnel were extremely diligent. They personally inspected the temperature of the truck ( it was 40 degrees) below the minimum temperature). The crew chief also brought the de ice manual for the truck to the flight deck. We informed the station manger that we could not depart until the truck was verified at the proper temperature ( by the ground crew) and that we would then de ice again and that the FO (First Officer) and I would both visually inspect before leaving the gate area. This entire evolution took 120 minutes. The station managers; gate personnel and especially the ground crew were beyond outstanding. The gist of the episode is that the de icer made the situation much worse by spraying improper temperature fluid and created ice and then informed us that the wing was clear. Had the flight crew and ramp crew not been diligent and inspected it could have been a problem. The de ice crew was improperly trained; completely unaware of procedure and dangerous. The contract de ice company at ZZZ needs to be trained properly in procedure; phraseology and  common sense or the contract needs to be awarded to a competent company.

column121: Departing during the waning stages of an intense storm. Winds were gusting close to 30 kts.. Windshear advisories were on the ATIS; however a flight landing 10 minutes before our departure reported only moderate turbulence with no mention of Windshear. Decided to let FO be the pilot flying. Climbing through 1;100 ft. MSL in a right turn to our cleared altitude of 4;000 ft.; the turbulence got very intense; with large; rapid; +or- 15 kts. fluctuations in airspeed. PF (Pilot Flying) called for flaps one; which I set; and thereafter he announced the autopilot was engaged. I had just changed to departure on the radio and then we were cleared to climb to 10;000 ft.; and to continue the right turn to our first navigation fix. PF called for flaps up; I selected the flaps up and then noticed the attitude of the airplane was falling below the horizon and we were starting to descend. I also noticed the PF trying to select 10;000 ft. on the altitude preselect. He was having difficulty setting the altitude selector as it was so turbulent ; so I stated: 'fly the airplane; we are descending'. The PF disconnected the autopilot and raised the nose after we reached about 3 degrees nose low attitude. During this time; our altitude dropped to about 1;300 ft. MSL (1;200 ft. AGL) and the GPWS 'Don't Sink' advisory sounded. We started to establish a climbing attitude so I directed my attention to setting the altitude preselect; setting the heading bug to our first fix; and the PF asked to also execute this fix in the FMS. After setting the FMS; I noticed our aircraft attitude was dropping below the horizon again and we were descending through 1;300 ft. MSL. Before I could command a correction; the GPWS 'Don't Sink' advisory sounded again; and the PF raised the nose. As we continued the climb; by this time the airspeed was climbing over 250 kts. and the aircraft attitude was raised to control the speed. The speed increased to approximately 287 kts; before starting to decrease. As the speed started to drop; the PF continued to raise the attitude of the airplane; and as we exceeded 25 degrees nose up I commanded the PF to 'lower the nose; our airspeed is decreasing; establish a pitch of 12 degrees'. By the time the airspeed stopped decreasing; our speed was about 5 kts. below the flaps up maneuvering speed. We accelerated and established a normal climb. From this point on; the rest of the climb was uneventful.

column121: Departing Runway XX Captain was the flying pilot and I was Pilot Monitoring. It was a normal takeoff until the Captain asked for the autopilot. About 3-6 seconds later we got a 'AP Trim is NU' caution message. Since we were only 700 feet above the ground the Captain turned off the autopilot and tried to trim the plane himself. He was putting in nose down trim but nothing was happening. During this time we got direct to ZZZZZ and climb to 7;000 ft. We started the turn and kept the plane climbing. During the turn I tried to put nose down trim to see if it would work on my side. It did not. Since we were not getting any messages on EICAS and the trim was still not working; we disconnected the stab trim and Mach trim and then reconnected. The plane was already in a nose high pitch attitude and once we reconnected; the nose high trim increased by an additional .4 units while the captain was trying to trim down. Once we confirmed that we disconnected the the stab trim and Mach trim at that point the Captain transferred the controls to me and he took the radios and started running the QRH. I started to slow the rate of climb of the aircraft and we asked ATC if we could stop the climb and maintain the altitude we were at. ATC gave us clearance to do so; the altitude was 5;000 feet. We were still heading towards ZZZZZ. Then we advised ATC and ask for delay vectors to return back to ZZZ. The Captain did the checklist for the stab trim caution message and we also did our check lists for landing. We then asked ATC for vectors to land on [Runway] XX. We landed with the trim at 8.8 and took off with a trim setting of around 6.8. During the whole fight we never put trimmed up. It was a successful landing in ZZZ. At we taxied to the gate without incident. The stab trim was not responding to our inputs.

column123: We were dispatched to fly on commercial flight to pick up the aircraft at the maintenance center. Concerns with COVID exposure while traveling on commercial airlines are aggravating. Upon arrival at the airport we were directed to contact the maintenance base to have their van pick us up. When I called; the base informed me that the van service was discontinued. I put in an on-line request for a taxi ride. The address given did not take us to the service center; and there was much confusion and aggravation dealing with the taxi driver to try to get to the proper location. Upon eventual arrival at the service center the aircraft was ready for us; and I ordered fuel. I talked to maintenance both before leaving and during the trip; verifying that all of the paperwork for the maintenance performed was completed to their satisfaction. While completing pre-flight paperwork I apparently overlooked that the flight crew that had originally ferried the aircraft in had written up the pilot seat as a discrepancy; and that the open write-up had not been dealt with; either by being fixed or MELed. Verifying no open write-ups prior to flight is a company SOP; and one that I feel that I normally do as a matter of course. I can only think that dealing with the major maintenance paperwork on the maintenance issues pushed the possibility of an open write-up not related to that work to the side; and I did not properly review the past flight logs in the flight can; thus missing the write-up. My aggravated mental state at dealing with airlines and COVID concerns; multiplied by the ground transportation snafus; were certainly contributing factors.When non-typical operations are being dealt with; stop and take the time to triple-check every detail.

column121: [I have concerns with] the COVID pre-takeoff PA; which now instructs passenger that flight attendants will collect trash during safety compliance checks. Topics of concern:1. Would this action not be a direct conflict with FAR 121.391 (d)? It is understood that collecting a few used cleaning wipes and some cups does not present an issue. Some may even consider it like collecting pre-departure beverage cups prior to takeoff. However; managing empty pizza boxes (and similar bulky items) will require flight attendants to unlock carts (and/or trash cart doors) since the openings are too narrow to accept such items (FAR 121.577 (c).2. The Flight Attendant could offer to return later for bigger items; but would that not require a judgement call during an extremely limited period? This adds a new distraction from more critical safety matters (seat-belts; tray tables; etc.). A Flight Attendant is responsible for (depending upon aircraft) checking for more than 20 items during routine pre-takeoff/landing compliance checks.3. The Flight Attendant must now carry a trash bag during compliance checks leaving only one hand free to steady themselves from a fall. It is confirmed that taxi surface movement is a high-risk period for injuries. Also; the revised policy now adds more time (additional duty) before being able to secure in a jumpseat.Knowing first-hand the history of Flight Attendant injuries related to surface movement; I strongly recommend the company reevaluate and consider changing to a more reasonable expectation of trash collection after takeoff.

column121: I was flying with my student in the designated practice area; working on a variety of maneuvers. There were 2 other company traffic in the practice area (both training helicopters); one of which was cleared to operate at 2;000 ft MSL and below. Without this radio-communication approval from the control tower; all helicopters are to remain below 600 ft AGL. I was unaware of this helicopter operating at 2;000 ft and below; as although the Control Tower cleared them into the practice area; I did not hear it; as my student was talking. Most of the time (but not always); the Control Tower will call up all other helicopters in the practice area to inform them of the joining company. This explicit advisory was not issued to my tail number; which in this scenario is why I was not aware of the company traffic. While my student and I were taking off in a normal takeoff configuration; we did not see the other involved aircraft which was entering a practice engine failure directly above us; flying in the same direction as us. It wasn't until about 200 ft AGL on the climb out that I (and not my student) saw the descending aircraft about 100 feet ahead of and above us. I quickly lowered the collective to arrest our rate of climb and decelerated to avoid a collision; and once the company traffic was well clear I proceeded to climb out in a normal profile. When questioning the other pilot and their student after the flight if they saw us; they said that the saw us on the ground; but did not see us take off. They were unaware that the near-miss had occurred. Control Tower not explicit warning us of the company traffic joining us. Not adequately visually clearing the area above me before take off. As per company SOP; this is normally only done when conducting a maximum performance takeoff maneuver. Not adequately listening to the Control Tower frequency. Other pilot not deciding to recover their descent well before 600 ft AGL; knowing that there are two aircraft operating at 600 ft and below. Company policy is recovery by 100 ft. Taking off to the south; despite Runway XX being active. However; it is understood in our standard operating procedures that all takeoffs in the north practice area should be made in the opposite direction when the winds are strong from the west and Runway XX is active; due to obstacle clearance and left crosswind avoidance. As the other pilot corroborated later; he was not able to confidently predict which direction we would be taking off in.

column121: ZZZ Approach was closed for staffing reasons due to COVID illness / quarantine on the midnight shift.  Sector X (my sector) was in control of the airspace.  Sector Y had Aircraft X arriving to ZZZ from the southeast.  The pilot dialed up the ATIS at ZZZ which told the pilot to come up on my frequency for a weather update. I read the weather to the pilot then sent them back to sector Y freq. I kept the datablock up on my scope assuming that I would get a hand off soon and clear the Aircraft X for an approach. Since ZZZ is really close to the boundary with [sectors] X / Y; the Controller decided to work the aircraft all the way into ZZZ.  I treated it like a point-out as did he although we made no official coordination.At the same time; I had another aircraft (Aircraft Y) about 60 miles north of ZZZ inbound to the field and was asking about runway conditions at ZZZ.  I had a number to call the field operations for updates because the TRACON /Tower was closed.   When calling from the line; I got a recording staying the 'This line is no longer in service and to hang up and try again.'   I asked the second Controller in my area if he knew of an issue with the phone number.   He got on the Supervisor's phone and called for an update.  The field ops told him about the snow on the runways as well as Runway X Left being closed for snow removal. This was not in our NOTAMs.  That Controller then ran down to the other area who was working the Aircraft X and told them what was going on.  Luckily the Aircraft X wasn't too low for radio coverage; the Controller issued them present heading and a climb back up to 6;000.  The Aircraft X was then put on my frequency where I let them fly out to the west a bit farther and set up for a turn back to the IAF for Runway X Right.  The plane then landed safely at ZZZ.There should have been formal coordination between Sector Y and myself on who was working the Aircraft X into ZZZ.  It doesn't change the fact that a runway was closed at ZZZ without a NOTAM in our system.  The only reason we found out was because of the Aircraft Y inbound from the north asking about updates on the field conditions and the other Controller making the phone call for me.  I'm not sure how long it takes for NOTAMs to populate in our system but it's not fast enough.  I guess they hit enter on the keyboard and immediately jumped in snowplows and took to the runway. The NOTAM did eventually populate in our system; but it was after this event took place.
column123: I was notified of a poorly handled situation on the mid shift.  There were several major breakdowns in communication causing a 'swiss cheese' situation that could have ended devastatingly. Likely some minor changes to ZZZZ/ZZZ (ZZZ ATC 0) Contingency Plan. At roughly XA:00 in the morning Sector Y was working Aircraft X; during the enroute/initial descent portion of the flight arriving ZZZ. Keeping in mind ZZZ Approach is ATC 0 and Sector X assumes ALL of their airspace with procedures in place. At some point Aircraft X calls Sector X; likely on a second radio while in communication with Sector Y; to obtain the weather since the ATIS is not updated hourly and instructs pilots to do exactly that for the latest weather and field conditions. Presumably the pilot was then instructed to return to Sector Y frequency since the flight was a little ways out (and no radar contact) where Sector Y proceeded to work the aircraft all the way into the airport with no coordination to Sector X. Sector X Controller proceeded to watch this unfold without attempting to initiate the coordination to Sector Y to say 'radar contact' or even 'point-out approved' since there was no traffic for this aircraft. This was wrong in and of itself for several reasons including questioning the reach of Sector Y frequencies.Sector Y has this aircraft set up for an instrument approach; runway unknown to Sector X. Simultaneously; Sector X is in communication with Aircraft Y; inbound to ZZZ. The pilot of this flight asked us for runway conditions. The Controller working the sector was unable to get a hold of ZZZ airport operations with the line for an unknown reason. The Sector X; A-side called on another phone and after a brief conversation with operations learned that operations had tried calling Sector X on frequency to inform us that Runway XL is closed while they clear the runway of snow. It was also about this time that the NOTAM populated in ERIDS (En-route Information Display System) which is definitely not enough time between NOTAM being received and giving [the] Controller time to see [the] NOTAM relative to the location and phase of flight to Aircraft X arrival; especially if NOTAMs had already been checked and issued at the initial descent per 7110.65. While this phone call was taking place; Aircraft X was on final at approximately 3;500 feet or less. A-side ran to Sector Y and asked what runway the flight is set up for and was told Runway XL and was immediately told to cancel approach clearance and climb aircraft to 6;000 runway heading and place the aircraft on Sector X's frequency. It's amazing that Sector Y's frequency was able to even reach the aircraft. With poor visibility and snow plows kicking up snow; the plows would never have been seen even if the runway had been.Recommendations:1. Airport operations not getting a hold of an actual person to communicate runway closure and in a timely manner.2. Sector Y working an aircraft into airspace that wasn't their own. Breakdown in understanding ownership of ZZZ1 or negligence?3. Sector X Controller not initiating 'radar contact' of this flight.4. Retrain OM's.  Many overnight OM's are not properly executing text files at time of ATC 0 placing ZZZ approach airspace at a sector that's adjacent to the actual sector being worked. Sector X is one scope on the mid at Sector Z. ZZZ approach is being opened at Sector X and more often than not; is NOT followed up with a CS message to combine with Sector Z. Until a few years ago; Sector X was the mid scope and text file needs updated. This second step was clear in an email prior to this period of ZZZ; ATC 0 but is being overlooked. Controllers in Sector X assume it's being done correctly by having the airspace next to them and don't speak up about it. So if an aircraft didn't call Sector X for weather; Sector X could potentially be completely unaware of Sector Y working aircraft into ZZZ as 'auto-pop' would happen on the adjacent scope. During this incident; ZZZ Approach was opened at the adjacent scope as I was told. That did not cause this though or factor into it; however.5. Airport operations told to contact ZZZ Center on frequency which was never going to work. Needs to be a phone call to center and nothing done until this takes place.It was discussed this morning after this incident that regardless of the weather; ZZZ (Sector X) shall reach out to airport operations for ALL arrivals to make sure they are clear of the runway. Supposedly one of the operators on the runway had a radio with a dead battery and obviously would not have heard a pilot calling short final or any other calls. Why wouldn't a radio be tested with another handheld and how could it have been unknown that it was dead?Changes to the ATC-0 plan may need to happen to stop this from happening again.

column121: Company Flights Aircraft X (event flight) and Aircraft Y had all the elements in play for a severe collision during taxi operations at ZZZ airport; had it not been for the keen and alert awareness of the First Officer (FO) on our flight.Other Company Flight Aircraft Y had just landed on Runway XXC; exited onto Taxiway B; and received clearance to back-taxi on Runway XXR full-length and proceed to the gate. Shortly thereafter Aircraft X received taxi clearance to taxi to Runway XXC via Taxiway P; cross Runway XXR; left onto Taxiway G; and join Taxiway EX.Both flights were taxiing toward the intersection of Runway XXR and Taxiway P when it is assumed that Tower saw the potential collision as both aircraft had 'ALL LIGHTS ON' indicating that Aircraft Y was taxiing with clearance on an active runway; and Aircraft X was preparing to cross an active runway with proper clearance. Tower then attempted to modify the taxi clearance for Aircraft X but made an error by initiating the call with Aircraft Y's call sign. The transmission was unfortunately interrupted by a third aircraft trying to transmit as the Tower was attempting to correct the call sign; resulting in the amended clearance transmission being unintelligible to both Flights X and Y.Aircraft X was underway at a nominal taxi speed; and Aircraft Y was observed taxiing at a higher-than-normal speed as they back-taxied toward the turnoff point at the end of Runway XXR. Taxiway P enters at a slight angle preventing the Captain of Aircraft X from clearly seeing any approaching traffic from his right. As the Captain of Aircraft X; we had full intention of entering the intersection as initially cleared. Just prior I initiated a Safety call by saying 'Clear left.' At that point the FO looked right and said; 'Wow; they're moving fast; and don't think they're intending to stop.' Hearing that; I immediately began a full stop of our aircraft prior to crossing the hold short line; followed by turning our lights off; and yielding to Aircraft Y; in case we were the ones in error with the crossing clearance. Startled that we had just avoided a serious collision; we discussed the possibility of us missing a clearance or how that collision seemed inevitable had we not made the final 'Clearing check' prior to crossing the runway. Because of the frequency congestion with Tower working all three frequencies (Clearance; Ground; and Tower) and the fact that we didn't actually cross the hold short line; we held any immediate inquiry as to the miscommunication of the clearance to ourselves.Upon further discussion among ourselves after departure; we were certain that we did not miss any clearances from ATC and that this was a certain potential mishap that needed further investigation to acknowledge the chain of events from going unrecognized in the future.  We discovered that both aircraft had the appropriate clearance to be where they were and that there was an attempt by ATC to issue an amended clearance to us. Tower initially called Aircraft Y then quickly attempted to correct to Aircraft X; but the transmission was interrupted by a third aircraft rendering the call sign and amended clearance unintelligible for either aircraft to be warned appropriately about each other.Due to the angle to which Aircraft X was approaching Runway XXR; there wasn't a good line of sight for the Captain to see any approaching traffic back-taxing on Runway XXR until it would have been too late. It was only due to the vigilance and discipline from the FO in effectively communicating the immediate danger that we were we able to avoid a severe collision given the circumstances.It is believed that Tower was operating at reduced staffing levels even though there were a lot of aircraft movements at ZZZ that evening. This was likely due to COVID protocols in place with ATC. The increased workload enabled him to issue clearances to both Flight X and Y to be on Runway XXR at the same time if timing was ideal. In thiscase; an amendment to the clearance was attempted to be issued; however; time was not in our favor for the Tower to initiate the call with the wrong call sign and be interrupted by a third aircraft making the transition intelligible by either flight.

column121: Getting radar vectors to intercept the final approach course to Runway 34L RNO;  ATC instructed us to fly direct to SPOON at 11;000 ft and intercept the localizer. The direct routing to SPOON took us on a westerly heading approximately 90 degrees to the final approach course. SPOON is defined as a radar fix on the approach chart and is D24.6 from the field. As such; we were reluctant to use the localizer to guide our turn to final and instead used GPS to navigate to SPOON and turn onto final. Upon overflying SPOON; the GPS commanded an aggressive; yet smooth; right turn to final. Once on final; we intercepted the localizer and descended on the glide path while observing the altitude restrictions at APIME; WAGGE; and EPOSE. The FO (First Officer) and I were fully 'dialed in' for this approach as we had briefed the procedure; identified the surrounding terrain; and associated threats. Landed uneventfully. Three days later I was advised ATC identified our airplane as one that lost acceptable separation with terrain during our approach. The FO was making his first trip to RNO and I had only been to RNO a few times in at least a few years. We were initially planning to fly an approach to the south until ATC told us to expect one to Runway 34L. The routing to SPOON put us at (approx.) 90 degrees to the final approach course with (from memory) an unreliable localizer signal at D24.6. That large angle and our reluctance to use the localizer so far from the field forced us into using the GPS which caused an overfly situation; and thus; and overshoot of the final approach course. I think getting a heading to intercept the final approach course inside SPOON and at a lesser angle would alleviate the overshoot possibility and the resulting loss of separation.
column123: We were cleared to and were proceeding direct to SPOON at 11;000 ft on a track of approximately 070 when we were cleared to intercept the localizer for the ILS 34L.  The Pilot Flying (Captain) and I discussed intercepting the localizer so far from the field (SPOON is 24.6D from the field) and the PF elected to stay in Nav [mode] until we had turned on to the final.  We saw the line the nav was going to take and that it was going to fly over SPOON and then turn us onto final with a slight overshoot and the PF verbalized this.  We had done an extremely thorough review of the RNO brief and of all of the pages in FD Pro and based on the clear weather and our awareness of the terrain hazards we concluded that this would be an appropriate course of action.  We overflew SPOON; 'nav'd' to the final approach course and then selected the approach mode and flew the rest of the approach and landing uneventfully. The extremely steep intercept angle and relatively close proximity to SPOON when we were cleared to intercept the localizer along with the far distance from the field.  Emphasize to both ATC and aircrew the ramifications of a steep intercept angle to final.

column121: Upon being vectored for the ILS approach to Runway XX at ZZZ; ATC cleared us to descend from 3;000 MSL to 2000 MSL. The PNF was distracted while trying to control the cabin pressure that had been wildly uncontrollable since the beginning of descent from FL410. As the PIC and PF; I set the Altitude Alerter to 2;000 and vertical speed to 700 FPM descent; with autopilot engaged. During the descent to 2;000 MSL; I briefly looked up at the Pressurization Control Panel to monitor the PNF progress in controlling the cabin pressure; I noted the cabin pressure was finally close to the aircraft's actual altitude. I directed the PNF to select 'RAM AIR' ON.  That action stabilized the cabin for landing. ATC called to confirm our 2;000 feet clearance limit and I realized that the aircraft did not level off at 2;000 feet and the autopilot was not engaged. I acknowledged our clearance to ATC; manually flew the plane from 1;700 feet to 2;000 feet and reengaged to Autopilot. Since the cabin pressure was finally under control; an uneventful approach and landing were completed. Due to the distraction of the cabin pressure control issues; as PF I briefly failed to monitor the aircraft flight profile. Since I had tasked the PNF to attempt to stabilize the cabin pressure; I take full responsibility for failing to continuously monitor the aircraft flight profile.No matter what cockpit distractions occur; it is incumbent upon the PF to continuously monitor the aircraft flight profile. And if using the Autopilot; PF should continuously monitor that it functions as programed and does not inadvertently disconnect.
column123: The flight went well up to the time of descent when the cabin pressure started to malfunction. All attempts were made to control the pressurization using ADC 1 & 2 and Manual control. As preparations were made for landing; air traffic control issued further descent to 2;000 feet and the flying pilot was in control of the aircraft with the auto pilot engaged. The aircraft did not capture the 2;000 foot altitude because the autopilot was inadvertently disconnected and the aircraft continued descent to 1;600 feet at which time the deviation was noted and immediately corrected.  The aircraft was subsequently vectored onto the final course and the rest of the approach and landing was uneventful.  The pilot monitoring should have noticed the altitude deviation as a result of the auto pilot not being engaged while manually controlling the pressurization and the pilot flying should have been aware that the auto pilot was not engaged. It is imperative that the pilot flying concentrates on flying the aircraft while the other attends to the malfunction and refers to the checklists.

column121: Day VMC. Conducted initial approach [Runway] XXR. PF (Pilot Flying) called missed approach into ZZZ [Runway] XXR due to windshear with airspeed loss below 500 ft. AFE (Above Field Elevation) with advancement in override thrust. Subsequently received windshear caution. After selecting TOGA and pitch up flew flight director. No windshear escape guidance provided as the windshear was not sustained. Thrust was advanced to GA (Go-Around) RSV as a precaution. Stable in the missed approach maneuver with no caution windshear; PF called Flaps 4 due to flaps full configured. Gear retracted at a safe altitude with positive climb rate. Flew ATC assigned runway heading with missed approach climb profile. Subsequent approach flown to the ILS profile with Flaps 5. Flew the glide slope to RWY [Runway] XXR. No windshear event occurred. Received wind report with gust factor 28 kts. Selected manual speeds to increase approach sped until 4-5 kts. until after passing 500 ft. AFE 'stable' call the target speed was reduced. Maintained visual descent rate with visual cues and instrumentation of the ILS. During round out to flare automation set the aural 'sink rate' message. FO (First Officer) announced correcting due to the aural call and confirmed with a cross check the sink rate was induced by maintaining descent rate with the descent maneuver to coupled round out pitch rate simultaneously for the landing maneuver; not due to windshear as the speed was stable. FO and CA (Captain) on debrief both acknowledged the aural alert at post flight and both agreed with given conditions the approach to landing was stable given the conditions. Touchdown was within LTP (Landing Threshold Point) distance.Second approach with Flaps 5 configuration allowed for a higher approach speed and acknowledging the wind factor with increase in target speed for gusty conditions allowed for less susceptibility for the same condition. Automation with sensor inputs from other automated systems is subject to its own set design limitations and may not reflect positive confirmation of the event with pilot judgment of the same situation monitoring the same event. Such as automation latencies detecting the windshear event prior to the windshear caution; or sink rate alert while the pilot is initiating real time assertive maneuvers in turbulent conditions. Inertial vertical speed descent rates measure acceleration as it filters out noise of turbulence conditions causing a lag as opposed to real time judgment of the flight crew.

column121: Training on combined sectors; moderate traffic; two practice approach aircraft in satellite airspace all other traffic in departure sectors.Aircraft X came off ZZZ on the published missed approach for the RNAV RWY XX approach; he checked in and was radar identified while in the published left turn towards the missed approach fix; ZZZZZ.  The trainee subsequently verified the pilot's previous request to return to ZZZ1 on an IFR clearance.  The trainee cleared Aircraft X direct ZZZ and instructed the aircraft to maintain 2;000'.  At the time; the aircraft was within a 2;000' MVA [Minimum Vectoring Altitude].  I believe both the trainee and I anticipated that the pilot would make a right turn direct to ZZZ1; not recognizing that a continued left turn may be more appropriate because the aircraft was already in the published left turn on the missed approach.  With the anticipation of a right turn in mind and the aircraft in a 2;000' MVA my attention as the OJTI turned to the other departure traffic; which was going to require the trainee to merge and weave multiple departures off multiple airports (ZZZ2/ZZZ3/ZZZ4) to get them on course and through our airspace.  This was an area the trainee had shown struggles in in previous sessions as well as earlier in this training session; so I was attempting to stay ahead and have a plan of my own if needed.  Upon reviewing the incident; I became aware that in the moments following Aircraft X's clearance I was suggesting an alternative course of action for one of the trainee's departures in an effort to illustrate a way to expedite getting a departure on course which also got them out of the way of succeeding departures quicker.  Unfortunately; this conversation kept my focus on the departure traffic as opposed to the continued turn that Aircraft X made into the higher MVA.  Aircraft X subsequently continued a left turn towards ZZZ1 and entered a 2;500' MVA at his assigned altitude of 2;000'.  The trainee was aware of the incident almost immediately.  The trainee issued a climb to 2;500' to Aircraft X when the aircraft was only a third or a half a mile inside the 2;000' MVA.  I was not aware of the situation until I heard the trainee issue the climb to Aircraft X.  I subsequently requested that we be relieved.  The trainee and I debriefed; after which I informed management of the incident when I requested time for myself and the trainee to review the incident and fill out our report.  To my knowledge; Aircraft X climbed to the MVA and subsequently landed at ZZZ1 without further incident.Numerous things could have prevented this occurrence.  Had the trainee climbed Aircraft X to 3;000' instead of descending them to 2;000' they would have been above the MVA.  Had the trainee left the aircraft on the published missed approach for even a few miles they would have climbed above the MVA and a subsequent clearance may have included a more appropriate altitude.  Had the aircraft made the anticipated right turn instead of continuing in a left turn they would have remained in the 2;000' MVA.  Had the trainee issued the clearance to ZZZ1 via radar vectors; I believe they would have assigned a vector that would have remained within the 2;000' MVA and avoided the situation.
column123: Recertification time on [positions] (departures) and Article 67 training on[positions](south satellite). Aircraft X departed ZZZ on the published missed from the RNV runway XX  approach. column121: Planned flight as normal; no limiting MELs were attached to the aircraft at any point during planning.  I received a call from the crew at asking for clarification that MEL XX-XX-X-1 meant that center tank fuel was unusable; I confirmed this was the case; that this MEL means that both center pumps are INOP and that any fuel in the center is trapped; I thought it was a generic question and didn't question the MEL on this specific flight. I believe the aircraft departed with approx 24.7 usable fuel with a MIN TAKEOFF fuel of 27.0.  After takeoff and at a safe altitude; I ACARSed the crew asking them to confirm the fuel available in their main tanks only; I determined this fuel was not sufficient to make it to RFD and advised the dispatch lead.  The crew agreed that a tech stop was in the best interest of safety and it was decided that ZZZ1 was a suitable gateway for this; the flight was diverted to ZZZ1 to add fuel.  Unfortunately; at no point during the pre-planning or planning stage of this flight; did I receive a call from Maintenance Control advising the MEL was being added; nor did the crew request an amended release before blockout advising that the MEL was not on their paperwork and thus not considered for the flight.  The call was a routine call in which I thought the crew was just asking for interpretation of a MEL.I would suggest to Maintenance Control that they advise all dispatchers that have that tail assigned of any MELs being added; unfortunately we don't always have the aircraft on its previous leg and thus when they advise one dispatcher of an MEL being added; the next dispatcher does not receive this information.

This system makes it very difficult to fly the arrival. Please know that this isn't pointing blame; but pointing out a problem. As PIC; the responsibility ultimately falls on me. column121: During the boarding process of Aircraft X at Gate; a passenger in her assigned seat was holding her carry-on bag on her lap. The carry-on had a vape charger inside the bag and the batteries started to smoke and meltdown. There was smoke and fumes in the cabin. An unknown passenger ran towards the front of the aircraft yelling that there was a fire in the back of the aircraft and for everyone to get off. The flight attendants made an announcement and commenced the Emergency Deplaning at the Gate procedure (which we had discussed in my pre-bridging brief to the FA's (Flight Attendants)). The Purser asked what to do and I told him to continue the process they had started; which was going very well with passengers calmly deplaning up the jet way. The First Officer alerted emergency response and got up from his seat to assist. I was then told by an unknown person; that the smoking bag had been removed from the aircraft by a dead-heading pilot. I ran the Emergency Evacuation checklist to secure the aircraft; grabbed the fire extinguisher (not needed) and stood at the door directing the passengers to continue up the jetway; 'do not take bags or stand in the jetway; and to proceed to the terminal.' I directed the First Officer to go to terminal. There were a few passengers slowing the process trying to grab their carry-on bag; but were directed to stop and continue to the terminal. Once all passengers were off; I directed the FA's to go to the terminal while I swept the aircraft to be sure all crew and passengers were off. I then proceeded to the terminal. At the terminal I found the crew and deadheading crew members at the door; several passengers and agents and the smoking bag lying on the floor next to the ticket counter. I then directed all persons to leave the area; and requested Law enforcement with/dogs and fire and rescue to the bag. Asked the gate agent to call medical assistance and found the affected passenger sitting in the terminal; which I directed Medical to her location. At that point I was alarmed that the threat had followed us to the terminal and was concerned as to its contents. I then briefed fire and rescue; Maintenance as well as corporate security and law enforcement. I directed the deadheading crewmember who had carried the bag to seek medical attention. We coordinated for the FA's to stay nearby to facilitate the eventual allowing of 5 passengers at a time to go back to the secured aircraft to get their belongings. The First Officer was having chest pain and went to the hospital. I declined medical treatment. And met the ZZZ Chief Pilot who assisted me in the process remaining. There were burns on the owner of the smoking bag; and she also went to the hospital. There were no other injuries or incidents associated with the emergency deplaning procedure...but there was some uncertainty among the many constituents affected by the procedure; gate; ground; maintenance. etc. I was relieved from duty with 'p' for the remaining duration of the trip. I received follow up calls from ZZZ Chief Pilot on multiple occasions and was grateful for his support. I also contacted directly Union Safety and spoke with [Representative] who provided assistance and guidance during and after the event. Overall the procedure works; but should be expanded to a joint training scenario. I was most alarmed to learn. That the (brave) deadheading crew member had carried the smoking bag with him during the deplaning and it eventually ended up in the terminal with no oversight. The direction was to deplane away from the threat; not take it with us.The cause was allowing of the charging device and vape apparatus onboard the aircraft as a carry-on. The positive outcome was due to emergency deplaning at the gate procedure and pre-briefing. Well trained and professional back-end crew was outstanding. First Officer reverted to training and promptly called fire and rescue. However once passengers were off; there was confusion and potential danger which needs to be mitigated for future events. Communication and full understanding and procedures associated are necessary.I suggest the need to continue the use of and to training of the 'Emergency Deplaning at the Gate Procedure'. Would recommend suggested briefings for the crew. Also believe joint training would be very beneficial to role play these scenarios...there is a lot going on and many potential pitfalls. This affects all constituents of the normal process; but also many others. Being released from duty by the Chief Pilot was appreciated; however as a reserve pilot; working to get my time for the month; Pay - No Credit does not help in any way. In fact it prevented me from flying another 4 day trip I could have held; and subsequently puts me at zero(0) hours going into the middle of the month.
column123: It was the first leg of the start of the sequence. I had just met the CA (Captain); for the first time; that afternoon. Along with the first time working with the FA's (Flight Attendants). Boarding started as normal; the CA and myself went about our preflight duties. We had finished all our checklists and were just waiting for the Gate Agent to inform us of boarding being complete. As we sat waiting to close up FA-1 shouts up to us 'We have a fire in the cabin'. In the time that it took the CA and I to get over the initial shock factor; the FA's immediately began an 'Emergency Deplaning' of the aircraft. From my advantage point I had no clue how bad the fire was in the cabin. I did not hear any call for an 'Evacuation'; or see any doors and slides deploying; so I assumed that the FA's were just doing the 'Emergency Deplaning'.The CA went to the QRH immediately. I got on the radio to ops and told them of our situation. That we had a fire onboard the aircraft; we were 'Emergency Deplaning' into the terminal; and we needed ARF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting).The CA and I had completed everything we could think of to help the FA's with the situation in the back. Still not knowing how bad things were in the cabin the CA instructed me to exit the airplane. I did so and then followed my 'evacuation' duties when outside the aircraft. As I exited the flight deck I found a clog of passengers not moving out the door. I made my way through them to find a group of passengers have congregated on the jetway. I instructed them to move and get in the terminal building. This helped the flow of passengers off the aircraft. I found one passenger in visible distress on the jetway. I did a quick assessment of the passenger and then asked if they were OK. The passenger complained of burns on their arm. It did not look bad so I asked if they could walk. The passenger said yes. So I got the assistance of another passenger to help them into the terminal. I also instructed them to take the bag that the hurt passenger said was theirs and was standing next to. Later I would find out this was the bag that was smoking. It was not smoking when I was on the jetway and I was unaware this was the threat on the aircraft. I never would have thought that the threat would be off the aircraft in the direction the passengers were going. Or taken off and left unattended.After the passengers were off the aircraft the FA's were coming off and then asked where the bag was. I asked 'What bag? The one on the ground in the jetway?' They responded Yes; that was the one that was smoking. At that point I realized that I sent it inside the terminal. I remembered what passenger had it and told the supervisor; that was on the jetway; that I could identify them to find that bag.The CA completed his final check of the aircraft and we proceeded into the terminal. The bag has been cordoned off at the gate and people were being kept away. The CA remained at the gate until ARF arrived. I took the FA's and proceeded to an unused gate to keep us together and away from the situation.The incident started with a passenger's bag there was no control over the problem. There was some confusion over what procedures were started and what roles the flight deck crew had in an 'Emergency Deplaning'.It was also confusing how and why the fire; smoking bag; was put onto the jetway. The use of the 'Emergency Deplaning' was very appropriate to this situation and did exactly what it was intended to do. However there is not a clear signal; that we knew of; that signals to the flight deck that an 'Emergency Deplaning' is in progress. There was also not an immediate action item; QRC; or QRH procedure to reference for an event like this for us on the flight deck to help. It felt as if we were making it up as we went along. column121: Upon descent on the RNAV arrival; the aircraft ahead advised 'moderate turbulence at 10;000 ft.… We as a crew evaluated the deviations options and concluded to stay on route and cross the next fix at 9;000 ft. The area north and south of course on the radar were shaded with darker colors. The current inflight night visibility was zero with moderate to heavy rain lightning and St Elmo's fire. Upon crossing the fix we begin to encounter moderate turbulence. The autopilot was engaged; 250 kts. speed selected. After passing the fix and right about when the smart turn over another fix began we received an immediate CLIMB RESOLUTION ADVISORY and a RED traffic appeared on the Multi-Function Display (MFD) in the 11 o'clock position.I; the Pilot Flying; began the TCAS TA/RA actions and call-outs disconnecting the autopilot; complying with the RA climb instructions. The Captain turned off the Flight Directors as per company procedures. Due to moderate turbulence the aircraft began to rapidly slow below the selected 250 kts.; so I; the Pilot Flying; selected TOGA (Take Off/Go Around) to equalize the descending energy and avoid a stall or near stall condition. With the lack of Flight Director (FD) lateral guidance the MFD became primary for lateral guidance for the turn over the fix; the red threat traffic appeared between us and turning left to rejoin the arrival. As we began to level off and reestablish vertical and lateral guidance ATC queried us. The Captain; who was Pilot Monitoring; was tasked with selecting the Flight Directors ON and selecting the desired modes to return us to course and altitude in a rather bumpy erratic flight condition. I; the Pilot Flying; with hands on a push to talk advised ATC of complying with a TCAS RA. As we began to turn back to course the previous red threat traffic reappeared yellow and a 'TRAFFIC; TRAFFIC' was heard; so we remained leveled off and slow turned towards the course. After establishing guidance; and positively managing the aircraft's speed and energy we began a turn towards the next fix. We as a crew were task saturated controlling the aircraft in moderate turbulence and complying with the TCAS RA and were merely queried by ATC; never advised of traffic by ATC or given any lateral guidance after stating we were complying with a TCAS RA. It was only several moments after we were reestablishing on course avoiding the traffic that ATC assigned a heading. Most disturbing during the irregularities of moderate turbulence; TCAS RA with traffic conflicting the turn; and turbulence induced energy state beyond authority of the auto thrust; ATC tries to immediately give us a phone number to call instead of any assistance in weather or traffic guidance.The portion of the RNAV arrival; during the event; has 6.5 miles to descend up to 2;000 ft.; slow 40 kts.; and smart turn 51 degrees; coupled with a very changing tailwind of 150 kts. at 20;000 [ft.] slowing to 36 kts. at 10;000 [ft.] and the aircraft's FMS plotting the deceleration to approach mode between fixes thus requiring manual speed selected management; it is a very busy part of the arrival.Casual factors were night with St. Elmo's fire; lightning causing a very dark outside and requiring bright instrumentation that is difficult for the eye to follow in moderate turbulence. Possible other factors of AUTO FLT FCU 1 FAIL immediately after the event. ATC was extremely busy. I think another big factor was ATC confusion of what we were experiencing; due to the fact we were both task saturated controlling the aircraft and avoiding a mid-air collision ATC communication became a lower priority. With reduced traffic separation ATC becomes an integral part of every flight; if the manuals would include 'advise ATC' as a step; and clear guidance on priority of traffic avoidance in relationship to lateral guidance and where it is seen or sourced this could help."

column121: We arrived just before our show time. I confirmed that the aircraft had been fueled the night before and was in the hangar (it was winter and I wanted to avoid frost on the aircraft) and I asked for a bucket to take a fuel sample. My First Officer and I made our way to the hangar and began getting the aircraft ready. I decided to take a fuel sample while he was finishing the preflight. The left tanks; fuel filter; and fuel system low point drains showed clear jet fuel with no contamination. I then went to check the right feeder tank and a large amount of water and cloudy fuel came out of the drain. The right main tank also had a significant amount of contamination but not as much as the feeder tank. I continued to sump the fuel a few more times and it was no longer making a layer; but the fuel was still cloudy. My First Officer had completed the preflight and I made him aware of the fuel contamination and I told him that I'd need to talk to maintenance before flight as I had never seen this much contamination before. I went ahead and had the aircraft pulled out and put on a GPU to warm the cabin before the passengers arrived. While that was happening; I sent the pictures to maintenance. Maintenance directed me to speak with maintenance and that the cloudiness needed to be resolved. I talked with maintenance and they acknowledged the pictures and started working on solutions to see if a maintenance tech could be found. I then checked in with the operations and informed them that the flight may need to be recovered. I then got back in touch with maintenance who said that they had reviewed the pictures and that continued draining of the fuel should cause it to clear up and that it may take several full sumps before it does. I then asked for another bucket and tried again to sump the right tanks. After 2 more sumps on each drain I was able to get clear fuel with no layering. I took pictures of the result and sent them to maintenance and we all agreed the problem had been resolved. I also asked my First Officer if he was comfortable with the result and he agreed. We then continued the flight as normal with only about a 15 min delay.

I greeted the owners and got them loaded and made sure the bags were loaded. During the baggage loading it became apparent I would have to increase the weight to match the weight of bags for the trip. I adjusted the weight in the waypoint app and waited for a valid release. The First Officer had briefed the passengers and we got into the cockpit and got ready to go while we waited for the release. We waited quite a while for the release as we began making phone calls and sending messages to try and see if the release was coming. Once I finally got through to the dispatcher on the phone and asked if the new release was coming soon. He responded 'what do you mean? You're in the air already.' I informed him that no we weren't we were still waiting on a valid release due to the weight change. Shortly after that we received a release from a different dispatcher which we verified the suffix was still the same as the last release and made our way to depart. A short time into the flight they gave us a reroute to a couple RNAV fixes and different route. We advised them we weren't RNAV and would like to remain on our route navigating by ground based navigation. It was at this point that I started to wonder if the suffix still wasn't correct for the airplanes condition. We continued without further issues. The entire process was truly exhausting having to review and keep straight in my head four releases and make sure they were done correctly; even if it wasn't already a new airplane as well as a recovery at the end of what was now becoming a long day. column121: I was conducting a training flight from ZZZ with a relatively new student; who is part owner of the aircraft (I am not an owner of the airplane). The lesson began normally with a preflight inspection by the student and an abbreviated inspection by myself; which showed no abnormality. There were five quarts of oil in the engine; I tightened the cap myself after double-checking. I personally watched the student add 10 gallons on fuel to the aircraft and sump uncontaminated fuel from both tanks immediately prior to flying. The run up was performed prior to takeoff with normal RPM drops on both magnetos and with application of carburetor heat. On takeoff the oil pressure and temperature read normal; and the engine was generating what appeared to be normal maximum power (~2;500 RPM). Takeoff and climb to the west were uneventful; with the student being the pilot flying. Several minutes into the flight I took the controls to demonstrate a maneuver. After performing a clearing turn at 3;000 ft. to prepare to demonstrate stalls to the student; I pressed the mixture in to prepare for full-power recovery from the maneuvers. Shortly after doing so; I noticed a drastic decrease in engine power (roughly 1;500 RPM maximum). After moving the throttle through most of its range to see if any setting would produce more power; I executed the engine failure checklist from memory (fuel on; mixture rich; carb heat on; magnetos on both; master on; primer in and locked). All items were configured correctly; I cycled each magneto individually to see if using one alone would produce more power; but this did not work. As I was doing this I was turning back toward land to the east and searching for a nearby grass runway. I requested priority handling to Approach; who assisted in locating ZZZ which was only several miles away and within gliding distance. A safe landing was made on the runway; which was in good condition and dry. When shutting down the aircraft; I noticed a sharp increase in RPM while pulling the mixture out to cutoff. I called the TRACON on the phone to let them know of our safe landing. After exiting the aircraft; I checked the oil level again; it was still at five quarts; and the cap had been tight. There was no obvious cause of the engine malfunction visible through the air inlets or the oil door. My student did find some acorns underneath the aircraft on the runway; the plane had recently undergone maintenance to remove debris in the engine cowling placed by squirrels that had gotten into the hangar. Several minutes after landing; deputies from the Sheriff's Department arrived to verify our safety; as they had been contacted by the approach controller. I was able to restart the aircraft normally; though in the full rich position the aircraft was not able to produce more than 1;500 RPM and ran very rough. With the mixture pulled out about two inches; I was able to generate a normal static RPM at full throttle. The aircraft was secured so that it could be inspected and repaired by the on-field A&P when he was available later in the week. I was informed by the student several days later that the mechanic found acorns in the air induction system.

At 150 feet AGL my student elected to go-around and when I questioned why they said; 'I cannot read any of the runway markings nor see the displaced threshold.' They were right to do what they did. The other aircraft was also not announcing enough or not announcing correctly or getting stepped on by other chatter or otherwise unintelligible. Another contributing factor was the other aircraft not having ADS-B Out installed. It wasn't required there but it would have greatly helped avoid the near miss. Given that we did hear another mention of Runway XX; I should have asked for their position since I didn't hear it the first time. In the future; I will break off opposite direction approaches much sooner when there is other traffic in the vicinity.

column121: I departed 52F from runway 35 for a straight out VFR climb enroute to ZZZ for pattern work. After departure; and during the initial climb; I visually observed a powered parachute maneuvering at approximately 1;200 feet MSL on the extended straight out departure path from 52F.  I then observed a second powered parachute operating at my current altitude of 1;500 feet MSL directly in my flight path (altitudes later crosschecked from my ForeFlight flight path replay). Since the second powered parachute was head-on I did not see him until the last minute.  I was forced to make an abrupt maneuver to the left (west) to avoid a midair collision.  I have since learned from other pilots based at 52F that this is a frequent occurrence in all areas around 52F; and at times powered parachutes have operated within the lateral and vertical traffic pattern boundaries of 52F; which seems to be contrary to 14 CFR part 103.13(a) and (b).  In addition; this type of operation is prohibited at 52F per the remarks section of the A/FD.  These types of operations are less regulated than drones and drone operators.  I am concerned that if allowed to continue without some type of mitigation or FAA intervention that it is only a matter of time before there is an accident. I would suggest either requiring some kind of formal training/testing/checking for powered parachutes or prohibiting these operations under (not just within) the all Class B airspace.

column121: I was flying on an IFR flight plan at assigned altitude of 4000'. I was granted the requested weather deviation and was flying outside of the weather depicted by FIS-B several miles in IMC conditions. Apparently; I flew into an embedded thunderstorm cell with both severe turbulence and violent downdrafts and updrafts which was not depicted by FIS-B weather with a 4 minute time stamp.I noticed the IAS had climbed dangerously high into the yellow arc while on autopilot (AP) maintaining an altitude of 4;000'. I reduced power to idle in an effort to maintain a safe indicated airspeed. While the AP was engaged and power reduced the IAS did not reduce sufficiently to the maneuvering speed but was rapidly climbing. I disconnected the AP and pulled the yoke back to reduce IAS. I then encountered severe turbulence and downdrafts forcing the aircraft to lose approximately 500 feet. In an attempt to stabilize the aircraft; I attempted to various throttle settings in an attempt to maintain altitude and heading with little success in controlling altitude or heading.The entire event lasted approximately 2 minutes with several calls from ATC offering assistance. During those calls I requested ATC standby until I was able to regain control of the aircraftThis was an isolated cell whose location was not accurately depicted by FIS-B weather radar returns. In regards to corrective actions on my part as pilot; I'd say to not trust FIS-B time stamps nor the weather depictions as being reasonably accurate. Further I'd extend my safety margin around weather depicted on FIS-B to a greater margin.The flight terminated without incident with my cancelling my IFR flight plan once out of IMC conditions and safely landing at the destination airport.
