column121: At XA:28Z; Aircraft X checked on the frequency asking for VFR flight following in the vicinity of ZZZ. He was given a beacon code and I displayed a data block on the radar scope; waiting for it to track up. After a minute I told the pilot that I did not have radar contact; and I didn't have a target in the area he stated. I verified his code and location; and had him reset his transponder after another minute went by. At XA:31Z I told him it might be necessary for him to climb before I could establish radar contact. He reported that he was starting a climb to 7;000 feet.One minute after he started his climb; at XA:32Z; I picked up a primary target in the area the pilot reported. I tried to verify the position of the primary target; but the pilot just responded that he was showing zero oil pressure and having electrical issues. As he was saying this; the data block correlated to the code and I radar identified Aircraft X and verified his location. My standard practice; something that I did less than ten minutes prior; is to radar identify; verify location and altitude; and give altimeter. I do it every time; and in that order. When I radar identified Aircraft X; there was no Mode C data; so I asked him to report his altitude. He reported that he was climbing to 7;000 feet and asked for help to get into ZZZ; he was showing zero on his oil pressure. I didn't circle back to the altimeter at this time.I issued Aircraft X a heading to set him up for a pattern into ZZZ. If his engine was about to quit; I wanted him lined up for an airport; not guessing what was below him. I told the CIC I was working a special aircraft; and the OM was quickly in the area. I didn't feel it was in good judgement to add on to the pilot's stress level by pointing out that he was experiencing an urgent situation. It was being handled as such.He asked as he rolled out if he was on the correct heading. I advised that he was 20 degrees off course; and that he should correct. He told me he was using his backup compass; due to electrical failure. That information made a lot of sense at that moment. The backup compass is a magnetic compass. It's one that bounces around as you turn it. The magnetic compass will continue to turn past the heading and then bounce back and correct as the airplane levels off and the compass stabilizes. This is something that an IFR rated pilot would be more knowledgeable about. No gyro turns; or turns with only the backup compass were part of my IFR certificate training. Due to this; I decided to give him small turns that would create an arc to final; and help him maintain better control and orientation.I told him to descend to 5;000 ft. and that I should still have radar contact at that altitude. He responded that believed he'd be able to poke through. I knew it would be minimal conditions; I still believed getting the aircraft set up for a runway was the safest places. As I gave him a turn to the left he stated that he was going to get into the clouds. I asked if he and the aircraft were IFR qualified. He said they were not. I asked if he could maintain VFR conditions. It sounded like he was trying; but didn't seem sure that he would.I told Aircraft X that he could continue down to 4;000 feet and gave him a heading to get him turned more toward the airport. About that time at XA:39Z; just eleven minutes into the situation; an aircraft inbound for ZZZ1 checked on. I issued the ZZZ1 altimeter. This aircraft would end up being held out for the [situation]. I then told Aircraft X he could descend at his discretion to 3;900 feet; but that was the minimum enroute altitude in the area; and the lowest I was comfortable advising him. He said he was starting to poke through at 4;100 feet. I gave him the position and distance of ZZZ1. He responded that he could see some ground.I had him continue his gradual left turn but saw a much more aggressive turn on the radar. I asked if he was circling down to stay in VFR conditions. He said he saw bases at 3;800 feet and it was an unintentional 360. Based on what the radar showed; it was not a controlled maneuver; and probably resulted from an unusual attitude due to spatial disorientation. I asked him to regain level flight; as to maintain control of the aircraft and not get into another unusual attitude. I asked him his altitude; he responded 3;680 [feet]. Up until this uncontrolled maneuver; every report was that he was in marginal conditions; but always seemed to have some visual capabilities. At this point the inability to maintain VFR was imminent.The aircraft showed a northeast heading; I asked him to make a slow turn. Being an IFR rated pilot myself; and seeing how easily he became disoriented already; I wanted to avoid a stall; spin or turning over the aircraft. In the clouds a turn can make your body feel like you are descending; and a climb can make your body think you are turning. A more abrupt climb or turn only magnifies this effect. At XA:43Z as I maintained focus on keeping the pilot's wings level; I offered the option of climbing back up into VFR conditions. He was in favor of the idea. He added that the engine had been running fine; and believed the zero oil pressure reading to be due to electrical issue; not engine issues. With that information I immediately reassessed the IFR conditions to be the most hazardous conditions in the situation.I saw the aircraft again start a west turn that seemed to increase in rate. I gave the aircraft his location and his observed turn. I advised that he level off and focus on flying straight and level. He did not respond. The maneuver seemed unstable and I tried to relay that he needed to get wings level; then start climbing slowly. Anything aggressive would cause greater disorientation. He said the engine was running fine now; no longer a concern. I told him that we believed it to be clear in ZZZ2; ZZZ3; and ZZZ4. He said that sounds nice. I wanted to get him into ZZZ3 if it was in fact clear. It was much closer; and based on his workload; fatigue due to stress; and equipment issues; I wanted him in the air the least amount of time possible. The CIC or the OM; I don't remember which; went up to the weather desk to get the most complete weather information available. Other controllers were also pulling weather at surrounding airports. I was focused on getting Aircraft X oriented and into VMC.I told him to fly his present heading and start a climb; advising that there was no traffic ahead. He responded that he was having trouble keeping his wings level. I advised back to straight and level and asked his altitude. The climb was giving him a sensation of turning and he was having trouble overcoming that. I should have advised him to focus on the instruments over his own sensations; but I did not think of it at the time.He said he was at 4;020 feet. I said give me level straight flight and then we'll start a slow climb. I wanted him to remain calm and know that we were going to work through it. He did not answer. Seeing what appeared to be straight flight on the radar scope I advised a shallow climb. He said he was trying to keep the wings level. At that point a VFR aircraft departing ZZZ1 was checking in. I called the traffic to that aircraft; advised the altitude was unknown; and asked Aircraft X to say his altitude. He did not immediately answer. Instead another aircraft keyed up; saying the other aircraft didn't look good on his TCAS and he needed to level his wings. Aircraft X then responded; he pulled into a stall; but was starting back up. I advised him to take it slow. At that point Aircraft Y verified ZZZ2 to be clear. I asked if Aircraft X was staying level. He said yes; 5;000 feet and seeing sunlight. I saw another turn on radar and had him level his wings once again. A minute later he reported on top of clouds and level. I told him maintain level flight; catch his breath; and if there were any airports he wanted to try to get to; we would get the weather for him. In my experience; it was best to remind him that he could exhale. He still needed to have the ability to fly the rest of his flight with electrical issues. I also offered him the opportunity to request an alternate airport. He had equipment that most likely needed to be repaired or replaced. I didn't want to send him somewhere that he'd get stuck. Aircraft X was maintaining a southeast heading and I asked him his altitude. He responded; 5;860 feet. I offered again; ZZZ2; ZZZ3; and ZZZ4. The pilot was happy with ZZZ2 because it was reported clear. I gave a heading for him to fly that would get him started turning more towards either airport as I waited for the weather information. I recommended going to ZZZ3 because it was the closest. The pilot agreed that ZZZ3 would be his first choice; then ZZZ2. Immediately as he said that; the information was back from the weather desk and I relayed it to the pilot. He said he wanted to shoot for ZZZ2 because it was clear and ZZZ3 was overcast. I gave a few more heading changes and turns to get him direct to ZZZ2. I also lost radar contact on him a minute later as well. I received another report that he should expect to be clear of the west edge of the moving weather some time before ZZZ2; and passed that along. I advised him that he appeared right on course; and I was relieved at XB:08Z.Ten minutes later; while talking to the relieving controller; the pilot thanked us all for the help he received and said he was feeling the love. He even asked to get a forwarding address to send me a bottle of good scotch. Additionally; when calling the facility from the ground; the pilot was very thankful for the services he received. He informed the OM that he had to change pants when he landed; and again wanted to send a thank you bottle for getting him to safety. It was not apparent at the beginning of the situation that the engine oil reading was due to an electrical issue. It was possible that it could have been a number of different factors; but I knew that he could lose his engine at any moment; and it may not sound rough right away. I wanted him to get lined up for a runway as safely and quickly as possible. I gave him the option to get down below the bases; but should have emphasized to maintain VFR; even though it is the pilot's responsibility. During a stressful [situation]; that would be a good reminder to give the pilot. Once the pilot gained confidence that the engine was running properly; I did everything in my power; and with all of my flight experience to keep the pilot focused on not getting into an unrecoverable condition; while maneuvering safely into VMC.During an imminent [hazard]; controllers have to make judgement calls on what is the most prudent and time critical course of action. Access to checklists during these situations would ensure that all services are provided. Controllers could check that they had provided all of the information possible without taking as much attention away from the imminent safety issue. An easier to use weather reporting system would ensure more weather reports are forwarded along from controllers. The current GI method can be tedious and the tie up keyboard use during busier sessions. ERIDS (En Route Information Display System) offers weather reporting by tapping on the information and hitting send. Using this system would increase the efficiency and result in more weather reports being available. Even just having paper weather slips that controllers can hand to a supervisor would improve efficiency.A working knowledge of flight instruments and factors of flight would allow better assistance to pilots in [hazardous] situations. Recurrent training that focuses on best practices during imminent situations would enhance controllers on seldom used skills.

column121: On the Arrival into ONT SoCal Approach assigned vectors to sequence behind a 747. We were vectored directly behind and above the preceding 747 for 26L when we were cleared for the visual approach to 26R. ATC advised to maintain visual separation. At that point; due to concerns of descending behind the heavy aircraft; I offset right of course and attempted to parallel the 747. My intention was to remain clear of the 747's wake vortices. As we continued the approach and began to converge with the other aircraft; ONT Tower issued clearance to S-turn to the right if necessary. At that point we were too close to the runway to make any effective maneuvers and still maintain a stabilized approach. We then received a 'Descend' RA and continued descending on the visual approach to 26R while the adjacent aircraft executed a climb and go-around from 26L. In retrospect I believe a better course of action would have been to discontinue the visual approach or ask for delay vectors to increase separation from the heavy aircraft. column123: Descending on the Arrival into ONT; SoCal Approach Control gave a maintain current HDG [instruction]. Once established on the 170 HDG; SoCal cleared us and the 747 visual approaches; 747 to Runway 26L and us to 26R and told us 'Caution wake turbulence and maintain visual separation with the 747'. The Captain did not want to be in a position to be at a 45 degree angle behind the 747; which would've increased the chances of getting into the wake of the 747; so as we were descending for the approach we received a descend RA and Aircraft Y executed a go-around for a climb RA. column121: Our alternate was ZZZ2 exactly because ZZZ3; ZZZ4; ZZZ5; and ZZZ6 were not suitable weather-wise. The original flight plan had fuel to fly ZZZ-ZZZ1; go-around and fly to our alternate of ZZZ2 landing with a fairly standard REMF; as I recall; certainly not enough fuel to shoot a second approach in ZZZ1 and comfortably divert to ZZZ2.This was our third and final leg of the day; following a ZZZ-ZZZ7 turn. It was our second day of a three-day trip and we felt reasonably alert. If we had to divert to ZZZ2; I suspect we would have been close to timing out in our block time; from a passenger standpoint; ZZZ2 made a lot of sense with the ability to re-crew in a base. By the time we blocked in ZZZ1 we had completed 7:30 actual flight time. I know I was tired at the end of the day. Time compression in ZZZ between second and third leg.1. The flight plan for our final leg was not yet available for downloading and consideration before top of descent ZZZ7-ZZZ (leg #2). Flight planning on the ground felt very time compressed.2. We were switching aircraft in ZZZ.3. We were supposed to have been boarded crew meals for our second leg (ZZZ7-ZZZ) but for some odd reason; the FO's hot meal was boarded and I was offered a hodge-podge of a snack box; beef jerky; a cookie; three dried apricots and a packet of honey. I snacked on that offering but needed to find a real meal back in ZZZ between flights.4. Please appreciate the 64 minutes on the ground is from parking brake set on Flight number; (inbound flight); complete the parking checklist; collect our belongings;  traipse over to a different gate (thankfully; the gates were close); download and review: Flight Number's OFP; NOTAMs; and aircraft maintenance and history; review weather on WSI iPad app; pre-flight a new aircraft; load and check the FMC; brief flight attendants especially on the weather conditions; receive an ATC clearance; departure brief between pilots; accomplish both the pre-flight checklist and before push checklist; and then release the parking brake for push-back.Given the lower ceilings and reduced visibility with snow-rain mix and strong direct gusty crosswinds in the TAF I felt it prudent to add contingency fuel. I called our dispatcher at the gate in ZZZ and we agreed to add approximately 30 minutes of fuel; specifically; 3;000 pounds. I had hoped that our dispatcher was cognizant the conditions forecast in ZZZ1 warranted more consideration than a milk-run; day; VFR landing; but truthfully; I had a whisper of uneasy misgivings. Perhaps I felt this was the fuel plan SABRE popped out and there could have been more... more human QA to it... perhaps. Then again; maybe it was nothing... yet the voice in the back of my mind wasn't letting up. Something felt unsettled. Was our dispatcher a little susceptible to Automation and Anchoring Bias... was our dispatcher's Situational Awareness appropriately elevated? Was her Review/Monitor/Predict loop firing on all cylinders? I decided: 'I'll set it aside for now--relax; captain--it's probably nothing.' (spoiler alert: it turned out to be nothing but the ambiguity of whether it was or not; before and during the flight was distracting.)I do not have the ATIS but I did reconstruct the conditions from a historical AWOS archive01 XA:51Z: 330/19G26 6SM -RASN BR BKN009 OVC016 02/01 A29.60 PK WND 3303301 XB:51Z: 330/18G27 3SM -SN BR BKN008 OVC013 02/01 A29.61 PK WND 3203201 XC:06Z: 330/16G29 3SM -SN BR BKN010 OVC015 02/00 A29.61 PK WND 3202901 XC:14Z: 320/16G24 2-1/2SM -SN BR BKN008 OVC 013 02/00 A29.61 PK WND 3202901 XC:23Z: 320/14G28 1-3/4SM -SN BR OVC010 01/00 A29.61 PK WND 3202901 XC:30Z: 330/18G22 1-3/4SM -SN BR BKN008 OVC012 01/00 A 29.61 PK WND 32029The ATIS stated ILS RWY XXL and RCC (Runway Condition Code) 5/5/5 at XJ:00Z; XXR/YYL and XY/YX CLSD; and variousCLSD taxiways. The RCC time stamp of XJ:Z caught my attention as being roughly 16+ hours old.[Aircraft type] landing crosswind component 'guidelines' in the Flight Manual Limitations Chapter:RCC 5 and 6: 40 knotsRCC 4: 35 knotsRCC 3: 25 knots'NOTE: The crosswind guidelines presented...... The use of these guidelines should be based on the current weather conditions and thepilot's ability and experience level.'Even with the recent uptick in flying the overwhelming majority of us are feeling 'rusty'. Generally; with my XX+ years flying experience it seems to come back fairly quickly but I definitely don't feel the same high level of finesse as I did a year ago. I'm aware of it; very aware. I'm working diligently to trap the errors and as minor as they seem there are more of them.Actively seeking and countering threats; setting the right tone on the flight deck; and ensuring we are working well with dispatch these are some of the best tools we have. Overconfidence bias especially in challenging conditions while none of us are flying as much as we usually do is probably at the top of the list. Going the extra step of resolving seemingly small ambiguities seems especially appropriate right now. Plan continuation bias; expectancy bias; and optimism bias creep into the mix a little more insidiously than usual. The ever-present threat of complacency has absolutely not waned. I wonder is Dispatch in the same boat? I suspect so. I want to be cognizant and understanding of that likelihood--we are a team and we need to lift each other up.A little over an hour prior to touchdown we began planning our ILS runway XX approach and landing with the most current conditions at the time. We reviewed the NOTAMs; assiduously marking up the myriad of closed taxiways on our -9 pages. We pulled landing performance data and reviewed it intently. With the strong direct and gusty crosswinds we might have preferred a flaps 40 landing on Runway YX but it was closed.I felt the RCC 5/5/5 at XJ:00Z (16+ hours old) was a remnant and if we just encouraged dispatch to make a call to ZZZ1 Tower; we could get something much more useful; more akin to an hourly observation. Actively countering the ambiguity of a very stale RCC given the worsening weather conditions. Making allowance that Dispatch is planning and monitoring somewhere between several and a small slew of flights they aren't going to catch everything. The ACARS reply from 'X Dispatch' for an updated RCC:'ZZZ1 CITY OPS SAYS 5/5/5.THEY WON'T UPDATE THE NOTAM/FICON UNTIL THERE IS SOMETHING SIGNIFICANT TO UPDATE.'Ambiguity not resolved. Concern we were being led down a path... heightened.With time for more nuanced decision points running out; I replied to X Dispatch:'Name; JUST WANT US ALL TO HAVE THE SAME UNDERSTANDING ABOUT HOW CRITICAL I VIEW A CURRENT AND ACCURATE FICON* WITH THE GUSTY DIRECT CROSSWIND TEMP/DP 02/01... I WILL NOT ATTEMPT A LANDING WITHOUT IT. IS THE 5/5/5 FROM XJ:00Z OR HAVE THEY MEASURED IT MORE RECENTLY... I WILL NOT ALLOW A GREEN BAY OFF THE ENDCOMPLACENCY FROM ZZZ1 CITY OPS TO SUFFICE. PLS INFO FODM OF THIS'(*FICON; I should have used 'RCC' instead)X Dispatch reply:'OKAY.I GOT THE [Flight Operations Manager] IN ON A CALL TO ZZZ1 TOWER. FODM IS UP TO SPEED ON THE CONCERN. THEY REPORTED: RWY XXL AT XS:54Z. 5/5/5. 100 PCT WET.AGAIN; THEY DO NOT ANTICIPATE TO UPDATE UNLESS THERE IS AN ACCUMULATION ON THE RUNWAY OR ANOTHER CHANGE IN CONDITION.'Did I feel like we were pushing a rope? Yes. Yes; I did. I felt like we were being dismissed and my confidence in X Dispatch was significantly diminished. I felt like X Dispatch was not proactively leaning forward in the saddle and was content to accept whatever ZZZ1 City Ops said. Rather than feeling supported; rather than feeling like the increased risk was being adequately considered and mitigated; I felt a certain inappropriate nonchalance had insidiously permeated. I feel like Ihad to kick up a ruckus to finally get an RCC 5/5/5 at XC:00Z--as the XS:54Z RCC was still 7-ish hours old... DURING a RASN event. Finally; I feel like the fact that nothing bad happened adds to the confirmation bias that it was much ado about nothing... right up until it's not nothing. And 'Not Nothing' happens in a blazingly fast moment.What could I have done differently and more effectively?I should have called X Dispatch from ZZZ7 on leg #2; asking her to work up our leg #3 early--I could have alleviated the time compression I felt on the ground in ZZZ.In retrospect; I wish I had noted the XJ:00Z RCC from the ATIS available in either FD Pro X or just pulled the ZZZ1 ATIS on ACARS before pushing and added resolving the stale RCC to the fuel increase phone call with X Dispatch.I should have used 'X' words in the ACARS messages with dispatch to convey the level of my unease.I should have started descent planning and landing in those conditions at Top of Climb (TOC) to allow more time to get 'the ball rolling'.I should have taken the time to call after the flight; to debrief with our dispatcher... really wish I had done that.Ongoing concerns/questionsX Dispatch:1. How early can I ask for a flight to be planned?2. What fuel contingency plan is appropriate in these meteorological conditions for delayed arrival (E.G.; holding while treating the runway) or the preceding aircraft doesn't clear the runway in a timely manner or a gusty wind event causes an unstabilized approach condition? To name but a few possibilities...3. What could I have done differently from X Dispatch's perspective? I would like the feedback to make me a better Captain.ATC:1. How long before an RCC gets updated? Is there an upper number of hours? 2 hours? 36 hours?2. In these particular conditions of strong gusty crosswinds and rain snow mix; what is an appropriate update interval to give us 'end-users' a reasonable level of confidence in the data?3. How are RCCs actually determined?I am going to end this unusual report with a few words from a recently would-have-been furloughed-but-took-advantage-of-voluntary-separation-program and much-liked coworker. It's important to recognize that Name was an administrative co-worker. He's not a pilot himself but he certainly recognized how important his part in the team mattered. We could all profit from his example. 'I made it my goal to make sure every pilot left the flight planning area with a clear head. No matter what issue they had coming in the door; when they went out to fly that issue was taken care of or they knew that I would do my best to take care of it and follow up with them on itsoutcome. I did not want to be the one to cause a distraction. I was proud to be the one who cleaned up the distractions.''...cleaned up distractions' ... Indeed.

column121: After landing on Runway 31 we exited at taxiway Tango. We told Ground Control we were going to gate. Ground Control instructed us to 'turn left on Bravo; right on Lima; taxi to the gate.' I have a lot of experience operating out of LGA; however; I have not landed there since the new terminal was built. I taxied south on Bravo and I identified taxiway Lima. It was dark and the new terminal is very bright. I made the right turn on Lima and saw gate straight ahead. I taxied toward the gate and suddenly; out of the darkness in front of me I noticed multiple; 2-3 foot tall; UNLIGHTED taxiway edge posts. I immediately stopped the aircraft and was able to make a hard left turn to barely avoid hitting the posts. It immediately became apparent that taxiway Lima is actually on about a 45 degree angle from off of taxiway Bravo vs what I thought was a 90 degree right turn. For whatever reason; there is an UNLIGHTED; 'false island' between Taxiway Lima and the ramp. Due to the conditions of darkness; a very bright new terminal and gate area; and unlighted taxiway edge posts; it was very easy for me to turn right onto taxiway Lima and then focus on taxiing straight ahead to gate right through the 'island.'

column121: I am writing this report due to the potential this type of incident has to distract aircrew; particularly the pilots.   I believe Purser X; was attempting to implement her own personal mask policy with respect to eating and drinking.  Even though I complied with her excessive demands after our first encounter; she immediately escalated the issue and contacted the flight crew (because I asked her name); thereby creating a potential distraction to the flight crew.Summary of events follows:  A couple of minutes after being served a drink; I was actively drinking and had my mask down.  Purser X; came by only a few minutes later and said I had to put my mask up.  I told her I was actively drinking and I had actually just set the cup down.  She said my mask had to be replaced between each sip.  I identified myself as an employee and told her I disagreed with her interpretation of the policy.  Of note; I have never had a Flight Attendant make such an assertion before.  I told her I was actively drinking and she said; that what I was doing was not allowed and reiterated; I had to put my mask up between sips.  She also immediately threatened to 'Go to the pilots' when I challenged her interpretation. I complied with her dictate; though I believed it to be errant; and put my mask up; dropping it only between sips of my drink thereafter.  Of note; the Flight Attendant deadheading adjacent to me left his mask down for long periods of time while eating and drinking; so it appears he had the same opinion as I did.  Afterwards; when she passed back by; I asked her if she would give me her name as I felt I needed to report this incident; since she threatened to go to the pilots and I considered her interpretation of the policy to be errant.  She refused to give me her name and said she was ' Going to the pilots' now; because I asked her name.   If Airline X intended her rule to be the standard; then I'm certain Airline X would specifically state that mask must be replaced between sips and bites as opposed to actively drinking or eating.  I reread the policy and I still believe her interpretation is errant.  I also checked with the ZZZ Chief Pilot office and they also believe there is nothing to support her interpretation of the mask policy.In summary; I believe her actions; specifically developing her own policy and her abrasive engagement has the high potential of creating additional conflicts with passengers and unnecessary distractions to the cockpit.

column121: On a calm clear day taking off behind an A319 with winglets we were cleared for takeoff just as they rotated. We were fairly heavy with tanker fuel so we rotated at about the same point down the runway. Between 500-800 ft. AGL we began to quickly bank to the right and ended up at approximately 50 degrees of bank. I immediately unloaded the aircraft with nose down force while continuously increasing left aileron. I pushed the thrust levers into APR thrust and turned on the Continuous Ignition as well during this maneuver. We recovered about 5-8 seconds after initial indication; notified ATC; and continued on without incident. I also checked with our flight attendants to verify that no one was injured and she said that no one seemed to notice. No aircraft damage was found.Calm air; heavy aircraft; and close separation.

I began to execute the memory items procedure for such an event but that procedure was interrupted when we realized there was no ABO (Aviator's Breathing Oxygen) available for use. Captain asked ATC to descend to lower altitude and I had asked the mechanic to bring me an oxygen bottle from the back; which I used. When we initiated the descent we had determined that cabin altitude was controllable.At FL360 we had experienced a Master Caution indicating a wing body overheat. We complied with the appropriate procedures per the QRH. About 20 minutes later; we received another alert; this time for CABIN ALT high. I began to execute the memory items procedure for such an event but that procedure was interrupted when we realized there was no ABO available for use. When we came to the pre-flight portion of the checklist; I pushed the oxygen test button on the FO (First Officer) side mask; and remember hearing a sound but I do not remember looking at the Oxygen Quantity Indicator like I always do. It is possible that we took off with an appropriate oxygen supply; and that it somehow changed during the flight. It is also possible that we simply took off without an appropriate oxygen supply.Captain asked ATC to descend to lower altitude and I had asked the mechanic to bring me an oxygen bottle from the back; which I used. When we initiated the descent we had determined that cabin altitude was controllable and no further incident had occurred enroute to ZZZ1 thereafter.We understand that the ABO may have been serviced for this particular aircraft. I recommend that every time such a procedure has been performed; that it be noted in the aircraft logbook so that the flight crew are aware. While I certainly would never not do a thorough preliminary pre-flight inspection myself again; if this suggestion is appropriate; I recommend a change to the FOM (Flight Operating Manual) that the preliminary pre-flight procedure be performed by the Captain and the FO.

column121: Arrived at the airport at XA:45. The station representative met us advising he had just received an email further pushing our departure back to XE:00. He also advised they were unsure as to whether there were even parts on hand to repair the aircraft correctly and wondered if it would even depart that day. We settled in the crew rest area to wait and see. At XC:51; I received a call from a Company A representative asking how we felt and if we were still good to fly. They said Maintenance advised they would have the plane fixed in about an hour. We advised we were good to go. I then called Dispatch to advise and keep them in the loop. The Dispatcher emailed us release revision 2. We reviewed it and headed out to the aircraft. As we arrived outside the aircraft; Maintenance was still aboard working on the aircraft. At XD:35; Maintenance finished with the aircraft. We then boarded the aircraft to find it on battery power and the GPU (Ground Power Unit) running but the over voltage warning light indicator on. We flagged down personnel to get a new GPU. At XD:45 the APU (Auxiliary Power Unit) was started. The replacement GPU arrived as the APU completed powering up. We then began our preflight. At XE:20; the preflight was finished. At XE:35; Maintenance finished the logbook and maintenance brief. We then blocked out. During this time I became aware of Company A Maintenance Control pressuring the on-site Company B maintenance personnel to 'line out' the other maintenance personnel's write-up stating 'Undocumented speed tape found concealing stripped and unsecured mounting screw to extruded MCD (Main Cabin Door) Manual Vent Door Drive (Pressure Vessel) cover panel'. This was found in Aircraft X's logbook. Maintenance Control wanted this done so as not to draw scrutiny to it by the FAA. Thankfully and appreciatively the Company B Mechanic refused to assist in this cover-up.This is the consistent behavior I have observed from the pressure Company C exerts on this operation to dispatch the aircraft on time at all costs. In the past several years I have submitted safety reports and FCRs (Flight Crew Reports) observing willful and wanton disregard of DDG (Dispatch Deviation Guide) procedures plainly written out. I've listened to Maintenance Control; on speakerphone; tell an on-site mechanic to 'Write whatever the hell makes the pilot happy to get that damn thing out of there.' I've had Maintenance Control denigrate me for not immediately pulling back into the gate with a problem but instead I followed procedure and called Dispatch for a three-way call with the problem. I've observed on numerous occasions and numerous stations Company B mechanics back-dooring the fuel sheets to make the numbers work instead of obtaining the fuel density to compute the numbers correctly to check the accuracy of the fueling process. I've had Company B mechanics on my jump seat share experiences of Maintenance Control telling them to check good" a system without actually testing the system. Thankfully as well; those mechanics told Maintenance Control their tickets were more important to them than their jobs. Both of those mechanics have since left Company B for more ethical workplace environments.My observation is the attitude in Maintenance Control is a mixture of arrogance and fear-driven to kowtow to this pressure. The pressure is passed down the chain from Company C to the executive level to the middle managers to the line supervisors to the line workers. This culture is a very dangerous one. It severely erodes the necessary safety and trust in the process required for it to work as it is designed. I have personally had so many of these instances where I have found incorrectly complied with DDG procedures both by blatant disregard and ignorance. I and several of my colleagues have experienced an extreme increase in time and concern when reviewing the log and maintenance procedures. I personally am not trained as a mechanic. The amount of items that we can see and have found greatly concerns us. Our concern is the amount of Maintenance egregious violations and errors we can see are so numerous and regular; how safe; complete; and compliant is the work; like the heavy checks and line maintenance behind the panels and cowlings that we cannot see. Our fear is this is going to lead to injuries; loss of life; and more aircraft damage and hull losses. The solution is straight forward and already established. Enforce strict adherence to maintaining the aircraft and equipment as directed by our FAA-approved maintenance program."

The hotel hands out a form which in part states that if you are caught outside your allowed radius of operation; your airline may lose its right to fly to this Country. The same rule applies to not having the tracking system on arrive or not submitting a daily health check.Cause - Lack of oversight and education from the inflight group.  Lack of following procedures from FA group.  I have to wonder if this important item is missed; what else are they missing?Each DH crew should be met at the gate by an in-flight Supervisor who ensures that the app is installed and a health check complete. column123: New on the aircraft; I had briefed the Captain I wanted to hand fly the aircraft; which he agreed was a good idea. We departed ZZZ on XXL and was cleared on the ZZZZZ1 4 RNAV SID.  In our turn towards ZZZZZ1 we received clearance to ZZZZZ2 on frequency XYA.B. When we checked in to XYZ.Z we received a clearance to FL230 and to fly direct to ZZZZZ. ZZZZZ is not on the SID or depicted anywhere on the SID. The Captain was unfamiliar but I was because I flew the same Flight the day before and we received the same clearance. I believe I spelt the fix out to the Captain and asked if I should I put the Autopilot on; which he responded 'no it's okay'. Just as he was typing it in and he executed it we heard the altitude alert caution and we were at 23;580 feet. I quickly reacted and proceeded back towards FL230 at the same time the Captain called ATC and stated 'Aircraft X at FL240'. ATC then cleared us to FL310 or FL330. column121: Aircraft X.  Ground Service personal brought Hazardous Cargo paperwork to the cockpit about dry ice being loaded in the aft cargo compartment and live animals being loaded in the forward cargo compartment.Normally live animals are loaded in the aft or bulk cargo compartments which are heated by engine bleed air. If carrying animals in the aft cargo compartments we make sure the cargo heat switches are in the high position which will warm and maintain the compartment temperature between 65F and 75F.  Due to the dry ice being loaded in the aft we are not allowed to have animals and dry ice in the same compartment.I was told by the ground service worker that they load live animals in the forward cargo compartment and do this regularly because the forward cargo compartment is heated. I explained that it is heated with cabin air that has flowed through the E & E compartments equipment ventilation system to cool the electronics and exhausted into the forward cargo compartment. We have no way of knowing what the temperature is in the forward cargo compartment is and no way of knowing if it is suitable for live animals.  We do have aft and bulk cargo compartment temperature indications on our air synoptic located in the cockpit. I asked Ground Personnel to swap the locations of the dry ice and live animals so that the animals could be kept warm for the flight in the aft cargo compartment.  I was told that this would be difficult to do because the dry ice would need to be moved to another canister and this would take time.  I asked to speak with the Ramp Supervisor and I spoke with the Station Manager. She explained that their ROM (Ramp Operations Manual) authorizes the loading of live animals in the Forward Cargo Compartment of the 777.  I explained that our Aircraft Operations Manual authorizes the loading of live animals in our aft or bulk cargo compartments only.  She explained that they have done this before and that I was not the first Captain to question this practice.I called the Dispatcher for the flight and discussed the situation with her thinking that she had seen this situation before and she had not.  She did some investigation and spoke with a mechanic and he told her that the forward cargo was heated. I explained to her what our manual stated and where live animals were to be transported.  The Station Manager directed the ramp personal to move the dry ice to the forward cargo compartment and move the live animals to the aft cargo compartment as per our operating manual.  I thanked her for her help and cooperation and explained that both of our manuals not being in agreement is a problem and that I would write this up so that we can get this discrepancy rectified so that we are all on the same page. The Ramp Operating Manual and the Aircraft Operating Manual not being in agreement on where live animals are to be transported caused a waste of time and effort.  Also; the animal's lives might have been in danger if the temperature was too low for the extended period of time of this flight. Both manuals (Ramp Operating Manual and Aircraft Operating manual) being in agreement would alleviate this problem.  Ramp Services and Flight [Operations] should get together and clarify the procedures for this subject.

At the beginning of the approach we had a tailwind and the descent angle of the approach caused us to be a little fast starting the approach. As the pilot monitoring I should have caught this issue sooner and brought it to the attention of the PF (Pilot Flying). Because of the speed the PF disconnected the autopilot/auto throttles and slowed the plane to the proper approach speed. During the turn onto final the PF was visual with the runway and let the nose drop which caused a momentary don't sink. He corrected and the warning went away. Still with the airport visual he tried to correct on the VASI and received another momentary don't sink call at around 700 ft. We continued the approach and the landing was normal. I don't have anything to add for [this report].I have learned many lessons from this very short flight. I haven't had much ZZZ experience and my FO (First Officer) who was PF has had very little. We tried to mitigate the possible issues by having a slow cruise speed of 210 kts. and trying to get ready for the approach early. We briefed the 3.4 GP and felt we were in a good position for the approach. With the unfamiliarity of the situation and the weather in ZZZ this day I missed the strong tailwind that was making our situation worse. This put us behind and we had to play catch up. It was turbulent the whole flight and when he disconnected the AP/AT my [situational awareness] went down because I was worried about his flight path at that time. As I look back at the event and if I could do this again I would have us discontinue the approach early and come around to try again. Once we continued and got out of the [weather] and had the runway visually climbing back into it in that terrain did not seem the safest option. But if we had bailed early it would have made the situation easier the second time.

column121: While flying into Burbank at night PF (Pilot Flying) / PIC (Pilot-in-Command) elected to do visual to [Runway] 15. Clearance was granted around JANNY [and] PF took a course that meant we would intercept the final approach course from the left of centerline. PM (Pilot Monitoring) noted that we were left of centerline and that there was terrain in the area. We crossed over the ridge line at the standard 5;500 ft. but thereafter while still left of centerline the PF started a descent. PM had terrain display up on MFD and was watching; there was never a yellow or red terrain ahead of the aircraft at anytime. Yet PM noticed that the radio altimeter was showing a reading while still left of centerline. The radio altimeter reading went below 1;000 ft. and got to around 800 ft. The PM called out the altitudes as soon as they were decreasing below 1;000 ft. and the PF took evasive action by disconnecting the auto pilot and stopping the descent. Almost immediately after the radio altimeter reading went away and we continued a normal descent to landing on [Runway] 15. Taking a visual to [Runway] 15 at night is unnecessarily risky. With margins very tight on the left side of the approach course; situational awareness is reduced at night. The benefits certainly do not outweigh the risks. We never received a GPWS yet we came within below 1;000 ft. of terrain on around an 8 mile final. It is easy to become complacent with your surroundings when you can not see them; so don't bother putting yourself in this situation... The company needs to put into writing that visuals to [Runway] 15 should not be allowed at night. As PM I should have called an immediate go-around the second I saw the radio altimeter go below 1;000 ft.

column121: We had walked into the hanger that morning and found out that we were doing an engine change. The engine had already been removed and needed to be installed. column123: On DATE on first shift at the ZZZ maintenance hangar; the right engine of aircraft X was being installed by the first shift maintenance crew. The individuals who performed and assisted in the task and include; myself (NAME2 RII Inspector); NAME (Maintenance Supervisor); NAME1 (Maintenance Supervisor); NAME3 (Maintenance Lead); NAME4 (Maintenance Technician); NAME5 (Maintenance Technician); NAME6 (Maintenance Technician); and NAME7 (Maintenance Technician). NAME8; Assistance Chief Inspector was also a witness to some portions of the task being performed. During the installation of the right engine the upper trans cowling 443AT; the lower trans cowling 443AB; and the upper and lower rear thrust reverser hinge line fairings 443BT and 443BB were damaged. Also there was damage to the forward engine mount on the pylon side. NAME (Maintenance Supervisor) was taking the lead on the job and operating the heavy duty forklift. Of the employees performing the task NAME had the most experience in doing this specific engine CF34-8C5 installation. NAME6 was the only technician besides NAME who had performed the specific installation task before and he had only performed it one time. Before the job started there was a safety meeting to discuss the possible dangers of the job. Everyone was assigned a position on the lifts; on the aircraft pylon; or on the ground. NAME8 present at the safety meeting and shortly thereafter I saw him from a distance talking to NAME about the task giving him some advice on how to install the engine and to make sure the task was followed exactly. Since I was on the lift and carrying out other duties I did not hear much of the conversation but it seemed more like an argument. NAME8 left the job site and we began to hoist the engine in place. NAME directed the mechanics to install the forward engine mount first because it was easier. NAME mentioned to us all that he had done at least five successful engine changes this way with no issues. At this point no one made an objection this. The two mechanics on the engine pylon; NAME4 and NAME5 aligned the forward engine thrust mount into place and torqued and safetied the nuts and bolts. They then attempted to align and fit into place the aft thrust mount. After a few minutes of trying the aft thrust mount would not fit into place. At that point myself and NAME6 double checked the manual instructions which we had on hand on the lift. We mentioned to all that the aft thrust mount should have been installed first according to the instructions the manual laid out. NAME stated that it should not matter and they proceeded to try again to fit the aft thrust mount into place. NAME3 kept saying that he thought some thing was binding where he was in the front side of the engine pylon. He mentioned this several times but because we were all in different positions around the engine we could not see was he was talking about. NAME3 asked NAME specifically if the panel 443BT is supposed to come off because it seemed like it was in the way. NAME replied that he had never seen that panel come off in his experience. They proceeded for another few minutes and then decided to remove the engine from the aircraft and put it on the stand to double check if anything was wrong with the engine mounts on the engine side. After the engine was secured on the stand. We found the above mentioned aircraft damage. A few minutes after the damage was discovered we did some more research. We found that the technicians that removed the engine the day before on second shift failed to remove panels 443BT and 443BB that are specifically mentioned in the removal task. We believe that this was the cause of the damage to the aircraft. With the panels installed there was not enough room to position the engine in place correctly. As an R.I.I. I rejected the installation in the maintenance software program and the maintenance staff asked for engineering relief for the damage. NAME then refused to sign the AMM task even though he took the lead on the job and operated the engine lift thereby performing undocumented maintenance on the aircraft.There were many factors that contributed to this incident. One was a serious lack of experience with this specific task. At other airlines they have an engine installation and removal team the handles all engine changes because of the complexity of the task and the teamwork it takes to do the job with five or more individuals. Most of the tasks frequently performed at ZZZ are done individually or with one helper. Only one technician on the job had performed the task more than one time. The complexity of the task meant that all involved had to read and understand a greater amount of technical data in a short period of time. Also the order of installation instructions were not followed because the most experienced technician claimed it was easier to perform the instructions out of order safely. Human factors also was a cause of this incident. The supervisor taking the lead on the job; NAME; has a reputation at ZZZ for being cocky and having a know it all 'one up you' personality. I have noticed that he has a condescending leadership style and likes to be condescending to his employees to make himself look good. Rather than train his people and build his employees up he would rather tear them down to make himself look better. I have been at Company almost six years and unfortunately Company management is full of people like NAME. I believe this creates a work environment that is intimidating and detrimental to open communication. People like NAME create a 'shame' environment where people are afraid to speak up when something is done wrong or doesn't look right to them. This creates and enhances human error.  Failure to read and understand the entire task and remove all the panels on the list for the removal task CRJ 900 AMM 71-00-00-000-801-A02-PSA led to the 2nd shift mechanics failing to actually remove the required panels. Failure to follow the installation order of specified steps in the task may have led to error also.More training by experienced technicians on more complex and team oriented task to train inexperienced technicians. In the manuals special notes to identify where the order of installation is a must and cannot be deviated from.(example: Note - Aft Thrust mount MUST BE INSTALLED prior to forward engine mount to avoid damage to aircraft and engine.) Better Leadership training for Supervisors with less than 3 years experience to avoid the cocky and condescending 'know it all' leadership culture. Make Maintenance Supervision and leadership responsible and accountable for the maintenance they perform on all Company aircraft. No running away and only making the mechanics on the floor sign something off when the job is not done right and something is broken.

By this time I had hollered for the FLM to come down and explain if they knew what was going on; and it was then I was told that ZZZ2 [Center] was ATC-0. We pulled up the approach plate at ZZZ [Airport] and I told Aircraft X to maintain 110 to not enter approach's airspace and gave the aircraft I think XYZ.AB to switch over.  Not two minutes later; ZZZ2 [Center] comes back up and helps me with necessitating the hand-off.  Not at any time was anyone working traffic aware of this issue with ZZZ2 [Center].  After this aircraft handling was done; I called Area B controllers and asked if they knew about the ZZZ2 [Center] Zero event and they said no that they had not heard anything.  Area B also is adjacent to ZZZ2 [Center] airspace.Later the FLM came back down to let us know the ZZZ [Approach] lines were back up and running.  This makes this Zero event even more frustrating to us in Area A since the routing and altitude that we give ZZZ2 [Center] aircraft going to ZZZ1 Approach requires us to call ZZZ Approach for a Point out.  So during this Zero event; we had no clue that we were actually in it; and then if we did know we would have had to do extra work just to get the procedure to work with ZZZ Approach.Another part of this is that the controller on RX1 never knew about this event as well because he had a ZZZ [Airport] departure at FL230 during this time as well; and according to the ATC-0 procedures we are to Radar Identify the aircraft when they come over to us.  I cannot be sure that this was done.  This aircraft... I don't recall the numbers or where he was headed.   Communication is a big deal in what we do.  It is highly irresponsible to not be told about something as important as an ATC-0 event in the facility.  All I needed was to know was who and when and we could have handled this situation the correct way.  We have routing for this exact situation; we have the procedures posted in the area; but if no one tells me what is happening then this type of event will continue to happen.

column121: In the upwind after VFR departure; Aircraft X advised that he wanted to return to the field. I immediately asked if he needed any help and he replied no. I told him to make left traffic. As he didn't indicate an [urgent problem]; I treated him like a regular aircraft who decided to return to the field. We get this all the time for all sorts of reasons. It was nothing out of the ordinary at that point. He was going to be next to land just as soon as I departed the waiting IFR Aircraft Y. In order to depart Aircraft Y I had to first turn two pattern aircraft out of the way early. As soon as the second aircraft - a touch-and-go aircraft- passed the threshold; I told Aircraft Y to LUAW (Line Up and Wait); which he read back and did. I informed Aircraft X (who at this point was approaching the midfield left downwind) that I would give him a base turn and landing in just a moment as traffic was in position. He again acknowledged without issue. I then told the first aircraft (a stop-and-go aircraft) to turn an early left crosswind when able and waited to tell the second aircraft (a touch-and-go aircraft) the same once he was safely established in the upwind. At that point; Aircraft X suddenly announced that he was turning base right now and had to land. I acknowledged the base turn and immediately told the upwind [touch-and-go aircraft] to start his early crosswind now; which he did and then went right to the Aircraft Y and cleared him for 'immediate' takeoff; which he didn't even acknowledge. I asked Aircraft Y if he'd started his roll; knowing Aircraft X was essentially now in a short approach. The Aircraft Y responded by saying he was 'holding position.' At this point I knew he hadn't been paying attention and there was no moving him out of the way in time. I told Aircraft Y to cancel his takeoff clearance and hold in position because any movement would have increased the likelihood of his being in the way of the inbound behind him. He acknowledged; 'hold position.' I then went right to Aircraft X and advised that I couldn't give a landing clearance because traffic was on the runway. He acknowledged but repeated that he had engine trouble and was coming in to land. I gave him the traffic on the runway and informed him that Aircraft Y wasn't moving. He responded that he would side-step around the jet and land in front of it. I repeated again to Aircraft Y to hold position and informed the pilot what was happening to help his situational awareness; telling him that a 'Aircraft X' would be coming around to land on the runway in front of him. He acknowledged and didn't move. Aircraft X landed without further incident and rolled out to the taxiway exit where he was taxied by Ground Control and met by Operations vehicles. If a pilot's aircraft indicates any sort of malfunction whatsoever on takeoff that prompts a request to return to the field; it should be required that the controller be made aware of this for priority and for a sterile runway. Otherwise we will just fit them right back into the pattern and treat them as any other inbound. This return to the field is a very common occurrence for all sorts of [non-priority] reasons. Barriers which might serve to deter pilots from declaring [urgency] or requesting priority should be removed so they can feel free to request the help they might need without repercussions. Additionally; changes should be made on both the controller and pilot sides in the event neither has time to [advise ATC]. When seconds allow for only the transmission of control instruction to prevent collision; neither party should be held liable for not having wasted precious time saying pointless words in that moment. The actions being taken alone speak to the [situation] without having to necessarily say as much.

column121: Aircraft X; ZZZZ-ZZZ1; Captain; First Officer; International Relief Officer; and 3 747 qualified ACMs. FO (First Officer) was Pilot Flying shortly after reaching cruise altitude the EICAS message 'Yaw Damper LWR' appeared. In a very brief time after; approximately 5 seconds; more messages began appearing; accompanied by numerous status messages. Ultimately; over the period of about 10 minutes 6 EICAS messages and 20 status messages appeared. They included faults on numerous unrelated systems--environmental; fuel; flight controls; hydraulic; navigation. I called the IRO (International Relief Officer) into the flight deck; ensured the FO focused on flying the aircraft; and began discussing the issues with the IRO. The IRO called one of the ACMs to the cockpit; who is a simulator instructor on the aircraft; and initiated a satellite call with Flight Control; who; in turn; connected us to countless resources on the ground. While the IRO and ACM were working on the situation with Maintenance Control; the FO and I began working on selecting places to land in case we couldn't resolve the issues. Options included ZZZZ2 (>500 miles in front of us); ZZZZ3 (288 miles ahead); and ZZZZ (>300 miles behind). While discussing these options; the remaining two ACMs requested to go down to the main cargo deck to check for any further evidence; which I allowed. They shortly came back and reported the odor of electrical smoke; but no visible signs of smoke. We decided to divert to ZZZZ2; declared 'Pan' with ZZZZ1 Control and proceeded direct. Many options for the arrival were discussed; including what checklists to run; what systems may or may not be available upon landing (Ground spoilers? Thrust reverse? Autobrakes? Anti-skid? Etc.). We discussed dumping fuel; but were unsure if that would even work; or from which tanks the fuel would come if it did work. We chose not to dump but to land overweight. As ACARS Flight Deck Performance was unavailable; Flight Control did a live calculation and provided us with landing distances for landing at 720;000 lbs. without thrust reverse or autobrakes. (The number; 5;800 feet; proved to be very accurate.) Now primarily focused on arrival and landing; we configured the aircraft slowly and very early; turning the autopilot off after each configuration change to ensure that we had control of the aircraft. This all led to an otherwise uneventful visual approach and landing on Runway XX in ZZZZ2. I manually deployed the spoilers on touchdown; the FO extended the thrust reverse levers (the levers fully extended; but the reversers did not deploy) and applied maximum manual braking. We stopped on the runway to allow the fire department to analyze the aircraft and brakes for fire indications; which were reported as negative. We opted to then taxi off of the runway and into a large taxiway intersection (XX and YY Taxiways) to allow access to the aircraft from all angles. We calculated brake energy and cooling requirements; and monitored the brake temperatures on the synoptic page. Because our calculations put us on the edge of the warning zone for fuse plug melting; we sat and did not set the parking brake and called for towing. Normal after landing and shutdown procedures were accomplished. The tow took approximately an hour to complete; during which the brakes cooled back to normal temperatures without any damage. There were many people and agencies involved; the aircrew; Flight Control; Maintenance Control; SME's; ZZZZ2 Gateway; and others; all of whom were ready on a moment's notice; helped tremendously; and performed their roles flawlessly. Thank you to all.
column123: After a normal climb to Flight Level 350 I began to exit my flight station when I heard the Captain call attention to the EICAS which at the time showed; I believe; two amber advisory messages; >YAW DAMPER LWR and RUD RATIO SNGL. Almost immediately thereafter several other EICAS advisory messages appeared on the primary EICAS screen along with a full page of status messages on the secondary EICAS screen. I immediately took my place back at the FO (First Officer) station and was advised by the Captain to resume Pilot Flying duties along with communication with ATC. Our IRO (International Relief Officer) was advised by the Captain to begin a patch with dispatch and begin troubleshooting measures with maintenance control. Among the three jump seating crew members was an instructor pilot who was also summoned to the flight deck for assistance. During this trouble shooting period it was determined that multiple systems including flight controls; hydraulics; pneumatic's and navigation equipment were all seriously degraded from normal. Also; it was decided that the two remaining jump seaters should go and inspect the main deck. Those crew members reported that no smoke was visible however a distinct electrical burning odor was present towards the front of the main deck. A diversion to ZZZZ2; including an overweight landing was agreed upon following all operating crew members vote. Clearance to ZZZZ2 was obtained with ZZZZ1 Radar and thus we began our diversion. I requested with ZZZZ1 a descent to FL250 so as to reduce the total time required to descend from altitude yet still provide for adequate differential pressure in case the need for equipment cooling override mode was required. After each initial flap configuration change we agreed upon disconnecting the autopilot momentarily to check flight control effectiveness. I found the aircraft to exhibit normal flying characteristics though slight porpoising occurred while on final approach as it was also discovered that the aircraft's right side glide slope was inoperable. I then disconnected the autopilot and hand flew the remainder of the approach to landing. During this landing it was pre briefed that the Captain would manually deploy the speed brakes and I would manually apply brakes as the auto deploy functions for both were disabled. I found the aircraft to have very effective stopping power as we stopped prior to the [Taxiway] XX high speed turn off. We remained on the runway with the parking break off while emergency vehicles inspected the fuselage and brakes for possible fire. Once it was determined that no visible fire was present we taxied clear of the runway onto a very large intersection at XX so that fire vehicles could more easily access the landing gear area if needed. We again held manual brakes only and did not set the parking brake during this wait for ground tow as our brake temperatures slowly climbed to a 6 on several indicators. After about an hour after landing we were towed to our parking gate. Incidentally; it was pointed out later on by the Captain that he was very quickly able to determine a possible diversionary landing site by his use of the 'Surface Conditions' line select item in the Weather Layers feature of our Jeppesen Flight Deck Pro app. Its simple and very intuitive red vs. green color gradation made the direction to turn from altitude a quick one; much quicker than having to dial up various ATIS frequencies. Perhaps this method could be stressed somewhat more during training? It was a great way to get a big weather picture of our surrounding area during an intense information overload situation.

column121: The purpose of this report is to point out a possible safety issue in regards to the no fly zones going to South America. Flying over South America there are two no fly zones; one in the Peruvian Airspace and the second one extends from south of Peru across the Andes mountains all the way down to the south of Chile. Those areas where depicted in our old paper navigational charts and every no fly zones had waypoints. Those waypoints where depicted; for example the no fly zone over Peruvian airspace had the following waypoints depicted on the old paper navigational chart as follows: NFZ01; NFZ02; etc.; up to NFZ06. Those way points are still on our Nav (Navigation) Database and can be still used for safety awareness by building the no fly zones on the secondary flight plan. When we switch to Electronic Flight Bag you can still see the no fly zones but the way points are taken away. Based on my experience; about 80% of the times that we fly to South America; the iPad loses his own ship due to lack of signal and you cannot use the electronic chart for reference to make sure that you are not getting over any of the no fly zones; especially when we are deviating from weather. The only place that we can find those no fly zones way points is in the diversion guide page XX. I always put those way points on the secondary flight plan so I can see them on the Nav Display just in case we have to deviate due to weather and the iPad loose the signal. On my last flight to Lima we had to deviate due to weather over the shore line and because we had those no fly zones on the secondary flight plan; we were able to stay away from that area. I been flying into South America for over XX years in different fleets and we always had use that procedure and the information was everywhere. Now we have lost that information when we switch from paper to electronic nav charts. We also are getting new pilots from other bases that never been in those routes before and the majority are not even aware of those way points; and have no clue how to find them and use them. I believe that in the name of safety; those way points should be inserted into the electronic navigational charts and the company should provide more information about those way points.If you need any additional information please don't hesitate to contact me.Thank you for your time and attention to towards this matter.Experience flying this division.As I mentioned before; I believe that in the name of safety; those way points should be inserted into the electronic navigational charts and the company should provide more information about those way points.

column121: Incident / Discovery: Maintenance work light / flash light found in the the nose landing gear wheel well which resulted in an air return of the aircraft.Aircraft location: Aircraft X B737-800 was located in the parking area at ZZZ Airport.Work Conditions: Night time; outside; no spot lighting or ambient lighting. Sky conditions clear. Temperature 30(s) Fahrenheit.On the night; Coworker and I were assigned to troubleshoot log X 'Unable to access APU bite' Per previous log entry of being suspect; I replaced the R735 relay in the J20 box; took us some time to locate the J20 box and the relay because the WDM and IPC were not clear on the exact location. 2-3 hours to locate on aircraft. This junction box is located behind the L/H rear pressure panel of the nose landing gear box structure. However; access was difficult to the box from the nose landing gear area due to the angle of access and aircraft height. In turn; I climbed into the E/E bay with a blue hand light; head lamp and a No. 2 Philips screw driver; maneuvered/positioned myself over the flight deck air supply duct along the left side of the nose wheel box structure to get better access to the J20 cover; Relay 735 and associated cannon plug for troubleshooting purposes. Coworker was in support from the nose landing gear wheel well to hand me various items I needed to work through the access structure.As documented in the log; the relay did not correct the issue so we continued to troubleshoot which required continuous access to the J20 box. I was mainly working from inside the E/E bay; not from the nose landing gear wheel well.As the night progressed and not finding any faults with the physical wiring; we reported to our lead where we were at. Was told that the aircraft is needed for a flight; document where we were at and close up the aircraft.We headed back out to the aircraft. When we got back to Aircraft X; I double checked the APU ECU security; checked the aft cargo bay for equipment and tools; closed the aft cargo bay door. I then proceeded into the E/E bay to secure the J20 box cover and check for security and check for tools and equipment. As I was doing this; Coworker was securing the nose landing gear wheel well pressure panel.After Coworker finished installing the panel; I went inside the flight deck to re-engage two circuit breakers and to pressurize the aircraft for the leak check of the pressure panel. Once pressurized; Lead performed the leak check of the pressure panel. When leak check was satisfactory; I depressurized the aircraft; powered down; closed the main cabin door and pulled the air stairs. Shortly after we met in the vehicle we had and began going over paper work.Coworker and I are somewhat new to avionics and have a lot to learn about the various differences between our fleet types and associated details of each. We are very capable of doing the work but would feel more comfortable to be paired with someone who is well seasoned in the avionics shop. It should be this way for anyone that is new. Since I have been in the shop; I have been paired mainly with inexperienced technicians who are learning the same way as I am; learn as you go. Common sense would dictate to pair a very experienced tech with a inexperienced tech; this promotes growth; development and prevents mistakes.I'm sorry that this unfortunate mistake took place and is an oversight I strive to never let happen; unfortunately it did. I will be much more vigilant in the future about tooling and equipment used for aircraft maintenance to make sure this will never happen on my end again.
column123: My co-worker and I received our assignment to work on the Aircraft X located [in parking]; a remote maintenance area (ZZZ). column121: I experienced a loss of full engine power during initial climbout from RWY 32 at ZZZ. I had the student notify Tower we wanted to return for landing. We were still able to climb and engine was running smoothly so I wanted to keep as low key as possible. When asked by tower we did not request assistance and did not require priority handling. We climbed to approximately 1;000 feet AGL as we entered left downwind. Just past abeam approach end of RWY 32 while on downwind engine experienced further reduction in power without moving throttle. I told Tower we were turning base at that time; added 10 degrees flaps and aimed for the approach end of RWY 32. As we rolled onto final there was a business jet in position for takeoff on the runway. I heard the Tower clear him for an immediate takeoff; then tell him to abort and hold position. The Controller then advised me they could not issue a landing clearance. I responded that I had to land and Controller told me about the jet in position. I replied that I observed the traffic and would maneuver to pass to the right so I would not overfly the jet; and come in around and land in front of him. I flew a few hundred feet to the right at approximately 300 feet AGL; did not fly over the jet and passed well clear of him holding in position. I then slipped the aircraft into the left crosswind; lined up and landed on Runway 32 about 1;500 feet down the runway. The engine was generating enough power to taxi and I utilized Taxiway XX and called ground control when instructed for taxi back to ramp. When I reviewed the event; I believe I incorrectly assumed that the tower controller was providing me priority handling; when in fact the Controller was not fully aware of my situation. I should have just requested priority handling either prior to or as I turned downwind so Controller knew not to have the jet line up and wait on the runway before me.

column121: Change in maintenance procedures after servicing or replacement of parts in the hydraulic systems.I was flying with LCA (name deleted) for my Latin America route qualification; to finish the Captain Upgrade syllabus.   We got a late start because of our gate being occupied by another aircraft experiencing maintenance issues.   Once we received our airplane X and performed all associated preflight flows; briefings; and checklists we pushed about an hour behind schedule.  I noticed that a leaky valve on the Yellow hydraulic system was replaced and a RON check had been performed that morning.  Taxi; take off from runway XX and the initial climb up through FL180 was normal.   Somewhere around FL200 the ECAM flashed a message; too quick for us to see what it was; about 30 seconds later it flashed again; and then another 2-3 times before the ECAM Message stayed displayed; hydraulic Y RSVR LOW LVL.  I was Pilot Flying; and called for ECAM actions.  LCA (name deleted) performed the ECAM actions and then consulted the COM for further instruction.  At this time we were nearing our cruise altitude of FL330.  I remained in control of the aircraft and ATC communications while LCA (name deleted) contacted maintenance through ACARS about our issue.  Dispatch and Maintenance both confirmed that a return back to ZZZ was the best course of action.   I requested a return to ZZZ with ZZZ1 center and stated we had hydraulic issues.   Center Cleared us back to ZZZ via direct ZZZ and the ZZZ Arrival.  The next communication with ZZZ1 I declared an emergency to get services in place for our arrival.   I proceeded to load the MCDU for our return to ZZZ.  LCA (name deleted) kept in communication with Maintenance and Dispatch during this time.  LCA (name deleted) also gave the TEST briefing to the lead Flight Attendant (FA); and made all PA's in both English and Spanish to the passengers.  Once we were established back towards ZZZ and we were caught up on our duties; I briefed the arrival and approach; we both discussed outcomes of the landing to be prepared for anything that may arise with our associated failure.  The loss of the Yellow hydraulic system would require us to bring the airplane to a complete stop on the runway because of the loss of Nose Wheel Steering.  LCA (name deleted) calculated a landing distance assessment; and went through the procedure for an overweight landing.   LCA (name deleted) took over control of the aircraft on the arrival because he has been flying recently and I haven't had a landing in the plane in 3.5 months; My most recent experience was a warm up and PC the week prior.  The arrival; approach; and landing were normal.  We landed and stopped on the runway XX; called for 'flight attendant stations'; Crash fire rescue inspected the exterior of the aircraft; and confirmed no hot spots.  Once given the all clear; the 'remain seated' announcement was made; we completed the landing checklist; shut down both engines with the APU running so the ground crew could hook up and tow the aircraft to the gate.   Once hooked up we were towed to Gate XX where we then deplaned and talked with maintenance about our issue.I believe the RA's functioned abnormally due to their antenna's prolonged exposure to snowy and icy conditions on the runway; taxiway; and ramp at ZZZ airport. I suggest an advisory could be sent out to keep the crews from being startled when this occurs in the conditions explained above. However; remind the aircrews to still comply with the terrain warning; whether it's an erroneous warning or not.

column121: After landing and during rollout on RW (Runway) XXR; we were instructed to 'make left turn if able and hold short of [Runway] XXL; then notify if gate was open'. As PF (Pilot Flying); I had already briefed during approach briefing that we would likely make left turn on [Taxiway] XX then hold short of [Runway] XXL to await further taxi instructions. As we decelerated and approached [Taxiway] XX; we noticed another airplane on Taxiway XY (around [Taxiway] XZ) facing east. We were initially uncertain if it was holding or continuing east so we were going to skip [Taxiway] XX and make next left. ATC stated that they were holding for us; so we made the turn on [Taxiway] XX. As we exited the RW (Runway); the CA (Captain) continued taxiing to cross RW (Runway) XXL even though we had been told to hold short. We were across the hold short lines when I queried him about holding short; but I was late in warning him to avoid the confusion and mistake of going so far. At same time; an airplane had rotated for takeoff on RW (Runway) XXL just prior to our position making it a more serious event. ATC never said anything to us as the event happened or immediately after; so I asked them if we should continue across RW (Runway) XXL. They replied in the affirmative and to contact Ground Control after exiting on other side. At no time did ATC comment on the event. We continued to the gate without further incident.Contributing factors were the confusion about the intention of the aircraft on Taxiway XY near the [Taxiway] XX exit we were instructed to use; the short distance between the parallel runways; and lack of coordinated and deliberate attention to the immediate situation we were in. I failed to give the CA a reminder we had been instructed to hold short of RW (Runway) XXL prior to him crossing the hold short lines. Neither of us confirmed both directions were clear prior to crossing even though it is SOP to do so and we had consistently been doing that up to that point. He said during our debrief he had momentarily looked down at his taxi diagram to confirm location of the potential crossing taxiways we might use before realizing too late we had taxied over the lines. I had also momentarily diverted my attention to try to contact ramp (per ATC's request about our gate availability); while assuming the CA had heard the hold short instructions and would comply. Again; we had already briefed this likelihood of taxi route and necessity of holding short of and eventual crossing of RW (Runway) XXL during the arrival/approach briefing during descent into ZZZ area. I had never received a query from ATC about gate availability in ZZZ; even though it's common procedure at other airports. Therefore; it affected my normal after-landing expectations and flow. That's not an excuse; but was definitely a factor.Weather was not a factor; nor was the lighting due to being midday. I don't believe fatigue or other physiological factors contributed either.
column123: CAVU. RNAV [Runway] XXR. FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying). Upon landing standard transfer of controls on roll out. I planned on exiting [Taxiway] XZ to [Taxiway] XY to get behind a Airbus on [Taxiway] XY. ATC states 'exit [Taxiway] XX hold short of [Runway] XXL on [Taxiway] XX' (and gate status I think).
