column121: Volume during this session was not particularly high; but complexity and workload changed quickly; and a sequence of events took my attention away from aircraft that didn't need much of it; including the aircraft in question. Aircraft X descending into ZZZ. My initial descent clearance was to 15;000 ft. An eastbound departure was potentially in conflict with 3 other aircraft; including Aircraft X. Deconflicting this aircraft took much of my attention during this time. Aircraft X ended up being no factor. Once clear of all other aircraft; I gave Aircraft X descent clearance to 11;000 ft. Read back was not as clear as I thought; but I had other things to worry about; including two aircraft simultaneously calling for VFR flight following and a conflict alert between VFR aircraft I was providing flight following to and a Mode-C intruder which took much of my attention because they were tracking to pass about 1 mile apart and the Mode-C intruder was climbing into the other VFR aircraft. Once that situation cleared up and as Aircraft X was descending through 12;000 ft. I received a call from FSS (Flight Service Station) which I decided to answer on the assumption that it would be a faster phone call than it turned out to be.Their request was for a Special VFR departure (SVFR). I had to take time to verify that SVFR was possible from this airport and since SVFR is a very rare request in my area of specialization I then had to look up the phraseology to give the clearance. By the time the clearance was delivered and read back; at least 2 minutes had passed. As I disconnected the FSS call; Low Altitude Alert showed Aircraft X at 7;900 ft.; descending below the MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) of 8;000 ft. I immediately issued a low altitude alert with a clearance to climb to 10;000 ft. immediately. After the pilot responded I advised the pilot that his descent clearance had been to 11;000 ft. and asked if he had ZZZ in sight. Pilot responded that he had the field in sight. I cleared Aircraft X for a visual approach and gave instructions to contact Tower. It did not appear that he observed the climb clearance that accompanied the Low Altitude Alert; and the aircraft was at 7;300 ft. when I cleared Aircraft X for a visual approach.It is difficult to recommend any actions or changes to prevent re occurrence. This particular sector is quite complex; with high terrain; military airspace; two approach control facilities; arrivals to and departures from ZZZ1 in all directions. Convergence between ZZZ arrivals/departures to the south of ZZZ and ZZZ1 arrivals/departures to the southeast of ZZZ1. Also ZZZ2 arrivals and departures to the northwest of ZZZ2 all come together in the vicinity of ZZZ3. Also several satellite airports where pilots cannot reach us on the ground resulting in FSS relays. 11 adjacent sectors adjusted for typical sector configuration with multiple combined but the actual number of individual adjacent sectors is much higher and a relatively heavy VFR workload. It can unexpectedly become quite busy; even with a small number of aircraft in the sector. When this happens; it usually entails coordination calls from one or both of the approach control facilities; the military controlling agency; FSS; and one of the 11 adjacent sectors; and often includes aircraft that require a higher-than-normal workload. The timing of these factors is not controllable; so when several things happen at once; it usually can't be predicted; it can become difficult to manage; and it's often over before a D-side (Radar Assist) can make it to the sector to help.

column121: There was some confusion going into work as I was notified at XA:00 pm for my XA:30 shift  and told not to report to work until XD:45 due to Level 3 cleaning that was taking place. When we arrived at work the control floor was empty and ZAU ARTCC resumed operations at XD:55am with no briefings at all. I was working the MID configuration which includes the following sectors (sector numbers removed) along with the following approach controls (ZZZ1/ZZZ2/ZZZ3/ZZZ4/ZZZ5). During my stint which started at XF:00 am and ending at XI:00 am around XX:50 ZULU I spoke with Aircraft X looking for the ILS to Runway X at ZZZ2. I asked the pilot if he had the current weather at the field along with the NOTAMs and the pilot responded with a yes to the weather and that he had read the NOTAMs yesterday. I then read what I thought was all the pertinent NOTAMs to the aircraft. I vectored Aircraft X for the ILS at ZZZ2 and cleared the aircraft in for the approach. I switched the aircraft to advisories and requested a timely cancellation due to a second aircraft being vectored for the same approach. Aircraft X soon cancelled his IFR and reported a down time along with the condition of the runway and that the ramp area was in a much worse condition. I inadvertently missed the snow removal NOTAM and was later on informed by management that Aircraft X had landed on a runway with snow removal equipment on it. Any usage of the active runway should require call to either the facility or on frequency to prevent any confusion on what is going on at the airport. Any and all NOTAMs that directly effect the runways should be better identified. ZZZ2 had over 15 NOTAMs listed at the airfield which all look identical; if the ones like snow removal were BOLD or even a different color it may help the next person avoid the same mistake I made.
column123: I was notified today upon arrival to work that Aircraft X had landed on a runway occupied by snow removal equipment at the time. I was unaware that this had happened. I was working the assist position when the aircraft was cleared for the visual approach. The Radar Controller had issued the weather and read the NOTAMs to the aircraft and neither of us were aware that snow removal was taking place at the airport. The aircraft canceled IFR prior to landing. I was not made aware of the hazardous situation until the following work shift. This is the third report that I have written on this type of event at this airport! Several years ago; I myself had an aircraft execute a missed approach due to snow removal equipment on the same runway. I of course submitted a report detailing the situation and offered recommendations to prevent the situation from occurring again. I received no feedback. I told my Operations Manager; who was aware of the incident; and was dismissed. I then took it to the local safety council who actually looked into it. However; after some time I was informed that the current procedures would remain in effect. No definite reason was given. If a runway is possibly occupied by snow removal equipment; an aircraft should not be cleared for an approach. Having an aircraft switch frequencies to contact the snow removal crew themselves to land obviously has many drawbacks. The snow removal crew should simply notify the control facility prior to entering the runway. ATC could then close the runway until notified that the snow removal crew has exited the runway. This could be done by radio or phone; thus preventing the situations that have previously occurred.

A slight north wind caused my track just slightly south of center line of final; well within reason; estimate one dot right. As I was correcting and back on centerline the GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning) sounded; when back on center line the GPWS stopped. column121: From Captain X - 'When I approached the gate for my flight the boarding agent was talking on the phone.  As a courtesy I waited until he was off the phone to identify myself (as working crew).  I overheard his side of the conversation and clearly heard him state that he was (now) aware that the first four rows of coach class could not be occupied due to weight and balance and that he would re-seat the passengers that were booked in those seats.  During my FA briefing I said nothing about those seats because there was no mention in my flight release that the first four rows of coach should not be occupied.  During pre-flight in the cockpit I called my Dispatcher to ask for additional fuel and an alternate and during this conversation nothing was said about the first four rows of coach not being occupied.  We pushed at XA:15Z and got airborne eight minutes later.  The closeout had a note about the first four rows not being occupied; but since I recalled the agent saying that he would re-seat the passengers in those rows I did not pursue it any further.  After climbing out of ten thousand I called the #1 FA and told him to make sure that no passenger changed their seats to the first 4 rows of coach during the flight and was then told that there were 3 passengers sitting in the first 4 rows of coach.  I called my Dispatcher to make sure we were restricted and was told we were.  I asked Dispatch to find out why those seats were assigned by the gate agent after I heard the agent acknowledge over the phone that those seats were restricted due to weight and balance and should not be used.  I also asked my FA to re-seat the 3 passengers and make sure the first four rows of coach remained unoccupied for the duration of the flight. I don't know why the agent who said he was going to re-seat the passengers didn't do it.  The passenger manifest clearly showed that at least one of those 3 passengers was assigned a seat in the first 4 rows of coach by the agent during our boarding process.'   To tag along with what Captain X said; the TPS did not have any weight and balance information about seat restrictions. The closeout did; but since Captain X knew that the gate agent knew about it already; we figured no one would be assigned those seats. For some reason; those passengers got assigned those seats; I assume because they were non revs and the gate agent was under pressure to get the flight out so they probably forgot about the restriction. Time pressure; gate agents are under a lot of pressure; and seem understaffed during COVID. Due to this; they should be commended for doing the work that they are. They should be thanked for making sure non revs make it on. The intense amount of pressure agents work under day in and day out; adds up and a mistake is bound to happen. This mistake; although a procedural mistake; was not one of extreme error. The margin of error built into weight and balance is wide. If weight and balance is truly as tight as 3 passengers; the FAA would make sure we weighed every single bag individually and get true cargo weights instead of averaging bag weights. We would also weigh passengers instead of simply assuming there are average summer and winter weights per passenger. The flight was completed successfully; transporting XX or so people across the country.Don't work gate agents so hard. Give them the tools they need to succeed and ease up on micromanaging. Let agents make real decisions and they will feel empowered to complete their tasks; like making sure 4 rows are empty on a flight. I could place the blame on the agent and make a bunch of suggestions and punishments up; but I'm tired of the culture of pitting work group against work group here. This is the only airline I've worked for where this practice is known and visible. We are all working toward the same goal of trying to save the airline industry. Let the agent know of the mistake and move on. We need to work together now more than ever.

ATC replied with 'roger.' Shortly following that; we were handed off to the next controller. When we checked in we mentioned our box input error and he said; 'No problem; proceed direct ZZZ1. How's that?' No further discussion with ATC. I immediately knew what happened and why. The FMS would not download our flight plan (not uncommon) so I built in manually. As I looked at the clearance I noticed the departure and selected it; but failed to assign the ZZZZZ1 transition. ZZZZZ1 appeared on our route packet as a different fix; not part of the departure and I fell for it. I had a lot of fixes and airways to type in so I focused on getting them correct and failed to notice how I had loaded the departure; without the transition. Ultimately we were missing 4 fixes in the legs page. I checked the first 5 fixes in the legs page to confirm the altitude restrictions since we were cleared to climb Via. Normally I check all the fixes but the other contributing factors today were no coffee or breakfast at this point. I wanted to get setup and ready so I could get coffee. Due to COVID; food and coffee was not available at the hotel so we catered it for our morning departure. Additionally; the pax showed up XX minutes early which squashed my plans to eat before we took off. Additionally; the lead pax birth date was incorrect on our brief so we were further distracted.Human error. I caused this event during the FMS setup. The pre-flight distractions becoming more and more common place with passenger related issues of catering and name details; today it got me. Another potential cause could be how the flight plan route is displayed on our packets. I'm used to seeing something like 'ZZZZZ.ZZZZZ1 ZZZ2; etc.;' as the FMS shows; but the filed route on our flight plan shows 'ZZZZZ ZZZZZ1 ZZZ2; etc.' Seeing it with the period would have drawn my attention to the ZZZZZ1 transition. Suggestions - For me; all things being the same again; if the filed route on our flight plan packet showed 'ZZZZZ.ZZZZZ1' this deviation wouldn't have happened today. Regardless of this and the distractions; I need to be more careful.

column121: During arrival to HAN; I was a jumpseat observer. We were at 2;000 ft. on the localizer; cleared for the ILS [Runway] 11 Left approach. Just outside the Final Approach Fix; I heard the Captain (Pilot Flying); say glideslope captured; and he set the missed approach altitude of 5;000 ft. in the altitude alerter. I was confused; because looking at the FO's (First Officer's) PFD (Primary Flight Display); I could see that we were below the glideslope; and it was no captured. I could not see the Captain's PFD to verify whether or not the glideslope was captured. The aircraft started descent from 2;000 ft.; even though we were not on the glideslope. I called out to check the glideslope and/or altitude. I did not have a hot mike; and maybe they weren't hearing me. The aircraft passed the Final Approach Fix approximately 500 ft. low. I called out the glideslope deviation again. The other jumpseat observer was also telling them to climb; and I yelled 'Go Around'. Then we got a GS caution with a line strike through the FMA on the PFD. At approximately 1;200 ft.; the go around was finally initiated with full scale deflection indicated on FO's PFD.During the surprise go around; we were instructed to maintain heading and climb to 5;000 ft. At some point the autopilot was disconnected; and situational awareness was deteriorating. The aircraft was veering to the right of track; 20 degrees nose up; and not following the flight director commands of 10 degrees nose up. I called out something like 'Who's flying the airplane; fly the airplane!' The flying pilot then steered back toward the flight director; regained control and the autopilot was re-engaged. After reaching 5;000 ft. we were vectored back for another approach to Runway 11 Left.Also of note; there was runway/taxiway construction at HAN airport that could have possibly created a glideslope anomaly. Though I could not see the Captain's flight instruments; it is possible there may have been a loss of glideslope indication at the start of the event. On the FO's PFD; I could see that the ILS was identified; and localizer/glideslope were displayed at all times.The Pilot Monitoring should have noticed on his instruments that the aircraft was not on glideslope; and should have called out the deviation immediately. When I saw the deviation; I was trying to alert the crew to fix the situation. I should have called out go around immediately.
column123: While inbound on the localizer for RNWY (Runway) 11L; the glideslope was captured and the 'G/S' FMA was active. Shortly after capturing the glideslope; the 'G/S' FMA blinked and had a yellow strikethrough. The glideslope then started to fall beneath us; while the autopilot tried to increase the rate of descent. The Pilot Flying switched to V/S [Vertical Speed]; and rolled in more V/S down to stay on glideslope with a more than normal descent rate. I instructed to 'level off; level off' followed by 'climb back to 2;000 ft. It was then I noticed the glideslope dot had blinked and reappeared at two dots high; indicating we were low. The Captain in the observer seat then said 'Go Around; Go Around'. The Pilot Flying initiated the go around with the 'TOGA' [Takeoff Go-Around] switches and sometime thereafter turned off the autopilot. He then hand flew the go around to 5;000 ft. and present heading. After notifying Tower of our missed approach; we were told to contact Approach frequency. During this event; with my seat position; I was only able to observe the Captain's PFD [Primary Flight Display]. After landing safely and gathering all facts observed between crewmembers; it was apparent that the autopilot tried to capture a false glideslope and failed; thus giving us the yellow strikethrough the 'G/S' FMA."

The student pulled throttle to idle and applied full brake pressure; the lack of grabbing action in the right main brake assembly caused the plane to veer even more sharply left; off the runway to the left and into the grass infield. No objects were struck by the plane and the student shut down and exited in a safe and timely fashion. The aircraft was reviewed by a company CFI and Maintenance Technician and returned to service after a change of brake pads. Speculation is that improper use of the braking system over time caused a [glazing] effect on both the pads and rotor that limited the grabbing ability of the system at the time of the incident. No harm came to persons or property; student was quickly and safely retrieved to the point of the flights origin and the aircraft was returned to service that same day.

The winds upon time of landing favored Runway XX and a right-crosswind component of about 10 knots was present at the time of the occurrence. No other traffic was in the pattern and the approach was stable throughout. The touchdown was in a three point attitude and did not bounce. On the rollout; the student improperly managed rudder control and the aircraft rapidly developed a significant turn to the left. As Instructor; I took control of the aircraft and stopped the ground loop from further developing. The aircraft departed the hard surface of the runway at roughly a 10 degree angle at a fairly slow speed and came to rest in the grass about 20 feet from the edge of the runway. Upon shutting the airplane down; both the student and I exited the airplane to assess the situation. No signage or lighting was hit nor was there any damage present on the airplane. The grass was smooth and no holes were present.The situation developed from a normal crosswind landing to a runway excursion quickly. The cause was an improper control input by the student that was not caught in time by me; the instructor. Despite not reacting in time to prevent the excursion; the aircraft did not ground loop and no damage was sustained by the airplane. Any corrective action would be on my part as the Instructor; to take control sooner before such a significant turn could develop.

column121: I was entering the traffic pattern at 45 degrees for a downwind entry for RWY14 at FIT. I had previously announced my intentions and location on the 122.7 CTAF. I did not see or hear the conflicting traffic during its go around and climb out from RWY14.  I was alerted to the traffic by an ADS B traffic alert on my iPad. At this point I could not see the traffic in my field of view. I turned 45 to downwind and added power to get away from the traffic.  Earlier I had heard the conflicting aircraft on the CTAF advising it was on the RNAV20 approach and would be breaking off the approach for a straight in to RWY14. Calls to the conflicting traffic before and after ADS B alert we're not answered.It all happened very quickly and I only glanced at the ADS B display; figuring my attention should be outside the airplane looking for the traffic. But the combination of repeated ADS B traffic warnings and not being able to visually see and avoid the traffic was quite stressful.  Today; I was able to get the conflicting traffic's flight path from flight aware and compare it to my own from Garmin Pilot. It appears the conflicting traffic did a low approach to RWY14 and a go around; making a left climbing turn close to my own flight path. From the flight paths; the time stamps; and the fact that I never made visual contact with the conflicting aircraft; I think it passed behind me; and estimate it may have gotten as close as 500 ft.Being more vigilant to visually identify and track what I thought was landing traffic; would likely have avoided this dangerous conflict. The fact that the conflicting traffic never responded to my radio calls should also have raised a red flag.

column121: I was on the ramp at the FBO which is located at the end of the taxiway. I had received my IFR clearance for departure on Runway 7 on the clearance frequency. I then switched to the ground frequency and requested taxi clearance. (It was now well after sunset) I was told to taxi to Runway 7 via Foxtrot. I left the ramp and made an immediate left. Upon reaching Foxtrot 2; I realized that I wasn't actually on Taxiway Foxtrot; but was on a parallel road which was intended for vehicle traffic; not aircraft. I stopped at Foxtrot 2 and notified Ground control what had happened. I informed them that I could make a right onto Foxtrot 2 to get on the Foxtrot Taxiway. The controller notified me to hold my position and that he would send an Ops (Airport Operations) vehicle out. About 5 minutes later the Ops vehicle arrived behind me. The ground controller notified the Ops vehicle that I had stated that I could make the turn onto Foxtrot 2. The Ops vehicle approved that which I did and I made the right onto Foxtrot 2 and then left onto Taxiway Foxtrot and proceeded to the hold line for Runway 7 without further incident.After making the wrong turn on what I thought was Taxiway Foxtrot I did see a sign with an F on it with a black background on my right which is why I thought I was on Taxiway F. As I proceeded towards Runway 7. I commented to my passenger that there were several dips in the pavement which was unusual. As I approached F2; I saw a red sign past F2 indicating no entry. That's what was literally the red flag. Fortunately; I was in a high wing aircraft which cleared all lights and signs. This may not have been the case in a low wing aircraft. This second road was not shown on my airport taxi diagram which might have helped. I don't know if anyone else had ever made this same mistake; but I think better signage would have helped. Perhaps a sign coming out of the ramp on F1 indicating 2nd left to Foxtrot or a red no enter sign like the one at F2 might have might have also helped. I had not flown into this airport in over 15 years. I did not request progressive taxi instructions because the route appeared to be very simple. I will be more vigilant during night operations at unfamiliar airports.

column121: My Recommendation: Because there is what I believe to be a low but uncertain chance that the primary pressure vessel of the Aircraft X has a current active failure; the aircraft should be immediately grounded; and an investigation be initiated into whether this issue is just a classification and engineering oversight; or indeed a failure to the aircraft's primary structure. Aircraft X (Boeing-767-300) is potentially operating on an inapplicable airworthiness sign off and may fly (already has flown) with a possible serious defect to the aircraft's primary structure (pressure vessel). Aircraft X arrived at ZZZ station December 2020. Upon arrival the following defect was found and recorded into the maintenance log book:Discrepancy: Undocumented Speed tape found concealing stripped & unsecured mounting screw to extruded Main Cargo Door (MCD) Manual Vent Door Drive (Pressure Vessel) cover panel.I notified Maintenance Control of the defect and submitted via email a proposal for a temp repair utilizing non-standard substitution parts available on-hand at our station that I hoped would allow for a timely repair keeping the aircraft on scheduled revenue flights despite the need for an Engineering Order (EO) and additional authorizations. After an appropriate time; an outline of maintenance action to be completed was submitted to our station for a yet unapproved EO numbered: XXXXXXXX; that was a substantial deviation from my own earlier proposed temp repair. This EO after performing a Detailed Visual Inspection (DVI) merely called for reattaching the panel in place with RTV-106 sealant; no hardware; and a covering of multiple layers of aluminum speed tape. Knowing that an external application of tape over a hole in the primary pressure vessel of an aircraft did not meet the basic criteria for acceptable maintenance standards; I contacted maintenance Control to inform them that we (aircraft technicians under my purview) at ZZZ would not be able to comply with the EO maintenance instructions as they were currently written because of the safety implications.After expressing my unwillingness to press forward with the draft EO I began receiving pressuring communications from various maintenance controllers; maintenance duty managers; and Company management; saying everything from 'just do it;' to 'it'll be fine.' Additionally; it was overheard in background talk on more than one phone call with maintenance controllers that they did not believe the panel in question was actually a primary pressure vessel fitting as I had asserted in multiple emails and phone conversations; and was merely a weather seal. Worried that I had somehow made an egregious mistake about the panel in-fact being a pressure hull seal; I enlisted both additional night shift mechanics to assist with a cabin pressurization leak check (referencing AMM 05-51-24-782-001) with the damaged MCD Manual Drive cover panel removed. As I operated the cabin pressure manually; utilizing APU bleed source; the two assisting technicians reported a strong; unrestricted flow of air emanating from the uncovered hole; while I was observing only 1 PSI indicated differential cabin pressure. Believing that this observation adequately supported my previous assertation; I terminated the test; returned the aircraft to its previous configuration; and felt confident that my continued refusal to repair the aircraft as outlined in the draft EO to be a safe and correct judgment call.The scheduled departure of the aircraft was altered from XA:15z to XE:00z. At XB:16z I received an email asking me to 'please call In to Maintenance Control to advise on current status of approved EO compliance;' (no approved EO had been received or transmitted to anyone at ZZZ station). Given the ongoing pressure from phone calls and condescending emails to comply with an EO I had yet to see; I advised [the] maintenance controllers that I would not be complying with the EO and to direct all future communications to be in writing. I then suggested at that point that they 'just AOG (aircraft on ground) ship the required parts necessary to return this defect to its original condition;' with the observation 'that the original undocumented speed tape repair has already been proven to fail;' as my own justification for non-compliance with an EO that called for doing the same thing; only with more tape.At XD:50z we received the first approved copy of the EO XXXXXXXX via email from the Maintenance Manager; which upon review was consistent with the advised sealant and tape repair already rejected. The scheduled aircraft departure was once again pushed back to XG:00z; well after the scheduled arrival of the oncoming maintenance day shift. At XE:15z I received a phone call from my Company Regional Manager asking me why I was not complying with the EO and then; regarding taping over a hole in the pressure vessel; to 'explain how this is a safety concern?' After briefly elaborating to him about how the loss of cabin pressure makes flight crews go to sleep and planes to become lawn-darts; he said that I would 'have coverage in terms of liability because the engineer signed off on three layers of speed tape.' After mutually disagreeing; he proceeded to switch the subject to asking me which maintenance technicians were coming in on day shift; then; seeming unsatisfied; continued to ask me about the status of other technicians not scheduled for shift. Several minutes after hanging up; another call was received from a subordinate technician; not scheduled to come in; inquiring as to what was going on and why the Regional Manager was asking him to come into work on his weekend and 'override' us. At the advice of another technician overhearing the conversations; I took a written note of the above quotes from the calls.With continued inquiries for resolution on the aircraft; the oncoming day shift Lead informed Maintenance Control that the EO was still unworkable as it was and reiterated that the original temp repair proposal forwarded to Maintenance Control that included substituted hardware installation would be a fix deemed acceptable and believed conforming with standard practices that we would still be willing to sign off on. Giving in; the Maintenance Controller agreed to get the hardware installation added to a revised version of the EO along with an additional step for a cabin pressurization check that the day shift Lead smartly felt necessary for repairs performed on the pressurized structure of an aircraft. With assurances that the revised EO would include the agreed upon amendments; the day shift Lead and myself expedited the repair to the aircraft in an effort to make the scheduled departure pending timely receipt of the revised EO. The cabin pressure leak check of the repair was then successfully accomplished with only a small movement observed in the repair at a peak indicated differential pressure of 4.5 PSI; and no leaks or excessive loss rates noted. Upon departing the aircraft to accomplish paperwork closeout we were greeted by the oncoming flight crew; who had apparently been kept apprised of the ongoing situation and wanted to personally thank us for looking out for their safety.At XF:18z we received the approved EO XXXXXXXX Revision 1. Required paperwork was completed; signed log pages were sent; flight crew was briefed; and the aircraft was returned to green status at XG:10z. The aircraft subsequently blocked out of the gate at XG:39z for a delay from scheduled departure of 39 minutes. Why is this a safety concern? Upon later realization and review; I have found several possible deviations to Federal Aviation Regulations (FARs); the airline General Maintenance Manual; and uncertainty to the validity of the accomplished repair that should be investigated immediately as it may represent a serious safety issue to the aircraft. Having been so narrowly focused on getting the point across to the necessary parties involved in the tribulations of Dec Xth that the damaged part was indeed part of the pressure vessel of the aircraft and that a workable repair would have to be tailored to the additional physics involved with that part of the structure; I failed to realize the broader implications of what a repair to the pressurized structure of an aircraft entailed in terms of adherence to regulations; maintenance policy; and accepted practices. The FARs define 'Primary Structure: is that structure which carries flight; ground; or pressurization loads; and whose failure would reduce the structural integrity of the airplane.' Even though steps were added to Revision 1 of the EO to conform the repair to acceptable practices 'equal to its original or properly altered condition;' because the installation hardware was a reasonably close approximation of the original parts; the additional step of adding three layers of overlapping speed tape is in direct contradiction to the airline General Maintenance Manual policy for its use:          -HIGH SPEED ALUMINUM TAPE-          High speed tape is a convenient material for use as an interim repair for          non-structural materials. Under no circumstances will it be used on primary          aircraft structure. A Log Book entry is required when high speed tape is           applied unless instructed to do so by an EO with DER approval.Under this policy; the use of speed tape in this manner is strictly forbidden and forgiveness when it comes to doing the maintenance under the provision of an EO only absolves the requirement of a log book entry for its use. However; even though agreement was made in Revision 1 of the EO for addition of attachment hardware and an added cabin pressurization leak check; the EO creator did not alter the original classification of the repair to acknowledge that the repair was in-fact being accomplished on an aircraft primary structure:          'The Main Deck Cargo Door Manual Vent Door Drive Cover is considered secondary          structure. The time limited repair per this EO is minor; and the temporary           repair per Part 1 does not affect the fit; form or function of the skin.'I would imagine this to be an oversight; and if it is; then an additional revision needs to be made which would at a minimum alter the category of the defect deferral and its associated time-limited re-inspections and permanent repair due date/cycles. If this is not an oversight; however; as this EO has been twice over reviewed and approved; and the MCD Manual Vent Door Drive Cover is indeed a secondary structure; then the original investigative cabin pressure leak test failed for a reason other than indicated (i.e. there is an existing failure of the primary pressure vessel somewhere internal to the Main Cargo Door). Which would in turn mean that a damaged secondary structure is now fulfilling the function of a primary structure pressure seal. I do not believe this to be the case; but; as the MCD is a modification from the original aircraft structure; the existing reference material available for my use to confirm the hypothesis that the cover plate is indeed a primary structure component is vague and uncertain. Tech Engineering likely has additional references not available at a line station that could perhaps shed light on the issue.Since issuing equivalent versions of the above safety report to both Airline and Company on [the next day]; Aircraft X has remained on a regular flight schedule with recurrent re-inspects per Part 2 of EO XXXXXXXX Rev 1; until receiving Part 3 Permanent Repair [4 days later]. I can currently find no record that any further investigation has been conducted.

column121: We were at FL410 in continuous light chop. The seat belt sign was on before we entered the known area of turbulence and remained on till we passed the turbulence. ATC [was] reporting light chop for the next 150 miles. I had the speed intervene window open. The N1 was set for turbulence penetration. The speed was Mach .76. Within a matter of seconds we were in severe mountain wave. The speed increased to Mach .80 and we were in the over speed band. The over speed clacker went off right away. We began losing altitude. I immediately reduced thrust which was ineffective so pulled the speed brake. The speed slowed to Mach .76. We lost 300 ft. quickly. Then the second wave hit and we climbed rapidly back to altitude then 200 ft. above the assigned altitude. The aircraft returned to FL410. The event was probably 30 to 45 seconds. During the event I had the FO (First Officer) seat the flight attendants immediately. I had the FO ask for a descent to FL390. We were given the descent. The FO reported the mountain wave and the trends to ATC. There was no traffic in the area on TCAS and none was reported by ATC. We reached FL390 with no further wave but the light turbulence continued. I checked the flight attendants in and they reported no one was up during the event. I reported the event to Maintenance as severe mountain wave and over speed. I reported the event to Dispatch as well. In my 25 years of flying I have never seen mountain wave this bad.

column121: ATIS was advising ILS approaches in use. We requested the RNAV Y for pilot proficiency reasons. The request was approved by the final approach controller. At the end of the RNAV arrival; we were put on the published heading and told to expect vectors onto final for the RNAV Y approach by the final approach controller. We requested but were denied direct both initial approach fixes to start the approach. We were given 2 vectors; the last being [Heading] 290 and the clearance to fly heading 290 maintain 4;300 ft. until established on the final approach course cleared for the RNAV Y approach as we were vectored toward the course between the initial approach fixes. The approach became challenging at that point because the final approach course and glidepath anticipation cues were not visible and therefore we were unable to arm the approach. Additionally; the 4;300 ft. restriction left us high rather than leave us in a position to descend to 2;900 ft. in the space between the initial approach fixes because the width of the lateral course at that point is much narrower than a localizer signal. The IMC and terrain rich environment added to the concerns at this point. I feel that part of this challenge was created by the technique US air traffic controllers are using to get aircraft onto RNAV approaches. Rather that clear an aircraft to a fix on the approach; they are trying to vector them onto final as they would for an aircraft flying an ILS approach. My first safety concern is that there is not final approach course to intercept when flying an RNAV approach such as the localizer transmitting out bound from the runway for many miles. Rather there seems to be courses from one fix to the next all the way down the published approach. When ATC says 'fly heading xxx until established on the final approach' there isn't a final approach to intercept. I question whether a clearance of that wording is procedurally correct on RNAV approach. There are no examples I can find in company manuals or the Airman Information Manual the depicts starting an RNAV approach at anywhere other than a fix on the approach. I have had this type of vector onto final clearance for an RNAV approach for RNAV approaches in other U.S. destinations also so I feel the safety threat posed by this type of RNAV clearance is widespread in the USA. I have never received a clearance like that outside of the USA. Outside the USA; I have always been cleared to fix to start the RNAV approach. My second safety concern is that if that type of RNAV approach clearance is correct; we do not train that at any point during initial or recurrent training. All of our simulator training clears the aircraft to a fix on the approach when cleared for an RNAV approach. If the type of ATC clearance we got is procedurally correct we never see it in training.

column121: During passenger boarding I started the APU to cool the aircraft. I selected the APU bleed on and immediately began to smell a foul pungent odor. I turned the bleed off and waited a couple minutes. I tried the APU bleed again and encountered the same pungent odor. I waited a minute to see if it was a temporary smell but it persisted. I turned the bleed off and wrote up the airplane in the maintenance logbook. The smell was predominantly in the flight deck and forward galley however passengers deplaning from the rear of the aircraft were inquiring about the odor. Maintenance checked to see if the APU was possibly over serviced. The APU checked out normal. Maintenance continued their work and eventually cleared the write up. When we returned to the aircraft to get ready to board all crew members again smelled the same smell. Although it was not as strong as before it was still there and seemed to get slightly worse if we turned the Number 1 Pack off. I again wrote the aircraft up in the maintenance logbook. No medical attention was requested or required for crew or passengers.As for the probable cause; no causal factors that I can think of. Maintenance said it could have been the fumes from an aircraft starting upwind of us however that wouldn't explain why we smelled it the second time hours later.
column123: APU was started in preparation for departure; upon turning on the APU bleed to begin cooling the aircraft there immediately was a strong fume that made my nose and eyes begin to burn. I told the CA (Captain) that was the bad fume smell we need to be careful about and said I was leaving the flight deck to stand on the jet bridge. The bleed was turned off and I left for fresh air. After multiple retries by MX (Maintenance) who agreed the smell was there the passengers and remaining crew were deplaned. Later the MX personnel had done nothing other than run the packs using the external air cart and were ready to sign the plane back into service; but simply walking into the galley every single crew member could still smell the fumes. We tried to isolate the problem pack by switching packs and the fumes became worse again. We then left the aircraft again. This is an ongoing problem worldwide in the industry. The potentially disastrous health consequences of this type of pyrolization should be addressed before more crew members and passengers are impacted.

column123: Climbing out; passing approximately FL280 in IMC conditions; with the CA (Captain) flying; we received an 'IAS DISAGREE' indication. I; the FO; got out the unreliable airspeed checklist in the QRH to look up the possible indications. After a few moments the indication disappeared and the IAS returned to normal. After beginning a descent the same indications returned and then disappeared as they had before. Passing approximately 16;000 ft. there was a large fluctuation in the CA's airspeed causing a large fluctuation in the autothrottles. The CA disengaged the autopilot and autothrottles. We transferred aircraft control since my indications seemed normal. The CA ran the QRH for unreliable airspeed [and] I flew the approach using the autopilot with the autothrottles disengaged to an uneventful landing.

column121: As we taxied out to our assigned runway of XXL in ZZZ; we received several EFIS COMP MON [airspeed disagree] caution messages. They would only stay on for a few seconds; then disappear as I would reset the master caution that would accompany the ding. Once we were cleared to 'line up and wait' on our assigned runway of XXL I taxied on the runway; and handed the controls to the First Officer (FO) and we waited for our takeoff clearance. A few moments later; we were cleared to takeoff with clearance of 'RNAV to ZZZZZ Runway XXL; cleared for takeoff.'  The First Officer then initiated the take off sequence. As she pushed the thrust levers forward and we started to move down the runway; yet another EFIS [Electronic Flight instrument System] COMP MON caution came on with an associated ding and master caution warning. I looked to ED1 (primary EICAS) to find the caution and said aloud 'continue.' and the The First Officer continued with the takeoff roll. As soon as I looked back at the airspeed indicator tape; I saw we already were at V1 speed; and Vr speed. So I said aloud 'V1; rotate' as soon as we rotated the STALL FAIL caution illuminated on ED1. The stick shaker activated shortly thereafter; followed by a warbling tone to indicated a stall had happened. I look at my airspeed indication 'tape' and now saw both red 'barber pole' indicators starting to come together. As I saw this; I quickly looked at the FO airspeed indication and back at the backup airspeed indication. I noticed they both were reading the same thing and said aloud; 'looks like we have a stall fail caution; and my airspeed is showing incorrect indications.' I then began to run the QRC and QRH for the stall fail and loss of reliable airspeed indications. After running the QRH; we promptly returned to ZZZ without incident and taxied to a gate.  According to Maintenance; water entered into the left-side pitot tube and caused an erroneous airspeed error; and potential STALL FAIL caution.

column121: The Captain and I met at the airplane in the morning and the first topic of discussion was the automated parking guidance procedure as neither of us had used the system yet and they appeared to be operating. We referenced the flight manual as well as the local notes concerning the system and still felt that we were not sure exactly what we were supposed to do approaching the gate. We asked rampers prior to departing and their explanation; which did not help much. We departed and further discussed our plan for approaching the gate in our briefing for the return leg. As we approached the gate 3 rampers were present and the guidance panel worked well and was intuitive. We found a Ramp Supervisor and he discussed the details with us and answered questions we had. The guidance in the flight manual is inadequate as it does not address definitively whether or not marshallers are required to be at the spot. It does not specify the procedure for requesting assistance from ramp personnel if required It does not address what to do in the event that equipment is in the safety zone. Finally; the guidance as to when the screen symbology is required references 'the nose of the aircraft passing the jet bridge' which does not apply to the Aircraft X in where the system is active. My interpretation and common sense answers to these questions are likely to create a safe operation but safe and compliant are not always the same thing.  We entered the gate area in compliance with the flight manual to the best of my knowledge and interpretation; however I feel that the guidance in the manual was inadequate. Part of the information we used to determine a plan for parking came from talking with rampers. They obviously have good insight but their word does not meet acceptable standards for determining compliance with a procedure. I would recommend a simple update to the manual that goes beyond description of the guidance panel and sets definitive procedures for entering the gate.

column121: There was a break before the next flight to ZZZ.  Flight attendants left the aircraft.  First Officer (FO) left the aircraft.  Captain left the aircraft as one of the FAs came back to the aircraft.  Captain came back to the aircraft.  Both FAs and FO were on board.  Also a Ramp Agent (RA) was on board sitting in the back of the plane resting.  One of the flight Attendants told the Captain she was concerned that the RA did not complete the security search.  From her perspective it seemed as if the security check was not complete.  Captain went back and asked the RA if he had completed the security search.  He said yes.  Captain asked what was involved with the search and he described that it was a visual search and where he looked.  Captain told the Flight Attendant that the Ramp Agent said he did it.  Flight Attendant was not sure because the RA hadn't lifted up the seat cushions and looked behind them or put the tray tables down as the FA had seen done in previous security searches.  Captain asked the RA if he could do the security check again and that there was a concern that it was not complete.  The RA started doing another security check lifting up the seat cushions in the first couple rows.  Captain went to the flight deck to prepare for the flight.  Captain assumed that the security check got completed the second round and all was good to go.  Flight departs for ZZZ; Captain and FO review the security section of Flight Ops Manual (FOM).  After arrival in ZZZ; the Captain goes to review the security section with FAs.  It is then that he hears that the Ramp Agent did not go completely through the cabin on the second time and check seat cushions and tray tables at ZZZ1.  The RA talked with another RA and then told the Flight Attendants that the search had happened and it was complete.  The Captain called the Duty Officer and had a discussion about the situation and the wording in the FOM.  Duty Officer told the Captain that he would call back after a few minutes while he made a call to find out what the Ramp manual says to do.  After the Duty officer called back to the Captain he referenced the Services Manual about aircraft search to and from ZZZZ; wording was not the same as what is in the FOM.  The Duty officer agreed that there is room for some confusion between the wording in the two manuals.  Captain decided to stop the operation and have ZZZ ramp agents do a Full Search before continuing on to ZZZ2.  A Big thank you to ZZZ RAs in knocking out a Full Search.         My thoughts (Captain) there is some confusion in how the FOM describes a cabin search and what a visual inspection actually is on the security form.Pay closer attention to details.  Don't assume anything; make sure everyone is on the same page in understanding of what's happening.  Ask questions; try and understand the full picture.  It's been awhile since our airplanes have made ZZZZ trips and it was the first time for our crew the other day since prior to COVID-19.  We need to show each other respect; and give grace in this super stressful time.  After talking with the Duty Officer; I more fully aware of the staffing issues with ramp; COVID-19 cases and just under staffing in different areas which has been extremely difficult.  I also see a value in debriefing the crew at the end of the trip or after abnormal situations as a learning time for all as we grow as professionals.

column121: We were fully boarded; with checklist Before Start To The Line complete. Flight Attendant B reported passenger submitted; when Flight Attendant A reported the ramp agents requested we contact Station Ops.  Operations informed us Flight Attendant B was being replaced on the trip by a reserve. I assisted Flight Attendant B off loading bags; and advised them to catch a breath and gather all effects. The pressure of the last minute situation and the ramp; and the timeline; needed to be ignored at that moment. The replacement flight attendant arrived; I assisted loading bags; verified ID and returned to the flight deck. Weight and performance numbers came up and the Captain stated ready for door closure. The main cabin door and cockpit door secured; weights entered and verified on FMS. Without communication from ramp agents; they re-opened the main cabin door. Flight Attendant A knocked on the cockpit door; which we opened. Flight Attendant A stated the First Officer was now also being replaced on the trip. I queried Crew Scheduling and was told name ordered me off the trip with no further information given. The replacement First Officer arrived and I offloaded the bags. The Captain was astonished that such an action would take place without communication; consult; or apparent consideration for safety of flight.Passengers expressed surprise; and some measure of concern and alarm. The main cabin door being opened without the crew's awareness is not a procedure I have seen before. Replacing crew members who are not ill at the last minute affects our morale and pocketbook; and creates unnecessary concern for the revenue passengers. Safety of flight is inevitably affected by this kind of turmoil; and it falls on the Company to alleviate stress and safety rather than contribute to it. The Company exercised authority in contradiction to common sense and safety of flight. The timeline; already compressed; became distressingly so given the apparent chaos this action caused in view of passengers. Ordering the ramp to open the main cabin door without communicating first to the crew is an extraordinary act of harassment and intimidation. If a pilot needs to be replaced on a trip for administrative reasons; surely that can wait until after a short turn is completed. This action requires the crew; the new crew; to re-brief and reinitialize a flight under stress; delays our passengers; compromises our timeline; and potentially costs us our bonuses. It should be taken only under extraordinary circumstances; which apparently do not exist. The Company should be an asset to safety of flight rather than a liability.

column121: On [Date 1]; I was reviewing paperwork on the current Aircraft X in the [Maintenance Visit] in ZZZ and noticed that a robbed transponder on Aircraft X was installed the previous night and did not get a signoff in the logbook releasing the aircraft for RVSM (Reduced Vertical Separation Minimum) operation. This aircraft was still scheduled to be in the [Maintenance Visit] for another 5 days so I just had the nightshift avionics tech complete the entry the next day. But I knew that the avionics tech that forgot the RVSM signoff on the [Maintenance Visit] also replaced a transponder on Aircraft Y during the overnight on [Date 2]. I pulled the paperwork from the night of [Date 2] and found that the #2 Transponder was changed to clear a MEL (Minimum Equipment List); but a RVSM release was not done in the logbook. I called Maintenance Control and told them what happened and Aircraft Y was inbound to ZZZ1 at the time so when it landed in ZZZ1; Maintenance went out and deferred the RVSM. The ZZZ Avionics tech that replaced the transponder is [Name].Found during paperwork reviewShould of; but did not realize the transponder is RVSMCalled Maintenance Control and had the system deferred (RVSM)[Parts Document] lists the PN (Part Number) of the transponders that go on our aircraft that are post ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast) mod. This PN [XXX] is not listed in the aircraft IPC (Illustrated Parts Catalog); so there is no statement (RVSM Critical Item) like all the other transponder PN's listed in the IPC. This statement (RVSM Critical Item) should be added to the [Parts Document]; to bring attention to it like the PN's listed in the aircraft IPC.
column123: On [Date 2] I was assigned to clear a Transponder #2 MEL (Minimum Equipment List) on Aircraft Y. I determined it needed a new transponder; however; we did not have the proper transponder in stock required for ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast) mod aircraft. I was directed to rob the transponder from Aircraft X which was the [Maintenance Visit]; after robbing (from Aircraft X) and installing (on Aircraft Y) the transponder; I went through the operation checks and everything was good. I went to sign off the paperwork and seen; from the beginning of Chapter 34 in the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual); that it was not CAT II (Category 2). I forgot that RVSM (Reduced Vertical Separation Minimum) isn't included in the beginning of ATA (Air Transport Association) chapters and since I picked the part number based on [Number] I didn't see the RVSM reminder note seen in the AIPC (Aircraft Illustrated Parts Catalog). I went to open the GMM (General Maintenance Manual) on the tech computer I was using and it wouldn't open. It was known within the base that PDF's can act up on the 2 provided tech computers. My ignorance of not remembering that RVSM wasn't included in the beginnings of ATA chapters; and not going into AIPC; and assuming that since RVSM wasn't downgraded it wasn't an RVSM component; along with my laziness of not confirming with a lead or Supervisor on their computers contributed to missing the RVSM release sign off. The plane made at least one flight with out having the RVSM release. The next night I installed new transponder in Aircraft X and Operations checked everything and since I assumed it wasn't RVSM the day before I repeated my mistake for the [Maintenance Visit on Aircraft X]; and didn't write up a RVSM release sign off. It was caught before the aircraft left and the other avionics technician went through the operation checks again and provided the RVSM release sign off.The day shift Supervisor caught the [Maintenance Visit] not having the release and knew that I did the aircraft the night before and seen that I didn't release that one either and took corrective action.I didn't put max effort into looking into seeing if the component was RVSM critical. I went off of a handful of assumptions and didn't double check with my leads or Supervisor. The [Number] didn't reiterate it was an RVSM critical item; the GMM PDF didn't want to load on the tech computers; RVSM isn't located at the beginning of ATA chapters like CAT II and RII (Required Inspection Item) are.Put RVSM in beginning ATA chapters like CAT II and RII. Add a reminder in [Number] that the transponder is RVSM critical component. Remove old transponders from stock that can't be used with ADS-B aircraft seeing that our whole fleet has ADS-B mod. Leadership verified wrong part number in stock the night before contributing to this issue being on 2 aircraft due to robbery. Update/upgrade/fix tech computers so we can open the files we need.

column121: On a training flight with a student; we had alternator failure an hour into our lesson. I did not notice the ammeter reading negative until the transponder began to flicker on and off. When I was troubleshooting; I asked the student to look at the ammeter; since it was on his side; and he told me that it was showing a negative reading; and that there was a red light. I immediately turned towards ZZZ1 and began to reduce the electrical load; hoping to lengthen the amount of time that we would have a working radio. At this point I checked into our traffic avoidance system; and noticed that there was heavy traffic at my airport of intended landing. I queued up Approach and told them the nature of my situation. I told them I wasn't sure if I would have enough battery to safely make calls to get into the traffic pattern; considering my transponder was dying. A few minutes later; right after they transferred us to Tower; who quickly cleared us to land; we lost all ability to communicate. We were unable to use our electric flaps on the landing. I taxied back to the ramp and gave Tower a call to see if I needed to fill out any paperwork; and they told me that they had taken care of it. In retrospect; I should have caught the failed alternator sooner. My student had noticed the light; but did not know what it meant; and his yoke was in the way for me to notice it. During our cruise checklist; that is one of the items that we check; and I did not notice anything wrong when we did the checklist 20 minutes prior. Additionally; after noticing the issue I could have just completely turned off the master switch and used pilotage to get us close to [the airport]; after which I could have turned the master back on and then used my radio. I had never had this happen before; so I was trying to make quick; confident decisions.

column121: This was my first flight at the controls of a tail wheel aircraft. I was in the left seat receiving flight instruction from the CFI in the right seat. A thorough pre-takeoff briefing including experience levels and positive transfer of controls was accomplished before departure.As we approached ZZZ; we briefed the fact there was a right crosswind with gusts and the appropriate actions to take regarding this. The approach was stabilized. A normal wheel landing was accomplished and the tail was successfully lowered to the ground. The left main tire failed; at which point the instructor stated 'my airplane' and I released the controls. The resulting swerve was not controllable and the airplane ground looped approximately 150 degrees; coming to rest on the runway. We immediately shut down the aircraft and exited. No propeller or wingtip contact with the runway occurred. The aircraft remained on the runway. No injuries occurred.
column123: The mission was to fly with 2 friends and give them tail wheel instruction. There was a crosswind from the right and we discussed crosswind correction and the plan. [The pilot flying] conducted the wheel landing and shortly after putting the tail down; the airplane started shaking violently. I thought this may have initially been a tail wheel shimmy; which was odd since it didn't shimmy since the tail wheel springs were replaced in month; but the airplane started veering to the left so I announced 'my controls' and corrected it with right rudder. The shaking got worse and the plane then swung around to the right and ground looped. The wings did not contact the surface and there was no prop strike. The airplane was then towed to the hangar where I worked with a mechanic to change the wheel and tire so that the plane could be moved while inside the hangar. I did identify some contributing factors. There was a strong right crosswind; it was my student's first landing; and I had previous issues with my tires slipping on grooved runways. They are 8.50 oversize tires. I do believe the left main tire went flat on landing; and with the strong crosswind and delay of taking the controls from my student; it was unrecoverable. I'm filling out this report to detail human factors issues that contributed to damage to my precious airplane; and as the investigation unfolds it will determine if there is need for additional caution when using larger tires.

I was able to find out who the pilot flying was and I called him to discuss. He said he was VFR; saw a mile wide hole in the clouds and wanted to descend which is when he turned toward me and descended. He said at one point he had me in sight but it was solid IMC. column121: This submission is not to report and accident; rather a serious incident under FAA and NTSB definitions. The day before the flight; my wife and I planned to attend a meeting in ZZZ1. I moved the helicopter out of the hangar and had it fueled to the 1/2 full point. We contacted the church where we were going and obtained permission and authorization to land on the property. Early the morning of the flight; I opened ForeFlight and briefed weather; winds; and the anticipated location; and sent a screenshot of the map and location to my rotorcraft instructor. He and I then had a conversation about the steps and procedures to assess the location once I arrived; and we discussed how to set up for the landing. At XA:00 my wife and I met our friends at the ZZZ airport; performed the preflight; calculated a weight and balance; loaded up in the helicopter and headed for ZZZ1. The weather was excellent with good visibility and cool temperatures in the 50's to 60's. After the 20 min flight; upon arriving at our landing zone; I circled twice as a part of our reconnaissance and did our steps of the 600 ft. recon: size; surrounding; surface; slope; safety and then the 300 ft. recon: wind; wires; way in; way out; where to auto. The landing was normal and I secured the helicopter and we attended the meeting and luncheon. After the luncheon; I went out to the helicopter and started my preflight. During my walk around; I walked out to the road next to the church and looked in all directions. I observed wires to the north across the highway; to the east I observed wires; the church building was to our south; and I cleared the area to the west visually; and saw it was open and unobstructed; the wind was from the west. Once the preflight was complete; I recalculated the weight and balance; all was good; we were more than 200 lbs. under the gross weight limit; and with the temperature in the mid 60s; performance showed to be real good; so we loaded back in the helicopter. After going over the passenger briefing and seeing that all passengers were buckled up and ready I started the helicopter. After all checklist items were completed; and the warmup was accomplished; I lifted into a stable hover; maneuvered up and out toward the highway. Once again I looked for any traffic; and noted that the intended flight path was into the wind; and to the west; was clear and unobstructed. As we were in the hover; I pushed forward cyclic and just as we started a normal takeoff; my front seat passenger said 'WIRE' and I suddenly saw a wire just ahead of us! I immediately applied aft cyclic and pulled up collective. I felt the impact with the wire; and I identified that the center of the highway was clear with zero traffic. I initiated an immediate landing. Approximately 2-3 seconds after not clearing the wire; we were on the ground; and I recall the landing as straight and level; firm and smooth. I shutdown the helicopter; made sure all passengers were out safely and well clear of the helicopter and off the highway. I then secured the helicopter. Next I installed the ground handling wheels on the helicopter and with the help of my passenger; we pushed the helicopter off the highway to the north; then 200 ft. up a side road and into my friend's side yard. At that point I was able to take a moment; thankful for all the help and assistance received; and beyond thankful for no injuries. To prevent a recurrence and to avoid this situation in the future: I contacted my flight instructor and walked through the incident scenario; and I have discussed how to avoid this situation in the future. This incident could have been avoided or prevented by driving by vehicle instead of flying. Also; this incident could have been prevented by performing and executing a confined area takeoff; thus avoiding areas that might have lines and wires. I did walk the area to be used for my takeoff path during my preflight; and I had already performed my 600 ft. and 300 ft. recon prior to landing; so by asking a larger area; and looking closer and further down the takeoff are; might have been of value.

column121: I am reporting my misinterpretation of the COVID relief provided by SFAR 118-1; which resulted in my acting as PIC beyond by required flight review date.My last flight review was in Month X 2018; so normally I would need another one by Month X 2020. But I saw a headline online (maybe from [organization] or another similar site) that the end dates had been extended due to COVID relief; so I didn't worry about the expiration too much - many official agencies have been extending deadlines for things like driver's license renewals etc.; and I assumed FAA had done the same.  So I flew once in Month Y and once in Month Z; the last flight being to take my plane to a maintenance shop for its annual.I then started thinking about getting a flight review; so I decided to read SFAR 118-1 to determine exactly what relief the FAA had provided and whether it would last until my plane was ready.  To my surprise; there were requirements about recent experience; type of operation; the need to take Wings courses; etc. - it was much more complicated than just an extension of time.But I determined that I did meet the requirements; provided I took the required Wings courses; I decided that both getting my plane back from an annual when it was finished; and traveling to a flight review were operations required by the FAR's and were thus permitted.  The annual took longer than expected; but I saw headlines that the relief had been extended with SFAR 118-2.  When the plane was ready to be picked up on Month C day 2; I took the required Wings courses and flew my aircraft back from the maintenance base; thinking that I had until Month C day 31 to complete a BFR.Then on Month C day 14 while preparing for my flight review later that day; I carefully read SFAR 118-2 so I could explain to the CFI how I had adhered to it. At that point I realized that while its relief should have applied to the end of my plane's annual; the delay in the annual's completion plus the fact that the FAA's further extensions did not apply to me meant that I had exceeded the relief allowed by SFAR 118.To summarize; the SFAR is new and complicated and I mis-interpreted it despite a good-faith effort to comply.I think the substance of the SFAR is reasonable now that I understand it; and although it's vague in places; I understand that it's an emergency regulation; so it doesn't seem too bad.  I think what would have helped me is a requirement that; in order to use the relief offered by SFAR 118; one of the required Wings courses should have been a tutorial on SFAR 118 itself.My flights past the Flight Review deadline were uneventful and I am of course no longer flying until my next Flight Review is complete (I started it on Month C day 14 as stated but the flight portion was delayed due to weather).  I doubt that SFAR 118 will be relevant much longer; but I think adding a Wings course the next time some complicated new SFAR comes out would go a long way towards increasing compliance and understanding.

column121: Please consider changing/eliminating the Deer Valley One procedure!The Deer Valley One obstacle departure is improbable if not impossible in a high-performance airplane.1. Chart does not tell you how close the turn is.2. Turn needs to be completed by 1.6 nm from end of runway! This alone should never never be permitted.3. Turn radius at 200 kts. is likely about 1.3 nm.4. 400 ft. V2 +10 flaps up igniters off Venr takes about 2nm min. And way longer in this scenario.5. And wait until you add what happened to me; a traffic call for departing traffic on parallel runway in the direction of my needed turn.6. That took time to find and alter course to avoid the traffic that was about 500 ft. away at the same altitude!6b. That traffic prohibited a turn to [Heading] 336 as required to occur at about 100 ft. if I was to make the turn in time.7. Then the TCAS resolution screen took time to resolve that first conflict.8. Then the instant that screen was resolved; a second additional 'traffic traffic' call occurred for another item of traffic that I could never visually acquire. Box said above and slightly ahead as I recall. Right near my course; so it was a serious safety concern.9. Then the second TCAS screen took time to resolve that second traffic call.10. Now it's finally time for 400 ft. V2 + 10; flaps up igniters off; recall Venr.11. By this time I'm coming upon 5;000 ft. considering engaging the autopilot; but the Flight Director is not aligned because so close and capturing.12. Stuff it down to capture; but overshot 5;000 ft. slightly.13. And now it's finally time to do the turn; but ATC asked what's up.Well ...How can you design a turn that needs to be completed in 1.6nm which would mean it must be started at about 100 ft. AGL = unsafe & no jet should turn before 400 ft. as trained.And look at the chart; no indication how close that is.And compounding my situation is that the PXR VOR was out of service.I submit it's impossible in a high performance airplane. Do it in the sim without telling the pilot in advance and with and without being a regular at the field; and I estimate you'll get max 10% compliance. column121: Aircraft X; ZZZZ-ZZZ1 was the continuation of a planned [refueling stop] for ZZZ-ZZZ1. Thus the passengers remained on the plane while there was a crew change and fueling. The crew inbound from ZZZ reported that the APU failed multiple start attempts after landing. ZZZZ Maintenance was working to fix the APU and was in and out of the cockpit and the lower E&E bay.Upon boarding the aircraft my FO requested that external air be connected to the aircraft. After some time we were told that air conditioned air was not available; as the airport had 'switched' over to heat. Wanting to get some (any) airflow on the aircraft we requested that it be connected. Again after some time we were informed that no external air was available at the particular gate. At that point we requested a start-cart unit be connected so that we could use it to run the packs. Eventually this was accomplished; but only after the passengers had been onboard without any cabin airflow for an extended time; perhaps 90 minutes.Early upon arriving in the cockpit; I called dispatch to inform her of the problem and to let her know that we'd keep her in the loop as maintenance worked the problem. During our initial time in the cockpit the two mechanics were coming and going and I multiple times; offered to get out of the cockpit to allow them access to the displays as they worked the problem. Eventually; I left as they were paying no attention to social distancing; often reaching over us to access the FMC keypad. Though they were wearing masks; they were often pulling them down to talk on the radio or the phone. Multiple times I had to ask them to replace their masks over their mouth and nose. I felt they were too focused on their work and forgetting the COVID precautions.After some time; my concern changed from maintenance getting the APU fixed; to them not being able to get it fixed. Normally; I'd have little to no issue operating a flight without an APU; however with the on-going pandemic there are additional considerations. I thus called the dispatcher and let her know of my concerns and asked if she would reach out to the Operations Center OM for what airline plans are for an inop APU in today's environment and to get more information / guidance to aide in our decision making. Eventually; I was informed that the Operations Center OM had simply said that 'We had to get the passengers to ZZZZ1.' This was not information; guidance nor helpful. My responsibilities are to do that safely and given the pandemic we needed more information to help us assess and understand the passenger safety implications. I was VERY disappointed with the lack of understanding; information and support from the Operations Center. Our dispatcher; and her relief; did a FANTASTIC job!I also attempted to find the information related to running the APU during the pandemic. Unfortunately; given the format; there is no way to read the titles without opening each one. It was too time consuming at that time; thus I was unable to access the needed information. The display really needs to be made user-friendly.The Dispatcher was able to coordinate with ZZZZ1 and we were told from the dispatcher that ZZZZ1 had external air and a start cart and could support a no APU operation. I asked that they be informed that we would plan on keeping an engine running until both external electric AND air were connected so as to maintain cabin airflow.We eventually agreed to accept the flight with the APU deferred believing that we had a viable operational plan; no thanks to the Operations Center. Upon arrival in ZZZZ1 there was much confusion; likely due to language barriers. It took some time to understand that there were local rules that prohibited them from connecting external air or a start-cart while an engine was running. Once we shut down the left engine it was +10 minutes before external air was connected to the aircraft.Given the on-going pandemic the key is airflow. Yet it appears there has been no planning or consideration of what to do in the event of an inop APU. I feel that on this flight we completely blew our promise to passengers and employees with regards to airflow and air filtration. I've continued to assess how I could have made better decisions; but can find no guidance or related plans. I'm not sure but perhaps refusing the aircraft and deplaning the passengers would have been safer from a COVID standpoint than leaving them on an aircraft without any airflow for such an extended period. I believe that we need to come up with some clear plans; guidance and actions to support a flight if we are going to operate with an inop APU. Perhaps we need to even ask if given the pandemic and Airline's associated messaging if we should even operate with an inop APU.I'm not sure why ZZZZ was unable to fix the APU; as the ZZZZ1 mechanics were able to identify and fix the problem in less than 30 minutes from block-in!

column121: After takeoff at approximately 1600 ft. there was a loud rumbling and shudder from the right engine with a loss of power from around 98 N1 to 27 N1. No vibrations or exceedances and engine remained running at idle with no response. After the thrust loss in the right engine we treated it as an engine failure and proceeded to clean up the airplane. I declared a Pan Pan Pan and notified ATC of the engine failure. After the airplane was stabilized we leveled at 3000 ft. and started the turn to downwind for the return to the runway. We initially started with the Engine Fire Severe Damage Checklist but switched to the Engine Stall Surge after we realized the engine was running fine at idle. Engine did not respond to throttle movements. I elected to keep it running since there were no vibrations or exceedances. Since the First Officer (FO) had the airplane well in hand I continued planning for the return and Flaps 20 landing. The approach and landing were uneventful and the Fire Brigade was standing by. We shut down the right engine clearing the runway. The Fire Brigade verified the engine and airplane were okay so we taxied to the ramp. Lessons learned: During the cleanup; I missed turning off the auto throttle arm switch hitting my flight director switch instead. Error was caught as FLCH and MCT (Flight Level Change and Maximum Continuous Thrust) was selected after flaps up as the auto throttles started to advance. I originally started in one checklist then switched due to the engine was still providing electrical; pneumatic and hydraulics at idle. Not sure I totally voiced that change to the FO but we did discuss leaving the engine running and agreed it was the best course of action. I used the Performance page in the ACARS to get landing data...it was cumbersome and could lead to errors. I changed the airport to pull up the runways but the fuel was as if we had flown to destination. I was able to change it but prefer the simple charts in the QRH when time is short. All in all; great CRM between us caught errors and made for a good outcome.
column123: After takeoff at approximately 1800 ft. there was a loud bang and the airplane shook as if we hit something. I asked the Captain; 'what was that?' I felt very comfortable with flying the airplane to let the Captain handle most of the managerial issues. We continued planning for the return and Flaps 20 landing. SOP saves the day.
