column121: On arrival into ZZZ from the south; we were vectored off of the ZZZZZ procedure and held high due to traffic. We had been previously queried as to our RVR requirements for [Runway] XXR. We were set up and briefed for CATIII approach to XXR. Just prior to ZZZZZ waypoint; we heard traffic ahead cleared to descend via ZZZZZ arrival landing north. We were then given clearance to descend via the arrival landing north and were unable to meet the new crossing restrictions. Due to 71 knot crosswinds our heading was 320. The vector we were given for descent was 340. This was assumed to be a 360 for descent. As we turned through a heading of 260 ish we were told to make an immediate right turn for restricted airspace. We complied. We continued on the arrival and had an uneventful hand off to approach.I believe that the ATC is currently overworked due to COVID cutbacks. Many communications are being missed in the last months because ATC are covering too many sectors. Our lack of fore warnings regarding the changes to airport configuration left us with inadequate situational awareness. We followed the vectors given to us with incorrect assumptions. I'm grateful that this situation was resolved without incident. My recommendation is that we begin to re-staff ATC to normal pre-COVID operation.
column123: Flight was left high on the ZZZZZ Arrival.   ATIS had us landing on [Runway] XXR.   We were cleared for the ZZZZZX but never informed by ATC that ATIS X special was issued at XA22z we only learned that there was a runway change due from listing to arrival aircraft in front of us.   We were now high for landing [Runway] YYL by 6;000 feet at the same time we were instructed to slow to 190 kts.  We can slow down but not go down at the same time.   We were instructed to fly heading 340 as we descended the controller once again said turn left 340 which we were on and we assumed he wanted us to do a 360 which is common to loose altitude and rejoin the arrival.   He was busy with several other aircraft left high the weather was poor in mild turbulence.  The next call was for us to turn I believe 040 because he said we are going to hit a restricted area.I was heads down retrieving the new ATIS as well and programming the FMS for a different runway.    This was a combination of change of runways; poor weather; and aircraft being left high by two controllers and high winds with an approach to mins.   This was a series of events that lead to an aircraft being out of position.When the weather is poor we cannot skimp on air traffic controllers they need to be tentative to aircraft and where they are going.   If the aircraft is out of position.  It should be quickly realize especially when a runway change has been posted and an aircraft may not have received the special ATIS.

column121: On take off from PLU; an unsafe condition took place that could have resulted in an aircraft collision.PLU's runway mid-point is higher than both thresholds. There's a taxiway that crosses over the southern threshold of the runway. I was departing from the north to the south. I made routine radio calls. Just prior to the midway point; I was off the runway and climbing; but I was not yet high enough to see the other end of the runway. At that point; another aircraft made a radio call that it was crossing the runway. No more than about a second later; I was high enough to see the end of the runway; and I saw the aircraft. It was passing left-to-right from my point of view. I veered left slightly and continued my climb.I don't know if the operator of that aircraft heard my radio call. The operator did not respond to my follow-up call that I was in the air departing and veering to the left. The operator could not have made the crossing threshold call more than a second or two before actually crossing the runway. I suspect the operator did not make a full stop prior to encountering the threshold.Had I experienced any sort of engine problem on my take-off roll or during the very early portion of the climb; the safest action would have been to land straight ahead on the remaining runway. However; in that case; I consider it likely I would have collided with the crossing aircraft.Threshold-crossing aircraft should listen to the radio before approaching the runway; and then should come to a complete stop before crossing the runway; should then only proceed with crossing after hearing no conflicting aircraft.

The FO was already the PF and I asked him to take radios as well. The passenger asked for a cup of water so passenger didn't have to wear the mask because she was 'drinking'. At this point; I sent another message asking for a customer service representative to meet us at the gate in ZZZ1 and explained to the Dispatcher everything the FAs had told me. About 5 minutes after that; the Fwd FA called up again. Again; I told the FO his controls; his radios. The FA then explained that the passenger was now starting to 'scream' on the plane and yelled very loudly; '#@%^! I'm not from [foreign country]!' While doing this; proceeded to flip off both FAs. I again messaged our Dispatcher with this information and now requested Security along with the customer service representative. The FAs and I talked back forth regarding passenger danger level. The passenger was remaining in the seat and making no other threatening gestures; so we did not see the need to declare an Emergency. We continued the flight to ZZZ1 with no further incidences. After landing; I had the FO call Ops just to make sure a customer service representative and security were waiting for us at the gate. Because the passenger had put on the mask and was making no further threatening behavior; we decided to make a note of it and continue. column121: Well; fatigue did play a role.  It slowed us down.  Earlier the hotel we were at started with construction outside at XA:00 am. Could the ERC (event review committee) pleased use all resources to ensure proper procedures and tooling are in place prior to tasks like this one being assigned. ZZZ does not need to be departing west bound departures off of the east side when ZZZ1 TRACON is landing XXR; especially when the weather is marginal like it is today. ZZZ TRACON needs to land the normal arrival runways and if they can't do this due to their staffing then they need to return to a regular schedule.  Most of us here are fed up with what is being asked of us and the safety of the system is quickly eroding to appease the users demands and ZZZ's TRACON staffing.

column121: Aircraft X was vectored to their final approach course approximately 3 to 4 miles in trail of a preceding Aircraft Y. We were VFR conditions but had low ceilings hovering around 1;000 feet. Aircraft weren't coming out of the clouds until a 1 to 2 mile final. When Aircraft X joined the approach they has an absurdly high overtake speed with the Aircraft Y in front of them of 80 plus knots. There was no way separation was ever going to be maintained. When the realization set in of what was happening Local Control issued instructions to cancel the approach and to climb to 3000 feet and to turn 20 degrees to the left.  I began coordination with Departure Control for a handoff with vectors to bring the aircraft back around for another approach. In the meantime Aircraft X advised Local Control that they were minimum fuel and were continuing the approach. Local Control advised me of this; so I canceled the coordination; and redirected my attention to an aircraft awaiting clearance. Then Local Control advised me that Aircraft X was indeed going around with the 20 degree left turn; and 3000 foot altitude assignment. Traffic was light; so I instructed Local Control to climb Aircraft X to 6000 feet and issue a turn to get them into the dispersal area as per our joint agreement. I again initiated coordination with Departure Control for the handoff; with Aircraft X climbing to 6000 feet and on a 100 or 105 heading.Then I came back to the aircraft on Clearance Delivery and had them read back their clearance. During the read back; Departure was trying to call me and say that Aircraft X needed to climb immediately for an aircraft that was departing southeast bound off a satellite airport. I responded that the altitude had been issued and would find out why Aircraft X stopped their climb at 3000 feet. I relayed the information to Local Control as I was receiving it.  Local Control told me that Aircraft X would not accept the climb due to their minimum fuel situation; which I relayed back to Departure. Departure Control requested we ship Aircraft X to them; so that they could maintain separation with the traffic departing the satellite airport which I relayed to Local. Local was able to get Aircraft X to climb to 4;000 feet before shipping them. There was a loss of lateral separation on final approach; but there may have been altitude separation; although I am not sure about that. The problem is that we are struggling with spacing issues on final and even have a collaborative work group established with Approach to resolve these problems. Approach is continually handing Tower these overtakes;  and less than coordinated arrival spacing for departure gaps; but Tower is always held accountable for the consequences of each event. This is the standard here at  even though the separation problem originates with the Approach Controller. Even our local management tends to initially stand behind Approach and their actions while pointing their fingers at the Tower controllers trying to tell us that what we did was incorrect; even though we are only trying our best to prevent an separation error from occurring or getting worse.  Standardize spacing requirements here at 3 miles or required and coordinated arrival spacing distances and never transfer communications of aircraft on final until there is less than a 30 knot overtake speed. In other words; follow the guidance in the 7110.65 and ensure separation before transferring communications to another controller. And on top of this; performance management to ensure controllers are being held accountable to the basic standards.

column121: ZZZ TRACON planned to surrender their ZZZ1; ZZZ2; and ZZZ3 sectors to ZZZ ARTCC initially around XA:00 pm local due to facility cleaning of a COVID-19 positive. Area X (controllers and management) objected to the proposed time frame and was able to push the event back to around XD:00 pm local.Shortly before the XD:00 pm acquisition of airspace from ZZZ TRACON; we learned that there would be no radar service to any of the City satellite airports. We were given the following stipulations: No IFR service to ZZZ4; ZZZ5; ZZZ6; ZZZ7; etc. No VFR Flight Following will be provided in ZZZ TRACON's airspace. Any IFR aircraft not willing to cancel IFR and proceed to their satellite destination VFR without any radar service from ATC will be kept out of ZZZ TRACON's and offered an alternate airport for landing in ZZZ Centers airspace.At XI:04z; ZZZ2 ARTCC called ZZZ ARTCC Sector XY to coordinate a possible emergency situation with Aircraft X. The aircraft (a type) was originally off of ZZZ8 to; as ZZZ1 ARTCC stated; 'Somewhere in the midwest' but changed his destination to ZZZ4 because a service center was located there. The issue affecting the flight was with a fuel pump trying to incorrectly pump fuel to a wing (or tank) that it wasn't supposed to. This was not an emergency at the time but serious enough to change the destination and have the aircraft inspected by maintenance.At XI:07z; the aircraft checked on with ZZZ ARTCC sector XY. As the situation developed; it was discovered through management that if the pilot declared an emergency; it would have no impact on the reduced level of service he would receive from ZZZ TRACON enroute to ZZZ4.Shortly after this time; I relieved CPC [Name] at [Sector] XY and began working the sector. Upon realizing the possible developing situation and the corner that I was being put in; I declared to continue under Article 65 of the 2016 FAA/NATCA CBA. My experience painted a picture of a night time; single-engine and (possibly single pilot); IFR flight being operated in IMC; with a fuel pump issue that likely could become an emergency situation; wanting to land at an airport that would have no radar service for the last 45 miles of flight; IFR or VFR. At some point Management requested the pilot provide an alternate airport. In a brief discussion with the pilot on the frequency; I suggested ZZZ because in my mind; it's the only airport that would have any kind of radar service. As the pilot reluctantly continued on to ZZZ4; he was forced to descend to find VFR conditions. It wasn't until he broke out of the clouds below 4;000 feet that he announced he could continue VFR. This now meant that this aircraft had to fly the last 45 miles to ZZZ4 at 3;000 feet. Any level of safety that altitude provides to an aircraft (in distress or otherwise) was forcibly sacrificed. Additionally; to remain clear of the Class Bravo; the flight was vectored to the east of side of the city toward the ZZZZZ way point and then northbound. The pilot mentioned his plan was to fly north from there and then turn west toward ZZZ4 and call the tower when he got 10 miles out. This added additional miles and flight time to the situation. Again: Single-engine (possibly single-pilot); night; IMC; with a mechanical issue and no radar service.At XI:33z; the pilot informed me that he could proceed VFR to ZZZ4; and radar service was terminated by ZZZ ARTCC.Other factors during this ZZZ TRACON COVID cleaning period:VFR aircraft off of ZZZ4 enroute to ZZZ9 could not maintain VFR and needed a short range IFR clearance with an RNAV approach clearance.Volunteer (call sign unknown) aircraft inbound to ZZZ9 requested and received radar vectors to the ILS [runway] X approach.Finally; at the end of the cleaning period; ZZZ TRACON suggested that ZZZ ARTCC just keep the airspace for the rest of the night which was agreed to by ZZZ ARTCC.Consider the impacts of Covid-19 cleaning; not to just the affected facilities but also the flying community.

column121: While enroute and at cruise altitude of 39;000 feet; with between 1:00-1:15 hrs of flight time remaining of a 3:40 hour flight: my stomach began to feel queasy; I started sweating; and in a short time felt the urgent need for a bowel movement. I advised the Captain of my need to use the lavatory and contacted the flight attendants. I quickly got out of my seat due to the urgency in my stomach and went to the door. When I stood up rapidly; I felt a rush of nausea as well as feeling light-headed. When the flight attendants knocked; I opened the door. The next thing I know I am sitting on the galley floor with a nurse sitting next taking care of me; with a doctor assisting. The doctor and nurse monitored my vital signs; which initially both blood pressure and oxygen levels were low. I began to feel normal shortly after they had me drink some water and ½ cup of orange juice; utilize the onboard oxygen and began to administer 2 bags of IV fluid. Blood pressure and oxygen levels returned to normal.I told them that I had been fasting and had not eaten for nearly 2 days. I also said I could tell I was dehydrated due to the limited amount of urine output on our first lavatory break 1-1/2 hours into the flight. Both agreed that this was probably a cause for what happened and called it a vagal response; which can cause a person to faint.Upon landing; we were met by paramedics at the gate. They took my vital signs to include a blood glucose test. After completing their assessment; they said I was fine and there was no need to take me to the hospital. After being released from the paramedics; the entire crew of went to the crew van and the overnight hotel.Medical Assistance provided a Hospital for me to be seen; to ensure I was medically able to fly (as a passenger) back to ZZZ. I went to the Hospital and received: initial screening; EKG; and blood tests to include Electrolytes; Hemoglobin; Triage Cardiac screen 'CUANTITATIVO; (INCLUYE TROPONINA I; BNP; MIOGLOBINA; CKMB Y DIMEROS D)'The doctor stated that I was in excellent shape and saw no problems or issues with any of my test results. I was released with no further action nor medications required.

column121: This event had to do with both Primary Flight Displays airspeed indications giving crew error readouts. The aircraft had been sitting outside during the snowstorm we had in the northeast. We followed deice and anti-ice procedures per Cold Weather Ops. Checklist. Passing through 210 kts (211) both IAS indications turned red indicating we were in a overspeed indication. Both landing gear and flaps/slat were verified up by checklist usage and visually from the cabin. With our resources we verified IAS were correct even though they were indicating in the Red. We ran appropriate checklist and verified aircraft performance charactertics utilizing all aircraft instrumentation. We advised the maintenance (coordinating with cessna) and agreed continuing on to destination would be the right decision with our situation. Both of us agreed with solution and agreed we we're safe to continue. Upon slowing in to ZZZ at 210 kts both Primary Flight Display IAS indications returned to Green Normal color. We landed with all normal indications. With my XX years of aviation commercial experience; I don't agree with the Cold Weather Checklist. It tells us to extend flaps to 35 for de-ice and 0 degrees for anti-ice. My experience has always kept Flaps up during both these procedures; so to prevent fluid getting on full flap area that sits under wing when retracted. Selecting Flaps once nearing runway so to prevent snow and slush from getting on Full Flap area would be a better practice; while protecting a major portion of flap area from icing conditions waiting to takeoff.Suggest looking at how we perform de/anti-icing procedures on the fleet.

column121: Normal (very early) departure.  We taxied out; ran checklists; lined up for takeoff; when I added power; we got the takeoff configuration warning horn.  We both saw immediately the flaps were not set. I notified tower we needed to exit the runway.  Exited the runway at the first taxiway.  I don't think our ground speed got above 25-40 (?) knots.  Set the flaps; re-ran the before takeoff checklist; notified the Tower ready; and completed the flight normally.Haven't been flying as much as normal.  First flight; very early morning.  Possible distraction(s). This is a humbling event.  I don't think I've done it in X0 years of flying.  There was nothing specific that I remember; but something interfered with our regular routine or 'flow'.   I did the 'after start' checklist and missed it; and we both did the 'before takeoff' checklist aloud and missed it.   I thought I was checking the position and the indicators carefully; but obviously I need to be more stringent; and will be in the future.
column123: When cleared for takeoff; and starting to line up and advancing throttles; a configuration aural warning activated because the flaps were in the up position. Neither of us realized the flaps in the incorrect position before taking the runway and I immediately took control of the aircraft and returned the thrust levers to the idle position; disconnected the auto throttle and cleared the runway; never exceeding 10-12 knots (still at taxi speed). Once clear of the runway; I commanded the flap lever to 1 and first officer moved lever to 1 and we got the green light. Ran the entire before takeoff checklist again and was cleared back onto runway for an uneventful takeoff and climbout.I had completed a 3 day trip late the previous night and this was an early XA30 departure time with minimum required rest. I stayed at the hotel and was interrupted in my sleep routine at around midnight by a noisy neighbor conducting a phone call in the room next to mine. Maybe I wasn't fully rested and still a little groggy.  My expectation was that the flap lever was placed to 1 after engine start and I was used to that routine so I didn't register that the flaps were not in the correct position. This was the first time this has occurred for me.Only suggestion is to double and triple check all items; especially configuration items; and to use the crew concept better.

column121: Flight was uneventful until cleared the ILSZ RWY 36 via direct QIT VOR at 18;000 feet assigned. A large build up was directly situated over QIT therefore ATC was asked for a left deviation due to the buildup. During the decent briefing the approach and contingencies were briefed; however; a storm disrupting the approach was not anticipated. A left deviation was started and I decided to proceed direct to point D111G as the best course of action. The FO had his terrain display in terrain mode allowing me to see any conflicts ahead. The FO correctly pointed out that going direct point D254I would be a better course of action and allow more time for the approach. I agreed and we asked for and was given direct to that point by ATC. At this point the situation was less than ideal. The weather was mostly cloudy with only brief glimpses of the terrain. I had the altitude of 10;500 feet in my mind thinking I was heading for my original point (D111G) when in reality we were required to be at 14;200 feet point D254I. I had started the descent when the FO pointed out the error and I immediately started to climb. At this point we were still not on the approach due to the weather. We were still proceeding direct to D254I. I was also slowing and configuring for the landing. I ended up disconnecting the autopilot in order to reestablish myself on to a stable approach. The terrain display never showed any conflicts and no verbal warnings of the system was encountered. I knew approximately where the aircraft was at all times. My error was in the decent altitude while forced off of the approach due to weather. We eventually did get on the approach; were stable when we broke out of the weather and had an uneventful landing. The large cell situated over the UIO VOR forced an unprepared diversion around it resulting in an off route decent in order to land. This in turn resulted in attaining a lower than desired altitude in heavily mountainous terrain. This was my first time into UIO. Although I reviewed the required airport familiar special qualification briefing; in this situation it was not adequate. I consider myself very experienced in mountainous terrain and I believe this particular field should require a Check Airman checkout. 'Picking the brain for gotchas' would have been invaluable.

column121: Everything during the preflight; engine start; and taxi out went normal. During the taxi out our clearance was picked up with a 5 minute void time. We had calm winds and [Runway] XX is the calm wind runway so we had briefed and planned for a [Runway] XX departure. There was work on the taxiway so it was going to require a back taxi to the end of [Runway] XX at an uncontrolled field. Coming out of the ramp we informed over the CTAF what our intentions were and taxied and held short of the runway. While holding short of the runway with some traffic in the pattern for [Runway] XX and a plane inbound on the GPS [Runway] XY doing a practice approach we realized we wouldn't get out in the 5 minutes. I put Center back in on Comm 1 and had my Captain on Comm 2 monitoring the CTAF. I asked Center for an extension explaining why we need it and they gave us another 10 minutes before the void time. I put the CTAF back on one and asked the Captain if I missed any important calls and he said no. We watched the plan in the pattern land [Runway] XX and I informed over the CTAF that we would hold short of the runway until the guy on GPS approach went missed and that we would then be back taxiing for full length takeoff on [Runway] XX. No one over the CTAF says anything else. We complete all checklists and are ready to go. After the GPS approach guy goes missed I inform over the CTAF that we are taking the runway and back taxiing on [Runway] XX. No one says anything. I looked right towards the [Runway] XX end and final and cleared that direction and the captain looked left towards the [Runway] XY end and final and cleared that direction. We then began our back taxi. During the back taxi I informed again over the CTAF that we were still back taxiing for a [Runway] XX departure. Nothing was said over the CTAF. We get to the end and line up for a full length departure. I inform over the CTAF that we are taking off [Runway] XX with a right turn out on the SID for a north departure. We wait a few seconds and nothing on the CTAF. We then began our takeoff roll with nothing out of the ordinary through 110ish kts. The runway was kinda of rounded and approaching V1 and cresting the rounded part of the runway I noticed something moving to the right of the runway. I said 'what's that?' Looked back down and it was V1 call out. At this time we realize it's an airplane that took off Runway XY and is making a left turn to our right. He was already a few hundred feet off the runway centerline and we were passed V1 so we continued with a normal departure sequence. During the departure we heard someone on the ground asking over the CTAF if the other plane had a radio. No response. It was asked a couple times with no response. We were asked by the person on the ground if we saw the plane. I was PM (Pilot Monitoring) so I responded with a yes and we asked for a radio check and were told that our radio was working. The other airplane finally responded saying he made at least 3 takeoff calls. The guys on the ground said that no calls were made from the other aircraft. He insisted again that he made the takeoff calls. Another plane flying just past the field who was on the CTAF also informed that he heard no takeoff calls from the other departing plane. We made a final call informing which direction our departure was and through what altitude we were climbing. Switched over to Center and had a standard flight the rest of the way. The cause was GA plane with a possible broken radio and or what seems to be more likely a wrong frequency tuned in was the biggest problem. If we had heard another plane wanting to takeoff in the opposite direction we would have never even started the back taxi let alone the takeoff. I'm not really sure what can be done about planes with no radios; broken radios; or wrong frequency's. We did everything to our power correctly and we were in no hurry with the extended void and were taking our time. Maybe operating even slower we could haveavoided being around the runway at the same time as this other plane. Hard to pin point something when everyone who was on frequency knew our intentions and what we were doing.

column121: On [a] flight to XNA we were cleared for the visual traffic pattern to land Runway 16. The Captain as the pilot flying had properly briefed the visual approach; to include the obstacles in the vicinity and highest obstacle on the approach plate. On right base; the Captain turned autopilot off with flaps 3 and gear down. I announced visual contact/no factor on the highest obstacles out the right window - a set of towers. We continued to slow and configure for landing and maintain an altitude of more than 1;000 ft. AGL. We received a caution from the GPWS; followed by a PULL UP verbal command. The Captain took the appropriate actions and immediately increased the airplane's altitude. We were in daytime visual conditions; and in accordance with company policy; determined we were still in a safe position to stabilize and conduct a safe landing after clearing the obstacle. We finished the turn to final; configured the aircraft for flaps 5 landing; completed the before landing checklist; were fully stable by 1;000 ft. and in a safe position to land the aircraft. Upon landing; we debriefed the situation; reviewing the approach plate for any obstacles. At more than 1;000 ft. AGL and no visual contact with an obstacle; we were unsure why the GPWS gave us the PULL UP command; but agreed that it was the most appropriate and safest action to respond to the command as we didGPWS PULL UP verbal command resulted in appropriate action of increasing aircraft altitude.A visual traffic pattern is one of the most difficult approaches we fly. I would suggest additional training during initial and recurrent training on distances and altitudes for different types of visual traffic patterns. I will personally work to improve my awareness as the pilot flying to ensure 1;500 ft. AGL on downwind and the 3:1 descent path ratio throughout the visual traffic pattern. I will review my flying skills to ensure I am flying this way as well. While I believe we took the appropriate action both during the event and after in the debrief; I will use this as a learning experience to ensure I am always a safe and skilled pilot.

column121: I departed ZZZ with the intent to ferry it to ZZZ1.  At the time of departure; weather was reported as overcast at 1;800 feet; visibility 10SM.  Field elevation is 2;500 feet.  Highest obstacle of the enroute corridor was indicated as 3;325 feet; per ForeFlight profile.  Reported weather allowed for a 1;000 foot clearance of the highest obstacle.  Upon departing and climbing to 3;200 feet; I could clearly see over all the hill tops along my intended flight path.  Approximately 10 minutes into the flight; clouds started to form and spill over from hill tops to the north and west into the adjoining valleys.  I executed a turn to avoid the clouds.  I decided I would return to ZZZ.  Suddenly; clouds started to form all around me.  The area around me was mountainous covered with thick forest. I felt that IMC was imminent so I initiated the IMC procedure.  I leveled the aircraft and started a climb; after adjusted power & airspeed settings.  I passed through the bottoms of 2 clouds as I started to set up the GPS for an instrument approach into ZZZ.  A moment later I was in a pocket clear of clouds with a large field next to a residence below me.  I decided it better to land VFR in the field than to continue IFR back to ZZZ.  I performed a descending orbit towards the field to get a clear picture of any/all possible obstacles.  A safe landing was performed without incident.  Notifications were made to Center.  After waiting approximately 2 hours; I was able to safely complete the ferry flight. Become IFR current within company.

column121: Just after completing a climb to 12;000 ft in an attempt to get above an icing layer; the company issued iPad mount fell off the windscreen on to the floor. Initially; I reacted to this by reaching down to pick it up; but simultaneously noticed the G600 displayed a GPS failure indication on the moving map side of the screen. At the same time TAWS (terrain awareness and warning system) gave an aural alert 'TAWS NOT AVAILABLE'. There were no additional audible alerts or visual annunciations. I initially thought this was simply a GPS signal failure and was starting to react accordingly; I then observed that the aircraft had entered a descending turn and immediately reacted with an unusual attitude in IMC recovery procedure. Given that the aircraft was in continuous light turbulence; in the clouds; at night; I was momentarily completely focused on ensuring the aircraft remained in a controlled attitude. A few moments latter I began taking stock of what I did and did not have. I observed the GMX200 screen off; GNS530 screen off; the primary GTX330 was off; and the autopilot was off. The G600 was giving associated GPS/AHRS and GAD43 failures. There were no other annunciations on the primary panel; and no audible alerts. My next focus was to re-establish navigation to my next known waypoint; the ZZZ VOR. I had previously tuned the ZZZ VOR into the NAV1 and NAV2; so I had manual navigation and DME via NAV2. Since the GNS430 and secondary GTX330 appeared operable; I immediately squawked 7600 as I had been out of contact with ZZZ1 Center (which was on COM1) and had obviously deviated heading/altitude at the beginning of the incident a few moments earlier. Not knowing what was happening to cause these failures and what might be failing next; setting the squawk may at the very least alert Center that I am having a problem. I also needed a few moments to sort out which frequency I needed to be on; as at this point the stress level was high enough I could not remember the frequency. I had to retrieve the iPad which was still on the floor in order to look at the chart screen for the frequency. Once back in contact with ZZZ1 Center I described the situation as best I could: some kind of electrical and/or communication failure as most of my avionics were now off. I elected for a diversion to ZZZ; now about 17nm away; and worry about troubleshooting the problem on the ground rather in the air in IMC at night. I was given vectors for a visual approach and landed without further incident.Having time to analyze the situation; and noting after landing/parking that the Avionics 1 & 2 were able to be switch back on; I conclude that the root cause of the systems associated with Avionics Bus 1 failing was from the iPad mount falling off the windscreen and hitting the switch on the way down. In personal reflection; I can recognize the irony that simply reaching over to check the avionics switches would have likely resolved the issue. But; the totality of the circumstances I had been suddenly faced with: 'an unexpected flight attitude deviation following an otherwise innocuous distraction; an initial observation of having a GPS signal failure'. Normally a failure of the GNS530/430; even if the failure was a complete loss of the entire unit; would not have resulted in the loss of the autopilot modes. Typically any normal failure of the autopilot is also accompanied by an audible alert. I had no immediate indication that the autopilot was off until observing the aircraft starting a descending turn. This precipitated the human factor contribution to the scenario of dealing with an otherwise unexplainable loss of avionics and uncommanded attitude deviation and no indication to which trained emergency checklist actions would be a prudent course of action. Overall troubleshooting based on system knowledge is a higher level brain function and at the time I did not have the luxury of 'stepping back' to think what might be going wrong. All that to say; there are no checklists specifically for an avionics failure (such as the switch some how getting turned off) or even what to do if the GPS fails. The assumed reactions remain in the realm of pilot knowledge and ability to troubleshoot the problem in lieu of following a checklist... in all likelihood with the assumption that the autopilot is still functional. This isn't a suggestion that we make a new checklist item; but rather the addition of random failure modes such as this during training to either establish situational memory or reinforce what to do if you don't know what to do. Finally; the root culprit of the situation... the iPad mount. This has been an ongoing 'issue' that has been simply tolerated by Company pilots. It hasn't been reported likely because we didn't think it was a big problem; would have never imagined it would lead to any problem; or have not been explicitly told that it is a problem if it occurs. There is also the ongoing back and forth with pilots who do not like having the mount and will remove it from the windscreen. The result is the mount ends up on the floor; getting dirty and damaged to the point that many of the suction cups do not effectively stay on the windscreen. In fact; in talking with another co-worker I discovered that this exact scenario happened to him during an AM departure a few weeks earlier and had hit both Avionics 1 & 2 switches. Since he saw it (and had the benefit of being VFR during the day) he just turned the switches back on and remounted the iPad. It has been my observation the suction cups seem to most frequently fail when climbing into colder temperatures; but this is not always the case. At this point; I believe it is safe to say that the current mounting system does not work... either by nature of system or as a result of the poor care and handling it as received over the past year or so. I will have to admit; the iPad mount coming off is something that I have observed and didn't report... and frankly should have reported and made a big stink over sooner. But I am now: at this point I do not believe the current iPad mounting system to be either effective nor safe.

column121: In ZZZZ loading was taking too long so I stopped our duty day because at our arrival point we would be over our legal XX hours.  I asked the company for hotel rooms for the crew.  The Handler informed us we would need to stay in a government designated hotel and undergo COVID-19 testing or stay on the airplane.  We chose the hotel.  The handler and a [company representative] informed us the immigration service of foreign country denied our crew entry into the country and we were not permitted to leave the airplane.  I asked the Directors of Operations; Safety; and Standards; and the Chief Pilots if this would be legal Rest for our upcoming Part 121 assignment and got no response from any of them prior to our new (after minimum rest time) departure time; so I asked my crew if they felt safe to fly and they all said yes; we departed. We were even warned not to leave the aircraft by the handler to walk over to our other company airplane on the ramp as it could subject us to serious consequences if we were detected by Immigration.   When we realized we had no alternate other than to obtain our Rest on board the aircraftA lack of planning on company Operations part in terms of how the Crew would be provided with normal hotel rest facilities should they get stuck in this location as we did.  Even if you book a hotel if Immigration won't let you leave to go to it it is of no use.I kept my crew 100 percent in the loop as to all communications and any of them were free to decline the 121 assignment after we obtained Rest on the airplane.  All of them told me they felt safe and were ready to fly.Plan for more than adequate time to load an airplane at this location.  X.X hours were allocated obviously that was not nearly enough.
column123: Though we were as a flight crew rested; alert and fully capable of conducting the flight safely; local authorities had denied our entry into the country. column121: Prior to entering the ZZZ Center airspace; during cruise at FL330; I had just returned back to my seat as 'as pilot monitoring' after using the rest room.  As a matter of practice; I read aloud the FMA parameters (which all appeared normal); upon taking my seat and assuming the role as 'pilot monitoring.'  Immediately after that; the Captain had also returned back to his seat as 'pilot flying' from his rest break; and exchanged his position with the IRO who had been occupying the captain's seat as the 'pilot flying' during the captain's break. At that time the Captain noticed that the aircraft had momentarily climbed to and leveled off at an indicated altitude of 33;500. The Captain immediately commenced a descent and returned the aircraft back to its original altitude of FL330; without any further consequence.We had become aware of the altitude when the Captain brought it to our attention In the cockpit. However; it was on the following day in ZZZ1 during my deadhead trip; that the captain recollected the event details and informed me that we had a deviation that may warrant the filing of a report. I believe that the aircraft may have climbed 500 feet and leveled off by the inadvertent touching of the altitude selector knob; either by the handling of the clipboard or by using disinfectant wipes in close proximity to the FCP; by one of the crew members; while getting in and out of the seats.  None of the crew members is sure of what caused the movement of the altitude selector knob and the gain in altitude.  The Captain immediately commenced a descent and returned the aircraft back to its original altitude of FL330; without any further consequence. As crew members; we were all equally surprised by the inadvertent deviation in altitude. Exercising greater level of situational awareness by all crew members; increased monitoring of the FMA; especially during the exchange of pilot seats and exchange of pilot roles while commencing and ending of crew rest periods.  Exercising extreme care during handling of clipboard and using disinfectant wipes in vicinity of FCP during flight.
column123: Aircraft wandered off of assigned altitude in excess of 300 feet in cruise flight. [It was identified] when the Captain pointed it out. Advise all flight crews to use extreme caution when moving things around or cleaning the FCP inflight.

column121: My duty day started in ZZZZ.  I was part of a 2-man crew; scheduled to operate ZZZZ-ZZZZ1-ZZZZ.  At the time I left ZZZZ; the TAF for ZZZZ had a small period of low visibility in the forecast; which was to occur while I was on the ground in ZZZZ1; and the weather was forecasted to improve to be above CAT I minimums prior to my arrival back into ZZZZ.  While on the ground in ZZZZ1; I was checking the ZZZZ weather and found out that the ceilings were WELL below CAT I minimums.  I called Flight Operations for a briefing and was told the same thing.  I decided to delay the flight for an hour to watch the ZZZZ weather and to 'time' my arrival into ZZZZ to coincide with the forecasted lifting of the weather.  Flight Operations then called me back and asked for me to delay another 30 minutes so we would arrive 30 minutes after the period of low weather in ZZZZ - I agreed; as it was a good idea.  I also knew that I was currently at an outstation where I really have zero options for adequate rest if we got stuck there since we can't deplane the aircraft without mandatory COVID tests and quarantine until test results come back negative.  So; in reality; flying to ZZZZ1 is really a gamble in the first place but; for sure; I knew that staying there wasn't even an option. I eventually departed ZZZZ1 at the newly determined departure time and flew towards ZZZZ.Through the use of ACARS ATIS updates as well as messages to/from the company - it was determined that the weather in ZZZZ had not cooperated with the forecast.  Visibility was 125 meters to 225 meters - well below CAT I minimums.  I talked with my First Officer and we decided to enter high altitude holding and set a 'bingo' fuel number for us to know when it was time to have to go to the alternate airport; ZZZZ2. We burned through our holding fuel and were forced to divert to our published alternate airport. That's where the real fun began.  This is the point where we found out that an alternate that looks good on paper doesn't always work in actual practice.  We landed; parked in spot XX; and sat; and waited; and sat; and waited some more.  It took almost an hour just to get a set of stairs brought to the aircraft - and took an equally long amount of time to get a GPU and wheel choked so I could release the parking brake. At this point; I became doubtful that we would have the duty time to allow us to continue to ZZZZ1 - and that feeling was mirrored back to me by Flight Operations on my first phone call to them.   A plan for crew hotels was then started; as well as the continued effort to contact our 'handler' there in ZZZZ2.  Next came the biggest issue...Customs.  The handler first started telling me that we can't stay there because we can't clear customs 'in their country'.  I reminded him that we were scheduled to land in ZZZZ; which is the same country - but he didn't care.  Clearly; the thought of a crew having to get rest at this published alternate airport hasn't been approached before?   Finally; after 4 hours on the ground; the handler comes to the aircraft; asks me to shut it down so he can take us to a hotel close to the airport.  I complied; and as soon as I carried my personal items downstairs; I was told by that same handler that it would be another hour before customs can clear us and to please wait on the aircraft - which was now shut down.  I opened the aircraft again and that's where we waited for almost 2 more hours before the handler came back to tell us that there is 100% no way we were gonna clear customs there at that airport.  At this point; we had absolutely no choice but to stay on the aircraft.  After talking it over with my crew; we decided that the only option would be to depart ZZZZ2 as soon as we were legally able to do so - even though sitting on the aircraft isn't actually 'rest' - we had no other options.  I talked with Flight Operations and they told me that we could depart at XA:00Z; which was another 3 hours from then.  Out of lack of betterideas; we agreed; got the plane ready; and blocked out at XA:01Z for ZZZZ.   The real point in this report is to illustrate that so many of our flight plans might look OK on paper; but when it comes time to actually put contingencies into practice; the plan immediately dissolves - leaving crews stranded without the ability to legally continue operating; and without the ability to obtain legal rest.  Vetting of our 'approved alternates' certainly needs to take place.Not properly vetting filed; 'approved;' alternate airports to facilitate crew egress between aircraft and legal rest facilities.Worked tirelessly with the ZZZZ2 handler to try to secure rest facilities for my crew.  When that failed; I worked with my crew and with Flight Operations to determine when we could 'legally' leave.Time and manpower needs to be put forth in this company to actually find out what processes would need to take place at alternate airports or at intermediate stops to allow crew members a place to get safe; legal rest when needed.

column121: Climbing out of ZZZZ to ZZZZ1 we were clear to unrestricted FL340. Empty of cargo we got to cruise level quick. We observed a pressure differential message and a rise 8.5 to 9.2 and up; as well as the cabin altitude rapidly climbing above schedule 7;000 ft quick; 8;000 ft and 9;000 ft at that point I told everybody; ' put the oxygen mask on' and verify the outflow valve. I pulled the QRH and read to comply with the rest of the procedure for level 3 cabin altitude while the Captain was at the controls and the radios. I selected the cabin pressure on manual and turn the knob slowly and fast and there was no response. Since we had no control of the cabin altitude that kept on climbing; the Captain on the radio requested a descend to 10;000 feet follow by the wads and requested land back in ZZZZ with runway in use and weather. We recycle the air system controller and try the cabin pressure controller knob again no response. Then set on auto for the landing in ZZZZ Runway XXR + 3;000 meters visibility night conditions. After landing I verified the outflow open and pressure differential. We parked on apron. During the flight we were asked by the controller if we where having an emergency; The Captain answered: 'no; but we were experiencing a pressurization problem and we needed to descend'. On the ground the mechanic showed us the lower pressure relief valve stuck clogged with insulation. I am not sure how to prevent this event from occurring again; but next time I get a clearance to climb unrestricted and I am close to another heavy aircraft; climbing on the departure maybe request a vector. But that was the furthest on my mind; because of night flying and terrain the only thing I could think about at that moment was climbing at a good rate.

My ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Broadcast) showed traffic 500 ft. below me; 12 miles out at my 1:30 position. This caught my attention because this condition indicates we will pass laterally very close. I heard Center alert the other aircraft about the traffic (my aircraft); but he was unable to get a visual. Center indicated my altitude was 7;200 ft. I turned on my taxi and landing lights to make my aircraft more visible to the other aircraft. We passed with 500 ft. vertical and about 150 ft. lateral separation. The other pilot called me on the phone later that day because he was concerned about a near miss (although he did get a visual on my aircraft just before we passed). His ADS-B indicated 150 ft. separation. My flights showed my ADS-B altitude 350 ft. lower than what it actually was; which was the cause for the other pilot's concern. I am reporting this to my avionics shop for repair; and in the future will pick up flight following earlier in the flight for better communication.

column121: I landed on Runway XX and my airspeed was approximately 76 knots. As soon as I touched ground; I slowed down in order to follow Controller directions. The Controller asked if I could make Taxiway Alpha X. By that point; I had already passed the taxiway and responded to the Controller in which I stated negative. The Controller's commands were to make a left turn at Taxiway Golf. I then proceeded to slow down and pulled back on the yoke to the turn left onto Taxiway Golf. Before fully exiting the runway; the tires of the plane became stuck on the snow ground and I was not able to move forward. The Controller questioned me and asked if I was able to move forward. I replied that I was unable to and that I was stuck in the snow. The Controller responded back and said hold tight; ground operations was on their way. As ground operations came; I shut off the plane and aided the ground operations staff in pushing the plane backwards. We successfully pushed the plane out of the snow.I started the plane back up and I was then able to make a U-turn back onto the Runway XX and taxi onto Alpha Y. The sign for Bravo (B) was not visible and I exited off of Alpha Y; made the left turn for Alpha and then right turn for Bravo.This experience taught me to avoid any taxiways that appear to have ice or snow on them. I also learned that I must make the judgement as being the pilot in command. As the pilot in command; I have the ability to deny requests made by Air Traffic Controller if I cannot adhere to their request promptly. I must note that it is important that all parties involved must remain safe; since safety is a priority of mine.

As the landing gear retracted; the aircraft's electrical system failed and I lost my radios and transponder. I flew the traffic pattern as I normally would until abeam the end of RWY XX; where I attempted to extend the aircraft's landing gear. The gear did not extend; so I departed the pattern straight out on a downwind to resolve the issue. After pumping my landing gear down by hand; I established communication with my cellphone with Maintenance on the ground at ZZZ; who made radio calls for me as I flew the aircraft in on final. I touched down and was able to terminate the flight without further incident. My main concern in filing this report is that after experiencing the electrical system failure; I did not have a functioning transponder. ZZZ is located within the Mode C Veil of ZZZ1; and a transponder is required while operating inside of the veil. Because of the electrical system failure; I was operating without a transponder. Based on the nature of this incident; the best course of corrective action that could be taken in order to prevent a recurring incident of a similar nature is for the electrical system to be examined and undergo whatever maintenance is necessary.

column121: I was Instructor Pilot; low time student pilot was in the left seat. We were practicing ground reference maneuvers; specifically S-turns across a road. Except we used the river as a 'road.' My thinking was that no traffic should be near us if we are 1;000 feet AGL (1;200MSL) at that location. Boy; was I wrong.My student had completed a few S-turns across the river and was just turning westbound to cross the river again when I noticed a target on our ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance - Broadcast) in display less than a mile to our right (north) -- actually; much less than a mile -- showing 100 feet below us; coming straight toward our right rear quarter. It looked like a 90-degree track compared to ours; meaning the offending aircraft was heading roughly 190 while we were heading approximately 270 (all magnetic). I took control immediately; raised the right wing; and looked intently to our right rear and all other parts of our right side in an effort to make visual contact. Alas; no joy.Since the ADS-B track showed he was likely to pass behind us; I went full throttle in order to give the other aircraft the best chance of doing so. That appeared to work; but we only knew that when the target (after what seemed like an eternity) moved to our left rear on its same heading. Finally; we were diverging. We both looked in the direction of the target; still no joy. Never saw the guy. Thank goodness for ADS-B in this case.Let me add that I was scanning for traffic the whole time my student was S-turning. Whenever he banked left; I took the opportunity to look under the raised (right) wing. When he turned right; the other raised wing. Nonetheless; no joy whatsoever.We were not monitoring any radio frequency at the time since we were not close to an airport traffic pattern nor in a designated practice area (the 'west practice area' near there is several miles west of our position). Now this: Thanks again to ADS-B; I was able to find both our flight tracks on FlightRadar24 (FR24). I identified the other aircraft's N-number; looked it up in the FAA database; found the owner's information; and called him. Nice; retired fellow on this third Cirrus; based at the airport 3 NM to our north-northeast; ZZZ. He had just departed ZZZ Runway XX and was climbing; per the FlightRadar24 track; via track 235 degrees at a ground speed of 132 knots. Our track at the time; per FlightRadar24; was 283 degrees with a ground speed of 71 knots. So roughly 50 degrees different in ground tracks; not 90 as estimated above.I asked the owner; who was the pilot in the Cirrus; if he saw us either visually or on ADS-B. He said he did not recall seeing us on either and that he did not get a traffic alert on his ADS-B device. I think we received an alert; but not positive in retrospect. I am just glad I glanced at the display when I did.The Cirrus pilot said that he always announces his takeoffs from ZZZ on the CTAF; which is Multicom 122.9. I admitted that I should have been monitoring that frequency for traffic awareness.I mentioned as gently as possible to him that the FAA recommends (via AC 90-66B; Non-Towered Airport Flight Operations) that airplanes departing a non-towered airport should fly straight out until reaching pattern altitude; then continue straight out or turn 45 degrees in the direction of the traffic pattern for that runway. This gentleman did neither. His FR24 shows that he went straight out off Runway XX for less than a mile; then turned 65 degrees!! To his right!! Even though Runway XX is a left-traffic runway. He did not seem impressed when I mentioned that to him; he was more eager to repeat that I should have been monitoring CTAF so we would have known he was departing.The upshot of our conversation for me was to guard the nearby CTAF whether or not I am in a location where I 'shouldn't' need to do so; and to realize that pilots operating at quiet; non-towered airports will do whatever they darned well please regardless ofany FAA guidance.Lastly; I offered to do his next flight review or IPC for free since I have never been in a Cirrus and would be eager to be his 'passenger.' Scolding him will not do any good; but perhaps by instructing him; should he decide to take me up on my offer; I may be able to remind him of proper non-towered airport procedures.

column121: I departed ZZZ on an IFR flight plan to ZZZ1. The aircraft had sat for roughly 3 days over the weekend before this flight and was difficult to start that morning (battery seemed weak). 40 minutes into the flight; the first symptoms of an electrical malfunction began to show up. I was roughly 15 nm from the IAF for the RNAV XX approach into ZZZ1 at 8;000 feet MSL; in actual IMC with light to moderate rime icing. I had just switched from ZZZ2 Center to the CTAF for the ZZZ1 airport when the auto-pilot for the aircraft unexpectedly disconnected. All of the lights on the autopilot control panel went dark; and the autopilot would not turn back on. Initially; I decided to continue the approach by hand and have maintenance check the autopilot malfunction on the ground. After briefly troubleshooting the autopilot; I returned to my instrument scan. At first glance; my HSI indicated that I was on Heading/Course. Needles were centered and heading bug was situated at the top of the instrument. But when I looked over at the Garmin 430 GPS; it indicated that I was off heading by 20-30 degrees. By the time I looked back towards my HSI; there was a 'HDG' flag starting to flicker in the top right hand corner. I looked across the panel at the co-pilot's instrument cluster and noted that the co-pilot's artificial horizon was flopped over; indicating a 45* right bank and 20* nose up attitude. The co-pilot's side DG was also off by 90* from my magnetic compass. As I looked back towards the pilot's side instrument cluster; my HSI began spinning around and around like a top.At this point; I had obviously determined that several of my gyroscopic instruments had failed; and I had difficulty determining which instruments were trustworthy and which were not. From this point on; I did my best to maintain straight and level flight with my remaining instruments and the Garmin 430 GPS ground track. I looked out the window at my wings (I was still in IMC and light to moderate icing [at] this point) and saw that during my troubleshooting I had enough ice accumulation that small 'horns' of rime ice were begging to grow on the leading edges and my de-ice boots were mostly white with a layer of ice. When I pressed the switch on the overhead panel to activate my de-ice boots; nothing happened. I immediately switched back to ZZZ2 Center and [received priority]; advising them that I had gyroscopic instrument failures and inoperative anti-icing equipment. I requested an immediate climb in an attempt to escape the icing conditions and find visual flight conditions before my remaining instrumentation failed; along with vectors back to ZZZ (which I knew had good VFR weather conditions...ZZZ1 conditions appeared to be worsening when I had last listened to the automated weather). ATC was extremely helpful and professional. Immediately offering any assistance they could; giving me no-gyro vectors towards ZZZ and approving a climb to 12;000 feet MSL. I had difficulty maintaining a heading and climb pitch-attitude initially; but got vaguely stabilized within a few minutes. Once stabilized; I noticed that the left alternator light was on; I attempted to re-cycle the alternator master switch twice without success. I then began to load-shed all electrical equipment which was not absolutely necessary for the continuation of the flight; and I advised ATC that I had experienced an alternator failure. 	I initially broke out of the top of the cloud layer and entered VMC around 10;000 feet roughly 15 minutes after the first indication of electrical failure. I had to request a higher altitude shortly thereafter as the tops of the clouds sloped higher towards ZZZ. ATC cleared me for a block altitude 8;000 feet to 12;000 feet; then eventually up to 14;000 feet; and authorized any course deviations necessary for me to remain in VFR conditions.Upon leveling off; I was initially concerned about what appeared to be a fairly significant performance loss. My first assumption was that it was due to ice build up on the wings/tail. In a level flight attitude; at 38 of manifold pressure and 2400 rpm (typical climb power) I was only getting 120 knots indicated airspeed. 160 knots to 170 knots indicated is more typical during cruise flight at a much lower power setting (30'/2300rpm). I alerted ATC that I was seeing abnormally low air speeds. But after a quick glance at my GPS (which was showing a 230 knots ground speed) I realized that the airspeed discrepancy was most likely due to pitot icing. ATC confirmed that they were showing me with a ground speed in the high 220's. By this point; the aircraft was out of icing conditions and flying just fine in VMC. So most of the potential danger had past. The last thing I had to do was search around for a hole in the clouds so that I could get back into ZZZ (there was an overcast layer between my aircraft and the ground). With the help of ZZZ3 Approach; ZZZ Tower; and several other aircraft in the area giving pilot reports; I found an opening near ZZZ4 and circled down for a visual approach into Runway XXL at ZZZ. The vast majority of the ice which had accumulated on the aircraft came off in the decent due to higher airspeeds and increasing temperatures. I landed without further incident; parked the aircraft; and immediately took down notes regarding the order of events while they were still fresh in my mind. I then called the Chief Pilot to relay what happened."

column121: While entering the downwind via the 45 for Runway XX; right traffic at ZZZ; we were following a Cessna. I was sitting in the passenger seat as the NFP (Non-Flying Pilot)/Safety Pilot observing my friends landing. We completed our landing checks and continued following the Cessna. As the Cessna reached our four o'clock position I told the PF (Pilot Flying) that he was clear to turn base leg behind the Cessna. We made our radio call; and turned to base leg. After we made another radio call to final; a young woman flying some sort of low wing canopy glass cockpit airplane turned directly in front of us and cut us off in the pattern. She did make a radio call announcing her turn to base. Approaching her turn to final she then queried 'how many airplanes are in the pattern and where are you'. I am sure she was completely unaware of our position. Out of the turn we were approximately less than a quarter of a mile at her seven o'clock position. Clearly she had no idea that she had just cut us off and was now on a simultaneous approach with another aircraft. The PF did not have the conflicting aircraft in sight until late after turning final. In the interest of safety; I took control of the airplane and elected to fly a parallel to her track. I passed by her left wing approximately 400 feet lateral distance and nearly level with her aircraft. Once I knew we were safely passed her aircraft I executed missed approach. We then came around for another successful landing to a full stop.
column123: As background; ZZZ was heavily congested with training and weekend aviators. The approach to the downwind leg was reported via UNICOM as 4NM southeast to enter a 45 - downwind entry. We coordinated spacing with another crosswind aircraft to follow us for spacing in the pattern. Our aircraft was operating with LED strobe lights and all landing lights for visibility to other aircraft.Reported downwind; uneventfully. And recognized the aircraft we were to follow and mimicked their pattern to minimize spacing conflicts. Reported our base turn to UNICOM; uneventfully. Our track on base leg was approximately 2 NM from the end of the runway. At no time was our location questioned by the conflicting near miss aircraft.Reported a base-to-final turn; uneventfully and unquestioned. Upon the completion of the turn to final; I focused on vertical alignment to the runway and did not see the conflicting near miss aircraft. The PNF (Pilot Not Flying); in a radio call questioned the conflicting near miss aircraft to determine her position upon hearing the UNICOM base report. After it was determined the conflicting aircraft turned inside of our location; resulting in cutting us off placing our aircraft in a hazardous flight profile; PNF took control of the aircraft in a professionally coordinated manner. At this time; the conflicting near miss aircraft was well within 1/4 NM and somewhat above our altitude; which was approximately 300 ft. AGL. Because of her proximity to us; and her apparently being unaware of our location; the resolution was complex. Keep in mind in her base to final turn (Right Hand pattern) with a low wing aircraft she would have then been unable to locate us visually. In a UNICOM radio call; the conflicting near miss aircraft questioned 'how many aircraft are in the pattern and where are you'; indicating her further lack of awareness to traffic as she was a close in final; an inappropriate time to establish traffic.Suspecting her unpredictable actions; we were prevented from a turn to side step since it would have blocked our ability to monitor her activities. Our inter-cockpit discussion created the point; given our closure rate; that our only recourse; in the interest of safety; was to parallel her path; fly past her which would have given her awareness of our location; then when ahead of the conflicting aircraft; we could safely initiate a missed approach; which we did.We remained in the pattern for another approach and full stop landing; uneventfully.

column121: After two right 360s we were told to extend downwind for runway X; and look for helicopter traffic (Aircraft Y) three miles west of the field at 700 feet. We called out traffic in sight; and continued. After Aircraft Y didn't respond to two radio calls; we were told to do another 360. It appeared as though Aircraft Y was still climbing as they passed in front from our left to right. After a controller change; Tower called our position to Aircraft Y; they did not respond. Shortly after that call; Aircraft Y made a sharp climbing right turn directly into our flight path. To avoid a collision; I took the controls and made a climbing left turn as sharp as I could. Shortly after I started that turn; Aircraft Y banked sharply to their right to avoid us. I can't put an exact number on the distance between us; but it was close enough that I felt the need to bank sharply towards traffic on final; and Aircraft Y banked hard enough for us to see the bottom of their helicopter. Once a safe distance away; we turned to rejoin downwind; and began a descent back to pattern altitude. After that; Aircraft Y asked tower to keep aircraft away from that area while they followed a pursuit. Hearing other aircraft have difficulty with separation; we departed the pattern to ZZZ1 to avoid a similar situation.It is normal for us to fly over helicopter operations at 500-600 feet while in the pattern at 1;100 feet. It is not normal to fly the pattern with unpredictable traffic at the same altitude.

column121: R-side working Columbus/Pike/Parkersburg airspace; Charleston Approach and Columbus Approach airspace at the same time. Having little effective contigency plan for approach controls shutting down. Working multiple aircraft into unfamiliar airspace with unfamiliar approaches to three airports all within 15-20 miles of each other; while managing holding aircraft; other enroute aircraft and aircraft wanting approaches to airports where we provide approach services. A laser event also occured around the ZZV VOR while this was occuring; with a green laser hitting an aircraft. Luckily no injuries were reported. Have a baseline contingency plan that includes aides for the controller; including LOAs between facilities; suggestions like establishing holding stacks; downstream speed reductions; local best practices used by respective approach controllers; etc. Also; try not to shut down an entire approach control facility during peak traffic times; especially on one of the busiest travel holiday weekends of the year.

column121: Aircraft X departure ZZZ IFR enroute to ZZZ1. I released the aircraft with a heading of 130 degrees & 2;000 ft. off Runway ZZ. This is a fairly standard procedure for releasing IFR aircraft off ZZZ when the metroplex is in a north flow. This keeps the aircraft away from the ZZZ2 finals which are just a few miles to the west of ZZZ. At the time; ZZZ2 was in the middle of an arrival push. Once the aircraft became airborne & I established communication with him I called ZZZ Tower & requested control so I could turn the aircraft back to the west across the ZZZ airspace. I turned Aircraft X westbound toward ZZZ1 & pointed him out to the appropriate ZZZ2 arrival sectors & handed him off to ZZZ TRACON. My plan was to keep Aircraft X low (2;000 ft. MSL) below the ZZZ2 finals where all the arrivals would be at 3;000 ft. MSL. A couple minutes later I noticed an aircraft in very close proximity to Aircraft X on a similar course. I called traffic but Aircraft X couldn't locate the aircraft. Due to the ZZZ2 traffic I couldn't climb Aircraft X for the traffic nor could I descend him due to the MVA of 2;000 ft. I again called traffic to see if Aircraft X could acquire the target visually. He still couldn't & the courses were converging while Aircraft X was overtaking the target. I called ZZZ Tower to see if they were talking to him or see if they knew what he was doing. They told me they thought he was heading to ZZZ3 which is very close to ZZZ1. The target had just departed ZZZ. I vectored Aircraft X to the north to in an attempt to increase the distance between him & the unidentified target. I then turned Aircraft X back to the southwest to go behind & to the left of the target to try & increase the separation even more. Once I was satisfied the two targets were safely separated I transferred communications of Aircraft X to ZZZ TRACON. I believe Aircraft X was on a heading of either 250 or 260 degrees at the time. It was brought to my attention later that while Aircraft X was on the heading I gave him when I transferred communications that he clipped a 2;100 ft. MVA while still at 2;000 ft. MSL. This occurred before the ZZZ TRACON controller was able to turn the aircraft. I didn't realize the heading would allow Aircraft X to clip the MVA. The MVA is a very small area; approx. 1-2nm wide 'shelf' of a larger MVA. I would not have given the aircraft a shortcut by taking him under the ZZZ2 finals. I was attempting to be as efficient as possible. However; with the amount of traffic in the area at the time I should have just taken him to the south off ZZZ & then westbound from there. This would've added approximately 30-40nm to his route but would've prevented this from happening. In the future I would also ask ZZZ Tower if they have anyone departing to the west who would be in conflict with this aircraft when I asked for control for a westbound turn. This also would've impacted my decision making.

column121: Prior to top of descent we briefed the NNCEE 1 RNAV Arrival into IAH.  The arrival says to plan on flying the RWY 8R transition.  So we briefed the ILS RWY 8R approach.  Houston Approach Control then told us to fly the RNAV (RNP) Y RWY 9 approach.  The CA was the PM and told the FO he would change the approach in the FMC.  After selecting the new approach the CA told the FO that there was a discontinuity at HOWLN.  By selecting the HOWLN transition two separate HOWLN fixes were created separated by a discontinuity.  The discontinuity appeared at the top of page two in the legs page of the FMC.  So the CA brought up the second HOWLN fix and entered it into the discontinuity boxes and assumed that this action closed the discontinuity.  But he never went back to page one to verify that the discontinuity was closed and he did not ask the FO to verify it as the FO was busy managing the descent.  The MCP displayed LNAV and VNAV were engaged and so did the FMAs.  Approach Control then said at HOWLN you are cleared the RNAV (RNP) Y RWY 9 approach.  So the CA set FAF altitude of 2;000 in the MCP.  The FO went through LAVSFT and at HOWLN (IAF) had me set TDZE of 100.  Then we both said why isn't the airplane turning?  Tower immediately cancelled our approach clearance and vectored us for the ILS RWY 9 approach.  The CA was on a larger scale than the FO and noticed that the magenta line showed both the RF leg turn inbound but also extended beyond HOWLN as well and said I think I did not clean up the discontinuity correctly.  The contributing factors were both pilots did not verify the legs page after the Captain cleaned up the discontinuity and the high workload environment in IMC.  Additionally it was the FO's first trip in over a month.

Passing through 2;400 ft. we made the decision to level off at 3;000 ft. and put our O2 mask on. I instructed the jumpseater to don his mask as well. I advised ATC as the First Officer was pilot flying. I coordinated an air return to the same runway we took off from and asked the tower to call our dispatch to notify of the diversion. Approach and landing was normal. I had Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting approach and inspect the plane before taxiing back to the ramp. Our mask were on until that point; but the fumes had subsided. The First Officer; did an amazing job; and I am grateful to have had such a professional with me at the time. We were only airborne for a total of 8 minutes. For hours after the event; I was short of breath and felt chest discomfort; a slight headache and inability to process thought. I elected to get checked out at the company provided medical center close by; escorted by Assistant Chief Pilot and was released. I am still not feeling 'normal' but hope to be by tomorrow. I feel as though I definitely took in some of the fumes; although it also seems that it was not for very long as I got my O2 mask on so quickly.

column121: Leaving ZZZ; we turned left on Taxiway XX out of FBO to taxi to [Runway] XXR. When we turned left; ground told us to expect 15 minute delay due to departures on the center runway. We therefore proceeded to wait to do the taxi checklist until we were holding short. Approaching [Runway] XXR; I switched to Tower; and within a matter of seconds we hear Company Traffic is on a 4 mile final; and from there I do not recall what I heard. I do not recall because we were then doing the taxi and before takeoff checklist. I remember going up and hitting all of the lights on; which in my mind I must have thought that we were cleared for takeoff; and not line up and wait. We both verified the runway; did all the checklists; took the runway and took off. We never got corrected by ATC to abort takeoff because we weren't cleared. Everything seemed normal; we then got handed off to Departure; and a few minutes later we got asked to copy down a phone number for a possible pilot deviation. At this point both my partner and I looked at each other confused; not knowing what we did. We arrive in ZZZ1; we call the number; they said if they needed us they would call us; they then called us on the Monday after the incident and told us that we took off without clearance. Apparently; I did read line up and wait correctly; though I do not remember what I said due to the last minute high work load. We were called the morning of Monday [Date] from the supervisor telling us what we did. I then told him our side of it. He told me he had to do a report; I told him we would do the same on our end.This occurred because of task saturation. We went from a very calm and slow environment; to a very fast; high workload and task saturated environment. Part of doing the checklists requires a lot of talking between the flight crew. Having to do two checklists; the end of a briefing; as well as listen to ATC all last minute; we clearly didn't hear/comprehend the full ATC instruction. Which; led to us taking off without a clearance. The fact that neither of us caught it; and still didn't know what happened until we got a call; just shows to me how fast we were working. That is a pure reminder to remember to take things slower to make sure this does not happen again.Both my partner and I immediately started doing a report from the incident; when we found out what we did. We made sure that we timely called the ATC facility on the day of the incident as instructed.This occurred because of task saturation. We were thrown off guard getting a clearance 10 minutes before we were expecting to; and were rushing to complete everything. Rushing is never a good thing. We should have stated that we need a minute to finish some checklists and not agreed to the clearance; and if there was ever a doubt in our mind that we didn't understand a clearance we should have double checked with the Tower.
column123: We were given taxi instructions from FBO via [Taxiway] XX to Runway XXR and told to expect a 15 minute wait at the end of the runway. I was Pilot Flying and made the decision to hold the taxi checklist until we got to the runway due to the short taxi and long wait for takeoff. Once we arrived at [Runway] XXR we switched to Tower and immediately was given clearance onto the runway. Due to the rush to get through the taxi checklist and before takeoff checklist; remember hearing traffic on four mile final and all lights being turned on; I thought we were cleared for takeoff. Once all checklists were done I preceded to takeoff. I do not recall hearing the lineup and wait instructions as my mind was rushed to complete both checklists. Looking back I clearly should have denied instructions to take the runway and take my time to complete checklists.We were notified after takeoff of a possible deviation and even at that time we did not know what we did. We called ATC after landing in ZZZ1. They didn't tell us what the possible deviation was and that they would call us back if needed. They called morning of [Date].I allowed myself to be rushed and became task saturated at a critical phase of flight by trying to rush through two checklists before takeoff and knowing traffic was inside a four mile final behind us. This prevented me in clearly hearing our instructions from the tower which was line-up and wait; not cleared for takeoff.Completed report after speaking with ATC on the morning of [Date]I allowed myself to be rushed and task saturated; trying to run two check lists after ATC instructions at the runway hold short line. Even though we had a short taxi and an expected 15 minute wait; I should have still ran the taxi checklist on the taxiway enroute to [Runway] XXR. If we had to wait the entire 15 minutes; I could've reviewed the taxi checklist again if needed. At the hold short once we were given instructions by ATC; I should have denied instructions to allow sufficient time to run the taxi checklist.
