column121: This was a rapid pressurization. After single engine start; I asked the FO (First Officer) to accomplish the single engine after start checklist. We received taxi clearance to Runway XXL. I began taxiing about 50 feet and the aircraft began pressurizing immediately. Everyone on the aircraft began feeling their heads squeezed together.  Immediately the EICAS gave a 'PRESN AUTO FAIL' caution. What would you do? Are you going to let the airplane keep pressurizing until it reaches 14;500 ft while simultaneously running the QRH and then aircraft drops masks mid checklist? I used my instincts and immediately stopped the aircraft; set the parking brake and pressed the 'dump' button near the pressurization panel to dump the pressurized air. I only knew to immediately do this because I've personally thought of this scenario plenty of times in situations where the boarding door was closed and external air condition was hooked up. I always thought to myself if the door couldn't open quick enough then I'd need to dump the air; so my instincts reacted as such when this actually occurred. This is not something I was taught; this is not something the company teaches; however it should certainly be a point of emphasis. Moving along; after I dumped the air; the aircraft began depressurizing as expected just enough for about 3 seconds and then immediately began pressurizing again. I unpressed the 'dump' button and pressed it again. Nothing happened. I did this instantly. Afterwards I pressed the manual pressurization button; and rotated it to 11 o'clock position and waited 2 seconds; nothing happened; I then rotated full clockwise but the aircraft kept pressurizing and I wasn't going to wait to run the checklist as the aircraft altitude kept climbing. I have read this checklist before and ran through this procedure on my own time once or twice due to curiosity; so I knew what to do personally. I then pressed the EMER CALL button to the flight attendant; and told him to immediately open the galley door. Keep in mind all of this happened within 15 seconds. I also told him the galley door because I didn't want passengers to panic and run out the boarding door thinking their heads were going to explode. This is how it felt. When the flight attendant opened the door; it slammed open; as expected; despite the pressurization knob fully rotated to the right. Then I ran the QRH. Keep in mind we were not losing pressurization; we were rapidly pressurizing; oxygen masks were not my immediate thought on the ground. The checklist says to don oxygen masks during rapid decompression. I made the PIC authority to open the galley door once the pressure would not dump properly because I knew it would completely depressurize the aircraft. After I ran the QRH; I called Maintenance and they wanted to MEL the Auto Pressurization; and have me continue with the aircraft to ZZZ; an airport with a field elevation of 3200 plus/minus 100 feet. One; I've never controlled pressurization manually in flight; and secondly I've never been to ZZZ; a high elevation airport. So I refused. Nonetheless; we went through the QRH; I ran through the proper steps from instruction from the book; and Maintenance. I did what the QRH said; which I actually did myself already; then I personally went to go close the galley door myself; in case it didn't properly pressurize. I at least considered running through the proper MEL procedure; however I was still not sold on taking the airplane. Once I closed the door; the same thing happened; aircraft began over pressurizing. I immediately opened the door again. I went back on the phone with Maintenance; after a quick discussion with my First Officer & flight attendant; I told Maintenance Control 'I will not take this aircraft.' He said ok; we ended the conversation; then I began coordinating with OPS for a gate return. I did not want to taxi with the galley door open; nor did I feel it was safe to close the door as well; so I simply turned off the #2 engine; the only one running; and asked to be towed back to the gate. I sent an ACARS message to Dispatch 'returning to gate; need new aircraft.' They responded 'copy.'  After a few minutes a tug came; we were towed; I blocked in and I then I called Dispatch and explained to him the situation. He said he'd call me back. In a few minutes he did; he said he spoke to Maintenance and they wanted to MEL the issue and keep the same aircraft; I refused again. The aircraft was not safe to fly. No one knew what the actual issue was; and unless you felt your head being squeezed in an airplane uncontrollably on the ground; you wouldn't know how that felt. I can't imagine what it would have felt like if we were flying at 3;000 feet and the aircraft wanted to over pressurize to a higher altitude and the dump feature didn't work properly; because opening the door inflight; is obviously not an option. A few minutes later Dispatch called and said they'd reach out to the Duty Manager and call me back.  The Duty Manager then called me; he said the same thing the Dispatcher said; to MEL the aircraft; and continue on the same plane. I respectfully refused again. The aircraft was not safe to fly. The Duty Manager then coordinated a new aircraft and I swapped to one about 30 minutes later. I must repeat; if you were not on the aircraft; you do not know how it felt. The crew was light headed; myself included; and the passengers had to have been as well. As a crew I felt we made the right decision; despite pressure to take out the same aircraft. About an hour later; when my new aircraft was being boarded; the previous aircraft was adjacent to us being worked on by Maintenance. In other words; it was not a simple MEL procedure. The aircraft was not safe to fly. Our new plane was just fine; we boarded; and proceeded to ZZZ safely and landed about 2 hours late. The QRH procedure is for inflight; and mainly focused on cabin depressurization; we were being over pressurized.  There wasn't enough time to run a QRH all while solving the issue as the aircraft continued pressurizing on the ground. I wasn't sure how much time I would have. There were children on board; I immediately thought about everybody; and since I knew opening the door would solve the issue; I made the decision to open. I didn't know of any other checklist action item would actually stop exactly what was happening. There isn't even a tab here for cabin over pressuring. You had to be there.

We scanned for traffic appearing to be around the 12 o' clock position of the aircraft. ATC issued a vector turning northeast bound which we complied with; however the TCAS RA went off immediately with a 'climb; climb' resolution. I disconnected the autopilot; put the thrust levers into the maximum position and adjusted the aircraft pitch to the vertical speed resolution. I believe we were about 9;000-8;700 feet before completing the RA TCAS. The separation showed about 300 feet. We climbed until clear of conflict to 9;500 feet and continued the ATC vector. After the 'clear of conflict' we leveled the aircraft; advised ATC of the TCAS RA and returned back to new given ATC clearance. We continued the flight to land safely at ZZZ. This was a huge learning experience to maintain separation and situational awareness of other aircraft and ATC instructions.

column121: We were descending via the DRLLR5 arrival for Runway 26R transition and we had everything briefed and ready to go. At a point ATC changed the runway on us from [Runway] 26R to 26L so we reloaded correct runway and its respective ILS approach procedure to back up the approach. We rebriefed the approach and reloaded all frequencies again so we were ready once again for the approach. At the end of the arrival there's a fix named ZOEEE; right upon crossing that fixed; my First Officer selected HDG sync; immediately follow by HDG mode. And just like that; we were auto sequenced for the approach. ATC then came to us with right turn for a right base followed by another right turn turn intercept the localizer for Runway 26L. At that point the FO (First Officer) armed APP and we confirmed APP1 was armed. So we continue with the approach but the airplane didn't intercept the LOC but instead it continued. Before we reached the final approach course I told my First Officer 'Be careful I don't think it's going to intercept' (he didn't acknowledge) right when we reached the course I told my First Officer 'turn now...turn now!' But he didn't; so at that point I said 'I have the flight controls' and I hand flown the airplane back the final approach course. At that point ATC came to us to let us know we were showing left of course to what my First Officer responded 'We are correcting. This happened like at about 3000 ft. AGL. After I restablished the airplane on it's final approach course I asked my First Officer if he wanted the controls back and he said YES. So I transferred the controls back to him. Then I quickly checked the information and I verified that the FMS was loaded with the ILS26L; we had a good preview with right identifier IJYV and we were showing an inbound course of 267 and APP 1 was armed. So I had to reach the FMS and I activated vectors then I forced V/L on the Pilot Flying side after asking the flying pilot if he agreed with every single step. Then the airplane's automation 'woke up' and the First Officer followed the FD all the way. We were stable at 1000 ft. and we continued to landing. I think the new FMS program has a glitch or something. Apparently it doesn't auto sequence the approach the same way. This happened in another aircraft which has the latest FMS update. From now on I'm not going to trust the auto sequence on the new loads and I am going to manually sequence it from a fix on the final approach fix. This should prevent the same issue from happening again."

column121: Typical peak afternoon departure.  Estimated 1hr late with 2 MELs; one unfamiliar. Flap system inoperative. About 25 minutes after show time finally got notice and it showed aircraft nearly fully loaded with 1 can to go. Went to aircraft and still pushed late.  After engine start got ECAM flaps extended.  Since flaps should have been fixed in the closed position I believed it was a problem.  Maintenance believed it was an expected spurious ECAM due to the MEL.  It took over 40 minutes to taxi to maintenance area; make calls to duty officer; and attempt calls to 2 tech pilots to finally have Maintenance on ground visually confirm that the notch flap on the left wing was not retracted and the ECAM warning was real.  Returned to gate; tail swapped and blocked out in just under 2 hours.  Nice job by everyone involved.  Flight to ZZZ was uneventful until approach control informed us the Tower was closed due to COVID.  We flew a box pattern while simultaneously looking at ZZZ1 as alternate (we could get there with 10;000 pounds of fuel due to Captain added fuel) and FO working ACARS to get non-Tower approval.  We briefed the details and flew an instrument approach in VFR conditions to an uneventful landing and block in at destination airport.  After block in I studied the events and our crew response and believed we did an excellent job under the conditions but noted the newest FOM revision required an alternate to operate to a non-towered airport; which we did not have.  The following morning; further study showed that the normally 24 hour Tower may have been closed due to COVID; but there was indeed a NOTAM for the closure which both I and the Dispatcher missed.The confusing MEL language refers to 'appropriate AFM performance restrictions are applied' led to longer than necessary hunt for those in the AFM when the only restrictions I could find are in the QRH.  The time I spent trying to make sure I didn't miss any restrictions could have been better spent studying the NOTAMs.  The closure NOTAM was found using the iPad app. which sorted the airport closure first; while company's provided NOTAMs sorted the closure near the end next to the airport inop lighting.  The requirement for the alternate seems to be a change in this week's FOM.The missing NOTAM closure is high workload human error sorting through pages of NOTAMs.  Lowering the workload by changing the MEL to point to the restrictions rather than creating a lengthy search would have helped. Company NOTAMs should be sorted more like the iPad app.

column121: While descending on the DRLLR5 into IAH; I asked the Captain a question regarding the flight and we began to converse about the topic. I continued to monitor the descent and we were on speed and on altitude all the way through MPORT. The Captain had the bottom altitude of MPORT (16;000 ft.) in the altitude selector and once past MPORT it was not changed to the bottom altitude of DRLLR (13;000 ft.). Since the altitude selector was still at 16;000 ft.; it looked as if we would be fine with the restriction at DRLLR according to the vertical guidance. 5 miles from DRLLR I noticed we were actually high and told the Captain we needed to increase the vertical descent. He increased the vertical descent while maintaining the speed restriction but we passed DRLLR 400-500 feet above the restriction. The flight continued normally and we continued on the arrival into the visual on 26R. This event was caused by a discussion about the flight leading to a monitoring breakdown. As Pilot Monitoring; I lost focus of the descent path and did not realize the bottom altitude of DRLLR was not set. By the time I realized and queried the Captain to increase the descent rate it was too late. I should have waited to ask a question until we were on the ground considering we were already on the arrival. This would have allowed me to monitor the descent rate more accurately and avoid being high at DRLLR. I also probably would have caught the altitude still being set to MPORT.

ECAM put us into ATL LAW (Alternate Law) and FO (First Officer) had to hand fly.  We asked for lower altitude and told ATC we wanted ZZZ1 and I sent ACARS to Dispatch.   I was running the COM and getting ATIS and found out ZZZ was showing 002OVC (200' Overcast) and 1 1/2 vis (Visibility).  I asked ATC if there was anything better for weather and he said the region was all the same.  We decided to go to ZZZ.  Once the COM was complete I called and briefed the FA's (Flight Attendants) and made PA to the passengers.  We decided that I would take over and fly the approach and landing. We briefed the ILS 11 Approach and the FO hand flew the Aircraft until about 15-20 mile final so I could take my time and take a few minutes to 'gather my thoughts.'  We started to configure early and we had to gravity extend the gear.  Now we were in direct law and started to fly the approach..  We saw the approach lights and continued and saw the runway at minimums.  We landed.  We taxied to the gate and briefed the passengers and deplaned.  I made the phone calls to Company; Dispatch and Maintenance.  Maintenance looked at the issue and found out there was HYD fluid all over and we had a bad O ring. They fixed the issue and we were about to land in ZZZ1 about 5 hours late.

column121: I was assigned to and present aboard a deadhead flight. I opted to occupy the center jumpseat of the cockpit for taxi and takeoff. The push-back and start-up from the parking spot at ZZZ were uneventful.After completion of the Before-Taxi Checklist; the Captain began a taxi to the southwest; along the ramp; in accordance with marshaller's instructions. At the southwest end of the ramp was a wing-walker with lighted-wands; and several other employees. As the plane approached the southwest end of the ramp; the wing-walker and other ground personnel passed out of my field-of-view and were not visible to me for the duration of the taxi; due to the visibility limitations of the jumpseat.The Captain then began the 180-degree right turn denoted by the ramp taxiway centerline. At the Captain's request; the First Officer monitored the right wing during the turn. Upon completion of the 180-degree turn; the aircraft appeared (from the jumpseat view) to be located on or near the centerline of the ramp taxiway. The Captain then requested the First Officer verify that the right wing was clear of obstacles. The First Officer turned his head far enough to the right to see the wingtip of the aircraft. He responded that the wing was clear; and that he had the wing-walker in sight.The Captain then began a left turn towards Taxiway F. The Captain's focus was on the turn. The First Officer monitored the aircraft which was giving way to us; as we [exited] the ramp. (The aircraft was approaching from the opposite direction; with its taxi-lights on; however; it had been stationary for several minutes prior to this point.) Passing through 20 degrees of left turn; a shudder was felt in the cockpit; similar to heavy braking.The Captain immediately brought the aircraft to a stop. All three of us in the cockpit made a visual inspection of the aircraft (from the cockpit.) The cause of the shudder was not readily apparent. At my request; the Captain checked the Main Body Gear Steering indications on the EICAS; to verify it was not the cause of the shudder. At that moment; (deadheading) Captain [Name] entered the cockpit and advised us that the right wingtip had separated from the aircraft.The Captain proceeded to start the APU; shut-down the engines; configure the aircraft for towing; and make contact with the ground crew. After the damage was inspected by ground [personnel]; a tow vehicle was connected. The aircraft was towed back to the parking spot; where the cargo was off loaded and the aircraft turned over to maintenance [personnel] for inspection.Immediately following the events described above; the right wingtip was discovered on the ground; adjacent to a ramp lighting tower located on the southwest end of the ramp. (This tower had passed off the right wing during the right 180-degree turn required to exit the ramp.) Ground personnel reported that the Tower appeared to have damage; in addition to the aircraft's own damage.Shudder notice after contact with obstacle.Inadequate ramp space/clearance from obstacles.Ramp space and access points need to be verified for sufficient obstacle clearance prior to operating at such location.

I suggest that all aircraft be required to turn on their landing lights during periods of difficult visual condition to include sun glare.

My own policy as Captain is to direct mask usage at all times possible while in the cockpit other than while eating or drinking or obviously in an emergency while using oxygen. I believe this to be congruent with CDC guidance for when someone needs to be in close contact with someone else who does not live with that person. This procedure is not perfect but the best I can come up with outside of pre-departure rapid COVID testing. As pilots we usually fly with new coworkers on every new trip and to date there is no way to determine that the person you are flying with is not an asymptomatic carrier of the virus.This whole situation is a failure of:The pilot group as a whole: We should do better than thisUnion: Our pilots are more at risk from death or injury from COVID than any other operational threatAirline: The safety protocol enforced outside the cockpit should extend inside as well; no exceptionsFAA: If none of the above will take action the FAA needs to step inMy First Officer on the flight associated with this report agreed in the briefing phase to comply with my directives for mask usage. During the flight I detected a problem though. I generally try to be friendly and conversational not only to pass the time in pleasant way but also to provide a comfortable environment to empower my First Officer to be a helpful partner in the flight.This wasn't to be on that flight and it culminated in my FO intentionally removing his mask on descent into ZZZ. Stating when asked about it that 'It is interfering with my duties.' The interference he was referring to was that I didn't hear the altitude ATC assigned and I asked him to ask ATC to confirm. I don't know how his mask interfered with ATC transmissions.I honestly think he was looking for an opportunity to remove his mask in defiance.I asked him to replace his mask and offered to work the radios if it's a problem.Later at the hotel I restated my objection to flying with someone who refuses to wear a mask and asked if that would be a problem in tomorrow's flight. He stated it would not.  There were no mask issues on that flight; however it was not the most pleasant environment; quite sterile.Mask-less cockpits are dangerous.Unfortunately this is not my first time experiencing the mask resistance in the cockpit.The current guidance on this is weak and shows a lack of leadership on all involved.My experience is that a surgical type mask does not interfere with my duties; is easily and quickly removed if necessary; and by medical consensus prevents contagious droplets from dispersing to a great extent.Please enforce mask usage and prevent the sickness or death of our brothers or sisters in the cockpit.

column121: Before push checklist and Ramp tower clearance to push were completed / obtained per procedures. Following standard pushback verbiage from the ground crew; I released the brakes. Pushback and No 2 engine start proceeded without incident. Ground crew instructed to 'Set Brakes' - at this time I read back 'Parking brake set; pressure normal' while the FO (First Officer) and I visually checked the red parking brake indicator for illumination and Brake Press gauge for 2800 PSI. Ground crew then announced 'Aircraft disconnected by-pass pin removed' to which I replied 'Disconnect headset.'Shortly after this statement the aircraft appeared to move forward unexpectedly. The ramp agent came back on headset with 'Set brakes set brakes' to which I applied brakes.Apparently the parking brake was not set; as we had intended and thought; and an uncommanded aircraft movement had occurred. The ramp agent came on the interphone and indicated that all was fine on the ground; and standard signals were given for ramp departure. Upon crew debrief; one of the threats that we identified was the sun shining into the cockpit; making the red parking brake light less apparent to the crew. Another threat was the general distraction of normalcy and not blocking out the sunlight's glare to verify aircraft condition.We are glad no one on the ground was injured and will learn from this experience.
column123: Before push checklist was completed. Received our push back clearance and the Captain communicated with the ground crew standard tow bar less pushback clearance and released the brakes appropriately. Pushback was completed uneventfully and during so we were cleared for engine start after which the Captain had me start the No. 2 engine. The ground crew instructed to 'Set Brakes.' I saw good brake pressure - 2800 psi; and what I believed to be the red Parking Brake light illuminated so I continued my duties of setting the packs appropriately.The ground crew announced 'aircraft disconnected - bypass pin removed' and I heard the Captain respond with 'Disconnect Headset.' Shortly after this the aircraft began an uncommanded movement forward; ground crew came on headset Immediately saying 'Set Brakes Set Brakes' to which brakes were applied and the aircraft stopped the slow roll and the Parking Brake was appropriately verified engaged at this time. The ramp crew came back on the inter phone and indicated all was fine on the ground; and standard signals were given for departure. Apparently our parking brake was not set after all when we initially thought; and upon debrief we both agreed the threats encountered were the glare of the sun on the parking brake light illuminating it more red than usual; as well as the general distraction associated with starting engines and push back tasks in general. We did not properly block the sun's glare and we should have been more vigilant to ensure it was set properly. We are both thankful nobody on the ground was injured and we will learn from this experience in order to prevent it from happening again.

column121: Aircraft was out of balance at start of my shift. It required the last row to be blocked. I sent a message to ZZZZ to do so and they did. At about 10 minutes before departure aircraft went out of balance again and I determined that the last 3 rows now needed to be blocked. ZZZZ called to find out why weights weren't generating and I advised that last 3 rows now needed to be blocked. He advised that aircraft was already out so I said I would handle it with Captain. I sent Captain that info via ACARS to block last 3 rows; but when I went back to double check the Load Program (LP) to verify that in fact the additional 2 rows needed to be moved and blocked; this time LP indicated that no rows needed to be blocked. I checked it 1 or 2 more times because it didn't seem right to me. LP again indicated no rows now needed to be blocked. So now I quickly sent Captain an ACARS to disregard moving the additional 2 rows of people as that would now be an unnecessary waste of time since no longer needed. I sent the disregard message and then released weights. Departure [load] control now did not indicate to block any rows-although row XX had been blocked from the beginning. As I thought about why LP would show 3 rows needed to be blocked; and then it indicated that we now didn't need to LP any rows; I checked the seat map (aircraft was airborne by then) and sure enough; Operations had gone in and shown last 3 rows blocked but never spoke with the crew. They should not have touched the seat map since they did not physically move anyone. And since they are not supposed to do that; it didn't occur to me that they had. But that is why LP did not show I needed to block rows; it was reading that the rows were already empty. I called Dispatch and asked them to find out from crew exactly which rows were blocked on take-off. The answer was just row 34-the last row. I verified with ZZZ; and they advised that they had not told crew to move anyone; they just showed passengers moved out of last 3 rows. I advised ZZZ never to indicate passengers moved seats unless they have physically accomplished the move. They understand now.

column121: I was Pilot Monitoring on flight [on] DRLLR 5 RNAV STAR to IAH. Aircraft X had one MEL for right FMS inoperative. Single FMS operation. We entered the STAR during preflight and 26R runway per the DRLLR 5 STAR. ATC instructed us to change to 26L just prior to MPORT. This changes the final point on the STAR from SKLER to ZOEEE. I entered the new runway and verified that no duplicate waypoints existed. I also verified and noted that the waypoint sequence on the MFD looked correct; noting the large gap between ZOEEE and BOZZZ on the 26L approach. I also noted the line on the MFD depicted from DOMNO to ZOEEE. For unknown reasons the airplane approached DOMNO; overflew DOMNO; and the autopilot went immediately into ROL mode and continued flying straight. It did not sequence to ZOEEE as expected. We noticed the change immediately; selected heading mode to start the turn to ZOEEE; and then re-engaged LNAV after verifying the FMS was sequencing properly to ZOEEE. As we started to sort out the flight path error; I was distracted when ATC issued heading calls and pilot deviation calls; which removed my attention from assisting the pilot flying. No other deviation occurred that we were aware of. Both pilots were fully engaged in managing the flight. We acted as fast as we could to regain flight path control. [I] suggest verifying the integrity of the FMS arrivals into IAH. Delay pilot deviation calls until on the ground and the airplane has been secured.
column123: We were on the DRLLR 5 arrival and planning for Runway 26R. We had checked the route for no double waypoints and all altitudes were correct. We were assigned Runway 26L and made the appropriate checks of waypoints and altitudes. At DOMNO the plane went into Roll mode and continued south. We saw it right away and began left turn as ATC told us to turn left and gave us a heading (070 I think). A few minutes later the controller gave us a phone number to call about a possible deviation. This plane had the #2 FMS MEL'd which may have contributed since we don't often operate with 1 FMS. Better planning for operations with one FMS. Closer attention while passing DOMNO; which has known issues. However we had no duplicate waypoints so this may be a new issue.

column121: Descending on the DSNEE 4 arrival from EMLLD; we became aware of congested airport environment with two different TCAS traffic alerts very close by. Approach had us at 190 knots departing DSNEE; and we were expecting the visual to runway 20R. We had gone to flaps 2 configuration. We were handed off late to the final controller; and when we switched over we heard a company call sign with nearly identical numeric as ours; cleared for the RNAV (RNP) Z runway 20R. We heard the other aircraft read back the clearance; we knew a VERY similar call sign was on frequency. We thought we might be cleared for the same approach. We checked in and asked if we were going to get the RNAV approach; and the controller said no; we were going to get a visual unless we asked for the approach. Shortly after; the controller cleared an aircraft to descend to 3000'; but neither of us were sure that it was our call sign. The First Officer (FO) attempted to clarify; but the controller was very busy and talking nonstop. We flew a few more miles; and before we could clarify he repeated the clearance to descend to 3000' and asked if we had the airport in sight. We called the airport; and said we were high. He cleared us to fly through final approach course and intercept from the right. FO read back the clearance; and we both agreed it was going to be tight. I immediately called for gear down and got the flaps to full; I also used the speed brakes as long as safely practical. We switched over to tower control; and I made the glideslope at approx. 1400' AGL; but we were still 40kts fast. I told the FO we were going to do a 'Soft Go'. At 1000' AGL I called for 'Go Around; Takeoff/around (TOGA)' and advanced the thrust levers to TOGA. I then called 'climb' as I brought the thrust levers back to what I thought was the climb position; but was actually the Maximum Continuous Thrust (MCT) detent. The tower initially held us to 2000'; so I reduced our climb rate - we were accelerating rapidly. As we cleaned up and were cleared to 3000'; the FO recognized that we were in MCT detent and brought it to my attention. By then we were clean and rapidly approaching 250 KIAS. I brought the thrust levers back to idle as we passed 260; and we saw a maximum speed of about 280 before we began to slow down again. I selected speed mode and set 220 KIAS; positioned the thrust levers in the climb detent and re-engaged auto thrust. We slowed and turned back into a right downwind for an uneventful visual approach and landing at SNA.Causes(1)	Late clearance to descend. SNA is challenging even when on a normal profile; and a few miles made all the difference.(2)	Task saturation. The L.A basin is one of the busiest airspaces in the world. Two Traffic Alerts and nonstop chatter from the approach controller indicated that he was task saturated; as well.(3)	Call sign confusion. The scheduling shop should never have had two call signs separated by one digit arriving at the same airport at the same time.(4)	Approach expectations. We were going to do a visual; and changed our setup and expectations when we heard preceding traffic approach clearance.(5)	Fatigue. Our FAR 117 duty day limit was 10 hours. We had been awake since 3.5 hours earlier to make sign-in; and were at 9:00 of our 10:00 limit when we arrived at SNA. When we knew we were too high to likely make a successful approach; we could have asked for a vector and more time/distance to descend. Flight scheduling needs to de-conflict call signs so very similar ones are not scheduled to arrive at the same airport at the same time. The ATC controllers seemed very busy; perhaps a few more controllers on-shift would help divide the workload better. Crew scheduling could alleviate fatigue factors by avoiding sequence builds that have crews flying into airports at the back end of their duty periods that are known to present unusual challenges (even if they aren't officially 'special qualification' airports).

column121: During cruise; observed oil entering cockpit through the firewall. Decided to make a precautionary landing. Uneventful approach and landing.Post flight inspection revealed a catastrophic failure of the fiber gasket in the Stratus Tools (Tempest) Model CO-300 spin off oil filter adapter. This is a known issue which has led to 3 fatalities and has recently been identified by the NTSB in a report 'Stratus Oil Filter Adapter Assembly Leaks' dated 30 NOV 2020. Note this was released just 17 days before my event. Please be advised. The NTSB refers to the manufacturer of the part by the parent company; Stratus; not the Tempest branded part most commonly known to pilots and mechanics. Previously this same part was manufactured by F&M.Key Takeaway- The NTSB needs to advise operators by using the Tempest brand to create maximum awareness. Better; the FAA needs to make this an Airworthiness Directive (AD) per the NTSB recommendation.Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association (AOPA) ran a story- 'NTSB Flags Oil Filter Adapter In Continental Engine Failures' (8 DEC 2020) and brought this to the attention of many pilots; myself included. Unfortunately; I did not know that Stratus (also F&M) is Tempest. Had that distinction been made clear; I never would have flown without checking the part as per the NTSB recommendation. I have since reached out to AOPA and asked them to re-run the story. Thus far they have only made the correction.I could never be so lucky again. I caught this failure in flight just in time in order to make a precautionary landing instead of a forced landing. Perhaps your good office could get this word out. If it can happen to me it can happen to anyone. Thanks for your efforts to be a PROACTIVE safety tool.

column121: On an empty repositioning flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 to then continuing on to ZZZZ. Preflight was normal; checking the site gauges on each engine indicated full oil quantities. After my walk around I briefed my First Officer that the preflight was normal and the oil quantities were full. Departure was uneventful and normal. I was flying the aircraft on autopilot navigating direct to ZZZ2 and we were in a normal cruise climb passing FL380 climbing to our assigned altitude of FL390 approximately 35 mins after departure from ZZZ when we noticed the oil pressure reducing rapidly to zero followed by the red CAS message 'right oil pressure low' The zeros turned to dashes and the CAS message and Master Warning extinguished. This happened a couple of times. Center cleared us to FL410 and we advised them that we would like to discontinue our climb and that we were working an issue. All engine parameters were normal except for the right engine oil pressure which was dashed and oil temp was slowly and steadily rising. I called for the oil pressure low checklist from the QRH. I continue to fly the aircraft on autopilot while my First Officer initiated the checklist in the QRH. We requested a diversion to ZZZ2 which was the closest suitable airport. We completed the Oil Pressure Low checklist verbatim and secured the right engine. Center gave us vectors for our descent for ZZZ2 due to being very close to the airport. We were cleared for the visual approach to Runway XXL backed up with the ILS an uneventful approach and landing was made without incident.

column121: On Day 5; the crew desk called me to assign me to a trip on Day 6 with a XA:40 report time.  I called in fatigued on Day 6 at approximately [3 hours prior]. I had just finished a 4 day trip from Day 2 to Day 5; with each day requiring subsequently later report times and the last 2 days requiring late or all night flying.  Additionally; even though this trip spanned 4 calendar days; it only included 2 sleep cycles.The previous 4 day trip created a significant cumulative sleep debt; as tracked my my Apple Watch. Day 1-Day 2; 6:38 of sleep at home prior to reporting for my 4 day trip. Day 2-Day 3; 8:44 of sleep in the ZZZ hotel. Day 3-Day 4; 5:26 of sleep after landing in ZZZ1; but I woke up at XA:00 am local time and had a XR:59 departure that night.  I attempted to take a nap prior to reporting for duty but I couldn't fall asleep and was awake for about 18 hours prior to flying a redeye. Day 3-Day 4; No sleep due to redeye.  I flew a redeye.  Extremely tired during the flight and took a 25 minute nap during cruise.  When I returned home; I slept from approximately XA:45 until the crew desk woke me from deep sleep shortly after XG:00.  After the crew desk woke me; I packed my bags and prepared for the new trip.  I attempted to go back to bed at XK:00 but could not fall asleep.  I realized that it was not safe for me to attempt to fly my 3rd transcontinental trip in 2 days so I called in fatigued. Day 5-Day 6; No sleep due to crew desk interrupting my recovery sleep from the previous redeye.Of note; my previous trip involved a significant cumulative clockwise circadian rhythm disruption in which every day required a later report time and each day flew later into the night.  Clockwise disruptions such as this are generally easier to tolerate compared to counter-clockwise disruptions.  However; this 4 day trip also was engineered to accumulate sleep debt.  Day 1 was 11 hours of duty and 20.5 hours of rest; which equates to a 31.5 hour long duty/sleep cycle.  Day 2 of my 4 day was 7:15 of duty and nearly 25 hours of rest; which was a 32 hour duty/sleep cycle.  Combined with each day's later duty periods; it was generally easy to fall asleep at the beginning of the rest periods.  However; it was not realistic nor possible to achieve 2 circadian rests or resets during the layovers; which meant that each day I would be awake for a longer period of time prior to reporting for late night flights.  This culminated when I reported for my redeye after being awake for 18 hours.  Upon landing I was absolutely exhausted and needed to catch up on the previous 4 days of missed sleep.  Unfortunately the crew desk interrupted this much-needed sleep and assigned me the new trip on Day 6.  In other words; the crew desk expected me to shift from my previous XM:00 pm and XS:00 pm local report times to a XA:40 am report time after disrupting my rest and being awake for over 12 hours.  Furthermore; the crew desk did not consider the larger picture of the 4 day trip and subsequent 2 day trip as a single 6 day long physiological marathon. column121: Arriving DEN on the CLASH2 arrival from the southeast; I planned and briefed an easterly flow arrival to land 17R. ATIS advertised 17R; 16L; 16R ILS; visual and RNAV Z approaches. I briefed for the RNAV RNP Z 17R. The final point for the arrival was QWIKE intersection and I left a discontinuity between that QWIKE and the QWIKE point starting the RNAV RNP Z 17R. Denver Center gave us a clearance to descend via the CLASH2 arrival landing south.The PM (Pilot Monitoring) and I confirmed that that was what we briefed and the FMC was properly programmed. The PM checked on with DEN Approach and we were told to expect RNAV Z to 16R. The PM installed that approach and I briefed the new arrival points and crossing restrictions on the CLASH2 that coincided with that runway; which were now a west downwind; the final fix being CLFFF. I briefed the approach as well. We did the same thing; leaving a discontinuity between CLFFF on the arrival and CLFFF as the IAF on the approach. The PM pulled the landing data for 16R and we briefed the changes on the engine-out missed approach which was slightly different then 17R. Approximately EVRLY intersection as we were descending through FL180; DEN Approach then said runway change; expect visual or ILS (I can't remember) to 16L. I remember it was at FL180 because it coincided with the altimeter change and the need to verify that VNAV is still able to maintain. The PM installed runway 16L and I did a briefing for the ILS 16L. This changed the FMC to an east downwind; the same fixes as for runway 17R but I did not note the changes in arrival fixes. As we were approaching JURKY intersection; I noticed on the FMC that the next waypoint was not what I was expecting. I had in my mind that we would be on a west downwind for the 16 runways. I said to the PM; it's not the correct fix next for runway 16R. The PM then asked DEN Approach to verify the runway assignment.Approach responded with a frequency change but did not respond to the request for runway clarification. This was at the point where we needed to go left or right depending on the runway. I thought it was 16R; so I went to the next fix for that runway; ROOTZ. As soon as the PM checked on with the next frequency; the Controller asked our runway assignment. The PM said we were trying to clarify. Approach then gave us 16R as a runway assignment. In fact; the previous clearance was for runway 16L. And that runway is an east downwind; not a west downwind even though the runway is on the west side of the airfield. This was absolutely my responsibility to ensure the correct runway and corresponding waypoints for the arrival. Going forward my personal correction will be to write down the runway assignment given by ATC each time it changes; whether on the yoke clip notepaper or on the iPad graphic. I also got complacent after doing 2 full briefings into DEN on a clear day. With the 3rd briefing; I did an abbreviated briefing. A full briefing; stepping through every arrival point would have caught it earlier. Additionally; as suggested by the Jump Seater; instead of clarifying the runway and having to verify the points quickly; I will ask ATC for the next waypoint they are expecting in order to give myself some time to figure out any ambiguities between the FMC and the chart. If we are adding to the data for DEN arrival deviations though...I didn't think this could happen to me. We briefed the threat of runway changes going into DEN. But DEN giving runway changes that impact arrival points without sufficient time for us to properly program and confirm was a contributing factor. Its 11.4 miles from EVRLY where we got the change to JURKY where the arrival splits. To reprogram; confirm; brief; get landing data and brief the engine-out profile changes while monitoring the descent is challenging.
column123: CLASH2 RNAV into DEN we initially planned for a Visual Approach to 17R backed up by the ILS. Initial Controller told us to expect 16R so we loaded RNAV/RNP 16R with the CLFFF transition to the approach; per ATIS. Cleared to descend via the CLASH2 arrival so we set 11;000 feet in the MCP (Mode Control Panel). ATC then advised us to expect Visual Approach to 16L. I then loaded the 16L ILS in the box and the Captain continued the descent on the arrival around the JURKEY fix. When the Captain started to brief the new arrival she noticed the arrival fixes did not match up with the new runway.I asked ATC to verify our runway assignment as all 3 of us in the cockpit were unclear at that point. After a pause; ATC gave us a new frequency instead of answering my query regarding which runway. At that point the Captain manually entered the ROOTZ fix. We changed our altitude in the MCP to correspond to the 13;000 feet minimum at ROOTZ while we checked in with the final Controller. Upon checking in the Controller asked us which runway we were planning on. I asked again which runway as we were not certain at that point. He then stated Visual Approach 16R. I updated the box AGAIN to the ILS 16R and; we were then given a heading and new altitude. The rest of the arrival and approach were uneventful.

column121: Departing Runway XXR ZZZ we were filed ZZZ1 Departure ZZZ transition then ZZZZZ [fix].  Upon receipt of CPDLC clearance there was a route modification that was obtained that had us routed via the ZZZZA3 ZZZZZ.  I loaded the flight plan per the CDU prompt and accepted the clearance and printed it out.  There was plenty of time as loading was delayed.  When I reviewed the loaded clearance it came up ZZZZA3 ZZZZA ZZZZZ.  I then went back to the DEP/ARR page and checked the runway and SID which I had previously selected to ensure it was still in the FMC.  I did notice that the routing had us now going south to ZZZZZ and thought the ZZZZA ZZZZZ was a short cut ATC wanted due to light traffic and time of day.  I also looked at the printout and didn't see the period between ZZZZA3 and ZZZZZ as in ZZZZA3 DZZZZZ verses ZZZZA3.ZZZZZ meaning that ZZZZZ was the transition.  Once we were airborne ATC cleared us directly to 12;000 which we were initially given 7;000 in the clearance.  ATC then came back and said maintain 12;000 unrestricted which in my mind validated the shortcut because usually you get the phraseology 'Climb via the SID except maintain XXX'. ATC then informed us our deviate and asked us if we were on the SID.  I said affirmative except from ZZZZA we were direct to ZZZZZ which was incorrect according to the clearance.  After getting to cruise the Captain and I discussed the situation looking at both the clearance; the FOM and the loaded routing from the CPDLC.  We realized that two errors were made.  When I loaded the SID I did not reselect the runway and SID with the ZZZZZ transition because when I checked it was in the box and because we both missed the period in the printout and ZZZZZ was on the regular routing I thought ATC wanted us to cut that part of the SID off because of low traffic volume.   It was pilot error and it's a difficult lesson.  I am fully aware that a period means a transition but I missed it on the printout and assumed ATC wanted a shorter routing which has become the norm is so many ATC environments with COVID.  I also realize that I will always double check every period on the CDU against the printout copy as it's easier to see.  In addition I will ensure that every modification in the future requires an input of both the runway and SID even when uploading clearances from CPDLC which I'm aware to do but I didn't see the period on the printout.  I take full responsibility for this mistake and I feel really bad I missed such a small but signification part of the clearance.   I know better so there's no excuses for this missed detail.
column123: First leg (and only leg) with FO; blocked XX mins late for loading; so not rushed. Filed FP was ZZZ1 ZZZ transition; ZZZ [VOR]; ZZZZZ; RXXX ....CPDLC had 'route change' (I was doing exterior prefect when it came): cleared ZZZZA3 ZZZZZ; RXXX ... climb via SID except maintain 7;000 feet. The actual printout was 'ZZZZA3. ZZZZZ'; which means the ZZZZZ transition with the 'dot' in between. We missed that dot. We both assumed the clearance was direct from ZZZZA to ZZZZZ. The ZZZ1 does not have ZZZZZ as a transition; yet it was on our filed flight plan. To add some justification for our assumption; the ZZZ1 goes way north and west before heading west. The ZZZZA SID went south of ZZZ [airport] and more direct west on course. Add that is was [early] in the morning (very light traffic plus Covid19 low traffic) we assumed we were cleared a more direct routing south of ZZZ [airport]. And the Controller gave us climb unrestricted to 12;000 which also made sense for the Direct ZZZZZ we had in the FMC. And then climb to FL340 but then stopped us at 15;000. But we were wrong. He questioned us and we discovered the actual clearance was the entire transition out to ZZZZZ. At that point he cleared us to ZZZZZ and to climb to FL340 again. No TCAS or other traffic was in the area. This was a crew error. We both were very disappointed with the mistake. We reviewed the FOM and saw our mistake. We have both done this correctly many times but the 'ZZZZZ' on the filed route threw us off. No other excuse. And as the Captain I take responsibility.

column121: A vibration / rumble was noticed during the No.2 engine start.   During taxi the Captain performed his flight controls check so fast that I was unable to keep up with the call outs. It had been this way the whole trip; in fact I had insisted that it be repeated on the 1st leg so I could correctly check the control position.  Whilst holding short of Runway XXL the Captain indicated he would turn the anti-ice off on taking the runway. I pointed out that the published ATIS reported runway conditions of 3;3;3 with 50% compacted snow; 50% compacted snow; 75% compacted snow. He was still inclined to turn off the anti-ice so I tried again suggesting should anything happen any investigation would focus on this. Reluctantly the anti-ice remained on and having lined up it was obvious that the runway was still significantly impacted by snow.  On departure I chose to call for autopilot 2 at approx 100 ft in case the controller was busy. This allowed me to notice during the initial turn towards / at ZZZZZ that on the E / WD the title Engine" was flashing as well as "N1 VIB" was flashing green 9.9. An increase in noise and vibration was perceived from the right engine. Anti-ice was reapplied and after a short while the indication reduced to 8.2. The indication returned to 9.9 after the anti-ice was turned off during climb and it remained this way until the engines were at idle during the descent. During cruise I suggested the possibility of a bad sensor; the Captain's opinion was that we had a vibration. Later during the leg I commented on the vibration and now the Captain's opinion was that we may have a bad sensor. We were initially cleared to FL360. As we approached level off the Captain requested a climb to FL380 earlier than the flight plan fix of ZZZZZ1. On reaching cruise I reduced then increased managed Mach by 0.01 to investigate the potential of a harmonic vibration. Once established at the new speeds there was no difference in the indicated vibration so I returned to the managed speed with the intent to divert should the situation deteriorate. The Captain took out his QRH and referenced the High Engine Vibration procedure. It was given to read and after a discussion the Captain elected not to follow it as it would require descending from cruise altitude. For the remainder of cruise the Captain returned to reading his magazine. I monitored the indications; changed assigned radio frequencies and from time to time closed my eyes to concentrate on feeling whether the vibration had changed or the ambient sound had changed. We began flying the arrival. During the descent; Approach instructed us to increase speed to 310 kts or better. I felt that this was a bad idea and expressed this by saying ' I don't want to do that ' and 'I am uncomfortable with that'.  'So what it's only 20 kts' was the reply and seeing no intent to inform Approach of our situation; I felt that I had pushed as far as I could and increased speed. The Captain gleefully declared that the vibration had dropped to 2.2. I countered stating that the engines were now at idle as the aircraft attempted to stay on the profile at a higher speed. It was at this point that I decided to reach out  and have myself removed from the trip. ZZZ1 was landing north with reported winds of 160/6 so a landing approach calculation was performed for the tail wind landing. On short final the Captain elected to increase Vapp unilaterally leading to a long float during landing. A new landing approach calculation for the new numbers was not performed. On landing I briefly deployed reverse thrust and quickly closed down the right engine before it could spool up and exacerbate the vibration problem. I moderated the thrust from the left engine and relied mainly on wheel braking to slow the aircraft. Control was passed back to the Captain at approx 60 kts for the taxi to the gate."

column121: During normal climb out of ZZZ; passing roughly FL240; we got a single CAWS Overspeed warning; FMA indicated FMS speed; however aircraft had accelerated into the MMO range I Reduced the speed from Mach .81 to .79 and pressed FMS speed to edit a new lower FMS speed. Reaching cruise at FL350 returned to normal FMS ECON Cruise .83 Mach Two hours into the flight; in cruise with no changes to pitch or power with autopilot on; aircraft started to overspeed by roughly 15 kts beyond the MMO in a couple seconds Both Primary Flight Display's indicated the same speed fluctuation We were alerted by the CAWS and the aircraft started to climb The First Officer took the controls as he was first to identify the problem; turned off the ATS reduced the power I pulled the speed brakes and called for the controls; reduced the speed from .83 Mach to .80 Mach Airspeed spread was about 60 kts and we were at optimum altitude Once the aircraft speed and altitude were under control; I reengaged the FMS speed and ATS These previous events; helped influence my decision making for the primary event.......All three crew members had been in the cockpit; with the door closed; together since departure I got up to use the lavatory about an hour west of ZZZ1; 3 hours into flight As I opened the cockpit door I detected a very strong smell of oily fumes I turned on the lights on the courier deck and the main cargo deck Air was hazy I went to the cockpit and got my flashlight turned off the lights on the main deck opened the smoke curtain and confirmed the presence of blueish smoke on the main deck in my bright flashlight beam I asked the Load Master to please come back to the courier station and check She confirmed the presence of smoke and fumes I returned to the cockpit and I ran the Emergency Non-Alert SMOKE/FIRE/FUMES checklist As per the checklist; I determined the source to be the Bleed 3 as the smoke smelled oily; not acrid; and I've heard of this problem in the past on this aircraft; also the Dangerous Goods Form did not list any hazmat on board and all systems were still functioning normally I turned off Bleed 3 per the checklist and started looking at nearby airports in my iPad The smoke began dissipating slowly I asked the First Officer to please go back and make sure the smoke is not coming from a ULD He returned after a few minutes and confirmed the smoke was dissipating and it was not coming from any of the cargo He said it seemed to concentrated above the wing box but dissipating I was reviewing the previous logbooks and current logbook pages for any smoke occurrences during the previous flights to help come to a decision to divert per the Quick Reference Handbook or to continue per the Quick reference Handbook Before I could finish reviewing the logbook Autopilot 1 disconnected; the aircraft started deviating from altitude and we got a LEVEL 2 alert for FCC 1B FAULT; a master caution and my flight director disappeared I immediately switched to Capt on First Officer Flight Director and stabilized the aircraft; checked all the parameters and engaged Autopilot 2 I called for the LEVEL 2 FCC 1B FAULT checklist After the checklist was complete; I consulted with the crew and made the decision to divert to ZZZ1 as it was a Company flight; it was en-route; weather was good; we were very familiar with the airport and we have maintenance there I gave the controls and communication to the FO and began running Checklist I told the FO to advise ATC that we would like to divert to ZZZ1 for technical reasons We were 39 minutes from ZZZ1 and cleared direct to a point on the STAR We advised NCC via ACARS of our diversion On the STAR when we were passing 11;000 ft at 245 kts; we were cleared to 6;000 ft; I reduced the altitude to 6;000 ft on the FCP and selected IDLE and confirmed on the FMA The aircraft began to climb instead of descend; speeds were normal and aircraft was in clean configuration w/ local altimeter set I disconnected the autopilot and hand flew thelast 50 miles We were cleared for ILS On final as we set Flaps 15 we got a LEVEL 2 FLAP DISAG; this was expected as the right outboard flap had been 'X' out since the FCC Fault We set flaps 35 Flaps showing 21/22/20/X on both PFD's I elected not to extend the flaps further or retract and retry to extend them as the airplane was light and controllable; runway was long and insight; weather was clear and winds were light I elected to maintain MIN auto brakes however I informed the crew I was going to use all 3 reverse and to advise tower that we would be rolling to the end Before landing checklist was completed I announced 'no green box' due to flaps not beyond 25 degrees We landed with no further incident and taxied to the ramp. Excellent job from my First Officer and Load Master They were invaluable to me during the flight. I identified the haze/fumes when I left the cockpit to use the lavatory I found the upper deck full of fumes. [Probable cause of the] smoke was Engine oil leaking into Pneumatic system [Probable cause of the] FCC issue is unknown. Followed SOP; make decisions while weighing input of crew. [As my response] recommended Preventative Maintenance.

column121: Today I taxied to the ZZZ strip with ATIS weather to ZZZ Runway XX. I noticed 4 or 3 maybe snow removal vehicles working around but not yet on the runway. I called in to the Tower and I introduced my airplane numbers and request for takeoff. The Tower asked me to repeat my call sign and I did.  The Tower told me to wait. I heard quite a bit (of half) the Tower radio traffic communication.  The Tower then told me I was cleared for takeoff and I confirmed.  I noticed that the snow removal vehicles all had backed off and so I took off successfully; without incident.  One of the snow removal drivers called into the Tower and told them I took off the strip.  I verified this and was told to call into the Tower later.  I called in and told the Tower how it happen from my prospective after my flight. They say they are passing the incident on. There was a southeast wind and in reflection; the Tower may have told me I was clear to take off southeast; which is from the lake; not the strip.  I should have reiterated my position on the runway when he asked me to repeat my tail numbers.  I do not believe I called for a southeast take off; but there was a southeast wind that I was in my mind.  I was also watching the snow removal equipment but believed he must have told them to back off on a different frequency. There was no other radio traffic until I was 8 to 10 miles away. The lake was empty and the Southeast water lane; frozen; is right in front of the Tower. He could have helped the situation if he said he could not see me. He did not see me take off at all. It was the snow worker that saw me. When I returned about an hour later the ATIS changed to MIKE and the strip was closed.  I had no issue landing on the lake to the southeast. I have flown out of ZZZ since I was a training pilot. I use the lake in the summer and occasionally in the winter. I regret this happened today; regardless that all was safe and there was no chance of any collision with truck or another plane.  It was my intention to follow ATC control; I am sorry if I heard/misinterpreted; or even possibly asked for the incorrect runway. I will certainly talk more to the Tower when they are short and listen more acutely.  I will be more certain of the runway as well and add it to my checklist as I am with wheels and skis. I have caught miscommunication from the Tower in the past coming in on floats but was able to talk it out.

column121: The incident occurred while on the initial climb from runway 25 at Orlando Executive Airport (ORL). The probable cause appears to be communication and pilot error. Our aircraft was a Aircraft X. The student and I were remaining in the pattern practicing touch and go landings. An Aircraft Y [faster aircraft] was following us throughout the pattern. Our call sign was occasionally [mis-stated] which contributed to the confusion. During our pattern practice we were told to extend our downwind and that Tower would call our base. While we were in the right downwind and extended right downwind for Runway 25; Aircraft Y was noticeably gaining on us as shown on our MFD's traffic feature. Our base was approved and we were number 1 cleared for a touch and go Runway 25. [Aircraft Y] was cleared for a touched and go number 2 behind us. While on short final; it was noticeable once again on the MFD that Aircraft Y was gaining on us significantly. Our approach speed in the Aircraft X is 65 kts. With the headwind component that day our ground speed was undoubtedly slower than 65kts. Aircraft Y was told by Tower to do an s-turn on final for spacing as it was apparent they were getting close. The problem arose on the initial climb out following the touch and go; Aircraft Y overtook our aircraft while on the departure leg at approximately 800 feet; resulting in a near miss.The traffic we were following was told to extend upwind and we were expecting to receive a similar instruction for ourselves. The confusion seems to have begun when Executive Tower radioed for Aircraft Y to continue in the upwind and that they would call their crosswind. We did not respond to this call; as we assumed it was intended for Aircraft Y.  Aircraft Y responded confirming to extend their upwind until their crosswind was called. This transmission must have stepped on the Tower's transmission because as soon as Aircraft Y was finished broadcasting; the end of tower's transmission came through with the only audible portion being '...end upwind.' (Most likely 'extend upwind.')  This stepped-on call was most likely a follow up to [us]; but Aircraft Y then responded to continue their upwind for a 2nd time. Tower then called for Aircraft Y to extend their upwind. At this point the instructor in Aircraft Y; clearly confused; read back the extend upwind instruction for the 3rd time. We realized that the extend upwind call to [callsign] was most likely for us and we continued the upwind as instructed with the traffic ahead of and behind us being on extended upwinds.During this time; we again noticed Aircraft Y gaining on us on the MFD traffic. We continued in our upwind climb as Tower called for Aircraft Y to follow traffic ahead to the right (us). They responded that they had us in sight as they continued climbing and closing in on our left hand side. This is the approximate time that [we] was overtaken by Aircraft Y at approximately 800 feet MSL. Aircraft Y passed by us at roughly 200 feet off of our left wing; while both of us were still climbing to pattern altitude in the upwind leg.

column121: I was approaching F70 from the southeast after a personal flight while making radio calls every few miles as I noticed on my ADS-B in several targets circling around the airport due to intense student activity.Someone made a radio call a few minutes before I was in the vicinity of another aircraft cutting them off on downwind too and I prepared myself for heavy traffic in the pattern and trying to find an opening so I could join the downwind.Upon entering the 45 for downwind I noticed visually an aircraft on the upwind taking off and repeatedly asked his intentions and if he could see me.There was no answer and seeing him proceed on runway heading I continued on the 45 for downwind being confident he wouldn't start a turn to crosswind until he reached close to pattern altitude as is recommended for the noise abatement procedure out of F70 for departures from Runway 18.Then I saw him maneuver for the crosswind maybe 500 feet below my altitude which was at pattern and make a radio call in that regards. At this point I had contacted him several times regarding his intentions and whether he could see me but without any answer.Seeing him turn and put me on the direct collision course with me although 300 ft. below me I decided to execute a 360 degree turn saw him coming extremely near me. Finally he acknowledged my presence in a subsequent radio call.I continued the full turn and reentered downwind.F70 was extremely busy that day with several schools on the field and at one point I saw no less than 5 aircraft in the traffic pattern. Needless to say a Tower is badly needed in that field for the safety of flight as the indiscriminate addition of several aircraft from several schools without any sort of coordination between those schools makes this urgently needed.A bit of courtesy goes a long way too and someone was nice enough to extend their downwind for me earlier in the day so I could depart as I had to hold short of the active runway at least 10 minutes as one aircraft after another was landing with no end in sight.On my side I should have waited outside the pattern on a hold in a safe area until there was no aircraft on upwind and the downwind leg would be fully opened; with adequate radio communications ensuring everyone in the pattern has knowledge of any other traffic with acknowledgement for all.This was my first experience with this field with that many aircraft in the pattern and the lesson learned here is to stay outside an uncontrolled field until there is fewer than a set limit of aircraft that one can set as personal limit.Such a personal limit is not taught at all as part of any training curriculum nor in the AIM in my knowledge.Most uncontrolled field are uncontrolled because of very low traffic but some reach levels just below the threshold needed for a tower and F70 seems to be in that category.Also the schools on the field could coordinate some kind of schedule among themselves so not everyone is up in the air at the same time. Poisson's law dictates things happen in bursts unless there is coordination to avert it.

column121: We were conducting Aircraft X at night into ABE; vectored from the north; and then given a clearance for a Visual Approach. As always; we had an approach set up; ILS 24; and while descending from the north side of the airport from 3;000 feet; the vectored altitude; to 2;400 feet; at an altitude of about 2;650 feet we received a one time (only 1) 'Terrain' warning from the TAWS (Terrain Alert Warning System); while descending very gently at about 300 feet per minute. We leveled off for a moment; there was no other terrain warning and never a 'Terrain; Pull Up' command; then as we intercepted the final; we continued to the 2;400 feet glideslope intercept altitude. There was a ridgeline north of the ILS course; which we had briefed on; but it did not show an altitude greater than 1;000 feet; so we did not think it would be a problem to start a shallow descent from 3;000 to 2;400 feet; especially at a shallow rate. This is a potential problem at night; as there are no obstacle lights on the ridge line; so I believe Approach should simply provide vectors to the ILS approach instead of just giving a 'visual.'  A little more work for ATC but a safer way of operating. Caused by ATC clearing crew to do a night visual instead of providing vectors; knowing that there are unmarked; unlit; terrain ridge lines to the north of the airport. Also caused by crew not requesting full vectors to the ILS at night. Most ATC facilities in small airports don't want to work that hard. Suggest that crews start asking ATC at small airports to provide vectors to the Approach being used to back up the Visual when in night VMC conditions; as a means to improve the level of safety; even if it means that ATC might have to work a bit more.

column121: The flight departed the from Gate X in ZZZ1 at XA:10z and proceed to flight level 200 to ZZZZZ intersection to join the arrival into ZZZ without incidence. At approximately XB:10Z while descending through 8;000 MSL for 7;000 MSL in IMC conditions with heavy rain and continuous light and occasionally moderate turbulence we received a single chime and an ELT ON Master Caution message was displayed on the EICAS primary page. Approximately one to two seconds later a very loud ELT signal began sounding through the flight deck intercom system. I notified ATC that we had an indication that our ELT had activated and that it was in error and could be disregarded. I further advised them that the ELT tone was sounding on the flight deck and it was making radio communication and flight deck communication very difficult. I turned the number two comm radio off of the guard frequency and reduced the volume; but it did not have any effect on the volume of the ELT. The First Officer (FO) began to attempt to find a resolution [in] the QRH and we attempted QRH procedure several times to try to silence the tone without success. The noise was deafening and flight deck communication and air to ground communication was very difficult.  At 4;000 MSL we were given a heading of 360 degrees then descended to 3;000 MSL and turned to a heading of 085 degrees and instructed to join the localizer for Runway X. At this time both aircraft localizers failed; and a red LOC indication was displayed on both PFD's.  We advised ATC and asked if there was a problem with the localizer.  ATC queried several other aircraft and all advised they were receiving the localizer.  We broke off of the approach per ATC instruction and attempted to set up for the ILS to Runway YL but could not receive any ILS signal.  I advised ATC that we would need a GPS approach and we were instructed to prepare for the GPS YL.  After having set up the GPS YL ATC advised that the wind had shifted and were now from 275 degrees gusting to 25 kts. We were further advised that the airport was now in a west flow.  We requested RNAV YY and began preparing that approach. We received radar vectors to RNAV GPS YY and completed the approach without incidence.Due to extreme flight deck noise from the ELT throughout the event communication on the flight deck and with ATC was very difficult. The noise and inability to communicate throughout added a high level of stress and complexity.  Continuous turbulence and instrument meteorological conditions were present throughout; with ceilings and visibility at or near minimums on arrival at the runway.  The double failure event coupled with the inability to sync the two MFD's due to a previously existing MEL added complexity and were additional threats. To mitigate these factors myself and my FO followed SOP to the extent that we were able. We resisted the urge to rush and after preparing the RNAV approach we briefed the approach; and the runway change items in an attempt to slow down the process and bring the flight back into the normal envelope as much as possible. In hindsight I wish that I would have tried the EMER function on the RCP (Remote Compensation Panel). I don't know if it would have helped but the noise made concentration and communication very difficult and it was very fatiguing. Overall I was satisfied with my actions and those of my FO given the circumstances and without the benefit of hindsight I thought that we met or exceeded expectations.

Before the pushback the ground personnel said all secure below; FOD walk complete; steering disengaged; standing by for parking brake. The ground personnel did not report any panels that were open. Some point above sterile we heard a thump noise. We then called the flight attendant to ask if everyone was okay. The flight attendant indicated everything was fine. We checked the EICAS and all the engine instruments were in the green. We then checked the MFD pages and everything was normal. We preceded onto the destination as there was nothing to indicate any abnormality. We have no way of knowing if this was related to the latches underneath the engine coming open. When we had arrived to the gate the ground personnel had told us that there was two latches underneath the engine hanging down. The two doors open underneath Engine Number 1 was the engine oil service door and the air turbine starter access panel. Me and the FO proceeded outside during the walk around to look at the access panels underneath the engine and relayed the information to Maintenance. The access panels had also caused holes in the engine cowling.The cause was the access panels underneath Engine Number 1 came open during the flight. During the preflight during before departure nothing was noticed abnormal.A thorough preflight was done before the flight. Nothing out of the abnormal was indicated by the FO or the ground crew. A thorough preflight was accomplished and should before every flight. No other suggestions at this time.

Autothrust disengaged and went into Thrust LK. Thrust levers were matched with power setting and IDP switches used. We had our route displayed in the ND on both sides and MCDUs were operating normally. ECAM displayed:AUTO FLT AP OFF (RED)AUTO FLT A/THR OFF (AMBER)L/G SHOCK ABSORBER FAULT (AMBER)Indications looked similar to an FMGC Dual Failure except we had both NDs displaying our route; our MCDUs did not go into a subsystem page and no FMGC (Timeout) was observed. The Shock Absorber Fault ECAM had me thinking this may be a different malfunction that I have never witnessed or a coincidence. We contacted Dispatch/Maintenance via phone patch using the 'CALL ME' function on ACARS. Maintenance was perplexed of what was causing our malfunction. They had us reset the Auto Flight C/B's B1 (MCDU 1) B2 (FMG 1) and hold. C/B's were reset with no change. We attempted the Long Reset in the QRH Dual FMGC Failure with no success. Mintenance had no other options available.ATC was advised of our equipment malfunction and our inability to remain in ZZZ airspace. We were cleared down to FL 27;000 ft.. Review of our fuel; weather and capabilities with my F/O. Dispatcher we agreed to continue to ZZZ1 with the caution that if we had additional malfunctions; we would consider ZZZ2 as a divert airport. ATC was given our new suffix with the inability to operate in RVSM airspace.Purser was informed of our status.Prior to touchdown at FL 27;000 ft. both FMAs began to populate. Autopilots and Autothrust became available. All malfunctions except for the STBY Pitot cleared. We reengaged the Auto flight functions and remained at FL 27;000 ft. We landed on Runway XX at ZZZ1. Malfunctions were recorded on in the ELB; including a information writeup of what happened. Technician met the plane and we explained what happened.
