column121: We started out vectored off our arrival by ZZZ Center to the southwest with several step down altitudes.  30 miles from the airport we found ourselves at 20;000 MSL which is about 10;000 feet higher than usual for a normal descent.  ATC; specifically ZZZ Center; was overloaded with aircraft going into south State X.  The Controller brought us around and eventually around 10;000 MSL he told us to go direct to the ZZZ airport.  At that time; we were about 15-18 miles away at just under 10;000 MSL.  A few minutes later the Controller asked if we had the field in sight to which we replied that we did; but we needed a vector because we were too high to safely attempt the visual approach.  We were given a left 360 degree turn and cleared down to 3;000 MSL also while given direct to the ZZZ airport.  Upon leveling off at 3;000 MSL we were in a cloud layer and couldn't see the field.  We requested lower and were given 1;500 MSL.  Once we reach that altitude; we could see the field and was cleared the visual approach to Runway X and to switch to Tower.On final; after fully configuring the aircraft; Tower told us to turn right to a heading of 180.  Very confused; we asked him to repeat the instructions at which point we executed a missed approach for a disabled aircraft on the runway.  Tower never actually told us to go-around.  We were given heading 180 and a climb to 4;000 MSL.  Following the level off we were instructed to hold present position however the aircraft will not hold present position on HDG mode.  It can only PPOS HOLD while on and active FMS leg with less than .25 NM cross track.  Knowing this; we told the Controller we needed a fix to hold and we were given the ZZZ2 NDB which doesn't exist in the database.  We instead requested the missed approach fix for the RNAV X approach.We weren't sure or told how long the runway was going to be shut down so the crew started to discuss diverting options which ZZZ1 was the only real viable option.  The FMS indicated it would take about 3;500 lbs of fuel and we had about 2;300lbs of reserve fuel on board.  From my quick calculation; I had to make a decision fairly soon considering the following:  we had about 5;700lbs on fuel on board; unknown runway closure; time; FMS calculation of 3;500 lbs of fuel required to ZZZ1; high volume of ZZZ Center traffic and high controller work load.  I sent a message to Dispatch informing them we would attempt one more approach and if unable to make it in we would divert to ZZZ1.We notified ZZZ Center Controller we needed to attempt another approach or we would soon have need to divert.  We were given vectors around and cleared for the visual to Runway X once again.  As the pilot flying; I opted to proceed direct to the FAF of the RNAV X and continue the visual approach.  At about the base leg portion I turned off the autopilot and turned towards the runway.  I believe that a slight turn inside of the FAF did not sequence the approach nor the glide path information which led to a position above the glide path.  I flew down to correct the glide path all while in and out of 1;000 FPM VVI.  I acknowledged the momentary deviations of descent and quickly corrected as I was now on the visual indications from the PAPI's.  On short final; a thermal briefly interrupted our descent and with a quick correction back to glide path I corrected the path for a safe landing.I believe the accumulation of all factors above could have led to a critically low fuel situation much quicker than expected.  I believe the saturation of airspace on a very busy travel day could have been underestimated in the current climate of understaffed controllers.  ZZZ Center controllers were so saturated with aircraft that any chance to hand an aircraft off to a visual approach whether it was really safe to do so or not was attempted.  Unsure about divert fuel and runway state created a high-importance; high stress moment of deciding when a divert should occur without having proper data supporting it.  Lastly; in a heightened sense of urgency with a tight turn inbound to the runway and sub-sequence 'Cutting the corner' led to the aircraft being in a position higher than the glide path.I would suggest the following for operations into ZZZ Captain only approach and landing.  I believe most captains take it upon themselves to make the approach and landing due to the short runway as it is.  There should be more 'hip pocket' information whether in the form of a bulletin or some other format that provides rough numbers of divert options; fuel required; routing; etc when a formal alternate is not filed.  I also suggest fuel planning take into account busy travel days and add as much fuel as practical for contingencies even on days with VMC conditions that does not preclude landing due to being over max landing weight.  I also believe during all forms of training (initial; recurrent; etc) special authorization airports and airports such as ZZZ are discussed. It is my suggestion that ZZZ be a mandatory training event.  I can tell you everything you need to know about flying to ZZZ2 yet we don't actually go there in the aircraft.  However; airports such as ZZZ are rarely mentioned when we fly there every week.  I suggest more 'hangar flying' where scenarios are discussed (such as this one) in a classroom/training environment to get captains to start thinking about scenarios such as these.  I'd also like to recommend that one or two approaches from ZZZ3 be included in our Jeppesen charts or company pages.  Should ZZZ be shut down for any reason and there is not enough divert fuel to safely make it back to the mainland there will be a 10;000 foot runway available; especially in IMC conditions.  Lastly; I suggest that pilots refrain from attempting to cut corners while approaching the runway from greater than 90 degrees.  Instead; they should fly the published approach in its entirety including glide slopes or glide paths so that they maintain a safe; stable approach to the runway.

column121: Reflecting back on this flight today; I fear we may not have obtained verbal landing clearance from Tower before touchdown on Runway X at ZZZ. This was my first flight in over two months; and was assigned with another Captain as my First Officer; with no one else present on the flight deck. I had also been on leave earlier in the year. Before we flew; I briefed that two captains flying together as a two-pilot crew complement is a threat; as it does not happen often; and there is an operational bias for the acting First Officer (co-Captain). During the descent; Air Traffic Control vectored us to a close-in base leg to Runway X. Approach Control asked us if we had the field in sight; and I elected to continue with a visual approach; which I believe now was not the best choice for myself. My acting First Officer momentarily lost sight of the field during my turn from base to final; however I had it acquired visually the entire time. I pointed out the field to assist; and the pilot monitoring re-acquired it. This should have resulted in a go-around to rejoin the approach; as this is a team environment; and a two-pilot airplane. I know I did switch the nose-wheel landing light to 'on' during the final approach leg; as that is SOP after being cleared to land; according to FOM. I was focused on flying the plane; slowing down early; and ensuring a stabilized approach.  I was not completely in tune with what my co-captain was or was not doing. Stabilized approaches are a topic often discussed in training; so it weighed heavily in my priorities on this day. My co-Captain (pilot monitoring) may not have switched to Tower as it was somewhat a high workload environment and unusual operation; at least to me.I should have recognized the threat of two captains flying together; along with my low state of landing currency; would lead to a chain reaction easily. I should have requested the full ILS to Runway X; or at least a longer final approach leg. I would recommend after a Captain returns to the line after a lengthy vacation; and in my case leave earlier in the year as well; to not pair up with another Captain; but only a highly current First Officer. Although everything was completely my responsibility; this would have eliminated the threat. I recognize that sound aeronautical decision making as it relates to all phases of duty; is the number one factor influencing safety; and it must be practiced even in high-workload environments.

I told him I wanted to wait till I had the new paperwork in hand and reviewed. Eventually the paperwork showed up and once we reviewed and did a few more items to finalize the preparation I turned around to notify the Load Master that I was ready for the cross check. The person said that they were not doing the cross check at that station due to COVID-19. I was surprised by his answer and said something like 'REALLY?' And he repeated his original statement. I told him I had not been notified of this situation and he said it was to reduce exposure on the flight deck.I gave him the paperwork that was completed but did not have the check marks related to the normal cross check process with the Load Master. In hindsight; I am skeptical about the answer I received and decided I should make this report to make sure that this situation is truly their process. If it turns out to be accurate we should possibly notify any crews that will be going into ZZZZ.This flight was already scheduled later than normal due to crew rest requirements and due to the delay in receiving the hard copy of the amended flight release it was running approximately 10 minutes later than the newly scheduled time. It was obvious that they were under pressure to get us moving and I was attempting to keep things standard and attempt to not introduce the opportunity to have errors.

column121: During boarding; the gentleman in [seat] XX1 got my attention to ask if he was in the right seat; so I looked and tapped on each person in the row to confirm for him. That is how I noticed the X Family was a party of 4. The mother was holding the child and I asked if the child was a seat or a lap as I didn't have her as a lap child in my list; but in her own seat. She said she has her own seat. And I asked if she was over 2 years. The mother said yes. I asked if they had a mask for the child reminding them of our policy and also reiterated that the child would need to be in her own seat for takeoff (FAR); landing and whenever the seat belt sign was on. The father stated that she's only two. I said yes; she's over two that's why she's required to have and be in her own seat. The father also said they were traveling internationally. (I believed they were traveling internationally when we got to ZZZ; but later in this situation the Supervisor who spoke to the family ascertained that they had come in from ZZZZ on Aircraft Y; where apparently the situation was not addressed on that flight).I offered to bring a mask and did. I informed the Purser and cockpit that there was both issues. While I was closing bins I walked past the family and they had made no attempt to rectify the situation. I also had to remind the father twice to fix his own mask. When there was no attempt to address the non masked child by the family I chat text for a Supervisor to address the situation since the door was open. The first Supervisor went to the seat and was there for a few seconds; I was concerned that it didn't appear the situation was addressed by the reaction of the family. The child still didn't have a mask on and no motion to attempt. I approached the Supervisor and asked him about it. He said he told the family. I informed him that I walked by their row and the child wasn't wearing a mask nor was there any attempt to get the child to wear one. The purser also spoke to the family.Another Supervisor came; and spoke to the family. I stayed at the front of the cabin to let them deal with the situation. Supervisor 2; Inflight supervisor came as we were now taking a delay.Supervisor 2 said that they could make an exception to the mask policy.I; as an employee who is required to be masked with verbalized and written termination warning from my company if I do not remained masked at work; is now telling me that exceptions can be made onboard the aircraft for passengers. I have never heard of this and am not aware of documentation of this.The passenger knows the child isn't allowed to be a lap child and they know that anyone over two is required to be masked.While I realize it's difficult for a young child I also acknowledge that Airline chose to pick this age for mask requirement likely to coincide with the FAA mandated age seat requirement. There is ample notification for these policies (during booking and check in); passengers personal responsibility is a choice. As is proactive parenting. After more than two decades of flying there are quite frankly cultural differences/ beliefs of non-compliance and this presents itself as complete lack of acknowledgment of our policies (or FAR's). I completely acknowledge that the flying public is a challenge at times; most follow the rules. This includes me; especially at work. While I'm completely capable of sympathy; compassion and compromise... I'm absolutely not when it comes to safety.I applaud Airline for enforcing the mask policy. I would encourage them to strive for consistency on a multitude of other safety issues that appear at times to go by the wayside in favor of on time departures and convenience. It is this mentality that creates inconsistencies and quite frankly makes my job harder to do.

column121: My flight began at ZZZ1 with the intent to fly direct to ZZZ for touch and goes and return to ZZZ1. I have flown this particular airplane multiple times with no issues. The start; taxi; and run-up were normal and no different than any other time; except that the strobe lights were blinking slower than usual but working as expected.The airplane was flown earlier; and no issues were reported; hence there was no reason to suspect a problem. I did two take-offs and landings before departing to ZZZ; I had no issues. During a normal approach to landing at ZZZ; all-electric equipment failed at an altitude of 300 feet from touching down on Runway XX. I was forced to immediately clear the runway and exit onto the first taxiway I saw; Taxiway XX; I had a disabled radio; transponder; and ADS-B.Although clear from the tower for a touch and go; I could not continue the flight safely with disabled equipment; therefore a go-around was not an option. Luckily; I have a handheld radio and was able to contact the control tower to explain what happened; and request directions to the parking area. I had to deviate from the touch and go clearance since I dint know what else was wrong with the airplane and continuing the flight would have been unwise.After arriving at the parking area; I talked to the mechanic who was only available by phone and asked me to go through my checklist again to troubleshoot the issue. I made multiple attempts to restart the airplane; loud cabin speaker noises could be heard as the power switch was turned on as if there was a short circuit in the system; but all fuses were okay and there was no power to start the engine. The mechanic determined that I had a dead battery and it could only mean that the airplane suffered an alternator failure on landing; grounding the airplane immediately.The flight club from which I rented the airplane has multiple airplanes of the same make and model and provided me with one so I could fly back to ZZZ1. The return flight was uneventful.

column121: Pre-flight planning with ForeFlight didn't show icing conditions where I encountered them in flight. The ZZZ1 live weather cams looked promising too. I should've used multiple resources instead of just ForeFlight. Years of multiple flights on this route gave me a false sense security. I was aware of a small storm moving in. I pushed my limits; trying to arrive before the storm while taking advantage of tail winds.These are all examples of what lead up to my problem. I encountered MVFR conditions over the mountains approximately 40 miles southwest of ZZZ2 at approximately 14;500 ft. I noticed light rime icing; air temp -20c. I climbed and notified ATC I would return to ZZZ due to weather. This was a safe decision. While Heading back at 17;500 ft.; it appeared I could make it safely over the top of the weather. I planned to overfly ZZZ2 and look for a safe opening in the weather. I had done this many times before and was still feeling complacent and confident. I informed ATC of my plans to turn around. This was NOT a safe or intelligent decision and caused my problem. I should have acknowledged my original weather concerns and continued back home. While close to ZZZ2 clouds built up vertically rapidly. I started icing up and informed ATC of my situation and needed to climb to FL 18;500 ft. I was at my service ceiling; with few options. Despite pitot heat and MVFR; my pitot tube froze up. I lost all primary instruments; switched to secondary steam gauges; also my O2 tank malfunctioned. This all happened in a matter of minutes. Lack of practice on partial instrument panel failures did not help my situation. I informed ATC I was unable to copy IFR clearances at this time.Maneuvering around building IMC icing conditions; on steam gauges; at my service ceiling; without O2; and now fighting headwinds was very challenging. Flying the plane had to be my sole focus and ATC understood. ATC made me a priority aircraft for me due to my unwillingness to copy my IFR clearance. As I headed southwest my instruments came back online and the weather improved. I subsequently picked up an IFR clearance. I requested lower; plus cancellation of IFR from ZZZ Center. ZZZ Center asked if I was still in distress. I assured ATC everything was fine now. I was no longer considered an aircraft in a priority handling situation. As a preventative safety measure; planes without deicing equipment should not fly near icing conditions even in VMC. Traditional VFR cloud separation rules; while legal are not always safe; especially when potentially hazardous conditions exist. A good preventative measure would have been not to fly at all that day.

I called out 'Speed' and he did not acknowledge so again I said 'Watch your speed.' By this time we were doing around 275 knots and I don't why but he thought we should continue the climb so he used the autopilot to begin to climb the plane. I immediately told him to maintain 7;000 and reduce his speed. The initiated climb resulted in an altitude gain of 400 feet and the Controller told us to maintain 7;000 feet. We returned to 7;000 with no other issues and slowed. I was told our delay was a result of staffing issues at ZZZ center because of COVID-19. This is by far the longest ATC delay I have experienced and I definitely know fatigue was a factor hear. Do I think we were unsafe? No; I do not. That being said I don't think we were the tip of the spear that late in the day. ATC was super busy on the radios and we tried calling several times to request higher to get out of the weather we were in to no avail. Under staffing; busy airspace; delays; fatigue; and weather all combined would be the problem in my opinion. As well as pressure to get the job done.

column121: On RNAV to Runway XX due to GS being inop on the ILS; winds; and airport conditions.  Outside FAF; attempted to extend Landing Gear and got only the 3 red UNLOCKED lights.  No landing gear operation.  Our airspeed was around 165 KIAS.  We attempted to recycle the gear and got exact same thing.  We executed a missed approach; [advised ATC]; and attempted to contact Dispatch on ACARS.  We tried several frequencies but could not make voice contact.  ZZZ1 airspace was undergoing some sort of COVID cleaning so not sure if that had anything to do with ARINC in that vicinity.  We just used the ACARS to communicate as best we could.  Dispatch texted that the only thing he was showing was LANDING GEAR NOT DOWN LOCKED (same as us) but had no other system malfunctions that he could see.  We followed the ECAM which instructed us to use the gravity extend.  We did; it worked; and we landed safely.  We texted Dispatch once on the ground that we made it safely; Maintenance came with the tug and towed us to the gate.  Passengers and flight attendants were informed in the air and on the ground as to what was happening.
column123: Just after midnight; outside the FAF to Runway XX at ZZZ; I was the PM and was asked to extend the landing gear. The gear failed to extend. Landing gear not down-locked. Recycled landing gear. No joy. Told Tower we needed to go-around to troubleshoot. Requested priority handling and then transferred controls; I was now PF while the Captain ran the ECAM and coordinated with Dispatch/Maintenance Control/FAs. I requested vectors away from the weather and near the approach so we could quickly join final when complete; requested they roll the trucks; and advised ATC we would need a tow off the runway. The Captain had difficulties talking with Dispatch and Maintenance over ARINC due to our low altitude (3;000) but was able to exchange some messages over ACARS with both. He ran the landing gear gravity extension checklist as directed by the ECAM. Landing gear came down. Captain updated FAs and made a PA to the passengers. We transferred controls and I was then PM for the final approach; visibility was poor due to a weather system. Rough winds and conditions but great landing by the Captain. Full stop on the runway. Crash truck circled and checked the plane out. Tow arrived and we shutdown motors and were towed to the gate.

column121: Deice in PIT is unsafeDeice in PIT done by [the FBO] on the general aviation deice pad near taxiways N and N5. When we arrived; the pad was unplowed; with no markings available. Lighting is poor. There were two deice trucks; one facing east and one west; with what appeared to be perhaps 125% of our wingspan between them. It's difficult to judge distance at night in the snow on a poorly lit ramp with lights facing us - but it was WAY too close. There is no specified aircraft operation zone. Were the vehicles in that zone? Who knows? Add that braking values on the ATIS were 3/3/3; and the ramp appears to slope slightly downward to the north.We did get the east-facing truck to back up so we could get parked; to do this I had to make a 120 degree turn (roughly from N5 into the ramp; I was able to widen out a bit) on this snow-covered; unplowed (and therefore unmarked) ramp. There are NO WINGWALKERS provided here - it's all on your own with only the driver and sprayer in the truck on duty as far as we could see. With a corporate jet; the building; and then a fence all within less than a wingspan this is simply unacceptable.To leave this deice pad; I had to add power to get through the unplowed snow. Notice that there was a building less than 150 feet behind me; and possibly the corporate jet there too although I think we got turned enough to not endanger them.While the folks in the deice truck were very professional; we did have to prompt them for the fluid type; etc. On the initial call to let us know they were done they only told us that the deice and anti-ice steps started 'x' minutes ago.We got it done. I'm only moderately sure in hindsight that it was safe enough. I can't be sure that when we got deiced we were completely off the taxiways. I am certain that if this setup continues someone will hit something. Why we don't use the vendor that *others* use is beyond me.

column123: I was the First Officer and pilot monitoring on this flight IAH. We were cleared to descend via the LINKK1 arrival except maintain 300 knots. Then; 320 knots. Then; as fast as practical until LINKK. Then we were cleared for the approach from RDFSH and maintain 210 knots until FESTA. We had 6000 feet in the MCP window as this was the bottom altitude for the STAR. After being cleared the approach; I failed to set a lower altitude. Shortly after RDFSH (and level at 6000') ATC asked if we were descending on the approach. We were immediately aware of our mistake and the captain began descending. GEYGR and SYYKO (the next two fixes on the approach after RDFSH) had mandatory altitudes of 4000' and 3000'; respectively. Because of our delayed descent after RDFSH; we were high at both of those fixes. The multiple airspeed changes on the arrival caused a distraction and I failed to notice that I hadn't set a lower altitude to continue the approach after RDFSH. That being the case; it was still my job as pilot monitoring to set the lower altitude and I failed to do it.

My recommendation is to change the [Taxiway] B1 sign to add the directional arrow to show turn or to rename the 2nd half of the angle/jog of Taxiway B1 to emphasize the direction of taxi that Ground wants us to take.

column121: On final; Runway XXL; ZZZ; Night; 1000 foot ceiling; Me (Captain) flying; gusty winds; very light load; FO low currency- only 150 hrs in type since hired 1 year ago; and has not been flying much. I was hand flying at 2;000 feet on normal ILS. Called for gear down; flaps 15 at approximately 2;000 feet and flaps 30 landing; check at about 1500 feet. FO ran check list; while I hand flew the approach. The winds were gusty; our target was +15 ref and it was night.  I saw flap refs change on airspeed tape; and glanced at gear lights when FO ran checklist; but I did not have full attention to FO duties since it was dark and gusty. We broke out at 1;000 feet; I called clear to land and set missed approach altitude. At 500 feet we simultaneously got the 500 auto call out and Too Low Flaps. I simultaneously; started a Go-Around (finger to toga button) and looked at flap gauge - which was at 25. But I hesitated on the go-around when I saw why we got the GPWS. I commanded flaps set to 30; which the FO immediately did. We were then about 350-400 feet and stable; and I continued to a normal landing. After landing I realized; even though there was adequate time to set the flaps to 30; I should have gone around. We debriefed after parking. The FO said he just missed the flaps in setting and checking on the checklist; most likely due to being low time in aircraft and rusty from time off. I missed his wrong setting; due to the dark and the gusty winds requiring my attention. I said I should have gone around; and that he as well should have told me to. I am confident if I had not immediately recognized why we got the too low flaps and immediately corrected it; I would not have continued.

column121: On Date; I was the assigned Captain on Aircraft X. The aircraft had the following MEL:APU shutdown during Engine 1 start action. Reset retry no help; request approval to apply MEL action. Applied MEL action; APU surges / rumbles during MES (main engine start) mode. It can carry both packs normally. When [the] First Officer and I were preflighting the aircraft arrived at the gate; the aircraft had already been completely boarded.  There was no ground air operating. During the preflight; the ground power failed and the entire airplane went dark.  Ramp personnel attempted to reconnect; but the airplane would not accept the power.  The Ramp Supervisor; talking with me through the open aircraft window advised he was going to get a second ground power unit.  Minutes later; with the aircraft still dark ramp [agents] attempted to connected power.  The aircraft powered for just at 30 seconds and went dark again.  The Ramp Supervisor stated the he knew both ground power units are working; yet the aircraft would not accept the power. I contacted the Duty Manager; briefed the situation and stated that I was refusing the aircraft.  He agreed; stating he would back my decision. I contacted the Dispatcher for the flight; who conferenced in Maintenance Control.  I explained the situation and that I was refusing the aircraft - unable to operate.  Maintenance Control stated that with both the APU and ground power not working; The aircraft could not be dispatched; so that technically it was not a refusal. During this call; passengers were becoming agitated and wanting off the dark aircraft.  Flight attendants and gate personnel began de-planing the passengers.  Several were taking video while in the dark airplane with no air. Maintenance arrived at the airplane during the passenger exit and advised they were able to get the power to work; 'the connection was not good.'The Dispatcher called; conferenced Maintenance Control; and we again briefed what I have stated so far in this report.  Both stated that the refusal was completely understandable and advised with questionable contingencies: what happens if the ground power doesn't work in ZZZ; what if it does work during an unplanned divert; etc.  additionally; with passengers filming; said it was the prudent call to refuse the aircraft. The aircraft was powered down so no MRM (maintenance report message) could be sent.

column123: First Officer came in after preflight and said [the] fueler had used pressure refueling port to fuel; she was almost done fueling by the time he saw and was able to say something. I called Ops (Operations) to mention the fueler had used a panel that was MEL'd and shouldn't have; gave Ops the truck number. column121: Captain (CA) was PF and First Officer (FO) was PM. We had a crew alert action of AUTOFLT FCU1 failure not far from our initial descent for the STAR. CA was working the crew alert issue and Center called saying what the CA heard was 'Flight ABC'; Direct ZZZZZ descend via ZZZZZ1' (CA was in the QRH; reading about or looking for the crew alert issue).  After talking with the FO on the ground in ZZZ; after the event; the FO thought the read back something like 'Flight ABC direct ZZZZZ for the ZZZZZ1.'  Then; PM made sure PF was inserting the bottom altitude of STAR in the FCU (Meaning PM understood the clearance to descend via the ZZZZZ1).  PF did insert the bottom altitude. Then; shortly afterwards; we hit some moderate turbulence and PF decided to start descend early because he could not read the QRH; hoping to get into some clear air.  Then we were told we descended and there may have been a flight deviation.  I did not think so at the time because of the clearance I understood.I believe there were several causal factors on this event. 1) Pilot Inexperience.  The FO was on the Type X aircraft and in March was awarded the Type Y aircraft.  But from March through December; all the FO did was go to Type Y training; and IOE.  This was the FO's first flight since IOE. The FO was going very slow making sure no mistakes were made. The PF was also going very slow to ensure all FO tasks were completed.  2) Task saturation (crew alert event; pilot inexperience; turbulence and clearance understanding). Combined; this put both pilots in a 'caution situation.'  The PF; was trying for something like this would not happen from the moment the flight started by making sure he was slow and deliberate on all his thoughts and actions. 3) Turbulence event. We descended early because PF had a hard time reading the QRH. 4) PF flying and completing crew alert actions.  In this case; it may have made a difference; but; I do not believe it would have made a difference; because the PM understood the clearance from Center was a clearance to descend Via;   and when the turbulence started; the person working the crew alert action would have said descend to get out of the turbulence the QRH could be read. The same outcome would have happened.Suggestions - Verify the clearance; no matter the circumstances...In this particular event; the PF should have verified the clearance knowing the proficiency of the other pilot may not have been 100%.  A pilot may be 'Current' with regards to the official written documents approved by the FAA; but they may have not been proficient...(I do not know how this can be fixed...)
column123: In preparation for descent; Status Page showed an inoperative system the CA/PF noticed. CA was in the process of investigating the crew alert message that caused it. We had a seasoned CA in the Jump Seat who was assisting in the lookup for the crew alert actions; if any; and the code was send to Maintenance. In that time; we received a call from Center to proceed 'direct to ZZZZZ for the ZZZZZ1.' I read the clearance back 'direct ZZZZZ for the ZZZZZ1 arrival'. I then conveyed to the CA/Pilot Flying 'direct to ZZZZZ; we can descend via the ZZZZZ1' and I backed CA up to set direct ZZZZZ in the FMS and dialed in the lowest altitude in the arrival for south landings. We verified the altitude. While inbound to ZZZZZ; we were at FL390 and encountered some occasions of moderate turbulence and continuous light chop. The CA/PF commenced a descent to avoid remaining in the turbulent conditions. I contacted the Center to let them know we were descending out of FL390. They called back to ask what was the reason for the descent. I stated we had encountered moderate to light turbulence and needed to descend to avoid it. They called back asking me to confirm the reason for descent was turbulence. I confirmed. Then; before we were handed off to the next frequency; the controller asked us to contact a number for possible altitude deviation. There was a misunderstanding; on my part; of the vertical clearance in the call with Center with the initial clearance for ZZZZZ1 and I passed that misinterpretation on to the CA/PF.It was my first flight in over a month; preceded only by sim events way back in September and just prior to OE. This was a threat up front. Hadn't flown in this environment in over 18 months. We had multiple distractions due to the crew alert and system loss being addressed; icing conditions and turbulence. The ATC frequency was covering high traffic volume so there was a significant amount of talking on the frequency. We had both been up very early in order to be ready at report time. My expectation bias led me to believe we were cleared to 'descend via' when we were cleared only laterally for the approach.We could have briefed the arrival prior to addressing the crew alert and done a transfer of control of the aircraft and radios. I could have had ATC repeat the clearance; once the PF was back with me; so that they could communicate directly what the intended clearance was. I could have stated the clearance exactly as it was read back to eliminate any 'single point' of interpretation; or misinterpretation.

column121: FL360 ISA -54C; REC MAX ALT (recommended maximum altitude) 39.8. MCDU weight 132.8. Green dot speed 229 KIAS. Vls 220 [lowest selectable speed for autopilot]. Takeoff Data Performance derived green dot corrected one knot per 1;000 feet above FL200 equals an under FL200 green dot speed of 213. A 213 KIAS green dot from 3.5.4 of the Performance Manual is the speed for a 141 knot jet (8;200 pound difference). FAC1 (flight augmentation computer) and FAC2 averaged to 140 kts. Flaps full landing. Vls 128 KIAS. MCDU Vapp was 123 (5 knots into the hook). Out of an abundance of caution; we added 10 knots to get to Vls+5. Landed uneventfully and under max landing weight even if you added in the 8-9 kts (worst case scenario). Documented all in the aircraft logbook. For the committee; this is the second 319 that has presented a large difference in MCDU weight vs. calculated weight from FAC1/FAC2 (which generates Vapp and Vls on a basic jet). Either the jets EOW (empty operating weight) is wrong; the software is corrupted or the alpha vanes are out of calibration. I think safety and maintenance need to do a deep dive in to the FAC's and alpha vanes and any software changes of late. The only other explanation is an error in the EOW which is hard to envision. I would like a response directly from the committee about this and [another] aircraft which was previously accepted in to report system. I am concerned that given the increase in the number of pilots who are not flying regularly due to schedule reductions; this could result in an incident or mishap.

column123: Cleared for takeoff Runway XX. Engines spooled up 'taxiing' up to takeoff point on Runway XX. With engines at 40% N1 pushed TOGA button and throttles advanced. We observed the white arcs advancing but the plane didn't seem to be accelerating normally. As I glanced inside to ensure the auto throttles were engaged (they were) the aircraft started to drift right. I tried to correct back with the rudder as we always do but it had no effect. As the right drift continued I rejected the take off and had to use almost full nose wheel tiller to correct back to centerline. We smelled burning rubber; so we taxied clear of the runway and had ARFF (Airport Rescue Firefighting) come inspect the gear and wheels. No problems found by ARFF. Tower had the runway inspected. Nothing found. I had ARFF follow us to the gate where we made an AML entry and had a lengthy discussion with Maintenance. During the takeoff roll the throttles never made it to Takeoff Thrust and I was looking outside the whole time; but the speed achieved was well below 80 kts. Probably around 40-45 kts. In addition; on taxi out when brakes were applied to stop in line they often 'chattered.'We suspected a brake problem or asymmetric thrust.I'm not sure why it happened. I've seen asymmetric thrust before and it is easily corrected with rudder to steer back to centerline. This plane was very difficult to get turning back to the left.

The flight continued without issue.This event was caused by lack of recent flight experience; as well as momentary task-saturation.This has not been a reoccurring trend for me during training or during revenue operations. I plan to continue to maintain a high level of situational awareness in the cockpit to trap threats before they become errors. I also plan to ensure I am making appropriate FCP selections when I am making an adjustment to our course.

The Captain was on the jetbridge with us and we were all in agreement that we needed to be sprayed before we could start boarding. column121: The landing was excellent; Rollout of the aircraft was straight and smooth. When reaching for the toe brakes; I had a left brake but no right break. The toe brakes are little round pads on the top outsides of each rudder and are not easily identified with your toes even with soft sole shoes which I wear to fly in. I did not realize my foot had slipped off or was not on it properly until it was too late. The aircraft took a left direction as I was wishing to slow down. I let go of the left brake and caught it/straightened it with the right rudder. Right after I had it straight; I removed my right foot to lift it higher up to engage the right brake. The aircraft took a sharp left direction went onto the grass which with then full right rudder and the right brake did not help. The slope away from the runway is very steep and the aircraft was not able to be brought back up onto the runway; so I kept it straight and aimed at the taxiway; With the airplane tailwheel not willing to provide steering since it was on grass and the slope was still steep; the aircraft slid over the other side of the taxiway. The aircraft refused to turn right with all my efforts; so my next choice was to hit trees and or a building; so I choose to ground loop the airplane to avoid the trees and building. NO damage was done to any property including taxi signs or even lights. The aircraft came to a stop 180 degrees to the landing direction. No one was hurt in any manner since the speed was not very fast. The right gear leg collapsed as it stopped and the prop hit the grass and broke one of the tips. The engine was shut down and everything was turned off. The Runway XX is a challenging runway since there is zero room for error.

We coordinated spacing with another crosswind aircraft to follow us for spacing in the pattern.Reported downwind uneventfully and recognized the aircraft we were to follow and minimized their pattern to minimize spacing conflicts. Reported [our] base turn to UNICOM; uneventfully. Our track on base leg was approximately 2 nm from the end of the runway. At no time was our location questioned by the conflicting near miss aircraft.Reported a base to final turn; uneventfully and unquestioned. Upon the completion of the turn to final; I focused on vertical alignment to the runway and did not see the conflicting near miss aircraft. The PNF (Pilot Not Flying); in a radio call questioned the conflicting near miss aircraft to determine the position upon hearing the UNICOM base report. For clarification; the safety pilot - PNF; is a seasoned 121 CA (Captain) and highly experienced in the PA24-250 with close to 2;000 hours in type. After it was determined the conflicting aircraft turned inside of our location; resulting in cutting us off placing our aircraft in a hazardous flight profile; PNF took control of the aircraft in a professionally coordinated manner.At this time; the conflicting near miss aircraft was well within 1/4 NM and somewhat above our altitude; which was approximately 300 ft AGL. Because of the proximity to us; and apparently being unaware of our location; the resolution was complex. Keep in mind in their base to final turn (RH pattern) with a low wing aircraft [they] would have then been unable to locate us.Additionally; as we both rolled out on final we were both nearly lined up on the centerline; the closure rate was approximately 42 FPS and without evasive action; contact would have occurred in about 30 seconds; short of the runway; all due to the difference in V-ref and approach speeds. The PNF recognized this before I had visual contact with the conflicting traffic and they took control of the aircraft and became the PF.The evasive maneuver was complex in that [the other aircraft's] intentions seemed unpredictable and we did not want to initiate a go-around with the associated high deck angle; which would interrupt visual conflict with the conflicting traffic. Communication from their aircraft was weak and seemed confused as they; on short final; radioed 'how many aircraft are in the pattern and where are you located'. We discussed the possibility that they may begin a go around and that would worsen the conflict since we may have lost visual contact and keep in mind... at this time we were behind their location and out of view.In the interest of safety; we chose to sidestep slightly left and to pass them on the level and then after we cleared the aircraft to begin a go around. The point we were trying to achieve was to maintain visual contact with the conflicting aircraft until we passed clear of their position.

column121: Aircraft X took off RIL climbing to 15;000 feet; at around 10;000 feet; Aircraft X informed me he was having a landing gear issue; could not climb further and needed to return to RIL right away. I sent him direct to RIL. He had good sight of the terrain and once he got the visual he was cleared the visual approach. Aircraft Y was another aircraft going into RIL north of the airport level at 14;000 feet with no approach clearance. Aircraft X appeared to be circling to the runway so I did not clear Aircraft Y into the airport. Aircraft X then popped back on the frequency saying they cannot land at RIL and need to go to [another airport]. Aircraft X at this point was 8;000 feet climbing eastbound still in priority handling status. I re-radar identified Aircraft X and had them climb to 13;000 feet to try to maintain positive Minimum IFR Altitudes. They affirmed they had good sight of the terrain. I called the traffic to both Aircraft Y and Aircraft X hoping to apply visual separation. Neither saw one another so they both remained 13;000 feet (Aircraft X) and 14;000 feet (Aircraft Y).Once able; I vectored Aircraft X south to get him away from high Minimum IFR Altitudes and the RIL approach corridor. I asked Aircraft Y 'if I turn you direct to RIL; do you think you can get a visual with the airport?' Aircraft Y responded he could. I then said 'Aircraft Y; cleared direct RIL' I then went back to Aircraft X and asked fuel remaining; souls on board; what altitude they could climb to; and then explained why 15;000 feet was not feasible. I offered GJT etc. While discussing options with Aircraft X; I noticed Aircraft Y leave 14;000 feet and begin their descent while still 3 to 4 miles from Aircraft X. I gave a traffic alert to Aircraft Y and told them to climb back to 14;000 feet immediately. I then gave the traffic alert to Aircraft X. Aircraft Y climbed back up; I gained the 5 miles and climbed Aircraft X up and gave Aircraft Y the visual approach to RIL. I issued Aircraft Y advisories.In this session I had two separate situations. A pilot deviation; an arrival rush; a handful of ornery pilots on the ground at RIL clogging the frequency looking for releases off the ground. Had RIL sector been separated out through our split frequency procedures; this may not have occurred. There was a lot of frequency congestion between the sector's two frequencies which blocked transmissions to the priority handling aircraft. We used to do this procedure and have been recently barred from doing it again. This procedure could have helped!

I did so but failed to verify that we were in VNAV. At 3800' the PM noticed we were below the 4000' restriction at GOOFY. I reversed the descent and started climbing back to 4000'. Next time I need to descend quickly; I will try to stay in VNAV if I am continuing on an arrival that connects with an approach with step-down altitudes. Also using VVMI to verify my level of automation after an altitude selection will trap this kind of error in the future.

column121: During push back from gate we started engine number 2 and disconnected from the pushback tug normally. We then noticed a faint burning smell in the cockpit that was present for only a moment. During this time we were positioned directly in front of a vehicle access road and there were multiple trucks driving in front of the aircraft. The First Officer and I discussed the smell and determined that due to the smell only being present for a short moment we were confident that it came from the vehicles near the aircraft. We then continued to taxi making a right turn on Taxiway Bravo. While taxiing; we received a call from the Flight Attendant. She told us that the back of the cabin was a little foggy. At this point I had two indications of a possible fire on board the aircraft; so I immediately contacted ZZZ ramp control and Requested Priority Handling and advised them that we had smoke in the cabin of the aircraft and needed to return to the gate. Ramp control cleared us to do a 180 degree turn and taxi to the gate and advised us that the rescue services were on their way. After making a 180 degree turn to get the aircraft heading back towards the gate; I then called the Flight Attendant back. I asked her if she had any updates on the situation with the smoke. She advised me that it was now mostly dissipated and that she had checked the lavatory and the cargo compartment and there was no evidence of smoke in either location. She also noted that she did not notice a smell of any sort during the time the smoke was primarily present. We spoke about the conditions of the passengers and she stated that the cabin was relatively calm and the passengers were doing just fine. I informed her that we would be returning to the gate for an expeditious deplaning. The First Officer and I discussed whether to perform the smoke fire or fumes memory action item but determined that it was not necessary due to the absence of smoke in the cockpit and due to the knowledge that the smoke in the cabin was dissipating. We then continued with the smoke fire or fumes checklist. The checklist had us push out both the re-circulation fan and the Gasper fan switches; and at this point a personnel from fire crash rescue started marshaling us into the gate. In order to return to the gate as quickly as possible to deplane the passengers; I made the decision to discontinue the checklist. To eliminate further potential sources of contaminated air entering the aircraft; I took it upon myself to shut off pack number 2 and the APU bleed at this time. Passenger number 1 was already off. We parked at the gate and performed a shut down checklist. We had the passengers deplane the aircraft using the mobile stairs at the gate. I don't recall the exact number of passengers we had on board but I believe it was less than 10; so deplaning was very quick. To ensure that the aircraft was not powered while emergency services personnel checked for the location of the source of the smoke; we immediately terminated the aircraft. EMS was present to ask each passenger of their condition and I was told that no one had any issue including the crew. Finally; I contacted Dispatch to inform them of the situation; and entered a discrepancy in the maintenance logbook.

We started getting a LOC flag prior to final approach fix. We broke off the approach and executed a missed approach. Knowing that there are many variables as to why we would not be getting reliable LOC information we elected to try a CAT II again but to a different runway. We go set up again for the ILS for Runway XXR. While intercepting we received a LOC flag again about 18 DME from the LOC. Again knowing that there are many variables that go into receiving a good signal we decided to give it a few more miles. We caught the LOC and GS and executed a CAT II to a landing. The only thing I can think that was improper about this circumstance was the continuation of a CAT II after receiving a LOC flag. It's being 18 miles out I believe we were in some gray area. At any rate we wrote up the LOC on the aircraft so that it could be ruled out as the cause. Perhaps the LOC on Runway XXR was not strong enough or there was interference from the proceeding aircraft causing the localizer. Or it was the aircraft itself. I think we did most everything right. It just felt weird to write up the LOC after a successful CAT II approach. I didn't see any reason we shouldn't try the CAT II we had plenty of fuel and had an alternate already specified.

Ontario was landing 8L and 8R; with good VFR weather and a light wind from the west. The crew descended on the Ziggy 7 arrival and was given a clearance to track outbound on 270 radial after Paradise VOR. There was a distraction trying to set up the tracking of a radial in the FMS by the pilot monitoring. As the pilot flying I decided to use the VOR and VOR mode to accomplish this. We complied with clearance and were cleared to 3;000 feet.After leveling at 3;000 feet a traffic report was issued for a helicopter at 1 o'clock and 4;000 feet. We were given a base leg heading of 320. After starting this turn an amber target showed up on the PFD (Primary Flight Display) at our altitude. I was looking out the window for traffic; in a matter of 2 seconds the Captain pushed forward on the controls; we got a TA/RA descend descend warning; I saw a small aircraft at 2 o'clock and 100 yards; I turned off the Autopilot and Autothrottle stopped the turn towards the small aircraft and descended to 2;500 feet. [We were] cleared to remain at 2;600 feet and received radar vectors to join the Localizer and landed 8L. The Captain was the pilot monitoring and the First Officer was the pilot flying. The ATC controller did make some kind of apology regarding the event. There was a minor distraction regarding the tuning of our radios. I had the VOR tuned and needed to make a switch to the ILS frequency. This took a matter of seconds to correct and we had the airport in sight the entire time.The Captain and I debriefed the event and felt we made all the correct decisions. The next day we confirmed how to track a radial using the FMS and LNAV mode. A note regarding small aircraft in vicinity might be a good idea. Knowing how to set up the FMS to track a radial would be helpful. Above all fly the airplane; keep your eyes outside; and expect the unexpected.
column123: Descending on the ZIGGY ARRIVAL ATC gave clearance to fly the PDZ 270 radial after PDZ. PM (Pilot Monitoring) was unable to input the radial to fly in LNAV and the PF (Pilot Flying) flew the radial using raw data. ATC gave clearance to descend from 4;000 to 3;000 with a right turn to a heading of 340 for vectors to 08L. ATC advised traffic (helicopter) in the turn at 3;500 and gave clearance to continue turn to 020. Helicopter traffic was never observed. On TCAS PM saw a target which appeared to be at 3;000 feet on the 020 heading and advised PF to stop turn. TCAS aural warning TA 'traffic traffic' annunciated and PM saw traffic as TCAS aural alert advised an RA 'traffic descend now'. PF and PM both pushed controls forward as conflicting traffic continued to descend and turn into the jets path. PM advised ATC of the new heading altitude deviation due to the RA. Conflict was resolved at 2;300 feet; PF leveled off and started climb back up to 3;000. ATC advised stop climb at 2;600 and continue turn to 020 to intercept 08L LOC with an apology for conflict. PF intercepted GS inside NAROD (FAF 08L) due to ALT (Altitude) assignment by ATC of 2;600 feet. PF and PM had field in site and terrain in site during all phases. ATC reported 'helicopter' traffic at 3;500. Both PM and PF did not observe the traffic on TCAS at 3500 nor saw any helicopter traffic in the initial turn. Controller change during the descent from 4;000-3;000 feet. Weather was VMC daytime.The clearance received to fly the 270R outbound caused PM and PF to be distracted. PM could not get the radial to input in the FMC and therefore the PF flew raw data. This created additional threats which created additional distractions at the low ALT 2;600 with terrain all around. Having had to use RAW DATA the radio panel had mismatched frequencies and MCP had mismatched courses in the selectors which caused FD to give incorrect LOC info. PM was able to configure the MCP/radio panel and EFIS in time to capture LOC before crossing LOC. It caused the PM to be heads down instead of assisting PF in confirming the airport in sight for a visual backup. During debrief both pilots agreed that asking for a climb back to 3;000 may have helped with visual guidance to help with positional awareness. The following leg PM/PF practiced input of radials off VOR stations to create a less threatening environment for the 'next time.'

column121: Upon gear retraction; after departure from [Runway] XXL at ZZZ; we heard a loud bang in the nose wheel well with an associated yaw of the aircraft. A burnt rubber smell was also detected and dissipated after 5 minutes. My thoughts ranged from; 'something hit us' to 'we blew a nose tire.' All engine and hydraulic indications were normal and the plane was flying fine with no control problems. I decided we had no immediate safety of flight issues and we continued the climbout. At 25;000 feet I had the First Officer take the radios and I messaged dispatch that I wanted to talk to Flight Operations. The Dispatcher and I talked briefly on the SATCOM and he put me on hold to get Flight Operations online. While waiting I ran through the QRH to see if there was a procedure for this issue and found 'Tire Failure.' That seemed to most agree with the possible problem and I was pleased to see that it called for us to proceed normally to the destination since that's what we were doing. Discussing what we knew with Flight Operations we all agreed that the problem was probably the tire and proceeding normally was the action we would take. Flight Operations also said they would call the Tower and Approach control to let them know we might have an issue.After level off the 'A' Flight Attendant came to the cockpit and asked if we heard a bang on takeoff. She said some of the 1st class passengers asked her if we were alright and she said that she was able to reassure them that we were. I told her what we suspected and that I would brief the FA's (Flight Attendants) near top of descent.We had plenty of time and I didn't want to get caught unawares so the FO and I briefed various scenarios and reviewed checklists including 'manual gear extension' and ' partial or all gear up landing'. By the time we were ready to brief the arrival I felt prepared to handle any scenario.Unrelated to the wheel issue; about halfway to ZZZ2 the FO fwd window overheat-light illuminated. We ran the checklist and never got it back so; knowing we had clouds and probably ice to descend through I opted to do the landing. I had considered it anyway; but that clinched it. Sure enough the FO's window was opaque until about the outer marker.ATC was ready for us thanks to the Flight Operations phone call. They set us up for [Runway] YYL and slowed us to 170 around ZZZZZ [Intersection]. I put the gear down at that time to give us some breathing room if it didn't come down. The nose gear was the first to show down and locked and I relaxed a bit. We told tower we anticipated a normal landing but they still asked for souls and fuel; which we gave them. They had an operations vehicle shadow us to check for debris. Touchdown was normal and the nose wheel felt fine when it made contact so we told Tower we could taxi in unaided.We were met by the ops manger and several mechanics. Disappointingly; the nose wheel and the well area looked perfectly normal. After all that build up; I admit I wanted to see some torn metal or bits of tire. It will be interesting to see what maintenance discovers.What I can say I learned from this; is that we have a solid system of communication at (Company).  The call to ATC by Flight Operations and Dispatch saved us a lot of on air negotiation for 16L. My FO contributed many helpful thoughts that aided our preparation for just about any gear scenario. The FA's took the news of a possible irregular landing calmly and knew what roles they would play should things get sticky. Although it all turned out to be much ado about nothing; it was a good test of the system and the system works.

column121: Departing ZZZ1 for ZZZ2 I was the PM (Pilot Monitoring) and the CA (Captain) was the PF (Pilot Flying). We planned a low altitude flight due to the shortness of the leg. Some altitudes in the legs page were edited to allow the lower cruise altitude to be selected. The flaps 10 takeoff went as normal (LNAV/VNAV). The PF called for flaps 1 as near as I can recall. I believe this is the case as most if not all of our previous legs had been flaps 5 takeoffs. I was distracted with a radio call or frequency change and I moved the flaps to 1 and did not catch the error. Shortly after that; the FMC changed to the descent phase and the speed bug moved to the flaps 5 maneuver speed; and the A/T (Auto Throttle) mode went from N1 to FMC speed; which resulted in the flaps 5 maneuver speed being the A/T target. As; or just prior to this happening the PF called for flaps up. I moved the flap lever to the up position; and since we were no longer accelerating got a momentary stick shaker. The PF instinctively lowered the nose reducing the AOA (Angle Of Attack). I increased the speed in the MCP window to get the A/T to command acceleration. The remainder of the flight was normal.Suggest crews be alert for unusual mode reversions when using low altitudes for cruise. I would probably use non VNAV takeoff procedures in the future. The big lesson is not new; vigilance absolutely has to be maintained during the 'red' parts of the flight path. The PM job is challenging and can be intolerant of errors.

column121: We were approximately 20 miles SE of the airport in the mountains on a sight-seeing flight. I was PIC (Pilot In Command) and the only pilot on board with 2 passengers. At 4;500 MSL the AWOS was intermittent because of the mountains. The MEF (Maximum Elevation Figure) on the sectional chart was 4;400 MSL and I was working my around some shorter hills. While experiencing some lighter bumps over a ridge; the 'GEAR IN TRANSIT' annunciator light lit up. I immediately checked to make sure I hadn't selected the gear handle down because we were too far away from the airport to have the gear down. The selector handle was still in the 'GEAR UP' position so my next instinct was to grab the emergency gear override and hold it in the 'UP' position to keep the gear from extending so far out. I checked the circuit breaker and everything seemed normal. I cycled the gear down and got 3 green lights and when cycled back up the green lights went away but the transit light never turned off. The AWOS suddenly kicked in and led me to decide on Runway 8 which meant I would cross the airport midfield and enter a tear drop for a left downwind to Runway 8. On the sectional I saw the altitude as 1;907 and decided to over fly the field at 2;500. In my mind 1;907 was pattern altitude and not the airport altitude. My mind was still on making sure my gear didn't fall down and create more drag for me that far away from the airport. About 1.5 miles to the south of the airport I once again communicated on the CTAF of my intentions to over fly the field at 2;500. One aircraft said they were back taxiing and going to depart Runway 8. As we approached the airport I felt like I was too low even though I was at 2;500 and then realized my mistake by how well I could see details on the ground. I quickly announced my intentions to climb up to traffic pattern altitude of 2;900 feet just before reaching the south side of the airport pattern which meant I was then climbing into the pattern instead of already being at the correct altitude. Directly over the runway we were back to 2;900 feet and I continued out to do a right hand turn and enter a tear drop to the left downwind. The gear came down fine and we landed safely. The combination of trying to troubleshoot an annunciator light while listening to incoming traffic and the intermittent AWOS left me to be distracted and mixing up proper altitudes for the pattern.Better self-briefing prior to arrival to an airport would have greatly reduced the chance of this occurring. Along with remembering that I had plenty of fuel and could have circled at a safe altitude to troubleshoot and then with a clearer mind come up with a plan to land at the airport normally.

column121: The mission was practicing landings at ZZZ on Runway XXR.  Weather was VFR.  All 4 fuel tanks were full at the start of the flight.  No issues were noted with the aircraft during preflight; taxiing; or run-up.  The plane behaved normally for the first two takeoffs and landings.  The engine had been running for approximately 40 minutes at that point; all drawing from the left main tank; with ~60% of the tank remaining. During the climb-out from the 3rd takeoff; at about 700 ft AGL; the engine had a momentary loss of power (lasting about a second).  In an effort to troubleshoot; I switched tanks from left main to right main.  A few seconds later; another momentary loss of power occurred (again lasting about a second).  Note that this was with everything in takeoff configuration; full throttle; max RPM; mixture full rich; electric fuel pump on; and carburetor heat was already on (keeping the carburetor temperature gauge above 40 deg F). At this point I felt there was a significant risk of the engine having an impending permanent loss of power and decided the most expedient option to get the plane safely back on the ground was to do a left 180 deg turn to land in the opposite direction on the parallel runway.  I stated the situation and my intention to the Tower over the radio.  The turn; descent; and landing on XXR were completed uneventfully.  There was no traffic actively using that runway at the time; so that wasn't a factor. At this point; it's unclear what the root cause was for the engine's momentary power losses.  I've contacted my local shop and have no intention of flying the plane again until after they investigate.  Of note; the engine stayed running seemingly normally at idle during the descent; landing; and subsequent taxiing.  However; during taxiing; the engine would run rough at any throttle setting above idle.  Also; during preflight; the tip tanks both had some water that was sumped out; but the main tanks (the only tanks used during the flight) didn't show any noticeable water when sumped.

column121: I had taken position after coming down from the tower working Ground Control. A priority handling had been coordinated with Aircraft X with an engine out. This had been coordinated at least 45 minutes prior to the aircraft's arrival. It was briefed from the relieved controller that this aircraft had requested 'wide vectors for an ILS.' In my judgement as well as the relieved Controller both of these aircraft would have arrived easily before Aircraft X came in on the ILS. I cleared Aircraft Y for the Visual Approach to the right parallel runway and decided to change the Aircraft Y to the left after they requested the ILS. Aircraft X changed his mind for the Visual Approach which I approved. I asked Aircraft X if they could visually follow the Aircraft Y and they said they would not because of wake turbulence. Since I did not issue a 30 degree intercept we coordinated with the tower to issue a go-around to Aircraft Y. We decided not to send the Aircraft Y around because he was established on the ILS even though I had not issued a 30 degree intercept for Aircraft X. In my opinion wake turbulence to a priority handling aircraft was more of a factor than a parallel runway approach.Due to the busy nature of this session I think splitting the radar position may have been warranted. The relieved Controller had been on position for over 1 hour and 45 minutes. Aircraft X changing his mind mid sequence also caused a lot of problems. I was wary of issuing delay vectors to an aircraft that was a priority handling.

column121: ZZZ1 Center had a positive COVID test from an individual in their building. The decision was made to go ATC-0 in the middle of the afternoon to perform a Level 3 cleaning.  I would completely understand the need to do the cleaning immediately; even if it was a high traffic time; if the individual had started not feeling well during that shift; or during the any shift in the previous 24 hours.  This was not the situation here. The positive test came from an individual that had not been in the building in X days!  Every Controller that had worked in the previous X days already had worked in a potentially contaminated area. There was zero benefit to go down at that time. The decision makers did nothing that was reasonable and responsible in this situation. Reasonable and responsible would have been to wait for a slower traffic period to get the clean accomplished. I had Aircraft X that had been in the air for 15+20 hours. I was forced to route him over an hour [out] of his way which put him in a minimum fuel situation.  We had MedEvac flights; on critical missions that were not allowed to pick up their patients.  I would hate to know how many passengers missed their connecting flights. We put our controllers; pilots; and flying public in an unnecessary unsafe situation.When an individual has not been in the building in the past 24 hours DO NOT CLEAN during a high traffic period.

column121: We took the aircraft that was returned to service after a large bird was ingested into the #1 engine on the previous flight. The #1 engine was started first prior to taxi out to ensure no issues with the engine. All engine indications after start were normal. The takeoff was normal with no abnormal engine indications. On departure just after retracting the landing gear; a strong smell from the previously ingested bird permeated throughout the aircraft. Shortly after; the forward lav smoke detector sounded. The aircraft was leveled off; and then we began to execute the Smoke; Fire or Fumes Checklist. Once stabilized on a left downwind with Departure Control notified; First Officer (FO) now flying; I contacted the Flight Attendants to confirm the status of the forward lav. They indicated that there was NO fire; just a very strong and pungent smell throughout the entire cabin. Fully aware that the cause of the alarm was the heavy fumes from the bird; we continued with the checklist and decided to discontinue the flight and return to the airport. We removed our masks; coordinated with Dispatch; and continued on downwind to set up for a visual approach and landing. Engine indications were normal the entire flight and the smell slowly dissipated. The forward lav alarm continued to sound; no fire though. No priority handling was requested. We landed uneventfully and taxied to the gate.The aircraft was returned to service after a bird was ingested on the previous flight. The engine contained a large amount of bird parts around the fan blades and some appeared to be ingested into the compressor section. Contract Maintenance cleaned and inspected the engine in coordination with Maintenance Control and signed off on the logbook. I did inquire of Maintenance about an engine run. They indicated it was not needed. I should have pushed them on it; as we were concerned about the large amount of bird guts all around the fan section. I did not inspect the engine after Maintenance completed their work and felt confident it was accomplished correctly; my mistake; should have crosschecked. The FO did a walkaround prior to departure and noted some bird parts still remaining. A borescope was not accomplished as Maintenance Control indicated it could be done within a couple of flight hours; most likely after the next flight since we were heading to a Maintenance base. Not sure Maintenance Control realized the significant amount of bird ingested into the engine. Could have communicated better with them.

column121: We were cleared for a visual approach following a Boeing 777 to Runway 25L at LAX. On short final we encountered what was most likely wake turbulence from the proceeding aircraft on short final ~300 feet AGL. This presented as a roll and shear to a headwind. This apparent shear to a headwind along with an addition of some thrust put me high on the profile and ~15 knots above target speed. The severity of the event was below what I would describe as an 'upset'. When the turbulence subsided we appeared to be in a good position to land; so I continued the approach and landed. Being high on profile and bleeding off the excess speed in the flare resulted in a touchdown that was most likely beyond the touchdown zone. Despite this we were in position; with normal braking; to exit at taxiway H8. Tower instructed us to exit at H9.
column123: Upon landing on Runway 25L at LAX we landed outside of the normal 3000 feet of the touchdown zone after being preceded by a 777 to landing during light tail wind conditions. The briefing and approach were completely routine. We had originally planned to land on 24R but we were prepared for a possible change to Runway 25L. We were told on downwind that we would be following a heavy 777 and could expect 25L. Conditions were clear and we had the aircraft in sight. As I reconfigured the aircraft for landing on the south runway; the Captain made the comment that he would be prepared to fly a dot high. The Captain flew as he briefed and we experienced mostly calm winds all the way down the glideslope. By 200 feet AGL; we were back on glide slope.  The aircraft sank somewhat and by 100 feet we were almost a half dot low when we started to feel some of the wake of the 777.  The winds were still light; about 300/7.  The plane was very controllable and the Captain pitched up and added power slightly to stay on top of the wake. In doing so; the speed increased almost 15 knots and I considered calling for a go around.  It still appeared that we were going to be touching down in the first 3000 feet so I allowed the approach to continue.  The Captain flared the aircraft so that it looked like we would touch down right at about 3000 feet.  Without trying to hold the aircraft off; the plane continued down the runway at what seemed like 1 foot. The aircraft finally settled a couple hundred feet later and we turned off the runway and proceeded to the gate without any further issues.This was a case where one limit almost being crossed led to another limit being crossed. It looked like it was all going to work out.  We have all encountered 'disturbed' air from a wake before on landing especially at busy airports like LAX.  The question is how much of an adjustment do you have to make and at what point do you go around.  This looked very doable.  We had plenty of runway and performance.  This looked familiar with a landing in the touchdown zone.  I only thought later and realized that the Captain had elected to do a flaps 40 landing in a 737-900ER.  I know I have not done many flaps 40 landings in a 900ER in the last couple years; so I think my sight picture was off a bit for the flare and the touchdown.  We may have also gotten a bit more of ground effect than what I would have imagined.  The speed did not bleed off as fast as I had anticipated.

column121: I was the pilot flying into ROA at night. We were at 6;000 abeam the airport on a left downwind for Runway 6. We were cleared for the visual approach and I asked for 3;000 feet to be set into the FCP (Flight Control Panel). I was aware there was a ridge we would need to cross on our left base turn; charted at 2;000 feet on the RNAV (GPS) Y approach plate. I planned to descend to 3;000 while turning base and turn onto final at HIVLU; charted at 2;700 on the vertical profile of the approach plate. I began a descent at 2;000 FPM just prior to turning base. On the base leg; I believe due to the rate of descent; a GPWS terrain warning occurred. I immediately increased the power; increased pitch; and arrested the descent. The warning stopped. The ridge was visible throughout the event and the aircraft did not descend below 3;000 until past the ridge and beginning a turn to intercept the final approach course. We continued and made a normal landing.Being unfamiliar with this approach I should have communicated my plan to the Captain and asked if he agreed. After landing we discussed the approach and he explained that we could have descended on downwind to 5;200; continued past the ridge; turned base at or just inside DIXXY; and then followed the descent profile on the approach plate. I agree with his assessment; that would have been a better course of action. In the future I will verbalize my intentions; particularly on approaches I am unfamiliar with; and have a discussion to collaboratively determine the best course of action.
