column121: After landing on Runway 12R; Tower instructed us to exit the runway at Taxiway C3; hold short of Taxiway C (parallel taxiway) and contact ground on 121.7. As we approached Taxiway C3; I saw an Aircraft Y taxiing northwest on Taxiway C with moderate speed. The Aircraft Y was approaching Taxiway C3 and it appeared that we had been instructed to hold short of Taxiway C so the Aircraft Y could pass in front of us right to left. As the CA (Captain) made the ninety-degree left turn to exit the runway onto Taxiway C3; I switched to ground control frequency 121.7 as instructed. The CA then stopped with the nose of our aircraft near the runway holding position marking on Taxiway C3. This left the aft end of our aircraft on the runway. The Aircraft Y then stopped short of Taxiway C3. As I was about to ask for clarifying instructions after switching frequencies; Ground Control instructed the Aircraft Y to continue taxiing and then asked if we were on his frequency. I responded that we were and then Ground Control instructed us to turn right on Taxiway C (behind the Aircraft Y that had by this point passed through the intersection) and then left on Taxiway B4 to our gate. As we taxied southeast on Taxiway C Ground Control advised us that we had created a dangerous situation by not fully exiting the runway. He informed us that a light general aviation aircraft had taken off while part of our aircraft was still on the runway. At the time it happened; I agreed with the CA's decision to stop the aircraft since we were unaware of the Aircraft Y's taxi instructions (we had just switched to Ground); and the appearance that the Aircraft Y may taxi through the intersection due to its rate of speed and remaining distance to C3. I also wondered why tower control had cleared an aircraft to take off while we still occupied the runway. On the taxi out for our return leg; we observed that there was a taxiway hold short line further ahead on C3 that would have allowed us to pull further forward; but our tail would still likely have been over the runway hold short line.Limited distance between the runway and Taxiway C. Lack of communication at a critical juncture: we were unaware of the Aircraft Y's taxi instructions as we had just switched to ground; and Tower didn't advise us of them when issuing us our initial taxi instructions (ie '... Aircraft Y will hold short.') The Tower Controller cleared an aircraft to take off while part of our aircraft was still within the boundary of the runway. The Ground Controller did not instruct the Aircraft Y to continue taxiing with a sense of urgency. Better communication from ATC. Better awareness of the location of taxiway hold short lines (of possible runway turn-offs) as a part of our approach brief.
column123: After landing on Runway 12R; tower instructed us to exit the runway at Taxiway C3; hold short of Taxiway C (parallel taxiway) and contact Ground on 121.7. As we approached Taxiway C3; I observed an Aircraft Y taxiing northwest on Taxiway C with moderate speed. The Aircraft Y was approaching Taxiway C3 and it appeared that we had been instructed to hold short of Taxiway C so the Aircraft Y could pass in front of us right to left. As I made the ninety-degree left turn to exit the runway onto Taxiway C3 at less than 12 knots of ground speed; the FO switched to ground control frequency 121.7 as instructed. I stopped with the nose of our aircraft near the runway holding position marking on Taxiway C3 because of the short distance to Taxiway C in front of us. This left the aft end of our aircraft on the runway. The Aircraft Y then stopped short of Taxiway C3. Ground Control instructed the Aircraft Y to continue taxiing. After the Aircraft Y passed Taxiway C3; Ground Control asked if we were on his frequency. When the FO responded in the affirmative; ground control instructed us to turn right on Taxiway C then left on Taxiway B4 to our gate. As we taxied southeast on Taxiway C Ground Control advised us that we had created a dangerous situation by not fully exiting the runway. He told us that a light general aviation aircraft had taken off while part of our aircraft was still on the runway. At the time; I felt that I could not have fully exited the runway considering the limited distance available to me on Taxiway C3. I also wondered why Tower Control had cleared an aircraft to take off while we still occupied the runway. On the next flight; we taxied out on Taxiway C. As we passed Taxiway C3 I noticed a taxiway holding position marking on Taxiway C3 that I had not observed on the inbound flight. Although the taxiway holding position marking appeared too close to Taxiway C; I could have taxied farther onto Taxiway C3 after exiting the runway on the inbound flight. If I had taxied to what I considered a safe distance from Taxiway C; our tail probably would not have been within the lateral boundaries of the runway; but it would have been on the runway side of the runway holding position marking on Taxiway C3. Limited distance between the runway and Taxiway C prevented us from fully vacating the runway while complying with the instruction to hold short of Taxiway C. The Tower Controller cleared an aircraft to take off while part of our aircraft was still within the boundary of the runway. The Ground Controller did not instruct the Aircraft Y to continue taxiing with a sense of urgency. When instructed to hold short of a taxiway after vacating a runway; stop the aircraft as close as safely possible to the restricting taxiway. Even if your aircraft is not completely clear of the runway; risk will be diminished by reducing the amount of your aircraft remaining within the runway boundary.

column123: I was acting as PM. Approaching ZZZ at night from the SW with a high overcast layer above. ATC had us on a downwind leg for [Runway] XXL at 4;000. The autopilot and auto thrust were engaged. Approximately abeam the end of the runway; ATC asked us if we had the field in sight. The CA/PF says he does; so I reported the field in sight. ATC then cleared us for the visual XXL. The PF then set 3;000 in the FCU and I confirmed and referenced the plate showing the FAF ZZZZZ at 3000. I believe the PF went open descent to 3;000 from 4;000. The PF then began his base leg turn. The intercept angle initially looked like it was going to join the final just outside of the FAF. As we approached 3;000 the PF continued the turn in. He asked me to set 2;000 into the FCU and set 1;000 v/s down. I complied as it appeared to me that the PF was trying to intercept the course and I assumed he was going to join inside of ZZZZZ/FAF. He readjusted his intercept to join the final at ZZZZZ or just outside it. By that time I began to realize we were getting low on the profile. I still had visual contact with the runway. At approximately that time; the airplane leveled at 2000 just inside of ZZZZZ and ZZZ tower advised us of a low altitude alert and to check our altitude with the current altimeter setting. I replied with our call sign. We continued at 2;000 until intercepting the glideslope and landed safely. We were approaching the end of a long duty day and it was a non eventful and quiet flight; so fatigue was a possible factor. I am also familiar with operating into ZZZ; so I was a bit complacent; as well as being in VFR conditions and being able to see the runway. Having both pilots confirm and verify any further altitude changes in the FCU after the setting of the lowest charted altitudes for the approach used.

As it happened I added power as we rolled wings level. We were about 20 degrees off heading; but the autopilot recovered to intercept the localizer; and we never lost any altitude. Like I said; it happened so quickly and recovered that I saw no need to disconnect the autopilot. We re-intercepted the localizer followed by the glide slope and shot the approach with no other concerns. I'm not sure if the winds were the reason or we hit someone's wake turbulence. column121: On the taxiway contacted Tower.  After check in we thought we heard 'clear for takeoff;' but neither of us were sure so I asked the First Officer to confirm if we were cleared for takeoff. The First Officer asked this question and the very clear reply was 'affirmative.'  We entered the runway and were subsequently told while finishing our line up on centerline to stop and hold position.  After a delay we were told of 'pilot deviation' and then cleared for takeoff.I allowed an 'affirmative' reply by Tower to suffice for a query on were we cleared for takeoff.  That is the root cause.  'Affirmative' is not the correct response and in retrospect I believe Tower perhaps misunderstood our query.  Choice of words and insistence on clarification.  I should have asked the First Officer to say 'Tower say again.'  Tower would then have repeated all instructions.  Looking back the word 'Affirmative' is not enough.  I allowed my leeway on foreign controllers English and accents to accept 'affirmative' for a cleared for takeoff query rather than insisting on hearing the entire standard 'cleared for takeoff' verbiage. The Tower could have easily misunderstood us and replied 'Affirmative' to what Tower believed was the question.

column121: The incident occurred during an otherwise uneventful reposition flight from ZZZ - ZZZ1. The PIC was acting as Pilot Monitoring; and the FO as Pilot Flying. The filed altitude was FL200; but the flight had requested and received FL220 approximately 45 minutes to an hour prior to the incident to escape some moderate turbulence.  At the time of the incident; the conditions were IMC with intermittent patches of VMC; light turbulence; and trace to light icing at about -23 deg C. The aircraft was on the western edge of the occluded segment of a frontal low. The first indication was the De-Ice Boots CAS. The FO remained Pilot Flying; and PIC attempted to troubleshoot the problem with the QRH. In addition; the QRH checklist was cross checked by the FO. Unfortunately; the problem did not reset; so the crew determined that it was not safe to remain in icing conditions without wing De-ice capability. The crew then examined alternates; eventually deciding on ZZZ2 due to the availability of a runway greater than 10;000 feet in length; its position behind (west) the front; and the prevailing conditions of unrestricted visibility and a 900 foot ceiling. The PM then informed ARTCC of the need to divert and received a vector for the ILS XX. During the descent; the PM calculated the required landing distance for the Flaps 0 deg Boot Fail scenario; the approach was set up and briefed; and the appropriate checklists were run. Due to the failure of the De-ice Boots; some mixed icing on the leading edge; clear runback ice on inside third of the upper surface; and rime on the underside of the airfoil accumulated during descent and approach.  The crew monitored the accumulation visually and by referencing the trim indicators to ensure that abnormal force was not required to control the aircraft. The approach and landing was conducted at Flaps 0 deg and in accordance with procedure for landing with inoperative boots.

column121: While on the visual approach into LEX Runway 4; inside the final approach fix and following the precision approach path indicator (PAPI) lights with two white and two red lights indicating on glide path; we started to feel we were low according to our actual sight picture. After referencing the electronic glide slope from the ILS we saw we were slightly more than half scale deflection low and corrected back onto the glide slope. We received a 'GLIDESLOPE' GPWS indication while correcting. When back on the glide slope we looked out at the PAPI again and saw it still showed two white and two red lights despite the change in glide path. The ILS chart for runway 4 does not mention that the glide slope and visual glide path are not coincident. I believe when we noticed we were low on the glide slope; the PAPI should have been indicating three reds and a white or maybe even four reds.There is something wrong with the alignment of the PAPI equipment for the runway. It should not have shown us to be two white and two red lights that low on the glide slope. The conditions were visual and easily fixed once we referenced the electronic glide slope fully.The Airport Operations Staff and the FAA need to conduct an alignment of the PAPI equipment. There could be a situation in low visibility or very dark conditions where an aircraft arrives at the minimum decision altitude; has the runway environment or approach lights in sight and relies on the PAPI to help keep the pilot's eyes outside to land; which could lead to an issue where they either see themselves as too high according to the PAPI (if it's aligned too low) or; if it only indicates two white two red at any altitude; may follow the PAPI to an unsafe landing either outside of the touchdown zone or short of the runway.

column121: About 10 minutes prior to scheduled passenger flight pushback at ZZZ; received a HAZMAT NOTOC (hazardous material notice to Captain).  There were 6 lines of HAZMAT of which 5 were normal but one stood out with lithium metal batteries; ERG (emergency response guidebook) code 12FG.  I queried the messenger about them; he said he could take a picture of the box to show me.  While he went to do that I discussed the situation with the FO (First Officer).  The battery weight was.15 kg or just a bit over 5 ounces and contained in equipment.  That size battery is similar in weight to our iPad batteries.  12FG code is risk of fire/heat/smoke with the additional risk Z 'aircraft cargo fire suppression system may not extinguish or contain the fire.  Consider landing immediately'.  When carried in our cargo hold; with passengers on board; that sort of risk gets my attention.  When the messenger returned with the picture I queried him about carrying that cargo in the cockpit or passenger compartment where we at least have our BCB battery containment bag; in case something went wrong.  He said they didn't know which box batteries were in so that wasn't possible.  It was almost push time so I called and discussed the situation with Dispatch.  They agreed with my concern and said they weren't experts on HAZMAT but could research who was or we could just remove the batteries in the interest of expediency.  We then opted for removing the lithium batteries for simplicity and timeliness.  After this was accomplished; we got a revised load closeout and were on our way about 20-30 minutes late.  The rest of our flight was uneventful.  Having reviewed FOM guidance on this issue previously; I consider it somewhat vague.  While the likelihood for these batteries to start burning is slim; the impact would be catastrophic and the ERG  code even warns us of this.  This could easily be mitigated by having an item like this in the passenger cabin or cockpit where FAs (flight attendants) or pilots could at least deal with the threat with the BCBs which are provided for an unlikely event such as this.  FOM  deal[s] with this and state or imply that these types of things should not be in the cargo compartment.  FOM addresses HAZMAT codes but really gives no guidance other than inspecting NOTOC paperwork for date; tail number etc.I've been involved in carrying lots of hazardous materials in aircraft over my career and believe I'm well versed on the risk vs reward of it.  While technically the NOTOC I received was legal per our FOM; the risk of these batteries also noted on the NOTOC; didn't appear to make sense from a risk management or an SMS (safety management systems) standpoint.  Thus my questions about better potential options.  If we are intentionally doing something like this; I; Dispatch; other pilots etc would probably be better served with more of a heads up on the decision process and other options sooner in the departure process.  Were we just doing the minimum legal or is there a more appropriate way in hindsight?  It certainly seemed like pushback time induced pressure discouraged discussion/questions about this sort of thing.

column121: While on a visual approach to [Runway] XXR; I was the PF. I hadn't flown in a month and a half or so; and the weather was conducive to trying to practice skills; so I turned off the AP/AT/FD. While over the ZZZ1 area; we received an RA directing me to level off. After complying with the RA; I began to descend to catch up to the approach; but at the altitude I was at; and the descent rate required to get back on the approach; I would not have been able to do so within stabilized approach criteria; so I conducted a go-around.The go-around was not smooth; and left room for improvement; but all call outs were made; and the checklists were accomplished. After passing through about 1;300 feet or so; we were assigned an altitude of 2;000 feet. The FO selected 2;000 feet and made the comment that we were about 700 feet away. We were climbing at a high rate as we were in TOGA (Still no AP/AT); and I was trying to get the plane slowed down; and arresting the climb rate; the FD began to turn to follow the missed approach for the ILS; as we had loaded it as the backup. We had yet received instruction as to what direction to turn; since we were assigned the visual approach. Between the FD turning and leveling off; it was at this point that I was focused on wanting the aircraft to continue straight on runway heading; and I flew through the 2;000 feet restriction; to my recollection by about 300 feet. The PM attempted to get some sort of instruction from ATC as to what they would like us to do; but struggled to get a word in on the radio. Finally they called and assigned us a vector. They also said since we went past 2;000; to level off at 2;500 feet. At this point; we had a moment; and was able to match up the information on the PFD with what I was wanting; and was able to add back in the AP/AT.This event felt like a culmination of a few problems. The root cause is that I; as the Captain; wasn't as prepared as I should have been. Having flown so little the last few months after upgrade sign off in month; I have been limited to just XX hours of total flying since month; my skill upkeep has been mainly book studying. While this is important; it does not replace being behind the controls of an aircraft.

column121: Operating at FL190. After cruise checklist was completed; cabin altitude was indicating approximate 10;000 feet. After 5 to 10 minutes' elapsed; I felt a change in pressure inside the aircraft. When I crosschecked the cabin altitude climb was indicating 4;000 feet climbing; a minute later; the cabin altitude warning illuminated. This was followed by aircraft memory item and checklist. I pulled O2 knob located left upper just left of the external power switch and as I pulled the mask I placed the O2 mask on emergency mode and no oxygen was flowing. I placed it back on normal operation and nothing happened. I switched the mic to the O2 mask and advised ATC for urgent descent 10;000 feet. I discovered that ATC was unable to hear me at all.  I looked over and the switch for the microphone was placed on oxygen mask and nothing seemed to fix the problem. The cabin altitude was indicating roughly about 20;000 to 21;000 feet from what I recall. I switched again to my headset and requested '...priority; need to descend now to 10;000 feet pressurization problems.' As soon as I talked to ATC; I started immediate descent memory item and checklist; while descending; I took the First Officer mask to see for O2 flow and no O2 was flowing; I double checked the O2 handle.  I pulled both located on the Captain left hand side upper and lower; and nothing resulted for O2 function. Since I was indicating 60 miles from my departure airport; I decided to return since for my judgment it was unsafe to continue the flight without O2 flow; no O2 mask microphone and pressurization problems. Upon reaching 10;000 feet the cabin stabilized and the cabin altitude indicator was no longer illuminated with a cabin altitude about 9;000 feet.ATC gave me instructions to descend to 5;000 feet and while at it; the cabin altitude started to jump 5;500 feet up followed by a descent to 4;000 feet and this continued all the way to 3;000 feet. At that moment; I was feeling uncomfortable since my ears where hurting and I knew I was not feeling 100%. At 3;000 feet; I turned off my bleed air and flew the aircraft unpressurized. Why ? I had 'ears popping' several times at this time and I wanted to make the little time left comfortable in order to make a safe landing; since this constant climb and descend from the cabin was making me feel really weak. Landed the aircraft successfully without any major issues. After landing Maintenance and Station manager met me at the airplane.  I took  time at the crew van to see if I felt better and I did.  This resulted in a maintenance write up for 3 items.  Unable to control cabin altitude; O2 Mask Mic not operating; O2 not flowing properly.

column121: After having sent 2 test balloons (party balloons with helium) to check winds and finding they both showed no more than 7 knots of wind and practically went straight up as far as I could see them. Only clouds in the visible area were small white cumulus approximately 10;000 feet high. I chose to launch my hot air balloon near in a dirt lot with no obstruction down wind and more than enough room to move around in case of wind gusts. Knowing I might experience some gusts of wind due to only one local airport having seen gusts up to 14 knots. During my entire set up and inflation; I hadn't experienced any gusts more than 10 knot. After inflating the balloon to an upright position and the balloon maintaining its usual shape and taking pressure as normal I asked the passengers to load into the balloon basket. I was still tied to the van with a 5/8' polyester yacht braided rope and started heating the balloon with a fuel tank only used for the purpose of inflation to buoyancy.Before I could heat the balloon to buoyancy the wind hit the balloon from the opposite direction pushing me toward the passenger van westbound. Then hit me again heading east at an estimated 30 knots while dragging the balloon to the end of the tie down rope. The rope then broke and the balloon began to drag across the large lot. I gave full power to the burners trying to heat the balloon into flight knowing I wouldn't be able to stop the balloon on the ground in that speed of wind before hitting something. We started to lift off the ground approximately 10 to 15 feet off the ground and the balloon started descending again toward a chain link fence. Once hitting the fence was inevitable I started opening the deflation port. It took an additional acre of land for the balloon to come to a complete stop on another chain link fence.After this was all over the wind had completely stopped; and had relatively calm winds the rest of the evening. All of the small cumulus clouds were completely gone after this incident with clear skies. Making me assume those clouds had dissipated causing outflow gusts of at least 30 knots. In total hitting 3 chain-link fences. All passengers and myself were unharmed with no injuries and no damage to the balloon to cause it to be unairworthy.

column121: The weather enroute to ZZZ1 wasn't too bad. I would characterize the clouds as scattered around 9;000 to 1;0000 feet with periodic cells of precipitation. Low temperatures meant icing conditions so we avoided all precipitation. Preflight planning weather briefing was in agreement with what we were observing; and we listened to each Automated Weather of the airports we passed.The area was nearly clear skies. Few clouds if any and no observed precipitation within 20 miles. Winds and clouds were moving east; following a cold front which passed the day prior. We encountered one broken cell at 10;000 feet off our left and few clouds off our right. We climbed to 11500 feet and passed above and well clear of that cell within a short period of time.We stayed VFR; away from known icing conditions and moisture. The ride was uneventful. On the ride back; I expected the same weather. Conditions at my destination were VFR with scattered clouds up high; and a nearby airport was reporting the same. I did not check one of the airports enroute.  Radar returns on the map showed the same few cells scattered without only light precipitation. In the same region we encountered what I believed to the be the same cell we crossed over in the previous flight. We took note of precipitation left; right and ahead to the left. With a large enough gap of scattered clouds ahead to the right. We continued; and I made the decision to climb up to 10;500 feet to determine the height of the clouds. The clouds which were still only 500 feet in height; were now based around 10;500 feet.I made the decision then to climb to 12;500 feet to cross over them. I knew we were less than 30 minutes from an area which previously was nearly clear skies. Upon reaching 12;500 feet; I started the timer and we continued to cross well above the layer. I would describe this layer to be 6/8 to 7/8 as there were often breaks where we could see ground and see that the layer was not very thick in height. Roughly 10 to 15 miles; 5 to 8 minutes we noticed the clouds were becoming higher altitude; and we were losing spacing from them. We maneuvered around them as best we could; but would need to climb to stay above them and away from icing conditions. I absolutely knew that we would not be putting the airplane into known icing conditions. At this point; turning back didn't seem to be any more promising than continuing on course. We had confidence that the weather in the area was better beyond this cell; and we just witnessed the weather make a change of heart behind us.At this point; I knew that things could turn worse. As contingency; we began direct course for an airport with good weather. In the event that we reached 30 minutes above 12;500 feet or encountered any ice; we would immediately descend through the nearest break and land the airplane.As we continued; the clouds continued to rise. Still broken and overcast beneath us; we were faced with few options. Climb higher; enter known icing; or drop through a break and hope there is not precipitation around which would become ice.Entering icing conditions was not an option; or if anything a very last resort. Hypoxia was our biggest threat at altitude; and we were well aware and cautious of any symptoms. Luckily; I have had the experience of an altitude chamber and know my symptoms and signs. But we had to climb higher to avoid the icing conditions. We climbed up to 14;500 feet briefly and descended back down when able. Then the weather cleared up; the clouds became scattered; and we were able to descend back down to 8;500 feet. A total time of 24 minutes was observed above 12;500 feet. I would estimate that only 2-3 minutes were spent above 14;000 feet. No signs or symptoms of hypoxia were observed. The remainder of the flight was VFR and uneventful.The challenge was the lack of weather reporting equipment to determine the weather enroute; but this is not an excuse. I will exercise more resources such as a phone briefing or additional charts next time. I will also remember to never expect the weather to remain the same. Next time I will remember my favorite motto; Plan for the worst; and hope for the best.

column121: Aircraft X was an arrival into PVU airport. He came to my sector from the northwest.  I had to vector the aircraft to get him in trail of SLC arrivals. I turned the aircraft in trail of a SLC B752.  As I turned the aircraft further north so final turn wasn't so tight; the pilot called the airport in sight. PVU was advertising Visual Approach Runway 13. I cleared the aircraft for the Visual Approach. They turned towards the airport; I shipped them to the Tower approximately 10 miles out when I saw them turning towards the airport. Almost immediately the aircraft started turning further south towards a 8;900 foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude descending out of 8000 feet. I called PVU and they said they were talking to him. I asked what they were doing and was advised the pilot stated they were making S turns or something. The aircraft descended to 5;100 feet 7 miles from the airport; elevation 4;497 feet.  At that point PVU called stating the pilot had lost the airport and was climbing to 9;000 feet. The pilot checked in with me heading 180 and climbing to 9;000 feet. I said roger. They then asked for vectors to an ILS and I stated I would when they were at Minimum Vectoring Altitudes. I vectored for the ILS with no further complications. I don't really have recommendations on my end. PVU after this incident continued to advertise Visual Approaches. My Supervisor did not want to fill out any paperwork on the incident; so they said nobody did anything wrong and to leave it at that. I felt like this should be reported somehow. The pilot was extremely low a long distance from the airport trying to scud run the Visual Approach. I knew visuals were iffy because when I descended the aircraft to 9;000 feet they were IMC; I turned them and descended them to 8;000 feet (also telling them to expect the ILS) and they called the airport. It's not surprising they were able to call the airport in sight at that point; the mountain sits below and often they can descend slightly and get the airport in sight. What's surprising is the pilot accepted the approach if clouds were that bad; that we didn't 'declare an emergency' for the aircraft when they lost the airport at 5;100 feet in an 8;900 foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude MVA; and that the supervisor wouldn't at least want to follow up with the pilot. I truly don't know why we wouldn't want to look at this further.

column121: We blocked in late after completing our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 after a diversion to ZZZ from ZZZ2; due to ZZZ ATC [Center] closures during our original flight. With an early report and the late block in; we fear we may have exceeded Flight/Duty time. On our flight from ZZZ2 near ZZZ VOR; we were informed that ZZZ Center was closed and would remained closed for several hours. We coordinated with Dispatch and decided our first alternate choice of ZZZ4; while closer would be unsuitable since we would have no access to customs should we need to deplane. ZZZ was agreed to be the best alternative. We landed and parked with no further incident. Once on the ground; we were advised that ATC would open at XA:00Z and we had a new flight plan for XAZ and an EDT of XA:40Z. We spent the following XX:23 [hours] in constant communication with Dispatch; ZZZ Clearance and Ground; scheduling; and operations. During this time; we were told that if we could get fuel; it was coordinated that we would be priority one for departure and our communications reflected that. The fuel truck took longer than expected due to lightning; arriving at approximately XA:45Z. At that time; we received a warning message for our [departure time]. I contacted dispatch and together with ATC; coordinated a new release which would allow for a [departure time] of XB:34Z. We were informed that we also had only 25 mins to get airborne from block out due to flight time regulations; but if we could do that we would be legal. We were cleared via the filed route and given clearance to depart. With efficient and professional teamwork from all involved; we were able to close; push; taxi; and takeoff in 19 minutes. Just prior to takeoff; we were given a quote 'short reroute' by ATC; which we believed would still allow for compliance with the FARs. We made changes and were off at XB:31Z; 3 minutes prior to [departure time]. We confirmed the route with dispatch immediately once time permitted (at approximately 10;000ft) via ACARS. We worked with ZZZ1 Center ATC and were able to receive two shortcuts; which further shaved off time from our arrival; which was still in time from the new numbers we received from dispatch. The flight was very busy due to the high volume of ATC communications; turbulence; avoiding thunderstorms; performing duties; and trying to maintain situational awareness. We also worked to double check our times; to ensure compliance. Once we switched to ZZZ Center; we received multiple delay vectors and made to reduce speed. Once with approach; we were slowed to 190 on the arrival and 170 prior to intercepting final at ZZZZZ for the ILS [Runway] XXR; a 20 mile final. On the ground we received a very short taxi of approximately 3 minutes to parked short of our gate. We then waited over 10 minutes for a ramp crew to show up. Official block in was at XD:01Z. Without the delay on the ramp and the excessive vectors and speed reductions; our computer had us in prior to XB:40Z; even with the routing by ZZZ Center. We completed our duties during and after the flight with no further incident. Honestly; I cannot say enough about the teamwork and professionalism of each of the crew members; dispatch; scheduling; and operations personnel involved with this flight. Each member was thorough and efficient in their duties and each was critical to the safety and completion of the flight. My feeling is that; if possible; last minute reroutes should be avoided if possible and ramp personnel ready to welcome aircraft upon arrival.

We were still over max landing weight; and needed time to run all the supplemental checklists and procedures; so we decided to land at ZZZ and burn fuel to get under max landing weight at the same time. The single engine ILS into ZZZ was textbook. We taxied off the runway; was inspected by CFR; and then taxied to the gate.The Low Oil Quantity checklist is not easily found; as it is not in the index as 'low oil quantity' or 'oil low quantity' and it only reference oil pressure in the index.There was no audio or visual alert; when the oil quantity was half what it was supposed to be. We just happened to catch the small indication on the lower screen; and watched it drop to zero. I don't think we could have caught it any faster than we did.

column121: We had no operational issues whatsoever. This debrief is simply an observation. The SNA Tower closed for COVID exposure and SNA has become an uncontrolled field. The flight experience of the GA traffic that saturates that airspace is typically very beginner level and a Control Tower is essential. Uncontrolled field operations were nothing short of chaotic at that airport; and I really do see a potential for an accident to occur. Simply put; the pilots that are operating at that airport don't have the experience they need to merge with airline operations. The radio was saturated; there was confusion of who's going to take the runway next; a twin engine airplane decided to do a 360 to provide spacing while a commercial aircraft was 4 miles behind them on final.  A small aircraft almost took the runway with an aircraft on short final. I saw another small aircraft make left traffic for [Runway] 20R when the traffic pattern is only right.  In my professional opinion; I suggest that SNA be only an IFR only operation only during non-towered operations.  The amount of threats at that field are countless. Every pilot has to start somewhere and I'm sensitive to that; but a new small aircraft pilot practicing landings; turning an early base while an air carrier is on final (hypothetical example; that didn't happen); has no business in such a busy environment without a Tower Controller there to mitigate risk.Again; there was no event. This is an observation. Lack of traffic management is the factor in a potential disaster.If there is to be no tower at SNA; it needs to be commercial or IFR only operations.

On a dry day with fillets; it would still be doable to make the turn. But with the taxiways in worse condition than I've ever experienced; we relayed to Tower the taxiway conditions and whether we could instead proceed straight via [Taxiway] X1 to X3 as the snow plow trucks were clearly visible on [Taxiway] X2. column121: ATC said there was rain on the field. There was a B737 flight ahead of us on the approach by 5 to 10 minutes. We were listening to both Approach and Tower to monitor their approach and landing. We discussed holding; prior to the preceding aircraft landing. The preceding B737 reported safe on deck; medium braking; and no issues. They said they broke out 300 feet above minimums; 500 feet above ground. This gave us confidence to conduct the approach and landing. We complied with the wet runway requirements on the 10-7 page (max braking).We were fully configured with flaps 30 by the final approach fix with the landing checklist complete. We were stable at both the 1000 feet and 500 feet calls. Approach was mostly smooth in the clouds with no turbulence. Auto throttles moved very little. The rain was moderate; maybe moderate to high. Once we broke out; we could see the runway the entire time. Wiper were keeping up; but on high. We broke out about 300 feet. Saw some ground before that; so knew we were close to breaking out. Saw the Runway End Identifier Lights at 300 feet and the runway edge lights and center line lights shortly after. Captain called 'approaching minimums' just prior to breaking out and I said I had the field in sight. The auto pilot and auto throttles were disengaged around 200 feet.Landed a little left of center line; but the right main gear was to the right of the center line. Nose was pointed down the runway. Landing was firm to hard. Flare was normal. Raised nose to arrest descent at 30 feet and power was at idle at touchdown. We were both surprised by the firmness of the landing. Nose wheel was set down normally. I thought we might have skipped a little bit; but the Captain did not think so. Maybe we hydro-planed then the tires grabbed. We immediately started sliding left. I don't remember us turning to the left. It seemed we were pointed down the runway but going left. I stepped on the right rudder; but it didn't seem to have an effect. The left main mount went off the pavement on the left side of the runway. It seemed to take a while to get it back on the pavement with full right rudder and full manual braking. With both pilots stepping on full manual brakes; the aircraft did not seem to slowdown. Never felt the brakes grabbing; and with max brakes; we should have felt the brakes grab. I do not know if that Captain was using the nose wheel steering to assist getting it back to the right.Once back on the pavement; we started to veer to the right; but never left the pavement on the right side. Once on the runway; we added full reverse. We put in full left rudder to keep it on the runway. We got the aircraft direction under control; but it was still pulling to the right with full braking and full left rudder. I think the Captain was countering the pull with nose wheel steering. The aircraft was still difficult to slow down.We exited the runway on the high-speed taxiway on the right at a slow speed and came to a stop just off the runway. Tower asked about our position and if we needed assistance. The aircraft instruments; indications and controls were all normal. The only noticed adverse indication was an 'anti-skid inop ' light. The Captain released the brakes and rolled forward a little to check for a blown tire and brake function. All seemed fine so we said we can proceed to the gate. The taxi in was uneventful.On the taxi in we informed Tower that we may have departed the paved surface and there may be Foreign Object and Debris (FOD)on the runway. After shutdown; the Captain got up and checked on the Flight Attendants and passengers. All seemed fine. One Flight Attendant said she was scared while it was occurring; but otherwise no adverse comments. They were obviously a little shaken at the time; but not excessively so. We contacted Company maintenance and wrote up the maintenance items that we knew about. Several of the Flight Attendants were working our deadhead flight back the next morning. Theystill did not seem to have any after effects from the event and were friendly toward us.Maybe the initial left drift was due to the right gear hydro planning while the left gear had full auto-brakes using anti-skid. Once the left gear returned to the pavement; it's ant-skid may have been damaged; causing the veering to the right under full brakes.
column123: Leg 3 of a transitioning First Officer on a 4 day 15 hour IOE (Initial Operating Experience). The First Officer had just flown the previous leg and done well. He shot the ILS Approach and flew a nice approach to a very nice landing. During the 3 hour sit prior to our flight we discussed the upcoming flight including the special airport requirements and 10-7 pages. Reviewed the flight plan NOTAMs and maintenance status of the aircraft. Noted the sequenced flashing lights to our planned arrival runway were out of service.First Officer made a nice takeoff and climb out to cruise and we continued to update the weather forecasts on the flight. Reviewed 10-7 pages decided to use max braking for training and for possibility of a wet runway. Worst weather report we saw was 4000 feet broken; light rain; and winds 240 at 8. Briefed the arrival and RNAV Approaches due to winds. We also briefed the ILS. Approaching top of descent asked Center which runway was in use. The ILS was the approach in use. Pulled up the landing data. Approaching with radar on noticed a cell and heard [an] aircraft ask for deviations. We asked for and received direct ZZZZZ on the arrival. Descending to 12;000 feet were cleared for the arrival and preceding aircraft ask for direct to a fix. There appeared to be cells just south of the approach. Approach informed us there was rain on the field; we discussed possible holding when we heard [another aircraft] cleared for the approach.I tuned VHF 2 to Tower frequency to get a heads up on the preceding aircraft. They were cleared to land and reported to Tower breaking out a few hundred feet above minimums landed and reported braking action medium. Approach cleared us direct to a fix and to report on the localizer cleared for the approach. Slowed toward 180 kts.; flaps 5 auto pilot on LNAV/VNAV; armed the app mode; made 2;500 feet call; reported established and was told to switch to Tower. Called Tower and reported 9 mile final was cleared to land. I believe Tower also said preceding aircraft broke out at 500 feet and braking action medium. Localizer and glideslope engaged set Touchdown Zone Elevation. Approaching the final approach fix gear down flaps 15 rolled speed back then selected flaps 30 and landing checklist.IMC and moderate rain but little to no turbulence or wind shifts. Passing approximately 1;000 to 800 feet saw ground and lights looking down called 1;000 feet then set Missed Approach altitude. Approach was stable and verified at 500 feet. Called approaching minimums slightly early approximately 400 feet to prepare for possibility of a go around. Approximately 300 feet broke out with Runway End Lights; High Intensity Runway Lights and runway center line in sight. First Officer disengaged the auto pilot and auto throttle approximately 150 to 200 feet. Still raining with wind shield wipers on high but could clearly see the runway environment. Short final dipped 1/4 dot low to try and land in the first 1;000 feet. Heard 50 feet just prior to crossing the threshold then 40; 30. At 30 the First Officer began the flare slowing the rate of descent then began reducing power. Everything appeared normal till the last 5 to 10 feet when it felt like the bottom dropped out to a firm to hard landing. Written up as a hard landing.There was no bounce. Power levers at idle and speed brakes deployed. I have used max auto brakes often due to the demo requirement for Operational Experience. Ordinarily they grab and push you forward in the seat. There was no such sensation other than a feeling the anti-skid was cycling and the aircraft did not appear to be slowing. I believe the nose was pointed straight down the runway and the touchdown had the nose just left of the center line. On touchdown the aircraft began to immediately slide to the left. I believe the aircraft hydroplaned after landing. The First Officer depressed full right rudder with no effect. First Officer was slow to go into reverse so I came on the controlsset max reverse and followed full right rudder yet the aircraft continued to slide left and the left main mount left the prepared surface. I used nose wheel steering to bring the aircraft back toward center line. All this happened immediately after touchdown or so I believe. As we continued down the runway with both of us standing on the brakes the aircraft began to slide toward the right side of the runway. With full reverse full manual brakes and what I believed to be full left rudder it required nose wheel input to keep the aircraft from leaving the right side of the runway. At no point in time did I feel the aircraft nose was pointed at or mostly toward either side of the runway from initial touchdown to stop.As we continued down the right side of the runway the aircraft still did not appear to be slowing normally. Approaching the high speed taxiway on the right side of the runway I elected to allow the aircraft to veer onto the taxi way. We had finally slowed where we were able to bring the aircraft to a stop. We were not 100 percent sure the left main mount had left the prepared surface so we discussed the possibility and the possibility of blown tires. Tower asked if we needed assistance. We did not note any usual indications or issues all instruments appeared normal. With the exception of the anti-skid fault light. I allowed the aircraft to roll forward checking the brakes which appeared to operate normally at slow speed and we had no indication of a deflated tire. I decided the aircraft could be taxied to the gate to deplane the passengers safely at slow speed and was cleared by Tower to do so. We also informed Tower there may be FOD (Foreign Object and Debris) on the runway. Uneventful taxi to parking with good clear area all the way into the gate. Performed the parking checklist then left the flight deck to check on the passengers and flight attendants. No injuries were reported. One flight attendant said she was a little shaken. Conferred with base ops then did a walk around with the contract mechanic. Called Company maintenance and made maintenance write ups.

column121: I am writing this because I'm concerned about the safety of the ZZZ - ZZZZ - Chengdu Airport - ZZZZ - ZZZ pairing.  Starting on date; it was changed from a 4 person crew to a 3 person crew. This is NOT SAFE. I understand why [it] changed is because the duty time went from XX:25 to XX:20 and so only 3 pilots are required.  I've flown this trip X times and it's challenging with 4 pilots let alone 3 pilots.  The primary purpose of this report is to identify this [pairing] as a safety event. My goal is to provide a corrective measure that will mitigate a safety issue; before it becomes a Incident/AccidentTHREAT: Personal Fatigue.  This trip is on the back side of the body clock with a late night pick up out of ZZZZ. This trip becomes close to a XX hour duty day because of the 1:10 ride from downtown [city] to the airport and back.  The flight from ZZZZ is often 2 hours longer than the flight coming back from Chengdu due to the Jet stream.  Often; because of this jet stream; there is moderate turbulence along the route; making sleeping in the bunk difficult.  The Captain must be in his seat for the take-off and landings for both legs.  With a three pilot crew; it is difficult coming up with a plan for breaks; especially on the shorter Chengdu - ZZZZ segment. The relief Pilot will hardly get a break; besides being upset for not getting a break; they will be very tired. The relief pilot is one of the most important people in the crew; and you want them alert. They often see threats before the flying pilots do; and can bring the threat to their attention.THREAT: Environmental.  Often there is low visibility in Chengdu and ZZZZ this time of year; increasing the work load. There is a X:10 break in Chengdu which is a very busy time for the pilots. We have to flight plan; pre-flight (with full suit) deal with the Chengdu police and customs. With the boarding of cargo (very noisy and moves the plane around a lot with loading of cargo containers) it is impossible to get any rest while on the ground.THREAT: Technical.  Chinese airlines are almost back to normal; leaving Chengdu is a very busy time for ATC. I have flown with new pilots that haven't flown China and between operating in meters and the difficulty with the Chinese ATC language it is impossible; and irresponsible leaving the flight deck out of FL180 to go on break. Because of this; it isn't until reaching cruise altitude until the Captain can start his break.  Meters can be challenging and causes a lot of missed ATC calls; or repeats. The 4th pilot is a huge benefit for listening to ATC and providing back up!I've flown this trip X times now; having 2 Captains and 2 FO's was by far the safest. It gave everyone a break and each Captain had a leg which helped mitigate stress; and fatigue.  With one Captain and 3 FO's it is not nearly as safe as 2 Captains; but it is bearable because you get more of a break. With one Captain and 2 FO's it is impossible to get a break; of good rest.Another thing the company needs to think about; this is China during COVID times.  The company realizes the difficulty of a layover in China for the crews. The duty time with 3 crews is reduced to XX hours. There can only be a X:10 delay in Chengdu before an extension takes place. After doing this trip X times I know for a fact that the likelihood of me extending is nil; due to fatigue.The mitigation is simple. Make it a 4 person crew.

column121: There is a trend with 737 windshields in that they no longer repel water when operating in rain. In addition; multiple aircraft I've flown have window crazing exacerbating the visual distortion in rain. In the past; I have contacted Maintenance and completed write ups which all resulted in being told there is no mitigation for this. Upon doing some research I learned Boeing used to have; and may still have; a procedure for applying Rain X to the windows. In the interest of safety; I'd like to suggest crazing be polished out of windows in accordance with Boeing's procedures; and some sort of hydrophobic coating be applied. It can be argued that windshields should be written up prior to accepting an aircraft; but there are two reasons this argument doesn't stand. First; a crew may fly an aircraft from an area with no rain to an area with rain and not realize the windows don't allow for adequate visibility until in the landing phase; and second; because I've attempted to rectify this numerous times either with Maintenance or through the reporting process with no changes being made. As far as writing an aircraft up after an event; I know there won't be anything done about it from past experience.

column121: Climbing to enroute altitude of 33;000 ft. MSL; received an advisory of malfunctioning outflow valve. Eventually; after being unable to establish control of cabin pressure altitude; failure of both automatic pressure controllers and no control over manual control; we requested priority handling and ATC cleared us to a lower altitude where we were able to maintain a safe cabin altitude. Diverted into ZZZ2. ZZZ2 Maintenance discovered on inspection that the aircraft fwd outflow valve had become obstructed from loose insulation material and prevented its operation.
column123: We had reached cruise at FL330 enroute from ZZZ-ZZZ1. The ECAM gave us an advisory that the cabin altitude was above normal. I was the PF (Pilot Flying). The Captain worked the problem. We noticed that the cabin altitude was approaching 8;700 ft. and had a trend to climb higher at 50-200 fpm. Looking at the pressurization schematic; we could see that the forward outflow valve was full open and should have been full closed. The aft outflow valve was normal at full closed. We referenced the QRH for all actions. The Captain switched the pressure controller to manual mode and attempted to close the forward outflow valve but it would not close. We discussed diverting to ZZZ2 and requesting priority handling. At a certain point; the ECAM indicated that both auto pressure controllers failed. As we could not control the cabin altitude in any mode; we requested priority handling and asked for a lower altitude. Initially; ATC cleared us to FL 240 and then later 16;000 ft. while we were descending. We were able to maintain terrain clearance and stay above the weather. We were cleared direct to the ZZZ2 airport and set up for an ILS to Runway XXR. We encountered moderate turbulence while we were at 320 kts. This caused the airplane to momentarily overspeed to about 335-340 kts. I slowed the airplane and we continued our descent. We flew an uneventful approach to Runway XXR and landed safely and taxied to parking. Upon inspection; we were told Maintenance discovered a piece of insulation stuck in the forward outflow valve the prevented it from closing. We later continued on with a separate flight to ZZZ1.

column121: I wanted to take a few minutes to relate to you my personal experiences during the events that transpired.  We were at the tail end of a lengthy four day trip; with the usual holiday related challenges; weather; maintenance; crew-placarding; lengthy sit times; de-icing etc. On the third day of the trip; we were waiting in line for departure on [Runway] XXL at ZZZ; when the tower informed us that the operation was shut down for a 'deep-cleaning' at ZZZ1 Center.  Having personally experienced the same the same scenario last year when both the ZZZ2 Tower and ground were shut down for a COVID spread throughout their Tower; it didn't take long for us to figure out the reason for the closure.Like everyone one else in our situation; we opened up the FOM and began compliance with the notification processes for the passengers; the Flight Attendants; and ZZZ Ops. My First Officer (FO) and I immediately began working the 14 hour duty day issue; (FO A was my second FO during the course of the trip; and he had a less restrictive duty day constraint than I did).  After nearly two hours at the hold short line; we began the process of finding a gate; with the intent to avoid the prospective government fines levied for lengthy delays. It was the usual chaos; with ZZZ Ops being overwhelmed by this unforeseen event.  As we approach the two hour FOM deadline for locating a gate; we were assigned DXX via ACARS.  While taxiing to the gate; we made multiple attempts to get guidance from Ops; Ramp; Dispatch; etc.; to see what the intent was for the passengers; my crew; and the aircraft. We were unable to get any specific guidance. Following our arrival at the gate; an Agent opened the main door; and told us that the flight would be cancelled. As directed by the agent; the passengers disembarked with their bags. Since we had seen no changes to our crew schedule; nor had we received any kind of communication from crew tracking; we assumed that the agent was correct regarding the cancellation; and as such; we began reviewing our required duty time obligations. Absent any further guidance; we subsequently put the aircraft 'to bed;' and once again we attempted to contact crew tracking; (no luck there).  Rather than exit into the terminal; we elected to continue to wait on the aircraft.After 20 minutes or so; a new Agent came down the bridge; and asked me if we were ready to board the aircraft. Needless to say; I was a bit astonished.  I asked her what the plan was; and she said that we were going to resume the flight to ZZZ3; ASAP.  I reminded her that the airspace was still closed; and that we had not received any contact from either dispatch or tracking; regarding an updated release; and that we would need additional fuel; lavatory/water service; and a resupply of the delay rations that the Flight Attendants had used for the passengers during our time spent waiting on the taxiway. I also told her that both of us; along with two of the Flight Attendants had duty-time issues that we have to calculate and resolve before departure.  She promptly replied and asked me; 'Captain are you refusing to board the aircraft?'I immediately realized that this was the standard pass-the buck/assign the delay language; that some Agents use in an attempt to intimidate Pilots. I took several deep breaths; before I stated to her in no uncertain terms; that we would need to at least begin to address the aforementioned issues; before we would be comfortable boarding the aircraft again.  Her reply was; 'Captain; are you refusing to board the aircraft?'  I answered that until we get some of these issues resolved; yes.  What was clear to myself; my FO and the number one Flight Attendant; is that this was clearly an attempt at pilot-pushing. [In my opinion]; this Agent had one concern; and that was to make sure that these passengers would become someone else's problem; (namely ours).Long story short; and after significant efforts by all involved; we reconstituted the flight and determined that without further lengthy ground delays that we would likely arrive in ZZZ3 within our respective 14 hour duty day window. We then performed our usual checklists; flows; refueling; new clearance etc.After push-back; start and taxi instructions were received; I made my first mistake of the flight; and turned in the direct opposite direction of ground's instructions on the taxi clearance. It was at this point that I realized I was a lot more tired than I thought.  My FO and I discussed this; and we agreed that though we were both somewhat tired; it was safe to proceed; and that we should just take extra time and precautions going forward.Mistake number two on my part was that when ATC changed our departure STAR; we briefed it at the gate; had it up on our iPads; but I had failed to enter it in the MCDU. After wheels up; ATC gave us direct-to clearance to a fix that wasn't on the legs page. My FO quickly realized that I hadn't entered the new departure STAR; and he rapidly remedied it on the MCDU. I was mad at myself for making this series of unprecedented and inexplicable mistakes. Those mistakes continued as we descended on the type of complex STAR with a series of 'at or above' altitude constraints; that confounds the logic on some of the older 'Basic' airplanes.Needless to say; we landed safely in ZZZ3 later that evening. After block-in; I determined that I was within my duty legality; by 20 minutes or so. It had been a very long day.  We had departed ZZZ4 that morning before the sun had risen; and we had left the gate at ZZZ for the second time; well after the sun had set. In summary; I had made many embarrassing operational mistakes during the course of the last leg; beginning with my pre-flight; push back; all the way through the descent into ZZZ3.  The only explanation for my numerous mistakes was fatigue. In short; I will never; ever; again allow the 'system' to push to me beyond my own personal safety limits. I will take my First Officers counsel more seriously when it comes to considering just how tired we are.Additional factors include that when you consider the cumulative effects of four and five day trips on us; along with a 14 hour duty period; it can be well beyond the average pilot's limitations to safely operate.  And while I don't blame the agent personally; (like everyone else; she was just doing the job in the manner that she was trained); and like everyone else she's just under time pressure.  As time has gone by at our company; it has become clear to me; that the safety culture at the top of this airline; is in many respects; mostly honored and kept in place; by those who of us; who are at the pointy end of the spear.In retrospect; the main causal factor was fatigue due to a lengthy delay.Two suggestions.  The first is that [in my opinion]; we need to take into account the cumulative effect of a lengthy four and five day trip on pilot fatigue.  The other issue is Gate Agent conduct and verbiage regarding flight Ops as it regards to boarding the passengers.

column123: Approximately 200 nm south of ZZZ we received our first indication of any issue with the blue hydraulic system. In level cruise flight we received an ECAM for HYD B SYS LO PR. While running the ECAM we noticed that the hydraulic quantity was low. The procedure calls for the Blue Electric Pump to be shut off; and as we did so; we monitored the quantity indicator. As it dropped; we received an ECAM for Hyd B RSVR LO LVL. After running the ECAM; finishing the QRH and conferring with dispatch we advised ATC for the loss of redundant systems. We chose to divert to ZZZ for a multitude of reasons including the nice weather; long runways; availability of ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) and the fact that it's a maintenance hub. We immediately received vectors and a descent from ATC for an arrival into ZZZ. The Captain finalized his briefings to both the flight attendants and passengers. We then updated the FMC; applied the landing distance procedure and landing calculations and briefed the descent and approach. We completed the RNAV to [Runway XX]; landed and had ARFF inspect the aircraft for any potential hazards or safety concerns. Once complete; we taxied to the gate and completed the diversion safely.

column121: The left yaw damper was deferred on the initial paperwork. Upon logbook review at the aircraft; the mechanic informed us the deferral was cleared which left us with no MELs. Pre-flight and taxi were uneventful. Shortly after takeoff with the Captain as PF; the L HYD QTY EICAS illuminated; followed by the L HYD ENG PUMP EICAS. As we were handed off to Departure on the ZZZZZ 5 SID; I saw the L HYD SYS PRESS; RUDDER RATIO; and YAW DAMPER EICAS messages momentarily appear; but they quickly extinguished without an associated Master Caution (that I can recall). The Captain elected to leave the Flaps at 5 and bugged the speed back accordingly. Departure cleared us to 10;000 ft.; but allowed us to stay at 5;000 ft. to run the QRH checklists. ATC provided vectors in the vicinity of ZZZ while we worked the problem. At the time the QRH was referenced; we had two EICAS messages displayed. The L HYD QTY checklist did not have any action items. The L HYD ENG PUMP checklist directed us to turn the engine pump OFF. Since I had momentarily seen the L HYD SYS PRESS message and the Status page indicated a loss of fluid in the left system (magenta RF); we referenced the L HYD SYS PRESS checklist; but did not perform any of the actions at that time since the EICAS was not illuminated. As we discussed a return to ZZZ; the L HYD SYS PRESS message reappeared; along with the YAW DAMPER and RUDDER RATIO messages; an associated Master Caution; and the SYS PRESS light on the overhead panel. We accomplished the QRH checklist up to the deferred items and advised ATC. The controller passed word of the priority handling to The Company at the Captain's request while we completed the DIVERT ACARS; got performance data with the L HYD SYS non-normal; and set up for an ILS to Runway XX. While on extended vectors; we tried extending the gear normally which resulted in a GEAR DISAGREE EICAS and POWER XFER UNIT Status message. In accordance with the deferred items on the L HYD SYS PRESS checklist; we accomplished the alternate gear extension procedures. Once turned back towards the airport; we attempted normal flap extension from 5 to 15. The TE FLAP DISAGREE message appeared; so we again followed the deferred items for alternate flap extension. I sent for performance data reflecting the new non-normal (L HYD SYS WITH TE FLAP DISAGREE) accounting for the Flaps 20 Vref 20 landing configuration. With the QRH complete; the Captain called for the applicable normal checklists and we briefed the approach with attention given to non-normals (manual speedbrake extension before right thrust reverser deployment; manual braking; etc) and how a go-around would be handled (gear would remain down; flap speeds; etc). Once handed off to Tower; we relayed that we would not have nose wheel steering. Our plan was to clear the runway onto a high speed taxiway to be towed; but if we couldn't stop by XX; we would probably have to shutdown on the runway for tow. Tower told us the runway was ours with CFR standing by and said they had notified Company of the need for tow. We had a jumpseater onboard that is another 757 First Officer. He had plugged a headset into the observer panel for assistance as needed and checklist backup. The Captain queried the crew as to if we thought everything was in order as we approached the FAF. We were in agreement that all checklists were complete and we felt comfortable with the approach and landing. The Captain landed; manually pulled the speed brake lever; deployed the right reverser; and conducted manual braking. He cleared [the runway] where we were met by CFR vehicles. After performing the After Landing flows (except leaving the flaps at 20); the engines were shutdown for CFR to inspect the aircraft/brakes. Once cleared by CFR; the priority handling was terminated and we were towed into Ramp by Company. There was not any visible hydraulic fluid on the aircraft exterior when maintenance first looked. We performed a Shutdown/Secure checklist; conducted aquick debrief with the mechanics to include the wording of the Captain's logbook write up; and left the aircraft with maintenance as we were directed to tail swap and continue to ZZZ1 under a new flight number. As the crew van arrived; hydraulic fluid was leaking onto the ramp from the left side of the aircraft while the mechanic continued to evaluate the problem. I still do not know what the root cause of the problem was and/or if there was anything that could have prevented the loss of fluid in the left hydraulic system. I feel our crew worked well together to safely recover the aircraft despite the backside of the clock showtime and it being our first leg flying together. ATC and CFR were very helpful throughout the event. I think our training prepared us for situations like this (heavy system hydraulic loss) and CRM principles were used to efficiently handle the issue to the best of our abilities at that time.
column123: Shortly after takeoff (ZZZ) and passing approximately 1;000 ft. AGL; we heard a caution aural and saw L HYD QTY EICAS Msg. There was also an audible thump sound and slight feedback through the flight controls (yoke). This was followed quickly by L HYD ENG PUMP Msg. We were flying the SID (I was PF) and the aircraft was in LNAV and VNAV. I called for A/P CTR CMD; confirmed the A/P FMA and that the A/P was in fact functioning properly. Initially; we remained on the SID while analyzing our problem. A quick check of the status page confirmed that the left hydraulic reservoir had lost a significant amount of fluid (high of .98 to low of .21; .30 after shutdown). We also had a momentary L HYD SYS Press message that extinguished and came back on later (on downwind). Considering an air turn back likely; I decided to keep the flaps at 5. We requested a level off at our initial altitude of 5;000 ft. We let ATC know we had a hydraulic issue and that we desired vectors for a likely return to Runway XX at ZZZ. With the initial 'aviating; navigating and communicating' complete we agreed that L HYD QTY was; at that point; our first priority. After running this checklist the L HYD SYS PRESS light came on continuously leading to the running of that checklist. Having reached the deferred items section of the checklist we briefly discussed contacting dispatch. I decided that a return to ZZZ was clearly the safest and best option and that direct notification by us would be more of a distraction than help. I decided to advise ATC and request ATC notify 'company' of our hydraulic system issue. This and quick divert message sent via ACARS; satisfied the notification requirement. We had good weather; a long runway (at a very familiar field) and were well below max landing weight. Before beginning the configuration process we completed our normal procedures; including after takeoff and approach checklists; and set up & briefed the ILS for Runway XX. We began configuring and quickly discovered that the PTU was not operating properly; requiring the alternate extension procedures for flaps and landing gear. After requesting and receiving landing data for our non-normal configuration (per checklist); we requested a vector to intercept final. With the assistance of our jumpseater we reviewed all the pertinent notes and made sure we had considered all the pertinent variables; no autobrakes; manual speedbrake extension on landing; R thrust reverser; only after speed brakes extended and no nose wheel steering (differential braking only) on roll-out. We notified approach and Tower of need to have aircraft towed to parking either from runway or after clearing runway (high speed taxiway). I planned to use differential braking to exit the runway; but wasn't sure how effective this would be. As it turned out; aircraft control was more than adequate for exiting via the high speed exit taxiway. After taxiing clear of the runway we stopped the aircraft and coordinated a quick inspection of the aircraft by crash/rescue and a tug to tow us to parking.

column121: While operating a part 135 trip from ZZZZ to ZZZ1 we experienced a runway incursion while departing on runway 14. The possible incursion happened at intersection Lima and runway 14 which is approximately 9000 ft. from the start of the runway. I am also confident that the other aircraft was a Medium Transport. At the time; the ground and tower controllers were operating on separate frequencies by two different people. Once holding short; we advised tower that we were ready for departure to which he responded for us to line up and wait as he had landing traffic a few miles out on runway 10. A few moments later; he cleared us for an immediate departure to which we thought he was trying to get us out before the traffic inbound for 10 landed. From our position on the runway; we could not see that landing traffic and could only go off what he told us earlier. As pilot monitoring; I completed the before takeoff checks and the pilot flying released the brakes and started to advance the throttles. As we rolled down the runway; I made the call of 'airspeed alive both sides;' and at that moment I could see in my peripherals that an aircraft far down the runway was approaching a hold short at intersection Lima. I called out to the PF (Pilot Flying) that there was an aircraft nearing the runway at a rather quick speed on the right side and keep an eye on him if possible. As we passed 80 kts and were quickly approaching V1 the aircraft began crossing the runway I called for an abort. It is hard to recall how long I waited for a response from the PF; but it had to have been about a half a second to a second and at that point I looked down again and we were passed V1. I called 'V1; rotate' and we took off and started the climbout. When we passed the aircraft that crossed; we were a hundred feet or so in the air and they were turning on to taxiway hotel. We climbed out as usual and once above 10;000 ft. the PF engaged the autopilot; and we began talking about the situation. My first question was if he heard me call the abort; to which he replied that he did. He then told me as he was processing everything; he made the decision that a high-speed abort would have been more dangerous as we were just about to rotate; and the incursion aircraft was still almost a mile down the runway from us. We had switched to Center at that point already and I took the second radio to call back Approach and let them know what happened. I informed the controller that we had a possible runway incursion; and that the Medium Transport was just finishing crossing the runway as we had taken off. They said the supervisor was following up with the situation; had no further questions and appreciated the report. When thinking back to the situation we were guessing that the tower controller wanted to get us out before the landing traffic on runway 10 while at the same time the ground controller wanted to get the Medium Transport across the runway before we took off. Due to runway crossing clearances being given on the ground frequency; we have no idea that was happening while we were given our takeoff clearance while on tower. Finally; we talked about the importance of when a decision is made; to verbalize it so that we remain an effective crew. When one pilot makes a decision without informing the other of that decision; especially at high speeds during takeoff; it is imperative that everyone is on the same page. We continued our way to ZZZ1 with no additional issues.The whole situation is complex and looking back it is hard to think of things we could have done differently. Due to operating procedures at the airport; we had no way of expecting that aircraft to cross in front of us down the runway as we executed out expedited departure. It is most important to maintain proper crew coordination and CRM through communication to remain a safe and efficient flight crew.

There was a lot going on during the crew change and I didn't think about having two Outbound Crew Members onboard before leaving the aircraft. column121: We were cleared for taxi to Runway 1. We exited the ramp at Taxiway D and proceeded southbound on Taxiway A. We were instructed to perform a 180 back to Taxiway A. The incursion did not present any immediate conflict to other aircraft. Another aircraft was simultaneously taxiing on the active runway for the north de-icing pad. The nearest arriving aircraft was greater than 10 miles away and had not yet been cleared to land.Upon further analysis of the error; we (the crew) determined that the short taxi certainly contributed to the confusion. The Holding Position sign for RWY 1-19 is situated on the northern edge of Taxiway A1 and angled to the northeast; in a manner that makes it very easy to miss when entering Taxiway A from Taxiway D. By the time the aircraft is established on Taxiway A; that sign is already abeam the aircraft. From the perspective of the pilot flying from the left seat; that sign is not visible in this situation. But the most significant factor in our misstep today was the nearly complete obscuration of the hold short line at the intersection of taxiways A and A1.

column121: There was no adverse event or situation on this flight. I am making this report out of concern for safety and to hopefully prevent a future accident.Flying into PDK; Peachtree Airport in Atlanta; last night was typical - IFR approach in IMC using the best low approach procedure at the airport; the ILS to 21L. On final; breaking out of the overcast; my copilot and I did not see the runway because it was not lit despite our having triggered pilot controlled lighting on 120.0. We repeated the procedure and the runway lit up. Landing was uneventful.Lighting at this airport is poor. PDK is located in an urban area and is surrounded by ground lights not associated with the airport. One pilot; reportedly told ATC that all he could see was a 'sea of lights' when asked to call the airport in sight at night. I have had the same experience on multiple occasions. The pilot controlled lighting is erratic; and it is on a different frequency than CTAF after the Tower closes. The typical visual approach we get is from the side where it is hard to see the runway lights even when they are all on; and the beacon is weak and usually obscured by surrounding obstacles at the approach altitudes we are typically given. Moreover; the PAPIs have been NOTAMed out of service for quite some time now; so there is no visual vertical guidance at night.In my opinion; this setup is an accident waiting to happen; hence this report.

column121: We were on our final phase of flight into ZZZ. It was IMC conditions with light snow upon arrival. The approach was ILS [Runway] XX. Upon landing; I used normal procedures with minimal braking for possible wet/icy runway and thrust reversers. All flight deck indications were as normal as we exit the runway and taxied to the ramp area for the conclusion of the flight. The next afternoon; we prepared to fly back to ZZZ1. The conditions had improved with clear skies and no precipitation. We began to taxi out to the runway completing all of the pre-flight checks and procedures. After takeoff; I began to execute the normal 'after takeoff checklist' with bringing the gear up. The gear did not retract and remained in the down and locked position. I am unsure if the gear came partly up or did not retract a small percentage at all. We climbed to 13;000 ft. and then 15;000 ft. attempting to resolve the situation. Once all procedures and attempts were exhausted; the decision was made to fly with the gear remaining in the down and locked position and head to ZZZ2. The airport weather was clear with light winds; and 10;000 ft. of runway. ZZZ2 was east of the mountains and clear of any weather. We attempted to burn as much fuel as possible as to not land overweight; flying at 17;000 ft. to also clear the terrain between our current position near ZZZ and ZZZ2. As we initiated our descent checklist and before landing checklist; our nose wheel steering was not illuminated and no indications of thrust reversers were available. Approach control and tower were notified of our situation and the possible need for Crash; Fire; Rescue upon landing.We landed at ZZZ2 without incident; I was able to taxi the plane off the runway using a highspeed taxiway. At that point; I stopped the aircraft and requested a tug to FBO on the field. There were no injuries to anyone on board the aircraft. The conclusion of events from information gathered from professional personnel; we encountered FOD upon landing at ZZZ or came in contact with ice buildup at some point during landing or touchdown. It is also possible that we could have encountered FOD upon takeoff the following day with our planned route to ZZZ1. Either occurrence of these two may have rendered our normal systems to function improperly.
