column121: On a normal approach to landing Runway XX at ZZZ airport; the aircraft experienced a temporary loss of engine power. We were on the middle glide path of the PAPI (2 red; 2 white) on runway centerline at approximately 200 ft. AGL. Approach speed was approximately 85 mph with 20 degrees of flaps deployed. The throttle was at a low power setting and the aircraft was sinking slightly below glideslope; so I pushed it in a bit to increase power. There was no increase in power so I pushed the throttle in further; eventually to full. With no change in engine sound or perceived power I continued the descent maintaining airspeed to the ground. As the aircraft was already low; we struck two approach lights (MALSR) and knocked them over. In inspection afterwards it appears that the lights struck the lower engine cowling and dented it. The plane touched down and at this point I contacted the tower letting them know we had a loss of power. During rollout engine power came back due to the pushed in throttle. I opted to shut the engine down at this point as the state of the airplane was not known. Once crews arrived I had already exited the plane and did not see much visible damage. With the fire crews there we opted to restart the engine to taxi off the runway with no further issue.I believe this incident could be caused by carburetor icing or perhaps a contaminant in the fuel system. The aircraft should have had approximately 20 gallons of fuel remaining at time of landing; and was in a stabilized decent so I would rule out temporary interruption of fuel supply. There was no indication of low fuel on either gauge and the fuel selector was set to both. A contaminant in the fuel system seems possible; though I am not sure what would make this kind of incident transitory. It's hard to say for sure; but I believe we were still hearing the engine running and not just the windmilling prop the entire time; so I don't believe the engine had shut off entirely at any point.Carburetor icing seems like the most likely explanation I can think of; but the symptoms are not consistent with how I was trained to detect it. At no time did we experience engine roughness during the flight; which I believed was a characteristic sign of carb icing. Prior to the descent to land; the aircraft was circling at 10;000 ft. for aerial observation. Power settings during the decent were reduced and I remember thinking that the throttle position used during the cruise descent was further in than I would expect for the observed manifold pressure. I had only flown this plane briefly before; so I didn't think much more of it; but if carb ice was the blame this was probably the main indication. At 2;000 ft. I was reducing to lower power settings and I activated carburetor heat. There was no roughness after this point that I would expect to associate with carb icing as it cleared.The fact that the landing after sunset and starting to get dark was not a major factor; aside from difficulty seeing what was below (besides the lights) as the plane came down short of the runway. Maintaining the approach speed close to best glide after power loss was important in avoiding any injury or more significant damage to the aircraft. Given the long length of the runway (9;800 ft.) I could have avoided hitting anything by planning to land above the PAPI glidepath.

column121: I was using a safety pilot and view limiting device to log instrument approaches to regain IFR currency. I was on climbout/missed approach from a low approach to a practice ILS X at ZZZ. I was told to by the Tower to 'proceed on course' after having previously told the Approach Controller I was headed next to ZZZ1 for the next approach. I was switched to ZZZ Approach at about 1;800 feet MSL on climbout and reported 1;900 feet for 3;000 feet direct ZZZ1. I was told 'Radar contact' and nothing else specifically.On climbout I was trying to set up my Garmin 430W for the next approach; and get a new program on the iPad (Foreflight vs. Garmim pilot I had previously used) to post the selected approach for ZZZ1 on the map. I had trouble with my glasses fogging up due to wearing a COVID mask in the plane and was experiencing updrafts/turbulence. The time to 3;000 feet was shorter than expected and due to the above distractions; I did not notice I was passing through 3;000 feet until I hit 3;250 feet at which point I reduced power and pushed the nose down. I was back to 3;000 feet within 15 seconds. I heard nothing from ATC regarding this; probably due to being VFR and no altitude restriction issued by ATC. I was able to verify all audio and events/altitudes due to a GoPro running to capture the flight.While I was VFR and there was no traffic nearby; if this was IFR; I would have had the same challenges and it would most likely been an altitude bust. There needs to be the same discipline applied to 'practice' instrument work as there is during the real thing in IMC; or the bad habits and distractions you allow during practice will seep into operations in general. I should have left the gizmo programming for level flight and popped the glasses off if the mask induced fogging was a distraction. I should have made the instrument scan primary rather than assuming I had more time than I actually had to program while getting to 3;000 feet.

I made the decision to divert to ZZZ3 and accomplished training enroute and landing late afternoon. Weather in ZZZ3 was IFR with a report that fog was believed to be moving into the ZZZ3 area. We refueled and departed for ZZZ1. Training was again accomplished enroute...landing was at night with 2;500 broken; 3;100 overcast and 3 mile in R and BR. This was the end of a long day that started early morning for a departure to ZZZ5 from ZZZ1...scheduled time was 1 hour 50 minutes with a 20 minute turn. Due to waiting for a dead heading crew member we left ZZZ5 one hour late; arriving ZZZ1 at noon. I picked up another FO and departed for ZZZ for a planned 1 hour 40 minute flight. Landing at ZZZ; we then departed for a planned 1 hour 40 minute flight to ZZZ1. As noted previously; we were forced to divert to ZZZ3; due to ATC Zero. I exceeded 8 hours but; felt that; per our FOM and the FARs; I was legal to start and finish because the divert to ZZZ3 was not planned and the scheduled times were within legal limits. Note that I had over 14 hours rest before the flying the following day and was off duty after the days flying was complete and no other flying scheduled for several days.The issue that bothers me is that I was accomplishing training at night and in solid IMC conditions...never again. There was some unspoken pressure to get the training accomplished due to approaching holiday and a lack of aircraft to accomplish the training during daylight hours. I also should not have pressed the flying...the start of the problem was the unplanned ZZZ5 turn due to the scheduled Captain timing out and for whom I was asked to cover. As soon as we knew we would have to divert to ZZZ3; I should have terminated any further training and proceeded to ZZZ1 as soon as ZZZ4 Center re-opened. Several 'takeaways'...I will not allow this to happen to me again; even though I believed (and believe) I was legal...fatigue was not an issue. The closest proximity of 2 aircraft in this situation is zero lateral and less than 100 feet vertical if the GSP arrival is on the glideslope and the VFR is in the GMU Delta airspace. However; it should not be taken for granted that aircraft on instrument and visual approaches will be at or above glideslope altitude. Since the VFR is under the GSP arrival; which is usually a jet; there are also wake turbulence issues.The Charlie and Delta airspace design is flawed. The FAA is either unwilling or unable to redesign the airspace to provide for the safety of the flying public.From my experience; the VFR aircraft involved are always inbound to GMU from SC72 (Chandelle). It is probably less than half a dozen aircraft that occasionally do this. When they depart GMU; they are instructed to fly over VPLOW when GSP Runway 4 is in use. If they were instructed to fly over VPLOW when inbound to GMU; the problem would be resolved. GMU Tower can instruct aircraft to remain outside the Delta and instruct aircraft where to enter the Delta; so there is no reason this solution would not work. It could be agreed to; briefed and implemented in 24 hours.This situation develops quickly and there are no guarantees that the controllers will see it before the RA or collision alert. When it is seen; or when the alarms go off; what does FAA management want the controllers to do?  Should we be breaking off the approach as a preventive measure?

column121: When arriving in BOI we were cleared for a Cat 3 approach. The visibility was reported at 1200 RVR with freezing fog and temperature -2. As we were shooting the approach; I elected to fly solid bug even though we had no ice detected. Once we entered the clouds I didn't want to be distracted by a possible Ice Detect message near the ground. But after passing 500 ft. an Appch Warn message appeared so I missed the approach. After the missed approach; I was trying to figure out what was not right and it occurred to me that I didn't have the Ref Speed switch on. So I selected it on and came in for another approach. By this time the weather had gone down to 1000 RVR. We shot the approach and landed. During the rollout the visibility was pretty good and as I was braking and slowing down I plainly saw taxiway E and I made the turn at E. After I had made the turn; tower told us to continue to the end of the runway and turn off at the end. We told them we had already turned off at E. They proceeded to have us cross the left runway at E and continue to parking. It occurred to us that low vis ops were in effect and we should have gone to the end of the runway to follow the lead off lights but tower didn't tell us to go to the end until we had already gotten off at E. The main cause of this was being distracted by the missed approach and trying to figure out why we got the Appch Warn. After we figured it out; the weather had gone down to 1000 RVR and it didn't occur to us about rolling out to the lead off lights. I was more concerned about shooting a successful approach. Another thing that didn't help was that company had shot an approach in front of us and we heard them get off at E. But the weather was 1200 RVR when they landed. I think we were expecting to be able to do the same thing based on what they did. After researching a little we found in the Flight Manual a cautionary note saying that I didn't need to proactively fly at solid bug in anticipation of getting ice. I could've flown open bug if practical and if we did get an ice detect message to not destabilize the approach presumably by increasing speed to solid bug and selecting the Ref Speed switch on when below 500 ft. If I had done this originally I wouldn't have needed to miss the approach the first time. I learned to pay attention to RVR values as they pertain to roll out and taxing; not just landing. 1200 RVR and below is a clue to remember that low vis ops are in effect even if tower doesn't say anything about it and to anticipate looking for lead off lights.

When I checked on with approach control the ceilings and visibility there were 400 ft. -4sm visibility. Once at the IAF it had dropped to 200 ft. and 1.5 miles of visibility and rapidly deteriorating. After the missed approach I had 48 minutes of fuel on board. I alerted ATC by saying I had 'Minimum Fuel' at which point they gave me priority vectors for ILS at the alternate. The approach was to minimums; but with the high intensity rabbit lights it was a successful approach and I made a full stop landing with 32 minutes of fuel. Factors were Fatigue/Hypoxia from a 6 hour flying day; my radio working as not as succinctly as it should have been; and impulsivity - trying to return home before dark to increase the odds of the approach being successful. I should have obtained more fuel at the prior airport despite my calculations of 1.5 hours after the return.

I stay at 4;500 until I make two-way contact with the Bravo.   It's incredibly busy - can't get a word in....I finally do and I was told 'Cleared thru the Bravo; climb to 5;500' - I repeat it back.   Then 3 minutes later; I hear my call sign again and was told 'State your request' - very confused at this point; I say I want the X route and I'm told.....'You better make a left 360 because you're about to enter Bravo and I haven't cleared you.'   Still very very confused; I make a left 360 - then he states; 'Make a right 360 - huh??  Then he says; ok - I see you're already making a left 360; stay with that.   Well; all that turning and confusion put me at around 5;200 (I was already climbing because I thought I was cleared).   So I'm pretty sure I went into that Bravo space just above 5;000 and I immediately dropped as fast as I could back down to 4;500.  1/2 way thru my turn I was cleared the Bravo and X route.Guys - I'm not a novice pilot - I've done these VFR routes many times.  I don't know what's going on with ZZZ Center.Here's what I think happened.....maybe someone was on UHF that I couldn't hear and that is who the Controller cleared through the Bravo - or maybe it was a similar tail number.I asked for clearance; heard it given to me; confirmed it back.  I'm super curious as to what exactly happened.We are trained - if you don't know - ask.  Well...that's only possible if you CAN ask and get into the frequency - I couldn't.   I would never have entered the Bravo but for the Controller telling me 'cleared thru the Bravo and climb to 5;500) - or at least I thought that was for me.If you're going to have VFR corridors - make them accessible - otherwise; just close them all down until you can staff them.  Had I known up front it wasn't available; I would have just climbed to 10;500 and flown over.As for me - I'm just going to go IFR unless I can get flight following from the Ground. column121: The Captain gave me the plane and started making calls on COM2 which I did not listen in on. Operations attempted a Dispatch patch which didn't work; Dispatch via airnav; Flight attendant calls; and PAs. Meanwhile I was flying the plane with automation; getting vectors from ATC; descending (I believe we were around 30;000' when we decided to divert); and fielding ATC questions to a limited extent. We were able to go and stay VMC at some point during this time although it was night.Maybe 6 minutes later the Captain was back with me and he took the airplane. At that point I started working the box with a bit of help from the Captain. I was still also handling most of the ATC calls at that point. We ended up getting direct to a waypoint that put us on a base to final for Runway XXL. Shortly thereafter they changed it to Runway XXR. Unfortunately I wasn't able to send for the numbers until we were turning final. I ran what I could of the descent checklist as I waited for them to come back. As they finally came up; Captain said it was too late; he would use green dot as a reference for landing. I expressed that I was OK with that and pulled myself away from the automation. Either shortly before or after this the Captain commented a different strange smell in the cockpit; I verbalized smelling it as well but am unable to describe it accurately- maybe some kind of fumes. Remember at this point we had a real concern that there was a fire with a fuel leak despite the lack of alarms or EICAS msgs.The Captain executed a very nice landing and I continued to communicate with tower on the dedicated frequency. We pulled off and came to a stop. Captain asked for a fire truck to inspect the plane which was accomplished without any abnormalities or fire indications found. We then proceeded to gate in the company ramp. At some point during this latter taxi the smell dissipated from the cockpit. I suggested not turning the APU on as it could have been the source of our issues. Captain agreed and asked me to notify Ops that we wanted to taxi in and leave engine 1 on while they hooked up the ground power. I relayed this and it took a while but was eventually accomplished. We shut down and medics came into the forward doorway asking to assess/treat folks. The flight attendants seemed to be the only ones reporting headaches/symptoms from the incident; especially FA2. Both FA2 and FA3 did a great job throughout the situation. I was especially impressed with FA2 doing her job professionally while in obvious distress after the cockpit door was opened. The medics basically had to insist on taking her for evaluation while the Captain stepped in to the forward cabin and volunteered to perform any of her FA duties necessary while the passengers deplaned. I remained in the cockpit monitoring the systems.Captain demonstrated superb leadership and decision making skills this night and I feel very lucky to have been working with him during this event.We talked to a variety of ground personnel and mechanics after a quick debrief. One mechanic firmly believed that de-ice fluid was ingested in the APU and that caused the odor. Captain and I were skeptical as we had not de iced all day and had been in heavy rain. The mechanic showed me the aft of the aircraft and there did indeed appear to be a small streak of fluid (not water) on the belly forward of the APU inlet. However to me it looked like the fluid came from the APU as the fluid was more concentrated there and disappeared as the streak moved forward on the small belly fin for maybe 8'. I took a few photos which should be attached. It's also noteworthy that we had this same aircraft for the last 2 flights (about 4.5 flight hrs) which included an identical takeoff from ZZZ.Unfortunately it took over an hour for everyone; especially the FAs; to complete all the required phone calls and documentation. We were unlucky enough to wait over 45 minutes for ground transportation during which we talked to crewscheduling and the contacted the shuttle company multiple times. We all got to the hotel after X pm truly exhausted from the experience and without an opportunity to get any dinner. Surprisingly I wasn't the only crew member to mention trouble sleeping as I unwillingly replayed the events over and over in my mind. In hindsight now it's interesting to evaluate myself going from the adrenaline spike during the incident; to the fatigue crash afterwards; to the inability to relax when I finally got to the hotel room. The following day which was supposed to be my day off was a deadhead home. That afternoon I evaluated my condition and thought it appropriate to ask for a later start for my next 3 day trip starting the following day. I will evaluate myself again on the next day and ask for yet a later time/day to join this next trip if necessary.Despite all the great training I've had to it was a valuable experience to go through this in real time. It was interesting as this evolved from a transient cockpit odor to a de facto emergency landing. We do get mild transient odors in the cockpit from time to time without consequence and I really thought this would be a similar outcome. I fully expected the flight attendants to report the odor gone as we continued the climb out and found myself a bit surprised to be going into ZZZ2 even though we literally had just been discussing it before the decision was made. After extensive reflection I feel like we handled the situation very well. I do think in hindsight that we could have communicated even more during that extremely busy descent. We both debriefed about looking at the landing weight during the descent; thinking it was okay; and deciding it better to land even if we were slightly over weight anyway but I don't remember either of us verbalizing it in flight. We also didn't discuss our obvious decision not to hold and run checklists which we both decided was not the best option. There is an argument to be made that it we had our hands full safely getting the plane down ASAP and those discussions were OK to save until later. In hindsight we probably should have [communicated the urgency to ATC] at some point. Initially the Captain and I had some uncertainty as to how strong the fuel smell was in the aft cabin but decided it was time to go to ZZZ2 regardless. As soon as we described the situation to ATC they treated it as an emergency and we were busy enough not to discuss or bother officially declaring it.

column121: I am aware that the pilot-controlled lighting frequency at PDK is different from the CTAF frequency of 120.9. I was on a VFR approach to PDK at night with a commercial instrument-rated pilot in the right seat when the Tower was closed. We both found it extremely difficult to find the PCL frequency buried in the Chart Supplement. We tried keying on multiple frequencies including CTAF 120.9 and UNICOM 122.95 but could not activate the runway lights. We heard another pilot attempting to turn on PCL on the CTAF frequency as well. I was able to continue to a safe landing by referencing taxiway lights and the runway environment illuminated by my own landing lights. After landing; we finally found the PCL frequency of 120.0 in the Chart Supplement and found that the lights were working. I understand that it is the PIC's responsibility to be aware of such exceptions to common procedures; but I think it would be highly beneficial; especially to those unfamiliar with the airport; to publish critical information such as PCL frequencies in a more accessible manner; e.g. on the sectional/TAC or on the airport diagram. An even better solution would be to consolidate the PCL frequency onto CTAF to reduce pilot workload in a critical phase of flight.

column121: I was departing ZZZ in a Cessna Citation 501. It was only me in the aircraft heading to ZZZ1. I taxied out to depart on Runway XX. Nothing was out of the ordinary. ZZZ Tower cleared me for takeoff on Runway XX. I rolled on to the runway and stopped when I was lined up on the runway. I took a look over my Crew Alert Messages of which there were none indicating. I also looked at my Engine instruments to make sure they were indicating normal; which they were. I advanced the throttles to my takeoff power. Once I achieved takeoff power; I took one more glance at my engine indicating instruments and they were still reading normal. As I approached around 70 kts. indicated on my airspeed; I heard what sounded like a HUGE bang from my left side. I immediately rejected the takeoff; I maintained directional control; and rolled off on to a taxiway as soon as I was at a safe speed. I shut down both the engines while on the taxi. Upon the exterior inspection of the aircraft; we discovered that left engine had a catastrophic failure. The front fan blew out the front of the engine which rolled down the runway. There was a big hole in the top of the cowling of the engine. There was also a small hole in the bottom of the cowling. All the rotor fan blades were destroyed and mangled. Oil was leaking all from the bottom of the left engine. We towed the aircraft back to the FBO where it currently sits. No one was hurt or injured during this.

column121: Enroute from ZZZ1-ZZZ2 [airport]; Aircraft X; [Date]. Approaching ZZZ3 [airport] ATC informed us that ZZZ2 [airport] was not accepting any aircraft. Asked ATC for amplification and was told ZZZ1 Center [had a] COVID issue. Advised ATC of intention to divert to our scheduled alternate of ZZZ4 [airport].  A couple minutes later; ATC informed us ZZZ4 [airport] couldn't accept any more diversions. We were just east of ZZZ3 [airport] so I informed Dispatch that we were diverting to ZZZ [airport]. Dispatch initially told us to go to ZZZ4 [airport]; but after I informed him ZZZ4 [airport] couldn't take anymore diverts; ZZZ [airport] was agreed upon. Landed at ZZZ [airport] and shut down on Gate X. I asked ATC about the delay. They told us about an hour. I informed the passenger and asked Dispatch for a new flight plan. It eventually came and I requested fuel. Pulled our clearance and received an EDCT of XA:X1L. Informed the passengers again. As we finished our cockpit prep for departure we are advised of a ground stop to ZZZ2 [airport]. I inform the passengers again. Called ZZZ [airport] operations to dump lavs and provide us with water and food. Lav cart was broken so we asked if we could use a [different airline] lav cart. [Different airline] said no. ZZZ [airport] only had one crew handling 2 diverts and their regular scheduled departures; so it was very difficult to get anything done. No food or water ever arrived. Received another EDCT of XC:Y1L. Aircraft Y gets tow bar hooked to their aircraft. I ask ops why the tow bar is hooked to the [other aircraft] and not us. I was told we had a passenger count issue. No one had left the plane at this point. Never figured out what the problem with the passenger count was. Aircraft Y tries to take our EDCT but we get another ground stop to ZZZ2 [airport]. About XB:Z0L; the agent finally gets back to us and we discuss deplaning. The agent makes the announcement and I follow up with another announcement about the delay; deplaning; and follow up about taking bags and boarding passes. I also inform them that rebooking needed to be done via phone because there was no one that could do it at ZZZ [airport]. 5 passengers deplane and one returns. We get another EDCT of XD:A4L. I inform Dispatch that that will exceed our MOT. Another EDCT is coordinated and we depart ZZZ [airport] at  XC:Y1L. Upon landing at ZZZ2 [airport] at XD:B6L aircraft are parked on every taxiway and holding pad. I inform Dispatch that we need to get a gate ASAP. Finally on gate at XE:C6L.Multiple EDCTs with a couple ground stops just kept dragging us along. Initial thoughts were to keep passengers on aircraft because once we got our fuel; flight plan; etc.; it was close to the original EDCT. After we received the first ground stop; I started thinking of the passengers. Thus; the request for food; water; and lav service. ZZZ [airport] personnel were overwhelmed and couldn't handle everything that was going on.This was a rare event that caused every plane going to ZZZ2 [airport] to divert. ZZZ [airport] operations was blind-sided and didn't have enough personnel to handle the demand that this caused. From a pilot perspective; there wasn't really anything we could do to prevent it.

column121: We landed in ZZZ with a Code 2 braking report. DOT had done a superb job of plowing and sanding the runway resulting in an actual braking action of at least Medium. It continued to snow during our approximate 30 minute turn while DOT continued to plow the runway. DOT stopped plowing when we commenced deicing. After our deicing and engine starts we commenced taxiing. Upon turning onto the runway the jet slid sideways across the runway. After correcting the slide I made a second turn onto the center line; experiencing a second slide. I determined Braking Action to be Nil. I set the parking brake and called DOT informing them we needed a complete plow and sanding of the runway. This took approximately 20 minutes. After DOT completed their work and issued a Braking Action report; we departed safely without incident.Crews should remain vigilant and remember Braking action changes rapidly with heavy snow.

column121: While conducting a FAR 91 reposition flight from ZZZZ to ZZZ; we were cleared to maintain a cruising altitude of Flight Level 260. Approximately three hours into our cruise; the Central Advisory and Warning System (CAWS) triggered a master caution and the LH FUEL PUMP and RH FUEL PUMP green indicator lights illuminated. About 10 seconds later they extinguished; only for another master caution to sound and the same lights to return; indicating a low fuel pressure situation. We ran the emergency procedure checklist for low fuel pressure. After completing the low fuel pressure checklist; we were unable to rectify the low fuel pressure condition and [advised] ZZZ Center. Per the low fuel pressure checklist; we diverted to the nearest suitable airfield. ZZZZ1 was the nearest suitable airfield. Center informed us that all nearby airports; including ZZZZ1; were closed at sunset and personnel were being contacted by ZZZZ Approach to turn the lights on at ZZZZ1. We conducted the RNAV RWY XX Approach to a visual landing at ZZZZ1 and parked the aircraft without further incident. The aircraft was then grounded. Lack of guidance in emergency checklist on time frame for both rate of descent to warmer air; as well as restoring boost pump switches to AUTO after descent to warmer air.

column121: I was scheduled to fly out of ZZZZ to ZZZZ1. While in cruise; I noticed the rudder pedals on the pilot side didn't mobilize as they should when pressed on to engage the brakes. I asked my SIC to perform the same checks on his side and he noted the pedals felt operational. We decided to continue our flight to ZZZZ1 and land taking into consideration that we might not have brake pressure and would have to perform a go-around and diversion to a longer runway. Rain had just ended in our destination and the runway was slightly wet. After touchdown; I try to engage the brakes to verify their status. Brakes started engaging on and off while we rolled on the runway. We decided to go-around. Before diverting to ZZZZ2 we acknowledge the fact that the runway was slightly wet and decided to try landing again. This second landing was firmer than the first one; I; as pilot flying; applied the brakes once more and this time around; no braking action was noticed therefore we decided to perform a go-around and divert to ZZZZ2. After touching down in ZZZZ2; brakes didn't engage appropriately; they were intermittent. After shutting down at the main ramp in ZZZZ2; deplaning and sending the passengers to a lounge; I talked to our mechanic on the phone and we both noted the brake fluid was lower than usual. The company flew another aircraft with a mechanic which happens to be also a pilot. He inspected the brakes visually and noted that the system looks fine. With that assessment; we accepted a ferry permit to fly back to base ZZZZ without passengers; for proper maintenance action. After touchdown in ZZZZ RWY XX and noting the fact that my 'now' SIC is a mechanic; I pushed on the rudder pedals to engage the brakes and try to assess what the issue was. This prompted no braking action. I communicated this to my SIC/Mechanic; and I increased pressure on the rudder pedals trying to note a response from the system with no luck. Eventually; after I kept applying pressure to the rudder pedals; the left and right main gear tires deflated disabling our aircraft in the runway. After this happened; we notified ATC (ZZZZ Tower) and shut down on the runway.

column121: We departed ZZZ part 91 to relocate Aircraft X to ZZZ1. Few minutes after crossing ZZZZZ intersection at FL370 in contact with ZZZ Center; I notice a red fire light blinking on left engine accompanied with both red master working lights. No indication of engine stall; no vibration felt; no lost of power notice.Within 5 seconds I retarded to idle the left throttle; 3 seconds later the 'ENG FIRE PULL' Handle light extinguish making me believe that was only bleed air leak in the sensing loop; but 7 seconds later; the 'T' handle again starting flashing indicating fire.I pulled the thrust lever in cutoff position; I pulled the 'T' handle and once the two arm lights where illuminated; I pressed left one first; seconds later when I realized that the fire light was continued flashing; I pressed the second fire extinguishers light to the same engine.Unfortunately; the 'ENG FIRE PULL' handle was still flashing; taking the decision to turn left to the closest airport.We were flying the [airway] eastbound at 85 nm from ZZZ; only 3 airports where closest before ZZZ; but no rescue services most likely or not enough runway available for our landing configuration (gear down; max flaps 20 deg).Since the checklist says 'land as soon as possible' and bad weather was in front of us; while my copilot was advising ATC I started my left turn while descending; circumnavigating the weather (during my 90 deg turn; I looked behind my left shoulder to see if a white or black smoke trail was left behind; but I couldn't see nothing); and after clear of mountains I continued descending to 5;000 feet where I preferred to maintain a low altitude and close to the shoreline if a ditching was necessary.During our diversion we had time to talk to the Controller where we answered every question he asked.Every question was answered at the moment and once we were established on the localizer about 20 nm out; the fire light extinguish. While on my final descent I asked the tower that the ground equipment if possible; to be waiting on the left side of the runway since I was requesting a visual confirmation if actual fire was still on the left side or not.After landing I stopped the airplane and I requested again a visual confirmation and the answer was 'they are on the way.' At that moment with the right engine running; I asked my copilot to open the upper main door since I never felt or saw fire and to have his visual confirmation from him.My intentions were to taxi the airplane out of the runway if no danger or fire existed.As soon as my First Officer opened the door; he gave me the visual that NO FIRE WAS ON LEFT ENGINE and I talked to the Tower that my intentions was to move the airplane out of there to the ramp. The Tower responded to not move since the fire truck was already in my left side. When I saw to my left; I saw a fireman with his hose in position so; I turned off the right engine shutting down everything and jumping out of the airplane. By the time I was stepping out; the fireman started to spray the left engine and I thought that finally a real fire was there.Few seconds later all the fireman started to spray with soapy water the hole airplane; from the cockpit; fuselage; wings and the two engines from the front side and from behind (right engine was only from behind).As soon as I see all that I started to ask the fireman if they saw actually fire; but no fireman spoke Spanish or English. I tried to speak with 5 of them but was a loss of time.By the time they finish spraying the airplane; people from different departments approached the airplane and as soon as I found one who could speak English I asked him to translate the only question I've been asking.'Did anybody see fire?''Can someone say if actually a fire was on either engine?'And the answer was 'No fire was detected by anyone.'After that; we proceeded to tow the airplane out of the runway.
column123: While following our route of flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 we leveled at 37;000 feet before entering ZZZ [Center] airspace just before the fix ZZZZZ. As we passed that fix; ZZZ Center switched us to ZZZ2 Center and before first contact was made; we had an indication of fire on the left engine.The Captain proceeded with the memory items procedure. He put the left power to idle and we were waiting for that light to extinguish; it did; but in about 8-10 seconds it started flashing again; giving the indication that fire might still be present. Then the Captain continued with the procedure of cutting out the engine to secure it and pull the T-Handle of the left engine; continued by pressing the ARM button of one of the fire extinguishers.The flashing light indicating the possibility of fire in the left engine continued; so the Captain pressed the second ARM button. In both intents to extinguish the light with the fire extinguishers the flashing light of the T-Handle never shut off. So the PIC decided to call on the requested checklist out of the planes QRH and initiated [expedited] descent. I; as the First Office went through the procedures on tab 5 'Engine Fire Shutdown' section of the QRH. I went through all the checklist out loud and twice to confirm everything requested was performed. Then followed the checklist to the single engine landing procedure on tab 14 abnormal checklist; and went through it twice and out loud.While the descent was performed; I advised ATC and asked for vectors to the closest airport; which in this case the only appropriate airport and closest was ZZZ1. The Controller first indicated to fly to a fix which I could not understand and when I asked about 2 times to spell it or give us vectors; he then instructed to fly to the ZZZ VOR. I immediately set the FMS and GPS to the VOR and ZZZ1 airport. The Captain continued VFR descent and decided to cross the mountains as soon as possible so that we can continue descending and get closer to the ground and shore and make a straight in into ZZZ1.While the descent was being performed the left fire; light continued to flash. The Captain took communications while I was setting the procedures into ZZZ1 on the GPS and FMS. In about 3 miles short of the airport. We noticed the light stopped flashing. The Captain requested the Tower to let the rescue and firefighters know that they were needed in our left side once we landed; they confirmed that they were ready and waiting for us. Once we landed and the airplane came to a complete stop I got out if my seat and opened the left exit door to verify if there was any fire present at the moment; I communicated to the Captain that NO fire was visible from the front of the engine and then he instructed for me to get out. As soon as I got out; he was still in communication with the Tower; he shut the right engine as instructed by the Controller and exited the airplane.Once we stepped away from the airplane the firefighters started spraying the left engine immediately through the front and back of the nacelle; and seconds after; another group of firefighters started spraying the right engine. I personally told the captain that if they were spraying is because probably; they saw fire but when I noticed them spraying the right engine too then we thought it was their protocol to follow.Once they stopped spraying the captain asked if they saw fire to several of the Firefighters but they could not understand what we were asking; it was not until a ground handler or someone that understood English approached the airplane and we asked him to ask them if someone saw fire; they answered that No fire was visible. We then proceeded to tow the aircraft out of the runway.Personally; I believe this could be a glitch on the system of the aircraft. I am not a mechanic so it's hard for me to say what might have caused the aircraft to give that indication of fire on the engine. We treated the indication as a real fire so the airplane couldbe secure and everyone on board too. I don't know if this could be a maintenance issue or if it has happened before. My suggestion is just to continue to give the progressive and preventive maintenance to the aircraft as they are required and for the pilots to continue to communicate with maintenance any issues given big or small as no matter how small it may seem it could lead to other problems in the long run. Definitely the airplanes have their years so the more they are used for the missions they are going to require more and more maintenance.

column121: During initial climb out (400 or 500 ft.) we heard a call from Medical saying that 'something's burning'. I looked behind and noticed the cabin was beginning to fill with a smokey hazy layer. The temperature in the airplane had increased and now the smoke was reaching the cockpit. I reset both bleed air valves in case we had a stuck valve; but this did not change anything. I told FO (First Officer) to turn off all fans in case that is the cause. I looked back again and I could visible see the smoke rising out of the rear right wall panel. We stopped the climb at 2;500 ft.; [advised ATC] and I made the decision to return back to ZZZ. I assumed control of the airplane and radios while FO completed checklist and set us up on the approach and calculated the weight of the airplane. He advised me that we were currently 500 lbs. overweight; I made the decision to still continue to the airport as I did not know the cause of the smoke and did not want to waste any time burning off extra fuel. We ultimately made a safe left base visual approach and landed 300 lbs. overweight. We were able to taxi into the ramp and shutdown and safely exited the airplane. We followed checklist and [Company] SOP.

column121: We were waiting to take off. The aircraft that took off ahead of us reported hitting birds on take off. The controller asked if they hit the birds directly over the runway; the crew confirmed it was. We were next for takeoff when the controller asked if we had heard the report from the aircraft ahead. We said we did. Tower then delivered a caution about possible FOD (Foreign Object Debris) and birds on the runway and cleared us for takeoff. We refused the clearance and asked that the runway be inspected. We were then informed that it would take a long time for an inspection; we said we will wait. This seemed to aggravate the controller. Tower continued to give takeoff clearances until eventually no one wanted to go until the runway was inspected. This seemed to expedite the runway getting inspected. Once it was deemed safe and free from FOD; takeoffs resumed.I then reached out to an airport authority and their ATC group. They informed me that they have an agreement between the ATC and the Airport Authority about such events. If at their airport that same report was made on takeoff they stated the runway would have been closed for an inspection. They also stated it takes less than 5 minutes At DFW I waited longer than that due to refusing the takeoff clearance.I then took the question to the APA National Safety Committee and asked what they knew about procedure when this happens. Coincidentally; on that call was another pilot that had the same thing happened to them at a different airport. As we have been researching this we are finding there is no standardization from airport to airport on this. Some airports have written agreements between ATC and Airport Authorities and others don't. Does this infer that certain airports take safety more seriously than another? It is factual that the Captain will always have final authority. But shouldn't ATC procedures across the system be uniform with regard to concerns with the runway condition? To give a takeoff clearance with no attempt to inspect the runway in order to keep traffic moving seems at odds with a culture of safety.

column121: On Date aircraft XXX had fumes/smoke in the cockpit smell noticed by the flight crew.The event occurred due to a razor blade that was left inside CBP1 possibly during a visit to ZZZ for the ADS-B modification in the middle of month of 2019 and I could have possibly left it there during the installation of breaker CBP1-XX during the mod. column121: We were flying to ASE and I was the Pilot Monitoring. As we approached Aspen; we were given vectors to intercept LOC E into ASE. We accepted clearance to maintain 13;000 ft until established and clearance to execute LOC E approach. As we were intercepting LOC we picked up visual with the airport and commenced descent towards it while having visual reference with the airport and all the terrain around. In the midst of all things happening quickly and the excitement of having visual with the airport; I failed to communicate to ATC my intention of executing visual approach. At some point we lost the visual with the airport due to a cloud layer just ahead of us; but not the terrain. At the same time ATC issued an altitude alert to us due to us being lower than what LOC approach altitudes called for. I advised that we had terrain in sight but lost the visual with the airport and said that we would be going missed and starting a climb. We got another altitude alert from ATC. We advised we are in a climb and asked vectors; until we decide what to do. We proceeded to ZZZ airport afterwards.  At no time we were in IMC conditions and maintained visual clearance from all the terrain. My mistake in this case was deviating from ATC clearance and going visual without communicating that to ATC. And also; not staying on a LOC due to a cloud layer over the airport. At no time was the aircraft in IMC conditions and we were maintaining clearance with terrain at all times. By all means the aircraft was never put in any unsafe condition.  I did learn from this experience to clearly and concisely communicate any and all of my intentions with ATC; so there is no misunderstanding at any point of the flight.

column121: I was the PF (Pilot Flying) on Aircraft X from ZZZ2-ZZZ1. I flew the RNAV RNP [Runway] XX approach with rain and wind in the vicinity. I attempted to configure early but a strong tailwind made it challenging. I encountered a wind gust which caused me to counter increasing airspeed by pitching up and slightly reduce power to maintain airspeed and continue configuring. This resulted in a position higher than anticipated. The PM (Pilot Monitoring) noticed this also and we articulated that. About that time; ATC directed a go-around. We executed the missed approach and climbed to 3;000 [feet] on vectors for another approach.Noting the conditions; I configured early for the second RNAV RNP XX approach. Rain and wind were still predominant throughout the approach but fewer gust excursions and we remained stable throughout the approach all the way to minimums. At minimums; we both had the approach lights and runway environment in sight and I continued the approach. As I turned final aligning with Runway XX; I lost sight of the runway environment due to the weather. The PM called go around and I initiated go around procedures. We climbed to 3;000 feet on vectors as directed by ATC. We communicated with one another and ensured we were both in the green; we had ample fuel; and agreed to attempt a third approach. On the third RNAV RNP XX approach; I configured early again and remained stable throughout the approach. The wind was still a factor though and required careful monitoring and aircraft correction to maintain a stable approach. Fully configured and in the vicinity of arriving at minimums; ATC advised a wind shift on the field of 330 degrees at 26 knots of wind. ATC asked for our intentions. Due to airline limitations on Maximum Tailwind Component for Landing; the PM told ATC we could not land and we would go-around. ZZZ1 Tower handed us off to ZZZ Departure and they advised us that they 'turned the airfield around' and they would give us vectors for the ILS RWY XY approach and we would be 'number 1' to the field. Again; the Captain and I communicated that we were both in the green; we noted that we had ample fuel; and we prepared for an ILS approach to Runway XY.After intercepting the localizer for the ILS to Runway XY; I configured fully and continued down the glideslope from the final approach fix. It was raining outside and was windy but we remained stable. Shortly prior to 1;000 feet AGL; it grew increasingly difficult to maintain a stable approach. I told the PM that I didn't feel comfortable; the weather was worsening; and it was likely that we would not be stable at 1;000 feet. We agreed and elected to go-around. Just as I began the go around procedure; we encountered a Wind Shear Warning and I proceeded with the Wind Shear escape maneuver. We exited the conditions quickly and transitioned to ATC's directives. We quickly agreed to divert to ZZZ3 and the PM informed ATC of our intention to divert. We climbed to 3;000 feet and flew vectors to ZZZ3.We flew the ILS RWY XYC approach and landed safely at ZZZ3 and taxied to the gate. We shut down the aircraft with approximately 7.4k pounds of fuel remaining. During the deplaning process; the Captain coordinated with the Maintenance and Dispatch and agreed to continue on to ZZZ1 as the weather cleared the area. We added fuel departing with 11.8k pounds of fuel. The Captain flew as the PF and I was the PM for the return flight to ZZZ1. The Captain maintained appropriate communication throughout the event. He communicated with the passengers explaining as best as possible what occurred and what we were doing to ensure their safety while doing our best to land at our intended destination. He kept the flight attendants apprised of the situation after each approach and we discussed each approach; verified we were both in the green; and maintained situational awareness at all times.
column123: Flew RNAV RNP [Runway] XX approach. FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying) and was configuring the aircraft early. He was at gear down; flaps 15; and we encountered a wind gust that drove the airspeed indication almost to redline. The FO raised nose slightly and reduced power to slow the airspeed in order to continue configuring the aircraft. As this occurred; aircraft got a little high. As PM; I noticed this and was in process of informing FO when ATC said that we looked a little high and to just go around. We executed the missed approach as directed by ATC and climbed on a heading to 3;000 ft. to vector for another approach.On the second RNAV RNP XX; FO configured the aircraft early and shot approach to minimums. At minimums; approach lights and runway lights were visible; but as we turned to final approach; visibility was lost.  I called go-around; and FO initiated go-around. We climbed on a heading to 3;000 feet. We communicated with each other that we were both in the green; had plenty of fuel; and prepared for another approach.On the third RNAV RNP XX; the FO had fully configured the aircraft; when ATC advised that the wind had shifted out of the north at 330 degrees and we had 26 knots of wind at our tail. ATC asked our intentions; I told them that we could not land with those winds and that we were going around. At that point; ATC handed us off to departure; and departure immediately advised us that they had turned the airport around and could give us an immediate left downwind to be number 1; shooting ILS Runway XY. FO and I communicated with each other that we were both in the green; had plenty of fuel; and prepared for an approach using the new runway.On attempt to Runway XY; we intercepted localizer and G/S. We had continual high winds indicating to me that the aircraft would not be able to remain stable throughout approach and landing. As PIC; I called for a go-around. FO communicated to me his agreement; and I immediately notified Tower of our intention to divert to ZZZ3. FO initiated the miss. As he did; we encountered a brief Wind Shear Warning. FO finished cleaning aircraft up and we diverted to ZZZ3 without incident.We were vectored to ZZZ3 and landed on Runway XYC and taxied to the gate with 7.4 pounds of fuel. I called Dispatch and she said we had plenty of fuel to get to ZZZ1 but as a precaution due to the frontal weather passage; she added more fuel and brought us up to 11.8 pounds. After the front passage; I flew the aircraft as PF uneventfully to ZZZ1. During all of the approaches and the divert I kept the flight attendants up to date and communicated with the passengers at all times. We exercised good situational awareness and followed SOPs during the entire flight.

column121: After trimming for level flight and while adjusting the prop for cruise; the airplane suddenly started shaking violently at a regular and high frequency. Thinking that something had gone wrong with the prop; I reduced throttle to try to reduce the severity of the shaking; but this had no apparent effect. Engine oil pressure and temperature were both well within the green range. We had just departed a nearby airport; so turned around to land. I noticed that keeping the nose of the airplane up required significant back pressure. Adjusting the trim appeared to have no effect. Enroute to the airport the shaking suddenly stopped. We continued to land without incident. After stopping the airplane on the ground we inspected the trim tab and found that it was stuck in nose-down position. Looking underneath the elevator; we found that the trim-tab control rod was not connected where it usually met the horizontal stabilizer. The end of the trim-tab control rod towards the stabilizer appeared to have been bent and broken. It appeared that at some point the rod broke and jammed. After replacing and reattaching the trim control rod the airplane is operating normally and has been returned to service. Speculation is that at some point the bolt connecting the rod had either partially failed or come loose; causing uneven stress on the control rod; eventually resulting in failure due to metal fatigue. The elevator trim cable had recently been replaced but it is not clear if the control rod had been touched as part of that work. Inspection of this connection point can be done simply and quickly during pre-flight and may benefit from increased awareness as a possible or likely point of failure.

column121: On Date at ZZZ airport; I fueled the airplane; conducted a preflight (includes checking oil quantity and taking a sample of all three fuel sumps); reviewed my direct course back home and updated my weather (VMC) for the short flight to ZZZ1. During the pre-takeoff checklist (engine run up); I notice a slight roughness in the engine. I leaned out the mixture control which cleared out the roughness. I set the mixture control for my takeoff; but not to full rich. I left it leaned out a little for the departure and climb. During my climbout; I always look for off airport landing spots (should I need one). I did not see any good locations and I told myself that I want 4;500 feet once clear of the Class B airspace altitudes. It was shortly after my desire to get to 4;500 feet MSL ASAP that the engine was not performing as it should in cruise climb. I applied full power and checked the engine instruments (all green; but RPM was towards the low end). I was getting a shallow climb at an airspeed of about 90. I then immediately performed the initial emergency procedure; carb heat on; mixture full (then adjust if needed) and check fuel selector on both. That seemed to bring the performance back; but not immediately. Shortly after that the engine then started to run rough. My thought was spark plug fouling or magneto (I know it was not a cylinder failure; because I have experienced that in a twin engine airplane). I adjusted the mixture control first. This is logical; because if you check the mags before the mixture control you could increase spark plug fowling. At some point through all this my mind went into altitude; altitude; altitude. Unfortunately; I had that 4;500 feet MSL in my mind. While dealing with the engine situation; I continued my climb to that altitude. I got the rough running engine cleared out.  Once I was done keeping the airplane in the air (dealing with low performance and then the rough running engine during the cruise climb phase); I checked my position and noticed that I was in ZZZ3 Class B airspace (west end of and close to the 6;000 feet MSL corridor; but I was in the 4;000 feet MSL corridor). I immediately descended below 4;000 feet MSL (3;800 feet MSL). Once clear of the Class B airspace/Mode C veil; I climbed back to 4;500 feet MSL. No airplane conflicts were noted. Once on the ground at the ZZZ1; I performed an engine runup and checked the mags full and leaned mixture settings. Both checked out okay. My plan is to check the oil; fuel and talk with a mechanic. I am confident that the fuel is okay since I checked it after fueling at the ZZZ (but I will check it again). I have cancelled my planned flying for the next week and no flying the Skyhawk until the items are checked out. Once I got home; I chair flew the scenario that I just experienced and realized that all my training and personal home chair flying has been geared to multi-engine; on an IFR flight plan and in radio communications. My scenario was single engine; VFR and not in communication. Do not get me wrong; I always review the emergency procedures before a flight for the airplane that I am flying. Also; the poor engine performance that I experienced did not seem to be carb icing. Since the air filter and bracket were replaced at the annual inspection; the carb air intake system will be looked at. What I learned and what I will do going forward so that this does not happen again:I learned that in my continued personal chair flying training that I need to go over single engine emergency; VFR and not in communications scenarios. This situation reinforced with me that single engine performance (VFR; non-communications) incidents come with a high workload especially when dealing with keeping the airplane in the air. It showed me that I became focused on keeping the plane in the air (altitude and rectifying the engine situation) and that navigating and communicating was lacking with this incident.   Going forward; in addition to reading theemergency procedures that I currently do for every plane that I fly and chair flying multi-engine scenarios; I will chair fly single engine (SE) scenarios. I need to emphasize aviate; navigate; and communicate in any SE situation. When flying under Class B airspace and within a Mode C veil do the following:1.	Obtain flight following when flying VFR; especially when flying in a Mode C veil. I would already be in communications should I need to report a problem.  2.	Mark along the course line a line with an arrow from the departure airport to the point when the plane will be cleared of the Mode C veil. Also; put a B next to this manually drawn line.3.	Apply a post-it-note on the instrument panel that I am in a Mode C veil airspace.I will talk to my Flight Instructor and review this flight to obtain feedback and discuss my ideas and additional ways to prevent this from happening again.

This indicated both ECS ducting systems were now overheating. At FL400; an additional alert was triggered: 'CABIN ALTITUDE HI;' signaling a loss of cabin pressurization.Actions Taken: Requested priority handling - Executed memory items for CABIN ALT HI (Don oxygen masks; establish crew communication; initiate descent).Requested priority handling with ATC and initiated a rapid emergency descent to 10;000 ft.Requested and received vectors to the nearest suitable airport: ZZZ.Maintained full control of the aircraft; monitored cabin and ECS parameters.Landed safely at ZZZ with no injuries or aircraft damage.Maintenance Findings:Following the flight; the aircraft was ferried to ZZZ2. After inspection; the following issues were identified:The RAM air valve was found fully shut; preventing proper airflow through the ECS during flight. This valve is designed to open in flight to allow ambient air for ECS cooling.Multiple ECS temperature sensors were found to be faulty; which likely triggered or contributed to the overtemperature alerts and misleading system indications.
